items.body:
# Korg Kronos 3 im Test: Die Workstation, die alles kann – aber zu welchem Preis?

## Test: Korg Kronos 3 Workstation Keyboard (Modell 2025)

## Neue Pianos, alte Schwächen

Test: Korg Kronos 3 Workstation-Keyboard (Modell 2025)

Korg hat 2025 den Kronos der dritten Generation vorgestellt, nennen wir ihn den Korg Kronos 3. Mit etwas Verspätung ist er bei mir auf dem Seziertisch gelandet und wird begutachtet. Optisch hat sich ja nicht viel verändert. Ob das auch im Innenleben so ist, lest ihr hier.

Was ist es? Der Korg Kronos 3 ist eine Keyboard-Workstation der dritten Generation, die mit neun eigenständigen Sound-Engines, SSD-Streaming und einer umfangreichen Effektsektion ausgestattet ist.

- Klangvielfalt : Neun unterschiedliche Synthese-Engines decken ein enormes Klangspektrum von akustischen Klavieren über Physical Modeling bis hin zu virtuell-analogen Klassikern wie MS-20 und Polysix ab.
- Bühnenbetrieb : Der bewährte Setlist-Modus ermöglicht mit 16 direkt abrufbaren Einträgen pro Bank eine hervorragende Übersicht und schnelle Umschaltzeiten im Live-Einsatz.
- Modellpflege : Die Neuauflage punktet mit einer um rund 60 Prozent verkürzten Bootzeit, einem reaktionsschnelleren Touch-Display sowie überarbeiteten Flügel- und E-Piano-Sounds.
- Einschränkungen : Das Bedienkonzept leidet unter teils überladenen Menüseiten mit sehr kleinen Schaltflächen, fehlenden dedizierten Hüllkurven-Drehreglern sowie nicht vorhandenen Oktavierungstastern beim 61-Tasten-Modell.
Inhaltsverzeichnis Korg Kronos 3 Workstation-Keyboard, Modell 2025 Das Innenleben Neuerungen beim Korg Kronos 3 Die 9 Sound-Engines Die neuen Sounds Die Bedienung des Korg Kronos 3 Der Grundsound

## Korg Kronos 3 Workstation-Keyboard, Modell 2025

Ich habe eine 61-Tasten-Version des Korg Kronos 3 bekommen, die momentan für 2.827,- Euro angeboten wird. Wie schon bei den Vorgängern gibt es auch je ein Modell mit 73 bzw. 88 Tasten, die dann eine RH3-Tastatur mit Hammermechanik verbaut ist. Der Kronos 88 bringt ein stolzes Gewicht von 23,8 kg auf die Waage. Im Vergleich zu einem Yamaha Montage M8X mit 28,1 kg ist er ein Leichtgewicht, verglichen mit einem Nord Stage 4 88 mit 19,6 kg dafür ein (kleiner) Sumoringer.

Korg Kronos 3 mit 61 Tasten

Die 61-Tasten-Version wiegt 14,2 kg. Die Tastatur lässt sich angenehm spielen, mir wäre sie etwas zu leichtgängig. Die Kalibrierung der Aftertouch-Funktion hat Korg sehr gut gelöst, indem man einfach den gewünschten Druck auf die Tasten ausübt und der Kronos das dann im Display anzeigt und speichert. Alle Controller und Taster sind mit denen des Vorgängers identisch. Leider besitzt der Kronos 61 keine Oktav-Up- und -Down-Taster. Bei einigen Presets hat man eine Oktav-Down-Funktion in den SW1-Schalter gepackt. Trotzdem – die SW1- und SW2-Schalter sollten ja für Klangveränderungen verwendet werden können. Ein Oktavschalter ist bei einem Instrument mit 61 Tasten Pflicht.

## Das Innenleben

So, nun einmal festhalten. Der Korg Kronos 3 hat:

- 20 Bänke mit 2560 Programmen, davon sind ab Werk 1792 belegt
- 14 Bänke mit 1792 Combinations, davon sind ab Werk 512 belegt
- 264 Speicherplätze für Drumkits, wovon 78 ab Werk belegt sind
Der Korg Kronos 3 ist im Grunde ein speziell konstruierter Computer mit einem Linux-Betriebssystem. Wie leistungsfähig dieser Rechner aktuell ist, lässt sich jedoch nicht herausfinden. Der Kronos kann seine Sounds nicht nur aus dem RAM (3 GB) auslesen, er kann sie auch von einer 120-GB-SSD streamen bzw. in Echtzeit wie ein VST-Softsynth erzeugen.

Ein Programm des Korg Kronos 3 kann entweder ein HD-1-Programm sein, das quasi einer „normalen“ auf Samples basierenden Klangsynthese entspricht, oder es ist ein EXi-Programm (Expansion Instrument). EXi-Programme können auch in einem Programm schon zwei verschiedene Engines beinhalten. So kann man in einem Programm den MS-20 mit dem Polysix kombinieren. Eine Combination (ich schreibe bewusst C statt K) besteht dann aus bis zu 16 Programmen (EXi oder HD-1), diee gelayert und/oder gesplittet sind.

Insgesamt besitzt der Korg Kronos 3 12 (!) Insert-Effekte mit 185 Effekttypen. Wenn ich 185 Effekttypen aufzählen müsste, wäre ich, glaube ich, bei 30 am Ende. Für die Summe gibt es noch zwei Master-Effekte und zwei Total-Effekte.

Die Anschlüsse des Korg Kronos 3 (USB nicht im Bild)

## Neuerungen beim Korg Kronos 3

- 60 % schnellerer Start (ca. 54 Sekunden)
- schnelleres Touch-Display
- neues Gehäusedesign mit schwarzen Holzseitenteilen und pulverbeschichtetem Metallgehäuse
- 256 neue Sounds, bestehend aus 128 neuen Soundprogrammen und 128 Sounds aus bestehenden Sound-Sets
- neuer Piano-Sound „Italian Grand“
- neues Tine EP I Early
## Die 9 Sound-Engines

Hier eine kurze Übersicht über die Sound-Engines des Korg Kronos 3:

- SGX-2 Premium Piano: Erzeugt akustische Flügel- und Klavierklänge auf Basis detaillierter Samples
- EP-1 Electric Piano: Modelliert klassische E-Pianos wie Rhodes und Wurlitzer mit authentischen Anschlag- und Vintage-Effekten
- HD-1 High Definition Synthesizer: PCM-basierte Sample-Engine zur Erzeugung von Instrumentenklängen, Drums und Synthesizer-Sounds
- AL-1 Analog Synthesizer: Analoge Synthese-Modellierung für druckvolle Leads, Bässe, Pads und klassische Synthesizer-Klänge
- CX-3 Tonewheel Organ: Simuliert klassische Hammond-Orgeln mit Zugriegeln, Percussion und Rotary-Lautsprechereffekt
- STR-1 Plucked Strings: Erzeugt Saitenklänge durch Physical Modeling, beispielsweise Gitarren, Harfen und experimentelle Klänge.
- MOD-7 VPM Synthesizer: Kombiniert Frequenzmodulation (FM), Waveshaping und PCM zur Erzeugung komplexer digitaler Synthesizer-Klänge, kompatibel mit der DX7-Library
- MS-20EX: Modelliert den klassischen Korg MS-20
- PolysixEX: Modelliert den klassischen Korg Polysix
Korg Kronos 3 – der Moment des Starts

## Die neuen Sounds

Der neue Piano-Sound gefällt mir gut. Er klingt deutlich brillanter als z. B. das ältere German Grand. Bei den Piano-Sounds scheiden sich ja die Geister. Dem einen gefällt der von Nord, dem anderen der von Yamaha usw. Ich finde, zu Hause auf den Monitorboxen in breitem Stereo klingt eigentlich so gut wie jede aktuelle Workstation sehr gut. Steht man dann auf einer Bühne und spielt dort den Piano-Sound, gibt es mitunter ein böses Erwachen. Man muss entweder laufend lauter und wieder leiser drehen, weil der Sound zu wenig Dynamik hat, oder er kann sich einfach nicht durchsetzen.

Die SGX-2 Piano-Engine des Korg Kronos 3

Das neue E-Piano (Tine EP I Early) gefällt mir auch gut. Es klingt oben etwas spitz, dafür setzt es sich möglicherweise besser durch. Aufpassen sollte man bei der Ausgangslautstärke. Der Sound hat bei mir in höheren Lagen immer verzerrt, wenn der AMP eingeschaltet war, obwohl Drive auf 0 gestellt war. Erst durch Reduktion des Volume-Outputs des E-Pianos hat sich das beheben lassen. Hier reagiert die Simulation also wie ein Original.

items.body:
# New EU Bureaucracy Index: EU law has more than doubled since 2010

November 24, 2026

## New EU Bureaucracy Index: EU law has more than doubled since 2010

edited by Swati Mestri , reviewed by Andrew Zinin

Swati Mestri

Scientific Editor

Andrew Zinin

Chief Editor

This article has been reviewed according to Science X's editorial process and policies . Editors have highlighted the following attributes while ensuring the content's credibility:

fact-checked

proofread

The new EU Bureaucracy Index measures the volume of EU law in force, and it shows a record high: At the end of 2025, the EU regulations and directives in force comprised around 47,600 standard pages, 118% more than in 2010. The volume of EU law has thus more than doubled in 15 years, and it continued to grow in 2025. The main drivers are sanctions regulations and new sets of rules in environmental, consumer and health law.

The EU Bureaucracy Index is compiled by professor Stefan Wagner of the University of Vienna, in collaboration with ESMT Berlin. It adds the European level to the Bureaucracy Index for German federal law , which ESMT published in March 2026.

The index covers all regulations and directives in force on Dec. 31 of a given year that were adopted jointly by the European Parliament and the Council or by the Council alone, each in its consolidated version. Legal acts of the European Commission are not included. As with the German index, volume is measured in standard pages of 1,500 characters each. The data come from Cellar, the database of the Publications Office of the European Union that underlies EUR-Lex.

The index does not count the number of legal acts. It measures their actual volume—that is, how much regulatory text applies at the EU level and ultimately affects companies, public administrations and citizens. Because EU law and federal law are measured in the same unit, developments at both levels can be compared.

If annexes such as lists, limit values and technical specifications are included along with the articles, EU law in force comprises around 90,800 standard pages (+85% since 2010). At the same time, there has been a shift in who makes the law: In 2000, 10% of the articles came from legal acts adopted jointly by Parliament and the Council; in 2025, the figure was 81%.

Eighteen of 20 policy areas have grown since 2010. Foreign and security policy saw the largest increase, with almost 12,900 additional standard pages. These are almost exclusively Council sanctions regulations with their lists of people, companies and goods.

In second place is law on the environment, consumer protection and health: Its volume has more than doubled, from around 4,300 to 9,800 standard pages. Outside sanctions law, no other area has added as many standard pages. This is driven above all by new sets of rules, for example on medical devices, renewable energy and industrial emissions. The Environmental Noise Directive alone grew by around 700 standard pages due to new calculation methods. Even when sanctions law is excluded, EU law has grown by 60% since 2010.

"EU law is growing almost twice as fast as German federal law," says Wagner. "Anyone who wants to reduce bureaucracy must also take the European level into account. Many of the obligations that companies in Germany complain about originate in Brussels. A national relief program alone will not solve the problem."

For companies in Germany, EU law and federal law add up. The Bureaucracy Index for federal law, which ESMT published this year, had already reached a record high. The volume of federal statutes in force rose from 24,765 standard pages in 2010 to 40,270 in 2025. Commercial law grew the most: 1,542 standard pages were added between 2022 and 2026 (+16.5%), more than in any previous period since the analysis began.

The articles of the EU regulations and directives in force alone now comprise roughly as many standard pages as all federal statutes combined. Including annexes, EU law is more than twice as extensive, and it is growing significantly faster.

The index does not assess whether individual regulations make sense. It measures the volume of the law in force. Sanctions law in particular is politically intended, and its extensive lists drive the figures up. However, the index shows where regulation has increased particularly sharply over the past 15 years, providing a basis for a targeted debate on reducing the burden of bureaucracy at the European level.

Provided by ESMT Berlin

Swati Mestri

Swati Mestri holds a bachelor's degree in Electronics Engineering and has worked as a content editor since 2019. She has experience editing research documents across technology, health care, and materials science, and has a particular interest in technology and space. Full profile →

## AI Twitter Recap

**Frontier Models as Research Engines: VP ≠ VNP, Protein Design and 948 Kernel Bugs**

- VP ≠ VNP, posted by two labs: An Anthropic GitHub repo reportedly contains a proof by an internal Claude research model that VP ≠ VNP. This is the algebraic analogue of P vs NP, posed by Valiant in 1979, and implies that polynomials such as the permanent lack small circuits over every field ([@kimmonismus](https://x.com/kimmonismus/status/2125131886271795290), [repo pointer](https://x.com/BlancheMinerva/status/2125085344555053363)). OpenAI's counter-release: OpenAI then posted its own proof and says it was "obtained on November 6, 2026." Neither lab named a model or published an announcement ([@AndrewCurran_](https://x.com/AndrewCurran_/status/2125289527531245998)).
- Scope: The result does not imply P ≠ NP, which still requires general Boolean circuit lower bounds ([@ZhihuFrontier](https://x.com/ZhihuFrontier/status/2125170512011944026)).
- Speculation: Curran argues that both labs are sitting on unreleased results and repeats unconfirmed rumors of cryptography breakthroughs. Treat this as opinion.
- Riemann proof clarifications: Levent Alpöge says the "250,000+ pages" claim was a joke. He released only the Lean code because he could not produce a readable writeup, and called it "full of garbage obviously, but compiles" ([@kimmonismus](https://x.com/kimmonismus/status/2125148979880964496), [@simonw](https://x.com/simonw/status/2125001984029921636)). Lineage claim: A Zhihu analysis traces Alpöge's key method to a short OpenAI proof excluding Landau–Siegel zeros. This is an attributed inference ([@ZhihuFrontier](https://x.com/ZhihuFrontier/status/2125200727140438125)).

One 13.8-day signal was independently confirmed by a SETI astronomer, and 49 TESS candidates were flagged ([@OpenAI](https://x.com/OpenAI/status/2125305606685053416)).

# Realitätsferner Dualismus

Maja Apelt | Rezension | 25.11.2026

## Realitätsferner Dualismus

## Rezension zu „Vergessene Soldatinnen. Frauen im Militär und in den Kriegen Europas seit 1600“ von Karen Hagemann

Karen Hagemann: Vergessene Soldatinnen. Frauen im Militär und in den Kriegen Europas seit 1600 Deutschland Berlin 2026: Suhrkamp 1056 S., 48 EUR ISBN 978-3-518-58840-6

Ihr neues Buch beginnt die deutsch-amerikanische Historikerin Karen Hagemann, Professorin an der University of North Carolina at Chapell Hill, mit einer Beschreibung der aktuellen Situation von Frauen in der Ukraine. Zwar stellen Frauen den Großteil der seit 2022 aus dem Land geflüchteten Menschen, zugleich dienen sie in wachsender Zahl in den ukrainischen Streitkräften. Dort sind sie vor allem in Verwaltung, Kommunikation, Logistik und Sanitätsdienst, aber auch in den freiwilligen Territorialverteidigungsverbänden tätig. Obwohl die Wehrpflicht nur für Männer gilt, lag der Anteil an Frauen in den Streitkräften 2016 bei 20 Prozent. Seit 2021 wurden „wehrdiensttaugliche Frauen aus über 100 Berufen, die für die Verteidigung des Landes von besonderer Bedeutung sind, verpflichtet, sich bei den Militärbehörden zu registrieren“ (S. 12). Sie haben demnach einen bedeutenden Anteil an der Verteidigung des Landes, in der internationalen Berichterstattung aber sind sie kaum sichtbar. Im Zentrum des medialen Interesses stehen „ukrainische Männer als heldenhafte Verteidiger des Vaterlandes und ukrainische Frauen und Kinder als verzweifelte Opfer des Krieges“ (S.13). Diese Darstellung, so hebt Hagemann hervor, erfüllt eine wichtige Funktion, wenn es darum geht, militärische Unterstützung und humanitäre Hilfe zu bekommen.

In diesem Auftakt werden die zentralen Leitlinien des Buches von Karen Hagemann bereits deutlich: Frauen haben in allen Kriegen wichtige Funktionen übernommen, sie wurden immer gebraucht, auch wenn man sie gerade im Europa des 19. Jahrhunderts aus den Streitkräften vollständig auszuschließen versuchte. Zugleich wurden sie aber in der Berichterstattung, im kollektiven Gedächtnis und lange Zeit auch in den Geschichtswissenschaften verdrängt. Allein als seltene Ausnahmen, als Amazonen oder der ihnen zugeschriebenen Geschlechterrolle zuwiderhandelnde Frauen, trafen Berichte oder Selbstzeugnisse von Frauen in den Armeen auf das wohl eher lüsterne Interesse einer breiteren Leserschaft. Das duale Geschlechterbild vom kämpfenden Mann und dem zu schützenden, weiblichen Kriegsopfer wurde durch diese selektive Inszenierung und Wahrnehmung produziert und reproduziert. Indem Hagemann eine umfassende Studie zur Lage und Rolle von Frauen in den europäischen Streitkräften und Kriegen seit 1600 vorlegt, zeigt sie, wie dieser Dualismus zwischen den Geschlechtern hergestellt wird, welche Funktionen er erfüllt – und sie belegt, wie realitätsfern dieser Dualismus ist.

Dazu hat sich die Autorin mit drei Fragen auseinandergesetzt: 1. Wie war der Einsatz von Frauen im Militär organisiert? 2. Welche Faktoren beeinflussen den Wandel des militärischen Einsatzes von Frauen und so auch deren individuelle und kollektive Erfahrungen? 3. Warum stellte es über Zeit-, Länder- und Systemgrenzen hinweg für Militär, Politik und Gesellschaft eine solche Herausforderung dar, den Einsatz von Frauen in Militär und Krieg anzuerkennen und sich daran zu erinnern (S. 21)?

Der Einleitung folgen vier Großkapitel: Das erste (S. 29 ff.) bezieht sich auf die frühneuzeitlichen Heere des 17. und 18. Jahrhunderts. Es geht vor allem um die Söldnerheere des Dreißigjährigen Krieges und den Siebenjährigen Krieg, an dem zahlreiche europäische Streitkräfte beteiligt und in dem unter anderem Kolonien und Handelswege von Interesse waren. Die Familien der Söldner und so auch die Frauen waren in diesen Fällen noch selbstverständlicher Teil des Trosses und übernahmen die unterschiedlichsten Funktionen in den Bereichen Versorgung, Ausrüstung, Schanzenbau und Plünderung oder Requirierung von Lebensmitteln und anderen Vorräten.

Im zweiten Großkapitel (S. 145 ff.) stehen Frauen in den Armeen des langen 19. Jahrhunderts im Fokus, vor allem in den Revolutions- und Napoleonischen Kriegen, den europäischen Kolonial- und Imperialkriegen, dem Krimkrieg und den deutschen Einigungskriegen. Die Autorin zeigt, dass der Versuch, Frauen und Familien gänzlich aus den Streitkräften auszuschließen, teilweise dazu führte, dass die Frauen, wenn sie in der Heimat zurückgelassen wurden, sich selbst und ihre Familien nicht ernähren konnten. Vor allem aber wurde offensichtlich, dass Frauen im Sanitätswesen und der Kriegskrankenpflege dringend benötigt wurden. Beginnend mit dem Krimkrieg (1853–1856) und verbunden mit dem Namen Florence Nightingale [1] etablierte sich über einige Jahrzehnte hinweg eine weibliche professionelle Krankenpflege.

Im Ersten Weltkrieg, dem das dritte Großkapitel (S. 347 ff.) gewidmet ist, wurden Frauen in immer mehr Bereichen benötigt, zunächst in der Kriegswirtschaft, da die Männer dort fehlten. Zunehmend kamen Frauen auch als militärische Hilfskräfte, Büroangestellte, Telefonistinnen, Etappen- und Nachrichtenhelferinnen zum Einsatz. Das galt gleichermaßen für die deutschen, britischen, französischen und US-amerikanischen Armeen. Die russische Armee hatte darüber hinaus sogar eigene Frauenbataillone.

Auch im Zweiten Weltkrieg, den das vierte Kapitel (S. 545 ff.) behandelt, konnten weder das NS-Regime und seine Verbündeten noch die Alliierten darauf verzichten, Frauen in den unterschiedlichsten Funktionen und in noch größerem Umfang als im Ersten Weltkrieg einzusetzen. Insbesondere in der Sowjetarmee und in den Partisanenverbänden kämpften viele Frauen, um ihre Heimat zu verteidigen und Deutschland zu besiegen.

In jedem Kapitel gibt die Autorin einen Überblick über die Geschichte der jeweiligen Kriege, die Streitkräfte sowie die Gesellschaften und erläutert die damit verbundenen Geschlechterverhältnisse. Vieles zeigt sie anhand von zeitgenössischer Malerei, Werbekampagnen oder Fotografien, die sie jeweils kritisch einordnet. Hagemann führt auch Dokumente an, in denen Frauen ihre Erinnerungen daran festhielten, wie sie den Krieg erlebt und mit welchen Motivationen sie sich beteiligt haben und erzählen, welche Schicksale sie erlitten. Gerade diese sehr konkreten Darstellungen machen die geschichtlichen Prozesse nachvollziehbar.

Aus mehreren Gründen halte ich das Buch auch über ein engeres Publikum von Historiker:innen hinaus für überaus lesenswert und gewinnbringend:

# Early-stage breast cancer gains first newly approved hormone therapy in more than 20 years

## Early-stage breast cancer gains first newly approved hormone therapy in more than 20 years

edited by Sadie Harley , reviewed by Robert Egan

Sadie Harley

Scientific Editor

Robert Egan

Senior Editor

This article has been reviewed according to Science X's editorial process and policies . Editors have highlighted the following attributes while ensuring the content's credibility:

fact-checked

peer-reviewed publication

trusted source

proofread

For the first time in more than two decades, the FDA has approved a new hormone therapy for early-stage breast cancer, marking a monumental shift in how the most common form of the disease is treated.

Estrogen receptor-positive (ER+) breast cancer makes up about 70% of all diagnoses. Known generically as giredestrant, this once-daily pill works by finding and destroying the estrogen receptors in breast tissue, effectively starving any remaining cancer cells of the hormone fuel they need to grow.

Following surgery, patients typically take daily hormone-blocking pills for up to 10 years to prevent the cancer from returning. However, standard therapies often come with harsh side effects that cause many women to abandon their treatment early, leaving them vulnerable to a relapse.

## Better protection with fewer side effects

This historic FDA approval introduces a highly effective, easier-to-tolerate alternative that is poised to change the standard of care. According to landmark data from the lidERA trial, published in the Journal of Clinical Oncology , this new treatment significantly improves disease-free survival and reduces the risk of the cancer spreading to other organs (metastatic disease). Crucially, this benefit was proven in both premenopausal and postmenopausal women.

"The approval of giredestrant is practice-changing as it is a better option over standard endocrine therapy for adjuvant treatment of breast cancer. It is better tolerated and has better efficacy as shown in the lidERA trial," said Madhurima Anne, M.D., FACP, chief of hematology/oncology at Hackensack Meridian Ocean University Medical Center and medical oncologist at Jersey Shore University Medical Center.

"For over 20 years, oncologists have had to counsel women through the difficult side effects of standard hormone therapies, knowing that if they stop taking their daily pill, their risk of relapse increases. Having giredestrant as a highly effective, easier-to-tolerate alternative is an absolute game-changer. It means we can finally protect our patients from a recurrence without asking them to sacrifice their daily quality of life," said Donna McNamara, M.D., breast medical oncologist, Hackensack Meridian John Theurer Cancer Center at Hackensack University Medical Center.

Publication details

items.body:
# Maybe Dark Energy Isn't so Inexplicable After All

The Universe as we know it is comprised of three "things": baryonic matter (planets, stars, galaxies, us), dark matter (still unexplained) and dark energy (really, really still unexplained). Of the three, dark energy remains the most challenging. It's "something" that's driving the acceleration of the expanding Universe but that's all we know about it. We can't see it, or even put a description to it, other than "it's mysterious".

This cosmic component accounts for about 70 percent of the known Universe's energy budget. Physicists have spent a lot of time trying to explain it, often invoking some hitherto-unknown fields, or exotic physical particles, or some kind of "cosmological constant" that is the same everywhere in space and time. Despite these and other attempts at explaining dark energy, physicists still don't know exactly what it is. However, there's hope that an explanation will come in our lifetimes. A team of scientists at Canada's University of British Columbia and the University of Sheffield (in England) have come up with a possible model that provides an explanation. They think dark matter may be a product of the same physics that governs the strength of the atomic nucleus. If that's true, then they could use the standard model of particle physics to understand this mysterious thing that is pushing the Universe apart.

Dark energy has many descriptions, which reflects our incomplete understanding of it. It could be a negative pressure that pushes space outward, although there’s no proof of that. It could be vacuum energy, which is an idea that there’s a background of energy that permeates all of the Universe. It’s also been called “quintessence”, which is a sort of imaginary “fluid” that fills space. Or it could be a combo of dark matter and dark energy, both yet unexplained. The wildest idea is that dark energy could be a wrinkle in the fabric of space-time, or even something leaking from another universe. All those explanations are fairly wild, and oftentimes in science, the simplest is the best explanation. That’s where the work in Canada and England is coming in handy, if particle physics can provide insight.

## Searching for a Quantum of Understanding

According to lead scientist Ariel Zhitnitsky of UBC, using particle physics means we don't need exotic explanations for dark energy. “Our theoretical framework suggests no new particles may be required at all,” said Zhitnitsky, who developed the theoretical ideas explained by the team. “The characteristic energy scale predicted from the QCD vacuum and gravity comes out close to the observed dark-energy scale today without having to introduce an ad hoc new field nor new parameter.”

What Zhitnitsky and others are talking about is a theory called quantum chromodynamics (QCD). It focuses on the strong nuclear force that holds quarks inside the protons and neutrons that make up atoms. QCD describes the actions of the strong force. Those actions could be affecting space, and in particular what it contains.

A NASA illustration of the strong force at work in an atomic nucleus. Credit: NASA

Space is never empty. Rather, it’s filled with subatomic fields and something called quantum energy. That's energy that exists in individual packets called “quanta”. This creates a “quantum vacuum” with properties that can affect space over large distances. Now, add in the fact that the Universe is expanding, and that has implications that need further explanation. The team, led by scientist Dong Ha Lee, proposed the following: as the Universe expands, the subatomic structure in the quantum vacuum responds differently as time goes by. That response generates a small energy shift that is just enough to drive the acceleration of universal expansion. The team points out that you don’t need new particles or other exotic things for this: the current particles are just fine, Lee suggested. “The idea that the quantum vacuum as described by QCD could have the right properties to account for the accelerated expansion of the universe is very intriguing,” said Lee.

## Testing a New Idea Using Standard Physics

So, if this idea holds up, it means that dark energy could have a connection to the strong nuclear force. Scientists could create models to test this using currently available physics models. The big test would be to compare it to cosmological data, according to Lee. ”Our analysis shows that such a model can reproduce the evolving dark energy behaviour suggested by current observations. This motivates further theoretical work to better understand how the QCD vacuum responds to cosmic expansion and to develop predictions that can be tested with future observations.”

When tested against real astronomical data including light from distant supernovae and leftover radiation from the early Universe, the team found that their model matched observations just as well as standard cosmological models. In addition, it offers a possible way to explain what is causing dark energy. The next step for the team is to keep refining their model and calculations in order to build as robust a model as possible. By that time, observations and data from the next generations of telescopes, such as the Nancy Grace Roman telescope, could prove very useful in testing ideas about the true nature of dark energy and its effects on the expanding Universe over time.

### For More Information

Could Standard Physics Explain the Mysterious Energy Driving the Universe Apart?

Evolving Dark Energy Is Vacuum Energy After All

### Carolyn Collins Petersen

Carolyn Collins Petersen is a long-time science writer and former astronomy researcher. She writes about astronomy and space exploration and has written 8 books, including the recently released 2nd edition of her Astronomy 101 book , countless articles, more than 60 documentaries for planetarium star theaters, and exhibits for Griffith Observatory, NASA/JPL, the California Academy of Sciences, the Shanghai Astronomical Museum, and the Lowell Observatory Dark Sky Planetarium. She is CEO of Loch Ness Productions . You can email Carolyn here .

# PrismML’s Bonsai 2.5 brings better coding and tool use to on-device AI - 9to5Mac

- Mac
- PrismML
- Bonsai
## PrismML’s Bonsai 2.5 brings better coding and tool use to on-device AI

Back in July, PrismML claimed its roughly 4 GB, 1-bit Bonsai 27B was the first AI model of its size to run on an iPhone. Now PrismML has released Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B, an update to the model it introduced in September.

The startup also drew attention when CEO Babak Hassibi told CNBC that Apple was evaluating its technology, as we reported at the time .

The new model is based on Qwen3.8 27B and keeps the same 5.9 GB footprint in its most compact format. This time, PrismML focused on helping the model handle longer tasks, including figuring out what to do when a tool returns an unexpected result or a step fails.

Bonsai 2.5 improved on six of the seven benchmarks PrismML highlights . Its SWE-bench Verified coding score rose from 60.8 to 75.6, while its AppWorld tool-use score jumped from 51.2 to 90.5. LiveCodeBench v6 dipped from 83.8 to 83.0.

What could that look like on a Mac? A coding assistant could inspect a private project, make a change, run the tests, and use the results to revise its fix. A document app could summarize a folder of sensitive files while keeping the processing on the device.

PrismML says Bonsai 2.5 runs on Mac, iPhone, and iPad through MLX. Its Apple silicon package is about 8.9 GB, and the model card walks through setup on a Mac . The weights are available for free under Apache 2.0.

For a closer look at how the model was compressed and tested, read PrismML’s technical white paper .

## US financial crimes bureau discloses ‘cybersecurity incident’

FinCEN’s alert comes in the wake of a reported breach of unclassified information at US spy agencies, including the CIA.

FinCEN’s alert comes in the wake of a reported breach of unclassified information at US spy agencies, including the CIA.

The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) disclosed on Tuesday that it’s investigating a “cybersecurity incident.” The bureau, which is part of the Treasury Department, said it’s looking into an “incident that resulted in unauthorized access to a limited subset of its systems.” It hasn’t offered any information about the full scope or source of the breach, but FinCEN has taken some systems offline as a precaution.

The news comes hours after The New York Times reported that the Central Intelligence Agency and Office of the Director of National Security discovered a breach of an open source intelligence system, exposing unclassified information. The Department of Defense, whose National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency was also reportedly impacted by the breach, declined to comment. The CIA and ODNI did not immediately respond to requests for comment. It’s unclear if the FinCEN breach is related. Americans have been on high alert about security incidents after a series of seemingly unrelated outages earlier this month .

Americans have been on high alert about security incidents

FinCEN’s role is to protect the financial system from illegal activity, including by combatting money laundering and terrorism financing. The bureau maintains financial transaction data and distributes it for law enforcement purposes. FinCEN also houses reports of suspicious activity that financial institutions file as part of the Bank Secrecy Act.

FinCEN says in its alert that banks can still file reports about suspicious activity online, but some services may not be immediately available. Filers that need to expedite their reports in the meantime can still call the Financial Institutions Hotline, which it says was not impacted by the disruption.

## Retributive Justice

Retributive justice is best understood as the form of justice committed to the following three principles:

- that those who culpably commit certain kinds of wrongful acts, paradigmatically serious crimes, morally deserve to suffer proportionate punishment;
- that it is morally right or intrinsically good—without reference to any further goods that might arise—for some (legitimate) punisher to impose the punishment they deserve; and
- that punishment must not be imposed in the absence of desert or exceed what would be proportional to the wrongful action.
While retributivism was for a long period of time disregarded as “a barbaric remnant of superstitious thought that more rational forms of society would sweep away” (Bennett 2014: 4446), recent work on retributivism has gained much support in the philosophy of punishment, making retributivist views among the dominant candidates for a positive justification of punishment. Still, critics continue to voice the charges of barbarism (Tadros 2011) and moral repugnancy (Scanlon 2008), and many features of retributivism—especially the notions of desert, proportionality, the normative status of suffering, and the ultimate justification for retribution—remain contested. Though theories of retributive justice have ancient and medieval roots, this entry focuses on contemporary conceptions of retributive justice.

## 1. Introducing Retributive Theory

### 1.1 On Punishment

Retributivism offers a justification of punishment. While the definition of punishment is itself a matter of controversy, punishment generally refers to the deliberate or intentional imposition of burdens or suffering on wrongdoers for an act or omission that the punisher believes to be (a culpable) wrong. (The entry on legal punishment discusses this concept in depth.) This definition includes both punishment as it is imposed by the state in the public sphere for the commission of crimes and punitive responses to wrongdoing in other spheres, including the private and the institutional. Still, the challenge of justifying state punishment is the most pressing, as the forms of punishment imposed by the state generally involve sanctions that are different in kind from and more onerous than those imposed outside the political sphere, paradigmatically involving the deprivation of basic human rights (to life, liberty, and property, among others).

Punishment is often analyzed in terms of two constituent parts: censure (or condemnation) and sanction (or hard treatment, that is, treatment that involves a hardship imposed on the person being punished, or at the very least the withdrawal of a benefit to which they would otherwise be entitled).

### 1.2 Basic Strengths and Weaknesses

### 1.2.1 Intuitive Appeal

Many share the intuition that those who commit wrongful acts, especially serious crimes, should be punished even if punishing them would produce no other good (see Darley & Robinson 2002). Consider, for example, being the sentencing judge for an offender who has been convicted of rape. How should you sentence him? You may have the intuition that he should not be “let off easy”. If so, you might think that this reflects the importance of incapacitating him, deterring him and others from future criminal acts, or publicly condemning the crime. But now suppose that he has since suffered an illness that has left him physically incapacitated so that he cannot rape or commit other violent crimes again. Moreover, he has enough money to support himself without resorting to criminal activities. You therefore have no need to take steps to prevent him from committing future crimes. Still, others might be emboldened if you don’t punish him. So suppose further that you could “sentence” him to spend his days on a tropical island of his choosing, where he can relax and enjoy himself, as long as he regularly reports to an island prison to be videoed in prison garb, footage of which is made publicly available, ensuring thereby that others harbor the false belief that he is suffering for his crime. If you believe that this could be done with no prospect of detection, should you choose such a sentence? Many share the intuition that this would be unjust. They believe that the wrongdoing should not go unpunished, even if punishment would achieve no other downstream good (see, e.g., Moore 1997: 98–101).

Not only is retributivism in this way intuitively appealing, the primary alternative, consequentialist theories of punishment that focus on deterrence, incapacitation and rehabilitation, seem to confront a deep problem: They have difficulty accommodating a core retributivist commitment, namely that these goals cannot justify imposing punishment on those who have done no wrong. They also have trouble explaining the discomfort most have with imposing disproportionately large punishments on those who have committed only minor wrongs.

Both of these sources of retributivism’s appeal have clear limits. The positive intuition can be challenged with the claim that it is merely the reflection of a morally dubious psychological propensity to feel an excess of what Nietzsche, in the Genealogy of Morals (1887), called ressentiment :

> a witches’ brew [of] resentment, fear, anger, cowardice, hostility, aggression, cruelty, sadism, envy, jealousy, guilt, self-loathing, hypocrisy and self-deception. (Moore 1997: 120)

And the argument that retributivism better justifies punishment than consequentialist alternatives presupposes that punishment is justifiable (for criticism of this premise, see Golash 2005; Boonin 2008), and that there are no alternatives that are better than both (for three alternatives, see Quinn 1985; Tadros 2011; Lacey & Pickard 2015a).

items.body:
# Real video of NYC lawmaker Jordan Wright's eye roll fuels lizard conspiracy theory

About this rating

Conspiracy theorists claimed the video served as evidence that "lizard people" walk among us. Wright reportedly told the New York Post that he's "obviously" a human.

A video circulating online appears to show a man rolling his eyes in a so-called "reptilian" fashion while standing behind New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani during a news conference.

The clip, which was posted on X , Facebook and other platforms, reignited a decades-old conspiracy theory claiming shape-shifting reptilians secretly hold positions of power, which Snopes has previously reported on.

Snopes readers wrote in to ask if the video was real or generated using artificial intelligence.

This is a real clip of Democratic New York City Assemblyman Jordan Wright, who reportedly told the New York Post that he is "obviously" human.

Wright's eye roll is visible in multiple credible livestreams of the news conference in question, which Mamdani held on Nov. 20 to announce a plan to shutter Rikers Island, the city's largest jail, by 2032.

For example, Wright's eye roll is visible at the timestamp 1:51 in a YouTube livestream posted by the official New York City mayor's office account, whereas USA Today's livestream shows the eye roll at 1:54 .

There's no evidence that the livestreams in question were enhanced using AI, nor would there be any reason to do so.

According to the New York Post, Wright said he has "no idea what was going on in that video."

"Obviously I'm a human being, and my humanity can be seen through my legislation like the $4 million for the WE ACT environmental justice center in Harlem," he reportedly told the Post. "I can't speak to any reptiles or aliens."

We reached out to Wright, who assumed office in the New York State Assembly in January 2025, to verify that he spoke to the Post and await a response.

## Background on reptilian conspiracy theories

As we previously reported , the "reptilian" conspiracy theory was popularized in the modern era by David Icke, a British man who is barred from holding events in countries like the Netherlands and Germany over antisemitic conspiracy theories.

According to the UK anti-fascist advocacy group HOPE not hate , " the 'reptilian theory' is just one element of the hugely convoluted narrative Icke has developed over his long career" that promotes longstanding antisemitic tropes.

In the United States, officials have previously examined whether the conspiracy theory was a possible motive for the Nashville Christmas Day 2020 bomber.

There is, of course, no evidence that a secret race of reptilians controls the world.

## DNGDNGDNG ~ Vestigio

There is something strangely archival about Vestigio , the latest album by Peruvian duo DNGDNGDNG (formerly Dengue Dengue Dengue). Its rhythms and sonic patterns have an uncanny familiarity, as though they belonged to an established musical tradition, yet their origins are difficult to locate precisely. They seem to come from a geographical territory that has yet to be mapped, let alone explored. The artwork by Joseph Melhuish reinforces this impression, depicting mysterious objects that might be archaeological remains of an unknown civilisation, past or future.

The recognisably Peruvian elements of their earlier releases have become harder to identify. As the duo explained in our interview, they are no longer interested in reproducing traditional rhythms but in extracting certain characteristics and rebuilding them in unfamiliar contexts. This is what gives Vestigio its peculiar character: the music feels familiar without quite belonging anywhere. Rhythmic structures drawn from different traditions are dismantled and recombined with influences from deconstructed club and drum and bass. On “Inercia”, fractured beats and abrupt shifts in rhythm create a sense of constant movement, an approach revisited on “Purpúrea”. Clipping, distortion and resonance are integral to the percussion itself, rather than effects added afterwards. The result is an ebullient album whose rhythmic vocabulary seems to have been invented from fragments of several different musical cultures.

There is also a darker side to Vestigio , most explicitly expressed in the closing track, “Noche Obscura”. Its title references the dark night of the soul , a period of spiritual crisis and eventual awakening. The voices declaring “Están matándonos” (They are killing us) and “¡Nunca más!” (Never again) give the piece an unmistakable political significance. As the duo explained, the track reflects their opposition to state violence and oppression, informed by Peru’s political reality but extending to conflicts and human rights abuses elsewhere.

The title Vestigio refers to something that survives a transformation. Here, traces of Peruvian musical traditions remain embedded in the rhythms, but their origins have become almost impossible to identify. What makes the album so intriguing is precisely this tension between recognition and disorientation: the sense of hearing something familiar while being unable to say exactly where it comes from.

Photo by Alejandro Loayza Grisi : Masks by Tween Muizen

To learn more, we reached out to Felipe and Rafael.

Vestigio is described as your most radical sonic departure to date, with familiar elements of your music broken apart and reconstructed. How did this transformation come about, and what traces of your earlier work, from Zenit & Nadir to Fiebre and Agita2 , do you recognise in the new album?

I think Agita2 was something of a precursor to Vestigio . It was already pointing toward the sonic direction we wanted to explore on the album. Maybe not every track, but several of them contain some of that essence.

There’s also something of the darkness of Fiebre , certain percussive elements, and some connections to Zenit & Nadir . I think the album contains a little bit of each of our previous records.

The idea was to take specific elements from our music, break them apart, and reconstruct them in a different context. Not necessarily to bring back a sound exactly as it was, but to transform it and take it somewhere else.

At the same time, we wanted to push the energy and intensity of those elements much further. I think that combination of deconstruction, reconstruction, and the search for greater intensity is one of the main ideas behind Vestigio .

In earlier interviews, you spoke enthusiastically about Afro-Peruvian polyrhythms and the possibilities of combining live percussion with electronics. On Vestigio , rhythm seems to emerge from the interaction of distortion, clipping and resonance, often becoming jagged and unstable. How has your approach to rhythm and sound design evolved, and what role do traditional Peruvian musical forms still play in your compositions?

On this album, we tried to work more with compositions built from scratch. We still use samples and recordings, but we don’t necessarily build the tracks around them anymore.

Now we’re more interested in capturing the essence or feeling of certain rhythms and musical elements, then transforming them and placing them in a different context.

Traditional Peruvian rhythms are still part of our musical language, but we no longer feel the need to reference them directly or reproduce them in a recognizable way.

That gives us more freedom to create music that doesn’t necessarily belong to a specific genre.

For example, there are elements of Pandilla music and other rhythmic traditions, but we’re not trying to recreate those sounds. We’re interested in taking certain characteristics, breaking them apart, and using them to build something different.

In that sense, the idea of breaking things down and reconstructing them also describes our current approach to rhythm and sound design.

Your back catalogue reveals an appetite for unlikely musical encounters, from reworking Chabuca Granda and Zambo Cavero to combining shoegaze with dembow on BambaPack . More recently, you’ve collaborated with Prisma on Abisal , while Vestigio features Los Hijos de Lamas , Siete Catorce and Only Now . What attracts you to these collaborations, and how do they challenge or expand your musical vocabulary?

We’ve always been interested in collaborating with artists whose music we admire. They’re usually projects we’ve been following for a long time and that make us curious, especially when we hear something that surprises us and makes us wonder how they came up with that sound.

I think an important part of collaborating is precisely that curiosity about how other people develop their ideas and what can happen when we combine them with our own.

Experimentation and fusion have always been fundamental to Dengue Dengue Dengue, so working with other artists is a natural extension of that philosophy. It allows us to bring in new perspectives and reach places we might not have reached on our own.

For example, collaborating with Siete Catorce was something we’d wanted to do for a long time. We started working on “Señal” in Berlin around 2015. After developing it for a while, we left the track unfinished for several years.

items.feedText: The Cerise project 1 was started almost 10 years ago at Aarhus University. Its goal is to develop formal methods to verify properties of capability machines, in particular involving non-monotonicity, and to prove end-to-end results in the presence of unknown code. Cerise has been extended to model different aspects of capability machines, and has involved work by and collaborations with several other universities, including Dominique Devriese’s research group at KU Leuven, and the universities of Cambridge and Edinburgh. items.body:
# From formal verification to bug-finding in CHERIoT

The Cerise project 1 was started almost 10 years ago at Aarhus University. Its goal is to develop formal methods to verify properties of capability machines, in particular involving non-monotonicity, and to prove end-to-end results in the presence of unknown code. Cerise has been extended to model different aspects of capability machines, and has involved work by and collaborations with several other universities, including Dominique Devriese’s research group at KU Leuven, and the universities of Cambridge and Edinburgh.

Cerise started as pen-and-paper proofs about idealised machines and focused initially on reasoning about control-flow integrity of encapsulation for stack-based calling conventions, but over time our research group has scaled up the approach along three dimensions. First, we made our proofs foundational: Cerise now builds on the Iris separation logic framework inside the Rocq theorem prover, which has been critical to ensure correctness despite the growing intricacy of our proofs. Second, we have investigated how to reason about a wider range of properties, e.g., involving MMIO and attestation. Third, we made Cerise work with an instruction set closer to the CHERIoT Sail model, and verified programs using those instructions.

When I started my PhD, CHERIoT had just been announced. I seized the opportunity to apply the verification techniques of Cerise to the CHERIoT switcher, for example to check that it isolates compartments and enforces no-capture. To that end, we started a sub-project of Cerise, which we call Griotte 2 .

As part of our verification effort in this Griotte project, we uncovered two bugs in the CHERIoT switcher: (1) the ability for a malicious (or buggy) scheduler to resuscitate an exited thread in a deprecated state, thereby getting access to a capability that it should not be able to have access to anymore, and (2) the ability for a malicious caller to leverage the stack high watermark register to trigger a fault in the switcher, thereby getting access to the callee’s stack frame and thus private data.

## Reasoning about unknown code

The CHERI/CHERIoT threat model includes interactions with unknown compartments containing arbitrary code, which can be buggy or malicious, and which can share objects in memory. Reasoning about arbitrary code is hard, because it requires characterising all the possible behaviours of that code. The challenge is that when trying to characterise what an unknown compartment can affect, we have to account not only for what it is passed directly (if an unknown compartment is physically passed a write capability to a region of memory, then it is behaviourally passed the ability to overwrite that region of memory), but also what it is passed indirectly—and this involves not only recursive access (if an unknown compartment is physically passed a read capability to a region of memory, then it is behaviourally passed the ability to acquire whatever ability is given by the capabilities in that region of memory), but also access through non-monotonic domain transitions (if an unknown compartment is physically passed a sealed entry point capability to a “counter” compartment’s incr function, then it is behaviourally passed the ability to affect the counter—but only by incrementing it). A unique feature of Cerise is the ability to reason also about the latter part of the challenge.

What makes it difficult to design such a characterisation is that it should at the same time be precise enough, and simple enough to verify the programs that we care about. At a very high level, Griotte defines a language to succinctly describe what is affected—and to state that something is not affected. The kind of properties that we want to describe are not only memory safety properties (if I share a buffer to the caller, then I have the guarantee that it cannot access the global data that I never shared), but also no-capture properties (if I share a buffer to the caller with its global permission stripped, then I have the guarantee that it cannot preserve a copy across calls), and many others (including secrecy, etc.).

## Separation logic and logical relations

Technically, we developed a reasoning system in two parts. First, we defined (and proved sound) a separation logic that allows us to verify known code line by line, showing that it satisfies expected pre- and post-conditions, and that it preserves the expected invariants. We used this both on the code of the switcher, and on the code of specific compartments of interest, for example a key-value store 3 . We designed this separation logic so it is reusable, and we expect that other such compartments of interest could be verified with it.

Second, we defined a logical relation in separation logic, which is effectively an over-approximation of the effect of unknown code that can be used by the separation logic to reason about a jump to unknown code (through the switcher) in one single step. As such, it works like a universal contract 4 for CHERIoT. Crucially, the frame rule of separation logic tells us that if we can establish that the resources (both in an informal sense, and in the technical sense of separation logic) of the caller are disjoint from those of the logical relation, then they will be preserved by the call.

For example, if calling unknown code with a capability to a shared buffer, while keeping some private data, the logical relation requires that the unknown code is only passed capabilities that are safe to share in a technical sense.

We then define a universal contract, stating that if an adversary has only access to safe to share capabilities, it can then execute safely and only produce other safe to share capabilities.

## Verification in the presence of compartments and a trusted switcher

We started by developing a simplified model of CHERIoT and a mini version of the CHERIoT-RTOS. In particular, we modelled the compartmentalisation mechanisms and the cross-compartment call path of the switcher. Our simplified model mirrors the main features of the CHERIoT hardware (including the new deep locality and deep immutability permissions). While our mini switcher doesn’t follow CHERIoT’s switcher instruction-by-instruction, it implements the same steps.

In this model, we proved on a range of small examples that the CHERIoT hardware-software co-design implements the expected memory-safety properties, and that the switcher’s overall design enforces both compartmentalisation and stack safety.

items.body:
Does a new map show the path of potential lead fallout from the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant? No, that's not true: The map in the post is clearly labeled as the snowfall accumulation forecast from the College of DuPage NEXLAB WOOF-NAM weather model. And what the post says is the North American Military model is really the federal government's acronym for the North American Mesoscale numerical weather prediction model.

The claim appeared in [a post](https://x.com/a_dose_of_wx/status/2125243331521515594?s=46) (archived [↗ web.archive.org](https://web.archive.org/web/20261124214535/https://x.com/a_dose_of_wx/status/2125243331521515594?s=46) ) by the @a_dose_of_wx account on X on Nov. 24, 2026. It read:

> BREAKING: NEW lead fallout map from North American Military model (NAM) as they move forward with plans to detonate 5 tons of unstable explosives at an Iowa ammunition plant.

This is what the map looked like on X at the time of writing:

*(Image source: post by @a_dose_of_wx on X.)*

The U.S. Army has scheduled a controlled detonation of 68 barrels (nearly 5 tons) of unstable lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, on Wednesday at 9 a.m. Central time (10 a.m. Eastern time), as [Iowa Public Radio reported](https://www.iowapublicradio.org/ipr-news/2026-11-24/reynolds-iowa-lead-azide-detonation-army-ammunitions-plant-ernst-grassley-middletown) (archived [↗ web.archive.org](https://web.archive.org/web/20261124224822/https://www.iowapublicradio.org/ipr-news/2026-11-24/reynolds-iowa-lead-azide-detonation-army-ammunitions-plant-ernst-grassley-middletown) ).

The map in the post does not show "lead fallout." It is clearly labeled as "snowfall accumulation" as the image below shows (red rectangle added by Lead Stories):

*(Image source: post by @a_dose_of_wx on X.)*

The image is from the [College of DuPage NEXLAB WOOF-NAM](https://weather.cod.edu/forecast/) weather prediction model (archived [↗ web.archive.org](https://web.archive.org/web/20261116220004/https://weather.cod.edu/forecast/) ). NAM is the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's acronym for North American Mesoscale numerical weather prediction model, not the North American Military model, as the post claims. Lead Stories was able to recreate the model map here:

*(Image source: weather.cod.edu/forecast.)*

The [U.S. Army](https://www.army.mil/article/297039) (archived [↗ web.archive.org](https://web.archive.org/web/20261124183120/https://www.army.mil/article/297039) ) published two maps on Nov. 24, 2026, on a page titled "Public Safety Advisory: Controlled, Mitigated Detonation of Unstable Lead Azide at Iowa Army Ammunition Plant." The maps did not match the map posted on X.

This is a screenshot of the first map on the page at the time of writing:

*(Image source: army.mil.)*

This is a screenshot of the second map on the page at the time of writing:

*(Image source: army.mil.)*

The [Associated Press](https://apnews.com/article/lead-azide-detonation-army-iowa-trump-83f1492cc5c3e358557f1170ea2a2d40) (archived [here)](https://web.archive.org/web/20261124225539/https://apnews.com/article/lead-azide-detonation-army-iowa-trump-83f1492cc5c3e358557f1170ea2a2d40) published a map from the U.S. Army showing the potential amount of lead dust deposited on surfaces after the explosion.

This is a screenshot of the map in the article at the time of writing:

*(Image source: Associated Press.)*

items.body:
# New leaks reveal the iPhone 18e will have a redesigned camera plateau - Engadget

- Big Tech
- Apple
## New leaks reveal the iPhone 18e will have a redesigned camera plateau

We've also got further confirmation the iPhone Air 2 will have a second camera.

Diego Thomazini/Getty Images Add Engadget on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover Apple seems to have adopted a new strategy for the iPhone launch, splitting it into two phases. After launching the premium iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo in September, Apple is preparing new versions of the lower-priced models — and it looks like they'll look a lot more like the more expensive iPhones. CAD images of the new iPhone 18e seen by Engadget show a redesigned camera bump on the back of the phone, similar to the one on the Pro models. The images come from a source familiar with Apple's supply chain who who had previously shared accurate tips on the colors of the iPhone 17 and iPhone 18 Pro before they were announced.

The current iPhone 17e doesn't have a camera bump — instead, the lens has a small protrusion and sits flush against the back of the phone, with the microphone and LED flash also embedded in cutouts directly in the rear glass. But according to CAD images seen by Engadget, Apple appears to be considering changing that with the iPhone 18e. The renders show an almost square camera bump measuring about 28 mm by 35 mm that houses the single rear camera, the LED flash and the rear microphone. It's somewhat similar to the camera module on the M5 iPad Pro (which you can see in the image below).

Interestingly, it seems that the iPhone 18e will be the only model to feature this new camera plateau. The same files include the CADs for the base iPhone 18 and the iPhone Air 2, both of which are expected to launch alongside the 18e next spring. The base iPhone 18 will keep the exact same design, but now with a thicker camera module — increasing from 3.45mm (0.14 inches) to 3.8mm (0.15 inches). Apple has been using the same 48-megapixel Sony IMX904 sensor for its base models since the iPhone 15, so a thicker camera module could mean new sensors or upgraded cameras.

As for the iPhone Air 2, the CADs seen by Engadget corroborate previous rumors that Apple's ultra-thin phone will feature a second rear camera — not a surprise given that its single lens was one of the main complaints about it . Although the Air 2 will remain 5.6mm thick, the camera module will increase in thickness from 3.45mm (0.14 inches) to 3.8mm (0.15 inches), with the two lenses aligned horizontally. Bloomberg' s Mark Gurman, the leaker Digital Chat Station and analyst Jeff Pu have all said Apple is adding an ultra-wide lens to the second-generation Air, and the CAD images back those reports up.

Also, the iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2 are expected to keep the same Dynamic Island as current models rather than the smaller cutout on the iPhone 18 Pro . Of course, these changes may end up being scrapped and never see the light of day, since Apple still has some time before they hit the stores next year.

items.title: New nose drops restore youthful memory and fight Alzheimer’s in aging mice
items.subtitle: A revolutionary new nasal treatment has restored youthful learning and memory performance in aging mice while preventing severe cognitive decline i…
items.feedText: Developed using technology similar to COVID-19 mRNA vaccines, the nose drops stimulate production of a brain-protecting protein that strengthens neurons and supports memory. Remarkably, the treatment preserved brain function without removing Alzheimer’s-associated plaques, suggesting a completely different way to combat cognitive decline.
items.body:
# New nose drops restore youthful memory and fight Alzheimer’s in aging mice

## New nose drops restore youthful memory and fight Alzheimer’s in aging mice

Researchers at the University of Sydney have created experimental nose drops that significantly improved learning and memory in older mice, bringing their performance back to levels seen in younger animals. The treatment also prevented severe memory decline in mice genetically engineered to develop Alzheimer's-like disease. Remarkably, the approach relies on mRNA technology similar to that used in COVID-19 vaccines.

The discovery, led by Professor Greg Neely at the University of Sydney's Charles Perkins Centre, could open a new path toward treating conditions that affect the brain. Potential applications extend beyond Alzheimer's disease to other neurodegenerative disorders, stroke, traumatic brain injury, and rare genetic and developmental conditions.

"If we can proceed quickly to clinical trials in humans, this approach could represent a world-first non-invasive delivery system to treat Alzheimer's that bypasses the blood-brain barrier," Professor Neely said.

The idea behind the research has an unusual origin. The team drew inspiration from Daniel Keyes' science fiction story Flowers for Algernon , which explores the limits of human intelligence through experiments designed to increase intelligence in laboratory mice and people.

How mRNA Nose Drops Restore Youthful Memory

The treatment works by delivering messenger RNA (mRNA), a type of genetic instruction that tells cells how to produce specific proteins. These instructions are enclosed in tiny fat-based particles called lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), which protect the mRNA and help it enter cells.

Once delivered through the nose, the mRNA instructs cells to manufacture therapeutic proteins capable of reaching the brain. In effect, the nasal tissue becomes a small drug-producing factory, creating substances that can support brain function.

"In aged mice, we saw learning and memory significantly increased, returning animal cognition to its youthful prime," Professor Neely said.

"What's exciting is that this was achieved with a simple non-invasive nasal delivery system that builds on the same underlying mRNA-LNP technology platform many people became familiar with during the COVID-19 pandemic."

The study, published in Advanced Science , used mRNA to stimulate production of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF). This naturally occurring protein helps neurons survive, form connections, and adapt as the brain learns and stores memories. Levels of BDNF tend to decline with aging and are also associated with Alzheimer's disease.

The results were striking. Older mice that received the nose drops performed about as well as young mice in standardized tests of working memory, spatial memory, and object recognition. These tests measure abilities such as remembering recently encountered information, navigating surroundings, and recognizing familiar objects. Untreated older animals showed the expected age-related deterioration in cognitive performance.

Nose Drops Prevent Alzheimer's-Like Memory Decline in Mice

To investigate whether the treatment might also protect against Alzheimer's disease, researchers turned to a widely used laboratory model known as 5XFAD mice. These animals carry genetic mutations that cause them to develop Alzheimer's-like brain changes and memory problems unusually early in life.

In this model, signs of Alzheimer's-related brain pathology can typically be detected by two months of age, with measurable cognitive decline appearing around four months.

The researchers began administering the BDNF-producing mRNA nose drops when the mice were two months old, around the time the disease-related changes first appeared. Treatment continued twice a week.

One of the most intriguing results was what the treatment did not do. Although memory and learning were protected, the researchers found no reduction in amyloid plaques, the abnormal protein deposits that accumulate in the brains of people with Alzheimer's disease.

That distinction could be important because many existing Alzheimer's treatments aim to remove amyloid. The new approach instead appears to help neurons remain healthy and functional despite the presence of these deposits. If the same effect can eventually be demonstrated in people, the two treatment strategies might be used together.

"Current Alzheimer's treatments largely focus on clearing these amyloid plaques," Professor Neely said. "However, just under a third of Alzheimer's patients have serious plaques but do not suffer from dementia, and these patients show naturally higher BDNF levels, suggesting if we raise BDNF, it's possible to live with Alzheimer's disease pathology."

"Our approach seems to work not by clearing plaques but by supporting the health, survival and connectivity of neurons themselves. It raises the possibility these therapies could eventually work alongside each other."

Bypassing the Blood-Brain Barrier Through the Nose

Getting medicines into the brain is one of the biggest obstacles in developing treatments for neurological diseases. The blood-brain barrier acts as a protective filter, preventing many potentially harmful substances in the bloodstream from entering delicate brain tissue. Unfortunately, it also blocks numerous drugs that scientists would like to use to treat brain disorders.

The nose offers a possible alternative route. Connections between the nasal cavity and the central nervous system may allow certain therapeutic substances to reach the brain without requiring surgery or injections directly into the brain or spinal cord.

"This is a very exciting proof of concept for a method to deliver mRNA-encoded cargo to the nervous system directly through the nose," Professor Neely said.

The team adapted mRNA technology built on the same clinically validated BioNTech platform used for COVID-19 vaccination. Instead of delivering instructions that prompt an immune response, the modified system provides instructions for producing proteins intended to benefit the brain.

First author Dr. Maria Bergamasco, from the University of Sydney's School of Life and Environmental Sciences, explained that the findings illustrate how mRNA technology could be used for purposes far beyond preventing infectious diseases.

"The success of mRNA vaccines showed these systems can safely deliver genetic instructions to cells," Dr. Bergamasco said.

"We wanted to see whether we could adapt that technology to deliver beneficial proteins to the brain in a completely non-invasive way."

Treatment Stimulates New Brain Cell Growth

The researchers also detected increased neurogenesis, the process through which new neurons are formed, in the hippocampus. This part of the brain plays an essential role in learning and memory and is particularly vulnerable to damage associated with Alzheimer's disease.

# wheybags' blog: Pokemon Childhood Version: A romhack where Mew is under the truck

- Tom Mason About
- Blog
- Projects
- Contact
## Pokemon Childhood Version: A romhack where Mew is under the truck

TL;DR I made a romhack which implements the most common urban legends from the gen 1 Pokemon games.

Catching Mew under the truck

- Spam A to increase catch chance
- Magikarp splash has a 1/256 chance to 1-shot KO
- Talk to Bill 100 times and you can go to his garden
- You can catch all three starters in Bill's garden
- You can catch Pikablu in Bill's garden
- You can battle Professor Oak after completing the Pokedex
- ... and of course, Mew is under the truck
The old fashioned way! I did not make the actual getting to the truck any easier. You have to either trade for a Pokemon that knows CUT, to avoid entering the S.S. Anne. Or, you can enter the ship and collect the CUT HM as usual, then backtrack to a trainer on the ship that you have not already defeated, battle them, and let them win. This will teleport you back to the nearest Pokecentre without triggering the S.S. Anne to leave.

### Download

I don't want to host the rom directly because Nintendo will eviscerate me. What I have below is a patching tool: select an original, unmodified ROM file that you ripped from your personal copy you've had since you were twelve, and it will patch it, and save the modified version. Under no circumstances should you use a ROM file ripped by anyone else, because that would be very naughty.

Select your Pokemon Red or Blue (USA, Europe) ROM to patch:

Source code available on github . Thanks to the pret/pokered contributors, without whose hard labour this would not have been possible. Also BTW I actually tried the Mew under the truck thing when I was a kid. I was devastated when it didn't work. Satisfaction at long last.

Now we’re building more auto plants than we…
items.body:
In declaring his high tariffs on imported vehicles a success, President Donald Trump often makes false and unsubstantiated claims about auto manufacturing plants in the United States.

For months, Trump has repeatedly made an [unsubstantiated](https://rollcall.com/factbase/trump/transcript/donald-trump-interview-roop-raj-fox-2-detroit-wjbk-october-25-2026/#56) [claim](https://rollcall.com/factbase/trump/transcript/donald-trump-speech-midterm-lincoln-memorial-remarks-november-2-2026/#43) that “we’re building more auto plants” in the U.S. than ever because of his higher tariffs, while also [falsely](https://rollcall.com/factbase/trump/transcript/donald-trump-interview-wayne-allyn-root-real-americas-voice-august-11-2026/) [claiming](https://rollcall.com/factbase/trump/transcript/donald-trump-speech-midterm-lincoln-memorial-remarks-november-2-2026/#43) [that](https://rollcall.com/factbase/trump/transcript/donald-trump-speech-midterm-lincoln-memorial-remarks-november-2-2026/#43) no new auto plants had been built in the U.S. in 40 or 49 years.

“Businesses are pouring in in order not to pay tariffs,” Trump [said](https://rollcall.com/factbase/trump/transcript/donald-trump-speech-midterm-lincoln-memorial-remarks-november-2-2026/#43), for example, in a Nov. 2 speech, citing announcements by Audi and Toyota to build auto plants in the U.S. “We went 49 years without building a new one. Now we’re building more auto plants than we’ve ever built before.” (On another occasion in August, he [said](https://rollcall.com/factbase/trump/transcript/donald-trump-interview-wayne-allyn-root-real-americas-voice-august-11-2026/) 40 years.)

We can fairly quickly dispense of the false claim that there have been no auto plants built in the last 40 or 49 years. We found that foreign automakers opened at least 19 new auto plants in the last 44 years, including 17 within the last 40 years, based on our review of company websites and a [2026 report](https://autosdriveamerica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/UPDATED-8.13.26_ADA_6X9_2026_8.5X11_rev.pdf) by a group that represents [12 foreign car manufacturers](https://autosdriveamerica.org/our-members/) with operations in the U.S.

Four new auto plants started production in the span of four years: Toyota’s [Blue Springs, Mississippi, plant](https://pressroom.toyota.com/facility/toyota-motor-manufacturing-mississippi/) in 2011; Volkswagen’s [Chattanooga, Tennessee, plant](https://www.vw.com/en/newsroom/everything-electric/inside-chattanooga-timeline.html) in 2011; Kia’s [West Point, Georgia, plant](https://www.kiamedia.com/us/en/media/pressreleases/3654/kia-motors-first-us-manufacturing-plant-starts-production-in-west-point-ga) in 2009; and Honda’s [Greensburg, Indiana, plant](https://manufacturing.honda.com/indiana-auto-plant/) in 2008.

More recently, a [Hyundai plant in Georgia](https://www.hmgma.com/our-facility/) broke ground in 2022 and started producing the IONIQ 5 in 2024. Also, Mazda and Toyota [launched a joint venture in 2018](https://mazdatoyota.com/who-we-are/our-story/) to build an auto plant in Alabama that [opened in 2021](https://pressroom.toyota.com/mazda-toyota-manufacturing-begins-production-on-2022-corolla-cross/) with the production of the Toyota Corolla Cross.

[Jonathan Smoke](https://perma.cc/WYZ7-ZJSN), chief strategy officer of Cox Automotive, also told us that Trump’s claim about no new auto manufacturing plants “completely ignores EV plants,” referring to electric vehicles.

In the early 2020s, Tesla launched one of its so-called gigafactories in [Texas](https://www.tesla.com/giga-texas), where the company manufactures the Model Y car and the Cybertruck (which will [end production](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/tesla-extend-cybertruck-production-backlog/) next summer). Tesla [selected](https://www.rgj.com/story/news/2020/07/22/tesla-austin-factory-location-earnings-call/5490790002/) Texas as its site for a new auto plant in 2020, during Trump’s first term, and [officially opened](https://www.forbes.com/sites/alanohnsman/2022/04/07/elon-musk-opens-teslas-giga-texas-that--he-says-is-the-biggest-us-plant/) it in 2022, although production started in [late 2021](https://www.edmunds.com/car-news/tesla-gigafactory-austin-grand-opening.html).

In December 2021, when Joe Biden was president, Rivian [announced](https://rivian.com/newsroom/article/rivian-to-site-second-manufacturing-plant-in-georgia) that it would invest $5 billion to build a second manufacturing plant in Georgia. In September 2025, Rivian executives and state officials held a [groundbreaking ceremony](https://web.archive.org/web/20260206134706/https:/georgia.org/rivian) for the new auto plant. Rivian executives [told investors](https://www.ajc.com/business/2026/08/rivian-says-construction-progressing-well-at-5b-georgia-factory-site/) this summer that construction is “progressing well” and production will begin in 2028.

Trump’s claim about the lack of new auto plants isn’t new. When he was president the first time, Trump made a similar claim in 2020 that there hadn’t been a new U.S. auto plant in “40 years.” As [we wrote](https://www.factcheck.org/2020/09/trumps-false-auto-industry-claims/) at the time, Volvo broke ground in 2015 on its [South Carolina plant](https://web.archive.org/web/20260206204227/https:/www.volvocars.com/us/l/hometown/), which opened in late 2017, and General Motors opened [a new assembly plant in 2006](https://www.gm.com/company/us-operations) in Lansing, Michigan.

So, Trump’s claim was false then and it still is.

## Tariffs and New Auto Plants

Trump’s other claim that “we’re building more auto plants than we’ve ever built before” because of his tariffs requires a close look at the inner workings of specific automakers.

But first let’s quickly recap what Trump has done to date. The Trump administration [officially announced](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/04/03/2025-05930/adjusting-imports-of-automobiles-and-automobile-parts-into-the-united-states) a global 25% tariff on imported autos and auto parts on March 26, 2025. The higher tariffs on autos took effect [April 3, 2025](https://perma.cc/5WKJ-2YF8), and on auto parts [the following month](https://www.kbb.com/tariffs/).

Since then, the U.S. reached trade agreements with Japan, South Korea and the European Union that reduced the auto tariffs to 15%, as explained in a [report](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R48549#:~:text=tariff%20action%20on%20automobiles%20and%20automobile%20parts%20) by the Congressional Research Service, and [10% on the first 100,000 vehicles](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/06/30/2025-12060/imports-of-automobiles-automobile-parts-civil-aircraft-and-civil-aircraft-parts-from-the-united) imported annually from the U.K.
