# Llm inflection points

# Three LLM inflection points in twelve months - Three LLM inflection points in twelve months Simon Willison’s Weblog Newsletter Sponsored by: WorkOS — Auth.md: signup built for agents. See how it works Three LLM inflection points in twelve months 24th November 2026 I gave a keynote at the AI Engineer Code Summit a couple of weeks ago, constructed around the idea that there have been three significant inflection points in the abilities of LLMs and coding agents in the past twelve months. Here’s the video of the talk. In this post I’m going to pull out the major inflection point theme and interrogate it more deeply. Coding agents in November 2025 Today, November 24th 2026, is the one year anniversary of the release of Claude Opus 4.5 . With hindsight, this was a consequential model. In the Opus 4.5 announcement, Anthropic said: Testers noted that Claude Opus 4.5 handles ambiguity and reasons about tradeoffs without hand-holding. They told us that, when pointed at a complex, multi-system bug, Opus 4.5 figures out the fix. They said that tasks that were near-impossible for Sonnet 4.5 just a few weeks ago are now within reach. This held up. Claude Code was 9 months old at that point, having been introduced alongside Claude 3.7 Sonnet on February 24th, 2025. Opus 4.5 was the first model I had used with Claude Code where the default result was generally the right thing. I hadn’t been using Claude Code as a daily driver because it didn’t feel reliable enough—I had to correct it often enough that it didn’t feel like a clear accelerant. The new Opus changed that. For most of the coding problems I faced on a daily basis, Opus would get them right . It was clearly faster than working through the problems myself. Also in November, OpenAI released GPT-5.1 Instant, GPT-5.1 Thinking, GPT-5.1-Codex, and GPT-5.1-Codex-Max. These had a similar effect on their Codex coding agent: it became reliably useful for many of my coding tasks. The timing was convenient, because the December holidays were upon us. A lot of people, myself included, spent December tinkering with these new tools to see what they could do. By January we were ready to use them for our actual work. Fable class models in June/July We got our first hint of Claude Fable in April, when Anthropic announced Claude Mythos and said that it was too dangerous to release , due to its improved cybersecurity capabilities. Mythos was a model that could not just find security vulnerabilities, it could also figure out how to exploit them. In June we got to see how good that model was for ourselves, with the release of Claude Fable 5—a defanged Mythos, that would solve most problems but would actively block you from using it for security work. After three glorious days... the US government took it away from us. Fable 5 was placed under export controls that effectively banned the model. We wouldn’t get it back until July 1st. For me, Fable was an inflection point because it introduced us to what I now think of as Fable class models . My definition of these: In June I wrote about how Claude Fable is relentlessly proactive , after I asked it to help fix a display glitch in Safari and it spun up its own pyobjc-framework-Quartz screenshot mechanism and a CORS-enabled localhost logging server to help resolve the bug. A more recent example of the power of Fable class models is my mysterious beep finder from a couple of weeks ago. I gave Opus 5.5 and then Fable 5.2 access to five WebAudio microphones in a room full of boxes and it was able to triangulate the source of an infuriating mysterious beep to within about 40cm. Give it a goal, give it the right tools, and watch it cook. I’d currently class Claude Fable 5, 5.1, 5.2 and Claude Opus 5.5 as Fable class (I think of Opus 5.5 as “cheap Fable”). GPT-6 Astra got there for me too, and I think the new Gemini 4 Neon may count as well. These now represent the baseline for what I expect from a frontier model. 3D modeling and game development in September/October Something interesting happened with frontier LLMs over just the past four months: they got really good at 3D modeling. Set them up with Blender or ask them to write Three.js code and they’ll produce credible models of almost anything you ask for. I first noticed this with Claude Fable 5, but it really kicked into gear with Opus 5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and most recently the Gemini 4 family. Here’s Gemini 4 Neon’s attempt at “Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data”, for example. 3D spatial awareness is crucial if you want to use vision LLMs for robotics. I don’t know if 3D modeling capabilities are a side-effect of the labs focusing on that or vice-versa. Back in August I experimented with having Fable 5 build me a raccoon heist game . It had 3D graphics, looked like a game, and played really poorly. GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra did a much better job but the game itself was still pretty dull after the first 90 seconds of play. I was somewhat relieved that designing a game that was fun appeared to remain a uniquely human pursuit. I even used that in a talk in September to reassure people that us humans still had a role to play! Then, I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 “This game isn’t fun enough yet. Make it a LOT more fun.” And it worked . My Command & Conquer-style RTS went from boring to deeply entertaining overnight, after Opus spent 12 hours playtesting new features and rebalancing the gameplay. Opus 5.5 was the first model I’d used that appeared to understand fun. I’ve since worked on several little game projects where prompts like “Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful” produced results that kept me engaged for significant amounts of time. Opus 5.5 came out on September 22nd, 2026. I’ve been to two different conferences since then where people showed me game projects they’d been working on that really did feel like proper, worthwhile games. The indie games scene has descended into a full-blown culture war over AI-assisted programming. A lot of people are calling GTA VI the last pre-generative AI blockbuster . It feels like another inflection point to me. Is Fable 5.2 an inflection point too? I’m still trying to decide if Fable 5.2 represents a new inflection point, or just another incremental improvement. I’m getting so much done with that model right now! It seems to have taste that almost exactly matches my own. I have been burning through all sorts of gnarly problems that I’ve been thinking about (or procrastinating on) for several years now. The release notes for Datasette 1.0a42 , 1.0a43 , and 1.0a44 —plus LLM 0.37 , 0.37.1 , 0.37.2 , 0.37.3 , and 0.38 — all in the last three weeks , represent a flood of fixes, features and improvements.

…

items.body:
Path Finder developer Cocoatech has been at this a long time. Twenty-five years, in fact. To celebrate its anniversary and the launch of its new website, the company has also [generously decided to spotlight some other longtime Mac developers](https://cocoatech.io/post/path-finder-turns-25-a-new-website-and-some-special-guests/):

> You can’t have a proper anniversary party without guests, so for our anniversary, we’ve invited five fellow independent Mac developers to join the celebration:
> Our guests are [DEVONtechnologies](https://cocoatech.io/post/devontechnologies-twenty-four-years-of-finding-connections/), [C-Command Software](https://cocoatech.io/post/c-command-software-twenty-five-years-of-making-the-mac-more-useful/), [St. Clair Software](https://cocoatech.io/post/st-clair-software-nearly-forty-years-of-making-everyday-mac-tasks-easier/), [Shirt Pocket](https://cocoatech.io/post/shirt-pocket-twenty-two-years-of-making-backups-less-frightening/), and [Stairways Software](https://cocoatech.io/post/stairways-software-thirty-one-years-of-making-the-mac-do-more/). We’ll be sharing the stories behind their applications, how they got started, and how their software has changed over the years here on this blog. We’ll finish the history series with a [look back at Path Finder’s own history](https://cocoatech.io/post/path-finder-25-years-of-making-the-mac-our-own/).

I use or have used apps from pretty much all these developers. Several of them remain indispensable to my workflow to this day. Every item in the series is linked above (on this Six Colors post, not the original) and can also be found [on this Path Finder archive page](https://cocoatech.io/author/alexandra/).

[Go to the linked site](https://cocoatech.io/post/path-finder-turns-25-a-new-website-and-some-special-guests/).

[Read on Six Colors](https://sixcolors.com/link/2026/11/cocoatech-celebrates-longtime-mac-developers-like-itself/).

# A Startup Tied to Donald Trump Jr. Could Get a Historic $15 Billion Loan From the Pentagon

## A Startup Tied to Donald Trump Jr. Could Get a Historic $15 Billion Loan From the Pentagon

## If approved, the money will go to Hadrian Automation to build a dozen factories for defense production. The company recently received a major investment from Trump Jr.’s venture capital firm.

In what would rank among the largest government loans in U.S. history, the Pentagon is considering extending $15 billion to a California-based startup with financial ties to Donald Trump Jr., according to interviews and records reviewed by ProPublica.

The award would be one of the biggest the federal government has given to a firm connected to the Trump family and would go to a defense contractor with a largely untested track record.

The startup, Hadrian Automation, has attracted over a billion dollars in private investment in recent months on the promise that it can build factories that use AI and robots to more efficiently produce precision components for defense, aerospace and other industries.

If approved, the loan would be almost twice the value of the entire company, based on estimates from a round of financing this summer. Hadrian announced that round of investment included “major participation by 1789 Capital,” the venture capital firm that Trump Jr. joined as a partner after his father was elected in November 2024. 1789 also invested in the company in 2025.

A spokesperson for 1789 Capital said it holds a “minority stake” in Hadrian, but the total size of its share has not been disclosed.

### Do You Have Information We Should Know About Donald Trump Jr.?

We’re still reporting. If you know anything about Trump Jr. or his businesses, please get in touch with our reporting team.

Robert Faturechi

Contact me, by email or securely on Signal, with tips about the federal government and Trump’s businesses.

The potential loan is 10 times the size of the largest deal the Pentagon has made in a recent lending spree.

According to Pentagon documents, a loan to Hadrian would be used to build a dozen “automated factories” in a partnership with other defense companies and potentially commercial ones to expand production of munitions, drones and other equipment.

The U.S. military has been dealing with a severe shortage of some types of munitions because of the wars in Ukraine and Iran, though it’s unclear if the factories are an attempt to address those particular shortages.

The size and structure of the deal would form an interdependence between the company and the federal government that could run afoul of long-standing guidance on how to protect taxpayer money, former Defense Department officials said. The government would use taxpayer money to vastly expand a fledgling defense contractor, which it would then presumably award contracts to, essentially paying the company money that it could use to repay the loan.

Pentagon staff have also raised several concerns about Hadrian, including its ability to expand and hire fast enough, the documents show.

The loan is under consideration weeks before Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress. The party’s leaders have vowed to use their new oversight powers to scrutinize the raft of contracts and other actions by the Trump administration that have financially benefited the Trump family and others who work in the administration or have ties to it.

Since the start of President Donald Trump’s second term, firms in which his elder sons hold stakes have won billions of dollars in federal backing. ProPublica recently reported on the Trump administration awarding nearly $40 million to one company to screen for Ebola and other infectious diseases. We also revealed how a White House aide intervened to secure a Pentagon loan of $620 million to Vulcan Elements, a rare earth magnet startup, a few months after 1789 Capital invested in it.

Responding to a question about whether the White House, Trump Jr. or 1789 lobbied for the loan, the Pentagon said in a statement that no company receives preferential treatment. “Outside affiliations, investors, or political connections play absolutely no role in the Department’s funding decisions.”

A Pentagon spokesperson also cast the loan discussions with Hadrian as being in “early stages” and disputed that the potential deal was for $15 billion. The spokesperson characterized the size of the Hadrian loan that is under discussion as not extraordinary, saying multibillion-dollar deals with other companies had been agreed to but not yet announced.

In a statement, 1789 Capital said it does not get involved in government contracts sought by the companies it invests in but is excited about Hadrian. “Our thesis is to invest in American companies that are rebuilding domestic industrial capacity and reducing dependence on China for critical supply chains that underpin our economy. Hadrian embodies the opportunity we see to strengthen America’s productive capabilities while pursuing compelling returns for our investors.”

Trump Jr.’s lawyer, Alan Garten, said his client played no role in Hadrian being considered for any contract and has no involvement with the company’s operations. “Don is a private citizen who has been building businesses and investing in companies since long before his father first ran for public office. He holds no government position and has never sought to influence government policies, regulations or decisions to advance or benefit his personal business interests,” his lawyer said.

Hadrian did not respond to requests for comment.

In the past, Trump Jr. and Eric Trump have described themselves as passive investors who aren’t involved in federal award decisions and said it is not a conflict for companies they hold an interest in to win government contracts.

1789 Capital’s first investment in Hadrian was announced in July of last year. That round of investments was co-led by conservative billionaire investor Peter Thiel’s Founders Fund. Hadrian said it would use that money to expand its shipbuilding and naval defense capabilities, and build a sprawling new factory in Arizona.

This March, the company announced a deal to make submarine parts for the Navy, which committed up to $900 million to the effort. And in July, Hadrian’s CEO became a significant donor to Republican groups, contributing nearly a half million dollars, campaign filings show.

1789’s second investment in Hadrian was announced in August in a round of financing that included participation from institutional investment managers. “This is just the beginning,” 1789 wrote in a LinkedIn post about the funding round.

items.body:
# Half of NASA's aging Mars fleet knocked offline by technical issues

Two of NASA’s four missions operating at Mars have suspended science operations after encountering separate technical issues in recent weeks.

The missions affected by the outages — hopefully temporary — are NASA’s Perseverance rover and Odyssey orbiter. Both are operating beyond their original design lifetimes. Perseverance is in its sixth year exploring the surface of Mars, having collected rock and soil samples for eventual return to Earth. The rover is now studying the rim of a crater that once contained an ancient lake of liquid water. Odyssey arrived in orbit around Mars in 2001, and is the longest-lived Mars mission in history.

## Losing its voice

The problem on Perseverance stems from the rover’s communications system. The rover has two redundant UHF radios for high-rate communications with a fleet of orbiters that relay data to Earth. A separate X-band system is available for direct-to-Earth communications at a lower data rate.

One of the rover’s two UHF radios was unresponsive when it powered up on October 30, triggering an automatic switch to the backup radio and placing the rover in safe mode. Ground teams at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California later discovered the backup UHF radio was transmitting at about half of its expected power output, NASA said in a statement last week.

“The team has stopped using both radios until they can evaluate potential causes of the issues and one or both are deemed safe to resume operating,” NASA said.

Perseverance is now transmitting signals directly to Earth in X-band, but the connection provides a “significantly lower data rate” than relaying signals through orbiters using the UHF radios. Mission managers paused the rover’s science operations “out of an abundance of caution” as they investigate the radio problem. Their initial focus is on getting the backup UHF radio running before turning their attention on recovering the primary radio, NASA said.

“The team is hopeful the rover could return to science by the end of November.”

The six-wheeled robot broke a record last month for the farthest any vehicle has driven on another planet. The Perseverance rover surpassed the 28.06-mile (45.16-kilometer) mark set by NASA’s Opportunity rover, which stopped working in 2018. Perseverance’s odometer now sits at twice the rover’s original goal for distance traveled.

## Running on fumes

The situation with the Odyssey orbiter seems more dire. One of the four reaction wheels used for pointing the spacecraft stopped spinning in early November, leaving Odyssey with two good wheels after the first one failed in 2013. The orbiter needs at least three wheels to keep it oriented correctly.

“Without the three reaction wheels, the spacecraft must rely solely on its hydrazine thrusters to remain oriented,” NASA said. The orbiter requires stable pointing to turn its solar arrays toward the Sun and its science instruments toward Mars.

Odyssey was running low on propellant before the reaction wheel malfunction, but managers were optimistic that with “extremely low” fuel usage, the orbiter would have enough to continue operating through at least the end of 2028, said Jeffrey Plaut, Odyssey’s project scientist at JPL, in a presentation earlier this year.

That assumed no failures in Odyssey’s three remaining reaction wheels. Without three healthy wheels, engineers estimate the spacecraft has enough hydrazine fuel to last one to two months, NASA said. The good news is ground teams had some initial success troubleshooting the balky reaction wheel. Further testing is necessary to determine whether the wheel is recoverable.

## Aging infrastructure

Odyssey is one of four orbiters NASA uses to relay data between Earth and the Perseverance and Curiosity rovers on the Martian surface. Curiosity is still driving and collecting data after 14 years on Mars. The other three relay craft are NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, which reached the red planet in 2006, the European Space Agency’s 10-year-old ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter, and ESA’s 23-year-old Mars Express spacecraft.

NASA lost contact with its MAVEN orbiter last December after 11 years of operations at Mars when the spacecraft suddenly spun out of control. An investigation could not identify a specific root cause, but engineers concluded that a radiation-induced single event upset or a software issue caused MAVEN’s flight computer to reboot, according to Tiffany Morgan, director of NASA’s robotic Mars Exploration Program.

The spacecraft’s inertial measurement unit failed to provide the computer with correct information on MAVEN’s orientation, causing it to spin in response to the faulty data, Morgan said in a November 9 presentation to the Mars Exploration Program Analysis Group.

NASA is preparing to send reinforcements to renew the agency’s presence at Mars. In September, NASA awarded Blue Origin a $700 million contract for the Mars Telecommunications Network (MTN), an orbiter dedicated to providing high-bandwidth connectivity between Earth and other missions operating on and around the red planet.

NASA wanted Blue Origin to complete the telecom orbiter by the end of 2028 and have it operational at Mars in 2030. But the Mars Telecommunications Network is on hold after Rocket Lab, which lost its bid to win the MTN contract, filed a protest with the Government Accountability Office . The GAO is expected to rule on the protest next month, at which time Blue Origin could start work on the NASA contract if the government rejects Rocket Lab’s petition.

Another Mars mission, SkyFall , could also launch in 2028. NASA aims to send three helicopter drones to Mars to explore the planet’s geology and weather from the air.

A perennial priority for Mars scientists is replacing the unique high-resolution mapping camera on the aging Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter. Such a capability will help identify landing sites for future robotic and human missions, including a potential mission to return Perseverance’s rock specimens to Earth.

NASA is in the very early stages of developing a mission concept that could take over MRO’s imaging capability, but there’s no firm schedule or budget for such an undertaking. NASA will likely rely on MRO for landing-site reconnaissance well into the 2030s.

items.body:
# New York and California Age Gating Rules Go Into Effect in the New Year

Come January 2027, everyday social media browsing in two of the country's largest states will look noticeably different. In California, AB 1709 (2026), AB 1043 (2025), and SB 976 (2024) are slated to take effect on January 1, 2027. Meanwhile, state attorney general regulations for New York’s Stop Addictive Feeds Exploitation (SAFE) for Kids Act take effect on January 25, 2027.

EFF has opposed these laws across legislatures , regulatory proceedings , and the courts . The core problem is simple: age-gating mandates trade away everyday user privacy and free expression under the guise of safety, while pushing platforms to gather even more personal data on users.

## What California’s Rules Say

Three interlocking California laws take effect on January 1, 2027, reshaping how platforms handle age checks and design features for young users. First, SB 976 (2024) requires verifiable parental consent before platforms can offer algorithmic feeds or nighttime notifications to anyone under 18. Second, AB 1709 (2026) goes even further by outright banning "addictive features," including personalized recommendation algorithms, autoplay, and endless scroll, for users under 16, even with parental permission. Third, the Digital Age Assurance Act (AB 1043, 2025) mandates age-assurance checks across devices (operating systems) and apps, serving as the enforcement backbone for those restrictions. Together with the California Attorney General’s proposed rules on SB 976 , which outline age-gating methods, accuracy, circumvention, and parental consent, these laws force platforms into a two-tier design that walls young people off from basic content-discovery tools, puts everyone's privacy at risk to prove their age, and has already drawn First Amendment lawsuits from social media companies against both SB 976 and AB 1709 .

For example: rather than minimizing corporate surveillance and data collection by passing stronger privacy laws, the SB 976 regulations encourage companies to evaluate behavioral patterns, collected user data, digital interactions, and metadata to estimate age (Sec. 561(a)(2)), alongside location data collected for other purposes (Sec. 565). Good privacy laws should discourage collecting that information in the first place, not reward broader tracking.

At the same time, these age assurance rules build in steep error rates and weak safeguards. They acknowledge that age-verification tools can misclassify young people as adults, allowing false-positive rates of up to 8% for 16-year-olds and 15% for 17-year-olds (Sec. 561(c)(4)(iv)). Yet the rules set no benchmarks at all for false negatives , meaning adults (especially 18- to 20-year-olds) are likely to be wrongly flagged as under 18. They also recognize demographic bias in facial recognition, yet offer no concrete fix, vaguely telling companies to take mitigating measures like correcting dataset imbalances (Sec. 563(a)(6)). While users can appeal wrong age estimates, the rules set no firm deadlines, meaning mistakes can drag on without a prompt fix, blocking user access (Sec. 564). Worse, requiring platforms to let users report others they suspect are under the age of 18 (Sec. 567) invites targeted harassment by bad actors , while rules telling companies to account for users trying to “conceal or misrepresent” their California location (Sec. 565) risk penalizing everyday VPN users .

## What New York’s Rules Say

Along the same lines as the California regulations, New York’s SAFE for Kids Act restricts personalized recommendations and nighttime notifications (between midnight and 6am) without required consent, and mandates that platforms run age assurance and determine user location. If a user does not verify their age or is estimated to be under-18, they will either be relegated to an account with no personalized recommendations and nighttime notifications (if the platform creates one), or prohibited from accessing the platform/service.

As we detailed in our December 2025 comments to the New York Attorney General, age-verification mandates inevitably chill access to online speech. And the final regulations introduce several troubling specifics.

The New York regulations use broad definitions for "age estimation," "age inference," and "age verification" (700.1(h)–(j)) that push companies to collect and retain more personal information from users. Even where privacy protections apply to that information, users cannot sue or enforce those rights themselves , since enforcement rests solely with the Attorney General (700.8). Worse, the rule’s definition of deletion appears to let companies " de-identify " age-assurance data and keep using it in that form, potentially feeding AI model training and creating re-identification risks if leaked or stolen. At the same time, platforms are required to hold onto records (including a user's age status and compliance data) for five years, increasing the risk of misuse or breaches (700.7(b)).

Echoing the problems in California, location and accuracy regulations bring further privacy and security risks. The regulations demand that operators must weigh all reliable location information and take reasonable steps to detect user efforts to “conceal or misrepresent” being in New York, which expands location tracking and threatens VPN use (700.2(d)(2)). On accuracy, the rules permit up to a 15% false-positive rate for 17-year-olds (700.1(b)), yet just like the California rules, say nothing about false negatives —meaning adults, especially 18- to 20-year-olds, are likely to be wrongly flagged as under 18. When that happens, the appeals process can take longer than 10 days, leaving misclassified adults locked out of standard features (or platforms altogether) for over a week.

## What This Means for Users in NY and CA

Under both states' regimes, many users will be pressed to hand over personal information just to access standard features like personalized feeds or notifications, while social media companies are encouraged to monitor (and monetize ) user behavior even more closely. Because these laws define "addictive feeds" so broadly that the label covers virtually every basic recommendation tool (including feeds built from who you follow, posts you like, or topics you say you are interested in), platforms face a stark choice: either build stripped-down versions of their apps without algorithmic feeds, likes, or notifications, or simply boot any account suspected of belonging to someone under 18. Either way, all users, and especially young people across both states, risk being shut out of major online spaces as they exist today.

items.body:
# Why there are still no non-WebKit browsers on iOS | The Mozilla Blog

## Why there are still no non-WebKit browsers on iOS

Firefox on iPhone is growing fast across the world. This is especially true in the EU since 2024, when the EU Digital Markets Act (DMA) started requiring Apple to let people choose their default browser; millions have picked Firefox, and daily use on iOS has doubled. People want to choose the browser on their phone.

But there remains an important limitation to what is available on iPhones: Apple forces all browsers on iOS to be built on Apple’s own browser engine.

This has meant that companies like Mozilla cannot easily bring the full range of Firefox features and functionality to iPhone users because many of these are built within our browser engine , Gecko. iPhones and iPads are unique in having this restriction. On all other major operating systems, including Apple’s macOS, people can access the Gecko-powered version of Firefox.

As a result of the DMA, Apple began allowing alternative browser engines on iOS in the EU. It published a set of conditions that companies like Mozilla must comply with to bring their own browser engine. At the time we said Apple’s rules made it “as painful as possible” for alternatives like Gecko. In the meantime, Japan also introduced new rules requiring alternative browser engines on iOS. Apple applied very similar conditions in Japan to those in the EU.

Nearly three years since Apple introduced these conditions in the EU and almost a year since Japan, not one developer has been able to launch a non-WebKit browser on iOS. The reason is simple: Apple’s conditions remain unworkable. The real test of any rule is whether it delivers the change it was meant to achieve in practice. Compliance on paper alone falls short of that test.

Since the DMA came into effect we’ve been working behind the scenes to test and improve Apple’s conditions so that we can bring Gecko to iOS users. Those efforts have so far largely failed.

One of the conditions requires us not to disclose non-public information related to the project, but here’s an example of what we are up against: to use Gecko, we can’t simply update the Firefox app people already use and love. We’d have to build a whole separate app, a second Firefox. Then we’d have to ask every Firefox user to download it, move their bookmarks, passwords and history across, and manually switch over, step by confusing step.

That’s a lot to ask of people who already made their choice. A significant proportion of people would understandably give up, including many who picked Firefox from the EU’s choice screen.

The conditions Apple imposes, including a level of user friction Apple would never accept for its own apps, mean that the open door feels more like a trap door.

Firefox users on iPhone chose an independent browser. They should get everything that comes with it, including Gecko, the last major browser engine not developed by a big tech company. We’ll keep pushing for a real level playing field, not an opening that drops independent browsers through the floor.

items.body:
# Court Orders Trump Media to Hand Over Truth Social Records in The Intercept Lawsuit

The Intercept and Freedom of the Press Foundation won a crucial victory against the Trump administration in court on Tuesday in a case challenging the president’s right to sell early access to his social media posts on Truth Social.

The ruling by Judge J. Paul Oetken in the Southern District of New York allows both organizations to seek limited discovery, offering a chance to peel back the layers on the president’s scheme to enrich himself through his public office. The Intercept and Freedom of the Press Foundation can request records from the president’s private media company on both the operation of its six-figure early-access model and whether other media companies have purchased a subscription.

Truth Social is owned and operated by Trump Media & Technology Group, a company in which the president holds the largest stake in a trust controlled by his son, Donald Trump Jr. The early-access model, known as Truth API, requires subscribers to pay $60,000 to $100,000 a month. The service offers a first look at Trump’s posts — where, as the White House has acknowledged , he often makes official policy announcements.

Most Read An Air Force Major Is Being Held in Solitary Confinement for Criticizing Trump on CNN Seth Stern ICE Spreads Misinformation About Securing Your iPhone. Here’s How to Really Do It. Noah Hurowitz, Nikita Mazurov, Karl Loftus Private Prison Told ICE Its Jail Was Worth $67 Million. ICE Bought It for Nearly Half a Billion. Jacqueline Stevens, Andrew Free

The lawsuit argues that the premium service violates the First Amendment rights of the public and the media to enjoy equal access to official government information. According to the lawsuit, Trump has published about 11,000 posts or reposts on Truth Social since returning to office.

## Related

### The Intercept Sues Trump for Selling Premium Access to Truth Social Announcements

The ruling will allow the plaintiffs “to get some answers about how this scheme works,” said Nikhel Sus, chief counsel at Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, who is representing the plaintiffs. The subscription service, he added, was “rolled out with minimal transparency as to how the actual functionality works and who has been subscribing to the service thus far.”

In October, The Intercept and Freedom of the Press Foundation requested a preliminary injunction arguing that the president should be barred from posting on his personal platform, Truth Social, as long as the premium service is in effect.

Oetken has not ruled on the preliminary injunction. But his decision on Tuesday is a “positive step forward,” Sus said. “The court didn’t explicitly say that it thinks our claims have merit, but the fact that it ordered discovery, we think, indicates that the court doesn’t think our complaint is non-meritorious because otherwise it wouldn’t have granted discovery.”

We’re independent of corporate interests — and powered by members. Join us.

## Join Our Newsletter Thank You For Joining!

Original reporting. Fearless journalism. Delivered to you. Will you take the next step to support our independent journalism by becoming a member of The Intercept?

## Join Our Newsletter

## Original reporting. Fearless journalism. Delivered to you.

David Bralow, The Intercept’s chief legal officer, agreed.

“We are grateful that the Court is allowing us to proceed with uncovering the nature of the scheme that violates our First Amendment rights,” Bralow wrote in a statement. “By continuing to allow President Trump to exclusively post official government announcements on Truth Social’s API, the President and the other defendants continue to provide preferential access to those who pay up to $100,000 a month to increase Mr. Trump’s personal wealth.”

Despite the initial victory, Sus noted, the court still has not ruled on the government’s motion to dismiss the case, nor the initial motion for a preliminary injunction. “So we still have to wait and see,” he said.

IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.

What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.

This is not hyperbole.

Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.

Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”

The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.

## We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.

We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.

In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.

That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?

items.body:
# 3 Questions: Tackling energy challenges in a changing world

### Press Contact :

Previous image Next image

Since the founding of the MIT Energy Initiative (MITEI) in 2006, the challenges facing the world’s energy ecosystem have become more pressing, with dramatic shifts in domestic and international energy policies, geopolitical instability, unexpected supply chain disruptions, and spikes in demand.

As MITEI celebrates its 20th anniversary, MITEI Director William H. Green reflects on two decades of energy research, education, and outreach. Green, the Hoyt C. Hottel Professor of Chemical Engineering, also describes a future shaped by a shifting energy landscape and by the urgent, ongoing need to solve the complex problems facing global energy systems.

Q: MITEI was founded in 2006 to bring MIT's energy researchers together around a shared goal of creating the solutions and technologies that will transform the world's energy systems. What do you consider to be some of MITEI’s most important impacts?

A: Over the years, I’ve seen MITEI from different angles. I’ve been a faculty member with research projects and graduate students supported by MITEI’s member companies. I’ve had undergraduate students working in my lab through MITEI-funded Undergraduate Research Opportunity Program (UROP) projects. I’ve also been involved in MITEI events as a speaker and panelist, and I’ve sought feedback from member companies to make my research more timely and relevant. Two-and-a-half years ago, I became the director of MITEI, affording me a whole new perspective. Looking back over the past 20 years, MITEI has funded more than 1,100 research projects, supported over 3,000 graduate students and postdocs, and brought nearly $1 billion in funding to MIT. All these elements contribute to sustaining a tremendous energy ecosystem at the Institute.

Twenty years ago, MITEI was formed in response to the deep interest of MIT’s faculty in energy problems. My predecessors as MITEI directors, Ernie Moniz and Bob Armstrong, built MITEI’s reputation, influence, and strong relationships with companies. Today, MITEI is not only responsive to the shifting interests of MIT’s energy researchers and MITEI’s member companies, but actually shapes the energy ecosystem on campus and beyond, especially through vehicles like our “Future of…” energy studies. MITEI makes critical and often long-lasting connections between MIT researchers and MITEI’s member companies. As a result, we know the energy research we are doing is solving problems that companies are struggling with today and anticipating for the future. MITEI and our member companies also provide MIT researchers with the support to do energy innovation, and some of these early-stage ideas become startup companies years later. About 65 companies have grown out of MITEI research or are directly connected with MITEI-funded graduate students or postdocs, and some of those companies have gone on to have a major impact on the energy transition.

Q: You became MITEI’s director in spring 2024, quickly mobilizing MITEI and the researchers and students with whom we work to tackle the energy issues relevant to our current times. Prior to this, how did your research and the MIT Energy Initiative intersect?

A: I was fortunate to work on a wide variety of MITEI projects before becoming director. Early on, I did MITEI projects focused on removing mercury, carbon dioxide, and sulfur impurities from fuel streams and on changing the properties of fuels to increase efficiency and reduce toxic emissions from engines. I was also involved in an important MITEI project to improve predictions of liquid-phase chemistry for energy applications. One component of that project was extremely successful, leading to development of fast, accurate, and generalizable ways to predict solvent effects on phase equilibria and on reaction rates and selectivity. The ability to predict the solubility of solids in different solvents has since attracted a lot of interest from the pharmaceutical industry. MITEI was critical in making the connections between my research group and industry, which supported these and other projects, even when the research was initially at the edge of my expertise.

One MITEI project I particularly enjoyed was the Mobility of the Future study, for which I served as the faculty director. That study, which was published in 2019 (before Tesla ever earned a profit), predicted that electric vehicles (EVs) would begin to be affordable enough to significantly compete with gasoline cars during the period 2025-30. Actual global EV sales have increased a bit faster than we predicted in 2019, in part because we did not anticipate the global conflicts that have raised world gasoline prices.

Most of my energy research projects were done primarily with MITEI-funded graduate students, or even UROPs. I-Yun Lisa Hsieh was a major contributor to the Mobility of the Future study and is now an associate professor at National Taiwan University, where she founded and leads their E3 Research Center for decarbonization and intelligent transformation of the energy system. I should also mention Yunsie Chung, the graduate student who did important work on solvent effects; she is now doing AI research as associate director, modeling and informatics, for Merck. Pierre Walker, a UROP who worked with Yunsie, completed his PhD at Caltech and is now a world leader in the thermodynamics of liquids and a postdoc at MIT. Another key student was David Couling, who did the mercury capture project. After graduating from MIT, he took a position in industry, going on to win the AIChE’s 2025 Industrial Progress award.

Q: What do you believe are the biggest energy challenges we are facing today and in the coming years?

items.body:
L ast week, Anthropic went public. The IPO was [heavily oversubscribed](https://www.wsj.com/finance/stocks/anthropic-prices-ipo-at-83-a-share-0290494c?mod=article_inline), spurring the company to sell more shares at a higher price than it had originally intended. The five-year-old start-up took in a record-breaking $81 billion from investors around the world, giving it a gobsmacking $1.5 trillion valuation and minting an estimated [600 centimillionaires](https://www.reuters.com/business/world-at-work/anthropic-ipo-mint-thousands-of-millionaires-2026-11-18/).

Nevertheless, the IPO arrived at a dour moment on Wall Street, and did not exactly brighten the mood. Investors had been selling off equities for weeks, spooked by rising interest rates, the midterm landslide, concerns about AI’s capacity to boost corporate profits, and Nvidia’s ouster of its allegedly honey-trapped CEO. When Nvidia’s board announced that it had unanimously reinstated Jensen Huang yesterday, its share price surged. Then it slouched back down, joining Anthropic stock, the S&P 500, foreign-equity markets, gold, crypto, and Nasdaq in the red.

The AI boom seems to be turning into an AI bust. Maybe we’ll end up thinking of it as an AI bubble. Maybe it will spur an AI recession. The worst possible outcome would be an AI financial crisis—and it is not a far-fetched outcome at all, given the astronomical sums, convoluted deals, and cavernous regulatory lacunae involved.

The question is whether the AI whatever-it-is will play out more like the dot-com bubble of the 1990s or the housing bubble of the aughts. In the former, Nasdaq lost 78 percent of its value and the country entered a brief recession. Still, the banking system remained solvent and the credit markets liquid. In the latter, the housing market faltered, the stock market collapsed, and the entire global financial system seized, precipitating the worst recession since the Great Depression.

*[[Read: A shameless valley](https://www.theatlantic.com/technology/2026/11/silicon-valley-shameless-nvidia/689549/?utm_source=feed)]*

The difference wasn’t the amount of money at stake. The collapse of the dot-com bubble wiped out more wealth than the collapse of the [housing bubble](https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/speech/bernanke20120413a.htm), as former Fed Chair Ben Bernanke observed in a 2012 speech. The difference was that the dot-com losses were transparent, widely distributed, and easily understood. People got excited about the World Wide Web; they bought stocks at absurd valuations; some of the companies they invested in proved to be duds; they lost money. The losses from the housing bubble, in contrast, were opaque, concentrated, and impenetrable. Where to even start? The erosion of lending standards, the explosive growth in derivatives contracts, the mispricing of mortgage-backed securities, the misguided faith in market [self-regulation](https://www.federalreserve.gov/boarddocs/speeches/1997/19970412.htm), the insufficient capital buffers, the regulatory gaps, the Sun Belt speculation, the low interest rates? I suppose it came down to one thing: Investors seemed like they were making a lot of different bets. But they were making one bet, on housing prices. And when that bet went sour, they panicked.

However the AI story ends, it is starting the same way that the dot-com and housing stories began—with trillions of dollars. Normally, software is relatively inexpensive to develop and cheap to scale. (Mark Zuckerberg wrote most of the code for Thefacebook.com by himself in his dorm, shelling out $85 a month for a server.) But ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude Code require a tremendous amount of “compute”—basically, computing power. So AI start-ups and Silicon Valley giants are spending $600 billion this year alone on silicon chips and data-center construction.

They aren’t footing the bill themselves. They are issuing shares, as Anthropic did last week. They’re selling bonds: Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Oracle issued $223 billion in debt in the first eight months of the year. They are also making arrangements with private creditors.

Here’s where things start to feel very 1996. The markets are making a massive wager on AI revolutionizing the business world, just as they made a massive wager on the World Wide Web revolutionizing the business world. The value of [AI-related stocks](https://www.goldmansachs.com/insights/articles/are-us-stock-market-valuations-outpacing-fundamentals) has climbed $27 trillion since the launch of ChatGPT, according to Goldman Sachs. Even given the recent correction, the country is in the midst of a hell of a bull market.

Yet the markets are making that bet on the basis of some awfully rosy assumptions. By 2031, AI-linked companies will need to generate $6 trillion a year in revenue to justify the cost of the [build-out](https://www.bain.com/about/media-center/press-releases/2026/global-ai-market-could-hit-%246-trillion-annually-by-2031-through-unlocking-value-and-innovation--bain--cos-7th-global-technology-report/), according to calculations by the consultancy Bain & Company. That is six times as much as American businesses and households spend on gasoline and other petroleum products each year, to give a sense of scale. It is eight times as much as U.S. firms shell out for software. It’s more than the country spends on *health care*.

AI revenue seems highly likely to fall short of expectations, while AI overhead costs seem highly likely to exceed them. Anthropic is committed to spending nearly $1 trillion on compute in the coming years. And many AI firms have hefty borrowing costs to deal with, as well as hefty infrastructure costs. CoreWeave, an AI cloud-computing firm, is spending a quarter of its revenue servicing its loans.

*[[Read: The economy is a hostage situation](https://www.theatlantic.com/technology/2026/11/ai-hostage-economy-nvidia-huang/689552/?utm_source=feed)]*

The disconnect between the two sides of the balance sheet is making the markets feel bearish. Some AI companies are having a harder time raising the cash they need to refine and run their algorithms. In time, that could force them to cancel construction projects and miss payments to their creditors, deepening the market rout. So would we end up in 2000, facing a sharp correction and perhaps a soft recession? Or in 2007, staring into the abyss?

items.body:
# Trump suggests Jensen Huang could have moved to China if not reinstated as Nvidia CEO: ‘Got a little blood there’

WASHINGTON — President Trump claimed Monday that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang could have become a leader in China’s artificial intelligence industry if he hadn’t been reinstated to the US firm — telling CNBC in a phone interview that the 63-year-old has “got a little blood there” despite being born in Taiwan.

“If we didn’t do this, I could see China coming in and saying to Jensen, ’Hey, how would you like to come to China?’ — He’s got a little [Chinese] blood in him. He’s got a little blood there — ‘How would you like to come to China and head up Huawei?’” Trump told CNBC in a phone interview, during which he called Huang, 63, a “national treasure” despite his affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

“If Jensen was angry enough, if he was treated badly, maybe he could do that.”

Trump pressured Nvidia’s board to restore the AI pioneer 11 days after he resigned — saying he gave the directors assurances that Huang wouldn’t face legal issues over his relationship with Alice Huang (no relation).

If Alice Huang or her Singapore-based Megaspeed firm violated US export laws by sending advanced Nvidia chips to China, “that wouldn’t be Jensen’s fault,” Trump argued.

The president, who returned late Thursday from a trip to China that included a trilateral summit with his counterpart Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, reiterated that “Jensen could take the next plane to China, and I guarantee you they would give him whatever he wanted.

“And then they’d automatically have you know all of the things. He never even suggested that. But I know how good China is, how professional they are, how cunning they are.”

Trump said during his nearly hour-long interview that he didn’t ask Xi if Alice Huang was a spy — a claim Beijing has denied though Megaspeed was under investigation by Singapore’s government and the US Commerce Department for allegedly flouting US export restrictions on AI chip shipping to China.

“You know, he’s in a class by himself. We would have lost him,” Trump said of Huang, who was sent to the US by his parents at age 9, cofounded Nvidia in 1993 and built it into one of the world’s most valuable companies .

“If I were President Xi, I’d say, ‘Hey, let’s get him over here real fast. He can have whatever he wants. We’ll give him Beijing. Okay, we’ll give him all of Beijing.’”

“Crazy things like that happen,” Trump said.

“I think he’s going to start off at an almost higher level. He’s apologized for indiscretion, which was unfortunate…. That’s what brought it to such a level because sex sells, fellas.”

items.body:
# Silence and Love

- Silence and Love – The Marginalian ABOUT CONTACT SUPPORT SUBSCRIBE Newsletter RSS CONNECT Facebook Twitter Instagram Tumblr Silence and Love By Maria Popova Music is the hand of silence cupped to hold the feeling of being alive, lifted to the lips and tasted. What differentiates music from noise is the touch of silence — the deliberate interstices between the tones, the still points in the rush of sound. As in music, so in life: “Listen to the silence inside the illusion of the world,” Jack Kerouac wrote to his first wife turned lifelong friend in reckoning with the meaning of life , “and you will remember the lesson you forgot.” Silence is the listening presence through which you hear the music of your own life, presence purified to become peace — a peace greater than joy and unburdened by understanding, a peace the other word for which may be love. There is no piece of music that has scored more of my waking days and my writing hours than “Spiegel im Spiegel” by the Estonian composer Arvo Pärt, whose virtuosity with sound springs from his relationship to silence — something he articulates with poetic concision in a series of reflections recently shared by his son: Silence is always more perfect than music. You must simply learn to hear it. Silence is utterly full. […] When we speak of silence, we must keep in mind that it has two wings: Silence can be both outside of us and within us. The silence of our soul, over which even external noise has no power, is actually more crucial. But is also much more difficult to achieve. A generation before him, Kahlil Gibran had captured this difficulty with piercing pointedness. “You talk when you cease to be at peace with your thoughts,” he charged in his timeless meditation on silence, solitude, and the courage to know yourself . Pärt puts it more gently: One does not have to speak. But one must love. One does not have to compose, one does not have to write a book. But one must love… If you do not speak, thinking, and even prayer, is clearer, and there is more space left over for love. I have always felt that the quality of silence two people can share is one of the great measures of love — something the young poet Babette Deutsch captured beautifully a century ago: SILENCE by Babette Deutsch Silence with you is like the faint delicious Smile of a child asleep, in dreams unguessed: Only the hinted wonder of its dreaming, The soft, slow-breathing miracle of rest. Silence with you is like a kind departure From iron clangor and the engulfing crowd Into a wide and greenly barren meadow, Under the bloom of some blue-bosomed cloud; Or like one held upon the sands at evening, When the drawn tide rolls out, and the mixed light Of sea and sky enshrouds the far, wind-bellowed Sails that move darkly on the edge of night. — Published November 24, 2026 — https://www.themarginalian.org/2026/11/24/silence-and-love/ — www.themarginalian.org PRINT ARTICLE EMAIL ARTICLE Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook

items.body:
# Tubbutec TR-8oh8 Upgrade Adds MIDI, 11 Instruments And New Sequencer Tools To The Roland TR-808

Tubbutec shared this video demo for TR-8oh8 , a replacement CPU and MIDI interface that expands the capabilities of the Roland TR-808 .

The upgrade adds 11 additional instruments, velocity-sensitive MIDI input and output, an expanded sequencer, and a set of tools for live rhythm manipulation while retaining the drum machine’s original sound circuits.

The updated sequencer provides 128 patterns in four banks, along with storage for 12 tracks. Patterns can be changed or edited while another pattern is playing, and tracks can be programmed on the fly. Each instrument can have four dynamic levels and four probability levels per step. A 12-style pattern generator can also create complete rhythms.

The 11 additional instruments use the TR-808’s existing sound circuits in new ways. They include an alternative bass drum, two additional snare variations, maracas, muted claves, an adjustable clap, a tunable second cowbell, felt and closed cymbal sounds, and a click-style hi-hat. A tom-noise instrument is also accessible via MIDI.

The MIDI input supports clock synchronization, velocity-sensitive drum triggering, and control-change messages. MIDI output can transmit clock and the TR-808’s sequenced instruments to external hardware or a DAW. Instrument note assignments can be configured with Tubbutec’s web-based tool.

The upgrade also adds 12 tools and performance functions, including live muting, a beat reslicer, a drum arpeggiator with Euclidean mode, 13 flam and ratchet patterns, adjustable swing, pattern generation, and a Grains mode that can use the drum circuits to create basslines and granular effects. The TR-8oh8 can reproduce the original machine’s timing behavior or use an improved clock mode.

Installation involves removing the original TR-808 CPU and fitting the replacement processor. The MIDI connections can use the existing DIN and pedal-switch sockets, avoiding the need to drill the case. Tubbutec also says the upgrade is compatible with the Din Sync RE-808.

Features:

- Replacement CPU upgrade for the Roland TR-808
- 11 additional instruments using the original analog sound circuits
- Velocity-sensitive MIDI input and output
- 128 patterns arranged in four banks
- Storage and recall for 12 user-programmable tracks
- Four dynamic levels and four probability levels per step and instrument
- Pattern editing while another pattern is playing
- 12-style pattern generator
- 12 tools, including mute, reslicer, arpeggiator, flam, ratchet, swing, and Grains
- Tunable, sequencable second cowbell and adjustable clap
- Configurable MIDI notes and firmware updates via MIDI SysEx
- Optional TR-8oh8 controller for direct access to additional parameters
- Compatible with the Din Sync RE-808
Pricing & Availability:

The Tubbutec TR-8oh8 is listed at €229 before VAT and shipping (approximately €272.51 including VAT) and is currently out of stock but available for pre-order.

items.body:
# Georgia Waffle House cuts cooling energy use by 40% with new salt-based AC system

November 24, 2026

## Georgia Waffle House cuts cooling energy use by 40% with new salt-based AC system

edited by Robert Egan

Robert Egan

Senior Editor

This article has been reviewed according to Science X's editorial process and policies . Editors have highlighted the following attributes while ensuring the content's credibility:

fact-checked

trusted source

proofread

In July 2025, a team of technicians walked into a Waffle House in Macon, Georgia. That month, peak temperatures hovered around 92 degrees Fahrenheit (33 degrees Celsius). In the restaurant's kitchen, where cooks fried patty melts, hash browns and waffles on an oil-slick grill, temperatures could feel just as hot, if not hotter.

The cooks kept sizzling while the technicians installed a machine out back and turned it on. Within minutes, the cooks came out. "What did you do?" they asked. "This is the first time we're not sweating in the middle of summer."

That Macon Waffle House test was the first real-world pilot for a new kind of air-conditioning system co-invented by researchers at the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) and the startup Blue Frontier.

Blue Frontier's air-conditioning system can run on far less electricity and cools and dehumidifies independently, which makes it quicker and less energy-intensive to convert hot, sticky air into comfortable cool. The invention can even store energy, so it can power itself during the hottest summer afternoons—even sweaty July days in Georgia—to avoid high energy prices and help prevent grid overloads and blackouts.

"It's a complete rethinking of how we condition air," said Eric Kozubal, a senior engineer at the NLR and one of the system's co-inventors.

That pilot was successful, both physically for those hot cooks and statistically: The system consumed 40% less energy than the building's previous air conditioner and cut operating costs by 65%, in part due to an 89% reduction in power use during peak grid hours when electricity costs are highest.

"We talk a lot about machines and energy," said Daniel Betts, the CEO and founder of Blue Frontier. "But society is made of people. And we are influencing that directly, you know, making people's lives better."

## The air conditioning tsunami

When Betts was studying to become an engineer, he realized energy was the machine behind all the machines. "It's super necessary for everything that we are. It's civilizationally critical," he said. And soon, he discovered that one specific machine consumes a huge portion of the energy produced globally: air conditioners.

Air conditioning can be like a tsunami: A trigger, like spiking afternoon heat, creates a wave of energy demand that can overwhelm power grids. That flood is temporary but maddening. A grid can only support the demand of its highest peak, and air conditioning is that peak more often than not.

When Betts visited NLR to give a talk, air conditioning came up yet again. "If there was a way to add efficiency and energy storage into the air-conditioning load," Betts told the crowd, then both energy and costs would plummet. Later that day, in a lab across campus, he met two NLR researchers who created something that could potentially do exactly that.

"Wow," Betts remembers thinking, "here are the wizards that have figured out the solution to the entire thing."

## A salty solution

Those "wizards" were Kozubal and Jason Woods, two senior engineers at NLR who co-invented a technology called the Energy Storing and Efficient Air Conditioner (or ESEAC).

More than half of the energy consumed by air conditioners goes to dehumidifying air. Conventional systems often overcool a room just to achieve a comfortable humidity level and must then heat it back up to the desired temperature.

But Blue Frontier and NLR's ESEAC system uses a salt-based liquid to pull moisture from the air—just like table salt absorbs water, infamously clumping on humid days. The heat from that now-dry air is then pulled into an adjoining heat exchanger, a device that can move heat energy from one medium to another. There, the air is chilled using evaporative cooling. Just like sweat evaporating from skin helps cool our bodies, evaporating water reduces the air's temperature to a comfortable level.

When the salt solution becomes too diluted to absorb any more water vapor, the system uses heat to evaporate some of the water and reconcentrate the salty liquid.

This salt-and-water system needs little electricity—just enough to power a fan and small pumps—and also consumes less energy as temperatures rise.

The technology was young, but Betts was "mesmerized by the potential," he said. A couple of years later, he licensed it to create an air conditioner that ran on the heat from a fuel cell. He launched his first startup, Be Power Tech Inc. Four years later, he shut it down.

"That's a really good idea. I stand by it," Betts said. "But it requires two new technologies to play together, fuel cells and the NLR air-conditioning tech."

Double new can mean double the risk, and risk can make investors nervous.

"It broke my heart, but a good entrepreneur is a glutton for pain," Betts said. "And I'm driven by the potential for innovation and the responsibility associated with knowledge and capabilities that we carry, right? We're here to leave the world a little bit better."

The wizards would agree.

## On to army bases and movie theaters

Betts went back to Kozubal and Woods at NLR. Together, they found a way to turn the original invention into an air conditioner that could power up when power is cheapest (or most convenient).

Betts licensed the technology again, and Blue Frontier was born.

Thanks to an add-on invention created by the NLR experts (something called an Electrically Driven Desiccant Regenerator), the new system could ditch the need for heat generated by a fuel cell and instead use the hot side of the refrigeration cycle to reconcentrate the technology's core salt solution. That reconcentration can happen at any time, enabling companies to recharge at night or during other periods of low electricity demand when prices are low.

"That new invention transformed the air conditioner into one that consumes 90% less electricity at peak, and 50% less year-round," Kozubal said. "It can be recharged like a battery, consuming electricity when it's cheap."

The journey from new invention to market success still had bumps.

"But this is again where NLR has been extraordinary," Betts said. "We found out how to jujitsu the physics into doing the things that we wanted to do."

NLR's experts and their "engineering rigor," as Betts said, helped confirm the idea could work. The laboratory's backing boosted investor confidence. Grants rolled in. It was time to turn their prototype into a product.

items.body:
NASA announced Monday that NASA+ content has found its first theatrical home at The Greenbelt Cinema in Greenbelt, Maryland, expanding the agency’s reach across major viewing platforms and bringing space even closer to home.

“The National Aeronautics and Space Act of 1958 calls us to share our story of space exploration with the broadest possible audience, and our partners help us accomplish that,” said Rebecca Sirmons, general manager of NASA+ at the agency’s Headquarters in Washington. “Artemis II captured the imagination of the Artemis generation, but we are just getting started. With Artemis III on the horizon and our sights set on building humanity’s first Moon Base, this is only the beginning of our story being told, and we’ll continue sharing transparent, engaging content every step of the way.”

NASA and The Greenbelt Cinema will kick off their partnership with screenings of the NASA+ original documentary “The Europa Concept,” which follows NASA’s journey to investigate the science driving future exploration of Europa, Jupiter’s icy moon. Dates for screenings will be announced soon on NASA.gov.

Future programming may include other NASA+ original content, in-person live streaming events of NASA’s Artemis missions, including the first crewed mission to the Moon under the Artemis program, additional Europa content, and more. NASA+ also will remain available for free, with no ads, through the NASA app and on the agency’s [website](https://plus.nasa.gov/).

Earlier this year during its [Ignition](https://www.nasa.gov/ignition/) event, NASA outlined a bold path forward for the agency, including increasing the cadence of [Artemis](https://www.nasa.gov/artemis) missions to the lunar surface, and building the first [Moon Base](https://www.nasa.gov/moonbase), among other agency priorities. Partnerships like this one help NASA maximize engagement with communities around the world by making the agency’s missions and educational content available to viewers on their preferred devices and channels.

## New Gemini setting lets you keep chat history, but turn off AI training [U]

Google is rolling out new privacy settings for the Gemini app that will let you “keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training.”

Update 11/24 : This new setting is now widely rolling out. On gemini.google.com, tap the settings gear icon to find a new “Gemini History” item at the very bottom. This opens myactivity.google.com/product/gemini with an On/Off dropdown.

Under “Help train generative AI models with,” you’ll find the new “Chat content including text & attachments” setting. It’s enabled by default.

> Your future chats won’t be used to train generative AI models, unless you provide feedback.

Training on “Audio and Gemini Live videos & screenshares” remains an opt-in preference.

Original 11/16 : Gemini’s existing Keep Activity setting “controls how long your chats are saved and whether they are used to train generative AI models.”

Google is now separating that preference into two new options.

## Top comment by Whispy_Snippet

This is huge. One of the major things Siri-AI users on iPhone like to point out is that while their assistant is a less capable portmanteau of Siri and Gemini, their queries are not used for AI training. Gemini on Android, on the other hand, offers the superior AI platform with the caveat that there is no way to opt out of training and still retain your chat history. Until now. Now users of Gemini on Android get the best of both worlds - the best of Google's AI models powering their AI experiences and their chat history siloed from AI training.

Win win.

The first setting is called “History” and lets you “control how long your history is saved.” If disabled:

> “…future chats will be saved for around 2 months and used to respond to you, process your feedback, and protect Google, its users, and the public, with help from human reviewers.”

The duration is currently 24 hours for chat context, and 72 hours to help protect Google, users, and the public.

The second setting allows you to “separately control whether your chat content, including text and attachments, is used to train generative AI models.”

> With this change, you will be able to keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training.

If Keep Activity is currently off, the two “new settings will both be off.” These changes are rolling out over the “coming weeks,” and Google is notifying users via email.

# Earth’s Water May Have Formed in This Fiery Furnace - Nautilus

## Earth’s Water May Have Formed in This Fiery Furnace

No ice deliveries needed

3:00 PM CST on November 24, 2026

It’s one of the most fundamental questions about life on Earth: How did water get here?

One possibility is that it was delivered as frozen ice by a bombardment of meteorites smashing into our planet’s surface. Another is that the chemistry of the early Earth somehow produced water from molten rock—a theory that’s the focus of a new study published in Nature Geoscience .

Read more: “ This Paradoxical Desert Landscape Is Filled with Fresh Water ”

The researchers behind the hypothesis are calling it “pebble rain” (or “pebble accretion”). What happens is silicate rocks with iron inside, drawn toward Earth by its increasing mass and gravitational pull, react with hydrogen in the atmosphere. Given the high speeds, high pressure, and high volume of incoming rocks involved, the subsequent chemical reactions could have stripped away the oxygen from the iron in the pebble showers, releasing water vapor as a by-product.

The researchers estimate that around 200 oceans’ worth of H2O may have been released in this way, supplying the planet with the magic ingredient for life. These pebbles would have been external visitors, like meteorites, but the water would’ve been formed on Earth rather than in space.

What’s more, the same process could plausibly happen on other planets as they form too—opening up new possibilities in our search for extraterrestrial life. “Previous ideas about the source of water to Earth rely on an external source, such as comets or meteorites,” study author Zachary Sharp explained in a statement . “Here we show that virtually any Earth-sized planet should have water by this newly identified mechanism.”

The researchers simulated the conditions of the early Earth in their lab with temperatures of up to 2,552°F, and heating silicate rocks in streams of hydrogen. Almost 80 percent of the iron oxide in the samples turned into metallic iron, producing water vapor along the way.

“Looking out over a large body of water, it’s hard to imagine that that water may have been produced four-and-a-half billion years ago in a hell-like atmosphere,” Sharp said, “but it very well may have.”

## Why you should be reading Helen Garner (and where to start).

Last week, The Paris Review announced the winners of its annual literary awards. In 2027, Australian author Helen Garner will be feted with the Hadada, a prize that recognizes a writer’s lifelong literary contributions. I am here as an independent body to hype this choice.

Garner—a novelist, journalist, and diarist—writes big-hearted heroines who are often on the edge of a crisis. Her other fans include Lauren Groff, Lily King, Rumaan Alam, and Ben Lerner, but we are legion. Why, you ask?

In a recent piece for The Guardian , Emma Brockes also praised Garner’s “ability to combine insight and erudition of the highest literary order with a style that is at times comically down to earth.” And it’s true—that earthiness is what makes her work indelible. But it’s also just the tip of an iceberg.

Here are three of Garner’s best known books (and why you should make like the Parisians and pick them up, stat).

Monkey Grip , Garner’s 1977 debut, sent a shockwave through Australia. This novel chronicles a woman’s doomed-from-the-jump situationship with a heroin addict who charms her intermittently as they orbit a communal living situation.

A little like Susie Boyt’s sleeper hit, Loved and Missed , this book beautifully captures the recurring heartbreak involved in loving an addict. But it’s never saccharine, or sanctimonious.

Following a bohemian Melbourne milieu that echoes the author’s own set at the time, Garner’s non-judgmental portrait of freewheeling radicals brought out the moralizers on publication. Nora, our heroine, ruffled feathers for depicting ambivalent parenthood administered with a very loose latchkey. All adults in this book are libidinally motivated. Drugs and sex are world-structuring forces.

But what’s most exciting is how naked the prose is about all of that want. In Garner’s matter-of-fact voice, Nora’s thirst for the grifting Javo is rendered tender, abject, holy, and pathetic by turns. She feels like a real and vulnerable person with a mighty human flaw. The best kind of protagonist.

My favorite of Garner’s novels is The Children’s Bach . Another tale of domestic upheaval ignited by a charismatic chaos agent, this book traces the happily partnered Athena Fox’s infatuation with a blast from the past. Against reason, she leaves her partner and two small children for… a rock star.

What follows is a little predictable, but as with Monkey Grip the pleasure is in experiencing that slow road to ruin. (Or is it ecstasy?)

The third person POV serves this book, which manages to texturize everyone affected by Athena’s choices. She feels like a modern Nora, in the Ibsen sense.

The Spare Room is a cool, slim, spiky book. I find this Garner still gnaws at me. Following two semi-estranged old friends who fall back together when one seeks harbor following a terminal diagnosis, this novel depicts the unpleasant side of caretaking and the indignity of illness.

This book asks some truly itchy questions. Such as, what do you do when your patient is delusional—and/or, you want them out of your house?

As in the other novels, our protagonist chafes against conventionality and obligatory mutual obligation. And her extreme honesty hits you like a glass of cold water. As always, there’s a nakedness to a Garner subject. She doesn’t flinch from depicting those ugly emotions or unwanted thoughts.

In a review for the Times , Daphne Merkin once compared Garner to other “laconic and wayward,” ladies who specialize in the “art of artlessness, like Jean Rhys, Jane Bowles and Paula Fox.”

I agree with wayward, but I think that artful eye is in a class all its own. Do yourself a favor and join the Helen hive. Today.

### Brittany Allen

Brittany K. Allen is a writer and actor living in Brooklyn.

items.body:
Noah Smith at *Noahpinion*:

“Pacing the frontier” so that alignment research can catch up might be effective in a world of steady linear AI progress. But in a world of sudden superexponential progress, AI alignment research will immediately be left behind. Even if there is a Singularity for understanding alignment, in a world with an intelligence explosion it will be the superintelligent AI, not us, that carries out that Singularity and decides on its alignment for itself.

A second point is that it’s not obvious why an intelligence explosion would be more dangerous than — or even distinguishable from — the type of rapid, non-explosive progress we’re already getting. Remember, AI going from “can’t add two numbers together” to “solves problems too hard for all human mathematicians combined” in three years is *not* counted as an intelligence explosion!

It’s clear that at the current rate of steady progress, AI will become superhuman in most domains in a fairly small number of years. Even robotics and other physical tasks [look conquerable](https://www.understandingrobots.org/p/openais-astra-model-is-shockingly) with the current type of AI that powers Claude and GPT. This means that AI will basically look like a god within our lifetimes, *whether or not* it looks like the kind of infinitely self-improving gods that populate Vernor Vinge novels.

This is why I’m not sure what an intelligence explosion means for our economy. It’s [easy to write down a model](https://aleximas.substack.com/p/will-ai-soon-lead-to-double-digit) in which smoothly increasing AI capabilities drive a smooth increase in GDP. But why should we believe a model like that?

More [↗ noahpinion.blog](https://www.noahpinion.blog/p/does-it-really-matter-if-theres-an).

items.title: Mitsubishi Electric Research Lab CEO on How He Reached the C-Suite
items.subtitle: The trajectory from researcher to top executive at a leading R&D organization doesn’t happen overnight.
