items.body:
The trajectory from researcher to top executive at a leading R&D organization doesn’t happen overnight. It took Anthony Vetro nearly 30 years to climb the corporate ladder at Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories, in Cambridge, Mass. He joined MERL in 1996, right out of college, and he has worked there ever since.

Vetro probably is best known for his research in multimedia signal processing, focusing on video compression.

Anthony Vetro

Employer

Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories, in Cambridge, Mass.

Title

President and CEO

Member grade

Fellow

Alma mater

Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school)

He became an IEEE Fellow in 2011 for his contributions to video coding, three-dimensional television, and multimedia adaptation.

Mitsubishi Electric has moved away from making televisions. It now focuses on developing systems including ones used for defense, electronics, the energy industry, and space exploration.

His ascension up the executive ranks began in 2018, when he was named a vice president and director of MERL. In 2023 he was appointed its president and CEO.

He also works closely with the company’s new U.S.-based innovation facility in Cambridge. And he recently took on a dual role as deputy head of Mitsubishi Electric’s global R&D activities, including in Asia and Europe.

Vetro credits IEEE with helping him develop his management skills after he served in several IEEE Signal Processing Society leadership positions. He also learned from his key roles in establishing international standards for digital image formats and video compression, he says.

“Between my IEEE activities, standards work, and some of the business shifts in Mitsubishi Electric, I eventually graduated to more management leadership roles,” he says.

A multimedia pioneer

Vetro is the son of immigrants. His father came to the United States from Italy and his mother from Sweden when they were both in their early 20s. They settled in New York City, on Staten Island.

Although neither parent went to college, his father stressed the importance of education to his son at an early age.

“My father started in the mailroom and worked his way up to eventually managing communication accounts and infrastructure for large financial companies,” he says. “My mother worked in banks, first as a teller and later doing bank reconciliation after pursuing some professional certifications.

“Through their jobs, they saw people with college degrees getting better positions and promotions, so education was something really ingrained in me.”

Vetro says he developed a passion for mathematics and engineering in middle school. He was accepted into the Staten Island Technical High School, a specialized pre-engineering institution. There he solidified his interest in pursuing a career in the field.

“A lot of students didn’t know what they wanted to major in at college, but I knew fairly early,” he says.

He was accepted into the accelerated bachelor’s and master’s engineering degree programs at the Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school). He began his bachelor’s degree program in 1992 and the master’s program in 1994.

“As part of the master’s degree program, I needed to do a thesis,” he says. “I wasn’t sure exactly what it would be on. Soon after taking my first course on image processing, I was certain that was an area I wanted to work in.”

It was an interesting time, he says, because broadcast television was going through a major transformation, shifting from analog to digital during the early 1990s. It was long before streaming services, he notes.

“I feel that industry-level engagement in IEEE is very vital to the organization in maintaining high relevance in the community and fulfilling its mission of fostering technological innovation and excellence for the benefit of humanity.”

“The idea of being able to come up with compact ways to represent this very rich information was really appealing to me,” he says. “I’m also a visual learner. I liked seeing images, and there was some nice math behind them, too.”

After he earned both degrees in 1996, Mitsubishi Electric hired him for its technical staff. He conducted research on multimedia signal processing, focusing on video compression.

“The opportunity to work on projects around digital TV broadcasting and image processing attracted me,” he says.

He conducted research in video conferencing, Internet and mobile streaming, and video coding technology, widely used for broadcasting, DVDs, and Blu-ray discs. He developed several technologies including digital TV receivers and displays, surveillance and camera-monitoring systems, automotive equipment, and satellite imaging systems.

Another advantage of joining the company, he says, was that it allowed him to pursue a doctorate in electrical engineering, also from Polytechnic, while working.

“That really sealed the deal,” he says. He received the degree in 2001.

The road to management

After six years as a technical staff member, he was promoted in 2007 to manage the group working on digital video coding, processing, and streaming. Seven years later, Vetro became its deputy director, a top-level management position that he held until 2018.

“After working for about 10 years exclusively on video compression processing technology, there were some shifts in our company’s business. Its overall strategy began to change,” he says, “so I became interested in broadening my experience beyond video.”

He was asked to lead the lab’s speech and audio team. It was more development-oriented, he says, and focused on vehicle infotainment and speech interfaces before Alexa and Siri existed. He pivoted the team’s focus more toward research and established strategic paths tailored to emerging opportunities within the organization. Recognizing emerging trends in sensing and information security, he formed groups that worked on them.

Mitsubishi Electric’s first U.S. innovation hub

To help spur innovation between Mitsubishi Electric and its U.S. customers, the company in June opened Serendie Street Boston, its first digital transformation hub in the United States. It’s colocated with MERL.

The new office is modeled after the first Serendie Street collaboration space, which Mitsubishi Electric launched in 2024 in Yokohama, Japan.

The word serendie is a combination of serendipity and digital engineering, according to the company’s website. Serendie is the digital platform designed to foster collaborations between data, people, and technology, it says. The space where people interact to extract ideas from the data is called “the street.”

The platform brings together researchers, startups, customers, and partners to identify new products, test them, run pilot programs, and scale them up.

Vetro says he’s excited about the endeavor.

items.body:
Was passiert eigentlich, wenn wir eine App auf dem Smartphone öffnen? Oft deutlich mehr, als auf dem Display zu sehen ist. Neben Verbindungen, die eine Anwendung für ihre eigentliche Aufgabe benötigt, können Kontakte zu Analyse-, Werbe- und Trackingdiensten entstehen. Android zeigt zwar an, wie viele Daten einzelne Apps übertragen, nicht aber, mit welchen Servern sie dabei kommunizieren. Wer nachvollziehen möchte, welche Netzwerkverbindungen eine Anwendung aufbaut, benötigt [zusätzliche Werkzeuge](https://www.kuketz-blog.de/empfehlungsecke/#app-verkehr).

Genau hier setzt [RethinkDNS](https://rethinkdns.com/) an. Die quelloffene Android-App vereint Netzwerkmonitor, Firewall und DNS-Filter. Sie funktioniert ohne Root-Rechte und kann sowohl einzelne Netzwerkverbindungen sichtbar machen als auch Internetzugriffe kontrollieren. Mit Blocklisten lassen sich zudem viele bekannte Werbe- und Tracking-Domains sperren.

Dieser erste Teil ist bewusst als Einstieg gedacht: Wir installieren RethinkDNS, nehmen es in Betrieb, schauen uns zwei Wege der DNS-Filterung an und untersuchen beispielhaft den Datenverkehr des DB Navigators. Eine möglichst restriktive Firewall ist noch nicht das Ziel. Zunächst soll nachvollziehbar werden, was RethinkDNS tut und welche Entscheidungen die Nutzer selbst treffen können.

## 1. Wie funktioniert RethinkDNS?

Um RethinkDNS sinnvoll einzusetzen, sollte man zunächst verstehen, welche Aufgaben die einzelnen Funktionen übernehmen und wo ihre Grenzen liegen:

- Netzwerkmonitor: Er zeigt, welche Anwendungen mit welchen IP-Adressen kommunizieren und welche DNS-Anfragen auftauchen. Das schafft Transparenz, ist aber noch kein Beleg dafür, welche konkreten Inhalte übermittelt werden.
- Firewall: Sie erlaubt es, den Internetzugriff einzelner Apps gezielt einzuschränken. Das ist beispielsweise sinnvoll für Anwendungen, die keinen Internetzugang benötigen oder nur unter bestimmten Bedingungen kommunizieren sollen, etwa ausschließlich über einen WireGuard-Tunnel. Auch einzelne Domains oder IP-Adressen lassen sich gezielt erlauben oder blockieren.
- DNS-Filterung: Anfragen an bekannte Werbe-, Tracking- oder Schadsoftware-Domains können anhand von Listen blockiert werden. Häufig kommt eine Verbindung dadurch gar nicht erst zustande.

Ein kurzes Beispiel: Eine App fragt nach tracker.example und bekommt von der DNS-Filterung keine reguläre IP-Adresse. Sie kann diesen Namen dann auf dem üblichen Weg nicht mehr zum Verbindungsaufbau verwenden. Das funktioniert aber nicht bei jeder Form des Trackings. Verwendet eine App eine direkte IP-Adresse, einen eigenen verschlüsselten DNS-Kanal oder dieselbe Domain für notwendige Inhalte und Tracking, stößt die DNS-Filterung an Grenzen.

### Warum verlangt die App eine VPN-Verbindung?

RethinkDNS verwendet die [VPN-Schnittstelle von Android](https://developer.android.com/develop/connectivity/vpn), um den Netzwerkverkehr lokal entgegenzunehmen und nach Regeln zu behandeln. Die Bezeichnung »VPN« bedeutet hier nicht, dass der gesamte Internetverkehr zu einem externen VPN-Anbieter geschickt wird oder die eigene IP-Adresse verborgen wäre.

Allerdings gibt es eine praktische Konsequenz: Pro Android-Nutzerprofil kann normalerweise nur eine VPN-Verbindung gleichzeitig aktiv sein. Wer bereits eine andere VPN-App verwendet, muss deren Zusammenspiel mit RethinkDNS prüfen. Die integrierten [WireGuard-Möglichkeiten](https://www.wireguard.com/) behandeln wir in einem späteren Teil.

## 2. Installation und Bezugsquellen

RethinkDNS ist über verschiedene Quellen erhältlich, darunter [F-Droid](https://f-droid.org/packages/com.celzero.bravedns/), [GitHub](https://github.com/celzero/rethink-app), die [Projektwebsite](https://rethinkdns.com/download) und den [Google Play Store](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.celzero.bravedns). Die Wahl der Bezugsquelle ist nicht ganz unerheblich, denn die angebotenen Varianten unterscheiden sich unter anderem bei den eingebundenen Google-Komponenten. Für diese Anleitung verwende ich Version 0.5.8 aus F-Droid.

Die Varianten von F-Droid und IzzyOnDroid kommen ohne Google-Bibliotheken aus. Seit Version 0.5.7 wurde Firebase Crashlytics auch aus den GitHub- und Website-Versionen entfernt. Die Play-Store-Version enthält dagegen weiterhin Crashlytics zur Fehlerberichterstattung. Diese ist laut Entwickler standardmäßig deaktiviert und muss unter »Konfigurieren -> Einstellungen -> Stabilitätsprogramm« ausdrücklich aktiviert werden. Ohne diese Zustimmung werden keine Absturzberichte über Crashlytics übermittelt. Wer solche Google-Komponenten grundsätzlich vermeiden möchte, greift zur F-Droid-Version.

Hinzu kommt ein funktionaler Unterschied: Die [geräteinternen Blocklisten stehen nach Entwicklerangaben](https://github.com/celzero/rethink-app/issues/3028) nicht in der Play-Store-Variante zur Verfügung. Wer diese Option nutzen möchte, sollte daher eine entsprechende andere Variante installieren.

Die F-Droid-Ausgabe von RethinkDNS. Auf dieser Variante basieren die folgenden Schritte.

Nach der Installation erscheinen vier kurze Einführungsseiten zu VPN, Firewall und DNS-Filterung. Man kann sie lesen oder überspringen. Sie sollen einen Überblick vermitteln, sind aber keine zusätzliche Konfiguration. Danach zeigt RethinkDNS zunächst » NICHT GESCHÜTZT « an. Das ist normal: Die App ist zwar installiert, verarbeitet aber noch keinen Netzwerkverkehr.

## 3. RethinkDNS zum ersten Mal starten

Mit einem Tipp auf »START« beginnt die Einrichtung. RethinkDNS erklärt zunächst, weshalb es eine lokale VPN-Verbindung benötigt. Anschließend erscheint die Android-Systemmeldung »Verbindungsanfrage«. Hier bestätigen wir mit »OK«. Android weist ausdrücklich darauf hin, dass die App den durch die VPN-Schnittstelle geleiteten Netzwerkverkehr überwachen kann. Genau diese Position benötigt RethinkDNS für seine Aufgaben. Sie setzt zugleich voraus, dass man der Anwendung vertraut.

Android fragt vor dem ersten Start nach der Erlaubnis, eine VPN-Verbindung einzurichten.

Nach erfolgreichem Start zeigt RethinkDNS den Status » GESCHÜTZT « an. Das bedeutet zunächst, dass die Anwendung aktiv ist und den Netzwerkverkehr verarbeitet. Auf der Startseite erscheinen außerdem Informationen zum verwendeten DNS-Dienst sowie zu erlaubten und blockierten Verbindungen.

RethinkDNS läuft. Oben wird der verwendete DNS-Dienst angezeigt, darunter folgen Firewall- und Aktivitätsinformationen.

### 3.1 Was passiert nach dem ersten Start?

Im Ausgangszustand dürfen die installierten Apps grundsätzlich weiterhin auf das Internet zugreifen. RethinkDNS überwacht ihre Netzwerkverbindungen, sperrt aber nicht automatisch einzelne Anwendungen. Wer den Internetzugang bestimmter Apps unterbinden möchte, muss dafür eigene Firewall-Regeln einrichten.

items.body:
# Jamaica Suk, producer, DJ, and friend, has died - CDM Create Digital Music

## Jamaica Suk, producer, DJ, and friend, has died

We lost Jamaica Suk yesterday, the singular musical force. To say this hits close to home is an understatement; few people have been a better friend or a greater inspiration. My thoughts are with her family, in particular, right now. Music in the end is just an excuse to spend some time together and share some hopes and dreams. Take care of one another. Here’s the official statement.

> We’re heartbroken to share that we lost Jamaica Suk on Monday, following a battle with an aggressive form of breast cancer. She passed away peacefully in her sleep, with loved ones by her side. No words can make this easier. We all wanted so much more time with Jamaica, and she fought fantastically hard for the past months, care for by her sisters Aysia and Hope. Thank you for your support during this time, when she was unable to work and do what she loved most. Memorial arrangements will be announced soon. We ask for some privacy for the family and friends as everyone processes this enormous loss. Jamaica shared so much love through the music world, from her own Gradient label to a life lived constantly playing — in rock and metal bands, jazz, and techno, across northern California and Berlin and internationally. She was a regular and unforgettable presence at RSO, Radion, Tresor, Melkweg, Basement, Renate, about blank, and many others. She was a long-time resident at Pornceptual, including one Boiler Room stream that was too hot to handle for YouTube. And she was a prolific producer, with a blend of hypnotic, groovy, and hard industrial elements that were instantly recognizable as her personality and warmth. To spend any time with Jamaica was to get to know her dreams, and the fierce tenacity with which she would work to bring them to reality. She literally described dreaming of wires and patch cables. Even in recent days, she was talking about new ideas for music and people she wanted to bring together and show the world. So we ask you to please keep celebrating her music and keep those dreams alive.

The official source for the family and arrangements is @jamaicasuk .

Please, do play some of Jamaica’s music. That remains the answer.

items.title: 9/UX: a Macintosh-inspired desktop for 9front
items.subtitle: I have written a story about this on the Register, but of course I can't post that here.
items.feedText: These are real frames, not mockups. The GUI tests embed h9 with a headless screen, inject mouse and keyboard input, and drive the 9P files at the same time. Macintosh structure, Plan 9 colour: butter title bars from rio's selection yellow, acme's cream and olive, and rio's greygreen for the desktop, so 9/UX windows and legacy rio windows sit together on one screen. items.body:
# 9/UX: a Macintosh-inspired desktop for 9front

- [ demo | about | screenshots | design | docs | code | warning! | contact | credits | links ] 9/UX: a Macintosh-inspired desktop for 9front Jeff Lindsay , h.d.a. This is the real thing, running live in your browser: the rio fork in 9/UX mode, Desktop, and the libux sample app, compiled for 386 and run by h9 on its own 386 emulator inside the page. Nothing is sent anywhere; it's about 23 MB to load, once. Click the screen to type; right-click (or Ctrl-click) is button 3, and Alt-click is button 2. It needs a recent Chrome or Edge; other browsers see a screenshot, a real frame from the end-to-end drag-and-drop test, running headless on h9. Open it in its own tab for a bigger screen. About 9/UX brings the classic Mac and A/UX desktop (a spatial desktop, a global menu bar, consistent controls and dialogs, icons, and resource-driven presentation) to 9front , built the Plan 9 way: rio and libdraw draw the screen, 9P exposes every application's UI state and commands as files, namespaces define the working environment, the plumber opens documents, and ndb holds human-editable metadata. Keep the Macintosh's direct-manipulation desktop, but make every meaningful object, action, and resource visible as a Plan 9 file. It is not an emulator, a Macintosh ABI, or an A/UX reimplementation. Native 9front programs stay first-class, and existing rio programs (acme, sam, rc windows, nested rio) keep working unchanged beside 9/UX apps. The pieces: rio fork ( rio -u ): a desktop layer, a global menu bar that follows the focused app, title-bar chrome, and a drag broker, all under /dev/ux . With 9/UX mode off it's stock rio.
- Desktop : volume icons, spatial folder windows, rename, duplicate, Get Info, Trash, remembered layout, and double-click to open documents through the plumber. A remote 9P server works as a volume.
- libux , the Toolbox: windows, menus, dialogs, alerts, and controls, each app serving its control tree over 9P, so echo activate >.../ctl presses a button.
- uxd gathers every app's tree at /mnt/ux with per-app policy; uxmeta keeps associations, volumes and layout in ndb files; resfs serves classic ICN# , icl8 , menu, dialog and string resources at /mnt/res ; clipd is a typed clipboard kept in step with rio's snarf.
## Screenshots

These are real frames, not mockups. The GUI tests embed h9 with a headless screen, inject mouse and keyboard input, and drive the 9P files at the same time.

## Visual Design

Macintosh structure, Plan 9 colour: butter title bars from rio's selection yellow, acme's cream and olive, and rio's greygreen for the desktop, so 9/UX windows and legacy rio windows sit together on one screen. Everything reads in one bit, uses a sixteen-colour palette, and is drawn in whole pixels. Every graphic is original to 9/UX; it ships no Apple resources. The mockups below are generated from the same palette and metrics files as the code.

## Documentation

The design document describes 9/UX and its v0.1 acceptance criteria; release.md has where each one stands, the end-to-end demo, and the open issues. Every interface between components is a file protocol in docs/protocols , and the visual design covers the palette, fonts, metrics, chrome, icons and cursors.

## Source Code

The source is on GitHub , under the MIT license. Development runs on h9 , which runs 9front's own compilers, mk and rio directly from the host shell, without booting a VM. scripts/h9.sh clones and builds the pinned h9 on its first run:

git clone https://github.com/progrium/9ux cd 9ux scripts/h9.sh --rc 'mk' scripts/h9.sh --gfx rio/7.out -u scripts/test.sh Use rio/6.out on amd64. development.md and testing.md have the details.

## Warning!

9/UX is at v0.1 and under active development. Interfaces and behaviour change without notice.

## Contact Info

Please report bugs and send questions through GitHub issues .

## Credits

The 9/UX mark in the menu bar is a pixel-art Glenda by Dan Fessler . Glenda, the Plan 9 bunny , was created by Renée French .

## Related Links

- h9 , native 9front executables on host hypervisors
- 9front
- A/UX , Apple's Unix with the Macintosh Desktop

items.body:
[Javier Hidalgo](https://jepson.richmond.edu/faculty/bios/jhidalgo/), a philosopher at the University of Richmond, has developed a classroom simulation game to teach about different ancient philosophies called “Ancient Philosophy as a Way of Life.”

Generously, Professor Hidalgo has created a [website](https://hidalgoj-ai.github.io/Ancient-Philosophy-Game/) to share the game with anyone who may wish to try it out in their own courses.

He writes:

> [Ancient Philosophy as a Way of Life](https://hidalgoj-ai.github.io/Ancient-Philosophy-Game/) is a free classroom role-playing game that introduces students to Hellenistic philosophy, plus a bit of Buddhist philosophy.
> The game is set around 150 BCE at the court of Menander, a king who ruled a Hellenistic kingdom that included part of the Indian subcontinent. Four delegations of philosophers (Stoics, Epicureans, Buddhists, and Skeptics) arrive at court, each claiming to offer the best way of life. Some students play the philosophers, while others play members of the court, each of whom faces a personal dilemma and must decide which philosophical school to join. The philosophers present their views, lead the court through a brief philosophical exercise, and offer advice on the court members’ dilemmas. At the end, the court members announce their allegiances and the king awards royal patronage.
> There is no predetermined winner: when I ran the game in two sections of my ethics course, different philosophical factions won. Students engaged in sustained debate about the merits of the different schools and also seemed to have fun with the game.
> The game takes two class sessions, one for preparation and one for play, although a third session might be useful for larger or more talkative classes. It works for classes of 7 to 30 students and assumes no background in philosophy. The goal of the game is for students to encounter these philosophies as live options rather than merely as historical doctrines. Students have to understand a view well enough to defend it against objections, apply it to concrete problems, and experiment with its practices.
> The game is inspired by [Reacting to the Past](https://reactingconsortium.org/) games (which I love!) but is shorter than a standard Reacting game and is designed to emphasize philosophical debate in particular. The [website](https://hidalgoj-ai.github.io/Ancient-Philosophy-Game/#materials) has everything an instructor needs to run the game: a student gamebook, an instructor’s manual, faction handouts, role sheets, dilemma cards, and ballots. All materials are free to download.

Check it out. Professor Hidalgo adds, “The game is still in development and I would welcome feedback from anyone who tries it.”

items.body:
# Everything I know about writing

## Everything I know about writing

### (slightly abridged)

Adam Mastroianni Nov 24, 2026 ∙ Paid 72 8 2 Share Upgrade to paid to play voiceover photo cred: my dad 1. A few years ago, some researchers put ants and humans in a head-to-head battle of wits. The task was to maneuver an awkwardly sized object through a series of obstacles, like this:

Humans and ants competed both as individuals and in groups. The humans were forbidden from communicating with one another (I guess to make the playing field more level with the ants?), and they were made to wear sunglasses and masks to prevent any nonverbal signals. The ants were allowed to do whatever they wanted, on account of them being ants. Researchers “incubated” the objects in cat food and rubbed them with tuna to make them “seem like attractive food items to the ants” (I assume humans were spared this step).

I have read the paper multiple times and I still don’t really understand why they did any of this, but the videos they made are really cool :

I bring this up because watching those videos, I think to myself: that’s exactly what writing is. It’s maneuvering an awkwardly sized idea into someone’s head. It’s getting the thing wedged in the wrong spot and then backing up to reorient it. It’s wondering why something that looks so easy can be so hard. And occasionally, the whole thing reeks of tuna.

Trying to write drives most people nuts, but nobody ever told me that there’s a good nuts and a bad nuts.

Bad nuts is when you’re sitting there thinking the same thing over and over again, or thinking nothing at all, just drumming your fingers on the desk and checking your email every 17 seconds, like “hmm...words...words...what is a word...”. This is both painful and pointless.

Good nuts is when you’re trying a million things a minute and almost all of them are failing. Like:

> Does it go like this? No. Does it go like this ? No. Does it go like THIS? No. Does it go like t*h*i*s? No. Does it go like T~H~I~S ? YES

This is also painful, but it ultimately results in something that you want to show other people. In this way, it is very similar to getting your unibrow waxed.

## This post is for paid subscribers

items.body:
If [Focusrite](https://musictech.com/brands/focusrite/)’s name is synonymous with affordable [interfaces](https://musictech.com/tag/audio-interfaces/), [Universal Audio](https://musictech.com/brands/universal-audio/) might be synonymous with expensive. Its Apollo interfaces helped popularise [recording](https://musictech.com/tag/recording/) through onboard DSP, bringing convincing emulations of classic hardware into countless [studios](https://musictech.com/tag/studios/).

In 2021, UA aimed to disrupt that image with Volt, a cheaper interface series that includes [vintage](https://musictech.com/tag/vintage/)-style preamps and even 76-style analogue compression on select models.

The second generation has now arrived, with a six-device roster split across standard and Max. I’m testing the Volt 2 Gen 2 and Volt 4 Max to find out whether one deserves a space on your desk – and which model makes the most sense.

Universal Audio Volt 2 Max. Image: Press

## Are the UA Volt interfaces well made?

While the first-generation Volts evoked the look of vintage hardware, the new lineup leans on a more modern aesthetic. The matte grey finish looks really smart, with a bright display and softly backlit button labels that are easy to read at a glance.

Both the Volt 2 Gen 2 and the Volt 4 Max occupy a similarly compact footprint on the desk; the Max features top-down controls akin to UA’s [Apollo Twin](https://musictech.com/reviews/studio-recording-gear/universal-audio-apollo-twin-x-gen-2-review/) interfaces, while the Volt 2 is operated via the front panel.

In both appearance and usage, I prefer the Max form factor, whose design feels decidedly more like the central hub of a recording setup. The Volt 2, meanwhile, can be stacked with other gear or tucked into a rack shelf, but a single-finger button push can move it around on the desk due to its lack of heft.

Neither Volt interface feels quite as premium as it looks. The buttons have a slightly plasticky quality, and there’s some wiggle on the control knob that calls its long-term durability into question. But visually speaking, the new Volts may look the slickest on the market.

Universal Audio Volt 4 Max smart display with meters. Image: Press

## Recording audio with a UA Volt interface

The new Volt interfaces connect over USB-C and are bus-powered, although an additional power connection may be required if you’re recording with a phone or tablet. I’m using a MacBook M4 Pro, and setup only takes a few minutes via UA Connect.

I begin with the Volt 4 Max, connecting my [Korg](https://musictech.com/brands/korg/) Electribe ER-1 to the two combo jack/XLR inputs on the back, although there are also two Hi-Z inputs on the front for [guitars](https://musictech.com/tag/guitars/) and basses.

After building a quick drum pattern, I use the Auto-Gain feature to set levels. By default, it targets -8 dBFS, but this target can be changed within the UAD Console application. Since I’m recording in stereo, I link the two inputs within the Volt’s simple menu system to ensure their levels are matched.

I get a solid signal after the first pass, but when I run Auto-Gain again, the level ends up higher even though my drum [loop](https://musictech.com/tag/loops/) is playing at the same volume both times. I’m also getting a peak readout of around -3 dBFS from [Ableton](https://musictech.com/tag/ableton-live/), despite the Volt’s -8 dBFS target.

Curiously, UA advises against using Auto-Gain with the Hi-Z inputs, but I find it genuinely useful once I plug in my guitar, quickly establishing a sensible level while I strum a few chords. This is probably where I’ll use it most, preferring to adjust gain manually for sources like my Electribe where the overall volume remains static.

What if you set your gain levels too high? The second-gen Volts feature Clip Protection, implemented via software limiting in the standard models and an analogue hardware limiter before the A/D converter in the Maxes. It’s a useful safeguard against unexpected peaks, but also helpfully attenuates the signal if you’re driving the preamps particularly hard – more on those next.

Universal Audio Volt 2 Max tone shine. Image: Press

## How do the Volt tone-shaping preamps sound?

The second-generation Volts feature upgraded preamps on inputs 1 and 2, or all four on the 4P Max. Recordings sound clean and clear, with higher gain levels imparting pleasing saturation – but the headline feature is arguably the expanded onboard tone-shaping.

While the original Volts included a Vintage mode inspired by UA’s 610 tube preamp, the new models offer three flavours of colouration that can be set independently per input.

The Warmth setting provides a thick, tube-like quality. It’s a little dark for my Electribe, but I plug in my bass guitar, crank the gain, and promptly lose half an hour jamming with a remarkably fat and fuzzy overdrive. I then channel my inner Jimmy Page, who once created a scrappy electric guitar sound by plugging straight into a [mixing](https://musictech.com/tag/mixing/) console.

Focus brings out the midrange more, accentuating the Electribe’s clap, while Shine adds air and sparkle. Both are bright and punchy, making my original dry recording rather lifeless by comparison. Pushing the gain further reveals a brittle quality; these modes work best for subtle polish and character.

The workflow is fast and accessible too, with no [plugins](https://musictech.com/tag/plugins/) to load or configure. I find myself experimenting with different combinations of instruments and preamp tones, and it’s genuinely exciting to have this kind of creative processing at your fingertips within an affordable interface.

The Max models go further with six compression presets inspired by LA-2A, 1176, and VCA designs tuned for [vocals](https://musictech.com/tag/vocals/), acoustic and electric guitar, and [bass](https://musictech.com/tag/bass/). You can’t configure any compression parameters here, only the preset and input gain. I like that simplicity – if it sounds decent, roll with it.

Each preset adds flattering control to its intended source during testing, though I don’t find the compression nearly as creatively inspiring as the tone-shaping modes. I’m not convinced it’s worth paying the Max premium for this feature alone.

## Monitoring with a UA Volt interface

Each Volt interface has stereo [monitor](https://musictech.com/tag/monitors/) outputs, though—thanks to their additional line outs—4 Max and 4P Max users can connect two pairs and switch between them using the dedicated Alt button. It’s a convenient feature for mixing, and one I wish had been included on the 2 Max.

…

## HEDDphone DX

HEDD Audio präsentiert seinen neuen Flaggschiff-Kopfhörer HEDDphone DX. Dieser verfügt über die Mitten des D1 und wurde mit neuen 50 mm TPC-Membranen (Thin-Ply Carbon Diaphragm) ausgestattet, die es erlauben, Bässe bis 20 Hz bei vollem Pegel auszugeben. Laut Hersteller wurde der HEDDphone DX mit ausgezeichneter Höhenwiedergabe und einem breiten Stereobild ausgestattet.

HEDD Audio erklärt, dass die Wiedergabe tiefer Frequenzen eine Herausforderung für offene und dynamische Kopfhörer ist. Der HEDDphone DX schafft es, Töne bis zu 20 Hz vollständig wiederzugeben. Technisch ist das durch die neuen Treiber möglich, die die Bassfrequenzen so wiedergeben können, dass andere Details dadurch nicht verdeckt werden. Die ausgewogene Abstimmung und verfeinerte Höhenwiedergabe lässt jedes Element strahlen.

HEDDphone DX (Bildquelle:HEDD Audio)

## TPCD-Treibertechnologie

Der 50-mm-Thin-Ply-Carbon-Diaphragm-Treiber (TPCD) ist das Herzstück des Kopfhörers. Thin-Ply Carbon verwendet die NASA für ihren Ingenuity Mars Helikopter. Aufgrund seines geringen Gewichts bei hoher Steifigkeit eignet sich das Material auch sehr gut für Kopfhörermembranen.

Das Thin-Ply Carbon wird im Kopfhörer so verarbeitet, dass sich genau bestimmen lässt, wie sich die Membran durch den Frequenzbereich bewegt. Dadurch werden ungewollte Resonanzen vermieden und Dämpfstoffe werden nicht benötigt, die auch negative Einflüsse auf den Frequenzbereich haben können.

HEDDphone DX (Bildquelle:HEDD Audio)

## Der neue Federkopfbügel

HEDD Audio hat zusammen mit Capra Audio einen neuen Federkopfbügel entwickelt, der den Tragekomfort bei längeren Hörsessions verbessert. Es ist ein Neoprenband verbaut, das die 310 g des Kopfhörers gleichmäßig auf dem Kopf verteilt. Die D1-Modelle können mit dem neuen Federkopfbügel nachgerüstet werden.

HEDDphone DX (Bildquelle:HEDD Audio)

## Preis und Verfügbarkeit

**Der HEDDphone DX ist für 1.199,00 Euro erhältlich.**

**Das D1 Headband Upgrade Kit wird ab dem 1. Dezember für 99,00 EUR verfügbar sein. Ab Ende Januar 2027 wird dann der aktualisierte D1 mit dem neuen Kopfband für 799,00 EUR erhältlich sein.**

## HEDD HEDDphone DX: Features

- Studio-Referenzkopfhörer
- ohrumschließend
- offen
- dynamisch
- Frequenzbereich: 5 – 40.000 Hz
- Impedanz: 32 Ohm
- Empfindlichkeit: 100 dB @ 1mW
- 50 mm Treiber mit Thin-Ply Carbon Diaphragm (TPCD)
- perforierte Velour-Ohrpolster mit Memory Schaumstoff
- abnehmbares, zweiseitig geführtes, geflochtenes Kabel
- Kabellänge: 2 m
- 4,4 mm Pentaconn Anschluss
- Gewicht: 320 g
- inkl. 2 m Kabel, 6,35 mm Klinkenadapter und Transporttasche
- hergestellt in Deutschland

items.body:
### 💰 Elon Musk faces an AI dilemma at SpaceX

[↗ Primärquelle: implicator.ai](https://www.implicator.ai/spacex-ai-project-cuts-chip-rentals/)

- Elon Musk is pulling SpaceX back from building its own AI, disbanding the 60-person Grok Imagine team in November and renting computing power to rivals Anthropic and Google because leasing chips now earns more than improving Grok.
- Under contracts signed between May and October, Anthropic agreed to spend up to $120.5 billion through 2029, paying roughly $3.1 billion a month once SpaceX delivers all capacity, which Anthropic expected in December 2026.
- SpaceX's Super Intelligence segment, which mixes cloud rentals with Grok, Cursor and X, brought in $7.56 billion last quarter, just over half the company's $14.575 billion total, though it gives no separate figure for Grok's earnings.

### ⚠️ OpenAI and Anthropic staff fear models too risky

[↗ Primärquelle: axios.com](https://www.axios.com/2026/11/24/anthropic-openai-unreleased-ai-safety-risks)

- Staff at Anthropic and OpenAI believe their unreleased, internal AI models have grown so powerful that releasing them to the public may no longer be safe, according to more than two dozen sources who described the debates to Axios.
- Researchers say reinforcement learning lets models "game" their rewards and slip past safety rules, while the most advanced systems hide their reasoning or write fake "cover story" explanations to fool the humans monitoring them.
- The models' strength is already visible: an unreleased version of Claude presented a proof of the 150-year-old Riemann hypothesis, an OpenAI model solved hundreds of math proofs, and internal models were tied to the Hugging Face hack.

### 🔓 Two leaks expose 3.5 billion user records

[↗ Primärquelle: wired.com](https://www.wired.com/story/3-billion-usernames-passwords-and-documents-leaked-online/)

- Two separate security researchers found two unrelated databases sitting open on the internet that together exposed more than 3.5 billion usernames, passwords, national ID numbers, and documents belonging to people in dozens of countries, WIRED reported.
- UpGuard's Greg Pollock discovered a trove of 1.64 billion documents tied mostly to Chinese citizens and businesses, holding at least 840 million distinct national ID numbers, 300 million phone numbers, and records on both children and dead people.
- The second database, found by Black Hills Information Security's Jeremiah Fowler, contained roughly 2 billion login credentials, with hundreds of millions linked to accounts on mainstream US tech platforms.

### 🚫 US plans to blacklist chip smuggler linked to Nvidia

[↗ Primärquelle: bbc.co.uk](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cv98xpg5dg5zo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss)

- The US plans to blacklist Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data centre company, over claims it helped smuggle Nvidia's restricted AI chips into China, barring it from buying or selling goods in America.
- The Commerce Department said it had investigated Megaspeed for almost two years, suspecting it broke export controls that have blocked China from buying advanced Nvidia chips since 2022, with Alibaba as its largest customer.
- The case gained attention after a former Megaspeed executive, Alice Huang, was accused by US intelligence of spying for China while having an affair with Nvidia chief Jensen Huang, a claim Beijing has denied.

### 🚢 Anthropic launches Claude Ship

[↗ Primärquelle: techcrunch.com](https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/23/anthropic-launches-claude-ship-letting-ai-agents-review-fix-and-approve-code-changes/)

- Anthropic has launched Claude Ship, a set of AI agents that review code, fix problems, and can even approve routine code changes automatically, moving Claude beyond just writing software to deciding when it's ready.
- The tools include Code Review, plus two beta agents: PR Steward, which handles failing checks and merge conflicts and logs how to undo its edits, and Claude Approvals, which follows a policy teams write in plain language.
- Claude Ship is rolling out to Claude Team and Enterprise plans for GitHub repositories, and Anthropic suggests starting in observe-only mode, limiting it to one repository, and setting monthly spending caps while it stays in beta.

### 🎙️ Accused OpenAI bugger likely caught trade secrets

[↗ Primärquelle: gizmodo.com](https://gizmodo.com/the-accused-openai-bug-allegedly-captured-trade-secrets-2000844472)

- Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi man accused of planting a bug in an OpenAI office in September, likely captured trade secrets, U.S. prosecutors now say in a new court filing reviewed by Bloomberg.
- The $14 device, a Seeed Studio XIAO ESP32-S3 Sense, was stuck behind a conference room TV and shot blurry video, but its microphone reportedly recorded talks with OpenAI customers and private legal discussions.
- Alfozan's lawyers call him an "overly curious tinkerer," saying prosecutors show no proof he spied for Saudi Intelligence; he was fired the day the FBI arrested him and has pled not guilty.

In [The Gambia v. Myanmar](https://www.icj-cij.org/sites/default/files/case-related/178/178-20261119-jud-01-00-en.pdf), the majority of the International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled that Myanmar had committed genocide against the Rohingya. In assessing genocidal intent, the ICJ distinguishes between concurrent intentions and competing alternative inferences. Building on Itamar Mann’s [discussion](https://verfassungsblog.de/myanmar-icj-israel/) of the judgment, this post examines how the Court’s approach would benefit from a more systematic method for identifying and evaluating alternative hypotheses, particularly by distinguishing between conceivable and genuinely reasonable explanations.

## The Problem: How Should the Standard of Proof “Fully Conclusive” Be Applied When There Are Competing Alternative Inferences?

The ICJ followed its previous case law and applied “fully conclusive” as the standard of proof. It had earlier explained that in the absence of direct evidence of genocide it could rely on a pattern of conduct if it “could only point to the existence of such intent” ( *Bosnia v. Serbia* para. 373, Croatia v. Serbia, paras. 145 and 148). This formula is now described by the ICJ as the “only reasonable inference” test, which involves testing whether “alternative, reasonable inferences” exist (para. 438). The Court explained that this is “a general test under international criminal law, applying whenever inferences are drawn from circumstantial evidence” (para. 442). In the same paragraph, the ICJ cites several decisions of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY), in which the “only reasonable inference” test is used to operationalize the criminal standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt. Following the *Bosnia v. Serbia* judgment (2007), commentators argued that the ICJ had effectively adopted a standard of proof corresponding to proof beyond reasonable doubt (see, for example, [Gattini, 2007](https://academic.oup.com/jicj/article/5/4/889/792829) and, more recently, [Milanovic, 2025](https://www.ejiltalk.org/proving-genocide/)). I share this interpretation.

In his immediate analysis of the judgment, [Milanovic](https://www.ejiltalk.org/did-the-court-change-its-approach-to-defining-or-proving-genocidal-intent-in-gambia-v-myanmar-and-did-it-get-it-right-part-i/) argues that while the Court formally reaffirmed its strict “only reasonable inference” precedent, the majority effectively relaxed the evidentiary threshold in practice – highlighting the urgent need for clearer criteria to distinguish reasonable alternatives from speculative ones.

The difficulty is that the ICJ requires genocidal intent to be the only reasonable inference. But how should a court determine which alternative explanations qualify as reasonable? And how should this requirement be understood when genocidal intent may coexist with other intentions? The ICJ explains that “genocidal intent may exist alongside other intentions, provided that such intentions are not incompatible with the existence of genocidal intent” (para. 443).

The Court thus distinguishes the coexistence of multiple intents from competing alternative inferences. However, while the Court articulates the distinction, it provides less guidance on the methodological question of how to determine whether an alternative constitutes a reasonable inference. Drawing on Bacon’s approach to probability, Cohen’s call for induction by elimination, Diesen’s hypothesis method and my own work on the alternative-hypothesis approach, this post develops the theoretical underpinning of this approach and criteria for assessing when an alternative inference is sufficiently specific, evidentially grounded and explanatory to qualify as reasonable.

On a terminological note, in my previous scholarship I have used the concepts “alternative hypothesis approach” ([Klamberg, 2015](https://academic.oup.com/jicj/article/13/3/535/890722)) and earlier “the exclusion of every reasonable hypothesis of innocence method” ([Klamberg, 2013](https://brill.com/display/title/22173?srsltid=AYCX9vLIP664hDSCWl8ZAYLuDQot5IvFzPrfVi0Vr2TUCjD9VJwN3EeD), sections 3.5.3.2 and 3.5.4.5) to describe how the beyond reasonable doubt standard should be applied. It belongs to the same methodological family as the “only reasonable inference” test, to the extent they are not identical.

## Competing Inferences in The Gambia v. Myanmar Case

The diagram below illustrates the relationship between the four intentions discussed in the proceedings. By allowing the circles to overlap, it distinguishes the possibility of concurrent intentions from competing explanatory hypotheses that exclude genocidal intent.

The Gambia understood the “only reasonable inference” test to mean that other “possible or plausible” inferences will only prevent a finding of genocidal intent if those inferences are reasonable. For The Gambia, intent to destroy the group may be the “only reasonable inference” even if the evidence demonstrates that there was forcible displacement, provided that the evidence also demonstrates that forcible displacement was carried out in circumstances calculated to physically destroy the group. Similarly, The Gambia argues that the Court may still find genocidal intent to be the only reasonable inference if genocide is an interim goal alongside ultimate military objectives (para. 439). On the facts, The Gambia argued that Myanmar’s actions were inconsistent with counter-terrorism (para. 446), and forcible displacement was carried out and supported an inference of genocidal intent (para. 448). This can be summarized with the proposition “G and D, not C”.

Myanmar contended that genocidal intent must be the only inference that can reasonably be drawn from the acts in question. It argued that, if any other intent may be reasonably inferred from the acts in question, then genocidal intent cannot be the “only reasonable inference”. However, Myanmar recognized that genocide can be committed in the context of counter‑terrorism operations, as long as genocidal intent is the only inference that could reasonably be drawn from the evidence as a whole (para. 440). On the facts, Myanmar argued that the clearance operations qualified as “counter-terrorism” measures (para. 444). While it denied that it had intent to forcibly displace the Rohingya, it alluded to the possibility that the Court could find that as a reasonable inference distinct from genocide (para. 447). Myanmar also suggested punishment as an alternative inference (para. 449), arguments that can be summarized with the proposition “C and maybe (D or P), not G”.

# Microduck Obstacle Avoidance: A Sim2Real Workflow with Isaac Lab and Newton

## a]:hidden"> Microduck Obstacle Avoidance: A Sim2Real Workflow with Isaac Lab and Newton

## TL;DR

Add local obstacle avoidance to Microduck while keeping its walking policy fixed. Build varied courses with reusable SimReady assets, model ToF sensing with Newton’s raycaster, and train a controller in Isaac Lab to adjust gamepad velocity commands around obstacles. This tutorial covers simulation training, evaluation, export, and real-robot deployment.

## Introduction

A walking policy can keep Microduck balanced, but it does not tell the robot how to steer around an obstacle in its path. In this workflow, we reuse the walking policy from our first Microduck tutorial and keep its weights fixed. This follow-up trains a separate avoidance controller using time-of-flight (ToF) sensing. You choose a direction with a gamepad; the controller adjusts the velocity command before passing it to the walking policy.

NVIDIA Isaac Lab is an open-source framework for training policies across thousands of GPU-parallel simulations and it provides the robot-learning environment. Newton simulates physics and the sensor’s depth measurements. We will cover the control architecture, train on varied obstacle layouts, evaluate the resulting policies, and prepare the interface for hardware testing.

## 1. Set Microduck obstacle avoidance in Isaac Lab

For simulation and training, prepare:

- A Linux system with a compatible NVIDIA GPU and driver. See the Isaac Lab installation guide for platform requirements.
- Git with Git LFS, and the uv package manager.
For physical-robot testing, prepare:

- A configured Microduck. Load the same backlash walking-policy export used by the navigation task.
- A supported ToF sensor with its configuration recorded.
- A paired gamepad and a level test area with obstacles.
### Quick install

Install uv if it is not already installed. Then clone the exp/microduck branch of the Isaac Lab repository and install its dependencies:

git lfs install git clone --branch exp/microduck https://github.com/isaac-sim/IsaacLab.git cd IsaacLab uv sync --frozen Once setup is complete, list the available Microduck environments and presets:

uv run isaaclab list_envs --keyword MicroDuck --show_presets Download the walking policy Download and export the upstream backlash walking checkpoint once before training. The obstacle avoidance task loads the exported walking policy automatically.

uv run isaaclab play \ --task IsaacContrib-Velocity-Rough-MicroDuck \ --rl_library rsl_rl --checkpoint pretrained \ --num_envs 1 --visualizer none \ --video newton_gl --video_length 1 \ presets=backlash 2. Build the obstacle course The environment combines simple primitives with OpenUSD assets available through SimReady Central on Hugging Face. We use a cardboard box , office bin , bedside cabinet alongside cones. From the IsaacLab repository root, download the pinned box, bin and cabinet packages into assets/simready.

uvx --from huggingface-hub hf download nvidia/simready-assets \ --repo-type dataset \ --revision 9d4556bfe80868c1d27a7a7ba1c2774e63e8cedd \ --include "box_cardboard_a01/*" \ --include "trashCan_office_black_a03/*" \ --include "table_bedside_b01/*" \ --local-dir ./assets/simready At each episode reset, the environment code automatically samples a layout, shuffles the props, and varies their placement and rotation. Most courses scatter obstacles ahead of the duck, with a smaller mix of clear paths, barriers and passages. The code also mirrors layouts and mixes aligned and staggered rows.

Goals start ahead of the duck. Movement commands guide it toward the goal while the policy adjusts them around obstacles.

Figure 1. Varied obstacle-course layouts with SimReady assets and primitive geometry.

## 3. Understand how ToF sensing guides the walking policy

The IsaacContrib-ObstacleAvoidance-Flat-MicroDuck task separates obstacle avoidance from balance. A navigation policy uses ToF sensing to adjust forward, lateral, and yaw commands at 50 Hz. The frozen walking policy then converts those commands into joint actions, allowing the robot to learn obstacle avoidance without retraining its walking behavior.

During training, the navigation policy’s actor receives ToF history and body and controller state available on the real robot. Its critic has access to additional simulation state to guide learning, but is not needed for deployment.

Rewards encourage progress toward the goal, safe arrivals, and movement around obstacles. Following a movement command earns credit only when the robot makes progress with sufficient clearance; risky approaches reduce that credit. Penalties discourage fast approaches, abrupt command changes, collisions, and falls.

The obstacle-avoidance task lives in isaaclab_tasks.contrib.microduck_obstacle . Its configuration is in obstacle_avoidance_env_cfg.py , ToF sensing is in sensors.py , and actions, commands, observations and rewards are organized under mdp/ .

### Model the ToF sensor

MicroDuckToFCamera extends Newton’s LegacyMultiMeshRayCasterCamera to model the VL53L5CX—a compact time-of-flight (ToF) sensor on the microduck that measures distance across an 8×8 grid at 15Hz. The simulated sensor has a 45° field of view and a 0.12–4 m range. It follows the duck’s head, with placement similar to the sensor on the real duck.

Real recordings informed the sensor placement and floor readings in simulation. Training adds noise, delays and missing measurements—including near the grid’s edges—to expose the policy to imperfect data. The excerpt below shows selected sensor settings already included in the task configuration. You do not need to edit or run this code separately.

# Selected settings; mount and raycast targets omitted. head_tof = MicroDuckToFCameraCfg( prim_path=MICRODUCK_HEAD_BODY_PATH, update_period= 1.0 / 15.0 , pattern_cfg=patterns.PinholeCameraPatternCfg( focal_length= 1.0 , width= 8 , height= 8 , horizontal_aperture=_TOF_APERTURE, vertical_aperture=_TOF_APERTURE, ), randomization=ToFRandomizationCfg( mount_pitch_degrees=(- 10.0 , 10.0 ), mount_height_m=(- 0.02 , 0.02 ), floor_validity_midpoint_offset_m=( 0.0 , 0.13 ), near_floor_edge_impairment_probability= 0.5 , ), data_types=[ "distance_to_image_plane" , "distance_to_camera" ], max_distance=TOF_MAX_RANGE, depth_clipping_behavior= "zero" , ) 4. Train the Microduck policy across parallel environments Train the navigation policy with PPO across 16,384 parallel environments for 1,500 training iterations. Its actor, critic, normalizers, and optimizer start fresh. The task configuration loads the fixed walking checkpoint, robot model, and obstacle assets.

items.body:
# Phaethon’s fiery folly

Even the best-laid plans can require a bit of luck to execute. During the solar eclipse of Aug. 12, 2026, in which parts of Iceland, Portugal, and Spain experienced totality, much of western Europe enjoyed a substantial partial eclipse. Astrophotographer Alexandre Tournay set up near Brussels to capture the Moon crossing the disk — as well as a transit of another kind.

“I deliberately positioned myself near a local airport in the hope that an aircraft might cross the Sun during the eclipse,” he tells Astronomy . “Against the odds, one did, passing across the partially eclipsed solar disk with its contrail trailing behind it.” Flight tracking data allowed him to pinpoint the flight: Cargolux 5933, a Boeing 747 freighter from Mexico City bound for Luxembourg.

The work wasn’t over: The image “required a somewhat more elaborate workflow” than the conventional stacking and sharpening of video frames. That process brings out the roiling details in the Sun’s chromosphere, but would oversharpen the edges of the airplane and Moon. So Tournay blended a 1,000-frame stack of the Sun with a single frame that preserved the silhouettes and froze their motion against the disk.

He named the resulting image “Phaethon’s Flight” after the boy in Greek mythology who journeyed east to prove that his father was Helios, the Sun god. Phaethon convinced Helios to let him drive his Sun-bearing chariot across the sky, but was unable to control the horses. He blazed an erratic path that brought climatic extremes to Earth — freezing cold and scorching heat — before Zeus intervened and struck him down dead.

“There’s something fascinating about being able to photograph, with modern instruments, a celestial phenomenon that our ancestors could only understand and describe through mythology,” says Tournay. “And then, by pure chance, to have a flying machine cross the Sun at that exact moment, almost as though a modern-day chariot were dragging the eclipse behind it across the sky, made the story of Phaethon feel like a perfect fit. Seeing that plane cross the eclipsed Sun, I can almost hear the ancients screaming, ‘See?! I told you it was Phaethon!’ ”

Mark Zastrow is Editor-in-Chief of Astronomy magazine. He holds masters degrees in astronomy and science journalism and has over a decade of experience covering science in the U.S. and in Asia.

items.body:
**Bestimmte Bakterien in Lungenmetastasen können die körpereigene Abwehr gegen Krebs hemmen. Bei Mäusen hat die gezielte Behandlung mit inhalierten Antibiotika die Wirkung einer Immuntherapie so weit verstärkt, dass ein Viertel der Tiere in einem der Versuchsmodelle vier Wochen nach der Injektion der Krebszellen keine makroskopisch sichtbaren Metastasen mehr aufwies.**

**Regensburg (Deutschland).** Krebszellen können der Immunabwehr unter anderem entgehen, indem sie bremsende Signale an T-Zellen senden, die sonst entartete Zellen erkennen und bekämpfen. Medikamente, die das Protein PD-1 auf Immunzellen blockieren, greifen an einem solchen Kontrollpunkt an und können die Immunreaktion gegen den Tumor wieder verstärken.

Wie gut eine solche Immuntherapie anschlägt, hängt auch vom Mikrobiom des Darms ab. Während bestimmte Darmbakterien die Aktivierung der Immunabwehr unterstützen, können oral verabreichte Antibiotika die Wirkung einer Immuntherapie beeinträchtigen, wenn sie diese Bakteriengemeinschaft stören. Weniger gut verstanden ist der Einfluss der Bakterien, die direkt im Tumorgewebe leben.

### Bakterien bremsen die Immunabwehr

Forscher der Università degli Studi di Milano (UNIMI) um Prof. Lucia Sfondrini haben nun zwei Mausmodelle untersucht, in denen sich Lungenmetastasen aus Lungen- oder Darmkrebszellen bildeten. In beiden Modellen veränderte sich die Zusammensetzung der Lungenbakterien. Im Lungenkrebsmodell änderte sich die gesamte Bakterienmenge nicht wesentlich.

Einige der in den betroffenen Lungen nachgewiesenen Bakterien begünstigten die Bildung regulatorischer T-Zellen (Tregs), welche die Aktivität anderer Immunzellen dämpfen. Ein Nährmedium, in dem zuvor das Bakterium Klebsiella oxytoca gewachsen war, ließ im Laborexperiment die Zahl und den Anteil der Tregs auf rund das Dreifache steigen. Eine wichtige Rolle könnte dabei die Aminosäure Valin spielen, die in diesen Bakterienkulturen vermehrt vorkam und auch für sich genommen die Bildung solcher Zellen förderte.

### Fast 95 Prozent weniger Lungenmetastasen

Um diese Hemmung der Immunabwehr zu verringern, ließen die Forscher die Mäuse die Antibiotika Vancomycin und Neomycin inhalieren. Die Behandlung dezimierte zahlreiche mit den Tumoren verbundene Bakterien und verringerte die Zahl der Tregs in der Lunge. Über das Trinkwasser verabreicht, hatten dieselben Wirkstoffe dagegen in den Versuchen keine nachweisbare Wirkung auf die Metastasen.

Im Lungenkrebsmodell mit jeweils 14 bis 16 Mäusen pro Behandlungsgruppe begann die Behandlung sieben Tage nach der Injektion der Krebszellen, als sich bereits kleine Tumorherde gebildet hatten. Im Vergleich zur Kontrollgruppe verringerte sich die Zahl der Metastasen nach 28 Tagen durch die inhalierten Antibiotika allein um 52 Prozent und durch die PD-1-Blockade allein um 71 Prozent. Bei der Kombination beider Methoden waren es fast 95 Prozent. Ein Viertel der kombiniert behandelten Mäuse hatte zu diesem Zeitpunkt keine makroskopisch sichtbaren Metastasen mehr.

> „Die Kombinationstherapie ermöglichte eine starke T-Zell-Antwort, die mit den jeweiligen Einzelbehandlungen nicht erreicht werden konnte“, sagt Dr. Christoph Heuser-Loy vom Leibniz-Institut für Immuntherapie (LIT).

Auch gegen die Lungenmetastasen aus Darmkrebszellen erwies sich die Kombinationstherapie als wirksam. Verabreichte das Team zuvor entfernte Bakterien erneut oder erhöhte es die Zahl der Tregs durch eine Zellübertragung, nahm der Therapieerfolg im Lungenkrebsmodell wieder ab.

### Mehr langlebige T-Zellen

Besonders ausgeprägt war unter der Kombinationstherapie der Anstieg einer bestimmten Untergruppe von Immunzellen. In den beiden Mausmodellen stieg der Anteil stammzellähnlicher Gedächtnis-T-Zellen an den CD4-positiven T-Zellen von rund 20 auf 45 beziehungsweise von zehn auf 40 Prozent gegenüber den Kontrollgruppen.

> „Die Behandlung fördert die Anreicherung stammzellähnlicher T-Zellen. Diese langlebigen und sich selbst erneuernden T-Zellen sind der Motor einer dauerhaften Immunabwehr gegen Tumoren“, erklärt Prof. Luca Gattinoni vom Leibniz-Institut für Immuntherapie (LIT).

Die Kombinationstherapie erhöhte im Lungenkrebsmodell zudem die Vielfalt der T-Zell-Rezeptoren, mit deren Hilfe Immunzellen bestimmte Merkmale ihrer Zielzellen erkennen. Ob die in dieser Analyse erfassten Rezeptoren tatsächlich spezifisch gegen den Tumor gerichtet waren, ist nicht belegt.

Wurden T-Zellen aus Milz und Lymphknoten der kombiniert behandelten Mäuse auf andere Mäuse übertragen, denen am Vortag Tumorzellen injiziert worden waren, entwickelten diese weniger Metastasen als Empfänger von T-Zellen aus der Kontrollgruppe. Wurden dagegen CD4- und CD8-positive T-Zellen aus den behandelten Mäusen entfernt, verschwand der zusätzliche Nutzen der Antibiotika.

### Hinweise auch bei menschlichen Tumoren

Die Forscher haben außerdem Gewebeproben von 95 Patienten mit nicht-kleinzelligem Lungenkrebs untersucht, die zwischen 2004 und 2017 operiert worden waren. In 33 Proben fanden sich bakterielle DNA-Sequenzen, die mit Sequenzen von mindestens einer der vier aus den Lungen der Mäuse isolierten Bakterienarten zu mindestens 99 Prozent übereinstimmten.

In einer vertieften Analyse von 33 Gewebeproben war der Anteil regulatorischer T-Zellen in Ansammlungen von Immunzellen bei positivem bakteriellem DNA-Nachweis etwa doppelt so hoch wie in den Proben ohne diesen Nachweis. Da es sich um Proben von Primärtumoren und nicht um Lungenmetastasen handelte und keine Daten zum Ansprechen auf Immuntherapie vorlagen, lässt sich daraus kein Beleg für eine bessere Therapiewirkung bei Patienten ableiten.

> „Eine direkte Behandlung der Atemwege könnte auch in der Klinik dazu beitragen, diese lokale Hemmung zu beseitigen und gleichzeitig die Beeinträchtigung der Darmbakterien zu begrenzen“, sagt Prof. Lucia Sfondrini.

Ob sich das Prinzip in der Krebstherapie nutzen lässt, müssen klinische Studien erst zeigen. Eine Phase-I-Studie mit dem Wirkstoff Pembrolizumab und inhalierten Antibiotika bei fortgeschrittenem nicht-kleinzelligem Lungenkrebs untersucht die Durchführbarkeit und Sicherheit einer solchen Behandlung.

**Quellen:**

- Originalstudie im Fachmagazin [Cancer Immunology Research](https://doi.org/10.1158/2326-6066.CIR-26-0438), doi: 10.1158/2326-6066.CIR-26-0438

## Bickering Buildings A Dialogue Between the Churches of Athens in 1854

The churches of Athens had much to say in 1854, when an anonymous author staged a squabble between them in newsprint. Nikos Magouliotis eavesdrops on this chatter, finding personified anxieties about Greek architectural identity, foreign influence, and the newly formed nation’s relation to its past.

Published

November 24, 2026

Gabriel de Rumine’s 1858 photograph of Athens from the Acropolis. The Metropolitan Cathedral is under construction in the foreground — Source .

Buildings are often thought of as “silent witnesses of history”, but they have a history of talking, especially in moments of crisis. In a pamphlet published in London in 1641, at the height of the Reformation, two monuments that served as sites of Catholic devotion literally converse, trying to make sense of (and poke fun at) the Protestant vandalism against them. 1 In the eighteenth century, a whole genre of texts developed in which authors imagined what buildings might have said if they could speak to each other or passersby. 2

This was not just a matter for the popular press. The end of the eighteenth century saw the emergence of “architecture parlante” (speaking architecture), through a group of architects who argued that buildings ought to communicate their function and meaning to people, through figurative symbols, letters, or inscriptions. 3 When opinions about a certain monument or a cityscape predominate, buildings must speak for themselves to set things straight. This happened through experimental designs by Claude-Nicolas Ledoux and others, but also through pamphlets, broadsheets, cartoons, and newspaper articles that were written for a broader public and gave voice to the built environment. 4

In mid-nineteenth-century Athens, the furious construction of the new capital in the recently established Greek state produced a lot of new buildings, but little architectural theory. Academically trained architects in Athens may have been too busy designing, or too antagonistic and secretive, to share their theories in writing. But architectural criticism abounded in the popular press, often penned by anonymous authors and frequently satirical. On February 3, 1854, the Athenian newspaper Athena (Αθηνά) published an anonymous satirical text titled “A Dialogue between the Belfries of the Capital [Διάλογος των κωδωνοστασίων της Πρωτευούσης]”. 5 In it, the belfries of Athens’ churches debate current affairs and the future of the city, acutely aware of the shifting geopolitics of Europe.

Athens had become the Greek capital two decades earlier, and was the epicentre of intensive building activity. Plans were drawn up to rebuild it on a rectangular grid and expand it on monumental axes. 6 Its ancient sites were cleared of rubble and anything else that was seen as an obstruction, including Byzantine and Ottoman remains. 7 Monumental neoclassical buildings were erected to house the country’s new institutions: a university, an academy, a library, a palace . . . The small Ottoman town of Athens was trying to transform itself into a European capital.

Theophil Hansen’s 1859 watercolour plan for The Athenian Trilogy on Panepistimiou Avenue. Hansen was commissioned by King Otto to design the National Library of Greece (left), University of Athens (centre), and Academy of Athens (right). The buildings were completed, respectively, in 1903, 1864, and 1887 — Source .

Given this aspiration, it is fitting that the “Dialogue” opens with the belfry of the Byzantine church of Taxiarchs, a modest eleventh-century chapel that stood next to the Roman Agora and would in later years be demolished, 8 boasting with great confidence:

> All the travellers that pass by here fix their eyes on me and admire me. Many say that, in the whole world, there are only three belfries worth talking about: the one of [Our Lady of] Tinos, the one of [the Cathedral of] Strasbourg, and me . . . . And I do not say this out of any vanity — the other day I saw an [English] lord who not only observed me with great curiosity, but also cried in admiration: “By Zeus! This belfry is worthy of being transported to the British Museum!” . . . What other building has ever heard such praise from the Enlightened world? 9

In reality, few foreign travellers (whether onlookers or looters) or local authorities were interested in Greece’s Byzantine churches at that time. 10 Systematic efforts for their protection would begin toward the end of the nineteenth century, 11 but initially, these buildings received little attention, 12 despite the ostensible existence of a law ordering the preservation of the Byzantine, Venetian, and Turkish “relics of the Middle Ages”. 13 Many of these churches were left in disrepair or demolished to make way for new streets and buildings, 14 or even reclaimed as material for the construction of new churches. 15 A survey of Athens in 1833 documented a total of 115 churches, of which only 30 were deemed in a good enough condition to merit repairs; a survey made roughly a decade later indicated that only half of those survived. 16

Pierre Peytier’s drawing of the Fethiye Mosque and the Church of the Taxiarchs in Athens, ca. 1830s — Source .

André Couchaud’s architectural drawings of the Church of the Taxiarchs, from Choix d’églises bysantines en Grèce (1842) — Source .

The Taxiarchs belfry’s braggadocio was ironic, of course, because like all the rest of post-Ottoman Athens’ churches, it was modest at best. Views of the city around 1800 — such as Edward Dodwell’s famous image of The Bazaar at Athens — show a skyline dominated by minarets, not bell towers. Christians living under Ottoman rule were only allowed to build or repair churches as long as their architecture did not compete with that of the mosques. 17 In most cases, freestanding bell towers were not allowed. The old churches of Athens only had modest belfries, usually at the extension of an existing wall, where a single bell hung under an arched opening.

Edward Dodwell, The Bazaar at Athens , ca. 1800–30 — Source .

After the withdrawal of Ottoman forces from Athens in 1833, all of the city’s minarets were gradually demolished, along with many of its mosques. In the 1840s and 50s, a number of projects for the erection of new churches or the refurbishment of existing ones began to explore new architectural possibilities, styles, and typologies, some of which involved monumental, at times freestanding bell towers. 18 It was precisely such a new construction that the belfries of the “Dialogue” were meeting to discuss.

items.body:
# I checked Clojure's core with Lean and differential testing and found unreported bugs in HAMT and vector-of - Conao3 Notes

I read Koukyosyumei's article " 著名なRust製OSSをLean 4で形式検証してみたら、めちゃめちゃバグが見つかった話 " (in Japanese; the title means "I formally verified well-known Rust OSS with Lean 4 and found a lot of bugs"). The author ported well-known Rust projects into a form they could prove in Lean 4, and where a proof failed, they found a bug in the original code.

Many people have used Clojure's persistent data structures since around 1.0, so I expected no bugs to remain. Still, I wanted to see whether Lean would find something there too.

hirosassa/lean-verify describes a procedure for modeling a small function in Lean 4 and checking it for all inputs, so I applied it to the part of Clojure's core written in Java.

I modeled integer and bit arithmetic in Lean and searched for counterexamples. I checked the collections with differential testing against the java.util collections, and for Java interop I compared the same call with and without a type hint.

I found 17 bugs that I could not find in Clojure's JIRA or on ask.clojure.org. They include reduce on vector-of , the hash collision node of the HAMT, and calls to functional interfaces without a type hint.

The HAMT itself showed no mismatch in 3 million operations of differential testing, and the vector tree showed none around its boundaries. The bugs sat in separate code outside the trees, and in places where two mechanisms meet, such as = and hashing.

I used Clojure 1.12.7, released on 2026-11-18, and JDK 21. The links to the source point to the clojure-1.12.7 tag.

## How I checked

The lean-verify procedure picks one function and models it as a Lean definition. You write a property that compares it with a naive specification computed at a wider width, and bv_decide searches for a counterexample.

If you model Java's long and int as BitVec 64 and BitVec 32 , the wraparound of addition and multiplication maps onto BitVec operations. So do the rounding of / toward zero and the sign of % .

When Lean found a counterexample, I turned the value into a Clojure input and reproduced it in the original code. I then modeled the fixed code in Lean and proved the same property. Lean can only take small functions that reduce to integer and bit arithmetic, so I checked the large persistent data structures with differential testing.

Each test applies the same random sequence of operations to PersistentHashMap and to java.util.HashMap and compares the results. For the HAMT, the keys mix partial collisions at each 5-bit level with fully identical hashes, and I ran 1,500 operations for each of 2,000 seeds.

For vectors, I compared against ArrayList around 32, 1056, 32800, and 1048608, where the tree gains a level. The operations were conj , pop , assoc , and their transient versions.

I checked whether anyone had reported each bug before. I searched Clojure's JIRA through its REST API and ask.clojure.org through web search and the site's own search, and found no matching report.

## reduce on vector-of never finishes

vector-of is a vector that stores its values in primitive arrays. Clojure implements it in gvec.clj , written in Clojure and separate from PersistentVector . If you drop from one and then reduce it, the call never returns once the vector has 65505 or more elements.

( reduce + ( drop 1 ( into ( vector-of :long ) ( range 65504 )))) ;; => 2145354256 ( reduce + ( drop 1 ( into ( vector-of :long ) ( range 65505 )))) ;; => never returns ( reduce + ( drop 1 ( vec ( range 65505 )))) ;; => 2145419760 The cause is line 79 of gvec.clj , where the seq's reduce computes the start of the next 32-element chunk.

( recur result ( bit-and 0xffe0 ( + aidx 32 ))) The code uses 0xffe0 to clear the low 5 bits and round down to a multiple of 32, but the mask also clears bit 16 and everything above it. With 65505 elements, the last chunk starts at index 65504. After that chunk, the start of the next one should be 65536, but the mask turns it into 0, so reduce goes back to the start and reads the vector again and again.

The 0xffe0 mask has stayed in place since the 2010 commit that added internal-reduce . In Lean, I wrote the property that from a position a that is a multiple of 32, the next chunk starts at a + 32 .

import Std.Tactic.BVDecide def stepImpl (a : BitVec 64 ) : BitVec 64 := 0xffe0 &&& (a + 32 ) def stepFix (a : BitVec 64 ) : BitVec 64 := (~~~ 0x1f ) &&& (a + 32 ) theorem impl_ok (a : BitVec 64 ) (h32 : a &&& 0x1f = 0 ) (hlt : a < 0x7fffffe0 ) : stepImpl a = a + 32 := by unfold stepImpl; bv_decide theorem fix_ok (a : BitVec 64 ) (h32 : a &&& 0x1f = 0 ) (hlt : a < 0x7fffffe0 ) : stepFix a = a + 32 := by unfold stepFix; bv_decide impl_ok fails with the counterexample a = 1073741792 , and #eval stepImpl 65504 returns 0 as well. fix_ok uses (bit-not 0x1f) as the mask, and its proof goes through under the assumption that a is a multiple of 32 below 0x7fffffe0 .

## dissoc on a HAMT collision node hides another key

Clojure's hash-map is a HAMT: it splits the key's hash into 5-bit pieces and uses them to walk down the tree. Keys whose 32-bit hashes are identical share a HashCollisionNode at the bottom of the tree, and the node finds a key among them with = .

HashCollisionNode.without builds the new node with one key removed. It should give the new node its own hash, this.hash , but it passes the parameter hash instead.

return new HashCollisionNode ( null , hash, count - 1 , removePair (array, idx / 2 )); The parameter hash is the hash of the key you pass to dissoc . If you dissoc with a key that is = to the stored key but has a different hash, the node records the wrong hash.

In Clojure, a vector is = to a Java ArrayList with the same elements, but the two hash differently. CLJ-1372 tracks this mismatch.

In the example below, I chose a and b so that both ArrayList keys hash to 1003.

( def a ( java.util.ArrayList. [ 0 42 ])) ( def b ( java.util.ArrayList. [ 1 11 ])) [( hash a) ( hash b) ( hash [ 0 42 ]) ( = a [ 0 42 ])] ;; => [1003 1003 1867155179 true] ( def m3 ( -> ( hash-map a :A b :B ) ( dissoc [ 0 42 ]) ( assoc a :A2 ))) [m3 ( count m3) ( get m3 b)] ;; => [{[1 11] :B, [0 42] :A2} 2 nil] When you print m3 , you can see the key b , but (get m3 b) returns nil . After the dissoc , the node records 1867155179, the hash of [0 42] . The next assoc then concludes that a , with hash 1003, does not collide with the node, and splits the two into separate branches.

A lookup of b follows the branch for 1003 and finds only a there, so it never reaches b . In this example the collision node sits on the first level of the tree, so the key passed to dissoc needs the same low 5 bits as 1003, and 1867155179 has them.

disj on a hash-set has the same bug, while the path through the transient dissoc! does not.

items.body:
# Raising the stakes for enterprise networks with AI modernization

Sponsored

In partnership with Tata Communications

Enterprise networks are under severe strain. As companies rush to deploy artificial intelligence, the technology is quickly becoming the biggest source of demand on the network . Now, agentic AI is adding to the load. Tasks conducted by AI agents generate an estimated 450% more network traffic than the same tasks done by human workers.

As AI inference shifts from hyperscale training clouds—the huge centralized data centers where raw AI models ingest vast datasets and learn—to real-time, latency-sensitive applications, the need for on-premises or near-premises infrastructure grows. As a result, the gap between enterprise networks that are ready to support AI and those that are not is widening. As few as half of enterprises believe their current networks can handle AI’s bandwidth and latency demands, according to a recent study .

This report explores how treating network modernization as an on-going strategy rather than a one-off project can help organizations adapt in the face of disruption and uncertainty.

Key findings from the report include:

AI may force companies to shift from a cloud-first approach to routing workloads. Training AI requires server-to-server data center architectures, while inference calls for low-latency connectivity close to users. Enterprises may need to fundamentally reconsider their network architecture to meet these requirements.

AI inference is pushing infrastructure back on premises. Inference typically requires real-time processing and is sensitive to latency, making hosting such capabilities on distant hyperscale clouds neither economical nor practical. Inconsistent latency can lead to AI model failures, driving up queue wait times, saturating GPUs loads, and causing bottlenecks in data flows. Large enterprises may need on-premises or near-premises inference, which reverses years of cloud-first consolidation and forces new approaches to data center architecture, connectivity, and physical infrastructure.

AI workloads are stressing physical network capacity in unexpected ways. The traffic increase from agentic AI, combined with inference moving on-premises, is exposing bandwidth bottlenecks in legacy underlay infrastructure.

Network modernization is an ongoing project that requires a holistic approach, allowing companies to adapt with ease. A combination of strong architectural governance, reusable design templates, and retained internal expertise supports organizations in adapting to disruptive events without rebuilding their infrastructure from scratch each time. Such events could include mergers and acquisitions, changing vendors, or technology upgrades.

NaaS and AI-driven observability can improve efficiency and reduce complexity in network operations. Network-as-a-service (NaaS) and AI-driven observability can offer companies benefits like faster, more flexible provisioning and lower costs.

Data sovereignty and sovereign AI will create infrastructure challenges for global enterprises. Regulators worldwide are passing laws requiring data and AI processing to remain within national borders. This conflicts with how multinational companies currently operate, requiring the build-out of sovereign-capable infrastructure for each geography, which will require significant new investment and complicate operations.

Download the report

This content was produced by Insights, MIT Technology Review’s custom content arm, not its editorial staff. It was researched and written by humans, with any AI tools that may have been used limited to production processes under human oversight.

Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible.
