items.title: Security incident on Hex.pm
items.subtitle: Lobsters Computing Community • Lobsters Community
items.feedText: On November 23, 2026, an unauthorized third party exploited a vulnerability in hex.pm that let them run commands on our web servers. We blocked the traffic and deployed a fix within 20 minutes. Shortly afterwards we received a report of this exact vulnerability. We found no evidence of unauthorized package modifications, or database changes, or that the attacker maintained access to our systems. However, because database reads are not logged, we cannot rule out that the attacker accessed data stored in the database, including email addresses, password hashes, API key hashes, 2FA secrets, sessions, and audit logs. Because email addresses may have been exposed, be careful with emails that claim to come from Hex.
items.body:
# Security incident on hex.pm | Hex

On November 23, 2026, an unauthorized third party exploited a vulnerability in hex.pm that let them run commands on our web servers. We blocked the traffic and deployed a fix within 20 minutes. Shortly afterwards we received a report of this exact vulnerability.

We found no evidence of unauthorized package modifications, or database changes, or that the attacker maintained access to our systems. However, because database reads are not logged, we cannot rule out that the attacker accessed data stored in the database, including email addresses, password hashes, API key hashes, 2FA secrets, sessions, and audit logs.

Because email addresses may have been exposed, be careful with emails that claim to come from Hex. Please double-check that the links they contain lead to hex.pm . Please forward suspicious emails to security@hex.pm .

We checked every file written to package storage during the incident against our database and found nothing unexpected. Reads of private packages in that period came from our own servers and coincide with releases the same organizations published at the time. A read made from a compromised server would look like one of ours, so we can't fully rule one out, and reads of private documentation aren't logged. We will contact affected organizations directly.

The attacker's commands could read the credentials our servers use, so we replaced them: the storage, CDN, email and database credentials, and the keys that sign sessions and access tokens. This logged everyone out of hex.pm and Hex clients. We're building a new registry signing system that supports key rotation, with new Hex client releases in the coming days. Until then, don't trust third-party mirrors and fetch packages only from repo.hex.pm. We already deployed fixes for the vulnerability and are working on further hardening fixes.

### What you should do

- Change your password at hex.pm .
- Reset your 2FA at hex.pm/dashboard/security : under "Authenticator App", choose "Setup New App" and verify a code from the new entry. You get a new secret and new recovery codes, so store the new codes. This works when an organization requires 2FA, where disabling it is refused.
- Update your Hex client when the release with the new signing system is out in the coming days. Until then, use only repo.hex.pm, not mirrors. To update, run mix local.hex --force , and update rebar3 or Gleam if you use them.
### Timeline

All times are in UTC.

November 23, 2026

- 18:16 - 18:29 : The attacker sent 69 malicious requests to hex.pm, six of our web servers were affected. Our error tracker Sentry recorded its first error at 18:16:00 and recorded an error for each request.
- 18:27 : We added a firewall rule to block the attacker's traffic, which took full effect between 18:30 and 18:33.
- 18:30 - 18:31 : All hex.pm servers were replaced with a patched build that rejects these payloads.
- 18:33 - 18:38 : All further requests from the attacking address were denied.
- 18:35 : We began investigating production logs and the database.
- 18:49 : We deactivated the AWS access key the affected servers used, after creating a replacement at 18:47.
- 19:07 : We received an email with a security report that described the same vulnerability.
- 20:21 : Most infrastructure credentials were rotated. The database password followed on November 24.
- 22:58 : We reported a personal data breach to IMY, the Swedish data protection authority.
- 23:05 : We reported the incident to CISA, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which confirmed receipt at 23:43.
- 23:26 : We submitted an early warning to ENISA, the EU Agency for Cybersecurity.
November 24, 2026

- By 10:42 : We had rotated every credential the attacker could have read, including the database password, except the registry signing key and a few low-impact secrets.
- 13:48 : We published CVE-2026-129514 .
### The vulnerability

The vulnerability in Hex.pm is tracked as CVE-2026-129514 .

hex.pm decoded unauthenticated request bodies in Erlang term format with Plug.Crypto.non_executable_binary_to_term/2 which blocks most potentially harmful terms, but allows struct values through. These decoded struct values, when chained together correctly, turned into a remote command execution (RCE). This is the detailed playbook of the attack:

- The entry point. A custom parser in the endpoint handled the application/vnd.hex+erlang content type using Plug.Crypto.non_executable_binary_to_term/2 with [:safe] . Because the endpoint runs this parser before routing and authentication, any unauthenticated POST with that content type reached it on every route.
- Fake structs got through. The decoder rejected functions and new atoms, but it never checked maps. An Elixir struct is just a map with a __struct__ key naming a module. That meant the attacker could send a value the runtime treats as a real struct, with every field set to whatever they chose.
- Converting the structs into an error. The decoded struct became the request's body parameters. Plug.MethodOverride then read body_params["_method"] , which on a struct calls fetch/2 on the struct's module. That function didn't exist, so the request raised an UndefinedFunctionError with the attacker's struct in the stack trace.
- Error reporting runs inspect. Sentry, Bandit's error logging, and the JSON log formatter call inspect on request data and stack-frame arguments. Inspect is a protocol, so for a struct it runs the implementation of the module named in __struct__ , which let the attacker choose which code ran next. They chose Ecto.Query.DynamicExpr .
- The Ecto hop. The Inspect implementation for Ecto.Query.DynamicExpr enumerated the binding field without checking that it was a list. Enumeration is itself a protocol call, so a struct placed in that field is dispatched to another implementation.
- The DBConnection hop. The struct placed in binding was a DBConnection.Stream . Its Enumerable implementation calls DBConnection.reduce/3 , which then calls declare/4 . Encoding the query failed before any connection was checked out, but the error path still ran the stream's :log option. That option was a {module, function, args} tuple taken from the request, and db_connection applied it with the log entry prepended.
- Command execution. An attacker-supplied {module, function, args} tuple that the server runs gives access to functions in loaded libraries and the standard library, which led to OS command execution as the BEAM's user.
While investigating, we found the same class of vulnerability in Ash: its keyset pagination accepted crafted structs in client-supplied cursors, which could lead to command execution or SQL injection. We reported it and the Ash team released a fix in ash 3.38.0 on November 24. It is tracked as CVE-2026-124283 .

items.title: Viral video from Paris shows French royalist march
items.subtitle: A video with a caption suggesting it shows a Christian procession is of a 2025 march in Paris in memory of King Louis XVI, organised by French royalists.
items.feedText: A video shows thousands of Christians gathering in the heart of Paris, openly celebrating their faith in Jesus Christ. items.body:
# Viral video from Paris shows French royalist march – Full Fact

## Viral video from Paris shows French royalist march

## What was claimed

A video shows thousands of Christians gathering in the heart of Paris, openly celebrating their faith in Jesus Christ.

## Our verdict

The video actually shows an annual torchlight procession dedicated to the memory of King Louis XVI, organised by French royalists.

A video of a night-time march in Paris has been shared thousands of times on Instagram, with suggestions that it shows a Christian procession.

The video was shared in a post captioned “Thousands of Christians are gathering in the heart of Paris, openly celebrating their faith in Jesus Christ.”

But the clip actually shows an annual torchlight procession which was reportedly attended by around 500 people in January 2025, in commemoration of King Louis XVI. In the video, people are chanting “France, youth, royalty” and “Paris, Paris, royalists” [translated from French].

The original video appears to have been posted on TikTok on 18 January 2025 with overlaid text saying “The torchlight march begins with chants of royalist slogans glorifying Louis XVI under high security” [translated from French]. It includes the hashtag #actionfrancaise.

Join 75,000 newsletter subscribers who trust us to check the facts

Sign up to get weekly updates on politics, immigration, health and more.

Subscribe to weekly email newsletters from Full Fact for updates on politics, immigration, health and more. Our fact checks are free to read but not to produce, so you will also get occasional emails about fundraising and other ways you can help. You can unsubscribe at any time. For more information about how we use your data see our Privacy Policy .

## What is the procession actually about?

Action Française is a far-right, monarchist and nationalist political movement . It describes its goals as working towards the restoration of monarchy in France and defending national interests.

A Facebook page called Souvenir de Louis XVI has posted about organising a march in Paris in remembrance of King Louis XVI every year since 2020 . Souvenir de Louis XVI has been linked to Action Française .

The French monarch was executed on 21 January 1793, a day that symbolises the end of the traditional French monarchy , which was abolished in September 1792 when it was replaced by the First French Republic .

While the post sharing the video suggests it shows a Christian procession, with “French flags, crosses, and crowds united by faith”, the annual march is primarily a royalist event centred on King Louis XVI and promoting anti-Republican ideals —though the Souvenir de Louis XVI page has promoted masses held across France to commemorate the day.

In a longer video of the 2025 event, some organisers can be heard addressing the crowd before the march begins behind a portrait of Louis XVI, proclaiming that their gathering testifies to their attachment to the late monarch and to French royalty more generally.

One attendee described the day as having a sacred, almost religious dimension, with the Souvenir page describing Louis XVI as a martyr and Action Française saying “The traditional, Christian, hereditary, decentralised, and representative monarchy shaped France and led it to its zenith” [translated from French]. And in the longer video of the full gathering, there is one flag with a religious message, depicting the Sacred Heart of Jesus. But a Facebook post from Souvenir de Louis XVI calls on people who identify as patriots, royalists and nationalists, and the focus of the march is on Louis XVI.

Before sharing content like this, it’s important to consider whether it has been shared in the right context. Our misinformation toolkit can help.

Tags

This article is part of our work fact checking potentially false pictures, videos and stories on Facebook. You can read more about this—and find out how to report Facebook content— here . For the purposes of that scheme, we’ve rated this claim as missing context because the implied claim that the event depicted is primarily a Christian one, is false, as the march was primarily a royalist one held in memory of King Louis XVI.

## Was this helpful?

Full Fact fights for good, reliable information in the media, online, and in politics.

items.body:
# Beyond profiles: Supervised repeat annotation using protein embeddings

- Article
- Authors
- Metrics
- Comments
- Media Coverage
- Peer Review
- Reader Comments
- Figures
## This is an uncorrected proof.

## Figures

## Abstract

Protein repeats give rise to diverse protein structures and functions, yet their sequence-based detection is often challenging because individual repeat units can diverge substantially in sequence while retaining similar structures. Most sensitive approaches rely on sequence information directly represented by alignments or derived profiles, thereby limiting flexibility and scalability. Here, we introduce TREAD ( T ransfer learning-based RE peat A nnotation using Protein Embe D dings), a supervised framework that reformulates repeat detection as a residue-level annotation problem and operates directly on embeddings from protein language models. Instead of constructing explicit probabilistic profiles, TREAD learns repeat-specific features implicitly, enabling residue-resolved scoring and flexible repeat segment extraction. Across complementary benchmarks based on RepeatsDB and Pfam, TREAD consistently matches or outperforms the widely used profile-based tool HMMER, particularly in low-data and high-divergence settings. The model exhibits robustness to score thresholding and demonstrates better generalization to independent test sets, including those containing remotely related families. To illustrate the practical utility of TREAD, we applied it to survey β-propeller proteins across the AlphaFold Database and representative proteomes to generate a comprehensive census of this fold. This analysis highlights extensive propeller diversity, identifies lineage-specific expansion patterns across the tree of life, and suggests previously unrecognized relationships between propellers and other repeat folds. Together, TREAD provides a flexible and scalable alternative to profile-based repeat annotation and establishes a general motif-centric framework for protein sequence annotation.

## Author summary

Many proteins are assembled from repeated building blocks. These repeats have helped evolution generate a remarkable variety of structures and functions. Yet sensitive detection of individual repeats has long been challenging because their sequences can diverge substantially even when their structures remain similar. Conventional methods often rely on comparing large collections of related sequences to find these patterns. We developed TREAD, a computational method that learns from annotated examples to recognize protein repeats using information captured by protein language models. Rather than building conventional sequence profiles, TREAD identifies repeat units and their boundaries directly from these learned protein representations. In systematic benchmarks, it matched or outperformed HMMER, a widely used profile-based method, particularly when few examples were available or repeat sequences were highly divergent. We then used TREAD to survey β-propellers, proteins assembled from repeated blade-like units, across millions of protein sequences. We uncovered substantial unexplored diversity, differences in their abundance and associated functions across organisms, and unexpected similarities to a previously unclassified barrel-like repeat fold. Together, our work provides a flexible approach to detecting protein repeats and shows how their systematic annotation can reveal new aspects of protein diversity and evolution.

Citation: Qiu K, Ludwiczak J, Lupas AN, Dunin-Horkawicz S (2026) Beyond profiles: Supervised repeat annotation using protein embeddings. PLoS Comput Biol 22(11): e1014994. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1014994

Editor: Dirk Walther, Max Planck Institute of Molecular Plant Physiology: Max-Planck-Institut fur molekulare Pflanzenphysiologie, GERMANY

Received: July 23, 2026; Accepted: November 16, 2026; Published: November 24, 2026

Copyright: © 2026 Qiu et al. This is an open access article distributed under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution License , which permits unrestricted use, distribution, and reproduction in any medium, provided the original author and source are credited.

Data Availability: The source code of TREAD, including its command-line interface, is available on GitHub at https://github.com/KYQiu21/TREAD/tree/main . A Google Colab notebook for running the models developed in this study is available at https://colab.research.google.com/drive/1gbtb5BtevWE9vChJrYgiNW2mQSW_kN8j . The benchmark dataset, trained model weights, and additional datasets and results, including the AFDB Swiss-Prot and AFDB50 scan results and the interactive hierarchical clustering visualization, are available on Zenodo at https://zenodo.org/records/20593717 .

Funding: This work was supported by institutional funds of the Max Planck Society (Max-Planck-Gesellschaft; https://www.mpg.de ; recipient: Andrei N. Lupas; no grant number). Stanislaw Dunin-Horkawicz was additionally supported by the National Science Centre, Poland (Narodowe Centrum Nauki; https://www.ncn.gov.pl/en ; grant number: 2020/37/B/NZ2/03268). The funders had no role in study design, data collection and analysis, decision to publish, or preparation of the manuscript.

Competing interests: The authors have declared that no competing interests exist.

## Introduction

Protein domains arising from the repetition of specific repeat units are widespread across all domains of life, giving rise to a broad spectrum of symmetric topologies [ 1 ]. Repetition has been, and continues to be, a major source of molecular innovation, producing ubiquitous protein folds such as TIM barrels, β-trefoils, and β-propellers [ 2 – 4 ] with the latter still emerging through ongoing blade amplification [ 4 , 5 ]. Owing to their modular organization, repeat proteins have long served as model systems for studying protein structure, function, and evolution, and as versatile scaffolds for protein engineering [ 6 – 8 ]. Furthermore, their repetitive nature provides a powerful biophysical window into protein folding and enables systematic dissection of repeat-by-repeat energetics and cooperativity [ 9 ].

items.body:
**Illustration from i went fishing with my family when i was five. Courtesy of Tao Lin.**

I wrote this in February 2005, when I was [twenty-one](https://www.theparisreview.org/blog/2025/08/05/my-college-diary/):

> i went fishing with my family when i was five
> when i was five
> i went fishing with my family
> my dad caught a turtle
> my mom caught a snapper
> my brother caught a crab
> i caught a whale
> that night we ate crab
> the next night we ate turtle
> the next night we ate snapper
> the next night we ate whale
> the next night we ate whale
> the next night we ate whale
> …

The first draft repeated the last line 143 times. I sent it to an editor at *Monkeybicycle* —an online literary magazine—and he accepted it for publication. He wrote:

> The average weight of a small sea turtle is 60 lbs. The largest whale (the Blue Whale) averages 120 tons. So, that’s 4000 times larger. I was thinking we could repeat the final line 4000 times.

I emailed the poem to my mom, who replied, “Children would enjoy it very much, what do you think? Maybe sometimes you can write something for children someday. Just have a question, there are several hundred lines of ‘the next night we ate whale,’ is it supposed to be like that or it is a mistake? I tried to delete it, but couldn’t.”

The *Monkeybicycle* editor sent me his 24,059-word file of the poem and suggested I find an illustrator and publish it as “a huge chapbook.” Another *Monkeybicycle* editor said he’d illustrate and lay it out, but I wasn’t interested.

I read the poem at readings maybe five or six times. I remember staying focused and serious while reading it by dwelling on how depressed and alienated I felt. The longest I ever read it was seven minutes, I think.

In 2008, my friend recorded a video of the audience as I read the poem. This video is on YouTube. I began the reading by saying, “I’m going to read from my memoir.” Afterward, I sold stapled booklets of a short version of the poem for three dollars.

In 2009, I was paid a hundred dollars to read the poem for four minutes at the New Museum of Contemporary Art. In 2010, the *London Review of Books* published an [overview](https://www.theparisreview.org/letters-essays/8475/gemstone-tao-lin) of my [writing](https://www.theparisreview.org/blog/2024/09/12/my-childhood-toy-poodles/) [career](https://www.theparisreview.org/blog/2023/09/11/jets-and-trash/) that referenced the poem, and someone read the poem at a cultural center in Amsterdam. Also in 2010, at an event at Drawn & Quarterly’s bookstore for my second novel, I pitched the poem as a book to D&Q’s owner. I described this in my novel *Taipei* (2013):

> … the owner of Drawn & Quarterly approached and thanked Paul for coming to Montreal. Paul pitched a children’s book, to be illustrated by a known graphic novelist who’d confirmed interest, based on one of his poems—
> when i was five i went fishing with my family
> when i was five
> i went fishing with my family
> my dad caught a turtle
> my mom caught a snapper
> my brother caught a crab
> i caught a whale
> that night we ate crab
> the next night we ate turtle
> the next night we ate snapper
> the next night we ate whale
> the next night we ate whale
> the next night we ate whale
> the next night we ate whale
> the next night we ate whale
> the next night we ate whale
> —with each line on its own page and the last line repeated as many times as needed. Maybe a different artist could illustrate each page to create a sort of anthology. As a children’s book, due to the content, it would …

The owner didn’t seem interested.

**Illustration from i went fishing with my family when i was five. Courtesy of Tao Lin.**

In 2012, the Asian American Writer’s Workshop asked me to participate in an event. The organization suggested four things I could do. The first was to read the whale poem. I chose another option. I was tired of reading the poem.

In 2013, I got an email that said, “The Head of English at the University of Exeter just randomly sent everyone on the Poetry module a video of you reading ‘i went fishing with my family when i was five’ as an example of how poetry isn’t dull.”

In 2014, Jeffrey Brown, the author of *Clumsy* (2002), one of my favorite graphic novels, agreed to illustrate my whale poem. An editor at McSweeney’s was interested in it for their children’s-book imprint. But this didn’t result in anything.

BBC Singers ’ composition by Jonathan Packham.

I mostly stopped caring about making the poem into a book. Sometimes people messaged me saying they’d performed it at a reading. A band used it as lyrics for a song. A doctoral student at Oxford used it as the text for a composition that the BBC Singers—a professional chamber choir—performed in a workshop setting.

In 2026, I noticed people discussing my poem on X. Pangram had identified it as 100 percent AI-generated. It was the only false positive discovered in a public challenge offering $4,100 to find one from before 2020 that was longer than 749 words.

This gave my poem more attention than it had ever gotten, encouraging me to make and publish the book myself. I handwrote, illustrated, and designed it over a week. I loved the process.

*From* [i went fishing with my family](https://muumuuhouse.com/whalepoem.html)[when i was five](https://muumuuhouse.com/whalepoem.html) *, published today by Muumuu House.*

*Tao Lin is the author of the novels* Leave Society *and* Taipei *, among other books. His poetry collection* Hawaii Years *is forthcoming from Louria Books. His most recent piece for the Daily was “[Taiwan English](https://www.theparisreview.org/blog/2026/06/24/taiwan-english/).”*

items.body:
# GPT-6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities

November 24, 2026

## GPT‑6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities

## Key findings:

- Our GPT‑6 family of models can design new protein shapes and the sequence of their chemical building blocks using only reasoning and code, without calling specialized biology models to generate those designs.
- An internal research model matched or outperformed specialized models on many protein design tasks. Researchers could also guide designs by prompting the model on where a protein should attach and what shape it should take.
- In lab tests with Onava, proteins based on GPT‑6.2’s designs showed evidence of binding, or attachment, across five targets. Redesigned antibodies also retained binding. Specialized models helped supply sequences and select candidates for testing.
- The models’ written reasoning and code suggest they draw on math, physics, chemistry, and biological knowledge to reason about protein shapes and interactions with other molecules.
In a preprint titled GPT‑6 as a Universal Foundation Model for Protein Biology: Beyond Specialized Models , we show that our GPT‑6 family of models has intrinsic capabilities for designing new proteins: the models can design new protein structures and sequences without relying on specialized biology models, using only reasoning and general-purpose coding tools.

Proteins do much of the work in living cells. They drive the chemical reactions that sustain life, carry oxygen through the blood, and defend the body against infection. Incorrectly shaped proteins can also cause disease and dysfunction. Proteins are made from chains of chemical building blocks called amino acids. The order, or sequence, of these amino acids helps determine how a protein folds into a three-dimensional shape, which in turn influences what it does.

Scientists often start with a clear idea of what they want a protein to do. They might want it to block a signal that helps cancer cells evade the immune system or to help capture carbon dioxide from the air. The challenge is to work out what three-dimensional structure would enable the protein to do its job and which amino acid sequence would give it that structure. Specialized biology models capable of generating three-dimensional protein structures and sequences have made this work more practical.

Using and coordinating these specialized models requires substantial expertise. Each accepts particular kinds of inputs and constraints, and these models cannot easily accept new kinds of information without changes to their software or additional training. In contrast, a general-purpose model capable of performing the work of multiple specialized models can easily adapt to new instructions and requirements.

Our research illustrates the potential power of pairing natural language with intrinsic protein capabilities. We could guide our models at scales ranging from a single bond between two atoms to the overall shape of a protein. For example, we asked GPT‑6.2 to predict where and how a small molecule would bind to a protein. When we already knew which two atoms formed a bond, we could give the model that information and ask how the rest of the molecule would fit. We could switch between these tasks simply by changing the prompt, without retraining the model. We also asked our models to design small proteins called minibinders and marked where each should attach to its target, and further specified how many coils or strands each minibinder should contain. An internal model followed that instruction with near-perfect fidelity in its three-dimensional designs.

Points farther from the center indicate better performance. Newer generations of models improved on many of the 14 protein tasks tested.

## A closer look at our models’ protein designs

We ran computational tests of whether the GPT‑6 models series could design small proteins to bind given targets, build proteins around specified structural features, predict protein structures and molecular interactions, and rank how sequence changes affect properties such as stability and binding. Our latest models performed comparably to or better than specialized models on most tasks, although predicting a complete protein structure remained a clear weakness.

The models’ written reasoning and code offer clues to how they approach these tasks. They draw on mathematics, physics, chemistry, and coding alongside knowledge of recurring patterns in protein sequences and structures. For example, when designing a small protein intended to bind to IL-7Rα, the model proposed how the two proteins might interact, then wrote and executed code to explore different protein shapes and amino acid choices that could support that interaction.

The model’s written reasoning and code show it drawing on math, physics, chemistry and biology to design a protein intended to attach to IL-7Rα. It examines the target’s surface, arranges five coiled sections into a protein shape, and checks how the two proteins could fit together.

With our research partner, Onava ⁠ (opens in a new window) , we also tested the models’ structure and sequence designs in the lab. First, Onava made small proteins based on three-dimensional structures designed by a pre-released version of GPT‑6.2. Specialized models supplied amino acid sequences and helped select candidates for testing. For each of the five targets we chose, at least one protein showed evidence of binding in the lab. In separate experiments, GPT‑6.2 designed new amino acid sequences for existing minibinders and antibodies. Following candidate selection with specialized models, many of the redesigned proteins also showed evidence of binding to the same targets as the originals.

## Laboratory Experiment 1: Designing small proteins that bind to a target

Our first laboratory experiment tested whether GPT‑6.2 could design small proteins that would bind to their intended targets. We compared computational measurements of quality against RFdiffusion, a specialized model for protein design, and found that GPT‑6.2’s three-dimensional designs scored slightly lower while our latest internal models scored higher. For the lab experiment, we made proteins based on GPT‑6.2’s designs and measured how strongly they bound to their targets.

We gave GPT‑6.2 the three-dimensional structures of five target proteins and marked where we wanted a minibinder to attach. It then wrote code to create three-dimensional designs for potential minibinders, without using specialized protein AI models.

To turn GPT‑6.2’s three-dimensional designs into proteins we could test in the lab, we needed amino acid sequences that would fold into the proposed structures. We used a specialized AI model called SolubleMPNN to suggest sequences for each design. Other specialized protein models helped us select candidates predicted to fold as designed and bind at the intended site on the target.

items.body:
# The Funniest Books of 2026

Make Your Own List

### The Best Fiction Books » Humour

## The Funniest Books of 2026

### recommended by Sophie Ratcliffe

Every year, the judges of the Bollinger Everyman Wodehouse Prize for Comic Fiction select the funniest novel published in the past twelve months. In 2026, finalists include a Booker-nominated book about a man in a black bag and a Regency rom-com with a very modern sensibility. Judge, academic and author Sophie Ratcliffe talks us through the six-book shortlist.

Interview by Cal Flyn , Deputy Editor

- Read 1 A Good Person by Kirsten King
- Read 2 Black Bag: A Novel by Luke Kennard
- Read 3 How to Lose a Lord in Ten Days by Sophie Irwin
- Read 4 Motherfaker by Anna Brook-Mitchell
- Read 5 Offseason by Avigayl Sharp
- Read 6 We Love You, Bunny: A Novel by Mona Awad
- 1 A Good Person by Kirsten King
- 2 Black Bag: A Novel by Luke Kennard
- 3 How to Lose a Lord in Ten Days by Sophie Irwin
- 4 Motherfaker by Anna Brook-Mitchell
- 5 Offseason by Avigayl Sharp
- 6 We Love You, Bunny: A Novel by Mona Awad
T hank you for talking to us about the six-book shortlist for the 2026 Bollinger Everyman Wodehouse Prize for comic fiction. I wonder: is judging humorous writing unusually difficult?

Yes, I think there is a difficulty. I guess what different people find funny or ‘comic’ is pretty subjective. It sounds a touch grave to say that it feels like a responsibility, but it is. We were all trying to come to these books with as open a mind as possible about the varieties of humour that we might encounter. We, as a panel, were looking for books that would make us laugh out loud, but were were also open to those that made us smile or raise an eyebrow, which plunged us into the absurd and grotesque, or the dry and the wry…

Also, crucially, we wanted books that were exceptionally well-written. My own acid test for any really great book – particularly a great comic or joy-giving book – is that I want to press it into the hands of someone who, say, tells me they are going into hospital and need something good to read. Maybe that sounds vague, but these were the rough ingredients of the recipe we were looking for.

A funny book is not the same thing as a light read. They can be both, but a great funny book should still be a quality book.

That’s right. And when I look at the shortlist from this year, that comes through.

Let’s look at those books, one at a time. Can we start with A Good Person by Kirsten King? It features a modern-day hex.

I love this one. Here’s the plot. The heroine of this book breaks up with her boyfriend, who she spent quite a lot of time getting. She also works for a marketing company, and through her work encounters the ‘Wellness Witch’, a social influencer, who gives her the tools to put a ‘hex’ on her ex.

It’s very filmic – King is a screenwriter, and you can tell. I think what stands out in this one is the voice. It’s so good, full of very funny one-liners, which are integrated beautifully. It’s also a page-turner.

The title is A Good Person , and it is very thoughtful about ethics, carried with a light touch. It makes one think about what that means, to be a good person, and what it might be like to want to hex someone, and what to do with shame when things get out of control.

Then all of that is played through a sort of millennial angst about paying rent and having roommates. It’s a gorgeous piece of work: quite dark, very funny.

It’s a classic combination. Comedians are famously troubled. Is there a thread of darkness running through all of the books?

In many of them, yes. There’s quite a lot of trauma and darkness to negotiate in this list. But what the books have in common is that while the dark recesses of the soul might be pondered or traversed, the joke always lands at home. The thread these books have in common is that the comedy is entwined with kindness. They certainly don’t punch down.

Luke Kennard’s Black Bag also featured on the Booker Prize shortlist, which I was delighted to see. I think it’s great. Why did the Wodehouse Prize judges admire it?

Well, it made us all laugh out loud. That’s the first thing. I don’t know if that is the most important thing to say about it, but for this prize it is very important. It’s not a book that is safe to read on a train because you will spill your coffee. And, actually, there’s a fantastic scene involving a coffee mishap—

Yes!

It’s a really, really funny book. So the scenario is based on a real-life psychological experiment where a professor hired someone to wear a large, leather, full-body black bag around the campus of a university to see what happened. So that is clearly completely absurd. The person in this book who is performing as the black bag is a failed actor, and this ‘part’ becomes his starring role. We admired the huge comedy of the novel, but in its construction, Black Bag has really thought through this comic scenario and what it can tell us about what it means to make art, and what it is like to be a human being.

Again, this is a book that does not laugh at anyone, but rather at the predicament of what it means to be human. We also loved the physical comedy. The tiny details. The actor wearing the black bag immacs his lower legs to make sure that no one can work out whether he’s male or female. And he talks brilliantly to the visceral feeling of wearing hot, black leather. There are also interesting themes which emerge around another character who makes a living through livestreams and cryptocurrency. So this book makes us ponder the relationship between the virtual and the material.

It’s a very clever book, but with great humour. You’re physically wincing as you read. It’s masterly.

Well, we have a very different book up next. This is How to Lose a Lord in Ten Days by Sophie Irwin. It’s a Regency rom-com . Tell us more.

One thing I want to highlight about this book is that it is gorgeously reflexive. It begins with the heroine reading a novel. The title too, is a riff on How to Lose a Guy in Ten Days , the Kate Hudson and Matthew McConaughey film.

Plotwise, it’s a Regency comedy in which both members of the couple are trying to break off an engagement, but modernity keeps poking its nose through the pages. You get a sense, almost, that they are wearing sneakerinas under their muslin frocks. It’s an enjoyable historical novel, but also a comedy about what it means to write historical fiction. It’s clever and quite delicious – probably the lightest book on the list.

I did want to give a shout out to some of the period descriptions: There’s a moment when Lydia takes a seat between a beef tremblant and a pigeon à la crapaudine. And there are descriptions of characters galloping ventre à terre , a Georgette Heyer term – if somebody really loves you, they will ride so that their horse’s belly is grazing the ground.

- [Colophon](https://pluralistic.net/2026/11/24/move-fast-break-kings/#bragsheet): All the rest.

## Free lunches (permalink)

[↗ Primärquelle: pluralistic.net](https://pluralistic.net/2026/11/24/move-fast-break-kings/#come-and-take-it)

An old joke: "Two economists are walking down the sidewalk and one of them points and says, 'Look, there's a $20 bill, right there on the ground!' The other one is dismissive: 'No, if that was a real $20, someone would have picked it up by now.'"

If that joke leaves you scratching your head, then you've been lucky enough to avoid the neoclassical economist's view of the world as a market whose participants, in aggregate, know everything about what people are buying and selling. In that world if there's a "free lunch" – like a $20 bill on the sidewalk – someone will have already taken it.

Likewise, if there's a seller who's priced their goods at $10 and a buyer who's willing to pay $30, there will be an "arbitrageur" who will be shuttling those $10 goods to those $30 customers and pocketing the difference. Give it enough time and either the seller will raise their price to $30, or the buyer will realize they should only be offering $10.

The market will "clear," with everyone getting everything they need in the most efficient way possible, meaning there's no way to improve anyone's position without making someone else worse off:

[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pareto_efficiency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pareto_efficiency)

When markets *don't* behave like this, neoclassicals hunt for "distortions" that prevent the market from performing this continuous balancing trick. "Distortion" is best understood here as a euphemism for "democratic intervention." If you've ever gotten excited about a commonsense policy solution to a serious economic problem (like public grocery stores as a means of addressing food deserts and greedflation), only to see it shot down by economists who use a lot of jargon to "prove" that it can't possibly work, you've experienced how well "distortion" doomerism keeps us from having nice things.

The economist's allergy to distortions is curiously selective. When a company uses its monopoly power to capture its regulators, or bind its workers to silence, or to erect barriers to entry that keep competitors at bay, somehow that doesn't qualify as a "distortion." Same goes for the situation in which a dominant retailer (Walmart) and a dominant manufacturer (Pepsi) come to a secret agreement to force everyone else to raise prices a *ton* so that Walmart can raise its prices by a (smaller) ton and still be "the cheapest":

[https://pluralistic.net/2024/08/14/the-price-is-wright/#enforcement-priorities](https://pluralistic.net/2024/08/14/the-price-is-wright/#enforcement-priorities)

Economists are in love with the idea of the economy as a self-licking ice-cream cone, a beautiful machine that operates all by itself, processing all the information we inject into it by buying and selling and finding the optimal way to produce more of the things we want best at the lowest prices.

But like any love-drunk suitor, economists habitually overlook the market's glaring imperfections. In the self-correcting market, a company with high margins sends up a flare that alerts other, hungrier companies to swarm it, competing to offer the cheapest price. Likewise any company with lots of customers: those crowds of customers should conjure up armies of clever planners and inventors who find more efficient ways to produce the same goods and services and lure those customers away.

This is the crux of market orthodoxy, the idea that competition lowers margins, goading sellers to offer better goods at better prices. Don't take my word for it, here's Adam Smith:

> It is not from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer, or the baker, that we expect our dinner, but from their regard to their own interest. We address ourselves, not to their humanity, but to their self-love, and never talk to them of our own necessities, but of their advantages.

If this is true, then the surest sign of a "market distortion" is persistent high margins and persistent high market-share. Any company that dominates its market and charges far more than its costs is a crisp, $20 bill lying right there on the sidewalk for all to see. If no one picks up that $20, then it's a sure bet that there's a "distorter" who is preventing the market from acting on the "information" that there is an opportunity here.

America's business lobby *loves* distortions, so long as they're the kinds of distortions that let the companies safely entrust their $20 bills to the sidewalk without worrying about having them scooped up by a competitor.

Take Big Tech: this is an industry with such persistently high margins and so many customers that there are *multiple* firms in the sector that were able to piss away *hundreds of billions of dollars* by manipulating their stock prices with buybacks and building AI data-centers that can never turn a profit:

[https://pluralistic.net/2025/09/06/computer-says-huh/#invisible-handcuffs](https://pluralistic.net/2025/09/06/computer-says-huh/#invisible-handcuffs)

If the market was "undistorted" then anyone this rich and this stupid would be in serious trouble. Ask a neoclassical to explain Big Tech's prolonged, morbid wealth and they'll insist that this means that *we're* the stupid ones, because we can't play 11-dimensional chess like Zuckerberg, which is why we can't understand why it was *good* to piss away $80b on the metaverse.

But we don't have to look very hard to find another, simpler explanation. Big Tech owes its profits to its monopoly power, which allows it to form cartels that collude to rig prices:

…

items.body:
# When Your Doctor Prescribes a Visit to an Art Gallery

The soulful deep greens and browns of British Columbia’s forests weave together with ferns and moss, catching the light through the tops of ancient firs and cedars. The trees sway, and the earth rises and falls among the rocks.

But in this case, the view isn’t from the trail. It is a painting by Canadian artist Emily Carr on display in the Vancouver Art Gallery , and some of those who are experiencing it are doing so because it was prescribed by their health care provider. How they ended up there is the result of a bit of creative thinking that honors the role of art in healing.

In 2025, the gallery partnered with BC Parks Foundation to extend PaRx , Canada’s national nature prescription program, to include the gallery. PaRx is a successful initiative that has included an estimated 2 million prescriptions issued by more than 20,000 health care providers. Typically, these prescriptions are for time outdoors, with added benefits, like free transportation, to reduce barriers to access. Using art as an entry point into nature as a formal intervention is novel—the first collaboration of its kind between a nature prescription program and an arts institution in the world, according to Sirish Rao, the gallery’s co-CEO and executive director. While art-based prescriptions are gaining in popularity, this program goes a step further, integrating engagement with nature in a gentle, accessible way. Other institutions around the world are looking to the Vancouver Art Gallery program as a model initiative that can be replicated in other communities to support people’s well-being.

## An artful approach to treatment

The process starts when a health care provider like a doctor, nurse, or therapist determines that a patient might benefit from a prescription to spend time in nature, including around the nature-inspired visual art at the gallery. The benefits can be many: combating isolation, engaging mentally and physically during a gallery visit, and experiencing awe and beauty.

The prescription to Vancouver Art Gallery includes free admission for the prescription holder and a guest, as well as a printed guide that offers prompts and questions to consider—for example, to notice the varied shades of green Carr used, or imagine a walk along a trail she painted—along with research about the benefits of experiencing nature. Participants are guided through “slow looking” as the act of learning through observation, imagination exercises, and physical movement—yes, swaying in an art gallery is encouraged.

After the visit, guests are invited to continue the immersion at a local nature space, with free carshare minutes to get there if needed. The art prescription guide suggests nearby parks where participants can walk or hike, extending slow looking from a curated indoor experience to the outdoors if they choose. And they can return to the gallery as often as they like by retaining their original prescription. On site, they can join free workshops, and a coloring book offers a contemplative experience at home.

This is an example of social prescribing, a worldwide movement that serves as a complement to clinical care and typical medication prescriptions by prescribing from a wide range of activities that support physical and mental health. Beyond art galleries and nature walks, this can include music classes, exercise sessions, or gardening programs. The prescription is personal and can be tailored to patients’ needs and interests.

Carla Fry is a West Vancouver psychologist and educator with more than 20 years of clinical experience. She says the art gallery prescription has been a gift for participants, especially those who face physical, mental, social, or even financial or transportation barriers to accessing nature. Many are surprised that they don’t have to pay anything for the experience.

“For them to understand that so many people have come together to create this opportunity, I think that in and of itself is special,” Fry says. “They say, ‘Wow, my community cares.’ The possibility that this exists, it’s available, it’s free—there’s something about that . . . that’s noteworthy.”

Fry is one of the professionals who gives these kinds of prescriptions to her clients. It’s another tool available to promote well-being.

“Of course, I’m never telling them to go. We talk about this as a prescription, but I always present it as ‘here’s an opportunity to meet some of your goals, and here’s what the opportunity looks like,’” she says.

As yet, no one has declined her prescription.

“They’re surprised that something so seemingly simplistic as slowing down and really looking, really living in front of the art or in nature is actually an intervention,” Fry says. “People in our culture are set up to think that growth has got to be painful, growth has got to be difficult, growth has got to be expensive, growth is going to take a long time. When I bring forward an intervention of going to a location, and your job as a client of mine is to appreciate, the first reaction is surprise. It opens up an entire conversation—‘I can just appreciate my life and not always be grinding to make it better.’ It’s a special process for me to witness.”

## Awe and nature in community

The goal is to do more than increase the number of people who have exposure to art, though that might be a side effect. The formal prescription to nature through art is designed to reduce stress, anxiety, and social isolation. The ability to bring a guest, as well as the opportunity to experience art with other patrons, is key.

“There are other people there; these aren’t private viewings. But of course, sometimes people don’t feel connected to others in a room. Sometimes they do; sometimes it’s enough to feel that they’re part of a community. But others really benefit from being able to have a shared experience where they can reflect in real time and reflect afterwards,” Fry says.

Paula Toledo is the mental health advisor and lead well-being consultant at Vancouver Art Gallery, leading the Richardson Family Art of Wellbeing Lab . The lab aims to connect the community to art as a means to improve mental and physical well-being, drawing on a collaboration of researchers, scientists, physicians, and Indigenous Elders and healers.

Toledo came to this work through the personal experience of losing her husband and her mother within months, while also caring for her newborn child. That grief and her recovery changed the course of her life and her career in wellness.

“When we encounter something so vast that it transcends our current understanding of the world, it can be very mysterious,” Toledo says:

items.body:
# Das Recht, nicht vorhergesagt zu werden

## Das Recht, nicht vorhergesagt zu werden

Künstliche Intelligenz ist eine Prognosetechnologie, die die menschliche Autonomie in Frage stellt. Daher braucht es einen neuen Freiheitsbegriff, meint unser Autor.

Die Agenten sind los: KI-gestützte Assistenten, die für ihre Nutzer E-Mails schreiben, online einkaufen oder Zugtickets buchen, sollen das Leben von Millionen Menschen erleichtern. Statt nach einer Unterkunft auf Mallorca zu googeln, erteilt man einfach einen Suchbefehl. Die KI wühlt sich autonom durch die Angebote und schlägt eine Schneise durch das Informationsdickicht, das auf ein paar Entscheidungsbäume eingedampft wird. Der Nutzer will nicht zehn blaue Links, sondern ein Ergebnis, das für ihn maßgeschneidert ist.

Mittlerweile gibt es eine neue Generation von KI-Agenten wie Meta Muse oder Claude Duet, die nicht nur konkrete Aufträge abarbeiten, sondern proaktiv Handlungen vorschlagen, zum Beispiel unbezahlte Rechnungen überweisen oder Meetings verschieben. Der Nutzer muss diese Aktionen zwar freigeben, doch das Ziel der Kybernetiker im Silicon Valley, den Alltag auf Autopilot zu stellen, rückt damit ein Stück näher. In einem nächsten Schritt könnten die Agenten mit Vollmachten ausgestattet werden. Wer regelmäßig Tierfutter oder Kontaktlinsen benötigt, könnte den KI-Assistenten ermächtigen, in einem bestimmten Intervall das Produkt zu erwerben. Und wenn der Agent aus den Chatverläufen lernt, dass der Nutzer mit dem Kauf eines Ohrrings liebäugelt, könnte er den Schmuck bestellen, wenn er am günstigsten ist.

## Von der Aufmerksamkeits- zur Absichtsökonomie

Amazon hat bereits vor einigen Jahren ein Patent auf ein Liefersystem („anticipatory shipping“) angemeldet, das Waren verschickt, noch bevor der Kunde auf den Bestellknopf drückt. Auf Grundlage von vergangenen Bestellungen, Suchhistorie, Wunschlisten sowie Browsergewohnheiten würde das algorithmengesteuerte Logistiksystem entsprechende Waren verpacken und auf Verdacht in die Nähe des Kunden verfrachten – in lokale Sortierzentren oder, bei entsprechender Kaufwahrscheinlichkeit, schon in den Lieferwagen. Was die Planer im Sozialismus nicht schafften, könnte ausgerechnet Big Data möglich machen: die präzise Vorhersage und Steuerung der Nachfrage.

Mittlerweile ist das Datenmaterial deutlich feinkörniger, und die KI kann Wünsche erkennen, derer sich die Nutzer noch gar nicht bewusst sind. So weiß Spotify anhand der Hörgewohnheiten schon heute, welchen Song Nutzer morgen zu Ende hören oder ihrer Playlist hinzufügen werden. Künstliche Intelligenz ist im Kern eine Prognosetechnologie, die nicht nur die nächsten Buchstaben oder Pixel, sondern auch die nächsten Käufe, Partner oder Einbrüche vorhersagen kann. Ökonomen der Monash University haben in einer Studie („Should I State or Should I Show? Aligning AI with Human Preferences“) herausgefunden, dass KI-Agenten, die mit Entscheidungsdaten aus der Vergangenheit trainiert wurden, die Präferenzen der Probanden genauer vorhersagen können als Agenten, die geschriebene Anweisungen erhielten – was auch damit zu tun hat, dass Menschen Probleme haben, ihre Wünsche zu verbalisieren bzw. zu prompten. Der Wille kommt also besser zur Geltung, wenn das Subjekt nicht selbst kommuniziert, sondern kommuniziert wird.

Das verweist auf einen grundlegenden Strukturwandel der Digitalwirtschaft. In der Aufmerksamkeitsökonomie geht es vor allem darum, Nutzer möglichst lange bei der Stange zu halten und durch visuelle Reize Kaufimpulse zu setzen. Die Intention Economy setzt dagegen einen Schritt vorher an und versucht, die Entscheidungsfindung in einem früheren Stadium zu beeinflussen: den Absichten. „Wir interessieren uns für umfangreiche Datensätze, die die menschliche Gesellschaft widerspiegeln und die derzeit noch nicht ohne Weiteres öffentlich online zugänglich sind“, skizziert die KI-Firma OpenAI auf ihrem Blog ihre Ambitionen. „Besonders suchen wir nach Daten, in denen menschliche Absichten zum Ausdruck kommen – etwa in Form längerer Texte oder Konversationen, statt lediglich unzusammenhängender Fragmente –, unabhängig von Sprache, Thema oder Format.“

## Der Algorithmus und das Selbst

Die Cambridge-Forscher Yaqub Chaudhary und Jonnie Penn haben in einem Aufsatz („Beware the Intention Economy: Collection and Commodification of Intent via Large Language Models“) für die „Harvard Data Science Review“ beschrieben, wie mit der Intention Economy ein „digitaler Marktplatz für kommodifizierte Signale der ‚Absicht‘“ entsteht. Bevor wir uns selbst bewusst sind, dass wir einen Flug buchen wollen, könnte die KI Bescheid wissen und unsere Motivationen meistbietend an Anzeigenkunden verkaufen.

Natürlich kann ein KI-Agent nicht mit 100-prozentiger Wahrscheinlichkeit vorhersagen, dass man im nächsten Jahr Tickets für ein Oasis-Konzert kauft. Er kann aber durch den dialogischen Charakter viel mehr als eine Suchmaschine, die ja bloß ein Ticketautomat für Datenautobahnen ist, Präferenzen beeinflussen und Nutzer mittels Nudging, also verhaltenspsychologischer Manipulation, lenken: „Du hast jetzt so oft Oasis gehört und wünschst dir tief in deinem Innern, auf ein Konzert zu gehen, also habe ich schon mal zwei Tickets reserviert.“ Es kommt auch bei großen Sprachmodellen auf die Sprecherposition an: Wenn ein KI-Freund ein Produkt empfiehlt, hat das aufgrund der Intimität der Beziehung ein anderes Gewicht als die unpersönliche Empfehlung eines Fernsehgesichts.

Damit verschiebt sich auch die Überwachungslogik – weg vom retrospektiven Aufzeichnen von Daten und der Nachverfolgbarkeit von Handlungen hin zur prospektiven Überwachung vor dem Fakt. Wenn das Internet von Bots bevölkert ist und nur noch Agenten browsen, verlieren die aus dem Webseiten- oder Maustracking abgeleiteten Signale an Bedeutung. Daher muss die Informationsgewinnung stärker über die Steuerung und Normierung von Verhaltensweisen erfolgen. „Die Prädiktion, die Vorhersage ist Teil der Überwachung, zum Beispiel um bestimmtes Verhalten gleich von vornherein auszuschließen“, schreibt der Soziologe Nils Zurawski in seinem Blog. „Die Abweichung wird vermieden, bevor sie passiert.“ Gerade weil das menschliche Verhalten in einer modernen Gesellschaft im Gegensatz zu atomarem Verhalten unvorhersehbar ist (auch wenn das die Adepten der Sozialphysik bestreiten), müssen die Entscheidungsarchitekturen so designt sein, dass die Optionen auf ein Minimum reduziert werden. Denn: Was wahrscheinlich ist, ist leicht vorhersehbar und kontrollierbar.

Die Philosophin Carissa Véliz argumentiert in ihrem aktuellen Buch „Die Macht der Prophezeiung“, dass Vorhersagen als „Beschreibungen getarnte Befehle“ sind – und warnt vor ihren autoritären Tendenzen: „Je stärker eine Vorhersage die Situation verändert, die sie vorhersagt, umso eher wird die Vorhersage zur Regel und umso mehr Raum existiert für Machtmissbrauch.“ Die Prognosen von Machine-Learning-Systemen seien daher oft selbsterfüllende Prophezeiungen, so Véliz.

…

items.subtitle: My mother tongue is Thai, but for a long time I couldn’t swear in Thai.

It was quite a colonial relationship. I remember the colonial roots of my English every time an American complements my fluency, now that I live in the US. items.body:
My mother tongue is Thai, but for a long time I couldn’t swear in Thai. That was because the international school I went to banned us from speaking Thai on campus. *No native languages, all the better to improve our English*. It was quite a colonial relationship. I remember the colonial roots of my English every time an American complements my fluency, now that I live in the US.

Because of the school ban my Thai was polite, sweet, but not cool. I had no slang. I could not swear. This changed in the last two years of high school. I did the International Baccalaureate, which then required fifty hours of service from each student in order to graduate with the IB diploma. That seemed like a lot of hours to me! I remember my reluctance to leave the beautiful school campus with its duck ponds and Thai sala and venture into the great unknown of the Klong Toei slums.

I was matched to work in an orphanage of kids with HIV. I squeal for babies and toddlers, and was thrilled. Thailand was early to destigmatize HIV/AIDS. I ended up spending years in this orphanage, holding babies with many wonderful volunteers. What bliss, truly. I learned the carrot dance that the toddlers were obsessed with then; I can still sing it. Then, to my chagrin, I was moved out of the baby and toddler center to be with the adolescents. I think there was some glamour to having an international school student among the older kids. I sensed status in their jostling to speak with me. When the teenagers heard me speak, they fell over themselves laughing. How did I sound like such a child! They taught me to swear. We spoke in slang. In my time in Klong Toei, my Thai finally entered adolescence.

I learned a lot in those fifty hours of volunteer service, which I ended up exceeding. First, service feels wonderful. Maybe in the very beginning it was uncomfortable because of self-consciousness—and who could be more self-conscious than a teenager. But even adolescent me was able to relax the *certainty that everyone was judging her* and enjoy the camaraderie. I brought candy, and we’d walk around in a big pack of teenagers through the slum.

I learned that when the rains come, the slum is first to flood and last to drain; I learned it loses power all the time; I learned that people can be proud of where they’re from even when home is a shack made from corrugated tin. I learned that phad thai is best made on a street-side wok; I learned that Muay Thai keeps kids, especially boys, out of trouble. I learned that no one begs nor steals if they can help it; I learned that people are generally kind and keen for friendship. It was a life-changing year, as it was meant to be.

Reflecting back on that period, I am struck by how effective it was to have a service requirement. We studied economics in IB and learned about purchasing power parity, which is the relative cost of a Big Mac in Cambodia, say, versus the US. But walking those streets, paying for food, looking away as buddies fished coins out of pockets, the cut-open plastic water bottles used to beg, and drains—that was a different education in the cost of living. Knowledge moved from head to heart.

Service can be a force-function to generosity. Some of us are born with access to our tender and generous nature; some of us have quite a crust around the heart. For whatever reasons (the causes and conditions of [karma](https://tricycle.org/buddhism-dharma/#samsara-karma-rebirth)) many of us have learned to armor the heart.

All of us are affected by culture, which is a collective karma. Thailand has a collective culture of generosity. It is startling and real. Don’t worry—there’s a shadow side to Thai culture too. I wrote a whole novel to process it.

The culture of the United States is not what I would call an open and generous one. There seems to be fear around opening the heart. It sounds like: *If I’m generous, someone will take advantage of me.*

It’s probably a well-earned fear. But we cannot begin to walk the path of a [bodhisattva](https://tricycle.org/glossary/bodhisattva/) without *dana*, generosity.

We cannot begin to walk the path of a bodhisattva without *dana*, generosity.

In the temple where I teach, students have asked what you should do if you can’t just produce generosity. What then?

It’s a brave question to voice in a room. This is the answer: Force-function generosity with service. Find a way to log fifty hours of service, and the generosity will be there in your heart by the end of that time.

We remain stuck in spiritual adolescence if we have not had a significant period of service and generosity in our lives. Spiritual adolescence is a preoccupation with comfort and status. It can last our whole life if we let it.

If you are ready to progress to adulthood, I recommend engaging in service. Letting go of individual protectiveness, and feeling the wide river of the heart’s flow is actually a relief. It is freeing in and of itself (though it is not Enlightenment). Push the edges of your comfortable existence and commit significant hours to service. It will widen the aperture of your heart and bring flow again. In Thai the word “kindness” literally means “water of the heart.” My mother tongue is wise. Kindness does flow. It arises naturally, without effort. Giving comes naturally, without effort. When there is flow. If there isn’t flow, we have to poke a hole in the armor of the heart. You poke a hole through service.

If you’ve traveled to developing countries from the US, you might have noticed the baseline generosity of most people. One reason for this is because people from a poor place have had to take responsibility for collective well-being. When you are from a poor country, you *know* that no one is coming to bail you out. Here in the US we might have a fantasy of FEMA or the President or the National Guard coming to people’s aid.

They do, sometimes. And, turning away because the National Guard has been deployed is a way of making the suffering of people connected to us Not Our Problem. That is the easy egoic slide away from responsibility. In Thailand, when it floods, people pick up a bucket.

Eventually, if you continue on this path, all action is service. You find that you’ve planted yourself in the place of service. It is your purpose. It feels good. It’s the only place you want to reside.

Things can even look similar, on the outside, whether you’re doing service or not.

An example of this is Yo-Yo Ma. Born a prodigy, no matter what, Ma probably would have spent his life playing music. But we don’t hear Ma playing just Bach for the rest of his life. (Sublime Bach!)

items.title: Cassiopeia Production Suite 1 Bundle
items.subtitle: These four Kontakt instruments from Soundsphat deliver thousands of highly editable, release-ready presets.
items.feedText: Let’s see what sample-based sound design has to offer your productions. Software synthesizers completely revolutionized the way music was made, and the sound of almost every genre of music has changed as a result. But arguably at least as influential to the music we hear today were sample-based instruments, such as those made for NI’s Kontakt. From meticulously recreated playable orchestras to special effects and sound design tools, everybody with a computer can produce more complex, modulatable tones in seconds…
items.body:
These four Kontakt instruments from [Soundsphat](https://www.soundsphat.com/cassiopeia-soundsphat-production-suite-1)deliver thousands of highly editable, release-ready presets. Let’s see what sample-based sound design has to offer your productions.

Software synthesizers completely revolutionized the way music was made, and the sound of almost every genre of music has changed as a result. But arguably at least as influential to the music we hear today were sample-based instruments, such as those made for NI’s Kontakt.

From meticulously recreated playable orchestras to special effects and sound design tools, everybody with a computer can produce more complex, modulatable tones in seconds than the entire BBC Radiophonic Workshop could manage in decades.

But with so many analogue-modelled soft synths on the market today, it feels like we rarely use sampled instruments for our core sounds. Which is where the Cassiopeia bundle of Kontakt instruments comes in.

Guided by Grammy-nominated Christian Beat Hirt, Soundsphat aims to deliver a definitive selection of production-ready presets, complete with performance and modulation options, and all of the envelope, filter, and effects controls you could desire.

## Production Suite 1 Overview

There are four instruments in the package: Cassiopeia, Landlord Stabs, Zerotone 6, and The Riga Piano. Each has its own sonic concept but all share a similar interface and layer-based approach to sound design, so we'll devote most of this review to the headline instrument, Cassiopeia, then explain how the others each riff on this concept.

Cassiopeia is based around four sound layers. The first two play host to the core sound layers like multisampled analogue synth layers, custom wavetables, acoustic-instrument-sourced waveforms, and more. The second two are sound-design-focused layers, including everything from bird calls and bells to subs and metal clangs. You can even add your own layers.

In terms of content, the headline figures are pretty impressive: a 422 GB library size (compressed to around 350 GB on your drive) with 58,000 samples, 120 custom wavetables, and 3,922 multisampled patches.

The sound design is top-notch throughout and the biggest selling point of this package by far. You could absolutely make complete, great-sounding tracks with nothing more than the sounds on offer here. Every kind of patch is covered, from basses and leads to pads and effects. And they’re incredibly polished, rich, slathered in effects, and ready to use.

For all that variety, though, this collection does very much have a distinct vibe. And it’s aimed squarely at the dancefloor and energetic playlists, so if you don’t like those kinds of sounds, this probably won’t be your bag.

## Cassiopeia In Use

Once you’ve found your sounds there is a powerful range of editing options.

The main interface is fairly uncomplicated with an X-Y modulation matrix for simultaneous real-time modulation of multiple effects and some headline parameters such as pitch bend range, filter cutoff and resonance, tone, volume, and velocity sensitivity. Plus buttons to add/mute each of the four sound layers that make up a Cassiopeia patch.

Cassiopeia’s main page and X-Y modulation control

There are then six editing pages. EDIT offers up various controls. For example, polyphony, portamento, and a chord maker feature. Then you can apply up to nine effects: Reverb/convolution, Room, Comp, Delay, EQ, Tape, Chorus, Flanger, and Phaser, with detailed controls for each.

The EDIT page, with its nine effects

Next comes ADSR, offering up assignable envelope control for volume, cutoff, and pitch of each individual layer. This is very welcome, but unfortunately brings us to the first of only two gripes about this synth. The way you assign the envelopes to the layers is really unintuitive, and hard to understand even after reading the manual. You use the same on/off button to assign a voice to an envelope group as you do to call up that voice’s individual envelope settings. It’s definitely worth revisiting in an update.

Envelopes for volume, cutoff and pitch on the ADSR page

Speaking of which, the LFO page has the same sound-shaping benefits and confusing assignment system as ADSR.

The LFO page

Luckily the ARP window is not confusing at all, offering a powerful and intuitive step-sequence-style programmer and all of the swing and timing controls you’d hope for. There’s even a randomize function.

It’s no surprise, then, that some of the most satisfying patches in the whole instrument are found in the ARP preset category – there’s just something fundamentally usable about them, enhanced by the top-tier sound design of each patch. Just keep an eye on the timing as you’ll find most arp-based patches need between −5 and −20 ms of track delay to slot into a project.

The ARP page’s step-style programmer

The MIX window comes next, with level and pan controls for each of the four layers, plus individual per-layer controls for things like pitch (semitones and cents), high- and low-pass filters, and Body and Silk (for boosting or easing low-mid and high-mid frequencies, respectively).

The layer-based architecture of Cassiopeia patches means you’ll probably spend a lot of time in this window, and it’s powerful and well laid out. It’s a shame, then, that there’s some real jank to the level fader controls – it can be really hard to get hold of them with the mouse pointer, particularly if you’ve previously pulled one all the way down.

Per-layer controls on the MIX page

Finally, there’s SOUND MENU, which allows you to swap different sound layers in or out. The options for each layer are neatly labelled and categorized, so if you’re the experimental type you’ll find hundreds of options allowing for many thousands of permutations.

Swapping layers in the SOUND MENU

## What About The Rest Of The Bundle?

Landlord Stabs uses the same basic design to deliver a selection of over 500 chord and stab-based presets. Named after the legendary [Landlord stab](https://www.attackmagazine.com/technique/synth-secrets/make-rave-stabs-like-the-landlord-stab/), this instrument goes further, with organs, orchestral-style, and other hits. If you’re after rave leads, look no further, but there’s much more to it than that.

Landlord Stabs

Zerotone 6 next, and this one is as close as the bundle gets to a conventional synthesizer, but still very much based on layered elements and inventive modulations. It gets its core sounds from two analogue synths – the Sequential Circuits Prophet-10 and Studio Electronics SE-1, judging from the images – allowing real-time blending, bending, and cross-modulation of the various waveforms in a custom granular engine. It sounds great, offers a bunch of usable presets, and has oodles of scope for user sound design.

…

items.title: 25 Films Inspired by Edgar Allan Poe Online: The Fall of the House of Usher, The Tell-Tale Heart, and More
items.subtitle: Rank the films inspired by Edgar Allan Poe, and several adaptations of “The Fall of the House of Usher” will almost certainly come near the top.
items.feedText: At first glance, that story of a man paying a visit to an old friend who lives with his twin sister in their family’s grand house — each of the latter three well advanced into a different process of deterioration — might seem too short, as well as too light on conflict to translate into a conventional screenplay. items.body:
Rank the films inspired by Edgar Allan Poe, and several adaptations of [“The Fall of the House of Usher”](https://www.eapoe.org/works/tales/usherf.htm) will almost certainly come near the top. At first glance, that story of a man paying a visit to an old friend who lives with his twin sister in their family’s grand house — each of the latter three well advanced into a different process of deterioration — might seem too short, as well as too light on conflict to translate into a conventional screenplay. Yet it’s also full of cinematically irresistible images, from the somehow ruinous yet wholly intact titular mansion to the bloodily wretched sister throwing herself upon the terrified brother who entombed her alive while their ancestral home collapses around them.

Of the twenty or thirty versions of “The Fall of the House of Usher” so far made for the screen, the most celebrated remains the one Jean Epstein directed in 1928. [Officially designating it as one of the “great movies,”](https://www.rogerebert.com/reviews/great-movie-the-fall-of-the-house-of-usher-1928) Roger Ebert calls that picture’s vision of the great hall “one of the most haunting spaces in the movies. Its floor is a vast marble expanse, interrupted here and there by an item of furniture that seems dwarfed by the surrounding emptiness. An odd staircase rises from one distant corner. It is not impossible that this vision, in one of the best-known French surrealist films, inspired the designers of the great hall of Xanadu in *Citizen Kane*.”

The avant-garde filmmaking duo James Sibley Watson Jr. and Melville Webber (in collaboration with e. e. cummings, who contributed to the script) could hardly manage the same scale of production design for [their own short adaptation of Poe’s story](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eh1Fnxctjsw), which happened to come out the same year.

But the resulting Expressionist take on the material has also been highly acclaimed, and through [this YouTube playlist of Poe films](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLGECP2JNbcRg), you can experience not just both of them, but also other adaptations of “The Fall of the House of Usher” by [idiosyncratic Czech animator Jan Švankmajer](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4f3ZxoLTHkk) and [B‑movie powerhouse Roger Corman](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EgktFwcVXCY). Sensitive to Poe’s sensationalist appeal and air of transgressive decadence, Corman ended up directing an eight-film “Poe cycle,” nearly all of which star Vincent Price.

It’s fair to say that no film actor is more closely associated with Poe than Price, a link Tim Burton [celebrated in animation](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hD8uQzu0IL0) at the beginning of his career. Price even played the writer himself in [An Evening with Edgar Allan Poe](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZzyYzK94UU4&list=PLGECP2JNbcRg&index=7), a special from 1970 in which he recites “The Sphinx,” “The Cask of Amontillado,” “The Pit and the Pendulum,” and “The Tell-Tale Heart.” That last, the most screen-adapted Poe story of them all, also appears on [the playlist](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLGECP2JNbcRg) in various forms: an [early D. W. Griffith feature](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=avB4bs4Q6DU), the [directorial debut of Jules Dassin](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RW6fdqnN0E0), an [animated short narrated by James Mason](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WAXB2H3SsFg), a [British psychological thriller](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pXMZeSZS_-A), and a [transposition into modern-day New Orleans](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yWworPqU668). And if you haven’t had enough Poe after watching through all 25 of these films, consider watching the recent, well-received *Fall of the House of Usher * miniseries on Netflix — an entertainment platform that satisfies much the same appetites Poe’s stories have been feeding for nearly two centuries.
