items.body:
This article explains how LLMs encode and process token position information by covering classic and contemporary methods like RoPE. It’s essentially a comprehensive journey where we will work through the mechanisms with visual examples, a little math, and a small PyTorch implementation. And, of course, we will then also look at how modern architectures adapt or omit explicit positional encodings.

Below, you can find a preview of which positional embedding choices are used in 2026 open-weight models. We will discuss these choices later after covering the underlying mechanisms.

Figure 1: A preview of the gallery’s 2026 architectures, grouped by positional encoding. Architecture figures taken from my [LLM gallery](https://sebastianraschka.com/llm-architecture-gallery/).

But why spending so much time writing/reading about this rather minor building block? LLMs keep evolving, and as I was preparing a new article on the latest LLM architecture trends this year, I realized that I never covered the positional information methods used in LLMs in any article so far. So, instead of letting the other article get out of hand, I thought it might make sense to publish this as a standalone building block for the upcoming LLM architecture and trends analysis.

Also, over the years, many readers have asked me for a tutorial on relative positional embeddings (aka RoPE) to follow up on the learned absolute embeddings used in GPT. It’s been on my TODO list for a long time, so I finally revisited my old draft and put this walkthrough together, which will cover

- different positional methods in LLMs;
- (finally) how RoPE works;
- what methods are used by recent open LLMs.

Note that this article assumes some familiarity with basic LLM architectures and works well as a follow-up to [Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch)](https://sebastianraschka.com/books/#build-a-large-language-model-from-scratch). If the concepts and computation of the attention internals, particularly query, key, and value vectors, are a little fuzzy, I recommend checking my [self-attention walkthrough](https://magazine.sebastianraschka.com/p/understanding-and-coding-self-attention) as a refresher:

The article is also very technical and likely too detailed for some. However, I really wanted to have this foundation out there for future articles to reference. And no worries, the next one will return to a more comfortable style.

**PS: I started experimenting with Substack’s new “perks” system. As a thank-you to supporters, I’ve added [image exports and metadata](https://magazine.sebastianraschka.com/perks) from the architecture gallery for you to use in your own analyses.**

PPS: If you are already familiar with how position embeddings work, feel free to fast-forward to Section 6, *Positional choices in modern architectures*.

Note that this article may be best read in a web browser than an email client. I recommend checking out the [web view here](https://magazine.sebastianraschka.com/p/understanding-positional-embeddings), which also has a navigation bar on the left side.

## 1. Where position information enters an LLM

Let’s start with the overall architecture. A tokenizer encodes the input text into token IDs. Next, the input token embedding layer of an LLM maps each of these IDs to a vector of numbers. We usually refer to these entries in that vector as “features” (similar to classic ML). The transformer blocks inside the LLM then modify these vectors using attention and feedforward layers. Lastly, the model’s output layer produces logit scores (converted into probabilities) for the next token.

The following shows this path in GPT-2 (a relatively classic LLM) and MiniMax-M3 (a more recent LLM released this year; a placeholder for most other recent LLMs). As we can see, the architectures are not too different from each other, but before we get to the positional information parts, let’s focus on the orange blocks for now (the token embedding layers) and the transformer blocks above them; the other architecture differences aren’t needed for this explanation.

Figure 2: Token embedding layers in GPT-2 and MiniMax-M3, highlighted in orange. (Side note: M3’s first three out of 60 feedforward layers are dense not MoEs.)

A token embedding layer, shown in the figure above, maps each token ID to a vector. Position information is then added afterward. Concretely, and as we will discuss in more detail later, GPT-2 adds a position vector to each token embedding before the modified embedding enters the first transformer block. On the other hand, MiniMax-M3 adds the positional information in each transformer block using a method called RoPE inside attention.

We will talk about these methods in more detail later, but first, let’s start with the big picture information explaining why explicit positional information is added or needed.

### 1.1 Why add positional information?

Consider the following two input sentences as a simple example:

- “The red fox jumps over the gray fox.”
- “The gray fox jumps over the red fox.”

Changing the word order changes which fox does the jumping, as illustrated in the following figure.

Figure 3: Changing the word order changes which fox jumps.

For the examples in this article, we will treat each word as one token for simplicity. (As you know, real tokenizers can split words into smaller subword tokens.) The first sentence then has eight token positions, from 0 through 7.

Figure 4: Token IDs and positions in the toy sentence.

# Assume the following small vocabulary.
# Real vocabularies typically have 50k to 200k entries
vocab = {
"The": 0,
"red": 1,
"fox": 2,
"jumps": 3,
"gray": 4,
"over": 5,
"the": 6,
}

(If you are interested in how vocabularies are built, check out my [tokenizer materials on GitHub](https://github.com/rasbt/LLMs-from-scratch/tree/main/ch02/05_bpe-from-scratch).)

Note that “fox”, which appears twice in the input sentence, gets the same token ID 2 in both cases. And since they both have the same token ID, irrespective of the position in the input sentence, they would get the same embedding vector from the embedding layer. (For those who are interested in more details on how this selection from the embedding table looks like, check [Appendix A](https://sebastianraschka.com/supplementary/positional-embeddings/#appendix-a-token-embedding-lookups).)

Now, let’s consider a regular self-attention mechanism with no positional encoding (and no causal mask), where every input token can attend to every other token in the input. In this scenario, swapping any two words, like “red” and “gray”, would still result in the same embeddings and attention scores between each token pair.

…

items.body:
*Housekeeping:*

- There will be a reader meetup in SF on December 10: [RSVP here.](https://luma.com/mk1c03jk)
- I’ll be in Stockholm on November 26 and made [a Luma event if someone wants to meet up](https://luma.com/8ga6l729). You can also dm me on Substack.

If you read writing advice, you’ll often stumble upon all of these rather abstract rules, such as “show, don’t tell,” “open the essay with a concrete story to engage people,” and so on. I don’t find advice like that useful at all. These sorts of maxims remind me of the small notes I might jot down to myself to remember the directions to a friend’s house—“left, right, past the oak tree, right.” Well, that might describe the right way, but it is a very rough map of the terrain, and if it turns out that the person who wrote the notes forgot to mention something—or perhaps was going somewhere other than you—their advice will lead you completely astray.

To develop a good toolbox, I find it much more fruitful to take the texts that I feel do whatever I want to learn best and read them slowly, repeatedly, with a pencil in hand. It’s like taking a slow, attentive walk around the neighborhood, getting a deep *feeling* for the landscape, for what it means to write at the highest levels. I will usually form a few theories about why the text is so powerful and I might spot a few techniques I can put into my toolbox, but these theories and techniques will be much more idiosyncratic and tentative than the ones I get from consuming writing advice: I will create tools that are meaningful to *my* projects, and my taste, and I will hold the tools with a light hand, knowing full well that they are just a rough guess, derived from a limited reading.

Last weekend, I did such a close reading of the piece that David Foster Wallace wrote about John McCain’s failed campaign for the Republican presidential nomination in 2000—the one that was originally published as “The Weasel, Twelve Monkeys and the Shrub,” a sprawling ~15,700-word essay in the April 13 issue of *Rolling Stone,* and later republished in a three-times-as-long “director’s cut” ebook called, first, *Up, Simba*, and later, *McCain’s Promise*. It is a New Journalism-derived sort of essay-reportage hybrid, where DFW travels around with the McCain campaign’s press bus, fails to interview any of the main players, and instead hangs around with the cameramen and sound technicians, but does little of the standard journalistic scene-setting and interview-quoting, in favor of a kind of writing that is a crossover between diary and essay.

I have read the book-length version of *McCain’s Promise* four times, I think, and the short version, once or twice. The immediate excuse for the last two + one rereads was that I wanted to understand how DFW integrates interviews and scene-setting into his essayistic reflections (and for the answer to that see this footnote1), but what I ended up focusing most on during the actual reading was the question: how on earth does he manage to make the reading so engaging and have such strong narrative momentum when most of it is just very long and detailed descriptions of the interior of a bus and the different kinds of phones people use on the bus and so on?

#### How DFW creates narrative momentum

items.body:
The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is a major setback for the US development of an open model ecosystem. Nvidia still has the financial interests in supporting open models, which are to avoid concentration in power among a few customers who would develop their own chips and reduce Nvidia’s profits, but supporting the open ecosystem is a tricky puzzle more than an engineering problem to grind out a solution on.

Nvidia’s business operations are famously extremely dependent on Jensen as an operator, so it is a consensus opinion that there are challenges ahead (or even more high-profile departures through chip-smuggling investigations or plain-old sharks circling more poachable talent). Nvidia’s number one goal is to stabilize the ship, deliver to customers in the next 24 months, and prevent implosion. Open models have been one of Jensen’s more ambitious, founder-style bets. He has been flooding the zone with funding in a way that will very likely dry up.

Interconnects AI is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

In this period, the open model economy is in its nascency. These are crucial years for establishing use-cases, revenue flow, and motives to continue training the next generation models. I discussed the sensitivity of these early years in my recent talk at Fireworks Forge ([slides](https://natolambert.com/slides/2026/fireworks/talk.html), [recording](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zsO5RktNB7k)). The core of the argument is one upside for open models, a reason to be optimistic, and one downside.

The positive case is that the open model economy has correctly latched onto “ownership of intelligence” and enterprise post-training as a crucial lane. What is to be determined is exactly how big the downstream market is.

The downside is that the true *long-term* benefit of open models, as truly commoditized intelligence, is very far from realization with compute in such short supply. In the near term, where [inference startups are also struggling to get enough chips](https://www.theinformation.com/articles/ai-inference-startups-quietly-buying-chips) (because Anthropic and OpenAI are buying so much capacity), there’s little margin competition on open-weight models. If open-source models are also served at giant inference margins, as we learned with DeepSeek’s [DeepInfer](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepinfer) release, they’re far from a commodity. In this paradigm, the closed labs with better economies of scale and integration from model to datacenter and chips will win. I expanded on this challenge in [my recent piece on the open model economy](https://www.interconnects.ai/p/how-well-can-we-measure-open-model).

Together, a lot still needs to go right for open models to be a meaningful economic engine. Jensen’s support, and protection, gave the ecosystem time to figure this out.

Jensen was more than a cheerleader. He would stop a lot of shit from going wrong once early winds were stirring. He was willing to use his power on open models.

There’s a major swell in Democratic government funding towards [candidates that want to regulate the AI industry, fostering “safety”](https://www.axios.com/2026/10/14/ai-safety-regulation-election-spending-50-million). Many of these people feel a need to do something and have general opinions that open models are unsafe, while not being educated on the complexities of their benefits. My biggest near-term worry is sloppy regulation at the state level, followed by national regulation. We’ve been [one, strong Chinese open-weight model away from a crisis](https://www.interconnects.ai/p/6-months-to-live-for-open-models) since this summer. It still holds – especially as we enter a new, turbulent equilibrium of cybersecurity. We have not seen a major hack driven by a popular Chinese open-weight model, but it is a matter of when, not if. We need someone to encourage caution and an ecosystem perspective when the “open-weight hawks” come hunting.

Knocking over the open-source AI domino today is easy — if done, unwinding the downstream concentration of power, reduction in safety research, and stifling of long-term innovation is far harder. On public data, it looks like balancing long-term innovation versus short term risks, but this is due to how horribly hard it is to measure the open model economy (e.g. the most valuable aspects of it run on private infrastructure). It’s a recurring challenge facing the ecosystem and my work.

As a brief aside, the extent to which the media ecosystem is revolving around timing today, rather than exact availability of information, is incredible. All of these Jensen affairs were known, but getting them out at the right time, right after the midterm political swing, took down the king.

The same goes for the Jacob Coxon brouhaha this summer. All of that safety culture around top labs was well known, but the right timing around datacenters and the Overton window made it a national issue. This could very well happen at some point for open model safety, as it tends to be harm, risk, or safety-related narratives that drive the modern media algorithms. I cannot imagine my work on open-science driving such a media cycle, because it will never happen.

[Share](https://www.interconnects.ai/p/open-source-ai-without-jensen?utm_source=substack&utm_medium=email&utm_content=share&action=share)

The only lasting solution to this is to incubate a truly frontier open model player in the US. For example, I agree completely with Dylan Patel, CEO of SemiAnalysis, on a core problem in the US open model ecosystem. From a recent ChinaTalk + SemiAnalysis [emergency podcast](https://youtu.be/2jqSNHWdHEY?t=1737):

> Jordan Schneider: I do want your guys’ take on just how bad this is, that Jensen’s now off the table for the future of American innovation. And we should talk about open models. I mean, he was the big champion, right? Dylan, you were talking earlier — I still don’t understand quite why someone didn’t just spend a few billion dollars and make something better than Kimi or DeepSeek and open source it.
> Dylan Patel: Not that easy. It’s not money, it’s talent, man. All of the most talented people primarily work at Anthropic, OpenAI, DeepMind, and Meta TBD, right? And then those who don’t are split across a hundred different startups. I mean, yes, Thinking Machines has a cracked team, but is Thinking Machines as good as Moonshot? No. Moonshot skill-wise is probably just as good as the US labs. They just have a big deficit in compute and deployment. So I think if we don’t have a scale advantage, then you don’t win. Yes, these smaller labs have spent a lot of money on models. But DeepMind, Grok, Meta have regularly fallen behind the frontier of Chinese labs, and they’re spending more. So it’s not just, oh, spend a few billion dollars and you can make a model that’s better.

items.body:
After a months-long investigation, Channel 4 News’s FactCheck team has obtained a dossier of exclusive new files on UK arms export licences to Israel.

The files give us major new insights into UK companies’ arms sales to the Israeli government during its war on Gaza, which has killed at least 75,000 Palestinians.

Our revelations raise questions about the former Conservative government’s policy on arms sales, as well as the current Labour government’s stated policy on the ongoing export of military aircraft parts.

We’re going to take you through the files step by step.

## The basics – what is an export licence?

When a UK company wants to sell arms abroad, it needs to apply to the UK government for an arms export licence – this document is like a permission slip.

Public data on these licences is limited. It doesn’t tell us whether the licences have actually been used to export weapons, or who in a given country would be using them.

But through repeated Freedom of Information requests to the Department for Business and Trade, FactCheck has now obtained several line-by-line snapshots of active arms export licences for Israel. The snapshots are from July 2024, July 2025 and July 2026.

Our new data captures which licences were active, not just for the country of Israel, but specifically for use by the Israeli government – which we understand means the Israeli military. And it also includes “usage notes”, which tell us whether a given licence has been used to export goods during a specific period of time.

## The Conservative government

On 7 October 2023, attacks on Israel by Hamas – which is proscribed as a terror group by the UK – left 1,200 people killed and 251 taken hostage. Israel then began its biggest ever bombardment of Gaza.

It was then that the International Court of Justice ruled there was a plausible risk of genocide in Gaza. Soon after, in April 2024, hundreds of UK lawyers, including former Supreme Court justices, issued a legal opinion saying that the UK must urgently suspend arms sales to Israel.

The then-Conservative UK government did not suspend arms sales.

Our first snapshot of new data reveals that, as the Conservatives were leaving office in July 2024, there were still 67 military export licenses left active where the Israeli government was an end user.

Those licences permitted the sale of a wide range of items – including parts for:

- combat aircraft
- military helicopters
- combat vehicles
- equipment for the launch and control of munitions
- military communications equipment
- military navigation equipment
- other military aircraft
- training ammunition, and more.

The total value of the active licences was around £164m. That represents an upper limit on what could have been exported under single issue licences. But the data also includes other types of open licence, which allow an unlimited value of exports.

We can reveal for the first time that, by July 2024, at least 25 of those 67 active licences had actually been used to send military parts to the Israeli government, since October 2023.

The licences that were used by UK companies to export goods during the war included licences for parts for:

- targeting equipment
- military aero engines
- combat aircraft
- military aircraft
- trainer aircraft
- parts for surface-to-air missiles.
- Targeting equipment refers to equipment which allows you to find, and aim weapons at, a target on the ground.

One of the used licences was a high value £25m licence for parts and software for “military aero engines”, which could include engines for military aircraft or drones. The data does not reveal the exact value that was actually exported. Another was an £88m licence for parts of “combat aircraft”.

The combined value of the used licences was around £150m. Again, this represents an upper limit on what would have been exported, and the actual value of the items sent was likely lower.

Two of the licences had been exhausted, meaning their full value was exported. These included one worth around £66,000 for trainer aircraft parts, and another worth around £109,000 for combat aircraft parts. It’s not clear whether the full value was exported during the war on Gaza.

We spoke to Professor Janina Dill, Dame Louise Richardson Chair in Global Security at the Blavatnik School of Government, University of Oxford. She told FactCheck that the UK “should have used [its] leverage” as a major arms exporter to Israel and “while there is a great deal of contestation around the question whether Israel is commiting genocide in Gaza”, it was “hardly contestable in 2024” that it was “committing grave breaches and war crimes”.

The Conservative Party did not respond to our repeated requests for comment about this story.

Israel has repeatedly denied the accusations that it has committed genocide or breaches of international law in Gaza.

## The Labour government

In July 2024, Keir Starmer’s Labour government entered power.

And by September 2024, the new administration said it wanted to suspend around 30 arms export licences for Israel, citing concerns over breaches of international law.

It said it was suspending exports that could be used by the Israeli military in Gaza. And it explicitly mentioned targeting equipment, and parts for military aircraft, including helicopters, fighter jets and drones.

But there were two big carve outs in the policy.

Firstly, Labour said it would continue to allow the sale of military training items, because they wouldn’t be used directly in conflict.

And secondly, the Labour government said it wouldn’t try to stop all exports of parts for the F-35 — a type of fighter jet used by Israel and NATO allies — because the exports went to a global pool that benefited multiple countries.

The Labour government refused to give us the full list of licences it suspended – even under Freedom of Information laws. It cited commercial sensitivity and confidentiality. It said if we figured out the names of the companies holding the suspended licences, we might, “potentially incorrectly”, link those firms to potential war crimes.

But by looking at the snapshots which the government did release, and comparing the active licences before and after Labour’s suspensions, we can corroborate some of what Labour announced about its suspensions.

For example, targeting equipment did disappear from later lists of active export licences, after Labour’s suspensions. As did other licences covering parts for military helicopters and combat vehicles. So that data fits with what Labour said it would do.

But many export permissions remained active under the Labour government.

Some of the licences that remained active for the Israeli government under Labour included parts for:

items.body:
Cover Image by [Gustavo Fring](https://www.pexels.com/@2206740/) from Pexels

*By Althea Need Kaminske*

Perhaps one of the more obvious pieces of advice that I give medical students about learning is to remember that our brains are in our bodies. Yes, I know that these are very smart, high achieving students who know quite a bit about anatomy and biology. But I also know that in an educational system and society that focuses so much on productivity, it can be easy to compartmentalize our lives. To become so focused on maximizing spaced retrieval practice (yay!) that we forget to prioritize sleep, nutrition, and exercise (boo!). In high-stress and fast-paced environments it can be difficult to remember that we are, ultimately, animals. Creatures that need sleep, a healthy diet, and daily walks.

A recent meta-meta-analysis by Singh et al. (2025) examined the effectiveness of exercise for improving cognition (1). The analysis included 133 meta-analysis, which themselves comprised a total of 2,724 randomized control trials. I’ll break down the results, but the overall finding was pretty notable: **exercise, even light intensity, benefits general cognition, memory, and executive function across all populations.**

The meta-meta-analysis classified outcomes into three categories: general cognition, memory, and executive function. General cognition was measured by scales like the Mini-Mental State Examination, Montreal Cognitive Assessment, and the Alzheimer’s Disease Assessment Scale - Cognitive Subscale which are used in medical settings to assess overall cognitive functioning. Memory was measured by instruments like the Wechsler Memory Scale and Verbal Learning Test which measure short-term memory and episodic memory. Executive function was measured by tools like the Digit-Span Test, Digit Span-Backwards, Digit-Span Forwards, and Trail Making Test Part A and B which measure visual and verbal working memory and attention.

## General Cognition and Exercise

There was a significant effect of exercise for improving general cognition. This effect was found across all age groups. The effect varied as a function of exercise type, with a moderate-to-large effect for exergames, and a small-to-moderate effect for aerobic, dance, mind-body, mixed mode, resistance exercise, and other. The effect of exercise on general cognition did not vary as a function of exercise intensity, however interventions that lasted for 1-3 months had the greatest effect on general cognition compared to interventions lasting 4-6 months or greater than 6 months. Finally, the beneficial effects of exercise on general cognition did not vary as a function of session frequency, session duration, or weekly duration.

## Memory and Exercise

There was a significant effect of exercise on memory. This effect was stronger in children/adolescents than in older adults (though benefits were still present in older adults). The effect also varied as a function of exercise type, with large effects for exergames, small-to-medium effects for aerobic, dance, mind-body, mixed mode, and resistance exercise. The effect of exercise on memory did not vary as a function of exercise intensity or intervention length. Further, the beneficial effect of exercise on memory did not vary as a function of session frequency or duration (there was an insufficient number of studies to draw conclusions about weekly duration).

## Executive Function and Memory

There was a significant effect of exercise on executive function. This effect was stronger in children/adolescents than in older adults (though benefits were still present in older adults). The effect also varied as a function of exercise type with exercises categorized as “other” as having a greater effect compared to aerobic, dance, exergames, mind-body, mixed mode and resistance exercise. The effect of exercise on executive function did not vary as a function of exercise intensity or intervention length. Further the beneficial effects of exercise on executive function did not vary as a function of session frequency, session duration, or weekly duration.

## Why does exercise benefit cognition?

The authors propose two potential ways that exercise improves cognition. First, there are several physiological mechanisms that might lead to cognitive improvement. The release of neurotrophic factors, increased vascularisation of the brain, greater dendritic spine density, enhanced synaptic plasticity, and reduced systemic inflammation (1). Your brain is in your body! Exercise improves overall brain health.

Second, the authors highlight the fact that exergames appear to be a particularly potent form of exercise. They suggest that this particular mode of exercise not only confers some of the physical benefits listed above, but may be particularly potent because of the challenging cognitive aspect of the exercise. Exergames require you to recall movements, recognize cues, and memorize steps.

## Exercise and ADHD

While there were benefits of exercise for all populations, the authors note that the benefit appears to be greater for those with ADHD. They highlight a few potential reasons for this. First, many of the studies examining exercise and ADHD involved children and adolescents, which is a population that was more responsive to exercise in general. Second, given that the hallmark of ADHD is struggles with executive function, they suggest that ADHDers simply had more room for improvement. Finally, they point out that one of the proposed mechanisms for working memory deficits in ADHD are altered neural activity in areas of the brain associated with working memory. Exercise may improve neural activity in these areas through enhanced blood flow and neuroplasticity. While further research is needed to test these theories, and to extend them to adult populations, this provides some initial evidence for a relatively low-cost tool for helping with the management of ADHD.

## Takeaways

Overall, I think the results of this meta-meta-analysis are really encouraging. Exercise - any exercise - can benefit cognition. Whether it’s a 20 minute walk after dinner, lifting weights, or breaking out the Nintendo Wii, adding movement into your routine can improve your cognition, memory, and focus.

My dog, Oden, who reminds me to go for walks every day.

…

items.body:
Welcome to the latest edition of “What’s new in Swift,” a curated digest of releases, news, and discussions from the Swift project and community.

To start things off, our guest contributor shares a timely reminder for anyone relying on CocoaPods:

> Hi, I’m Dave Verwer, co-creator of the [Swift Package Index](https://swiftpackageindex.com/) and now part of a team at Apple working on a public, cross-platform package registry for Swift. How developers find, share, and manage dependencies across the entire ecosystem is something we think about a lot.
> CocoaPods is a dependency manager for Swift and Objective-C Cocoa projects. The project began in 2011, before Swift was publicly available and long before the Swift Package Manager (SwiftPM) existed. For many people who started developing with the iPhone SDK, it was a first look at what a dependency manager could do. Today, Swift has expanded across platforms, and SwiftPM has become the standard for managing dependencies everywhere Swift runs.
> Following a two-year sunset period that began in 2024, the [CocoaPods project will stop accepting new pods and pod versions on December 2nd, 2026](https://blog.cocoapods.org/CocoaPods-Specs-Repo/). With that date less than a month away, I wanted to make sure this milestone is on your radar, and to share what it means for your projects. If your project still uses CocoaPods, this change won’t immediately break your builds. All current pods and versions will still be available, just in a read-only state. However, with pod authors no longer able to publish updates, if you haven’t switched to SwiftPM yet, now is the time.
> Most pods in your dependencies that are still being maintained will already be compatible with SwiftPM, and the easiest way to check is to look for them on [Swift Package Index](https://swiftpackageindex.com). Every package in the index is a SwiftPM package, and if you find any incompatible pods, you can search for an alternative so you don’t leave yourself with unmaintained dependencies.
> I’d like to extend a personal thank you to everyone who worked on CocoaPods for creating and maintaining it for the last fifteen years. Their work shaped how the community shares code, and it helped lay the groundwork for the modern, cross-platform package ecosystem Swift has today. I also want to express my admiration for how the team managed this sunset and communicated the transition so clearly.

Now on to other news about Swift:

## Videos to watch

- Tim Condon’s ACCU 2026 talk, [Incrementally Migrating C++ to a Memory Safe Language with Swift](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LMQ21X6_2FQ), shows how Swift’s C++ interoperability lets you adopt memory safety incrementally, without rewriting everything at once.
- [Building Android App with Swift: First-Hand Experience](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AibwYt3esbk) is a conversation with Pierluigi Cifani, who describes how his team shares business logic and ViewModels between iOS and Android, with native UI on each and Skip bridging the two, in apps like Polymarket.
- Want to build Minecraft mods in Swift? A recent iOSDC Japan lightning talk, [Creating a Minecraft Java mod with Swift](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=r_A44OiLASw), shows how, using swift-java to interoperate with Minecraft Java Edition. The speaker’s [blog post](https://note.com/1mash0/n/n107a49ec76a3) has the slides and more demo videos. The talk is in Japanese, with an auto-dubbed English track available on YouTube.

## Community highlights

- Did you know Optional has a take() method? John Sundell’s [Interesting ways of using Swift optionals](https://www.swiftbysundell.com/articles/interesting-ways-of-using-swift-optionals/) goes beyond if let, with take(), switching directly on optional enums, and a small isNil(or:) helper that works with key paths.
- What happens when you let the compiler check your whole website? Sindre Sorhus [rebuilt his site in Swift](https://sindresorhus.com/blog/swift-website), moving off Astro so that broken links and bad metadata become build errors.
- Two server-side frameworks, one team’s experience. [Don’t Underestimate Swift](https://wearecommunity.io/communities/mobilepeople/articles/8881) shares what engineers at EPAM learned building backends with Hummingbird and Vapor, and how those services compared against FastAPI and Node.js.
- A [preview of Embedded Swift support in Swift Testing](https://forums.swift.org/t/preview-embedded-swift-support-in-swift-testing/90281) shows nearly the whole API, including @Test, #expect(), and custom traits, running in Embedded Swift. It has been tried on WASI in Safari, a Raspberry Pi Pico 2, a Playdate, and a Game Boy Advance SP.

## New package releases

- [Swift Kafka Client](https://github.com/swift-server/swift-kafka-client/releases/tag/1.0.0) has reached 1.0.0. The client for Apache Kafka, the event streaming platform, is built on librdkafka and works with structured concurrency, with built-in metrics through swift-metrics and static Linux builds.
- Robotics meets Swift. [swift-ros2](https://github.com/swift-ros2/swift-ros2) is a native client library for ROS 2, the robotics framework. It runs on Apple platforms, Linux, Windows, and Android, and version 3.1.0 recently added a topic graph API for discovering what’s available on a robot network.
- [Perfect-NIO](https://github.com/PerfectlySoft/Perfect-NIO), the HTTP layer of the Perfect server framework, has been rewritten on SwiftNIO and Swift 6 concurrency. Version 0.1.0 uses async, @Sendable route handlers, and 0.2.0 adds WebSocket message size limits.

## Swift Evolution

The Swift project adds new language features through the [Swift Evolution process](https://www.swift.org/swift-evolution/). These are some of the proposals currently under review or recently accepted for a future Swift release.

**Under active review:**

- [SE-0559](https://github.com/swiftlang/swift-evolution/blob/main/proposals/0559-unicode-bidi-class.md) Add bidiClass to Unicode.Scalar.Properties - If your code lays out or transforms text that mixes right-to-left and left-to-right scripts, you often need to know how specific characters behave. This proposal adds bidiClass to Unicode.Scalar.Properties, so you can look up a character’s bidirectional class in Swift without needing to bridge to external libraries like ICU.
- [SE-0560](https://github.com/swiftlang/swift-evolution/blob/main/proposals/0560-swiftpm-build-configuration-conditional-target-dependencies.md) Build configuration conditionals for target dependencies - This proposal would let you conditionally include SwiftPM dependencies based on whether you’re building for debug or release. By adding a new configuration condition, you could link a debug menu only into your debug builds, or a crash reporter only into your release builds.

**Recently accepted:**

items.body:
In contemplating the theory of general relativity, Albert Einstein imagined [a falling lift in which people are performing experiments](https://archive.org/details/evolutionofphysi033254mbp/page/n245/mode/2up):

> One of the observers takes a handkerchief and a watch from his pocket and drops them. What happens to these two bodies? … [F]or the outside observer they are both falling with the same acceleration. But so is the lift, with its walls, ceiling, and floor. Therefore: the distance between the two bodies and the floor will not change.

This notion of the equivalence between gravity and acceleration, which he called “the happiest thought of my life,” came to Einstein in 1907. Interestingly, Lewis Carroll had explored a similar scenario in 1889:

> ‘One can easily imagine a situation,’ said Arthur, ‘where things would necessarily have no weight, relatively to each other, though each would have its usual weight, looked at by itself.’
> ‘Some desperate paradox!’ said the Earl. ‘Tell us how it could be. We shall never guess it.’
> ‘Well, suppose this house, just as it is, placed a few billion miles above a planet, and with nothing else near enough to disturb it: of course it falls to the planet?’
> The Earl nodded. ‘Of course — though it might take some centuries to do it.’
> ‘And is five-o’clock-tea to be going on all the while?’ said Lady Muriel.
> ‘That, and other things,’ said Arthur. ‘The inhabitants would live their lives, grow up and die, and still the house would be falling, falling, falling! But now as to the relative weight of things. Nothing can be heavy, you know, except by trying to fall, and being prevented from doing so. You all grant that?’
> We all granted that.
> ‘Well, now, if I take this book, and hold it out at arm’s length, of course I feel its weight. It is trying to fall, and I prevent it. And, if I let go, it falls to the floor. But, if we were all falling together, it couldn’t be trying to fall any quicker, you know: for, if I let go, what more could it do than fall? And, as my hand would be falling too — at the same rate — it would never leave it, for that would be to get ahead of it in the race. And it could never overtake the falling floor!’

(From [Sylvie and Bruno](https://www.google.com/books/edition/Sylvie_and_Bruno/OTcTEQAAQBAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&pg=PT67&printsec=frontcover).)

items.title: Homo Erectus May Have Lived in the Rainforest at the Same Time as Denisovans
items.subtitle: Homo erectus, an extinct archaic hominin, was the first human species to migrate out of Africa and is considered to have been an ancestor of many o…
items.feedText: H. erectus was thought to have died out in mainland China around 400,000 years ago, although they held on in Indonesia for another couple hundred thousand years. But a new discovery may change that timeline. The discovery of hominid teeth in the southern Chinese caves called Baxian and Naxian were dated to somewhere between 324,000 and 184,000 years ago. items.body:
*Homo erectus*, an extinct archaic hominin, was the first human species to migrate out of Africa and is considered to have been an ancestor of many other hominin species. *H. erectus* was thought to have died out in mainland China around 400,000 years ago, although they held on in Indonesia for another couple hundred thousand years. But a new discovery may change that timeline.

The discovery of hominid teeth in the southern Chinese caves called Baxian and Naxian were dated to somewhere between 324,000 and 184,000 years ago. They were analyzed by their proteins, and eight of the nine teeth were determined to be from *H. erectus*. The ninth tooth appears to be Denisovan ( *Homo longi* ). So not only did *H. erectus* hang on longer than we thought, they existed at the same time and area as Denisovans. That doesn't mean they lived together, since the bones and teeth may have been carried into the caves by porcupines (I am not making this up). It also contradicts the notion that *H. erectus* didn't survive well in a rainforest, which that area was all those years ago. [Read more about this discovery](https://arstechnica.com/science/2026/11/homo-erectus-lived-in-the-rainforest-alongside-denisovans/)at Ars Technica.

(Image credit: [Ryan Schwark](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Homo_erectus_diorama_at_the_Hall_of_Human_Origins_at_AMNH.jpg))

Toy photographer [SirDork](https://www.sirdork.com/) (Jared Middleton) showed how he captured an incredibly realistic action shot of a [Spider-Man](https://laughingsquid.com/every-spider-man-radioactive-spider/) action figure on the riveted green girders of a bridge. Skillful close-ups of Spidey’s perch on the truss and specialized lighting worked together to make the image look as if it were happening in real life.

> Perfect Spot for Spidey

SirDork also shared the equipment he uses to get shots like this.

> Camera: Sony A7III
> Lens: Sony 40mm f2.5
> Lighting: Lume Cube Tube Light Mini
> Figure: DBToys Netman

SirDork, who’s based in New York, has also shot for [Disney](https://www.disney.com/) and [Warner Bros.](https://www.warnerbros.com/) He posts videos about collecting action figures and photographing them on his [YouTube channel](https://www.youtube.com/@sirdork730).

items.body:
The surprising benefit of a common enemy

Sallust’s Theorem is that fear of an external enemy promotes internal social unity.

Perhaps more pertinent is the other side of Sallust’s Theorem: the absence or removal of an external enemy leads to internal moral decay and conflict.

Sallust, or more fully Gaius Sallustius Crispus, was a Roman historian and politician around the time of Julius Caesar. Remarkably, several of his works have remained intact to be read over 2000 years later.

Sallust describes unity in the face of common enemies and decline in their absence at several points in the history of Rome’s Republic. His strongest example is the fear of Carthage.

Here’s Sallust in his work The War with Jugurtha, chapter 41 (Latin terms included):

“…before the destruction of Carthage the people and senate of Rome together governed the republic peacefully and with moderation. There was no strife among the citizens either for glory or for power; fear of the enemy (metus hostilis) preserved the good morals of the state.

But when the minds of the people were relieved of that dread (formido), wantonness and arrogance naturally arose, vices which are fostered by prosperity. Thus the peace for which they had longed in time of adversity, after they had gained it proved to be more cruel and bitter than adversity itself.

For the nobles began to abuse their position (dignitas) and the people their liberty (libertas), and every man for himself robbed, pillaged and plundered. Thus the community was split into two parties, and between those the state (res publica) was torn to pieces.” (quoted from Neal Wood, see below)

Sallust sees Rome’s rise and decline as a psychological progression from liberty through glory and ambition to avarice (greed).

You may remember Carthage from the Colosseum scene in the film Gladiator, where Maximus is forced to represent the Carthaginians in Rome’s great victory at the “Battle of Carthage.” It doesn’t go to plan.

Tim Marshall introduced me to Sallust’s Theorem in his fascinating and relevant book Prisoners of Geography. He summarises Sallust’s idea in terms of alliances: “alliances are only strong with the fear of a common enemy.”

In some ways, Sallust’s Theorem is about the danger of getting what we want. We may resent a demanding boss, a fierce local rival, a struggle to build ourselves up from nothing, or a powerful business competitor, yet find that they gave us purpose and brought out the best in us as a group. We can miss them when they’re gone.

—

I believe the term Sallust’s Theorem was introduced by Neal Wood in Wood, N. (1995). Sallust’s Theorem: A Comment on “Fear” in Western Political Thought. History of Political Thought, 16(2), 174–189.

items.title: A hardware-aware open-source framework for design space exploration of mixed-signal spiking neural networks
items.subtitle: IntroductionEnergy-efficient neuromorphic computing at the edge requires simulation tools that can capture the non-ideal behavior of mixed-signal s…
items.feedText: The framework supports multiple neuron models, including Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF), Hodgkin-Huxley (HH) and Axon-Hillock (AH), together with non-volatile analog synapses based on floating-gate transistors and ReRAM devices. By incorporating device-level non-linearities directly into PyTorch-based training and inference, the tool enables optimization of physical synaptic parameters rather than idealized abstract weights.ResultsThe framework is evaluated on standard neuromorphic benchmarks, including N-MNIST,…
items.body: IntroductionEnergy-efficient neuromorphic computing at the edge requires simulation tools that can capture the non-ideal behavior of mixed-signal spiking neural network (SNN) hardware while supporting system-level design exploration.MethodsThis work presents an open-source hardware-aware simulation framework for mixed-signal SNNs that enables comparative analysis across neuron, synapse and architecture choices. The framework supports multiple neuron models, including Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF), Hodgkin-Huxley (HH) and Axon-Hillock (AH), together with non-volatile analog synapses based on floating-gate transistors and ReRAM devices. By incorporating device-level non-linearities directly into PyTorch-based training and inference, the tool enables optimization of physical synaptic parameters rather than idealized abstract weights.ResultsThe framework is evaluated on standard neuromorphic benchmarks, including N-MNIST, DVS Gesture and Spiking Heidelberg Digits (SHD). For each model dataset configuration, it reports classification accuracy together with hardware-oriented metrics such as silicon area, power consumption and quantization sensitivity. In addition, mismatch analysis has been implemented to capture the impact of real silicon fabrication-based effects, such as device-to-device and transistor-level variability, on network behavior.DiscussionThese capabilities enable cross-layer design space exploration and help identify neuron-synapse configurations that best satisfy application-specific constraints on accuracy, energy efficiency, area and hardware fidelity.

items.body:
**Die europäische Office-Suite läuft nicht mehr nur im Browser, sondern jetzt auch als App direkt auf dem Mac – auf Wunsch sogar komplett offline. Seit dem Sommer will Euro-Office eine europäische Alternative zu Microsoft 365 und Google Workspace sein, bislang allerdings nur im Browser. Damit ist jetzt Schluss: Nextcloud hat vor knapp einer Woche fertige Desktop-Version veröffentlicht, die neben macOS auch Windows und Linux unterstützt.**

## Euro-Office unter neuem Namen

Die App heißt Nextcloud Office Desktop, unter der Haube steckt aber Euro-Office. Die Suite ist ein Ableger von OnlyOffice und wird von einem Bündnis um Nextcloud und IONOS entwickelt. Seit dem 9. Juni gibt es sie als stabile Version 1.0., [Apfelpage berichtete](https://www.apfelpage.de/news/euro-office-startet-am-9-juni-europas-office-alternative-kommt-zunaechst-nur-im-browser/). Wer lieber direkt beim Projekt bleibt, findet auf GitHub unsignierte Builds oder baut die Suite selbst aus dem Quellcode.

## Offline arbeiten, lokal oder in der Cloud

Der größte Unterschied zur Web-Variante ist die Offline-Arbeit. Dokumente lassen sich lokal speichern und ohne Internetverbindung bearbeiten. Ihr legt dabei selbst fest, welche Dateien auf dem Rechner bleiben und welche in die Cloud wandern. An Bord sind Programme für Texte, Tabellen, Präsentationen und PDFs. Neben den Microsoft-Formaten DOCX, XLSX und PPTX öffnet die Suite auch die offenen Formate ODT, ODS und ODP.

## Eigene Schriften, Signaturen und Passwortschutz

Wer schon Nextcloud nutzt, verbindet die App mit dem eigenen Konto, auf Wunsch auch mit mehreren Servern gleichzeitig. Anschließend bearbeitet ihr Dokumente gemeinsam mit anderen in Echtzeit. Neu ist außerdem der Zugriff auf die Schriften, die auf dem Rechner installiert sind. Das ist vor allem für Firmen mit eigener Hausschrift praktisch. Fehlt einem Teammitglied die Schrift, zeigt die App dort eine Ersatzschrift an. Im Bereich „Schutz“ lassen sich Dateien digital signieren, sofern ein passendes Zertifikat vorhanden ist. Außerdem könnt ihr Dateien mit einem Passwort schützen und anderen nur Kommentare, das Ausfüllen von Formularen oder nachverfolgte Änderungen erlauben.

## Großer Schritt, aber nicht ohne Haken

Damit verschwindet die größte Schwäche, die Euro-Office seit dem Start hatte. Ganz ohne Haken ist das Projekt aber nicht. OnlyOffice hatte Euro-Office im Frühjahr Lizenzverstöße vorgeworfen. Im August kündigte Nextcloud an, Code und Lizenzhinweise an eine neue OnlyOffice-Lizenz anzupassen. Offiziell beigelegt ist der Streit allerdings noch nicht. Mac-Nutzer mit Intel-Rechner gehen außerdem leer aus. Privatanwender haben mit Pages, Numbers und Keynote ohnehin schon eine kostenlose Lösung, daher richtet sich das Angebot vor allem an Firmen und Behörden, die Nextcloud nutzen und ihre Daten in Europa halten wollen.

### Preis und Verfügbarkeit

Nextcloud Office Desktop ist kostenlos und quelloffen und steht auf der Website von Nextcloud zum Download bereit. Auf dem Mac setzt die App einen Apple-Prozessor voraus, eine macOS-Mindestversion nennt Nextcloud nicht. Für Windows gibt es Versionen für x64 und ARM64, für Linux Pakete für Debian, Ubuntu und Fedora.

items.title: Uncorrelated perspectives
items.subtitle: After I sold my company, I had to learn about long-term investing.
items.feedText: The best books all emphasized the importance of owning a diverse portfolio of uncorrelated assets that rise and fall independently. If one crashes, the rest don’t. Don’t put everything into stocks or real estate or commodities or any one market. Don’t put it all into America or Europe or Asia or any one place. Don’t over-invest in what’s popular or familiar. Invest equally into the entire world economy. I apply this metaphor to worldviews. You start with the perspective of your parents and culture. But you are o…
items.body:
After I sold my company, I had to learn about long-term investing.
The best books all emphasized the importance of owning a diverse portfolio of uncorrelated assets that rise and fall independently.
If one crashes, the rest don’t.

Don’t put everything into stocks or real estate or commodities or any one market.
Don’t put it all into America or Europe or Asia or any one place.
Don’t over-invest in what’s popular or familiar.
Invest equally into the entire world economy.

I apply this metaphor to worldviews.

You start with the perspective of your parents and culture.

But you are over-invested in one or two worldviews.

You have to deliberately diversify - to intentionally invest in other perspectives.

When your government or media says some country is the enemy, it’s a good sign that place has an uncorrelated perspective.
The governments have conflicting interests, but the people there are not bad people.

When another culture feels completely foreign, weird, and wrong, it means you are under-invested in that worldview.

Even in your own country, right versus left or whatever.

When the “other side” seems crazy, you need to balance your portfolio.

Invest some understanding until you hold some of those perspectives.

If people can predict your opinion on something, based on your opinion on something else, then your worldview is too correlated.

To be an independent thinker, own a diverse portfolio of uncorrelated perspectives.

items.feedText: Jehovah’s Witnesses were targeted by the Nazis specifically for their refusal to salute Hitler, display the swastika flag, or serve in the military; 4,500 were sent to concentration camps, and 1,800 died during the Nazi era. The more than 1,000 documents, photographs, drawings, letters, and reports that make up the archive were collected and saved for decades by Annemarie Kusserow, one of 11 children from a Jehovah’s Witness family that lived in the town of Bad Lippspringe in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany. Acc…
items.body:
Five years after the Jehovah’s Witnesses sued the German government over ownership of an archive tracing one family’s persecution by the Nazi regime, the files have been returned to the religious organization, [reports](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/23/arts/design/kusserow-archive-nazi-abuses-jehovahs-witnesses.html) the *New York Times*. Jehovah’s Witnesses were targeted by the Nazis specifically for their refusal to salute Hitler, display the swastika flag, or serve in the military; 4,500 were sent to concentration camps, and 1,800 died during the Nazi era.

The more than 1,000 documents, photographs, drawings, letters, and reports that make up the archive were collected and saved for decades by Annemarie Kusserow, one of 11 children from a Jehovah’s Witness family that lived in the town of Bad Lippspringe in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany. According to an oral history [published](https://perspectives.ushmm.org/item/oral-history-with-annemarie-and-waltraud-kusserow) by the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum, the Kusserow home was searched by the Gestapo 20 times, and the Kusserow parents, Hilda and Franz, were the first to be arrested, in the mid-1930s. The children eventually ended up in prisons, concentration camps, or training schools. Two brothers, Wilhelm and Wolfgang, were murdered by the Nazis, and another survived the war but died shortly after from tuberculosis contracted at Dachau.

At the time of her death in 2005, Annemarie Kusserow’s will stated that her family’s archive should go to the Jehovah’s Witnesses. But one of her brothers, Hans Werner Kusserow, had the archive in his possession at the time, and in 2009 he sold it to the Bundeswehr Military History Museum in Dresden. This was “especially troubling,” the Jehovah’s Witnesses’ official website [notes](https://www.jw.org/en/news/region/germany/Amicable-Settlement-Reached-in-Annemarie-Kusserow-Archive-Case/), given that her brothers lost their lives due to their pacifism.

The parties came to an “amicable agreement” on November 19, which was formalized the following day by the Higher Regional Court of Cologne. The museum and the Jehovah’s Witnesses agreed to keep the details of the settlement private. A Kusserow relative told the *New York Times* it is “a great relief that at last we will have these precious documents back where Annemarie always wanted them.”

items.body: In October, U.S. President Donald Trump sold his eleventh-hour deal to secure diesel from Russian President Vladimir Putin—pausing sanctions that his own administration had imposed—as a boon for the negotiations to end the war in Ukraine. The arrangement, he wrote on Truth Social, was intended to keep Russia at “the bargaining table.” Of course, it was always obvious to observers that the gambit had as much or more to do with bolstering the U.S. economy and stemming a massive victory for the Democrats in this month’s midterm elections, and in that, it failed.Cynics have grounds for questioning all of Trump’s moves when it comes to Russia and Ukraine. He clearly dislikes Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and shows a marked preference for illiberal leaders, especially those willing to give him easy wins. Still, a stopped clock can be right twice a day. And concessions such as the fuel deal are exactly what might move Russia and Ukraine closer to peace, even if they are not wholly motivated by public-spiritedness.

items.body:
** The latest on Trump’s approval rating**

**Updated November 24, 2026**

After rebounding slightly to 38 percent, Donald Trump’s approval rating is back on the downswing. **Today, 37 percent of Americans approve of the job he’s doing, while 60 percent disapprove**.

Show more Show less

Just 18.9 percent of Americans *strongly* approve of Trump, dangerously close to the 18.3 percent who *weakly* approve. If the president continues to get less popular, those figures could flip in the not too distant future. **-EMD** **, 11/17/26**

**See also: [Iran War support dashboard](https://www.natesilver.net/p/iran-war-polls-popularity-approval).**

This is the landing page for Silver Bulletin presidential approval ratings. We’ll regularly update the charts below as new polls about Donald Trump’s approval rating come in.1 This page is designed to be [viewed on the web](https://tinyurl.com/3fzxm9wc) rather than in our email client or in the Substack app.

[Click here for more information on how the average works](https://www.natesilver.net/p/silver-bulletin-polling-average-methodology). The Silver Bulletin average weights more reliable polls heavily — you can **[find our latest pollster ratings here](https://www.natesilver.net/p/pollster-ratings-silver-bulletin)**.

### The topline: So, just how popular is Trump?

Our default average reflects a combination of all polls, whether conducted among adults, registered voters or likely voters. If a pollster releases multiple versions of the same survey, we use the all-adult version of the poll before the registered voter version.2 This is because all Americans have a say in how popular the president is — whether or not they vote.

### The polls: What do the surveys say?

Each poll gets an “influence” score based on its pollster rating, its sample size, its recency, and how often a pollster is publishing numbers.3 Sometimes, surveys with mediocre pollster ratings have more weight in the model just because they were conducted very recently or polled more people.

Inevitably, there’s a lot of disagreement from survey to survey, not just because of [statistical variation](https://www.natesilver.net/p/dont-let-randomness-make-a-fool-of) but because pollsters have [long had trouble pegging down Trump’s popularity](https://www.natesilver.net/p/polling-is-becoming-more-of-an-art). By clicking on the “adjusted results” tab, you can see how [the “house effects” adjustment](https://www.natesilver.net/p/silver-bulletin-polling-average-methodology) that corrects for these predictable differences works in our model. You can also **[click here to download every Trump approval poll in our database](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/e/2PACX-1vS-FKWVTTFtJT6u56e0bqdfoMcXvDO1DUChsJ3jQAMB2lZk2SMqVfmg7dGjclTYkYWz-Pm5lfcLPjp4/pub?output=csv)** — including some additional details not shown in the chart below.

### The issues: What do Americans think of Trump’s policies?

Pollsters don’t just ask about Trump’s overall job approval, they also ask about how well he’s dealing with different issues. We’re tracking how the public feels about Trump’s handling of four topics: the economy, immigration, trade and tariffs, and the cost of living.

[↗ natesilver.net](https://www.natesilver.net/p/trump-approval-ratings-nate-silver-bulletin)

items.feedText: Autistic people often meet criteria for anxiety, depression, and other psychiatric conditions; co-occurring psychiatric conditions are more prevalent in the autism population than in the general population.1 Psychotherapy is a first-line treatment for many psychiatric conditions, such as anxiety and depression, but appears to serve autistic adults less well than it does others: an analysis of the UK National Health Service Talking Therapies found a reduction of depression and anxiety symptoms among 8593 autistic adults, but lower odds of reliable improvement and recovery, and higher odds of deterioration, than in matched non-autistic peers.

Saturday Night Live [ran a skit](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-X9dxL17t1k) for an eldercare service that was simply calling your sister to take care of things. Many people related, because it is actually happening. [For Bloomberg, Lisa Jarvis has the numbers](https://www.bloomberg.com/opinion/articles/2026-11-18/snl-sister-skit-about-the-us-eldercare-crisis-is-too-relatable?accessToken=eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzb3VyY2UiOiJTdWJzY3JpYmVyR2lmdGVkQXJ0aWNsZSIsImlhdCI6MTc5NTEyMTQ3MiwiZXhwIjoxNzk1NzI2MjcyLCJhcnRpY2xlSWQiOiJUT1A1Q0NLR1pBSk8wMCIsImJjb25uZWN0SWQiOiIzRDhGMEEzMTc2MDc0NUM5OTg4NkFCNzA1NDk2RUNEQSJ9.8Rm4_qRQDNrQl5SG6qxNGsTkbi7DGmEbfQ1N588AByU):

> And the pressure is only mounting as America gets older and sicker. Time devoted to caregiving more than doubled between 2020 and 2025, rising from 9 to 23 hours a week, according to a recent survey of working Americans conducted by the insurance provider Guardian Life. The majority (57%) are caring for elderly relatives. The same survey found women were five times as likely as men to say they’d left the workforce to care for someone, whether that was an elderly parent, a spouse, a young child or a special needs child.

items.body:
# Linke schliesst Emde aus: Eine Hürde weniger für Rot-Grün-Rot

## Linkenfraktion schliesst Vanessa Emde aus : Eine Hürde weniger für Rot-Grün-Rot

von Markus Gross

Vanessa Emde ist raus aus der Berliner Linksfraktion - und auf dem Weg zu Rot-Grün-Rot haben Linke, Grüne und SPD ein Problem weniger. Das letzte wird es wohl nicht bleiben.

Vanessa Emde wurde aus ihrer Fraktion ausgeschlossen. Sie war wegen ihrer Haltung zu Israel unter Druck geraten. Für die Regierungsbildung in Berlin ist es ein wichtiger Schritt.

Vor Raum 311 im Berliner Abgeordnetenhaus herrscht ein gewaltiger Medienrummel. Drinnen im großen Sitzungssaal diskutiert die Linksfraktion lebhaft über den Ausschluss von Vanessa Emde. Es scheint, als würde die halbe Republik auf ein Zeichen warten. Schafft es die Fraktionsführung, die aus ihrer Sicht widerspenstige Abgeordnete rauszuschmeißen?

Nach zweieinhalb Stunden steht fest: Vanessa Emde ist nicht mehr Mitglied der Fraktion Die Linke . 33 Abgeordnete stimmen für ihren Ausschluss, sechs stimmen mit Nein, es gibt vier Enthaltungen. Die nötige Mehrheit von 30 Stimmen wird erreicht.

- Umstrittene Abgeordnete: Vanessa Emde aus Berliner Linken-Fraktion ausgeschlossen
Sichtlich angespannt verkündet der Fraktionschef der Linken, Tobias Schulz: "Wir haben keine Möglichkeit mehr gesehen, mit Frau Emde weiter zusammenzuarbeiten." Sie habe sich nicht an Partei- und Fraktionsbeschlüsse zum Thema Antisemitismus gehalten. "Ihr Ausschluss ist folgerichtig", so Schulz weiter.

ZDF-Korrespondent Stephan Merseburger ordnet aus Berlin den Fraktionsausschluss Vanessa Emdes ein.

## Unterstützer empfangen Emde mit Jubel

Als Vanessa Emde den Fraktionssaal verlässt, wartet schon ein zwölfköpfiges Unterstützerkomitee auf sie. Es gibt Jubelrufe, als sie erscheint, Umarmungen und Zeichen der Solidarität. Emde bezeichnete ihren Ausschluss in einem Statement als Ergebnis einer "medialen Hetzkampagne".

Ihre Fraktion habe offenbar dem Druck von SPD und Grünen nachgegeben. Sie wolle ihr Mandat behalten. Ihre Unterstützer ruft sie dazu auf, sich zu "organisieren". Kämpferisch ihr Schlusswort:

> Wir sehen uns im Kiez und wir sehen uns am Streikposten! In diesem Sinne: Yalla, yalla, Klassenkampf, Freiheit für Palästina! „

Vanessa Emde

## Grüne und SPD sehen positives Signal

Die möglichen Koalitionspartner SPD und Grüne begrüßten den Ausschluss von Vanessa Emde. Werner Graf, Co-Chef der Grünenfraktion, gab sich zufrieden: "Die Entscheidung zeigt, dass für israelbezogenen Antisemitismus in einer rot-grün-roten Regierung kein Platz ist" . Steffen Krach, Co-Chef der SPD-Fraktion, der zuvor vehement einen Ausschluss Emdes gefordert hatte, ergänzte:

> Die Entscheidung der Linksfraktion ist eine gute Nachricht für die weiteren Koalitionsverhandlungen. „

Steffen Krach, Co-Chef der Berliner SPD-Fraktion

Die Berliner Linke hat die Abgeordnete Vanessa Emde aus ihrer Fraktion ausgeschlossen. Den Schritt hat man sich laut dem Fraktionsvorsitzenden Schulze nicht leicht gemacht.

## Antisemitismus-Vorwürfe gegen Emde

Vanessa Emde, mit über 46 Prozent direkt gewählte Abgeordnete in Neukölln, hatte zuvor mit ihren israelkritischen Aussagen immer wieder für Diskussionen gesorgt. Zuletzt hatte Emde in einem Instagram-Post das Existenzrecht Israels als jüdischer Staat angezweifelt. Ihre Kritiker werteten das als antisemitisch.

Der Zentralrat der Juden zeigte sich tief besorgt und forderte die Linke zum Handeln auf. Auch SPD und Grüne, die möglichen Koalitionspartner, waren verstimmt und machten den Ausschluss Emdes zur Bedingung.

- Schuster: Ausschluss von Emde "nur ein erster Schritt"
Bei den Grünen schaltete sich zuletzt sogar die Bundespitze ein. "Wenn das scheitert, kann ich allen nur abraten, in eine Regierung mit einer politischen Führung zu gehen, die in der eigenen Fraktion keine Macht hat" , hatte die Grünen-Co-Vorsitzende Franziska Brantner noch der "Frankfurter Allgemeinen Zeitung" vom Dienstag gesagt.

Die Berliner Linke hat die Abgeordnete Vanessa Emde aus der Fraktion ausgeschlossen. Was bedeutet die Entscheidung für die Partei und die Regierungsbildung in Berlin? ZDFheute live analysiert.

## Misstrauen bei SPD und Grünen bleibt

Mit dem Ausschluss Vanessa Emdes ist eine der größten Hürden auf dem Weg zu Rot-Grün-Rot in Berlin aus dem Weg geräumt. Doch Entwarnung bedeutet das nicht. SPD und Grüne bleiben misstrauisch. Der Vorwurf, in Teilen der Linken gebe es ein strukturelles Problem mit antisemitischen Tendenzen, ist längst nicht ausgeräumt.

Auch innerparteilich ist der Konflikt keineswegs beendet. Sechs Gegenstimmen und vier Enthaltungen zeigen, dass Emde weiterhin Rückhalt in der Fraktion hat. Wie sich ihr Unterstützerlager künftig positioniert, dürfte für die Koalitionsgespräche entscheidend werden. Der Politikwissenschaftler Thorsten Faas findet: "Der Ausschluss ist nicht so überzeugend, dass jegliche Diskussion innerhalb der Linken beendet ist." Das Bündnis bleibe in einem Schwebezustand.

Vorerst aber können alle Beteiligten aufatmen: Die Gespräche gehen weiter. Bis zum Jahreswechsel soll ein Koalitionsvertrag stehen. Anschließend müssen Linke und SPD noch ihre Mitglieder überzeugen. Doch bis dahin ist es ein weiter Weg - und das nächste Personalproblem womöglich nur eine Frage der Zeit.

Markus Gross ist Redakteur im ZDF-Landesstudio Berlin.

items.title: 11 Things Jensen Huang Actually Said at His First All-Hands Back at Nvidia
items.subtitle: The newly reinstated CEO discussed his daily therapy sessions, his reputation as a “tech bro,” his disdain for succession planning, and his relationship with President Trump.
items.feedText: The newly reinstated CEO discussed his daily therapy sessions, his reputation as a “tech bro,” his disdain for succession planning, and his relationship with President Trump.
items.body:
# 11 Things Jensen Huang Actually Said at His First All-Hands Back at Nvidia

Jensen Huang is going to therapy for 90 minutes a day, rethinking his management style , and says that violating Nvidia’s code of conduct isn’t necessarily a fireable offense. That’s just some of what the newly returned Nvidia CEO told staff during his first all-hands meeting on Tuesday.

Here are some of the most striking things Huang said during the meeting, according to remarks reviewed by WIRED. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

On self-improvement: “I go to therapy every day for an hour and a half. And it's been helping me a lot.”

On accountability: “There are rumors on the internet that apparently I'm a tech bro, and therefore I’m back. Apparently, I'm a tech bro, and because I wear a super nice jacket, that I'm above the law, and I’m above the code of conduct. That is not true. It won't be tolerated. That is not true. It won’t be tolerated, and it wasn't tolerated here.”

“If one of you were to violate a code of conduct, what does that mean? If you were ever to violate a code of conduct, it is not appropriate. I just wanted you to know, it is not right, it's not appropriate, it won't be tolerated. But ‘it won't be tolerated’ does not mean, the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door. Facts, circumstances, a lot of assessments. And your management team will still make the decision. That is what is in the best interest of the company and its employees, with all the facts and circumstances.”

On his management style: “The intensity I bring elevates everybody else. But I can go too far. When I go too far, it hurts people, it belittles them, it disempowers them. And that’s not right. And so I need to go figure out how I'm going to bring the intensity, the crazy intensity, to the field.”

On women at Nvidia: “I believe we need to create and continue to sustain a safe environment for all of our women. And if I did anything that put that in jeopardy, I cannot tell you how sad I am, and I'll do everything I can to fix it. We will not tolerate that.”

On succession: “All day long, this company can run autonomously, and you saw it. I promise you, whether I'm here or not, this company is wired up to execute, execute, and execute, and deliver on financial results and financial results.”

“I also didn't believe in succession planning. Let that sink in. I don’t believe in succession planning. I think it’s flawed. The idea of succession planning is not flawed. What people think succession planning means is flawed.”

“There’s a reason why we don’t have succession planning, it’s not because we are unaware of the word. I’m the longest-running tech CEO in history.”

On politics : “There [were] also rumors that apparently I'm back because the highest levels of our government wanted me back. That is also completely untrue. Our board of directors performed their duty as they should have.”

“It is absolutely true that President Trump really, really loves our company,” Huang told employees. “He gloats about Nvidia. You know he does. But there’s a question about politics. Are we now political? Are we partisan? I wanna be very clear with you. President Trump is the United States president. He is my president. And I’ll do everything I can to help this president be informed about how he could make decisions that are in the best interest of our country. … We have to do it, and whoever the next president is will be my president, and I will do exactly the same.”

“Don't think for a second that politics ever play a role in this company, not even a little bit. We are the most apolitical company. I don't love that we talk about politics here. Take it home. I love that we talk about work here.”

# Kommentar: Vanessa Emde und die Berliner Linke – dieser Ausschluss war überfällig - Meinung - SZ.de

Vanessa Emde nach der Fraktionssitzung. Christian Mang/REUTERS Es ist richtig, dass die Partei, die künftig die Regierende Bürgermeisterin stellen will, diese Abgeordnete aus ihrer Fraktion ausschließt. Zu diesem Kraftakt darf man gratulieren - und noch einen Wunsch äußern.

D ie Linkspartei im Berliner Abgeordnetenhaus hat Schluss gemacht mit Vanessa Emde. Das ist nicht schön, aber es ist richtig. Die Abgeordnete, die seit Monaten ihre Parteifreunde auf Trab hält und sich immer weiter verzettelt hat in Provokationen zum Nahost -Konflikt, ist am Dienstagabend aus der Fraktion ausgeschlossen worden. Ein Kraftakt war das für ihre Partei, vor allem aber eine Demonstration. Die Linke will Berlin regieren, zusammen mit Grünen und SPD. Wenn das überhaupt gelingen kann, dann nur auf Basis eines unmissverständlichen Signals: Mit Judenhass gezündelt wird nicht in der Stadt.

items.body:
# 2035 came early

> tl;dr trynix.dev boots GUI programs now. Try solitaire , GL gears , xeyes , a voice , the weather over curl , or Firefox .

I remember watching the talk The Birth & Death of JavaScript by Gary Bernhardt and falling in love with the whimsical yet dreadfully serious unfolding of the story of how JavaScript will come to dominate all software.

Others have noted the inevitability of JavaScript’s dominance, so perhaps it was not surprising that Atwood’s Law holds true.

> Atwood’s Law Any application that can be written in JavaScript, will eventually be written in JavaScript. — Jeff Atwood, 2009

I highly recommend watching the talk if you have not already seen it, but the short and skinny is a lookback from 2035 and how JavaScript came to be the defacto language for all software.

In Bernhardt’s retelling of events, the date is worked back from 2035, however unsurprisingly, large language models have rapidly sped up the timeline. What was once perceived to be the end-state at 2035 has arrived years earlier and you can witness it unfolding at trynix.dev .

One of the most impressive creations I’ve managed to build leveraging nixpkgs-multiverse is https://trynix.dev .

It still baffles my mind that I can run any Nix package , over 300,000 distinct package versions, straight from my browser. Truly insane capability. I was however a little dismayed at the speed of the QEMU emulation in the browser. It was slow enough that the creation tipped more towards novelty than practicality.

I woke on November 20th and saw Domen Kožar sharing a single message in our TacoSprint Discord channel: unkernel.dev

It was the fast browser Linux experience I had sought to achieve, but with Nix .

> Aside What is unkernel ? It is Linux compiled to WebAssembly, allowing the kernel and system components to run at wasm speed while only user programs are emulated. It was published by Pooya Parsa on November 19th, 2026.

In an AI induced manic frenzy, I adopted the new engine along with a slough of long-wished features almost immediately.

The proof is in the pudding: unkernel delivers remarkable speed improvements over qemu-wasm , 1 1 With a very healthy set of patches applied to make it even faster. especially on first runs where kernel work dominates. The new engine is able to deliver 2x to 32x faster performance depending on the workload. 2 2 The benchmark page tracks both engines over time, measured through the real page and shell.

JavaScript & WebAssembly nirvana.

Amazingly not only does the kernel boot quickly, it also enables networking, full-fledged graphical and audio experiences directly in the browser.

Windows. A program’s Wayland surfaces are composited in the page by wland , and they float over the terminal you started them from.

GL. The VM includes a minimal Mesa build with only the virgl driver, compiled to WebAssembly, rendering through your browser’s WebGL2.

Sound. The VM has an ALSA sound card, and can play audio through your browser.

Network. curl , git clone and pip install work. Each TCP connection goes over one WebSocket to a Wisp relay. 3 3 Thank you to @_pi0_ for adding trynix.dev to his Wisp relay allow-list.

The best joke in Bernhardt’s talk is a browser running inside another browser: the Windows GIMP under Wine, in Chrome, in Firefox. Of course, I had to try it with trynix. 😈

Here is Firefox in trynix , and it loading trynix.dev , and then loading Firefox again inside itself. 4 4 Don’t get too excited: this took over 4 hours. The inner Firefox needed JIT disabled, the middle one ran without GL, and the outer page used a Wisp relay on my laptop since wisp.unkernel.dev cannot reach itself .

Sit and bask in that insanity. That is Firefox, on Linux compiled to WebAssembly, in a Firefox tab, loading the site and then loading Firefox again inside itself. 🤯

2035 came early.
