items.body:
We live in a world with so many monolithic apps and services, dominated by giant companies. So one of my favorite things is to explore little software niches that haven’t been captured by the major players. Instead of one or two pretty samey apps, you can end up with a whole forest of wild variations on the theme, each fueled by developers making specific choices about how to present information and serve users.

When I compare these apps, I realize that there’s really no right or wrong—there are just choices, some of which might work for me, some of which won’t. I’m not offended when an app isn’t made for me, but I can be delighted when an app does slide perfectly into my life.

After a year of using [Television Time](https://sixcolors.com/post/2016/02/keeping-on-top-of-peak-tv-with-television-time/) (not to be confused with the now-defunct [TV Time](https://sixcolors.com/member/2019/01/applications-folder-tv-time/)) to log my TV viewing and (more importantly) let me keep track of what we’re watching next and what we’d like to get to next, I discovered an app that just served me better.

That’s [Skipper](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/skipper-tv-movie-tracker/id6780667490), Yoav Zoldan’s new app, available for $30/year or $3/month. What sold me on it is that its primary screen is a list of shows I’m watching with the next episode marked, sorted in a way that makes sense to me. I only want to interact with the app in a handful of ways: seeing what to watch next, checking the box indicating that we watched it, and occasionally searching to add a show that I might be interested in watching next.

Television Time required more swiping around and entering detail views, and one thing I’ve discovered about myself is that I prefer apps that are optimized to present all the information I want in one place, and which limit the number of swipes and taps required to navigate around. Skipper hit that sweet spot for me—your mileage, of course, may vary.

Skipper has a lot of other features, including a very clever one that compares your watch list to your streaming service subscriptions and can nudge you to drop that service you’re not actually using, complete with a calendar of when shows you watch will be returning. (I know, I know, I shouldn’t have subscribed to BritBox. I have no time to watch it!)

It’s not entirely accurate—it doesn’t seem to understand that I watch sports on YouTube TV and things that are not shows on YouTube Premium—but it’s a smart feature that could help a lot of people who are not inveterate streaming subscription sickos like me.

Just as there are many TV-tracking apps, there are many, many podcast apps. I’ve [been using Overcast for ages](https://sixcolors.com/link/2024/07/overcast-turns-10/), and it just fits into how I want to listen to podcasts. I spend as little time as possible picking what to listen to (there’s my optimization streak again) and have Overcast configured to give me that.

But there have been other podcast apps that serve other, equally valid, points of view. [Castro](https://sixcolors.com/post/2016/08/castro-2-inbox-triage-for-podcast-episodes/) really made its name by not just offering a beautiful interface, but a clever “triage” system that brings new episodes into an inbox. Then the user manually decides what’s worth adding to the play queue. Clearly that approach clicked with a lot of people, making Castro a fan favorite even through its ongoing business challenges and [different owners](https://sixcolors.com/post/2023/11/castro-podcast-app-goes-down-and-may-be-dying/).

Which brings me to an impressive new podcast app that’s been designed to appeal especially to Castro fans: Ben Rice McCarthy’s [Tripod](https://benricemccarthy.ghost.io/tripod/). Ben is a really talented designer, and the app looks gorgeous and works well. It’s built around the same Inbox concept as Castro, so Castro users will feel right at home. I got to beta test Ben’s app for a while, and was incredibly impressed—especially at how it works on the iPhone Duo.

That all said, I am just not the target audience for Tripod—and that’s okay. The way Overcast works for podcasts is the way I want to work. Quite frankly, the idea of having another Inbox to check does not fill my heart with joy, even if the podcasts found therein would bring me that joy. That’s on me, not on Ben, and not on Tripod.

So if you watch TV like me, you should try [Skipper](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/skipper-tv-movie-tracker/id6780667490). And if you’re not like me, you should try [Tripod](https://apps.apple.com/redeem?ctx=offercodes&id=6824844745&code=WELCOME&ref=benricemccarthy.ghost.io). That’s the beauty of these app niches; they don’t have to be all things to all people, they just need to find their audience and serve them well.

items.title: At a Doomed U.N. Conference, Saudi Arabia and Other Oil States Pushed Hard for an Unproven Climate Fix
items.subtitle: Activists unsatisfied with the second draft text at COP31 hold a silent protest outside the plenary hall, where delegates meet during the United Na…
items.feedText:
20. Yasin Akgul/AFP/Getty Images

A United Nations-sponsored negotiation on climate change collapsed Sunday amid bitter standoffs over how to slow the warming of the planet and who will pay for it. During the two-week summit, oil- and gas-producing nations blocked any mention of phasing out those fuels — a step scientists uniformly agree is a prerequisite to addressing global warming. Instead, petrostates, led by Saudi Arabia, pushed for an aggressive expansion of carbon capture technology as a way to reduce the…
items.body:
Activists unsatisfied with the second draft text at COP31 hold a silent protest outside the plenary hall, where delegates meet during the United Nations Climate Change Conference at the Antalya Expo Centre in Turkey on Nov. 20. Yasin Akgul/AFP/Getty Images

A United Nations-sponsored negotiation on climate change collapsed Sunday amid bitter standoffs over how to slow the warming of the planet and who will pay for it. During the two-week summit, oil- and gas-producing nations blocked any mention of phasing out those fuels — a step scientists uniformly agree is a prerequisite to addressing global warming.

Instead, petrostates, led by Saudi Arabia, pushed for an aggressive expansion of carbon capture technology as a way to reduce the pollution their fuels cause.

Today, carbon capture facilities operate at a tiny fraction of the scale promised, are riddled with failures and setbacks, and show no signs of being able to overcome those hurdles at the pace that the U.N. suggests would be needed to mitigate global warming, [reporting by Drilled and ProPublica](https://projects.propublica.org/why-carbon-capture-cant-solve-climate-change/) has found.

The role of carbon capture was just one cause of discord in Turkey at the 31st annual U.N. climate summit, known as the Conference of the Parties. But it reflects a culmination of [decades of effort](https://www.propublica.org/article/wedges-climate-research-bp-fossil-fuel-princeton) by fossil fuel companies, and the nations most dependent on them, to slow a transition away from oil, coal and gas in part by pressing for methods like carbon capture, which theoretically allow for the use of their products and cleaning up carbon pollution at the same time.

Over the course of two weeks of negotiations in Antalya, drafts of the summit’s main political accord were stripped of language encouraging such a transition even as specific targets were added to expand carbon capture and storage, or CCS.

One draft released Nov. 16 included language encouraging a transition from fossil fuels alongside a recommendation to scale up carbon capture — where greenhouse gases are caught from industry, or filtered from the air, and injected underground — so that it removes at least 500 million tons of carbon dioxide a year by 2035.

Currently, however, the carbon capture industry buries [only a sliver of that amount](https://projects.propublica.org/why-carbon-capture-cant-solve-climate-change/) and has struggled for three decades to meet even the lowest-end projections, leading many climate experts to conclude that it will never be a practical solution to climate change.

“The effort by bad faith petrostate actors to block any agreement at #COP31 on fossil fuel phaseout in favor of (hypothetical future) carbon capture is the best evidence yet that moral hazard FUNDAMENTALLY compromises carbon capture as a climate solution,” wrote Michael Mann, a prominent climate scientist at the University of Pennsylvania, in a [Bluesky post](https://bsky.app/profile/michaelemann.bsky.social/post/3n2vxe4blj22y) Sunday.

As it stands, most CCS is used to squeeze additional oil from aging fields, so critics say setting global goals for it would lead to further subsidy of oil production, rather than limit or reduce the amount of CO2 that reaches the air.

Behind the scenes in Antalya, some 700 carbon capture lobbyists were registered as attending, up from 531 at last year’s summit in Brazil and more than the combined delegations of all 14 Pacific Small Island Developing States, according to an analysis of U.N. participant lists by the Center for International Environmental Law. Forty-five of those representatives were granted entry to closed-door negotiating sessions. The center has not completed a similar analysis of lobbyists for other technologies.

The agreement — and its emphasis on CCS — “really had the fossil fuel industry’s fingerprints all over it,” said Romain Ioualalen, the global policy lead for the nonprofit Oil Change International, a research and advocacy group pushing for a phaseout of fossil fuels.

A coalition of nations, including the European Union, rejected the proposal outright.

For years, tensions at the annual climate talks have tended to break down to three camps: Saudi Arabia, Russia and other oil-producing states — at times with tacit U.S. support — which argue for an approach that prioritizes slow changes in the energy system in service of economic stability; the wealthy, industrialized nations, which push for an energy transition but resist measures to pay for both the transition and damages caused by warming; and the low- and middle-income nations, which will sign on to fossil fuel phaseout only if other powerful economies commit to supporting the cost of their transition.

Carbon capture remains just one part of that larger debate, which included other ways to clean up energy sources. But its weight in this year’s talks reflects long-standing efforts to tie climate action to its success, as well as a failure to enact any other meaningful agreement that would slow the rate of CO2 emissions in the first place.

For more than a year, ProPublica and Drilled have investigated the history of carbon capture and storage and the decades-long effort by oil companies to validate it in the scientific community and at the U.N. Our reporting has found that [industry funding contributed to influential CCS research](https://www.propublica.org/article/wedges-climate-research-bp-fossil-fuel-princeton) at universities, [petrostates pressed the U.N. to validate the technology](https://www.propublica.org/article/carbon-capture-storage-fossil-fuel-sally-benson) without supporting evidence and [climate modelers have assumed it can work](https://www.propublica.org/article/carbon-capture-and-storage-climate-models) at an enormous scale, despite the technology’s troubled real-world track record.

In the closing session, a delegate from Panama explained that the country could not support the language in the final COP31 text in part because “it wagers too much” on CCS “instead of calling for deep changes.”

Vanuatu, a small island nation in the Pacific that is especially vulnerable to rising sea levels, warned that the text “risks legitimizing continued fossil fuel dependence” and that carbon capture must not become “an excuse to prolong the fossil fuel era.”

But Saudi Arabia, speaking on behalf of the 22 countries in the League of Arab States, insisted CCS was an essential part of a “package of solutions” to address climate change.

“If indeed the climate challenge, as some have mentioned today, is so important,” the Saudi delegate said, “it makes no sense that solutions, concrete solutions, which is what this COP was meant to represent, will be taken off the table.”

items.body:
According to internal memos reviewed [by Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/business/microsoft-declares-code-red-after-historic-outage-internal-memos-show-2026-11-24/), Microsoft has declared a "Code Red" overhaul of its engineering response practices after the [November 12 outage](https://arstechnica.com/gadgets/2026/11/microsoft-details-how-three-problems-combined-for-a-global-outage/) that lost access to Exchange Online, Teams, and Outlook for users worldwide.

Per the memos, Microsoft 365 Core President Jason Henderson described the outage as having the most customer impact in the history of Exchange Online. In a separate memo, Henderson wrote that an urgent production fix in a recent incident took five to six days to reach worldwide saturation. Microsoft's target for its most urgent security fixes is to move from detection to safe worldwide deployment in one hour. "Needless to say, we aren't here yet," Henderson wrote.

The memos, which Reuters reviewed but Microsoft has not published, outline the response to the November 12 disruption. The company's [post-incident report](https://tianyin.github.io/misc/pir_microsoft_365_11-12-2026.pdf), dated November 20, attributed the downtime to an undetected Windows scalability defect introduced in July, which caused lock contention in the gateway processes. A Teams traffic failover then dumped additional load onto infrastructure already under stress, as maintenance had left nearly 14 percent of gateway server capacity offline at the time of the incident.

[Read full article](https://arstechnica.com/gadgets/2026/11/microsofts-historic-cloud-outage-exposed-an-engineering-fog-of-war/)

[Comments](https://arstechnica.com/gadgets/2026/11/microsofts-historic-cloud-outage-exposed-an-engineering-fog-of-war/#comments)

items.body:
Signal announced an update to its mobile apps on iOS and Android that seeks to curb issues with AI agents accessing private chats. This is a useful new barrier against a problem we’ve been highlighting this year in our Encrypt It Already campaign. And good news, it’s enabled by default so you don’t need to do anything except update the app.

Over the last year, both Google and Apple* have released AI features in their operating systems that can read the contents of apps. One of the ways it can do this is through screen analysis. Google calls this feature “Intelligent Screen Context,” while Apple refers to it as either “Onscreen Awareness” or “Visual Intelligence.”

Apple now provides a way to block Siri AI’s access to apps, but by default every app is available to Siri AI, so it’s up to the user to go in and put these guardrails up. Signal requests that protection on your behalf. Google doesn’t currently offer any sort of similar option. So Signal on Android does the best it can, by turning off screenshots when it detects an AI assistant attempting to access the screen. Signal’s solution helps ensure that, unless you go in and change the setting yourself, it defaults to the most private option.

While this is a clever solution to the current issues facing Signal (and potentially useful for any other app that does its best to promise privacy), we need all operating systems to provide stronger methods and clear documentation to developers so they can safeguard their users without needing to jump through hoops. Both developers and users should have the tools they need to safeguard their own data from AI agents and other AI tools.

*Apple is an EFF donor. EFF donors do not influence our agenda or our positions.

items.title: Why a Case Against ICC Sanctions Is a Major Victory for Palestine Human Rights Work
items.subtitle: A federal judge on Monday ruled that the Trump administration may not punish Americans for sharing evidence of Israeli war crimes with the Internat…
items.feedText: The ruling also blocked the administration from meting out punishments for sharing information with three sanctioned Palestinian human rights groups and a prominent United Nations official. The Monday ruling is the broadest challenge yet to an executive order issued by President Donald Trump in the early days of his second term that has been used by U.S. officials to issue sanctions against the ICC; the Palestinian groups al-Haq, al-Mezan, and the Palestinian Center for Human Rights; and U.N. special rapporteur…
items.body:
A federal judge on Monday ruled that the Trump administration may not punish Americans for sharing evidence of Israeli war crimes with the International Criminal Court. The ruling also blocked the administration from meting out punishments for sharing information with three sanctioned Palestinian human rights groups and a prominent United Nations official.

The Monday [ruling](https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.nysd.668333/gov.uscourts.nysd.668333.50.0.pdf) is the broadest challenge yet to an executive order issued by President Donald Trump in the [early days of his second term](https://theintercept.com/2025/01/22/trump-israel-settlers-west-bank-sanctions/) that has been used by U.S. officials to issue sanctions against the ICC; the Palestinian groups al-Haq, al-Mezan, and the Palestinian Center for Human Rights; and U.N. special rapporteur Francesca Albanese.

> “It was kind of expected that they would make the preliminary injunction permanent, but the universal part is huge.”

The order, which came as a result of a [lawsuit](https://theintercept.com/2026/07/15/trump-sanctions-international-criminal-court/) filed in July by Democracy for the Arab World Now, or DAWN, and the Taxpayer Alliance Against Genocide, is the latest setback to efforts by the Trump administration to undermine the efforts by the ICC, Albanese, and others to hold Israel accountable for crimes against humanity.

“This landmark ruling dismantles a core part of Trump’s ICC draconian sanctions regime,” said Omar Shakir, executive director at DAWN. “The court has affirmed that every American has the constitutional right to advocate for justice on Palestine without fear of reprisal.”

While previous rulings against Trump’s executive order applied more narrowly — including an October preliminary injunction in the ICC case that prevented punishments against the plaintiffs — this is the first ruling against the sanctions that protects all Americans.

“The main difference is that this was expanded to be universal, meaning it doesn’t just protect the people who filed the lawsuit in the first place,” Michael Schaeffer Omer-Man, the Israel-Palestine director for DAWN, told The Intercept. “It was kind of expected that they would make the preliminary injunction permanent, but the universal part is huge.”

[Related Trump’s Sanctions Against the ICC Are Unconstitutional, Rights Groups Say](https://theintercept.com/2026/07/15/trump-sanctions-international-criminal-court/)

A spokesperson for the White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but in a [legal filing](https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.nysd.668333/gov.uscourts.nysd.668333.46.0.pdf) earlier this month, attorneys for Trump argued that his original executive order did not represent a restriction on free speech.

Another previous ruling that applied narrowly came in a [case brought by a pair of university professors](https://www.justiceinitiative.org/litigation/gabor-rona-and-lisa-davis-v-donald-j-trump-et-al) who challenged the administration’s prohibition on working with the ICC. Joseph Pace, a lawyer for DAWN and the Taxpayer Alliance Against Genocide, said this ruling also helped overcome some of the limitations in the professors’ successful case.

“It didn’t stop the administration from enforcing the sanctions against anyone else,” he said, of the decision in the professors’ case. “Nor did that decision say anything about the Palestinian NGOs or Albanese” — neither of which had been sanctioned yet at the time of the ruling.

“The permanent injunction, though, is what’s called a ‘universal injunction,’” Pace told The Intercept. “That means the government can’t penalize anyone for providing (or receiving) First Amendment-protected services to or from ICC, Albanese, and the NGOs.”

## “ Challenging These Crimes”

In his ruling, U.S. District Judge Jesse Furman found that the so-called services provision of Trump’s order — which threatened penalties for anyone “providing services” to the ICC, Albanese, or the three Palestinian NGOs — was unconstitutional because it undermined the First Amendment rights of people seeking to provide non-financial services to human rights advocates.

[Related Inside the Trump Administration’s War on the International Criminal Court](https://theintercept.com/2026/11/17/trump-icc-sanctions-war-crimes/)

In a statement, Taxpayer Alliance Against Genocide co-founder Anna Marie Stenberg said the ruling by Furman provided immediate clearance for her organization and others to resume work with the ICC, Albanese, and the three Palestinian organizations.

“We challenged Trump’s Executive Order on the ICC because we refused to let his regime intimidate us into silence while it used our tax dollars to fund crimes against humanity,” Stenberg said. “This victory means that others can join us in challenging these crimes without fear of punishment for exercising their First Amendment rights. Ordinary people have a right to seek justice, and our government cannot take that right away.”

[Read our complete coverage Chilling Dissent](https://theintercept.com/collections/chilling-dissent/)

Trump’s Executive Order 14203, issued in February 2025, called for financial penalties against the ICC under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act. It barred Americans from providing financial assistance or services to further the court’s activities. Trump’s order explicitly cited the court’s investigations into Israel as a justification for the sanctions.

The order led to sanctions by the Trump administration against Albanese, who has consistently drawn the ire of pro-Israel officials for pursuing investigations into [Israeli war crimes](https://theintercept.com/2025/05/03/eu-israel-palestine-war-crimes-accountability/). The sanctions barred her from entry to the U.S. and froze her assets in the country. Albanese challenged the sanctions and a judge threw them out in May, but they were [reinstated](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/5/28/us-returns-palestinian-rights-expert-francesca-albanese-to-sanctions-list) later that month.

items.title: Agentic system personalizes physical controls to help users “DJ their art”
items.subtitle: In 2017, Apple removed the home button from its iPhones.
items.feedText: Users lost a convenient, tangible control — part of a larger shift to digital buttons, knobs, and sliders we also see in cars (like with radio presets and air conditioning) and kitchens (see smart fridges). items.body:
In 2017, Apple [removed the home button](https://apnews.com/article/ad9e1a52b5dc4d48bc55256a1124315b) from its iPhones. Users lost a convenient, tangible control — part of a larger shift to digital buttons, knobs, and sliders we also see in cars (like with radio presets and air conditioning) and kitchens (see smart fridges).

We can’t leave physical controls behind entirely, though. They tend to be more convenient and efficient — think of how you can use a physical gaming controller without looking at it — and, at times, more precise, like when you use a dial to get the volume just right. But tangible controls are typically preprogrammed to do a specific thing, minimizing their usefulness.

A new system called “[TangiMap](https://yunyi-zhu.github.io/tangimap/),” co-developed by an MIT graduate student and researcher at MIT’s Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL), helps bring tangible control back to your software. The system personalizes the physical controls on everyday devices by mapping digital widgets onto tangible inputs, turning things like editing photos, animation, performing music, and creating 3D models into more dynamic and tactile experiences. Just as a DJ’s pads switch between triggering cues, loops, and samples, TangiMap gives a device’s controls entirely new roles.

But how, exactly? TangiMap relies on an AI agent, or semi-autonomous programs that “think” and complete well-defined tasks, to find and act on context about the software you’re using, your tendencies, and the device used to control that program. To gather the required context, the agent can draw on sources such as the program’s API (the rules that let programs talk to each other), an MCP server (a standard that connects AI agents to apps), or a screenshot interpreted by a vision-language model. Then, the agent uses a large language model to put all the info it's gathered into a file before mapping specific digital functions to physical controls.

“TangiMap builds on our broader vision of reprogramming common objects to be more dynamic,” says Yunyi Zhu ’20, MEng ’21, a doctoral student in the MIT Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science and a CSAIL researcher whose advisor is MIT Associate Professor Stefanie Mueller. “Here, AI agents help us adapt physical controls to whatever we’re working on. We want to bring back physical controls so we can interact with our devices eyes-free, the way you adjust a car’s volume without looking away from the road. Physical controls also let you adjust several settings at once, like tweaking brightness and contrast together when editing an image, which is hard to do on a screen.”

The system helped the researchers turn a standard mixer into a photo-editing controller. That way, they could adjust color in Adobe Lightroom, with a complementary visualization of those controls displayed on their screen. The team did the same with sound-mixing software, so that performers can adjust their music in real-time with their own inputs to knobs and faders.

The researchers also reprogrammed a simpler mixer to work with the 3D modeling program Blender. Their interface included an area where users can type in a prompt, and once the model was generated, users could adjust features like shininess on a mixer using physical controls. Within Adobe’s Character Animator software, TangiMap connected specific expressions and movements to buttons on a control pad so users could animate (or “puppeteer”) a cartoon character live.

Zhu and co-author Chang Xiao, an assistant professor at Boston University, [presented their tool at the ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3830398.3830602) earlier this month.

Zhu and Xiao created a custom user interface (UI) for each application. While that adds another layer of personalization to the creative process, the team is hoping to create a more streamlined system that helps the designer to generate the UI for their device by taking a picture.

The researchers are also considering the physical aspects of user interactions. They want to use more ergonomic devices and also ensure that TangiMap accounts for where users position their hands when doing different tasks. For example, users typically hold a mixer differently when they’re using it to make music than, say, when playing a video game. You may want controls mapped closer or further apart, depending on what you’re doing.

Zhu is hoping to do a user study to get more feedback about TangiMap, and whether this kind of “smart DJing” could indeed improve those experiences. But the dynamic reprogramming she ultimately envisions is even more ambitious.

“The same way our phones and computers generalize to a range of tasks, we want other objects to be more intelligent,” she says. “I would like to build physical items that use an AI agent as a brain to decide what to reprogram into. They could understand what to transform into, given a specific situation.”

A chemical jar, for instance, could tell you if it’s sealed correctly when asked, and when you want to see what it’s typically used for, the container would instead display that information. While that kind of versatility and interactivity is a ways off, more powerful agents and more intricate fabrication pipelines could bring everyday objects to life.

Their work was supported, in part, by Google’s Gemini Academic Program Award.

items.body:
Charlie Warzel, writing for The Atlantic (gift link):

> The rationale for this rally is that Huang is the central figure
> of the AI boom — that Nvidia, which powers the AI economy and
> props it up with the company’s investments, is basically an
> exoskeleton around Huang. With him, AI progress and U.S. tech
> leadership can continue apace; without him, the music stops,
> investor confidence falters, and the AI bubble pops. On November
> 9, I [wrote](https://www.theatlantic.com/technology/2026/11/jensen-huang-chinese-spy/689357/) that, in the eyes of Silicon Valley and Trump,
> Huang was too big to fail. For 11 days — the window between
> Huang’s departure and his return — it looked like I was wrong and
> the shameless era of lol nothing matters in American politics
> and technology was winding down. Nope!
> The professed logic of those calling for Huang’s return was
> [nonsensical](https://www.theatlantic.com/technology/2026/11/silicon-valley-model-collapse/689505/). The venture capitalists and shareholders
> argued that American dominance in the AI race against China
> depended on Huang’s ability to do whatever he pleased. This
> impunity included allowing Nvidia leeway to potentially skirt U.S.
> export controls and get chips into China, and sleeping with an
> alleged Chinese intelligence asset. You might be forgiven for
> missing the genius of the argument.

The other side of this coin is that Huang’s personal dishonesty — not just to his family but [to the entire Nvidia company](https://daringfireball.net/linked/2026/11/08/huang-betrayed-nvidia) (which, I guess, [includes his family](https://www.businessinsider.com/madison-huang-growing-influence-at-nvidia-jensen-daughter-2026-11)) — and disregard for U.S. national security policy *do not matter*. It’s one thing to believe (as I do) that a romantic indiscretion shouldn’t necessarily be cause for firing. It’s another thing entirely to argue that integrity doesn’t matter.

Even just putting aside the fact that Donald Trump is singularly responsible — in an objectively unprecedented way — for Nvidia’s board reinstating Huang, the whole thing is part and parcel with Trumpism itself. Should a single extramarital affair rule someone out from elected office? No. But does a [lifetime of lecherous behavior](https://daringfireball.net/linked/2020/09/06/trump-cohen-the-act), an entire [string](https://www.nickiswift.com/913028/the-real-reason-marla-maples-and-donald-trump-divorced/) of [failed](https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/was-donald-trump-accused-of-sexual-assault-prior-to-the-2016-election/) marriages, and a [documented long-term friendship with the world’s most infamous pedophile](https://www.wsj.com/us-news/law/trump-jeffrey-epstein-letter-birthday-book-analysis-0bbeeaf6?st=i3v3VX) suggest a man might be fundamentally unfit for leadership?

[★](https://daringfireball.net/linked/2026/11/24/warzel-nvidia-economy)

items.body:
The Wall Street Journal, “The Frantic White House Push to Get Jensen Huang Back” (gift link):

> What followed were a frantic 48 hours in which the president, the
> vice president and other top administration officials relayed
> Blanche’s assurances to board members as they rushed to rescue a
> leader Trump hadn’t even heard of when he began his second term.
> “The response from the market has been very positive,” Trump said
> in an interview with The Wall Street Journal Monday evening. “That
> really shows the decision was right.” Nvidia stock notched the
> largest one-day market cap gain on record for a U.S. company.

If the entire stock market and U.S. economy is held together by investor faith in Jensen Huang, it’s a bubble and it will burst.

> On Sunday afternoon, the board met for a marathon session
> and spent hours talking to Huang, people familiar with the
> matter said.
> Huang disclosed to the board additional affairs beyond the two
> that had been widely reported, but he was contrite about his
> behavior, people with knowledge of the discussion said.
> After conversations with Huang about the importance of candor and
> honesty, the board ultimately decided that having him return was
> the best path, the people said.

Yours truly, back on November 12, after Reuters found Huang’s third girlfriend (an executive assistant at Nvidia):

> What’s the over-under at? If it’s 4.5, I’ll take the over.

“Additional affairs beyond the two that had been widely reported” takes us to at least 4, but sounds like more than that.

[★](https://daringfireball.net/linked/2026/11/24/bet-the-over-huang)

items.title: How to Touch the Nothingness Behind Everything: Kahlil Gibran on the Seven Selves
items.subtitle: A self is an illusion, and yet it is the place where we live, the costume the naked soul wears to survive in the world.
items.feedText: A self is a forest. A self is a ship. Above all, a self is a sum of selves, contextual as a chameleon, conflicted as a parliament. Which self takes the reins of our character and conduct at any given time is a function of which animating passion takes possession of us. But though we may be governed by different selves at different times, our task is to discover — and to heed — the higher, truer self that hovers above them all like the shadow of a mountain, impervious to the passing winds, holding up the sky of l…
items.body:
A self [is a forest](https://www.themarginalian.org/2026/11/09/pando/). A self [is a ship](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/03/08/plutarch-the-ship-of-theseus-ted-ed/). A self [is an illusion](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/10/21/iris-murdoch-unselfing/), and yet it is the place where we live, the costume the naked soul wears to survive in the world.

Above all, a self is [a sum of selves](https://www.themarginalian.org/2024/04/10/parts/), contextual as a chameleon, conflicted as a parliament. Which self takes the reins of our character and conduct at any given time is a function of which animating passion takes possession of us. But though we may be governed by different selves at different times, our task is to discover — and to heed — the higher, truer self that hovers above them all like the shadow of a mountain, impervious to the passing winds, holding up the sky of life.

[Kahlil Gibran](https://themarginalian.org/tag/kahlil-gibran) (January 6, 1883–April 10, 1931), who thought deeply about [the art of becoming yourself over the sweep of life](https://www.themarginalian.org/2023/04/04/youth-and-age-kahlil-gibran/), takes up this question in one of his signature parable-poems found in his 1918 classic [The Madman](http://www.amazon.com/Madman-His-Parables-Poems/dp/0486419118/?tag=braipick-20) ([public library](http://www.worldcat.org/title/madman-his-parables-and-poems/oclc/242642&referer=brief_results) | [free ebook](http://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/5616)).

The poem unfolds as a taxonomy of the core animating passions we live with and suffer by — sorrow, ecstasy, infatuation, hate, longing, creative possession — each a trap, a cage, a dooming fate the sufferer yearns to rebel against. Then comes the seventh self, seemingly the most pitiable, for it is the self that appears to live in pointlessness, perpetually facing the void, but in the end the freest: Only the empty self that lusts for nothing can touch the essence of everything. (Gibran would have appreciated [the Japanese concept of ma](https://www.themarginalian.org/2026/09/07/ma/).)

Kahlil Gibran

> THE SEVEN SELVES
> by Kahlil Gibran
> In the stillest hour of the night, as I lay half asleep, my seven
> selves sat together and thus conversed in whisper:
> First Self: Here, in this madman, I have dwelt all these years,
> with naught to do but renew his pain by day and recreate his sorrow
> by night. I can bear my fate no longer, and now I rebel.
> Second Self: Yours is a better lot than mine, brother, for it is
> given to me to be this madman’s joyous self. I laugh his laughter
> and sing his happy hours, and with thrice winged feet I dance
> his brighter thoughts. It is I that would rebel against my weary
> existence.
> Third Self: And what of me, the love-ridden self, the flaming brand
> of wild passion and fantastic desires? It is I the love-sick self
> who would rebel against this madman.
> Fourth Self: I, amongst you all, am the most miserable, for naught
> was given me but odious hatred and destructive loathing. It is
> I, the tempest-like self, the one born in the black caves of Hell,
> who would protest against serving this madman.
> Fifth Self: Nay, it is I, the thinking self, the fanciful self,
> the self of hunger and thirst, the one doomed to wander without
> rest in search of unknown things and things not yet created; it is
> I, not you, who would rebel.
> Sixth Self: And I, the working self, the pitiful labourer, who,
> with patient hands, and longing eyes, fashion the days into images
> and give the formless elements new and eternal forms — it is I, the
> solitary one, who would rebel against this restless madman.
> Seventh Self: How strange that you all would rebel against this
> man, because each and every one of you has a preordained fate to
> fulfill. Ah! could I but be like one of you, a self with a determined
> lot! But I have none, I am the do-nothing self, the one who sits
> in the dumb, empty nowhere and nowhen, while you are busy re-creating
> life. Is it you or I, neighbours, who should rebel?
> When the seventh self thus spake the other six selves looked with
> pity upon him but said nothing more; and as the night grew deeper
> one after the other went to sleep enfolded with a new and happy
> submission.
> But the seventh self remained watching and gazing at nothingness,
> which is behind all things.

Couple with Gibran on [silence, solitude, and the courage to know yourself](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/11/21/kahlil-gibran-prophet-talking/), then revisit Hermann Hesse on [discovering the soul beneath the self](https://www.themarginalian.org/2024/02/18/hesse-soul/).

### donating = loving

For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing *The Marginalian* (which [bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings](https://www.themarginalian.org/2021/10/22/brain-pickings-becoming-the-marginalian/) for its first fifteen years). It has remained free and ad-free and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, no assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If this labor makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider lending a helping hand with a [donation](https://www.themarginalian.org/donate/). Your support makes all the difference.

### newsletter

*The Marginalian* has a free weekly newsletter. It comes out on Sundays and offers the week’s most inspiring reading. Here’s [what to expect](https://mailchi.mp/brainpickings/janna-levin-rebecca-elson-anne-lamott-james-gleick). Like? [Sign up.](https://www.themarginalian.org/newsletter/)

## Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater)

NASA’s Space Reactor-1 (SR-1) Freedom, the first fission-powered spacecraft to travel beyond Earth orbit, cruises past Mars in this artist’s concept, demonstrating nuclear electric propulsion in deep space.

NASA completed a major review for [Space Reactor-1 (SR-1) Freedom](https://www.nasa.gov/mission/space-reactor-1-freedom/) and locked in key elements of the spacecraft, which is targeted to launch in 2028 and demonstrate nuclear electric propulsion in deep space for the first time.

Experts from across the agency, the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE), and industry met at NASA’s Glenn Research Center in Cleveland for a major SR-1 mission design review in October. Several key decisions were made, propelling the mission from an early concept toward a defined spacecraft design.

“SR-1 marks a pivotal step in how we travel through the solar system,” said Steve Sinacore, SR-1 Freedom program director. “This mission will be the first freight run on the railroad of the solar system, and the decisions we’re making now are laying the tracks for every nuclear-powered spacecraft that follows.”

Planned for launch in late 2028, SR-1 will use both nuclear and solar power to deliver [SkyFall](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/skyfall/), a capsule carrying three next-generation helicopters, to Mars. Once deployed, the helicopters will study Martian geology and climate history, explore new terrain, and search for signs of subsurface ice.

As NASA prepares for more ambitious exploration missions, future spacecraft and surface operations will require significantly more power than current systems can provide, particularly in environments where sunlight is limited or unavailable. SR-1 will demonstrate how fission power can enable long-duration missions, pave the way for reliable surface power systems to support NASA’s future [Moon Base](https://www.nasa.gov/moonbase/), and enable exploration deeper into the solar system.

## Key design decisions

The SR-1 Freedom spacecraft design has evolved since NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman first introduced the concept in March at the agency’s [Ignition](https://www.nasa.gov/ignition/) event, where leadership shared plans to develop a fission-powered spacecraft in time for the next Mars launch window.

One significant change is to use a shorter boom than the one shown in early illustrations. The boom separates the reactor from the spacecraft’s main body, known as the Power and Propulsion Element. The shorter boom will reduce weight, simplify assembly, and help streamline the spacecraft’s design.

Planned for launch in late 2028, Space Reactor-1 (SR-1) Freedom will use both nuclear and solar power to deliver SkyFall to Mars. This infographic explains the components of the spacecraft.

NASA and DOE experts also determined that improvements in shielding and spacecraft design will allow the reactor to operate closer to the rest of the spacecraft. This will simplify integration while maintaining the radiation protection needed for spacecraft electronics and the SkyFall payload.

Teams are continuing to evaluate other key design features, including the number of radiator panels on SR-1, output power levels of its [nuclear power module](https://www.nasa.gov/centers-and-facilities/glenn/sr-1-freedom-advances-with-progress-on-nuclear-power-module/), and how long its reactor will operate. These decisions will help shape the final spacecraft design and ensure it meets mission objectives.

In addition, the team is modifying the spacecraft’s [Power and Propulsion Element](https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/america-underway-in-space-on-nuclear-power.pdf?emrc=6b069185e993a) by updating its communications system for the journey to Mars. SR-1 Freedom will use larger X-band antenna dishes to send data across deep space back to Earth. Further maturation of the spacecraft plans will focus on reducing risk, simplifying the design, and staying on schedule.

NASA awarded a $39.3 million contract to Johns Hopkins University’s Applied Physics Laboratory to develop the heat rejection system for the spacecraft’s nuclear power module. The system will remove excess heat generated by the spacecraft’s nuclear power system, allowing it to operate safely and efficiently. The lab is working with the company Advanced Cooling Technologies as a key strategic commercial partner for providing the critical heat pipe and composite radiator technologies that will enable the system to meet the demanding mission requirements.

Awarded under the Aerospace Research, Development, and Engineering Support II contract, the contract action ensures the Applied Physics Laboratory team will design, build, test, and evaluate the system, along with producing the hardware needed for flight. The heat rejection system is a key part of demonstrating nuclear electric propulsion in space and will help lay the groundwork and industrial production foundation for future high-power nuclear systems used in deep space exploration.

## Updated mission profile

Along with the spacecraft design, teams have defined the mission timeline and planned operations.

After launch and once the spacecraft has left Earth orbit, SR-1 Freedom will activate and gradually increase reactor power. The reactor system will operate for an initial period of time before shutting down. During this period, the spacecraft will collect and send performance data back to Earth. Solar arrays will then provide power as it cruises to Mars.

NASA’s Space Reactor-1 (SR-1) Freedom, the first fission-powered spacecraft to travel beyond Earth orbit, cruises past Mars in this artist’s concept, demonstrating nuclear electric propulsion in deep space.

After delivering SkyFall to Martian orbit, SR-1 Freedom will restart its fission reactor, collecting additional data on the spacecraft’s performance in deep space.

“By refining the design and advancing this architecture, we’re not just building a spacecraft, we’re establishing the foundation for a new era of reliable, efficient transport beyond Earth orbit,” Sinacore said. “What we learn from SR-1 Freedom will shape the future of exploration for decades to come.”

With key design decisions advancing and teams across NASA, DOE, and industry working together, SR-1 Freedom is moving toward its 2028 launch goal. The mission will demonstrate new capabilities for nuclear-powered transportation and help establish the foundation for future exploration beyond Earth.

To learn more about NASA’s efforts in nuclear power in space, visit:

[https://www.nasa.gov/space-nuclear](https://www.nasa.gov/space-nuclear)

# YouTube's iconic iOS app icon may soon return with new customizable icons [Gallery]

- YouTube
## YouTube’s iconic iOS app icon may soon return with new customizable icons [Gallery]

The iconic YouTube app icon that looked like a retro TV found on iOS might be making a comeback, with new customizable icons showing up behind the scenes of a new YouTube update.

In the early days of the iPhone, Apple built a custom app for YouTube on iOS before Google built its own. That included an app icon that looked like a retro TV and it was later replaced when YouTube’s official app launched on the platform.

Now, that icon might be coming back.

Android Authority spotted several new app icons YouTube for Android is testing in its latest beta update (v21.47.483-BETA). These icons seem to be tied to a new feature that would allow users to customize the homescreen icon for YouTube, and includes seven designs in total including two throwback designs. One is the aforementioned retro TV icon used on iOS, which was never on YouTube for Android, and another is an old stacked YouTube logo design.

Users would be able to change the app icon via a new setting in the app near the “Appearance” section, but nothing is live just yet. We also don’t know if this is Android-only, if this is limited to Premium subscribers, or when this might debut.

That said, it’s very fun to get these throwbacks, and we’ll be excited to see this functionality go live.

items.body:
# This Well-Known Butterfly is Actually Three Species in Disguise - Nautilus

## This Well-Known Butterfly is Actually Three Species in Disguise

A new discovery after 250 years

3:00 PM CST on November 23, 2026

Sometimes discovering a new species is a question of looking a little bit closer at wildlife we already know all about—which is how the Colobura cryptica butterfly has been identified in the tropical rainforests of Central and South America.

Butterflies of the Colobura genus are found all over these areas, and for more than 250 years, C. cryptica has been hiding in plain sight as the Colobura dirce species. In 2001, researchers realized that C. dirce populations actually included a second, distinct species, which was formally named Colobura annulata in 2001. Now, we have a third.

Read more: “ What a Massive Butterfly Count Reveals ”

It was caterpillars being studied in Venezuela that offered a big clue: They lacked the pale body markings seen on the other two species. As adults, these butterflies are harder to tell apart (what are known as cryptic species), but the differences in the caterpillar patterns prompted researchers to take a fresh look at 670 specimens stored in museums.

Alongside DNA analysis of those collected in the field, as well as careful comparisons of the wings of adults, the third species emerged. “It’s crazy to think about,” study author Anisha Sapkota said in a statement . “These butterflies look almost exactly the same and are found in the exact same place at the same time.”

In adult butterflies, C. cryptica is tricky to spot even for experts. All that tells it apart physically is the uniformity of the width of a gray band along the wing, and how well the wings reflect ultraviolet radiation. As disguises go, it’s pretty effective. The genetic comparisons were definitive though, and so, the new species is official—the end result of some careful caterpillar observations.

Now that researchers are aware of all three species, they can start to look at how their distributions and habits vary across Central and South America. The study authors think that even though there’s a lot of overlap in where these species live, that vertical stratification may have played a role in their isolation and eventual speciation. C. cryptica and C. annulata are usually found in forest canopies, while C. dirce more typically live in the undergrowth.

Another open question is how the butterflies recognize mates of the same species, with such minor physical differences. It’s possible that UV coloration is involved here too. UV-reflecting scales are relatively common across moths and butterflies.

Whatever the case, they’re certainly three of a kind.

items.body:
Today, the [Booker Prize Foundation](https://thebookerprizes.com/the-childrens-booker-prize) announced the “Great Eight” shortlist of titles for inaugural Children’s Booker Prize, which will be awarded annually beginning in 2027. The Children’s Booker is the latest off-shoot of the prestigious Booker Prize (most recently awarded to M. John Harrison’s [The End of Everything](http://bookshop.org/a/132/9798217438655)) and celebrates fiction for eight- to 12-year-olds, written in or translated into English and published in the UK or Ireland. The winner will take home £50,000 and the Booker Foundation will be donating at least 30,000 copies of the shortlisted books to children across the United Kingdom and Ireland.

“Any of these books stands comparison with any adult book, whatever the category, on its own terms,” said Frank Cottrell-Boyce, Chair of the Children’s Booker Prize 2027 judges, in the shortlist announcement. He, along with fellow judges Sanchita Basu De Sarkar and Lolly Adefope, narrowed down the shortlist from 89 submissions and will be joined for the final decision by four young people: Ibrahim (12), Lainey (12), Luna (8), and Myla (11).

Here’s the shortlist:

Guy Bass, illustrated by David Roberts, [The Worst Thing That Could Possibly Happen](http://bookshop.org/a/132/9781454975045)

Catherine Bruton, [Tadpole Summer](http://bookshop.org/a/132/9798887774466)

Eoin Colfer and Andrew Donkin, illustrated by Giovanni Rigano, [War](http://bookshop.org/a/132/9781464261251)

Iqbal Hussain, *The Night I Borrowed Time*

Liz Hyder, illustrated by Tom de Freston, The *Teller of Tall Tales*

Mikey Please, *The Rambler’s Curse*

Jessica Scott-Whyte, illustrated by Becka Moor, *Séamus Almost Famous*

Shaun Tan, [Hometown](http://bookshop.org/a/132/9781646146987)

The winner will be announced in a ceremony on February 2, 2027.

items.body:
Todd Cronan at *nonsite*:

Matisse often expressed his deepest sentiments about the world in his still lifes, and in his late works there is a sense that the world outside the canvas is impinging, seemingly violently, on his “figures.” The still-life creatures that inhabit his universe often appear harried, threatened, and vulnerable. Consider, for instance, the insistent partitioning of space in the late still lifes. The vertical wallpaper and curtain in *Black Philodendron* appear, at first, as decorative motifs, but they are also, on second glance, bars of a cage. Notice how the first bar of the curtain at right *severs* the leaves from a lemon at the upper edge of the table. It appears that the lemons on the table are less circling the plate than *fleeing* their containment within frames (table, dish, and picture). Mirroring the lemon at the edge of the plate, the stem of a lemon at right has broken through the edge of the table contour, a pictorial event that appears more “hopeful” than the jailbird lemon on the plate.

items.body:
In March of this year, a flurry of emails and text messages from a half dozen reporters around the world disrupted my quiet Saturday morning. An Iranian news agency had aired a week-old video of what appeared to be a U.S.-made Tomahawk missile hitting a school. News reports claimed that the strike killed more than 175 people, most of them children. The U.S. president and military denied responsibility. In the age of generative AI and all things deepfake, everyone—including me—was skeptical of the video’s authenticity.

I get this type of request a lot. For the past three decades, I’ve been developing mathematical and computational techniques to analyze and detect manipulation in digital media. Over this time, I think it’s fair to say that I, like most people, have approached visual recordings with a “presumption of authenticity”: If a skeptic claims that a recording is fake, the burden of proof is on them.

In today’s world of generative AI, however, I think we need to shift this stance to a “presumption of fake.” That is, the burden is now on the creator to prove that their content is real. While this new stance may seem unfair to legitimate creators, I think it both reflects reality and points to a future where we will once again be able to trust that most online media is what it appears to be.

The Forensic Approach to Deepfake Detection

Even last March, I was already tilting toward a presumption of fake. My initial response to the reporters was something along the lines of, “I am suspicious of the video because the quality is low, it emerged weeks after the bombing, and it is only being distributed by an Iranian news agency with a less-than-stellar record of accurate reporting.”

Given the potential implications—if the video was indeed real, however, I resigned myself to spending my Saturday morning analyzing it.

I first reasoned that if the Tomahawk missile was digitally added to each frame of the video without taking into consideration the camera motion, we might see a physically implausible missile path. So I aligned the video frames using a stationary background landmark as a reference. In the updated video, the missile did, in fact, move in a nearly linear trajectory. (See the yellow dots in the composite shown below.)

I next asked if the size (in pixels) of the missile in the video was plausible. Under some reasonable assumptions, I estimated that the missile in the video corresponded to a 6-meter Tomahawk at a distance of approximately 100 meters. The distance seemed plausible from the scene and was also consistent with the delay of 0.3 seconds from visible impact to the sound of impact, given that sound travels at 343 meters per second.

A composite photo composed of frames from a video of the Tomahawk strike reveals the missile’s trajectory.Hany Farid; Source: Mehr News

Despite the mounting evidence, though, I struggled to refine my answer for the reporters.

My skepticism was fueled by a recent study I worked on with colleagues at the University of California, Berkeley, that showed how hard it is to distinguish real from fake videos. Observers are now so suspicious of videos in general that they have trouble convincing themselves that a video is real.

But after a few more hours and a few more analyses with the missile video, I finally decided that it was authentic, and I gave the reporters my updated view.

This analysis marked a turning point for me. I realized I was just like the participants in our study: The lack of artifacts was not enough to readily convince me a video is real. I had flipped from a presumption of real to a presumption of fake.

Signaling a Video’s Provenance

When the visual record is no longer reliable, what can we do?

The types of forensic analyses that I routinely perform do not currently operate at internet scale and speed. But provenance signals can. These signals include content credentials and watermarks that are inserted or embedded at the time of creation or recording.

Credentials that follow the C2PA standard, for example, attach a cryptographically signed manifest to a photo or video at the moment of capture; this metadata records the device, the time and location of the recording, and any subsequent edits. Because the manifest is signed, any tampering with either the content or its history can be detected later by machine. Watermarks, like Google’s SynthID, embed an imperceptible signal directly into the pixels or audio samples that identifies the content’s origin.

Apple recently took these ideas a step further. On some of its newest iPhones, the camera sensor can cryptographically sign the raw pixel data as it’s captured. That signed data is then developed into a reference image saved alongside the normal, editable photo. Anyone can then compare the two and see exactly what, if anything, was changed.

These provenance signals are often criticized as being only a partial solution or vulnerable to attack. This is true if we think of them as mechanisms for catching bad actors. But that’s not what they’re supposed to do. Their purpose is to let good actors prove that their audiovisual recording is what it claims to be.

Provenance signals thus need not be adversary-proof. Instead, these signals are part of a new reality in which consumers, journalists, and the courts must adapt to a presumption of fakeness. If enough good actors adopt these mechanisms, they can begin to drown out bad actors. In other words, we have to switch from a model of “catch the bad actors” to “empower the good actors.”

Real-Time Verification

This switch from trust to distrust of digital media has expanded to include routine video calls.

In September 2024, for example, Senator Ben Cardin (D-Md.), then chair of the Foreign Relations Committee, received a video meeting request from Dmytro Kuleba, who until a few weeks earlier had been Ukraine’s foreign minister. During the call, Cardin became suspicious when, out of character, Kuleba pressed him on whether the U.S. should allow Ukraine to fire long-range missiles into Russia. Cardin ended the call. Later, the State Department confirmed that Kuleba had never requested the meeting, and the Senate security office warned staff that foreign adversaries, possibly Russian, would likely try similar faked meetings again.

All it takes to conduct this type of impersonation is a face swap or avatar deepfake, along with voice conversion, both of which substitute the speaker’s face and voice for deepfaked versions in real time. These technologies are readily available in commercial products and open-source libraries and run on nothing more powerful than a modern laptop.

This video illustrates the current state of face-swap deepfakes.

Farid’s Company GetReal Shows How Real Deepfake Videos Look Today

Your browser does not support the video tag.
Firms that verify provenance have to move fast to detect real-time deepfakes. Hany Farid, GetReal

items.subtitle: Viele nutzen einen VPN, um sich gegen IP-Tracking zu schützen.

items.body:
Viele nutzen einen VPN, um sich gegen IP-Tracking zu schützen. Aber gerade Youtube, wo sehr umfangreichen Verhaltensdaten entstehen, funktioniert über VPNs oft nicht – vor allem, wenn man Videos über Drittanbieter-Apps, Downloadtools oder mit Werbeblocker schauen will. In diesem Artikel stelle ich einen einfachen und kostenlosen Trick vor, mit dem man statt VPN eine neue IP über das Smartphone bezieht. Über die recht neue App »[5G Proxy Pro](https://f-droid.org/en/packages/com.tokyoxpa3.androidproxy/)« kann man diese IP auch in einem einzelnen Browser oder per Kommandozeile am Desktopcomputer nutzen. Am Ende des Artikel liste ich dann noch Ideen auf, um dauerhaft einen 5G-Proxy für Youtube im Einsatz zu haben. Der Trick hilft natürlich auch bei anderen Schutzmaßnahmen, die einen VPN benötigten.

**Nicht für Einsteiger**: Dieser Artikel ist für Fortgeschrittene. Die Tipps sind Bastellösungen, die für manche Personen möglicherweise nützlich sind, um eine Alternative für einen IP-Wechsel zu kennen. Damit ist nicht immer automatisch mehr Datenschutz erreicht. Probleme wie DNS-Leaks oder unbemerkte IDs von Apps müssen beachtet werden.

Gut zu wissen

### Das Problem mit manchen alternative Frontends

Nicht alle alternativen Youtube-Frontends und Apps schützen vor IP-Tracking. Vor allem die bekannten Android-Apps NewPipe, PipePipe und LibreTube fragen die Daten direkt bei Youtube ab. Das kann man teilweise in den Einstellungen ändern, zum Beispiel bei LibreTube. Andere Projekte nutzen „Piped“-Instanzen, so dass die IP geschützt ist. Aber wenn Piped-Adressen über das Terminal genutzt werden, können sie ebenfalls direkte Youtube-Verbindungen herstellen. Das Setup also besser einmal mit PCAPdroid oder einem Netzwerk-Sniffer oder über die DNS-Abfragen prüfen.

## 1. Warum man sich gegen IP-Tracking schützen sollte

Viele Websites geben deine IP-Adresse an Werbefirmen weiter, die dann Verhaltensdaten für einen Haushalt ganz ohne Cookies speichern können. Ausführlich habe ich das 2024 in diesem Artikel beschrieben: [IP-Haushaltstracking bei Google und Drittanbietern](https://www.kuketz-blog.de/ip-haushaltstracking-bei-google-und-drittanbietern-was-es-ist-und-wie-man-sich-schuetzt/). Wenn du Glück hast, wird das IP-Tracking über eingebundene Drittanbieter ausgeführt, die man mit einem klassischen Werbeblocker deaktivieren kann. So ist das beispielsweise bei Spiegel Online mit Einwilligung. Bei großen Plattformen wie Youtube passiert das aber serverseitig und man kann es nicht blocken. Die Technik wurde bis 2024 von Google auch ohne Einwilligung eingesetzt. Daher ist grundsätzlich Misstrauen angebracht, ob Google sich beim Haushaltstracking an die DSGVO hält.

Gut zu wissen

### Grundidee: Google/Youtube und andere IP-Tracker nur über eine zweite IP nutzen

Im Idealfall eines perfekt geschützten Haushalts könnte man das IP-Tracking durch Google, Shops oder Nachrichtenseiten einfach ignorieren: Man bekäme über Nacht eine neue IP-Adresse, eventuell erzwungen mit einer Zeitschaltuhr am Router beziehungsweise dem Flugmodus über Nacht am Smartphone. Wenn man alles perfekt konfiguriert hat, kann Google die Aufrufe aus dem Haushalt nur für jeden Tag zusammenknüpfen, nicht aber für einen längeren Zeitraum. Voraussetzung dafür wäre:

- Kein Browser im Haushalt speichert Cookies von Google
- Keine Apps im Haushalt senden eindeutige Installations-IDs an Google Firebase
- Keine smarten Geräte wie Fernseher senden IDs an Google
- Im ganzen Haushalt werden keine Websites, Apps oder Geräte mit Drittanbieter-Logins betrieben, die Anmeldeinformationen an Identitätsprovider weitergeben, beispielsweise über Zalando oder einen Cloudanbieter.

Da dieses Szenario aber im Alltag und mit mehreren Haushaltsmitgliedern sehr schwer oder gar nicht zu erreichen ist, besteht die Grundidee von VPN oder Proxy als Trackingschutz darin, gezielt problematische Seiten – also vor allem werbefinanzierte Seiten mit spezifischen Interessensdaten wie Youtube, aber auch Nachrichtenseiten, bei denen man eine Einwilligung geben muss – über eine zweite IP zu leiten. So minimiert man zusätzlich zum Werbeblocker das Risiko, dass sehr viele problematische Verhaltens- und Interessensdaten langfristig in einem Haushaltsprofil gesammelt werden. Das IP-Tracking wird also nicht verhindert, sondern abgetrennt.

## 2. Spontane Variante: Flugmodus-Trick mit googlefreiem Smartphone

Wer GrapheneOS oder ein ähnliches googlefreies Android installiert hat, hat gegenüber Stock-Androids den Vorteil, dass weder ein Google-Login noch eine Werbe-ID mit dem Smartphone verknüpft ist. Wenn man nun Wifi deaktiviert und dann einmal den Flugmodus an- und wieder ausschaltet, bekommt das Smartphone vom Mobilfunkprovider üblicherweise eine neue IP-Adresse. Das muss nicht sein, daher sollte man es zunächst testen: Einfach vor und nach der Neuverbindung eine der vielen IP-Serviceseiten aufrufen – leicht zu merken ist [ip.me](https://ip.me/) von Proton, werbefrei dafür [stat.ripe.net](https://stat.ripe.net) von der europäischen Internetregistry). Wenn ein solcher IP-Wechsel stattfindet, hat Google ein wichtiges Merkmal weniger, um die Youtube-Nutzung mit den vorherigen Aufrufen auf dem Smartphone zusammenzuführen. Vor allem wenn man trackingfreie Drittanbieter-Apps wie Newpipe oder einen Privatsphäre-Browser auf dem Smartphone nutzt, ist man so gegenüber den wichtigsten branchenüblichen Trackingmethoden geschützt.

Wenn man für diesen Trick ein eigenes **Profil** anlegt, hat man zwar einen etwas besseren Schutz, weil andere Apps oder Websites nicht versehentlich gestartet werden können.

Aber was viele nicht wissen: Apps, die im Eigentümer-Profil im Hintergrund laufen dürfen oder die anderweitig vom System aktiviert werden können (beispielsweise Signals Verbindungen zu Amazon AWS), **laufen auch bei einem Profilwechsel im Hintergrund weiter**. Also auch wenn beispielsweise Signal nicht im Zweitprofil installiert ist, laufen die Verbindungen aus dem Eigentümerprofil weiter. Andersherum ist das nicht der Fall: Die Apps aus Nebenprofilen laufen nicht weiter, wenn man zum Eigentümerprofil zurückwechselt. Daher nutze ich für mein Setup RethinkDNS, um vor dem Wechsel alle Apps im Eigentümerprofil abzuschalten, bevor man wechselt.

Das will man verhindern: Diese Netzwerkverbindungen öffnet mein Android, obwohl ich ins Zweitprofil gewechselt bin, in dem diese Apps nicht installiert sind. Sichtbar wird das nur mit einem externen Sniffer, den ich auf meinem Router laufen lasse. Die Datenverbindungen zu Signal sind im Eigentümerprofil weiter aktiv. Außerdem stelle ich fest, dass die Gopro-App aus dem Eigentümerprofil aktiv ist, obwohl sie dort keine Hintergrundrechte hat. Google Firebase erhält hier vermutlich eindeutige Installations-IDs. Eben weil es so viele Möglichkeiten gibt, wie Google eine dauerhafte ID aus dem Haushalt erhält, empfehle ich das umständliche Vorgehen mit einer extra IP, einem Zweitprofil und RethinkDNS im Eigentümerprofil.

items.title: What the End of Anonymous Writing Means for Academia
items.subtitle: A reader who asked to remain anonymous (seriously) pointed me to an article about the impending end of anonymous writing.
items.feedText:
Large language models are getting increasingly good at identifying the authors of human-written text. In a preprint, “Frontier models need only one text to unmask its human or AI author,” a team of authors claim that:

Given a single text and a simple zero-shot prompt (no web access, tools, candidate lists, or writing samples), frontier models can answer “who wrote this?” at three increasingly specific levels: (1) whether an AI or human wrote it, (2) if an AI, which lab, and (3) if a human, often exactly who. Th…
items.body:
A reader who asked to remain anonymous (seriously) pointed me to an [article](https://www.theargumentmag.com/p/say-goodbye-to-anonymous-posting?) about the impending end of anonymous writing.

Large language models are getting increasingly good at identifying the authors of human-written text. In a preprint, “[Frontier models need only one text to unmask its human or AI author](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26216),” a team of authors claim that:

> Given a single text and a [simple zero-shot prompt](https://github.com/denizbt/unmasking_authors/blob/main/prompts/RQ3/holistic.txt) (no web access, tools, candidate lists, or writing samples), frontier models can answer “who wrote this?” at three increasingly specific levels: (1) whether an AI or human wrote it, (2) if an AI, which lab, and (3) if a human, often exactly who.

The authors asked LLMs to provide the identity of different kinds of often-anonymous writing, such as peer reviews and internet comments.

Their findings:

> The best-performing model we test is Claude Fable 5.2, which names the reviewer of 56% of private peer reviews and the username behind 31% of recent Reddit comments.

It appears that your writing is more likely to be outed as yours if some previous writing of yours was in an LLM’s training data, or if you a lot of your writing is available online. And once a model becomes familiar with you, your writing is very likely to be identified as yours:

> Even when a text is brand new, a model can identify its writer from what it learned about them elsewhere; i.e., once that knowledge is in the weights, the writer cannot do anything about it. This leaves people with the largest public footprints, such as active social media users or established authors, permanently exposed, since paraphrasing the text does not completely remove the deanonymization risk. Moreover, the set of vulnerable writers expands as models improve… Maintaining anonymity is especially important for peer review. Our private lab review data comes from only six writers, but a study across thousands of private peer reviews is underway.

Having an AI disguise your writing style by paraphrasing your writing does diminish its recognizability somewhat, but not entirely, the researchers report.

One commenter on the paper, Kelsey Piper, [writes](https://www.theargumentmag.com/p/say-goodbye-to-anonymous-posting?), “We’re witnessing a total erosion of the ability to write anonymously online,” though “the process is still incomplete. Not everyone should consider themselves deanonymized yet. But the erosion is happening.”

Regarding peer review, she writes:

> [T]he institution of anonymous peer review does not look like it will hold up any longer. The space of possible reviewers for a given academic article review in a particular discipline is pretty small; stylistic tics are sufficient to confidently distinguish between them.

Suppose the LLMs get quite a bit better at identifying the authors of anonymous text. What would that mean for the future of peer review? Well, while some reviewers have regularly opted to forgo anonymity, that is typically a privilege exercised by the relatively senior and secure members of the profession. I wouldn’t expect many more to join their ranks. Nor would I expect academia to be content relying on the forbearance of, say, curious authors or grant judges, to preserve anonymity.

There are [alternatives to peer review](https://dailynous.com/2022/02/07/why-a-crowd-sourced-peer-review-system-would-be-good-for-philosophy-guest-post/). Will the erosion of anonymity push more branches of academia to embrace these alternatives?

Or will it be a reason to use AIs even more in academia, say, as peer reviewers? After all, recently [one set of researchers found that](https://gking.harvard.edu/files/peerless.pdf):

> AI-generated article reviews are now better, by every measure we could construct, than reviews written by well-compensated human experts and judged to be of unusually high quality by journal editors and authors.

The study was performed on quantitative social science papers, not philosophy papers, but of course this technology is only a few years old; who knows how it might develop, and how rapidly.

Discussion welcome.

**UPDATE:** Shen-yi Liao [provided](https://bsky.app/profile/liao.shen-yi.org/post/3n32y4m2mgs2v) a direct link to [the prompt the researchers used](https://github.com/denizbt/unmasking_authors/blob/main/prompts/RQ3/holistic.txt). Try it on an unpublished piece of your writing. I gave ChatGPT [the prompt and the introductory section of an unpublished talk I wrote](https://chatgpt.com/s/p_6b05bf5973a08191aa93b52e7a43d0ed) a couple of years back and it identified me as the author with.62 confidence. You can read its report [↗ chatgpt.com](https://chatgpt.com/s/t_6b05bff752448191821da26c86cb9f2b). I fed it a referee report I wrote and it returned my name with.55 confidence.

items.body:
If you tend to work with [Novation](https://musictech.com/brands/novation)’s keyboard controllers, we’ve got some good news for you. Today, Novation has released a free v2.0 firmware update for the [Launchkey MK4](https://musictech.com/reviews/controllers/novation-launchkey-mk-4-review/) and [FLkey 2](https://musictech.com/reviews/controllers/novation-flkey-2-review/). Alongside general improvements, the update also gives a major facelift to the controllers’ arpeggiators, two-way plugin integration, tweaks knob behaviour, and more.

The update introduces six new arpeggiator types, meaning that both keyboard controllers can now utilise up to 14 different arps. Changes have also been made to allow users to route the output of your three chord modes or external MIDI input directly to the arpeggiator – a change that will make make it easier than ever generate sequences.

- READ MORE: [Black Friday 2026: Our favourite deals on music gear, plugins, and DAWs](https://musictech.com/news/gear/best-black-friday-music-tech-deals/)

As well as this, Arpeggiator Snapshots have also been introduces to store your preferred arpeggiator settings, with the option of saying up to eight unique set ups.

Elsewhere, the update also adds two-way integration to the Novation Play software instrument. Users will also be able to monitor their parameters as they’re being adjusted from their keyboard’s OLED display.

Novation has also introduces a new Pot Style encoder curve. This comes as a ‘requested’ feature from Novation’s community, tweaking the firmware to allow each controller’s knobs to behave in a more “traditional” sense, with fixed potentiometers.

**The v2.0 firmware is free and available now. For more information, head to [Novation](https://novationmusic.com).**

items.body:
**Mit dem DW-8K emuliert Cherry Audio den legendären Korg DW-8000 und erweitert den hybriden Vintage-Synthesizer von 1985 um zusätzliche Funktionen. Ich schätze den warmen, lebendigen Klangcharakter des DW-8000 ebenso wie seine angenehm überschaubare Synthese-Architektur. Falls ihr mehr über den Klassiker erfahren wollt, ist das [Bonedo-Feature Korg DW-8000 Vintage Synth](https://www.bonedo.de/artikel/korg-dw-8000-vintage-synth/) sicher interessant für euch.**

Der Korg DW-8000 im neuen Gewand: Cherry Audio liefert mit dem DW-8K mehr als eine reine Emulation.

Ein gebrauchtes Original kostet derzeit etwa 400 bis 600 Euro – ich selbst habe noch einen Korg DW-8000 im Studio stehen. Kann der Cherry Audio DW-8K, der regulär 69 Euro kostet, klanglich mit dem Original mithalten? Ist das Plugin am Ende sogar die praktischere Lösung für die tägliche Musikproduktion?

## Cherry Audio DW-8K Highlights

- Emuliert den Korg DW-8000 originalgetreu und integriert sein charakteristisches Digital Delay.
- Im Dual-Layer-Betrieb lassen sich zwei Sounds schichten oder auf der Tastatur splitten.
- Erweiterte Filtermodelle und Rauschtypen, ein Sub-Oszillator sowie eine Modulationsmatrix erweitern die klanglichen Möglichkeiten.
- Zu den Extras gehören ein Step-Sequenzer, interne Effekte und Parameter-Automation.
- Die mitgelieferte Sound-Library umfasst über 400 Presets, darunter auch die 128 originalen Factory Programs.

## Was hat Cherry Audio am DW-8000 verändert?

In den 80er-Jahren hätte ich mir für den DW-8000 zusätzliche Oszillator-Wellenformen gewünscht. Cherry Audio geht mit dem DW-8k jedoch einen anderen Weg und erweitert den Klassiker vor allem um zusätzliche Klanggestaltungsmöglichkeiten: Der Synthesizer bietet einen Dual-Layer-Betrieb, bei dem sich zwei Klang- und Effekt-Setups unabhängig voneinander konfigurieren lassen. Außerdem stehen bis zu 16 Stimmen pro Layer zur Verfügung.

Neue Perspektiven: Der Cherry Audio ermöglicht Layer- und Split-Kreationen mit zwei unterschiedlichen Klängen.

Auch im Oszillator-Bereich hat sich einiges getan. Neben den drei zusätzlichen Soundparametern Phase, Fold und Drive gibt es jetzt auch einen Sub-Oszillator und verschiedene Rauschtypen. Das ursprüngliche analoge 24-dB-Tiefpassfilter des Korg DW-8000 wurde im Plugin um die Filtertypen Bandpass und Hochpass ergänzt.

Der originale DW-8000 ist bekanntlich kein großer Modulationskünstler. Mit der neuen Modulationsmatrix von Cherry Audio ändert sich das jedoch grundlegend: Insgesamt 57 Modulationsquellen und 107 Modulationsziele lassen sich hier miteinander verknüpfen.

Die Klangerzeugung ist leistungsfähiger als beim Original – neue Filter und eine Modulationsmatrix.

Wie von anderen Cherry-Audio-Plugins gewohnt, gehören auch ein Arpeggiator, ein 16×4-Step-Sequenzer und eine umfangreiche Effektsektion zum DW-8K. Letztere umfasst rund 25 FX-Typen, darunter auch ein Shimmer Reverb. Ebenfalls mit an Bord ist das originale Digital Delay des Korg DW-8000.

Ein Software-Synth à la Cherry Audio: interne Effekte und ein 16×4-Step-Sequenzer.

## Wie komfortabel lässt sich der Cherry Audio DW-8K programmieren?

Die GUI bildet fast alle Parameter des DW-8K auf einen Blick ab. Das ist sicherlich gut gemeint, wirkt auf mich allerdings etwas überladen. Ich ertappe mich dabei, wie meine Augen ständig leicht nervös den Bildschirm absuchen. Eine deutlichere und vielleicht auch farbliche Abgrenzung der einzelnen Bereiche könnte hier für mehr Übersicht sorgen. Insgeheim vermisse ich die Einfachheit des DW-8000 und würde mir von Cherry Audio eine Easy-Edit-Page wünschen, die sich tatsächlich auf die wichtigsten Parameter beschränkt und diese übersichtlich präsentiert.

Abgesehen davon ist die Bedienoberfläche klar strukturiert und in drei Hauptansichten unterteilt: Keyboard, Motion und Effects View. Gemessen an den zahlreichen neuen Möglichkeiten lässt sich der DW-8K außerdem erfreulich unkompliziert programmieren.

## Wie authentisch klingen die Factory Programs?

Auch diesmal hat Cherry Audio mehrere erfahrene Sounddesigner engagiert und eine beachtliche Factory Library mit über 400 Sounds aus den üblichen Klangsparten zusammengestellt. Die Klänge sind zwar meist gelungen und unterstützen auch Poly-AT- und MPE-Controllern, treffen aber nicht immer den charakteristischen Vintage-Sound des Korg DW-8000.

Über den Browser findet ihr viele und gute Presets für den schnellen Einsatz des DW-8K.

Anders formuliert: Für meinen Geschmack schießt Cherry Audio hier etwas übers Ziel hinaus. Ich hätte mir eher schöne, unkomplizierte Brot-und-Butter-Sounds gewünscht als moderne, ambitionierte Interpretationen. Allerdings ist es durchaus verständlich, dass Cherry Audio die erweiterten Möglichkeiten des DW-8K demonstrieren möchte. Für die Hörbeispiele habe ich zwölf Factory Presets ausgewählt, die meiner Meinung nach den ursprünglichen Charakter des DW-8000 am besten einfangen.
