## Lassen Sounds vom originalen DW-8000 importieren?

Der Import von Originalsounds geht ganz einfach: Zieht einfach die SysEx-Datei aufs GUI des Plugins. Anschließend erscheinen die importierten Sounds als neue Bank im Preset-Browser. Ich habe das einmal mit meiner Library „Atmospherika“ ausprobiert. Sie enthält Pads und andere Programs für Ambient und klingt ganz anders als die Factory Sounds von Cherry Audio.

Nach dem Import bin ich ziemlich begeistert: Der Cherry Audio DW-8K fügt zwar automatisch einen Reverb hinzu, den es beim Original nicht gibt, dafür klingen die Programs aber sehr nach meinem DW-8000 – warm, breit, organisch und charaktervoll. So gefällt mir der hybride Vintage-Synth. Sieben Programs spiele ich als Kostprobe an. Das letzte Demo ist übrigens ein A/B-Vergleich zwischen Cherry Audio und Full Bucket Music.

## Cherry Audio DW-8K – momentan fast alternativlos

Eigentlich hatte ich erwartet, dass Korg selbst irgendwann eine Emulation des DW-8000 veröffentlichen würde. Stand jetzt (November 2026) ist es dazu aber noch nicht gekommen. Damit ist der Cherry Audio DW-8K tatsächlich bislang das einzige kommerzielle Plugin, das den charakteristischen hybriden Vintage-Sound des Originals überzeugend einfängt und umfassend programmierbar macht.

Kaum zu glauben, aber der FB-7999 ist momentan die einzige Alternative zum DW-8000-Klon von Cherry Audio.

items.body:
### 🔄 Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO

[↗ Primärquelle: wccftech.com](https://wccftech.com/nvidia-reinstates-jensen-huang-ceo-board-of-director/)

- Nvidia has brought Jensen Huang back as president and CEO and a board member, effective immediately, weeks after he resigned over an admitted affair with a Singaporean data center executive tied to banned US AI chips in China.
- The board voted unanimously to reinstate Huang after talks with him and senior US government officials, saying it was confident his return posed no national security risk and that interim CEO and CFO Colette Kress had served well during the gap.
- A committee of independent directors will finish investigating a reported foreign intelligence effort targeting Huang, a separate national security committee will oversee trade compliance, and Nvidia is now hiring a new chief compliance officer.

### 🚗 Tesla says new FSD is 25x safer

[↗ Primärquelle: digitaltrends.com](https://www.digitaltrends.com/cars/tesla-fsd-v15-rollout/)

- Tesla has started releasing Full Self-Driving v15, which updates its whole driving network and, the company says on X, handles safety-critical situations 25 times better than before.
- Tesla says the 25x figure refers to the critical intervention rate after an upgraded vision encoder was trained on millions of internet videos, and the update adds a live Reality View showing what FSD plans to do.
- The release improves detection of signs, potholes, animals, and speed cameras, slowing for cameras unless you cancel twice at one spot, and adds Bike Rack Mode, but it stays a supervised system.

### 🛑 OpenAI urges rival labs to cap AI training

[↗ Primärquelle: unite.ai](https://www.unite.ai/openai-proposes-shared-ai-development-limits-tied-to-safety-milestones/)

- OpenAI's chief scientist Jakub Pachocki asked rival AI labs to agree on shared limits for frontier model training, warning that safety and monitoring research could fall behind if pretraining speeds up as soon as 2027.
- Pachocki published OpenAI's internal log-perplexity scores, a measure of how well a model predicts the next word, showing GPT-3.5 at about 0.99 and GPT-4 at 0.91, with new skills emerging below 0.8.
- He proposed that developers not cross perplexity-based thresholds until oversight research hits a clear milestone, such as a successor to chain-of-thought monitors, and jointly set evaluation norms, red-teaming, and transparency standards.

### 🧠 Meta AI chief says superintelligence is arriving

[↗ Primärquelle: nerds.xyz](https://nerds.xyz/2026/11/meta-ai-chief-superintelligence-warning/)

- Alexandr Wang, Meta's chief AI officer, warned in a post on X that superintelligence is coming and said humanity should refuse any "handover" of control to AI, with the next year being a critical period.
- Wang pointed to a formal proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, a 167-year-old math problem about prime numbers, which Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge worked out with Claude and two Lean proof-checking groups confirmed as correct.
- His biggest worry is AI automating AI research itself, with labs using one model to design a better successor until humans signing off can no longer truly check the work, something he calls "recursive self-improvement."

### ⚠️ US intelligence chief warns of more tech outages

[↗ Primärquelle: cnbc.com](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/22/jay-clayton-tech-outages-faa-microsoft-thanksgiving.html)

- US intelligence chief Jay Clayton told Americans to expect "bumps in the road" and more tech outages as companies and the government upgrade their systems to handle the AI age, speaking on CNN's "State of the Union."
- The warning follows a nationwide ground stop a week ago that the FAA blamed on router upgrades flooding systems with data, plus a Microsoft Outlook outage the company tied to an earlier network capacity upgrade.
- Officials have brushed off claims the outages, which also slowed bank transactions, stemmed from a coordinated or AI cyberattack, with Bessent comparing the glitchy security patches banks are applying to a vaccine's temporary side effects.

### 🛡️ CrowdStrike buys Zscaler for $43.9B

[↗ Primärquelle: implicator.ai](https://www.implicator.ai/crowdstrike-agrees-acquire-zscaler-which-develops-network/)

- CrowdStrike has agreed to buy network security firm Zscaler in an all-stock deal valuing it at roughly $43.9 billion, pushing the endpoint security maker into cloud network protection, which both companies call cybersecurity's biggest market.
- Zscaler shareholders get 1.135 CrowdStrike shares each, worth about $260 per share, a 34% premium, and will own around 15.9% of the combined company, whose founder Jay Chaudhry keeps running the Zscaler business and joins CrowdStrike's board.
- CrowdStrike expects about $1 billion in extra yearly revenue and $500 million in cost savings, with roughly 8,000 Zscaler customers it can sell to, and plans to close the deal in the second half of its fiscal 2028.

items.body:
Je konkreter die Vergesellschaftungspläne in Berlin werden, desto lauter fordert die Union ein bundesgesetzliches Einschreiten. Spätestens als bekannt wurde, dass Linke, Grüne und SPD in Berlin rund 160.000 Wohnungen vergesellschaften wollen, konkretisierten sich die Eckpunkte eines möglichen „Investitionsschutzgesetzes“ des Bundes. Danach sollen Vergesellschaftungen nur bei nachgewiesener „zwingender Notwendigkeit“ zulässig sein, wenn andere wohnungspolitische Maßnahmen bereits ausgeschöpft wurden. Zudem soll die Entschädigung 80 oder sogar 100 Prozent des Verkehrswerts betragen. Innenminister Dobrindt will damit in eigenen Worten „deutlich machen, dass willkürlicher linker Vergesellschaftungs-Fetisch mit dem Grundgesetz nicht vereinbar ist“ ([ZDF](https://www.zdfheute.de/politik/deutschland/dobrindt-immobilien-wohnungen-enteignung-100.html)).

Bereits die Gesetzgebungskompetenz des Bundes wird aus guten Gründen bezweifelt (siehe [Laven](https://verfassungsblog.de/ein-bundesweites-vergesellschaftungsverbot/)). Doch selbst wenn der Bund ein solches Gesetz erlassen dürfte, zieht das Grundgesetz hier materielle Grenzen. Art. 15 GG ist kein wohnungspolitisches Notfallinstrument – die Verfassung erkennt Vergesellschaftung als eigenständigen Zweck an. Wer Vergesellschaftung von der Ausschöpfung sämtlicher wohnungspolitischer Alternativen abhängig macht, verkennt diesen Zweck.

## Kein Grund zur Aufregung?

Aber von vorn: Warum sollte ein solches restriktives Investitionsschutzgesetz verfassungsrechtlich überhaupt problematisch sein?

Das Bundesverfassungsgericht hat bereits klargestellt, dass Art. 15 GG keinen Verfassungsauftrag zur Vergesellschaftung enthält ([BVerfGE 12, 354 363 f. – VW-Privatisierung](https://opinioiuris.de/entscheidung/1117)). Der Wortlaut stellt die Vergesellschaftung vielmehr in das Entschließungs- und Auswahlermessen des Gesetzgebers. Außerdem lehnt es das BVerfG ab, in das Grundgesetz eine bestimmte Wirtschaftsordnung hineinzulesen, und betont stattdessen dessen „wirtschaftspolitische Neutralität“ ([BVerfGE 4, 7 (17 f.) – Investitionshilfe](https://opinioiuris.de/entscheidung/818)). Das bedeutet auch, dass die Verfassung dem Gesetzgeber eine große Gestaltungsfreiheit zugesteht und die jeweilige demokratische Mehrheit ihre wirtschaftspolitischen Vorstellungen umsetzen darf; selbstverständlich auch mit einer starken Betonung rein privatwirtschaftlicher Formen (Kempny, in: Dreier, 4. Aufl. 2023, GG Art. 15 Rn. 17).

## Die Besonderheiten des Art. 15 GG

Allerdings muss der Gesetzgeber, wenn er denn tätig wird – und das sind absolute Basics des Verfassungsrechts –, den Vorrang der Verfassung beachten (Art. 20 Abs. 3 GG). Er muss Gesetze so gestalten, dass sie mit den Inhalten und Wertsetzungen des Grundgesetzes vereinbar sind, und er darf keinesfalls unbegrenzt über Normen von Verfassungsrang verfügen (Heusch/Ullrich/Posser VerfassungsR-HdB/Heusch, 1. Aufl. 2024, Rn. 32 ff.).

Das Grundgesetz bildet dabei eine Rahmenordnung, innerhalb der sich der Gesetzgeber zu bewegen hat, auch um zwischen mehreren Alternativen seine (rechts-)politischen Programme zu gestalten. Um zu bestimmen, wo diese äußeren Rahmenlinien bei Vergesellschaftungen verlaufen, sind die Besonderheiten des – durchaus eigentümlichen – Art. 15 GG zu beachten.

Nach der Befreiung von der NS-Diktatur war die Meinung verbreitet, dass Großkapital und Monopole die Machtübernahme der Nazis befördert hatten. Das Grundgesetz enthält deshalb den Bonner Kompromiss: Das Eigentum wird als individuelles Privateigentum geschützt, soll aber gleichzeitig dem Wohle der Allgemeinheit dienen. Deshalb sind – unter bestimmten Voraussetzungen – auch Enteignungen möglich (Art. 14 Abs. 2, 3 GG). Von der Enteignung strikt zu trennen ist die besondere Möglichkeit, Grund und Boden, Naturschätze und Produktionsmittel nach Art. 15 GG in Gemeinwirtschaft zu überführen. Die Vergesellschaftung entzieht also nicht konkret-individuelles Eigentum, um öffentliche Aufgaben zu erfüllen. Ihr Ziel ist vielmehr die Überwindung privatnütziger Strukturen. Mit anderen Worten ermöglicht Art. 15 GG die Ablösung einer Wirtschaftsform, die auf privatem Eigentum und individueller Gewinnerzielung basiert, hin zu einer an Gemeinwirtschaftlichkeit ausgerichteten Umgestaltung des produktiven Eigentums – alles natürlich unter Entschädigung derjenigen, die von der Vergesellschaftung betroffen sind (Axer, in: BeckOK GG, Art. 15 Rn. 5).

Die Besonderheit dieser Regelung beschreibt Krüger ([zit. nach Oerke 2025](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/397400656_Art_15_GG_als_kollektives_Verfassungsrecht_Zur_notwendigen_Ausgestaltung_kollektiver_Entscheidungsstrukturen_in_einem_Sozialisierungsgesetz/fulltext/690e54864baee1659191991c/Art-15-GG-als-kollektives-Verfassungsrecht-Zur-notwendigen-Ausgestaltung-kollektiver-Entscheidungsstrukturen-in-einem-Sozialisierungsgesetz.pdf?_tp=eyJjb250ZXh0Ijp7ImZpcnN0UGFnZSI6InB1YmxpY2F0aW9uIiwicGFnZSI6InB1YmxpY2F0aW9uIn19)) eindrücklich:

> „Art. 15 ist der einzige Satz des Grundgesetzes, in dem nicht der Einzelne, sondern die Gesamtheit als Gesellschaft, als Wirtschaftssubjekt und als Eigentümerin positiv bewertet wird.“

Ob man Art. 15 GG dann als kollektives Grundrecht sui generis ([Oerke 2025](https://univerlag.uni-goettingen.de/handle/3/isbn-978-3-86395-674-5)) oder mit einem Großteil der Literatur als Erlaubnis- bzw. Ermächtigungsnorm versteht, spielt für den materiellen Gehalt zunächst eine untergeordnete Rolle. Entscheidender ist das hinter der Norm stehende Telos, von Teilen der Berliner Expertenkommission treffend beschrieben, als sog. [„wirtschaftspolitische Offenhaltungsnorm](https://www.berlin.de/kommission-vergesellschaftung/_assets/abschlussbericht_vergesellschaftung-grosser-wohnungsunternehmen-230627.pdf?ts=1702396025)“ (Abschlussbericht Rn. 114).

Die Mütter und Väter des Grundgesetzes wollten die Wirtschaftsverfassung bewusst offenhalten. Sie schufen die Möglichkeit, die wirtschaftliche und gesellschaftliche Entwicklung durch staatliche oder weitere Formen vergesellschafteter Unternehmen anders zu steuern als über die „[invisible hand “](https://politischeoekonomie.com/der-verdrehte-mr-smith/) des Marktes. Denn die unsichtbare Hand kann die Ökonomie demokratischer Kontrolle entziehen [(dazu ein Überblick).](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/economic-democracy/)

Dazu passt auch der eindeutige Wortlaut. Art. 14 Abs. 3 S. 1 GG bindet bereits die Enteignung nur an eine offene Formel, das „Wohl der Allgemeinheit“, die der Gesetzgeber ausfüllen muss. Art. 15 S. 1 GG formuliert hingegen:

> „Grund und Boden (…) können zum Zwecke der Vergesellschaftung (…) in Gemeineigentum oder in andere Formen der Gemeinwirtschaft überführt werden.“

Auch wenn dahinter praktisch natürlich weitere mittelbare Ziele stehen, setzt die Verfassung Vergesellschaftungen damit als Selbstzweck.

items.body:
# RoboTrack: Point tracking for real-world robotic manipulation

## a]:hidden"> RoboTrack: Point tracking for real-world robotic manipulation

🤖 Models | 📄 Tech Report | 📊 Data | 💻 Code | 🌐 Project Page | 📈 Benchmark

Deploying robots in real-world settings requires reliable perception throughout an interaction. To pick something up, a robot needs to follow the positions of its gripper and the object as they move. In a laboratory, a robot handling a pipette must keep track of its tip while aligning it with the opening of a tube. These tasks become harder when nearby objects clutter the view, the gripper obscures the object being handled, or the viewing angle changes.

One way to help robots follow these interactions is to track specific locations on the objects they handle. This is the idea behind point tracking . Given a location in one video frame, a tracker estimates where that same point appears in subsequent frames, when it is occluded, and where it reappears. These trajectories can help robots learn from demonstrations, plan and guide movements, and model how objects respond to actions.

Robotics systems often rely on off-the-shelf trackers to automatically annotate motion in videos and provide feedback during execution. And current trackers score well on established robotics benchmarks, suggesting they could be ready for wider use in real-world systems. We wanted to see whether those results hold up across the varied scenes, viewpoints, and object interactions robots encounter in practice.

We introduce RoboTrack , a benchmark and training data suite for point tracking in robotic manipulation. RoboTrack-Bench contains 307 human-annotated videos from DROID, Ego-Exo4D, MolmoAct 2 , and EgoVerse, covering different robots and human hands, cluttered scenes, and first- and third-person viewpoints. To study how training data affects tracking in these settings, we also extend MolmoSpaces , Ai2’s simulation ecosystem for robot learning, to generate dense point tracks from simulated robot manipulation trajectories. This pipeline produces RoboTrack-15M , a new synthetic training dataset targeted toward robotic manipulation.

RoboTrack is a benchmark and training data suite for point tracking in robotic manipulation. Built on MolmoSpaces, RoboTrack-15M (top-left) generates point tracks for training. Training with this simulated data improves tracking on real manipulation footage. RoboTrack-Bench (top-right) provides human-annotated point tracks in real manipulation videos.

Our evaluations show that leading trackers score much lower on RoboTrack-Bench than on existing robotics benchmarks. Adding RoboTrack-15M to an existing tracker’s training improves performance on real manipulation video, with gains extending to other tracking benchmarks. We bring these pieces together on a real robot, using the resulting tracker to help guide pipette handling in wet-lab tasks.

Today, we’re releasing both RoboTrack components and two new point tracking models: RoboTracker and RoboTracker-Warp . RoboTracker is a fine-tuned AllTracker model using our techniques and data, while RoboTracker-Warp is trained from CoWTracker. Both models improve average AJ across the three robotics benchmarks compared with their respective released baselines, and RoboTracker-Warp achieves state-of-the-art performance on four out of the five benchmarks we evaluated. We’re also releasing our paper describing the work and evaluation results.

## RoboTrack-Bench: A benchmark for point-tracking in real-world manipulation

RoboTrack-Bench at a glance. Examples from each source dataset (307 clips and 2,522 human-verified tracks in total). MolmoAct 2 and EgoVerse show one embodiment per panel. DROID and EgoExo4D show synchronized ego (top) and exo (bottom) views.

RoboTrack-Bench expands evaluation beyond controlled tabletop setups. It contains 307 videos from DROID, Ego-Exo4D, MolmoAct 2, and EgoVerse, annotated with a total of 2,522 point tracks. The videos show robots and human hands manipulating objects across cluttered scenes and first- and third-person viewpoints. Small objects can be difficult to follow against a busy background, and grippers often hide the objects they hold.

Every track in RoboTrack-Bench is annotated and verified by humans. We ask annotators to prioritize points that move or become occluded rather than the many static background points in robot videos. Following the TAP-Vid annotation approach, annotators use motion estimates to help trace each point through a video. They label each track as belonging to a robot or human body, a manipulated object, or a static object to support future analysis of performance on each group. A second group of annotators checks every track frame by frame before it’s included in our curated data.

To support research in multi-view pointing, correspondence, and tracking, RoboTrack-Bench contains a subset of 33 video pairs that were recorded simultaneously from two cameras. We annotate the same physical points in both views, synchronized across frames, connecting different views of the same interaction.

## Point trackers struggle on real-world manipulation

We evaluated four leading trackers – CoTracker3, BootsTAPNext, AllTracker, and CoWTracker – on RoboTrack-Bench and four other benchmarks: RoboTAP (real-world tabletop manipulation), RGB-Stacking (simulated manipulation), and DAVIS and Kinetics (general video). We report Average Jaccard (AJ), which measures tracking accuracy and visibility prediction; higher scores are better.

RoboTrack-Bench is harder than existing robot benchmarks . Every final tracker we evaluated scores lower on RoboTrack-Bench than on RoboTAP, the only other real-video robotics benchmark. Their score drops by 3.0 to 6.6 AJ. Even the strongest off-the-shelf tracker, CoWTracker, drops from 70.5 AJ on RoboTAP to 63.9 on RoboTrack-Bench. The drop holds across models despite their different architectures and training data, indicating RoboTrack-Bench identifies weaknesses across multiple trackers.

RGB-Stacking rewards synthetic training more than real-world ability. BootsTAPNext is TAPNext trained further on 15 million real videos. That extra real-world training raises its RoboTrack-Bench score by 5.1 AJ (55.1 to 60.2), but lowers its RGB-Stacking score by 9.5 AJ (75.0 to 65.5). RGB-Stacking is built from simulated block stacking, and it ranks the Kubric-only model higher, while real manipulation video ranks them the other way around.

A lead on the older benchmarks does not carry over. CoWTracker leads CoTracker3 by 4.7 AJ on RoboTAP, but by only 2.1 AJ on RoboTrack-Bench. AllTracker’s 2.7-point lead over CoTracker3 on RoboTAP shrinks to 0.8. BootsTAPNext, the strongest model on DAVIS, falls 3.7 AJ behind CoWTracker on RoboTrack-Bench and even trails the Kubric-only AllTracker (60.2 vs 61.4 AJ), despite its training on 15 million real videos.

items.body:
This moon lamp is a hot Christmas tip from designer Phoebe Watts (see below)

Gingko Design

The *New Scientist* Christmas gift guide is assembled by our crack team of science editors and experts. If you’re struggling for gift ideas, you will find unexpected and ingenious suggestions for amateur astronomers and animal and nature lovers, as well as those fond of food, beauty and puzzles. And surely that covers all of us?

Space reporter Leah Crane recommends the science-themed jigsaws from Nervous System

Nervous System

## Puzzlingly beautiful: a science jigsaw

If you’re looking for a quick and easy jigsaw to breeze through while watching holiday movies, Nervous System puzzles probably aren’t for you. But if you want something that’s part puzzle, part work of art, and that will keep you transfixed for hours, they’ll definitely do the trick. Nervous System makes laser-cut wooden puzzles with uniquely shaped pieces and science themes, and they are absolutely beautiful. I’m particularly a fan of their geode puzzles, featuring concentric wiggles of bright colour, including wiggly sides that defy every puzzler’s instinct to start with the edge pieces. For even more of a challenge, they make infinity puzzles that can be assembled and reassembled many different ways – those have no edge pieces at all, and some don’t even have a picture on them! Nervous System also sells absolutely stunning jewellery, lamps and sculptures, but to me the puzzles are the real show-stoppers.

*[Nervous System puzzles](https://n-e-r-v-o-u-s.com/shop/line.php?code=12), from $45* *(£32)*

**Leah Crane**

The CL Companion 8×30 binoculars, as recommended by senior editor Chelsea Whyte

Swarovski Optik

## Zoom in: splashing out on binoculars

The eccentric filmmaker Werner Herzog famously declared that he travels with only a second set of underwear, a map, a toothbrush and a set of binoculars. I don’t travel quite so lightly, but on my next trip, I definitely want to add a pair of nice binos to my baggage. I tested out three sets at varying price levels, taking them down to my favourite spot on my local river and out to my backyard during a clear night with a half-moon overhead. The Nikon Prostaff P3 8×42 binoculars are extremely well balanced and were the most comfortable in my hands. They were particularly well-suited for twilight and brighter. The other Nikon set I tried was the Stabilised 12×25 S, which is much more compact. For my small hands that was fine, and the stabilisation was marvellous at reducing any shaking, both while looking at something fixed like the moon or moving quickly to track an eagle fishing for dinner. The stabilisation requires batteries, so these are probably best – suited to the more prepared adventurer. The stand – out pair was the CL Companion 8×30 from Swarovski Optik. I’ve never seen anything look better than they did through these lenses. They let in an enormous amount of light, making the world look like the brightness has been turned up. And the moon’s craters looked stunningly crisp. For the birdwatcher, wildlife lover or stargazer in your life, these would be a worthwhile, although pretty major, splurge.

[Nikon Prostaff P3 8×42](https://www.nikon.co.uk/en_GB/product/sport-optics/binoculars/prostaff-p3-8x42?srsltid=AYCX9vLs5ncI6HPlo5sBgjGvJMpg-fwoIXxVhpKnBpAwPs2nALhePgBl) *, £159*

[Nikon Stabilised 12×25 S](https://www.nikon.co.uk/en_GB/product/sport-optics/binoculars/stabilized-12x25-BAA951WA?srsltid=AYCX9vIQO-5VpLRqqZa1k-oTWDWJxcoA0T9NmHmL3efXmO7iqSY_WY8e) *, £729*

[CL Companion 8×30 from Swarovski Optik](https://www.swarovskioptik.com/gb/en/outdoor/products/binoculars/clc?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=142839797&gbraid=0AAAAADuZMWsTJfg7C3tdkNR3WEGyQnHhN&gclid=CjwKCAiA5Y_YBhBbEiwAK5Dl7Xg1oKi9uHrtavOf8IoNM3VkIv16Ry6Udy-K-JyvO9EZp_jBA61RRxoChEIQAvD_BwE) *, from £1070*

**Chelsea Whyte**

Podcast editor Rowan Hooper’s tip this Christmas: the Magenta 5 bat detector

Widcare

## Sounds good: a bat detector

Thomas Nagel’s famous 1974 essay, “What is it like to be a bat?”, argued that we can never fully know the experience of being a bat (or any other animal). I have been testing that argument with my fantastic bat detector. The device picks up on the ultrasound frequencies emitted by bats as they fly overhead and converts them into clicks that we can hear. It also displays the frequency of the squeak, and that allows us to identify the species. In my London back garden I get mostly pipistrelles, our smallest bat at just 4 grams. Nagel is right – I don’t know what it is like to fly and catch moths by echolocation. But it is quite thrilling to hear the clicks as a bat swoops past in the dark, and that experience has got me a little closer to appreciating what it is like to be a bat. There are several options available, but I used the Magenta 5 bat detector from Wildcare.

*[Magenta 5 bat detector](https://www.wildcare.co.uk/bat-detector-starter-kit-10-to-bct.html), £105*

**Rowan Hooper**

Editor Catherine de Lange recommends the Timeshifter app

Natee Meepian/Timeshifter

## Time for bed: a jet lag app

If you have a jetsetter in your life, they are probably by definition the kind of person who is tricky to find a gift for. So why not gift them something money can’t buy (well, almost): an end to jet lag? Many moons ago, I was on a journalism fellowship about sleep at Harvard Medical School, when I visited the lab of sleep scientist Steven Lockley. I was fascinated by his experiments, including work he was doing with NASA astronauts, which looked at circadian rhythms, sleep and what happens when our bodies are out of sync with the natural rhythms of the day. Aside from astronauts, many of us who remain earthbound can still feel these effects – especially those who do regular shift work or long-distance travel. What’s more, a body clock that’s out of whack can have serious health consequences.

I followed Lockley’s research closely over the years, and he was generous enough, whenever I travelled back to Boston, to make me a tailored jet-lag plan – when to sleep or nap in the days before and during my flight, as well as when to wear sunglasses and drink caffeine, all based on what time my flight was and the time difference. Fast forward about a decade, and this service is no longer a personal one – Lockley has created an app called Timeshifter, which allows users to plug in their flight details and instantly receive a step-by-step plan to minimise jet lag. There’s a version of the app for shift workers, too.

I recently tried it on a trip to New York, purchasing a one-off plan rather than the subscription, and I can honestly say that I barely felt any jet lag at all – while my husband was falling asleep in his sushi at dinner.

*[Timeshifter app](https://www.timeshifter.com/), $6.99/month or $69.99/year* *(£5.30/month or £53/year)*

**Catherine de Lange**

items.body:
**Die natürlichen Salzunterschiede zwischen Flusswasser und Meerwasser lassen sich zur Stromgewinnung nutzen, doch die berechnete Leistung solcher Osmose-Systeme ist oft zu hoch angesetzt. Ein neues physikalisches Modell zeigt nun, dass nicht nur die Membran, sondern auch die angrenzenden Wasserkanäle berücksichtigt werden müssen. Andernfalls kann die erzielbare Leistung um mehr als das Hundertfache überschätzt werden.**

**Beer-Sheva (Israel).** Wenn sich Flusswasser und Meerwasser mischen, verteilen sich die im Meerwasser gelösten Salze auf ein größeres Wasservolumen, bis die Konzentrationsunterschiede ausgeglichen sind. Ein Teil der bei diesem Vorgang freiwerdenden Energie lässt sich mithilfe von Osmosekraftwerken in Strom umwandeln.

Eine Variante dieser Stromgewinnung ist die sogenannte umgekehrte Elektrodialyse. Dabei trennen elektrisch geladene Membranen die Salz- und Süßwasserseite, wobei ihre winzigen Poren bevorzugt Ionen einer bestimmten elektrischen Ladung passieren lassen. So kann aus dem Unterschied der Salzkonzentrationen eine elektrische Spannung entstehen, mit deren Hilfe sich ein Strom erzeugen lässt.

### Nicht nur die Membran ist entscheidend

Forscher der Ben-Gurion University of the Negev (BGU) um Prof. Yoav Green haben nun untersucht, warum vereinfachte Modelle für solche Systeme oft zu hohe Leistungen vorhersagen. Statt nur den Nanokanal innerhalb einer Membran zu betrachten, beziehen sie in ihre Berechnungen auch die beiden größeren Wasserkanäle ein, die an dessen Enden anschließen.

Das Modell beschreibt, wie sich die Verteilung der Salzionen und das elektrische Potenzial innerhalb des Systems gegenseitig beeinflussen. Um ihre Rechnungen zu überprüfen, haben die Forscher diese mit numerischen Simulationen der zugrunde liegenden physikalischen Gleichungen verglichen. Sie gehen dabei von einer einfachen Salzlösung mit Eigenschaften ähnlich denen von Kaliumchlorid aus und lassen den Ionentransport durch die Bewegung des Wassers unberücksichtigt.

### Zusätzlicher Widerstand bremst die Stromgewinnung

Wie die Berechnungen zeigen, tragen auch die größeren Wasserkanäle zum elektrischen Widerstand bei, obwohl sie deutlich breiter als die Poren der Membran sind. Je nach Geometrie der Kanäle verringert sich die berechnete gewinnbare Leistung durch ihre Berücksichtigung um mehrere Größenordnungen gegenüber der idealisierten Betrachtung der Membran allein.

Auch die Salzkonzentrationen spielen dabei eine entscheidende Rolle. Bei konstantem Verhältnis der beiden Salzkonzentrationen geht die Stromstärke bei kurzgeschlossenen Elektroden im Modell mit Wasserkanälen bei sehr geringen absoluten Salzkonzentrationen gegen null, während das vereinfachte Modell ohne diese Kanäle einen konstanten Grenzwert liefert.

Zudem ergibt sich ein Unterschied zwischen den optimalen Bedingungen für Stromstärke und Leistung. Die Salzkonzentrationen, bei denen sich der Berechnung zufolge die höchste elektrische Leistung erzielen lässt, stimmen nicht genau mit denen für die maximale Kurzschlussstromstärke überein.

### Ansatzpunkte für effizientere Osmose-Systeme

Dem Modell zufolge könnte es sich daher lohnen, die Elektroden möglichst nahe an den Membranen zu platzieren, um den elektrischen Widerstand der Wasserkanäle zu verringern. Die Berechnungen liefern zudem einen Maßstab, an dem sich die experimentell erzielte Leistung unterschiedlicher Membranmaterialien und Anordnungen messen lässt.

Ob die vorgeschlagenen Änderungen auch in technischen Anlagen zu den erhofften Leistungssteigerungen führen, muss noch experimentell untersucht werden. Das Modell könnte aber auch helfen, den Ionentransport bei der Meerwasserentsalzung, in Nanoporen-Sensoren und in biologischen Ionenkanälen besser zu beschreiben.

**Quellen:**

- Originalstudie im Fachmagazin [PRX Energy](https://journals.aps.org/prxenergy/abstract/10.1103/xnd6-226l), doi: 10.1103/xnd6-226l

items.body:
*This is today’s edition of* [The Download](https://forms.technologyreview.com/newsletters/briefing-the-download/?_ga=2.179569122.736533416.1649661040-405833893.1649413289), *our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.*

### Data centers are getting their own natural gas power plants

One of the biggest obstacles to building a data center is getting approval to connect to the grid, a wait that could last as long as a decade. Some developers won’t wait and are instead building their own off-grid gas power plants to fuel the AI boom.

As of October 2026, developers had announced plans for more than 100 such gas power plants at data centers in the US. But bypassing the grid brings its own problems, from worsening climate emissions to potentially higher energy bills for everyone else.

[Find out how the push for gas power could shape the grid—and the climate—for decades](https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/11/24/1149622/data-centers-natural-gas/?utm_source=the_download&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=the_download.unpaid.engagement&utm_term=*%7CSUBCLASS%7C*&utm_content=*%7CDATE:m-d-Y%7C*).

*—Casey Crownhart*

### A legendary philosopher isn’t buying Anthropic’s consciousness argument

Before going public last week, Anthropic named the possibility of AI consciousness as a risk factor for investors, warning that it might introduce new rules to protect its models. But that stance came under fire from an inconvenient source: one of the philosophers who helped shape our understanding of consciousness in the first place.

Thomas Nagel, best known for his essay about what it’s like to be a bat, was blunt. “Here are some of the smartest people on the planet being completely idiotic,” he said. He argued that producing language isn’t enough to establish consciousness. But other philosophers disagree.

[Here’s why language has become central to the debate over conscious AI](https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/11/23/1149569/a-legendary-philosopher-isnt-buying-anthropics-consciousness-argument/?utm_source=the_download&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=the_download.unpaid.engagement&utm_term=*%7CSUBCLASS%7C*&utm_content=*%7CDATE:m-d-Y%7C*).

*—James O’Donnell*

[This story](https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/11/23/1149569/a-legendary-philosopher-isnt-buying-anthropics-consciousness-argument/?utm_source=the_download&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=the_download.unpaid.engagement&utm_term=*%7CSUBCLASS%7C*&utm_content=*%7CDATE:m-d-Y%7C*) **is from The Algorithm, our weekly AI newsletter.** [Sign up](https://forms.technologyreview.com/newsletters/ai-demystified-the-algorithm/?utm_source=the_download&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=the_download.unpaid.engagement&utm_term=*%7CSUBCLASS%7C*&utm_content=*%7CDATE:m-d-Y%7C*) **to receive it in your inbox every Monday.**

**The must-reads**

*I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.*

**1 Huang’s Nvidia return has lifted markets and put Trump under fire** US stock indexes had their best day since April 2025. ([NBC News](https://www.nbcnews.com/business/markets/stocks-rebound-ai-tech-selloff-nvidia-rcna610833))
*+ Trump made up to $15 million on his Nvidia holdings.* ([Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/24/donald-trump-nvidia-stock-jensen-huang-stock-market))
*+ He reportedly saw Huang as vital to US open-weight AI.* ([Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/world/us/trump-saw-nvidias-huang-protector-open-weight-ai-models-sources-say-2026-11-23/) $)
+ *The US has also finally blacklisted Megaspeed.* ([BBC](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cv98xpg5dg5zo))
*+ Open-source advocates wanted Huang back.* ([MIT Technology Review](https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/11/16/1148624/the-open-source-movement-wants-jensen-huang-back/?utm_source=the_download&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=the_download.unpaid.engagement&utm_term=*%7CSUBCLASS%7C*&utm_content=*%7CDATE:m-d-Y%7C*))

**2 COP31’s collapse has revived calls to end the consensus rule** It effectively lets any single country block a deal. ([Axios](https://www.axios.com/2026/11/23/un-climate-talks-meltdown-aftermath))
*+ But changing the rule would itself require consensus.* ([Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/nov/23/failure-cop31-calls-urgent-reform-un-climate-summits))
*+ Rare wins at the talks included a new electrification pledge.* ([Nature](https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-026-03827-0) $)
*+ Our climate models have a major blind spot.* ([MIT Technology Review](https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/10/29/1147735/climate-models-blind-spot/?utm_source=the_download&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=the_download.unpaid.engagement&utm_term=*%7CSUBCLASS%7C*&utm_content=*%7CDATE:m-d-Y%7C*))

**3 Russia could launch a nuclear-armed satellite as soon as next month** The warning comes from intelligence shared among Nato allies. ([BBC](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9x2er1ry2mzo))
*+ Such a weapon could destroy thousands of satellites at once.* ([FT](https://www.ft.com/content/dd00f616-1fef-4a26-a5f9-2b1bf83cc489) $)
*+ The Kremlin has dismissed the claims as propaganda.* ([Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/23/russia-nuclear-weapons-space-german-intelligence))

**4 Google wants to make a 24/7 AI TV channel starring you** Its new patent imagines shows and ads built around each viewer. ([404 Media](https://www.404media.co/google-wants-to-make-a-24-7-ai-tv-channel-youll-be-the-main-character/))
*+ They would be generated from your viewing history.* ([Gizmodo](https://gizmodo.com/google-wants-to-make-ai-tv-shows-starring-you-2000844299))

**5 Oregon and Virginia are suing SpaceX over Grok’s sexualized images** Grok’s “spicy mode” produced explicit images of women and children. ([NYT](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/23/technology/spacex-lawsuit-ai-sexualized-images.html) $)
*+ Deepfake porn is stealing people’s bodies.* ([MIT Technology Review](https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/05/14/1137161/ai-porn-nonconsensual-deepfakes-takedown-piracy-copyright/?utm_source=the_download&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=the_download.unpaid.engagement&utm_term=*%7CSUBCLASS%7C*&utm_content=*%7CDATE:m-d-Y%7C*))

**6 Prosecutors say an ex-OpenAI engineer bugged company meetings** One appears to have involved a foreign government. ([Bloomberg](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-23/openai-staffer-likely-captured-secrets-on-hidden-bug-us-says) $)

**7 Signal has joined banks and airlines in blocking AI agents**
It’s urging Apple, Google, and Microsoft to give apps more control. ([CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/24/signal-airlines-banks-ai-limit.html))
*+ AI agents are not your “coworkers.”* ([MIT Technology Review](https://www.technologyreview.com/2026/06/29/1139849/ai-agents-are-not-your-coworkers/?utm_source=the_download&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=the_download.unpaid.engagement&utm_term=*%7CSUBCLASS%7C*&utm_content=*%7CDATE:m-d-Y%7C*))

items.body: Ischaemic disease presents a significant challenge in medical science due to its widespread manifestations in the body and its tendency to only become overt in its late stages, beyond where current intervention methods are effective. Diseases such as coronary heart disease and peripheral artery disease (PAD) represent leading causes of death and are detrimental to quality of life. Focussing on the latter, PAD incurs an amputation rate of around 25%, largely owing to microvascular disease that prevents tissue recovery even after revascularisation. Current methods for investigating PAD either cannot chart specific vascular determinants, such as with in vivo imaging, or deform and remove subjects from longitudinal studies, such as with ex vivo tissue sampling. Presented to aid live research, computational modelling can collate information and build models of ischaemia using available information and provide a reasonable approximation of the disease’s chronology and thus support understanding and advance research of PAD. Proposed here, is a 3D in silico model of ischaemic disease in the limb using a system of purpose-built platforms. Starting with a real micro-computed tomography image of the murine hindlimb, a realistic vessel bed was generated using vascular graphing software, ViGiL. From here, the model was realised in a defined pressure gradient via flow-modelling software, numPTI. With the base model of lower limb arteries, collateral vasculature was generated throughout the vessel space. This provides a bypass system for adaptation post-ischaemia. Upon ischaemic induction, the collateral bed responds to the loss of flow and successfully adapted to recover flow with similar density and distribution of diameters in collateral arterioles (p>> 0.05). Moreover, a satisfactory flow recovery of 50% was achieved after 6 days, showing that the model can reflect the specific vascular environment in which disease is incited. The proceeds of this study lay the groundwork for truly realistic ischaemic models including moving towards a predictive model than can signify when and where key indicators of PAD manifest.

items.body:
[Janet Flanner-Solita Solano papers](https://www.loc.gov/pictures/item/95507085/), Library of Congress. Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Georges_Gurdjieff.JPG).

My first mistake was to draw a connection. The flyers appeared all at once over the telephone poles of my neighborhood in the East Bay, with contact info provided on the kind of tear-away strips more typical of a HELP WANTED or FOR SALE notice, only here the subject read: AN INTRODUCTORY DISCUSSION: G. I. GURDJIEFF. The accompanying copy spoke of spiritual methods and cosmic scale; the words seemed to promise some tremendous synthesis between part and whole, spirit and matter, individual and collective. More prosaically, they advertised a series of public meetings to take place in Berkeley. My second mistake, I think, was to write an email expressing interest.

Where had I heard the name Gurdjieff? The question took me several minutes of standing in front of the poster to answer. I must have missed the crossing signal before remembering with a start that the life’s work of the Russian-born mystic, teacher, sacred choreographer, and occasional composer of piano music [George Ivanovich Gurdjieff](https://www.theparisreview.org/blog/2020/10/22/the-lesbian-partnership-that-changed-literature/) had—for me at least—everything to do with a small, neglected corner in the [short fiction](https://www.theparisreview.org/authors/4476/joy-williams) of [Joy Williams](https://www.theparisreview.org/authors/4476/joy-williams).

Photograph by Drew Dickerson.

“Gurdjieff in the Sunshine State” appears in Williams’s 1990 book *Escapes,* but is among the very few stories not to make it into her nearly comprehensive collection *The Visiting Privilege*, published twenty-five years later. I have never understood the logic behind its exclusion any more than I can claim to understand the story itself—in which G. astral projects to Florida, where, as a specter, he observes a roller rink, drinks a Tab, and chats briefly with what may be the ghost of Katherine Mansfield. By virtue of being disincluded from Williams’s collected work, this story of an esotericist feels in turn to have become itself esoteric, tucked away and little read. Even Williams’s own mentions of the story seemed charged with the force of mystery. “There is a Gurdjieff story in Escapes,” she wrote to her editor, the late Gary Fisketjon, in 2011. “I was going to write a whole mess of these stories on Gurdjieff but haven’t, you’re probably happy to know.”

The historical Gurdjieff was no stranger to hermetic situations. He traveled widely during the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. In the course of his itinerary between the Mediterranean and southwest Asia, he absorbed the teachings that would result in his syncretistic blend of Sufi, Hindu, Zen, and Christian tendencies. But the articulation of his thought in a system and set of practices later known as the Fourth Way would come to be passed between generations, making Gurdjieff one of the most influential figures in what we today call the New Age Movement.

Some of this biographical picture was imparted at the first public meeting I attended in the auxiliary room of a Unitarian Universalists Fellowship Hall. For practical purposes the scene might have been lifted straight out of the fiction of Williams herself—from “The Country,” say, in which a group of denominationally wide-ranging seekers meet weekly “in one of the many, many rooms” of an Episcopal church to discuss the question: “Why Are We Here?”

I took my seat in a circle of folding chairs under a framed black-and-white portrait of Gurdjieff that someone had arrived early to hang. It was the first time I’d seen a picture of him. His eyes were enormous. Introductory talk proceeded gnomically. Most present seemed to have been steeped in one or another Gurdjieff-adjacent current. All were capable of trading words as tokens in a kind of code I had trouble grasping.

“I was brought here out of interest in the work of Maurice Nicoll.”

“Yes, well. Nicoll certainly had a lot to say, didn’t he? Maybe he ran out of things to say by the time of his fifth book. You should read Ouspensky.”

“I’m wary of Ouspensky. Remember what Gurdjieff told him: if you understood half of what you know, you’d be my teacher.”

Why were we there? Newcomers were encouraged to share our answers to this question. I owned up to my literary detective work in tracking down this reference of Williams’s, so marginal in her body of work as to be secretive. I also said that I wanted to enjoy a closer relationship to [God](https://www.theparisreview.org/blog/2013/06/03/3-stories-of-god/), which was true.

Motivations varied. One woman mentioned a near-death experience several months ago that convinced her of the need for greater spiritual attunement. Another spoke about how, after a childhood spent being told to shut up, she was now emboldened to want to find her voice. Someone else detailed a fairly fresh LSD episode before producing a decorative knife that he told us had been forged from the metal of an authentic meteorite. The ceremonial blade looked no shorter than six inches.

Georges Gurdjieff, 1930. [Time](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Time_-_1930.03.24_-_62_-_Georges_Gurdjieff.png), Public domain, via [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Time_-_1930.03.24_-_62_-_Georges_Gurdjieff.png).

*Experience* certainly struck me as a keyword in the group’s talk, in the sense of a spiritual experience’s spontaneous flash of insight that leaves one wholly changed. *Vibration*, too, was in frequent currency. *Self-observation*. *Self-knowledge. Self-remembering.* One first-time visitor’s chancing upon the term *wish* was met with a gasp. The wish, it seemed, was fundamental. The lights were dimmed. The scent of patchouli was strong. Boredom was my prevailing attitude—shot through at odd intervals with the numinous feeling that somehow anything at all might be possible.

Others seemed less impressed. An attendee identifying himself as a veteran of workshops in human development at the Esalen Institute complained, not without cause, that we’d certainly heard the name Gurdjieff plenty. But what did he teach in specific terms? What did he promise? We’d been told Gurdjieff had answers. I felt my own small disappointment with the session, mired in personal anecdote, without much in the way of a survey of Gurdjieff’s system.

“You’re right to ask,” said one man. “Gurdjieff works by allegory. He says of his writing in *All and Everything*: ‘I bury the bone so deep that the dogs have to scratch for it.’”

…

## The Debt Trap (permalink)

[↗ Primärquelle: pluralistic.net](https://pluralistic.net/2026/11/23/grasshoppers-v-ants/#)

Smoking is very stupid. I was a smoker for 17 years, from ages 13-30. I was very stupid to start smoking. That stupidity only came into sharper focus a few years ago, when I got a cancer diagnosis (don't worry, I am now cancer-free):

[https://pluralistic.net/2024/11/05/carcinoma-angels/#squeaky-nail](https://pluralistic.net/2024/11/05/carcinoma-angels/#squeaky-nail)

In my defense, I'll point out that I was just a kid when I started, but also, smoking belongs to a class of pernicious problems whose insidiousness is rooted in the distance between their causes and effects:

[https://pluralistic.net/2021/06/03/i-quit/](https://pluralistic.net/2021/06/03/i-quit/)

I've often said that if a little tumor had sprouted immediately after I took my first puff, I never would have taken a second one. Now that I've actually had the experience of being told that I have a tumor, I can say *definitively* that I would not have taken that second puff. An economist would tell you that I was engaged in "hyperbolic discounting": underpricing a future cost and overvaluing a present pleasure:

[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperbolic_discounting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperbolic_discounting)

But I don't think that tells the whole story. Sure, I was engaged in hyperbolic discounting, but *why* was I doing that? What was it about smoking (as opposed to, say, French-kissing light-sockets) that led me to apply a hyperbolic discount to the costs of smoking? I say it was the attenuated relationship between cause and effect. It's not just that we undervalue the price of smoking: it's that we struggle to arrive at a correct price for smoking in the moment, because the intellectual knowledge of cancer statistics is in no way comparable to the visceral experience of a cancer diagnosis. Estimating the "cost" (emotional, physiological, monetary) of a cancer diagnosis is *hard*, especially if you're young and have had the good fortune of a life untouched by close contact with agonizing illness and death.

The point I'm making is that the discount isn't just hyperbolic, it's hyperbolic *because* it relies so much upon guesswork, without comparable experiences to anchor your estimate.

What's more, it's this same *attenuated causality* (in which cause is separated from effect by so much time and space) that allowed the tobacco industry to sow so much profitable doubt about the connection between smoking and cancer. Sure, *some* of the policymakers who let Big Tobacco off the hook were doubtlessly in their pocket, reliant on campaign contributions or beholden to a party that was in some queasy, cozy relationship with these death merchants. But the reason Big Tobacco was able ( *is* able) to get away with killing us for so many decades is that you don't get a tumor with each puff.

I believe that *most* of the policymakers who reasoned their way into doubting the connection between smoking and cancer were ensnared by this attenuated causality. They might have had low morals and low intellect, but the factor that made them such easy marks for Big Tobacco's death-hustlers was this wide, long gap between cause and effect.

This cuts both ways: if you're a policymaker of low intellect and morals, you can rig your policies to put their consequences a long way off in the future, which might give you time to escape to a lucrative private-sector career with the industrial interests who benefited from your chicanery. Or (if you're a Mitch McConnell-adjacent flesh-eating ghoul who plans to die only after centuries in office, chin red and slick with the heartblood of the innocent), you can put so much time and space between your fuckery and the ruin it brings that the voting public fails to connect your actions with the consequences. After all, no one ever lost money betting against the American public's object permanence.

For example, Trump's Big Bill was designed to make its deepest cuts – to Medicaid, rural hospitals, the increased tax-load on workers to advantage their bosses – *after* the midterm elections. The cynical reasoning isn't hard to follow: We'll just tell voters that all the bad things they've been told about the coming cuts are Fake News, and then, after the cuts arrive, blame their post-midterm misery on Biden, communists, trans people, immigrants, and the phases of the moon.

This cheap trick may be deplorable, but you should also save some anger for politicians who enact *good* policies but refuse to take account of this principle. Take Biden's 2021 plan to lower prescription drug prices. This started off as a rule that would end the longstanding, outrageous policy that bans Medicare/Medicaid from negotiating with pharma companies. Yes, you read that right: when Uncle Sucker buys drugs from Big Pharma, the government just asks the pharma companies how much public money they'd like, and then the USA writes the companies a check for whatever sum they name, no questions asked. That's why the US pays 300% more than any other advanced nation for its drugs.

…

items.body:
When I moved from the San Francisco Bay Area to a small, rural town in Vermont, I wanted to find a way to contribute to the local community. Knowing there was a significant senior population here, I reached out to the town librarian with hopes of helping elders share their stories.

The local historical society took interest in this idea, which led to an exhibit at the 159-year-old Tunbridge World’s Fair, and a book series entitled *Folk Life: Tunbridge Oral Histories*. The first two print runs sold out. The second collection of stories has just been published, and people are already asking who will be featured in the third.

What is it about life stories that strikes such a universal chord? And why is it important—and even imperative—to share our stories with others? I interviewed oral historians, teachers, and a digital storyteller to discover more about why the age-old tradition of recording oral histories continues to make such a significant impact for individuals and communities.

## Fostering connections and reflection

Storytelling is, according to scientific research, a biological shortcut to human connection. [Uri Hasson](https://blog.ted.com/what-happens-in-the-brain-when-we-hear-stories-uri-hasson-at-ted2016/) and fellow researchers at Princeton University discovered that the brains of the storyteller and listener physically sync up while a story is being told, promoting social connection, trust, and empathy.

The more emotionally affecting the story is, the stronger this connection becomes. As emotions and tension rise, hormones are released, including oxytocin, the “bonding hormone”; dopamine, which sharpens focus; and cortisol, which promotes attention and alertness as conflicts in the story arise. These hormonal responses enhance both the listener’s memory and connection to the storyteller.

For Erin Barnaby, a digital storyteller and 11th-generation Tunbridge native, oral histories create a connection not only to people, but also time and place. “My dad recently sold his house to my uncle, a house that he built on land that my grandfather had given to him. I love to hear him tell stories about the shifting of the land, from sheep farms to dairy farms and the shift from open pastures to forests.”

Even when the subject matter might not be instantly relatable, the process of listening to another’s stories still creates a profound interpersonal connection. Esther Ehrlich, who worked at [UC Berkeley’s Oral History Center](https://www.lib.berkeley.edu/visit/bancroft/oral-history-center) for six years before launching an oral history business of her own, experienced this sense of connection firsthand:

> I was assigned an interview with a former medical malpractice insurance guy, which initially didn’t interest me at all. And then lo and behold, after interviewing this man, I found him absolutely fascinating. What I came to discover was that by the time we were done, or even partway in, I came to love every single person I interviewed. I would feel connected to them and them to me.

## Providing unique perspectives

From that biological and psychological basis, oral histories make a critical social contribution.

According to the [Oral History Association](https://oralhistory.org/), “oral history is the oldest type of historical inquiry, stemming from the oral traditions of myriad cultures across the globe, predating even the written word.” These personal stories expand upon the narratives of history books, allowing people from varied walks of life to share their unfiltered experiences and perspectives. Indeed, many works by trained historians rely on oral histories.

The founders of [Voice of Witness](https://voiceofwitness.org/), a nonprofit dedicated to advancing human rights by amplifying unheard voices, believe that oral history “can democratize history, contribute to narrative change, and illuminate issues and events in a profoundly powerful way.” Enabling individuals to safely share their stories opens people’s minds to fresh perspectives and vantage points.

While oral histories are limited to an individuals’ memories and are by nature subjective, they remain incredibly valuable in their ability to paint a portrait of time and place. Plus, their narrative-driven format brings history to life in a more memorable way than date- and fact-focused textbooks.

Helen Marks, a former history teacher who has spoken to thousands of students about her experience as a hidden child in Belgium during World War II, has observed that when a person shares their stories, it brings that part of history to life:

> I am among the few surviving hidden children who are willing and able to talk about their experiences in the Holocaust. Reading numbers on a page does not create the same impact as someone standing or sitting in front of you describing a moment that was frightening or was so foreign they didn’t know what to do.... I think that when you connect a face, no matter what the face looks like, you get a wholly different reaction than when you read a page full of facts.

## Leaving a legacy

Throughout the interviews I conducted for *Folk Life*, the importance of leaving a meaningful legacy was a common theme. “That’s the reason we share our stories,” says Marsha Higgins, a history teacher for nearly 40 years. “It makes us feel like we matter.”

Higgins taught students to create personal narratives from a young age. Decades later, former students still express their thanks for her guidance in teaching them the importance of recording their experiences.

“I encouraged students to write down things that happened to them. It’s helpful to know at the time, you’re creating chapters in your life, that your story is just as interesting as anybody else’s.”

Like Marks, Higgins grew up around immigrants from Europe. “And they all had stories,” she says. “Whenever we got together, somebody would tell me a story. How do you make conversation without one? It’s just so much a part of who we are.”

“I think everyone wants to know that they have made a positive difference,” says Marks. “That they did some good, that their being here wasn’t just a fleeting moment of nothingness, but that they contributed something. They reacted to something. They gave something. So when you tell stories, that’s where you learn about people and what they value.”

## Gaining newfound awareness

Neal Allen, a coach and author (most recently of *Good Writing: 36 Ways to Improve Your Sentences* with his wife Anne Lamott), spent several years as a hospice volunteer. During that time, he helped a number of people share and record their stories.

“Every week I had one or two clients who were dying, and I spent time fluffing their pillows, listening to their stories and how they approach death. The funny thing is we were always asked, ‘Oh, isn’t that hard?’ It was quite the opposite. It was really quite extraordinary.”

items.body:
While my husband kept his eye on the light plastic kickball wavering indecisively in the air above, his arms upraised to catch it for the out, his feet scuttled side-to-side on the bumpy field, as he tried to position himself perfectly. It was his birthday, and we were playing a celebratory game with our extended family at his parents’ house an hour away from ours. After triumphantly catching the ball, he collapsed abruptly to the ground and, when we rushed over, he immediately told me to take him to the ER because he knew a bone had broken. I hate to admit that one of the first things I looked at—silently, selfishly—was which leg was hurt.

Right leg. Driving leg. At that moment, I knew that I was in for what my therapist friend would later call a “growth opportunity.”

Up until that point, my husband had done all of the driving for our family of four, us and our 13-year-old twins; I pinch-hit only when he went out of town. Living previously in Beijing, Brooklyn, and then downtown Boston had obviated most any need to drive, and my skills were basic anyhow, as my immigrant parents had severely limited my mobility as a suburban teenager. In the decade since moving to Cambridge and buying a car, my slight fear of being behind the wheel had deepened into a full-on phobia. The road seemed increasingly like a slippery sheet of ice, unpredictable and dangerous, and I clung to public transit, which is better in Boston than in most American cities though far from comprehensive.

I had always maintained that being terrified to drive in greater Boston was a rational response. Based on accident statistics, Allstate has ranked Boston as America’s worst city for drivers for eleven straight years. There is the running of red lights, the “banging” of “ueys,” the weaving through former-cow-path streets, the traffic jams, the rush hour daredevilry, the cutting off, the honking, the flicking off, the jaywalking, the lawless bicycling, the urgency, the rage, the tailgating. Indeed, it was this last behavior that set me off more than any other. I can picture it now: the heat in my rearview mirror, the voice inside my head that said, *You’re going too fuckin’ slow, you’re a pathetic driver, you need to get out of my way and off the road, you don’t deserve to be here—oh look, an Asian woman, of course.*

Unfortunately, the porous emotional boundaries that had served me well to date as a writer were terrible for a driver. Every time I got behind the wheel, I felt squeezed by the time-is-money capitalist python and crushed down by the country’s sexism and racism; the entire experience of being seen, judged, and honked at was psychologically harrowing. My cringing fear translated into a self-abasing timidity, and I let every single person who wanted to cut in front of me cut. Flash, flash; flash, flash.

After the ER trip that put my husband’s broken fibula in a temporary cast, I managed to pilot the car the hour home on the highway. After his surgery, he was ordered to keep weight off the foot for at least a month, and I prepared to take over the driving. Weekend drum and tennis lessons, weeknight capoeira lessons. I was finally going to learn to drive in Boston.

My instinct on my first drive was to flick loving-kindness at all the other drivers around me as I drove. *May you be happy—and you—and you—and you—and you.* This was a practice I’ve had on and off for the past two decades, ever since I sat my first weeklong silent retreat at the Insight Meditation Society, a loving-kindness focused program led by vipassana teacher Michele McDonald, who counseled us to take a light approach. If you’re sitting on the subway, you can just flick [metta](https://tricycle.org/magazine/metta-practice/) quickly at people, one by one, she said. You don’t have to make it something big and serious. I was living in New York at the time, and it was easy to feel barricaded or hostile or shrunken, especially when crammed into the tin can of the subway with strangers, and flicking loving-kindness at fellow riders shifted something in me—it expanded me, softened me, softened the space between me and others, woke me to the present. When I did the same while driving, it worked similarly, creating a radiant force field through which all the cars moved and related to one another. I could impute positive intentions to drivers I’d read earlier as only erratic, selfish, or terrifying. Even when confronted with impatience and rage, through the practice I learned that those feelings did not have to become mine. Each time I drove, my mind grew quieter.

Of all of the categories of people one can send loving-kindness to (self, benefactor, friend, neutral, difficult), I’ve always found the self the hardest, or at least I’ve found it hard to receive my own good intentions, but in this time of forced growth, I had to try. I returned to the [Metta Bhavana](https://dharmaseed.org/talks/3512/): *May I be safe, may I be peaceful.* In this mindset, when I had to make a turn, I realized that I didn’t have to peel out in front of oncoming traffic in a death-defying manner, no matter what the person behind me insisted. I could simply wait until there was a gap in traffic or someone let me go. And they did. There’s actually a lot of kindness out on the roads, in moments people do seem to understand that we’re suffering through this abominable system together and a little kindness can shift the whole system. These kindnesses, and my own, enabled me to enter the slipstream of humanity as an equal. Before, I used to flash my lights, urging others to turn out of terror, but slowly and through practice, I began to do it mainly to be part of the web of the road. I’ve become more confident about driving exactly how I want; after all, these roads are my roads too. And I admit that on some days I do hit the gas instead of flashing my lights because there are places I need to get to on time too.

…

items.body:
*A trained car mechanic who plays 150 BPM trance in a shirt and tie, and checks his tracks by dancing around his room. Meet Davyboi*.

In recent years, trance and its faster, more euphoric relatives have found a new generation of dancers across Europe. Among the DJs who have built a following on the back of that revival is Davyboi, a Munich-based DJ and producer with Polish roots. His sets usually sit between 148 and 155 BPM and draw on trance, eurodance, and hard house in equal measure.

Going out in a city where hard techno dominated, he wanted more melody and uplift than most nights offered, so he began playing the records he wanted to hear himself. That approach, delivered in his trademark shirt and tie, has since taken him to Gotec, Rotterdam Rave, and Into The Woods Festival.

We asked him to introduce himself for Introducing, our series on up-and-coming producers and DJs, many of whom have gone on to much bigger things.

## Who are you?

I’m Davyboi, a DJ and producer. I love fast music, big melodies and dancing just as much as the people in front of me. You’ll usually find me behind the decks wearing a shirt and tie.

## Where are you from?

I’m from Munich, Germany, with Polish roots.

## What do you sound like?

Mostly trance and eurodance, but I also love groove, gabber and makina. It’s fast and energetic, with plenty of melodies and vocals. I want people to dance, sing along and have a good time together.

"Your problems are someone else’s dreams"

## Why should we follow what you’re doing?

If you love dancing and getting a bit carried away with your friends, I think we’ll get along. That’s what I enjoy most about a night out, and it’s the feeling I want to share when I play. I’ve also got plenty of new music on the way that I’m excited for people to hear.

## Which of your tracks sums you up? Why?

“Discotheque,” my collaboration with Mika Heggemann. It’s a good introduction to the energy I like bringing to my sets. When I make music, I always ask myself whether I’d enjoy dancing to it if someone else played it. That’s a big part of why I chose this one.

## What have you got coming out in the near future?

My remix of BUNT.’s “I Need You” is coming, and I’ve been busy working on more tracks. There are a lot of ideas I’m excited about, but I want to give each release a little time before moving on to the next.

[quote align=right text="I don’t really feel like I’ve had to give anything up completely."]

## Who or what is your biggest influence, and why?

A lot of it comes from being on the dancefloor myself. Some nights really stay with you, especially when a DJ plays something you weren’t expecting, and it completely changes your mood. I still think about those experiences when I’m choosing music. I know how much a good night can mean to someone.

## How did you get into DJing OR producing to begin with?

I was going out a lot in Munich, where hard techno was very present. I enjoyed the energy, but I wanted to hear more melodies and uplifting tracks too. Eventually, I started putting together the kind of music I wanted to hear on a night out. Coming from the crowd still influences how I play today.

## What are three things on your studio shopping list?

A monitor, a height-adjustable desk and [Nexus](https://refx.com/nexus/) to use in [Ableton](https://www.ableton.com/shop/live/?affiliate=F4nlA735). A few things to make working on music a bit more comfortable and give me some new sounds to play with.

### Who or what have you sacrificed for your art?

I don’t really feel like I’ve had to give anything up completely. It’s more that fitting everything in has become harder. Seeing my friends in Munich takes more planning now that I’m away so often. I still want to make time for them, even when things get busy.

## What’s been your favourite place to play so far?

[Thuishaven](https://thuishaven.nl/) is a favourite. I really love playing for Dutch crowds, and that’s a place I’m always happy to come back to.

## Where can we hear your music?

Mostly on [SoundCloud](https://soundcloud.com/davyboii), where you can find my tracks and mixes. My releases are also on Spotify, Apple Music and the other usual platforms.

## What one song would feature on the soundtrack to your life?

“Tokyo Drift” by Teriyaki Boyz. I trained as a car mechanic and got into tuning cars quite early. That song reminds me of that time, which I look back on really fondly. It always puts me in a good mood.

## What motivates you?

Knowing that people have made an effort to come and see me. Some bring their friends, some travel quite far, and some have been looking forward to that night for a while. I really appreciate that. Seeing them enjoy themselves makes me want to keep improving and give them a reason to come back.

## Tell us an interesting fact about yourself.

I get up and dance to my tracks after working on them. It helps me hear things differently. Sometimes a section seems fine while I’m sitting at the laptop, but when I’m moving to it, I realise it goes on too long. So dancing around my room is actually part of the process.

## Complete this sentence: At heart I’m just a…

…raver who ended up behind the decks.

## What’s the best bit of advice you’ve received?

“Your problems are someone else’s dreams.” I take it as a reminder to appreciate what I get to do. It helps me keep some perspective.

## Where will you be in five years’ time?

I’d love to reach more people with my music and make something that means something to them, whether it helps them through a difficult day or becomes a song they share with their friends. Knowing that something I made could become a small part of someone’s life would mean a lot to me.

**Davyboi and DJ Cringey "Naughty" is out now. [Listen on Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/track/67MB3IlBzSxG6Q9SGh7qXF?si=3fcc2aea3dfb4851). Buy on Bandcamp.**

**Find Davyboi on [Instagram.](https://www.instagram.com/iamdavyboi/?hl=en)**

items.body:
For most of scientific history, women who made contributions to various fields have been sidelined or ignored in favor of male colleagues, who reaped fame, professional recognition, and cash rewards that come with prestigious prizes like the Nobel. Cornell historian of science [Margaret Rossiter](https://sts.cornell.edu/margaret-rossiter) coined[the term “The Matilda Effect”](https://www.openculture.com/2025/12/matilda-effect.html) to describe sexist bias in the sciences. Rossiter’s work and popular reappraisals like book-turned-film *[Hidden Figures](https://amzn.to/2HTG1jS) * have inspired other women in academia to search for forgotten female scientists, and to find them, literally, [in footnotes](https://www.openculture.com/2019/02/womens-hidden-contributions-to-modern-science-get-revealed-by-new-study.html).

When systematic discrimination limits opportunities for any group, those who do receive recognition, the exceptions to the rule, must often be truly exceptional to succeed. There has been little doubt, both in her lifetime and in the many decades afterward, that Marie Curie was such a person. Although forced to study science in secret at a clandestine “[Floating University](https://www.openculture.com/2016/07/marie-curie-attended-a-secret-underground-flying-university-when-poland-blocked-her-other-women-from-advancing-their-education.html)” in her native Poland—since the universities refused to admit women—Curie (born Marie Salomea Sklodowska in 1867) would achieve such renown in her field that she was awarded not one, but two Nobel Prizes.

Curie and her husband Pierre shared the[Nobel Prize](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1903/summary/) [in Physics](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1903/summary/) with Antoine Henri Becquerel, discoverer of radioactivity, in 1903. The second prize, in Chemistry, was hers alone in 1911, “in recognition of her services to the advancement of chemistry by the discovery of the elements radium and polonium, by the isolation of radium and the study of the nature and compounds of this remarkable element.” Curie was not only the first woman to win a Nobel, but she was also the first person to win twice, and the only person to win in two different sciences.

These are but a handful of achievements in a string of firsts for Curie: denied positions in Poland, she earned a Ph.D. in France, awarded the degree in 1903 by the [Sorbonne](https://www.sorbonne-universite.fr/en/university/history-and-heritage/history), the same year she won her first Nobel. “Her examiners,” notes the site [Famous Scientists](https://www.famousscientists.org/marie-curie/), “were of the view that she had made the greatest contribution to science ever found in a Ph.D. thesis.” Three years later, after Pierre was killed in an accident, Marie was offered his professorship and became the first female professor at the University of Paris.

Curie succeeded not in the absence of, but in spite of the sexist obstacles placed in her path at nearly every stage in her career. After she received her doctorate, the Curies were invited to the Royal Institution in London. Only Pierre was permitted to speak. That same year, the Nobel Committee decided to honor only her husband and Becquerel. The Academy relented when Pierre protested. Curie fell victim to a wave of xenophobia and anti-Semitism (though she was not Jewish) that swept through France in the 1900s, most famously in the so-called “Dreyfus Affair.”

In 1911, the year of her second Nobel, Curie was passed over for membership in the [French Academy of Sciences](https://www.academie-sciences.fr/en/). It would take another 51 years before the first woman, [Marguerite Perey,](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marguerite_Perey) a former doctoral student of Curie, would be elected to that body. That same year, Curie was persecuted relentlessly by the French press, the public, and her scientific rivals after it was revealed that she had had a brief affair with physicist Paul Langevin, one of Pierre Curie’s former students.

But no matter how many men in positions of power wanted to deter Curie, there always seemed to be more [influential scientists](https://www.openculture.com/2017/12/read-the-dont-let-the-bastards-get-you-down-letter-that-albert-einstein-sent-to-marie-curie-during-a-time-of-personal-crisis-1911.html) and politicians who recognized the supreme value of her work and the need to help her continue it. After her second Nobel Prize, her native country finally recognized her with the offer to direct her own laboratory in Warsaw. Curie turned it down to focus on directing the Curie Laboratory in the Radium Institute of the University of Paris, which she founded in 1914, a major achievement and, again, only a small part of her legacy.

Curie is known, of course, foremost for her exceptional scientific work, but also for opening doors for women in science all over the world, though much of that door-opening may only have happened decades after her death in 1934, and much of it hasn’t happened at all yet. Incidentally, in the following year, the Curies’ daughter Irène Joliot-Curie and her husband Frédéric Joliot-Curie were jointly awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Since then, only seven other women have claimed that honor, and [only five women, including Marie Curie, have won the Prize in physics](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/are-the-nobel-prizes-missing-female-scientists/?redirect=1), out of 230 winners total.

There may be nothing yet like gender parity in the sciences, but those who know where to look can find the names of dozens of women scientists running women-owned companies, women-founded research institutes and academic departments, and, like the famous Curies, making [major contributions to chemistry](https://www.thoughtco.com/famous-women-in-chemistry-609453). Perhaps not long from now, many of those exceptional scientists will be as well-known and widely celebrated as Marie Curie.

Note: An earlier version of this post appeared on our site in 2019.

items.subtitle: Neue Technologien können Sicherheitsrisiken bergen, zugleich werden ihre Gefahren mitunter überschätzt.
