items.body:
arXiv:2611.31329v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: Attribute reduction in incomplete information systems is difficult because missing values break the equivalence-class structure of rough set theory. We propose the Conservative Overlap Fuzzy Rough Set (COFRS) model. Each object is described by its set of present attributes. The similarity of two objects is a weighted overlap on the attributes present in both, divided by the fixed number of attributes |A| instead of the size of their union, so missing values are penalised globally and are not matched as wildcards. From this similarity we define a soft dependency degree based on weighted granule consistency, and we search for reducts by greedy backward elimination in O(|U|^2 |A|^2) time. We show that the relation is symmetric and non-reflexive, that the dependency degree is not monotone, and we give a sufficient condition under which monotonicity holds. On 11 UCI benchmarks with missing rates from 0.15% to 20.46%, COFRS gives the smallest reducts on average (4.1 attributes, against 5.0-11.2 for Tolerance-RS, a range-threshold variant Tol-RS_tau, Zhou-RS and the min-aggregation variant COFRS-min). The difference is significant against Tol-RS_tau, Zhou-RS and COFRS-min (Holm-adjusted Wilcoxon p<0.01) but not against Tolerance-RS (p=0.56), and it is small against the Jensen-Shen selector (adjusted p=0.084). At equal reduct size, COFRS selects more informative attributes than random subsets. With a kNN classifier the methods do not differ significantly in accuracy, F1 or G-mean; with an RBF-SVM they do, and COFRS ranks last. The gain is therefore compactness, not predictive accuracy.

items.body:
Within a few hours of each other ([timeline](https://x.com/eliebakouch/status/2123804091297976653)), two mathematicians claimed independent proofs of the Riemann Hypothesis, the most famous open problem in mathematics ([Scientific American](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/dueling-claims-of-riemann-hypothesis-proofs-emerge/)).

- Levent Alpöge of Anthropic first made his Claude-driven proof in a [note](https://alpo.ge/remark.pdf) released with Lean code (1.3GB worth, ~250,000 page equivalent) rather than a full paper. [Elliot Glazer](https://x.com/ElliotGlazer/status/2123792743503933774) confirms that the formalized statement is GRH and puts the chance of a Lean bug well under 1%. So if it finishes compiling with no extra axioms, it is probably correct, and no human will ever have read all of it…
- …prompting Alessandro Masullo to release his 940 page, 100% human, [work in progress proof](https://math216.wordpress.com/2026/11/20/hurried-announcement-alessandro-masullo-grh/) he had been working on for the last 12 years (and had been undergoing secret manual review and revision per [Kevin Hartnett](https://x.com/KSHartnett/status/2123847664064241799)).

This is the third in the trilogy of frontier math breakthroughs, following from the [Navier Stokes](https://latent.space/p/ainews-openai-reports-navier-stokes/) solutions and the [Quasi-Riemann](https://latent.space/p/ainews-quasi-riemann-hypothesis-openai/)bounding, but it doesn’t feel over. OpenAI's September [Navier-Stokes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.08144) claim is still the cautionary tale: critics argued that its Lean proof did not match the natural-language result. Both AI-claimed Millennium Prize results will take years to verify.

Apart from the incredible accomplishment of the most famous problem in mathematics, one cannot miss the contrast that the AI-written solution is **probably correct but incomprehensible**, and the other solution is**probably technically incorrect but understandable**.

**Sponsored by** [Agentfield.AI](http://agentfield.ai/)

Open models are ready. Most coding harnesses aren’t. On DeepSWE, CodeAF finished #1 of ten on the same open model, ahead of Claude Code, at the lowest cost per fix.

[Try CodeAF](https://agentfield.ai/github/codeaf/?utm_source=latentspace&utm_medium=newsletter&utm_campaign=latentspace-261119&utm_id=latentspace-261119-codeaf&utm_content=codeaf)!

As Levent eloquently put it: “ **Claude far outpaced me near the finish line**. No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.”

This also ties into other AI themes we’ve covered on the podcast and on this newsletter:

- The nature of Slop: Levent says “ I am presenting the world with a complete argument before having mastered a massive neighbourhood around its mathematics. It being obviously inappropriate to attempt to post some massive unreadable travesty of "slop", I decided to only present Lean. ” One of the key tenets of the [No Slop Manifesto](https://latent.space/p/ainews-the-no-ai-slop-manifesto/) is that you should understand what you ship (“ Slop is when we put less effort into producing something than we ask the consumer to spend understanding it. ”). And yet, this giant pile of Lean is verifiably correct and is incredibly significant in human history. Should we have delayed its release by a decade simply because we didn’t understand every single bit of it?
- Weak to Strong alignment: the typical experience of using agents is Strong to Weak - we are general intelligences guiding not-as-smart AI to do things we know how to do well. We also often expect AI to automate most work “within distribution”, and expect it to run into more trouble at the limits of capability where the “centaur” pattern of human-AI-collaboration is required. Levent’s lived experience is the opposite - collaborating with Claude only in the early stages and then leaving him far behind with the critical parts involving automorphic forms on higher-rank groups. We are starting to need [Weak to Strong](https://openai.com/index/weak-to-strong-generalization/)[alignment](https://openai.com/index/weak-to-strong-generalization/) — the open ended domain of controlling AI smarter than us.

items.body:
On Nov. 24, 1947, the U.S. Navy launched the first Aerobee rocket into the sky, but it never reached space.

Aerobee was a suborbital sounding rocket designed to study [Earth's atmosphere](https://www.space.com/17683-earth-atmosphere.html).

After World War 2, the United States started [reusing erman V-2 rockets](http://www.space.com/17858-bumper-v2-launch.html) for this kind of research. When they started running out of [V-2 rockets](https://www.space.com/v2-rocket), the United States constructed its own rockets that were similar but cheaper to build and to launch. In the weeks leading up to the first Aerobee mission, three test flights were launched.

Those tests used a dummy version of Aerobee with a live booster to see if the two stages would separate properly. On Aerobee's first real flight, the rocket flew about 35 miles high. That's below the 62-mile (100 kilometers) upper limit for the [boundary of space](https://www.space.com/karman-line-where-does-space-begin). (NASA and the U.S. military typically consider 50 miles the edge of space.) Mission control cut the flight short after about 30 seconds, because Aerobee started to yaw, and they wanted to keep it from going completely out of control.

The first Aerobee sounding rocket launched on Nov. 24, 1947 under a project led by the U.S. Navy. (Image credit: U.S. Navy)

## Why it mattered

Billed as the "[most successful sounding rocket of the space age](https://www.oxfordreference.com/display/10.1093/oi/authority.20110803095353746?p=emailAkQhgmA8CoLKQ&d=/10.1093/oi/authority.20110803095353746)," the initial Aerobee rocket was suborbital rocket designed to launch experment payload of up to 100 pounds (45 kilograms) to an altitude of 75 miles (121 kilometers) or so.

"The Aerobee was designed to carry instruments aloft to collect data on the upper atmosphere and to place small animals in a weightless condition for physiological studies," the U.S. National Museum of the United States Air Force [wrote in a mission overview](https://www.nationalmuseum.af.mil/Visit/Museum-Exhibits/Fact-Sheets/Display/Article/198112/aerojet-aerobee-rocket/). "It was launched by a solid-propellant booster engine of 18,000 pounds thrust that burned for only two and a half seconds."

An Aerobee suborbital sounding rocket of the type designed to study Earth's atmosphere. (Image credit: NMMSH)

While the first Aerobee rocket did not reach [space](https://www.space.com/24870-what-is-space.html), many more made successful launches in the decades that followed.

Engineers made a steady stream of upgrades to the the Aerobee rocket, allowing to fly higher and launch heavier payloads into space. It was an Aerobee rocket that launched two Phillipine [monkeys](https://www.space.com/19505-space-monkeys-chimps-history.html) on a mission to study how the effects of rapid launch acceleration might affect their bodies, an experiment that was among the frst human physiology tests that paved the way for [human spaceflight](https://www.space.com/space-exploration/human-spaceflight).

More than 1,000 Aerobee rockets have launched since then, and the last one flew in January of 1985.

Want more space history? Check out our[full On This Day In Space Story archive](https://www.space.com/tag/on-this-day-in-space) and watch our[On This Day In Space videos on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLCE-SVF9BSTdloyi4P9TmQVTp9Q2zTb27).

items.body:
A flurry of hyperactive and melodic percussion establishes the unmistakable rhythmic vocabulary of Nyege Nyege Tapes before a burst of laughter rounds off the 33-second introduction to *3OK*, a fitting elevator pitch into the record’s unruly, exuberant world. Yet beneath the apparent chaos lies an intricate rhythmic architecture, bringing together **Zoë Mc Pherson**‘s deconstructed club experiments,**Jay Mitta**‘s breakneck Tanzanian singeli and**DJ Diaki** ‘s electro-balani.

Born out of extended improvisational sessions at Nyege Nyege’s Kampala studios in 2022 and aboard Hamburg’s former fishing vessel MS Stubnitz in 2023, *3OK* takes its title from the three musicians’ shared expression of approval, a simple “OK” bridging the absence of a common spoken language. Their spontaneous exchanges, sometimes stretching to an hour and constantly changing tempo, subsequently became the raw material for Mc Pherson’s painstaking reconstruction. The intricate breakbeat manipulations of [States of Fugue](https://sfx-space.bandcamp.com/album/states-of-fugue-sf02) and [Pitch Blender](https://sfx-space.bandcamp.com/album/pitch-blender-sf04) meet the frenetic momentum of Mitta’s [Tatizo Pesa](https://nyegenyegetapes.bandcamp.com/album/tatizo-pesa) and the increasingly elaborate production of his recent [Kazi Kwanza](https://nyegenyegetapes.bandcamp.com/album/kazi-kwanza). Rather than smoothing out their differences, Mc Pherson finds ways of making them coexist.

On “222”, recurring, reverb-drenched motifs open up pockets of space within the frantic percussion, creating overlapping planes of sound. “Singeli on TV” develops this spatial play further, its circular patterns and submerged electronic textures seeming to rotate at different depths. The six-minute “Stubnitz” is the record’s most sustained excursion into rhythmic delirium, its relentless momentum gradually acquiring an almost trance-like intensity. “Drill”, meanwhile, introduces an almost symphonic quality, its densely layered electronic gestures suggesting instrumental sections competing and converging amid the rhythmic onslaught.

Throughout, pitched figures double as percussion while drum patterns acquire melodic contours, the different elements becoming almost impossible to disentangle. There is also a distinctly cartoonish humour to the music, with rubbery synthesizers, exaggerated pitches and abrupt interruptions. Yet much of this playfulness was already present in the original sessions. Mc Pherson’s intervention was less about adding further absurdity than giving the material a sense of dramatic progression, allowing particular motifs to emerge from the relentless flux.

The closing “Orchestra”, featuring DJ Diaki, has something of an afterparty atmosphere. Its interlocking motifs and playful exchanges feel less like a grand finale than the musicians continuing to bounce ideas off one another after the main event, restoring something of the spontaneous camaraderie from which the project emerged.

[Jingxin Wang](https://www.instagram.com/wjx_hasnoenglishname/)‘s artwork, depicting three psychedelic eyes with intersecting orbits, offers a fitting visual analogy. Each musician retains a distinct perspective, yet their trajectories continually overlap, collide and realign. For all its escalating tempos, abrasive textures and irrepressible humour, *3OK* never loses its sense of collective purpose. There is order in this chaos, even if it rarely stays still long enough to reveal itself.

To find out how the combo came together I approched **Zoë Mc Pherson** directly.

**3OK began with jams with Jay Mitta and DJ Diaki, which you later took away and developed into the finished album. How did you approach that material in the studio — what made you decide that a particular spontaneous exchange should remain recognisable, while another could be cut up, reorganised or transformed completely?**

Oh my, this is a very good question, actually! This process took a lot of thought, and a lot of time too, and I’m really happy with where it ended up.

I wanted the essence of our encounter to come through, but I also wanted to share finished material: tracks that could become a mini album. I thought a lot about the musical balance between our parts, and about the match that brought Jay and me together for the residency: the Singeli / Jay side and the bass / breaks / Zoë side. Diaki comes in on the intro with his voice, and on the last track with several of his recognizable pads. I kept the jam sessions with the three of us for side B of the tape, since they have a more live feel.

I also thought about each person’s role and involvement. We were in different positions, with different privileges too: living in Africa or in Europe, being a man or a non-binary person, knowing more or less about the music industry. That made the project even more interesting to me.

When we jammed, we were all equally involved. Afterwards, Diaki and Jay felt the rough jam recordings already worked as finished tracks, and they trusted me to finish the work the way I envisioned it. It took me a moment to step into that role, because I cared about keeping everyone’s involvement balanced. I checked with them several times, and they were happy to let me run with it Honestly, I get it, it was a lot of work!

The jams kept changing BPM, so I couldn’t just chop and edit quickly, and the recordings were mono, so I had to give them more weight. I edited everything, replayed melodies with other synths and extracted parts, and the jams became my inspiration material. They were 20-minute to one-hour pieces that changed every couple of bars, full of precious memories of us playing together.

I didn’t want to make a Zoë Mc Pherson EP. I wanted everyone’s engagement to be present while bringing my own vision forward. So I followed the sounds I loved most: nostalgic, sad EDM synths and hyperactive, almost glitching rhythms that are clownesque and dark at the same time. I think it’s a really original match of music. I haven’t heard anything like it before, and I don’t think anyone has.

I was lucky to have friends in the studio, most of whom had seen us perform in the main room at Berghain during CTM Festival. Kasimyn (Gabber Modus Operandi and Hulubalang), DJ Scotch Egg and my friend Darin listened with me and helped me carve the tracks down and bring our different roles to the front.

Side A is the produced version. Side B includes a snippet of a live set, so listeners can hear where the music came from and nerd out on how this sound evolved. I’m proud of it!

**You, Jay and Diaki didn’t share a common spoken language during the original sessions, and the title comes from the three “OKs” that signalled everyone was happy with what was happening. How did that affect the way you listened and responded to each other, and did the absence of verbal discussion allow things to happen that might otherwise have been talked out of existence?**

…

items.body:
A new Belgo-Dutch investigation uncovered a network of over 750 Facebook pages spamming the platform with AI-generated stories targeting Belgian and Dutch audiences. Many of the pages and sites appear to be run by a Vietnamese company named BeeUp. In a world first, Ngo Dang Hung, the CEO of BeeUp, agreed to speak to journalists on camera. Lead Stories is proud to have contributed to this joint effort by fact-checkers from Belgian public broadcaster VRT, the team of "Pointer" at Dutch public broadcaster KRO-NCRV and Dutch fact-checking website Nieuwscheckers from the University of Leiden.

You can read their reporting here:

- Pointer: [Vietnamese nepnieuwsfabrieken verklaren 70 BN'ers onterecht dood op Facebook](https://pointer.kro-ncrv.nl/vietnamese-nepnieuwsfabrieken-verklaren-70-bners-onterecht-dood-op-facebook) ("Vietnamese fake news factories falsely declare deaths of 70 Dutch celebrities on Facebook")
- Pointer: [Zo hebben we Vietnamese nepnieuwsfabrieken ontmaskerd die BN'ers doodverklaren](https://pointer.kro-ncrv.nl/zo-hebben-we-vietnamese-nepnieuwsfabrieken-ontmaskerd-die-bners-doodverklaren) ("How we unmasked the Vietnamese fake news factories who falsely declared deaths of Dutch celebrities")
- Nieuwscheckers: [Vietnamese nepnieuwsfabrieken spammen Facebook vol uiterst rechtse propaganda over Nederlandse politiek](https://nieuwscheckers.nl/nepnieuwsfabrieken-in-vietnam-spammen-facebook-vol-uiterst-rechtse-propaganda-over-nederlandse-politiek/) ("Vietnamese fake news factories spam Facebook with far right propaganda about Dutch politics)
- VRT: [Vietnamees spamnetwerk verklaart BV's dood op Facebook: zo gaan ze te werk](https://www.vrt.be/vrtnws/nl/2026/11/17/vietnamese-nepnieuwsfabrieken-check-spamnetwerk-onterechte-doods/) ("Vietnamese spam network declares Belgian celebrities dead on Facebook: here's how they do it")

While some of the mass-produced content posted by the pages consisted of relatively benign content such as fictional stories about family relationships and gossip about soap operas, they also published several viral stories falsely announcing the deaths of Dutch and Belgian celebrities (including the Dutch king and Belgian cycling legend Eddy Merckx) and in some cases they dipped into politics as well. The investigation uncovered almost a million posts made in the past two years, a staggering number made possible by the mass deployment of artificial intelligence tools.

This isn't exactly a new phenomenon:[a quick search](https://leadstories.com/cgi-bin/mt/mt-search.fcgi?IncludeBlogs=1&search=Vietnam) of the archive of fact-checks here at Lead Stories that mention "Vietnam" brings up dozens and dozens of results, many going back years. We mentioned such networks [as far back as 2021](https://leadstories.com/hoax-alert/2021/09/fact-check-fraudulent-votes-not-revealed-this-is-foreign-spam-network-video.html) and started using the term "Vietspam" or "Viet Spam" on our site in [2025](https://leadstories.com/hoax-alert/2025/11/fact-check-scam-bait-posts-falsely-claim-patel-and-other-celebs-paying-off-school-lunch-debts.html) to refer specifically to these types of pages and websites. We even published [this warning about fake fan pages](https://leadstories.com/analysis/2025/10/fact-check-prebunk-beware-of-fake-fan-pages-spreading-false-claims.html) back in October 2025: many of the pages we found published completely made-up stories featuring various celebrities. Sometimes the stories were positive (the celebrity being philantropic, doing good deeds, winning awards), but in other cases, the stories would cast a celebrity in a negative light (connecting them to various political causes they did not support, making up quotes or even declaring them dead or gravely wounded or ill).

In our own monitoring of such pages we came across at least 300 of them targeting American audiences with stories about U.S. celebrities, sports teams and politicians so far. We've seen stories mentioning over 500 different U.S. celebrities, ranging alphabetically from rapper 50 Cent to New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

The network (or ones similar to it) appears to be active in multiple countries. Swedish Källkritikbyrån found content aimed at Swedish audiences and [linked it to a Vietnamese company named BeeUp](https://kallkritikbyran.se/vietnamesisk-klickbetesfabrik-bakom-sommarens-svenska-ai-bluffar/).in the summer of 2025 (BeeUp also features heavily in the new Belgo/Dutch investigation). Indicator spoke of how the pages [thrived under Meta's relaxed moderation](https://indicator.media/p/celebrity-slop-hoax-pages-thrive-under-meta-loosened-moderation-caitlin-clark-colbert-lebron-vanessa?utm_source=indicator.media&utm_medium=newsletter&utm_campaign=briefing-x-wants-humans-and-ai-to-fact-check-together&_bhlid=57de87732c68ea2e6660fc55851f32e34802f98b) in August 2025. Nieuwscheckers [looked at the Dutch extent of the phenomenon](https://nieuwscheckers.nl/vietnamese-pulpproducenten-verdienen-via-facebook-aan-massameuk-over-misdaad-sport-en-soap/) in September 2025 while [VRT focused on the Belgian angle](https://www.vrt.be/vrtnws/nl/2025/09/23/vietnamese-beheerders-achter-vlaamse-facebookpagina-s/). Polish Demagog spotted [Vietnamese pages targeting Polish users](https://demagog.org.pl/fake_news/viet-spam-dotarl-do-polski-profile-na-facebooku-promuja-fake-newsy-o-politykach/) with this type of content in the spring of 2026. Around the same time, Political Capital [found pages in Hungarian, French and Polish](https://politicalcapital.hu/news.php?article_read=1&article_id=3699). AAP saw [Australians being fooled by such pages](https://www.aap.com.au/factcheck/the-fake-political-news-pages-fooling-countless-aussies/) in March. Canadian CBC found [pages targeting Canadian audiences](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/vietnam-canadians-fake-ai-9.7318612) in September 2026. And only a few days ago [Spanish Maldita saw the same type of pages spreading Spanish content](https://maldita.es/investigaciones/20261118/granja-vietnamita-paginas-facebook).

Lead Stories gave the latest Belgo/Dutch investigative effort a hand by providing some of the tricks and strategies we used to find such pages in the past. We also helped with some of the manual classification of the content and analyzing the monetization model. Surprisingly, according to data we cross-referenced with [What To Fix's Monetization Archive](https://www.monetization.wtf/), most of the pages in the network were not monetized directly on Facebook. This means any ads that did appear on the posts on Facebook only made money for Meta. It turns out the publishers actually paid Meta to run ads promoting the pages to gain more followers.

…

items.body:
Former Health and Human Services Department adviser Calley Means has misleadingly suggested that the new mRNA influenza vaccine from Moderna isn’t safe and doesn’t work well. Less is known about it because it is a new vaccine, but trial data suggest it works better than standard flu vaccines and does not have any serious safety risks.

For the first time, some Americans have the option to receive an mRNA vaccine to protect against seasonal influenza. In August, after a review that found the benefits of the vaccine outweighed the risks, the Food and Drug Administration [approved](https://www.fda.gov/vaccines-blood-biologics/vaccines/mflusiva) the shot for people ages 50 and up.

The American Academy of Family Physicians has also [endorsed](https://www.aafp.org/assets/image/upload/v1791920850/pdf_2026_through_2027_influenza_guidance.pdf) it as one of several recommended flu vaccines, including it among preferred options for those 65 years of age and older.

The new vaccine was tested in a large, randomized controlled [clinical trial](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2516491) against a standard flu vaccine. The trial included 40,703 people. The group that received the Moderna vaccine had around 27% fewer cases of lab-confirmed illness from influenza than the group that received the regular vaccine, with no apparent major safety risks.

Means, a prominent [figure](https://www.statnews.com/2024/10/07/calley-means-casey-means-conservative-voices-of-chronic-disease-crisis/) within the “Make America Healthy Again” movement and brother of [withdrawn](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cr5p4pp1407o) surgeon general [nominee](https://www.factcheck.org/2026/03/factchecking-claims-in-casey-means-surgeon-general-confirmation-hearing/) Dr. Casey Means, has distorted trial data and some circumstances surrounding the vaccine’s approval to imply in recent interviews that the vaccine is dangerous and ineffective.

Speaking on Joe Rogan’s podcast on Nov. 6 after [resigning](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/rfk-jr-adviser-calley-means-resigns-amid-growing-maha-discontent-over-lack-of-progress) from his HHS role last month, Means [said](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dMBBOawFy_4&t=5791s) the vaccine “didn’t work,” with an “almost negligible” reduction in flu, and came with “massive side effects.” When Rogan asked him what these side effects were, Means replied, “It can’t be definitively said, but there were deaths.” Means did not correct Rogan when, in following along with Means’ commentary, the podcast host said the vaccine would “kill people.”

“The FDA sent a study back on the Moderna mRNA vaccine showing that there were deaths in the study group, and showing that it had a paltry absolute benefit, and that there were severe side effects, and they asked for another study to begin,” Means also [said](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/calley-means-health-and-human-services-face-the-nation-transcript-11-08-2026/) in a Nov. 8 [interview](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Bal2ks8NN9Y&t=2237s) on CBS News’ “Face the Nation.” An advisory committee ultimately “approved a vaccine that the FDA thought was not safe and effective,” he continued.

Dr. [Anna Durbin](https://publichealth.jhu.edu/faculty/798/anna-p-durbin), director of the Center for Immunization Research at Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, told us that Means’ statements “are not accurately reflecting the safety or efficacy of the vaccine.” Durbin is a [member](https://www.fda.gov/media/194955/download) of the FDA advisory committee that reviewed data on the vaccine and voted unanimously that the benefits outweighed the risks.

The FDA did not find that deaths in the trial were vaccine-related, as we’ll explain. The agency also found the vaccine was effective compared with a standard-dose vaccine. But because the standard vaccine already works to reduce illness from flu, the absolute difference was relatively small — even though the results showed Moderna’s vaccine was superior. In addition to providing another flu vaccine option now, having an approved mRNA flu vaccine platform [could help](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2853094) in the future if there is a flu pandemic, since mRNA vaccines can be rapidly updated.

Screenshot of Calley Means from CBS News’ “Face the Nation.”

Means’ remarks are also contradicted by reporting about the events at the FDA. In February, Dr. Vinay Prasad, then the Trump administration appointee in charge of vaccines at the FDA, initially prevented the agency from reviewing Moderna’s vaccine submission, [reportedly](https://www.statnews.com/2026/02/11/moderna-flu-vaccine-application-rejected-by-prasad-overruling-fda-staff/) over the objections of FDA staff, according to STAT. Prasad [objected](https://static.modernatx.com/pm/6cef78f8-8dad-4fc9-83d5-d2fbb7cff867/38ab7558-636c-40d1-b49a-c8f51a7afa1a/38ab7558-636c-40d1-b49a-c8f51a7afa1a_viewable_rendition__v.pdf) to the design of the primary clinical trial used to test the vaccine. The trial compared the mRNA vaccine to a standard-dose flu vaccine, and not the vaccines preferentially recommended for adults 65 and older.

The FDA, however, had previously approved Moderna’s plans, and the company was seeking an approval for people 50 years of age and older, not only those 65 and older. Prasad did [not cite](https://static.modernatx.com/pm/6cef78f8-8dad-4fc9-83d5-d2fbb7cff867/38ab7558-636c-40d1-b49a-c8f51a7afa1a/38ab7558-636c-40d1-b49a-c8f51a7afa1a_viewable_rendition__v.pdf) safety concerns when he initially rejected Moderna’s submission, and he [reversed his decision](https://www.statnews.com/2026/02/23/fda-lobbying-efforts-grow-under-trump-administration/) after complaints from Moderna and, according to reporting from [multiple](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/02/18/fda-reverses-course-on-moderna-flu-shot-bid-00785799) [news outlets](https://www.cnn.com/2026/02/19/politics/midterm-elections-trump-health-care), White House intervention. (The White House has denied being involved.)

Once review was permitted to begin, FDA staff and a committee of independent vaccine [experts](https://www.fda.gov/advisory-committees/advisory-committee-calendar/vaccines-and-related-biological-products-advisory-committee-june-18-2026-meeting-announcement) reviewed the data on Moderna’s vaccine and each [concluded](https://www.fda.gov/media/194955/download) it [supported](https://www.fda.gov/media/194140/download?attachment#page=10) the vaccine’s approval. The committee does not approve vaccines but makes recommendations that the FDA then can accept or reject.

…

items.body:
Release: datasette-charts 0.2a0

I introduced this new charting plugin for Datasette yesterday. Today it's gained integration with Datasette Agent, so now you can ask chat for a chart and it will create one for you using the same underlying chart suggestion and generation tools.

Here's a demo video, recorded on agent.datasette.io where you can sign in with GitHub to try the plugin yourself:

Download the video (MP4)

I prompt Datasette Agent to "Use #stats to show sqlite-utils downloads over time as a chart" - where typing "#stats" opens a table search box. It shows me a chart inline in the chat, and when I click "Open in the chart builder" it opens the chart in a panel along with the table page. I use the table page to switch to a chart of "datasette", then when I ask the agent "what does the chart show?" it notices that I changed the content in the panel and describes the new Datasette chart to me.

Here's a Markdown export of the chat from the video.

items.title: App Report: Music, man
items.subtitle: We’re striking up the band with some musically inclined macOS and iOS apps this week.

items.body:
We’re striking up the band with some musically inclined macOS and iOS apps this week. In some cases, these apps augment music-subscription services like Apple Music, but the main point is to let you enjoy the music stored on your Apple device in new and different ways.

If you’ve got an app that marches to the beat of its own drummer, let us hear about it. Email apps@sixcolors.com with a description of the macOS or iOS offering you want to bring to our attention. We won’t be able to write back due to the volume of submissions we get, but we’ll certainly give your app a look for inclusion in a future column.

## Needl

Many people still collect vinyl records, though I can’t claim to be one of them. My daughter, however, is known to pick up the occasional album at record shops and flea markets, and an app like [Needl](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/needl-vinyl-record-collector/id6754252048) could help her get a handle on her growing collection.

Using Needl on your iPhone, you can scan the barcode on the album cover to import information about it onto your phone. (A Cover Scan feature identifies albums by the sleeve artwork, but you’ll need the Pro version for that feature.) Once imported, you can choose the edition/pressing of the album; Needl also lets you log the CDs and cassettes you have on hand.

Besides providing a handy glance at your record collection, Needl lets you keep a wishlist, shows the value of records if you’re looking to sell or buy and even offers AI-powered answers to questions about the artist or album. (One complaint: in the version I tested, a suggested Try Asking box remained on the screen, making it hard to see the complete answer.)

There’s a basic visualizer feature in the free download of Needl, but upgrading to the $20/year Pro version adds a custom visualizer and live lyrics feature to the app. (Weekly and monthly subscriptions are available, too.)

Perhaps the greatest value of Needl comes from its ability to connect to music services like Apple Music, Spotify and Tidal, as you can thumb through your collection and decide what kind of song or record to play next.

## Albumary

[Albumary](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/albumary/id6797989082) brings a different look to music management for the songs and albums stored on your Mac. Instead of the database structure found in the built-in Music app, Albumary adopts the look of a real-world music store, as you thumb through your collection like you would through a store rack full of records.

You can organize albums and singles by genre, decade or alphabetically, and flip through them by clicking on a stack of records pulled out of the virtual shelves. Flipping over a cover shows you a list of songs, the genre tags and album credits, including — in some cases — the personnel playing on the record.

In an especially nice touch, playlists from your music library are organized as cassettes in the Albumary interface. Anyone who assembled their own mix tapes in the ’80s and ’90s will appreciate that approach.

You can use Albumary for free for 21 days. After that, you’ll need to pay $18 to keep your virtual record store intact on your Mac.

## Truffle

If you’ve spent a long time assembling a music library, you’ve likely got a lot of entries missing things like cover art, album info and other bits of data. [Truffle](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/truffle-music-tag-editor/id6806763735?mt=12) is a macOS app for the completist in all of us, as it will analyze the songs you own looking to fill in any missing details.

Truffle does this by checking for sound rather than file name. Even more important, the app gives you control over imposing any changes, as you’re given the chance to approve the cover, artist, album year and genre data retrieved by the app. Owing to the developer’s roots as a hobbyist DJ, Truffle also works with Traktor, Serato and Rekordbox collections.

You can try Truffle for free, with analysis of up to 100 tracks. Unlocking the full app costs $50.

## Katalog

Like Truffle, [Katalog](https://musickatalog.com) is built for people who are serious about collecting music, having amassed a lot of tracks over the years. Katalog’s developer says the app can open a 91,000-track library in less than a second, so the 2,500 or so tracks I have stored on my Mac are no match for it.

Katalog looks a lot like what would have happened if Apple had kept the old iTunes interface in place and then just kept adding to it. It sorts your library by the usual information — artist, title, album, genre and so forth — while adding other categories for serious music fans and DJs like BPM and Key. A number of categories in the side menu like acapella, instrumentals, remixes, masters and more let you further sort your tunes out by type.

Katalog boasts four different modes for viewing your library, including a few aimed at people who make their own music and store it on their Mac. I particularly like the Prep interface aimed at building playlists with songs that have complementary keys and beats.

For basic music playback, Katalog is going to come across as overkill. Instead, this app is for music creators, DJs or people with extensive collections that include rare and offbeat tracks. Basic features in Katalog are free, and if you buy a support license for $30 to unlock extra features during the app’s beta process, those features are yours for life. Otherwise, the extras will cost $30/year once Katalog 1.0 ships. You can try everything out for 30 days right now.

## GroovSide

We started out with vinyl, and that’s what we’ll return to at the end of this column — at least vinyl in the virtual sense. [GroovSide](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/groovside/id6826888565?mt=12) offers a new look for enjoying music on your Mac by replacing your desktop with an animated turntable that spins as you play songs from either Apple Music or Spotify.

GroovSide is serious about the turntable motif. If you’re playing a full album, the animation will show the record flipping over when you reach the second side of the playlist. Single songs appear as 7- or 12-inch records. And the album art appears in the center of the record with title, artist and playback info also showing up on the screen.

It might take some fiddling to get GroovSide to work properly. I wasn’t seeing the animations when I first tested the app, but after emailing with the developer, I learned that I had to go into GroovSide’s settings to turn off a Pause When Covered toggle — a setting that I’m guessing was affecting the app since I was testing on a MacBook Air and GroovSide was looking to help preserve battery life. After making that adjustment, though, GroovSide worked as advertised.

No one’s going to pretend that GroovSide performs a vital function. It’s all about the whimsy, giving you a more interesting way to control music playback. For some listeners, that’s more than enough to justify the $5 cost of GroovSide.

items.title: Delayed Cancer Treatment. Missed Medication. How a Popular Insurance Plan’s Use of Prior Authorization Hurt Patients.
items.subtitle: Richie Jones at Stone Mountain Park in Georgia this month.
items.feedText:
Jones and his doctor repeatedly tried to get his insurer, Ambetter, to cover his cancer treatment. Jones often visits the park for quiet reflection. Matt Odom for ProPublica

Felicia tried everything she could think of to get her insurer to cover the only treatment that made a difference in her years-long effort to manage her obesity. items.body:
Richie Jones at Stone Mountain Park in Georgia this month. Jones and his doctor repeatedly tried to get his insurer, Ambetter, to cover his cancer treatment. Jones often visits the park for quiet reflection. Matt Odom for ProPublica

Felicia tried everything she could think of to get her insurer to cover the only treatment that made a difference in her years-long effort to manage her obesity.

In 2024, after her insurer denied her coverage for medication despite her doctor’s order, the 38-year-old Texan sought the help of consumer advocates. She crafted a detailed appeal. She sent it not just to the head of the Fortune 500 company that oversaw her health insurance plan, but also copied the secretary of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services and the chair of the Federal Trade Commission.

A short time later, someone called from a number she didn’t recognize. It was Kevin Counihan, CEO of her health plan, Ambetter.

Felicia, who asked to be identified by her middle name due to her fear of reprisals and so that she could share sensitive medical information, calmly told Counihan that she hoped that “something gets done right by me and by my health.”

“I have tried everything in the formulary. I exhausted all options,” she explained on the call, which she recorded and shared with ProPublica.

Kevin Counihan, who was CEO of Ambetter and had once overseen the federal Affordable Care Act marketplace, conceded that a customer’s reported experience with his company had been “a tremendous inconvenience and a real pain in the neck.” Brooks Kraft/Getty Images

A veteran health insurance executive who had once overseen the federal Affordable Care Act marketplace, Counihan conceded on the call that Felicia’s reported experience with his company had been “a tremendous inconvenience and a real pain in the neck.” But he assured her that “we really want to get you what you” and your doctor “think is the most appropriate medication for you.”

“I’m working on it as fast as possible,” said Counihan.

Counihan’s call was a rare acknowledgment from the company’s top brass of a pervasive problem. Ambetter, the most popular plan on the ACA marketplace, has one of the worst track records of delaying or denying medical coverage by refusing to cover the costs.

ProPublica has found that Ambetter last year denied these kinds of requests — known as prior authorization — at a higher rate than any other large insurer on the ACA marketplace. Our analysis of Ambetter’s own data, along with interviews with more than two dozen recent customers, sheds new light on the vast and sometimes illogical nature of how the company can block access to care.

Each dot below is a marketplace plan in Texas, sized according to the number of prior authorization requests it reported in 2025. Plans further to the right deny those requests at higher rates. Ambetter plans are shown in red.

In Texas, where Ambetter’s denial rates were above 32%, the company initially refused to pay for a medical scan for a patient with Stage 4 colon cancer because the doctor hadn’t ordered a cheaper, less precise scan first.

In Iowa, where Ambetter’s denial rate was 31%, it approved a patient’s colonoscopy but denied a request for the bowel prep that all patients must drink in advance of the procedure.

In Kansas, where Ambetter’s denial rate was 26%, it stopped covering an anti-inflammatory treatment for a patient with Crohn’s disease because it wanted the patient to try a different drug.

A ProPublica analysis of nearly 200 federal marketplace plans across the country found that Ambetter had the highest denial rates in most states where it provided data.

Ambetter plans had an average denial rate of 25% in states where the company reported data for last year. That’s substantially higher than the 16% average denial rate for all marketplace plans.

Our analysis is [based on data](https://www.authdenied.com/) that federal regulators required marketplace plans to report and publish for the first time this year. The requirement is intended to offer greater transparency into how often insurers restrict care by denying prior authorization for treatment.

Since the ACA marketplace launched in 2013, there has been little transparency around how often insurers request — and deny — prior authorization. Insurers use prior authorization to limit spending on treatment, equipment and prescriptions. They say it is also intended to ensure that doctors try less expensive and less invasive treatments before pricier ones. Health insurance experts said that the process of how or when prior authorization gets used is largely a black box.

U.S. Rep. Craig Goldman, a Republican from Texas, sponsored a bipartisan bill that would require marketplace plans to disclose more information about their use of prior authorization. “These companies represent these individuals — and yet denying them coverage and not being transparent with what they will be able to cover,” he said. “They’re just not there for the best interest of the people.”

Four former heads of state insurance departments who reviewed ProPublica’s findings said that Ambetter’s high denial rate was such an outlier that current regulators should examine further.

“This is stunning — and not in a good way,” Mila Kofman, a former insurance superintendent in Maine who now oversees the District of Columbia’s ACA marketplace, said of Ambetter’s denial rate. “This is something insurance regulators need to understand. There’s a huge opportunity for regulators to address the improper use of prior authorization.”

## We’re Investigating Prior Authorization. Help ProPublica Understand Your Health Insurance Denial.

[↗ Primärquelle: propublica.org](https://www.propublica.org/getinvolved/propublica-health-insurance-prior-authorization-reporting)

ProPublica is looking into the ways health insurers’ use of prior authorization impacts patients. We need your help to figure out if the process is still leading to delayed or missed treatments, tests, medical equipment or medication.

[Share Your Experience](https://www.propublica.org/getinvolved/propublica-health-insurance-prior-authorization-reporting)

Sarah London, CEO of Ambetter’s parent company, Centene, recently said in a statement on its website that it was “[creating a more predictable and transparent experience](https://www.centene.com/news/ahip-partnerships-prior-authorization_progress.html)” for its customers. That statement followed growing backlash against the industry and a push to limit the practice of prior authorization.

…

items.body:
Last week, news broke that a mathematician had used AI to help crack one of the biggest outstanding problems in math: a proof of [the Riemann hypothesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_hypothesis). The news follows several other major breakthroughs in math that have either been enabled by or managed entirely by large language model-based systems, a development that has left the entire field of mathematics in a state of upset.

It's too early to say much about the proof itself—mathematicians are still in the process of digesting it. But we can say a little about how the proof came about, and what it tells us about the state of math.

## Tackling Riemann

The Riemann hypothesis dates from the mid-1800s and was formulated by (you will be surprised to learn) Bernhard Riemann. There's not an obvious way to describe the details of the actual hypothesis simply, but it has implications for the distribution of prime numbers. This gives it significance for areas ranging from number theory to cryptography. As Wikipedia accurately states, "It is considered by pure mathematicians to be one of the most important problems in the field."

[Read full article](https://arstechnica.com/ai/2026/11/whats-going-on-with-the-riemann-hypothesis/)

items.title: EFF to Congress: Mass Surveillance Is Too Important to Shove into Must-Pass Bill

items.feedText: Now, with the program set to truly turn off within the next few months, surveillance hawks and national security maximalists are rushing to renew this secretive power by shoving it into a must-pass bill, like a continuing resolution to fund the government or the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) or an end of year, rushed, funding bill to prevent a shutdown. items.body:
In June 2026, the surveillance authority Section 702 of FISA expired absent a consensus among lawmakers over the terms of its reauthorization. Now, with the program set to truly turn off within the next few months, surveillance hawks and national security maximalists are rushing to renew this secretive power by shoving it into a must-pass bill, like a continuing resolution to fund the government or the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) or an end of year, rushed, funding bill to prevent a shutdown. This would be both undemocratic and suppress any real chance at reform. In an effort to prevent that, EFF has singed into a letter with over 25 civil liberties organizations, including the ACLU, Color of Change, and the Brennan Center, to urge Congress not to allow such a significant and dangerous program to be tacked onto a must-pass bill.

The letter says: “The NDAA is among the most important bills Congress considers each year. It should not be used as a vehicle to circumvent or to cut short this long-running bipartisan debate over Americans’ civil liberties and constitutional rights, nor to force lawmakers to choose between supporting our national defense and ending warrantless spying on Americans. Adding language in the NDAA conference to reauthorize Section 702 that has not been fully debated and voted on would be a serious procedural and substantive failure, and a betrayal of the democratic process.”

You can read the entire letter here.

Section 702 grants the government authority to compel a telecommunications company to hand over data to the National Security Agency (NSA) in an attempt to protect national security by monitoring communications overseas—but this is only a piece of what the law does. Because we live in a globalized world, communications between people in other countries and in the United States often gets hoovered up. Once it does, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and several other agencies give themselves permission to search through U.S. persons’ data without a warrant. This is unconstitutional, undermines our right to private communications, and creates a dangerous and potent tool for would-be despots who might use that communication to discriminate, marginalize, or punish people based on their identities and political beliefs.

This is not the kind of policy Congress should be considering without necessary reforms, open debate, and the ability for lawmakers to vote against without forcing them to vote “no” on all defense policy.

We once again urge Congress not to put Section 702’s future in a must-pass bill like the NDAA.

items.body:
After years of being able to hide behind Republicans’ blatant mismanagement and intentional sabotage of the healthcare system, Democrats will now have to put forth their own plan to save our crumbling healthcare infrastructure. Whether the party can agree on what that plan is remains to be seen.

The middle path has been dubbed “Medicare for More.” It’s been framed variously as a first step toward Medicare for All and as a half-measure to relieve the pressure to pass the more expansive healthcare agenda. Now backed by Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, the presumed next speaker of the House, the policy would lower the eligibility age for the public retiree health system; expand dental, vision, and hearing care; and provide universal coverage for children.

> “We’re in the wealthiest nation on Earth, and we’re running out of excuses for why Americans don’t have universal healthcare.”

But the plan would maintain the status quo for people ages 26 to 55 — many of whom saw their Affordable Care Act healthcare premiums spike after December 2025, when enhanced subsidies expired for an estimated [22 million people](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/02/24/aca-enhanced-subsidy-expiration-effects.html) as a result of [Republicans](https://theintercept.com/2025/11/10/democrats-republicans-government-shutdown-aca-deal/)’ so-called Big, Beautiful Bill.

“We’re in the wealthiest nation on Earth, and we’re running out of excuses for why Americans don’t have universal healthcare,” Rep. Summer Lee, D-Penn., wrote in a statement to the Intercept. “The mandate from voters is change. The American people literally cannot afford to return to the status quo.”

[Progressives](https://theintercept.com/2026/11/04/midterms-democrats-agenda-congress-iran-ai/) have vowed to pass Medicare for All, a sweeping proposal to establish a national public health insurance program

Polling suggests broad support for Medicare for All, particularly among Democratic voters. A Kaiser Family Foundation poll found that [94 percent](https://www.kff.org/public-opinion/current-and-historical-public-opinion-on-medicare-for-all-and-other-national-health-plan-proposals/) of registered Democrats support the policy — and roughly 79 percent of all adults polled favor the federal government doing more to help provide health insurance.

Despite Medicare for All’s growing popularity, Jeffries, a New York Democrat, remained skeptical of the policy throughout the midterms. In August, he [told](https://www.facebook.com/MeetThePress/posts/hakeem-jeffries-says-medicare-for-all-is-not-legislation-he-currently-supports/1410117684318565/) “Meet the Press” that he did not support it, emphasizing that since joining leadership he has declined to co-sponsor Medicare for All legislation.

[Related Luigi, a Year Later: How to Build a Movement Against Parasitic Health Insurance Giants](https://theintercept.com/2025/12/04/luigi-mangione-health-care-insurance-costs/)

Jayapal, who has [reintroduced](https://theintercept.com/2025/05/02/briefing-podcast-pramila-jaypal-democrats/) her [signature legislation](https://theintercept.com/2021/03/19/deconstructed-medicare-for-all-health-care/) every session since 2019 and plans to do so again in the next Congress, said wins from candidates who ran on Medicare for All in this year’s midterm elections have helped to push leadership on this issue. She specifically cited the success of purple-state candidates like Sen.-elects [Abdul El-Sayed](https://theintercept.com/2026/07/31/democrats-michigan-el-sayed-stevens-left-moderate/) in Michigan and Troy Jackson in Maine, who invoked the policy again and again on the campaign trail — and won.

At a meeting of the Congressional Progressive Caucus last week, the Washington congresswoman said that Jeffries agreed to two out of three of the caucus’s requests on Medicare for All. First, he agreed to support the initial phase-in of the Medicare for All Act, which Jayapal says she has been pushing him on for “the last couple of months.” The plan would greatly expand access to healthcare for most Americans by simultaneously lowering the Medicare eligibility age and covering everyone under the age of 18. ** **

Second, he agreed to get a Congressional Budget Office score on the full Medicare for All act. The [CBO score](https://www.cbo.gov/cost-estimates/faqs) estimates the cost of any given legislation, which gives members a chance to weigh the financial impact of a bill before casting their vote.

But Jeffries declined to support their third request: a markup of the full “Medicare for All” bill in committee. Markups allow committees to make amendments to a bill before it gets voted on in front of the full House — making it substantially easier to pass.

Still, Jayapal believes there is a path forward for her bill. She said that she has spoken with both new members and incumbents “who haven’t been on it before” and now say they want to co-sponsor the bill, and she believes that with more of the caucus’s support, Jeffries could support a bill markup in the future.

It appears that attacks on the policy have become less effective with voters over time. Private insurance companies have long supported anti-Medicare for All messaging, Jayapal pointed out.

Opponents of the public healthcare proposal argue it will create longer wait times, raise taxes, and separate people from their preferred doctors. But as the state of healthcare in the United States has degraded and become more dystopian, Jayapal said, “none of those attacks work when people are already experiencing $20,000 in premiums, when they’re already being told they can’t have care by an AI model or by a private insurance company.”

[Related Corporations Are The Real Healthcare Fraudsters, Inspector General Report Shows](https://theintercept.com/2026/07/31/immigrants-healthcare-medicare-fraud-scam/)

Regardless of what the public wants, and even if Democrats can agree on a vision, the mercurial commander-in-chief remains an obstacle. The Democrats’ 56-seat Senate majority is significant but not veto-proof, and President Donald Trump has previously [called](https://www.beckersasc.com/asc-coding-billing-and-collections/a-socialist-takeover-everything-president-trump-said-about-healthcare-in-the-state-of-the-union/) Medicare for All a “socialist takeover.” On Saturday, he [told](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/donald-trump/abdul-el-sayed-catches-trumps-attention-pitch-trumpcare-rcna610626) Fox News there’s a “chance” he would work with Democrats on healthcare — but it would not be the legislation Democrats “want.”

Jayapal says she’s not holding out much hope for collaboration.

“I don’t think much about Trump in this particular moment,” she said. “I think we just need to do the thing that we know Americans deserve and want, and then let’s send it to his desk. And if he signs it, great. And if he doesn’t, he will be the one that is not allowing Americans to have healthcare, and then we can sign it when we have the trifecta.”

items.body:
As the U.S. expands its reliance on renewable energy, a considerable amount of excess electricity will be generated by solar and wind power plants. A new study explores how this energy could potentially be harnessed by certain technologies or production processes, reducing costs and increasing energy efficiency.

Researchers from MIT and Georgia Tech studied future situations in which the build-out of solar and wind farms has scaled up enough that 80 percent of the electricity supplied to customers in the U.S. is generated from renewable sources. They modeled systems with different mixtures of wind and solar power capacities.

They found that solar and wind farms could produce as much as 10 percent more power than the grid could immediately use or store in electricity systems that cost-effectively meet demand with 80 percent renewable energy. If not utilized, this excess electricity would go to waste.

This finding holds true even when the cost of energy-storage devices like batteries is low, and it remains largely consistent across the U.S. in many future scenarios.

The researchers’ model reveals when excess electricity will likely be available. It shows that periods of excess will generally occur in the spring and fall and usually persist for several hours at a time.

This predictability presents an opportunity for some industrial processes that, with the right scheduling and capacity scaling strategy, could use this otherwise excess energy. Examples include raw materials grinding and even electrified steel production. The excess could also be tapped to help meet the growing electricity demands of data centers.

While it can be more challenging to run industrial processes intermittently than continuously, the predictability of potential excesses helps, the authors say. Additionally, strategies like designing less-capital-intensive machinery, or even sharing equipment across manufacturing sites, could also be useful.

“In this era where there is a need for additional electricity, where demands are growing to support data centers and other end users, we wanted to understand what this excess electricity will potentially look like so we can design processes to benefit from these excesses. Our work can help technology developers and other stakeholders plan for future infrastructure needs and start innovating toward these technologies now,” says Jessika Trancik, a professor in the MIT Institute of Data Systems and Society (IDSS) and a senior author of this study.

She is joined on the paper by lead author Micah S. Ziegler, a former IDSS postdoc who is now an assistant professor at Georgia Tech; Aliza Khurram, a former IDSS postdoc now at the Toyota Research Institute; and Shannon Y.S. Hwang a PhD student in IDSS. The research [appears today in Joule](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2542435126003673?dgcid=author).

**Examining excess**

Wind and solar energy are variable resources because they are dependent on weather. During periods when supply exceeds demand, operators often take measures to either store the excess or reduce energy production altogether.

But “another way to think about that curtailed energy is as an opportunity to use this excess electricity for some other processes,” Trancik says.

“Excesses could instead be used productively in a range of processes including making materials and training AI models,” Ziegler adds.

To help engineers design processes to utilize this resource, the MIT researchers modeled the dynamics, durations, and frequencies of excess energy events.

They used an energy systems model to study systems that combine wind, solar, and energy storage to meet different percentages of electricity demand in many future scenarios. The model can also simulate how these systems might operate hourly over decades.

They fed this model 40 years of data that captured weather extremes and fluctuations in wind and solar resources across the United States. They also incorporated technology-related factors, such as the cost of building different types of batteries or other kinds of energy storage, as well as electricity demand profiles for specific regions.

“All these costs are changing, so we wanted to study many different combinations of technologies to help people plan amid all this uncertainty about what the future power system is going to look like,” Trancik says.

They designed the model to handle this enormous amount of data, while balancing the level of detail so the problem was computationally tractable.

In the end, the researchers found that significant amounts of excess energy would be generated in electricity systems that meet a significant portion of demand with renewable energy. Even when systems are designed to minimize the costs of delivering renewable energy, the amount of potentially excess power available would regularly double the amount used to meet demand.

“We found that considerable excess energy could be available even in systems with very low-cost storage, including at costs an order of magnitude lower than what battery storage costs today,” Ziegler explains.

“There is a huge amount of renewable energy that might be wasted in these cost-optimal systems, and there is not as much sensitivity to location as one might have thought. This energy is broadly available across the U.S.” Trancik says.

The model shows that the greatest potential periods of excess energy would occur in the spring, with smaller amounts of excess available in the mid- to late fall. These excess periods typically continue for seven to 12 hours, usually occur midday through the afternoon, and sometimes last for multiple days.

**Leveraging surplus energy**

Because these excess energy patterns are somewhat predictable, scientists and engineers could design processes to capitalize on this resource, Trancik says.

“In many of the scenarios, excess energy was often available for seven to 12 hours continuously, which suggests this duration could be a good target for technology developers and system planners when they design and schedule processes,” Ziegler explains. “When the same characteristic is found consistently across a wide range of possible energy systems, it can be considered more robust to our uncertainty about the future.”

For example, some industrial machinery, like electric arc furnaces in steel production or mills for grinding raw materials, could be switched on and operated during these times.

This electricity could also power equipment to manufacture products used seasonally, like fertilizer or concrete, which tend to be used more during spring, summer, and fall, and less during the winter. This coincides with several periods where more excess electricity is available. The energy could also power flexible computing, such as AI training processes that can be scheduled for times of day, or even months, when excesses are more likely available.

items.body:
*Updated at 6:06 p.m. ET on November 23, 2026*

Americans learned several things over the past few days. The most recent news is that Jensen Huang, after a nanosecond of disgrace for an affair with a woman [allegedly connected to Chinese intelligence](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/22/us/politics/alice-huang-china-spy-agency-nvidia.html), is back in control of Nvidia, the giant corporation that makes some of the world’s most advanced AI chips. Another is that China’s Communist regime has gotten its hands on the chips. The markets, as usual, have reconfirmed that they prefer profit to politics: Nvidia’s stock price jumped more than 30 percent on the news of Huang’s return.

But most important, Americans learned—yet again—that their president does not care about the national security of the United States. In fact, he is so aggressively resistant to any notion of security that his actions have become almost indistinguishable from those of a hostile foreign agent.

Step back for a moment and consider this sequence of events. The married Nvidia boss was caught in a sexual relationship with a woman named Alice Huang. (She is not related to Jensen, but I will use first names here to avoid confusion.) Alice, during this affair, worked for Megaspeed, a company in Singapore. Megaspeed bought Nvidia chips, and then [found ways](https://www.wsj.com/tech/li-ming-megaspeed-nvidia-chips-china-6260d836) to get them to China, despite U.S. export controls. She also reportedly maintained contacts with the Ministry of State Security, the Chinese intelligence agency, while carrying on with Jensen.

(Some reports call Alice an “agent” or a “spy,” others refer to her as an “asset.” The distinction makes little practical difference in Jensen’s case. Someone who is employed by an intelligence agency, has professional training, and may be acting under a false identity, is an *officer*. *Agents* and *assets* are people recruited from private life, outside of the organization, who have a cooperative relationship, in varying degrees, with such an agency but aren’t actually employed as spooks. Either way, Jensen was literally in bed with someone who was reportedly in bed with Chinese intelligence.)

*[[Josh Tyrangiel: Three theories of Jensen Huang’s resurrection](https://www.theatlantic.com/ideas/2026/11/jensen-huang-nvidia-reinstated/689546/?utm_source=feed)]*

All of this certainly looks bad. It gets worse. The United States government, including President Trump, was [warned by American intelligence](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/us/politics/trump-china-trip-nvidia.html) that Alice was entangled with Beijing. In fact, Trump was warned *twice* in seven months, including once during a briefing by Marco Rubio aboard Air Force One in May as Trump was headed to China for a state visit. This must have been awkward, because shortly afterward, Jensen Huang boarded Air Force One and joined the U.S. delegation for the trip to China.

Trump ignored these warnings—or more accurately, in classic Trump style, he pretended not to know about these issues. “I’d certainly check with the intelligence people,” he [said,](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/09/us/politics/trump-jensen-huang-spy.html) just before his most recent visit to China. “They could have been mentioned. Certainly, it didn’t make much of an impact on me.”

Clearly not. Nor did these warnings move Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick, whose former company, [Cantor Fitzgerald, has significant ties to Nvidia](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/13/howard-lutnick-nvidia-jensen-huang-china-cantor-fitzgerald.html), including financing some of the firms that were buying its chips.

The company is now run by Lutnick’s son.

Trump’s reaction to all this? When Jensen was discovered and had to leave his company, Trump got right to work [trying to put him back](https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/11/20/trump-defends-jensen-huang-after-alleged-chinese-spy-affair/) in the big chair at Nvidia. “I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance. You know, we’re a country of second chances.” [Nvidia wasn’t having it](https://www.washingtonpost.com/technology/2026/11/16/trump-says-he-would-not-mind-jensen-huangs-return-nvidia/): Internal sources at the company made clear to reporters that Jensen Huang would not be reinstated.

So what changed in a matter of days? Nothing, except that the president apparently brought the American intelligence community into the fray to give Jensen a clean bill of health. At least that’s how it sounds from the Nvidia board’s public statement: “In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”

The national-security process is slow and deliberative for a reason; people with even modest clearances who have been accused of minor infractions have had to wait months, sometimes even going to court, before being allowed back to work. An executive working with some of America’s most exotic technology commits adultery with a foreign citizen who has ties to a hostile government, and is credibly accused of funneling highly restricted American technology to a hostile intelligence service—and the U.S. security mandarins give the guy a thumbs-up after a *week*?

Trump likes Jensen, he likes money, he likes the markets, and he likes Lutnick and his family. So perhaps he told the American spooks to sound the all-clear so that Jensen could get back to work. Trump indicated as much today when he told CNBC that he spoke with Nvidia’s board members. “I spoke to them, let me put it that way. And I convinced them.”

In a [statement](https://truthsocial.com/@realDonaldTrump/posts/117666141823845971) on Truth Social, Trump said: “The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct.” That means exactly nothing. Saying that Todd Blanche does not “possess evidence” is an artful formulation meaning that Blanche does not have a file in front of him from the intelligence community detailing Jensen’s acts, some of which might have been dangerous even if they were not “unlawful.” (As any government employee can tell you, any number of “lawful” activities, including carrying lots of debt or having emotional problems, can sink a clearance and a job.) And because of Trump’s pressure to clear Jensen, it’s unlikely he ever will.

…

Sumathi Reddy, writing for The Wall Street Journal (gift link):

> The U.S.’s loss of what is known as [measles-elimination status](https://www.wsj.com/health/u-s-loses-measles-elimination-status-as-historic-resurgence-sickens-thousands-b95e8780?mod=article_inline) is a massive public-health defeat that begs a question:
> How long will it take to regain it?
> Based on other countries’ experience it could be up to five years,
> say doctors and epidemiologists. But that assumes the federal
> government is a robust and willing participant proactively working
> on measles vaccination.
> Without that, it could take even longer.

Nilay Patel, in the headline of his endorsement of Kamala Harris two years ago: “[A Vote for Donald Trump Is a Vote for School Shootings and Measles](https://www.theverge.com/24282022/kamala-harris-endorsement-presidential-election-2024)”.

items.feedText: When the Inquisition persecuted Galileo for advancing the rude truth that Earth is not the center of the universe, the charge against him was heresy — the same charge on which Joan of Arc was burned at the stake for her crusade for political reform. items.body:
### “If we are to be true and worthy heretics, we need not only new heads, but new hearts, and, most of all, that new emotional imagination… begotten of enlarged sympathies and a more sensitive habit of feeling.”

**UPDATE 2025: This book is now [back in print](https://www.amazon.com/Alpha-Omega-Jane-Ellen-Harrison/dp/1961341417/?tag=braipick-20) as the third title in [Marginalian Editions](https://www.themarginalian.org/editions/). When the Inquisition persecuted Galileo for advancing the rude truth that Earth is not the center of the universe, the charge against him was heresy — the same charge on which Joan of Arc was burned at the stake for her crusade for political reform. We have had many words for heretics over the epochs — rebels, radicals, freethinkers — but they have always been the ones to dislodge humanity from the stagnation of the status quo, to illuminate our blind spots, dismantle our unexamined biases, and jolt us out of our herd mentality. Without those devoted to seeing reality more clearly and possibility more wildly, we would still live in a world haunted by superstition and governed by dogma. The power and dignity of this most courageous human mindset is what the pioneering classicist Jane Ellen Harrison** (September 9, 1850–April 15, 1928), who brought the culture of Ancient Greece to the modern world, explores in her magnificent essay “Heresy and Humanity,” found in [Alpha and Omega](https://www.amazon.com/Alpha-Omega-Jane-Ellen-Harrison/dp/1961341417/?tag=braipick-20) ([public library](https://www.worldcat.org/title/769418)) — the out-of-print essay collection that gave us Harrison on [the art of growing older](https://www.themarginalian.org/2022/09/10/jane-ellen-harrison-crabbed-age-and-youth-alpha-and-omega/), published just as humanity was being dehumanized by its first World War.

Jane Ellen Harrison

Harrison writes:

> The word “heretic” has still about it an emotional thrill — a glow reflected, it may be, from the fires at Smithfield, the ardours of those who were burnt at the stake for the love of an idea.
> Heresy, the Greek hairesis, was from the outset an eager, living word. The taking of a city, its expugnatio, is a hairesis; the choosing of a lot in life or an opinion, its electio, is a hairesis; always in the word hairesis there is this reaching out to grasp, this studious, zealous pursuit — always something personal, even passionate… To be a heretic today is almost a human obligation.

In a sentiment Bertrand Russell would echo in [timeless manifesto for freedom of thought](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/05/18/bertrand-russell-free-thought-propaganda-doubt/), Harrison adds:

> The gist of heresy is free personal choice in act, and specifically in thought — the rejection of traditional faiths and customs.

Art by Olivier Tallec from [Louis I, King of the Sheep](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/10/14/louis-i-king-of-the-sheep-olivier-tallec/)

A century and a half after Emerson inveighed that [“masses are rude, lame, unmade, pernicious in their demands and influence,”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/05/04/emerson-masses/) she considers what makes heresy so difficult yet so necessary to the health of society:

> All traditional views are held with such tenacity, such almost ferocity, because they belong to the class of views induced, not by individual experience, still less by reason, but by collective, or, as it is sometimes called “herd,” suggestion. This used to be called “faith.” The belief so held may or may not be true; collective suggestion is not in the least necessarily collective hallucination. Mere collective suggestions — that is the interesting point — have the quality of obviousness; they do not issue from the individual, but seem imposed from outside, and ineluctable; they have all the inevitableness of instinctive opinion… Hence they are held with an intensity of emotion far beyond any reasoned conviction. To doubt them is felt to be at once idiocy and irreverence. Inquiry into their rational bases is naturally, and in a sense rightly, resented, because they are not rationally based, though they may be rationally supported. It is by convictions such as this that a society of the homogenous kind — a society based on and held together by uniformity — lives and thrives. To attack them is to cripple and endanger its inmost life.

Observing that the development of science is what pivoted heresy from damnable to desirable in society, Harrison contrasts sensemaking by empiricism with sensemaking by authority:

> Science classifies, draws ever clearer distinctions; herd-suggestion is always in a haze. Herd-suggestion is all for tradition, authority; science has for its very essence the exercise of free thought. So long as we will not take the trouble to know exactly and intimately, we may not — must not — choose… We must follow custom; we must accept the mandates of [those] who enforce tradition.
> […]
> Science opens wide the doors that turned so slowly on tradition’s hinges, and opens them on clean, quiet places where we breathe larger air… It is well to remember our debt to science — our inward and spiritual as well as material debt.

Art by [Rockwell Kent](https://www.themarginalian.org/2022/02/15/rockwell-kent-wilderness/), 1919. (Available as [a print](https://society6.com/product/the-star-lighter-by-rockwell-kent-1919_print?curator=brainpicker) and as [stationery cards](https://society6.com/brainpicker/cards?sort=new?curator=brainpicker).)

And yet, Harrison argues, the heretic needs more than science — the heretic needs humanity. She writes:

> Science broke the binding spell of herd-suggestion. For that great boon let us now and ever bless and praise her holy name. She cleared the collective haze, she drew sharp distinctions, appealing to individual actual experience, to individual powers of reasoning. But by neither individual sense — perception nor ratiocination alone do we live. Our keenest emotional life is through the herd, and hence it was that, at the close of the last century, the flame of scientific hope, the glory of scientific individualism that had blazed so brightly, somehow died down and left a strange chill. Man rose up from the banquet of reason and law unfed. He hungered half unconsciously for the herd. It seemed an impasse: on the one side orthodoxy, tradition, authority, practical slavery; on the other science, individual freedom, reason, and an aching loneliness.
> […]
> We live now just at the transition moment; we have broken with the old, we have not quite adjusted ourselves to the new. It is not so much the breaking with the old faiths that makes us restless as the living in a new social structure.

Art by Olivier Tallec from [Louis I, King of the Sheep](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/10/14/louis-i-king-of-the-sheep-olivier-tallec/)
