items.body:
NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Services 25 mission, or Northrop Grumman CRS-25, will deliver about 11,000 pounds of science and supplies to the International Space Station. The mission will be the third flight of the company’s Cygnus XL, the larger, more cargo-capable version of the company’s solar-powered spacecraft.

The Cygnus XL will launch aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. Following arrival to the station, astronauts aboard the space station will use the Canadarm2 to grapple the spacecraft before ground controllers robotically install it to the Unity module’s Earth-facing port for cargo unloading.

NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Services 25 mission will launch on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket to deliver research and supplies to the International Space Station.

NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Services 25 mission will deliver approximately 11,000 pounds of research and supplies to the International Space Station.

NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Mission 25 will launch from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida.

NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Services 25 spacecraft is named in honor of NASA astronaut James “Jim” A. Lovell Jr. Lovell flew four missions, including Gemini VII, Gemini XII, Apollo 8, and the Apollo 13 mission around the Moon.

NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney will be on duty during the Cygnus spacecraft’s approach and rendezvous. Watkins will be at the controls of the Canadarm2 robotic arm, ready to capture Cygnus as Delaney monitors the spacecraft’s arrival.

## Science highlights

In addition to food, supplies, and equipment for the crew, Cygnus will deliver several new experiments aimed at improving drug delivery for cancer and osteoarthritis treatment, predicting cancer spread, advancing treatments for muscle loss, improving radiation sensing, and supporting food production for future long-duration missions. This research includes:

### Cardinal Muscle 2.0

Preflight image of the Biocell bioreactor system used to maintain engineered muscle tissue samples as part of the Advancing Therapeutic Treatment of Sarcopenia (Cardinal Muscle 2.0) investigation. Aboard the International Space Station, this investigation tests the effects of potential therapeutics on human muscle cell cultures. The research may help accelerate development of treatments for age-related muscle loss on Earth and support astronaut health during long-duration missions.

[Cardinal Muscle 2.0](https://www.nasa.gov/mission/station/research-explorer/investigation/?#id=9031) uses the microgravity environment to explore potential treatments for muscle loss. Muscle atrophy and strength loss experienced by astronauts after spaceflight share many features with age-related muscle decline on Earth and occur more rapidly in microgravity without exercise. Researchers will use a muscle tissue model to test different Food and Drug Administration-approved drugs used to treat other conditions can be repurposed to prevent or reduce muscle loss.

### DNA NANO B

A confocal microscope image shows a human cartilage cell, with its nucleus stained in blue, following delivery of Janus Base Nanoparticles (JBNp) and the subsequent release of bioactive mRNA (pink) that was translated into function protein (green). Biomimetic Fabrication of Multi-Functional DNA-Inspired Nanomaterials via Controlled Self-assembly in Space (DNA Nano Therapeutics-Mission 2) continues prior research on in-space manufacturing of nanomaterials that mimic DNA and have applications for vaccines and regenerative medicine.

The [DNA Nano B](https://www.nasa.gov/mission/station/research-explorer/investigation/?#id=9654) investigation uses microgravity to manufacture tiny, DNA-inspired particles designed to deliver medicine into dense tissues, such as cartilage and solid tumors. Microgravity may enable more uniform particle assembly, helping researchers refine production methods. The results could advance targeted treatments for cancer and osteoarthritis on Earth.

### ARES

Preflight image of an Active Radiation Environment Sensor (ARES) unit undergoing ground testing in a thermal vacuum chamber. This investigation monitors radiation in habitable spacecraft environments and has exposure awareness and warning capabilities for Human Landing System crews. Testing aboard the International Space Station helps researchers validate the technology for future exploration missions.

The Active Radiation Environment Sensor ([ARES](https://www.nasa.gov/mission/station/research-explorer/investigation/?#id=9537)) will test a small radiation monitoring device to support future Artemis program and lunar missions. The system is designed to integrate with spacecraft systems and provide real-time radiation monitoring inside crew living areas. The results could inform radiation monitoring strategies and crew safety measures for future exploration missions.

### ENCAPSULATE-1

Preflight image of colorectal microtumors grown within Encapsulate’s biochip. The investigation, Encapsulate nVasive: Unraveling the Enigma of Metastasis – Flight 1, or Encapsulate-1, grows copies of patients’ tumor samples aboard the International Space Station to study how cancer cells move and interact in microgravity. Results may help researchers develop further testing to predict a patient’s risk of metastasis and support more personalized cancer treatments.

[Encapsulate-1](https://www.nasa.gov/mission/station/research-explorer/investigation/?#id=9594) uses miniature replicas of patients’ tumors to study how cancer cells move, invade surrounding tissues, and potentially spread. Researchers aim to develop a space-based diagnostic tool that could predict cancer progression months or even years in advance, improving early detection and treatment decisions for patients on Earth.

### OHALO III

Preflight image of Utah State University’s OHALO III module with a variety of plants growing from the Utah Re-usable Root Modules. This facility aims to validate plant water delivery, volume optimization, and advance knowledge on crop production, which could inform design decisions for future plant systems on deep space missions.

[Ohalo III](https://www.nasa.gov/mission/station/research-explorer/investigation/?#id=9272) is a new plant growth facility designed to help food crop production on future long-duration missions. The mostly automated system uses innovative water recovery and air exchange technologies to grow a variety of crops. This research could help lead to better food production methods to keep crew healthy and fed on future exploration missions, including those to Mars.

items.body:
# New Species of Flying Frog Discovered in Indonesia - Nautilus

## New Species of Flying Frog Discovered in Indonesia

And it’s got a very unusual way of laying eggs

1:00 PM CST on November 22, 2026

New species can be discovered in all sorts of ways . In the case of Rhacophorus kurniatia , a type of Asian flying frog that’s only just been identified, it involved a trek deep into the Mekongga Mountains in Indonesia, to a secluded lake where thousands of frogs had congregated.

“We were moving up the mountain, and we came across this big pond covered in these green frogs,” Alan Hitch, one of the authors of a new study about Rhacophorus kurniatia , explained in a statement . “They were all over. You don’t really see frogs in big congregations like that. This was something super special.”

They were quickly identified as being flying frogs, from the Rhacophorus genus. The large webbed feet, for gliding between trees, were the main giveaway. Further analysis revealed something not seen in other Rhacophorus species, though: The frogs deposit their eggs in gelatinous masses hanging above or near water, rather than in the typical foamy nests.

Distinctive, pointed snouts, as well as differences in the calls made by the frogs, confirmed that this was a species that hadn’t been observed and documented before.

“The team looked at hundreds and hundreds of specimens of frogs to describe the new species,” study author Andrew Engilis Jr. said in a statement . “Sometimes species can look the same, but their behavior is different and their genetics are different—these are called cryptic species. This frog is an example of that. It looks very similar to other Rhacophorus , but its genetics and behavior show that it’s very distinctive.”

The identification of R. kurniatia is the culmination of four years of work on the Indonesian island of Sulawesi, which is close to Borneo. Expeditions carried out by the researchers led them from sea level to the highest mountain peaks—with the new flying frog species discovered some 6,100 feet above sea level.

And there’s a bittersweet reason for the naming: The flying frog’s scientific name was chosen as a mark of respect for renowned herpetologist Hellen Kurniati, who died in 2024. She was one of the leading researchers studying amphibians and reptiles in Indonesia. She also helped to discover the new species that now shares her name.

John Kaag at The American Scholar:

items.body:
John Kaag at *The American Scholar*:

In 1946, she sent Gershom Scholem her essay “Zionism Reconsidered.” He was furious, accused her of betraying her people, and demanded that she recant. She defended herself but ended her reply not with an argument but with a question: Could they still be friends? She warned him against becoming “a fanatic for truth,” said he had unleashed “an orgy of truth-telling,” and wrote the sentence Berkowitz’s book keeps returning to: “A human being is far more valuable than his opinions.” In 1963, after Arendt published *Eichmann in Jerusalem,* Scholem charged her with lacking love for the Jewish people. She agreed. “I love in fact only my friends and am fully incapable of any other love.” A people, she said, is an abstraction. One cannot love it. Friendship is loyalty to particular persons, not to positions, and that is why Arendt thought it a sturdier foundation for a shared world than truth, certainty, or being right.

items.body:
Many farmers and ranchers in eastern Colorado are curious about artificial intelligence, but they don’t have a local tech-savvy person to show them how to use it. Xue “Alice” Dong has made that her job.

Dong, an IEEE senior member, is an extension regional specialist with the Colorado State University Extension, CSU’s outreach arm. She works in Logan County and serves a 10-county farming area in Colorado’s northeast corner. Her job is to turn university research into practical help for the people who live there.

Xue “Alice” Dong

Employer

Colorado State University Extension in Logan County

Title

Extension regional specialist

Member grade

Senior member

Alma maters

Inner Mongolia Normal University, in Hohhot; Beijing Normal University; State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry, in Syracuse; Colorado State University Global

She built the AI-Powered Agritourism Chatbot (AgriTourismAI.com), which helps farmers and ranchers launch and run “agritourism” businesses. Agritourism is when farmers open their property to visitors for fun, education, or shopping events. Familiar examples include pick-your-own fruit orchards, lessons on how to grow vegetables, and sales of handmade products.

Dong also teaches workshops where she shows farmers and ranchers how they can use AI tools to help grow and manage their business.

She says she sees herself as a link between the university and the countryside.

“We [extension specialists] act as a bridge,” she says. “We bridge our campus to the rural communities we serve.”

Many farmers and ranchers are older, and they typically have no technical training. Often their children and grandchildren have left the farm to work in a city or otherwise aren’t around to teach them about new tools. Without help, the benefits of AI could pass the farmers by. Dong’s workshops give them a way in.

Dong was named a finalist in the 2026 GenAI for Good Challenge for her AgriPivot AI Agent. The challenge was organized by IEEE Humanitarian Technologies and theU.N.’s International Telecommunication Union, and her project was selected from 318 teams across 79 countries. She also won the 2026 Award for Innovation from the National Extension Technology Community (NETC), and both the 2025 national and Western regional Educational Technology Awards from the National Association of Community Development Extension Professionals (NACDEP).

She has secured seven competitive grants totaling more than US $250,000 as principal investigator or co-principal investigator, including funding supported by the Department of Agriculture’s National Institute of Food and Agriculture.

An early love of design and problem-solving

Dong was born in Beijing. Both her parents are doctors.

As a child, she liked drawing new and inventive things. Sketching, she says, lets her picture solutions to problems in her head and put them on paper as practical designs.

That habit grew into a way of relating to her surroundings.

“I’ve always had a passion to create something tangible that can solve problems in the real world,” she says.

She doesn’t credit a single mentor for the direction her life has taken. Instead, she says all her teachers helped lay the groundwork for her career.

She attended the Inner Mongolia Normal University, in Hohhot, an institution that trains teachers. She earned two bachelor’s degrees there in 2013—one in geographical science and one in education.

She then earned a master’s degree in curriculum and instruction from Beijing Normal University in 2016.

That year, she moved to the United States to continue her graduate studies at the State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry, in Syracuse. She earned a master’s degree in environmental biology in 2020.

From outreach to extension work

After earning her second master’s degree, she joined Paul Smith’s College, in Paul Smiths, N.Y., as an education and outreach coordinator.

She managed several national watershed projects to protect rivers, lakes, and aquifers. Watersheds are areas of land from which water drains into bodies of water.

She also undertook invasive-species-prevention projects, wrote grants to secure project funding, and designed two educational websites and several outreach publications. One website, Maintain the Chain, helps lake residents, boaters, and visitors from around the world keep invasive species out of the Fulton Chain of Lakes in New York’s Adirondack Park.

In 2022, she joined Stewards of the Coast and Redwoods as program manager. The nonprofit, based in Guerneville, Calif., works with California State Parks to protect, restore, and educate the public about the parks along Sonoma County’s coast and the Russian River area. The region is known for its redwood forests, wineries, and resort towns.

She left in 2023 to join the CSU Extension as a regional specialist, a title she still holds.

Her employer is part of the Cooperative Extension System, a nationwide network run by land-grant universities, schools founded with federal grants to teach farming and other practical subjects. Extension faculty and staff share what researchers at their universities learn with the citizens of those states.

The cooperative system operates on three levels. It is overseen federally by the Department of Agriculture’s National Institute of Food and Agriculture, managed statewide through land-grant universities, and delivered locally by county offices and Extension agents across more than 3,000 counties.

The work goes well beyond farming, Dong says, also covering community and economic development, health initiatives, and the 4-H program, which teaches children hands-on skills in agriculture, science, leadership, and citizenship.

Extension faculty members’ performance is judged on their research, teaching, and service to the community, Dong says—similar to the way professors in academia are evaluated. The difference, she says, is the audience: Professors teach students; most extension specialists teach adults, including farmers, ranchers, and community leaders. The setting is different, too. Dong doesn’t commute from the campus to the countryside; she lives and works in it. Her office is in Sterling, a small rural town. But her projects serve the whole state, and many of the people she helps live one to four hours’ drive away. So, most of her work with farmers and ranchers happens by email, phone, and virtual meetings. County fairs, farmers markets, and agricultural events give her chances to meet large groups of them in person.

She can’t just hand Colorado residents research findings and expect them to figure out the information they need, she says.

“We need to translate that research into something more practical, and easier to use, that farmers and ranchers can understand immediately,” she says.

items.body:
## Re-Design

Wer den Kuketz-Blog in den vergangenen Wochen regelmäßig besucht hat, dürfte es bemerkt haben: Hier hat sich einiges verändert. Was ursprünglich mit ein paar kleineren Anpassungen begann, ist schließlich zu einer umfassenden Überarbeitung des gesamten WordPress-Themes geworden. Sowohl auf dem Smartphone als auch auf dem Tablet und Desktop präsentiert sich der Blog nun in einem neuen Gewand.

Dabei ging es mir nicht einfach darum, alles etwas moderner oder schicker aussehen zu lassen. Im Mittelpunkt stand die Frage, wie sich die vielen Inhalte übersichtlicher, angenehmer und möglichst ohne unnötige Ablenkung darstellen lassen.

## Weniger Ballast, mehr Übersicht

Die [Startseite](https://www.kuketz-blog.de/) wurde grundlegend neu gestaltet. Kurzbeiträge und ausführliche Artikel sind nun deutlicher voneinander getrennt und werden in einer übersichtlichen Kachelansicht präsentiert. Auch die Navigation, die Suche, die Darstellung einzelner Beiträge und zahlreiche kleinere Elemente wurden überarbeitet. Wer lieber chronologisch stöbert, findet sämtliche Veröffentlichungen weiterhin in der [Sitemap](https://www.kuketz-blog.de/sitemap/).

Auf größeren Bildschirmen ist die bisherige Seitenleiste verschwunden. Stattdessen bekommen die Inhalte mehr Raum. Auf mobilen Geräten wurde die Darstellung ebenfalls umfassend angepasst. Alles soll besser zusammenpassen und unabhängig von der Bildschirmgröße ein möglichst einheitliches Erscheinungsbild bieten.

Auch unter der Haube hat sich einiges getan. Zahlreiche Altlasten wurden entfernt, bestehende Funktionen vereinfacht und der Code aufgeräumt. An einem Grundsatz halte ich dabei weiterhin fest: Das Theme kommt ohne JavaScript aus. Für eine gut funktionierende Webseite braucht es schließlich nicht für jede Kleinigkeit ein zusätzliches Skript.

## Über Geschmack lässt sich streiten

Natürlich ist mir bewusst, dass ein neues Design nicht jedem gefallen wird. Manche mochten die bisherige Darstellung, andere werden sich erst an die neue Aufteilung gewöhnen müssen. Das ist völlig in Ordnung. Gestaltung ist immer auch Geschmackssache, und Veränderungen brauchen manchmal etwas Zeit.

Mir war vor allem wichtig, dass der Blog seinen Charakter behält. Er soll kein überladenes Nachrichtenportal werden, sondern ein Ort, an dem Inhalte im Mittelpunkt stehen. Mit möglichst wenig Ablenkung, einer klaren Struktur und einer angenehmen Lesbarkeit.

Ob mir das gelungen ist, müsst letztlich ihr entscheiden.

## Fertig – aber Feedback ist willkommen

Die Überarbeitung ist inzwischen abgeschlossen. Das neue Design steht und ich bin mit dem Ergebnis zufrieden. Trotzdem kann sich bei einer so umfangreichen Umgestaltung natürlich irgendwo noch ein kleiner Fehler eingeschlichen haben. Gerade unterschiedliche Browser, Geräte und Bildschirmgrößen bringen manchmal Überraschungen mit sich.

Deshalb freue ich mich über eure Rückmeldungen. Was gefällt euch? Was könnte besser sein? Und falls euch Darstellungsfehler oder andere Probleme auffallen, gebt mir gerne über die [Kontaktseite](https://www.kuketz-blog.de/kontakt/) Bescheid. Besonders hilfreich sind konkrete Hinweise, möglichst mit einem Screenshot.

Auch kritische Rückmeldungen sind ausdrücklich willkommen. Schließlich soll der Blog nicht nur mir gefallen, sondern vor allem für euch gut funktionieren.

Eines bleibt bei aller Veränderung unverändert: Der Kuketz-Blog steht weiterhin für unabhängige, kritische und möglichst verständliche Beiträge rund um IT-Sicherheit, Datenschutz und digitale Selbstbestimmung.

Die Verpackung ist neu. Der Anspruch bleibt derselbe.

Viel Freude beim Lesen und Stöbern!

👇

kuketz-blog.de wird vollständig durch Spenden unserer Leser getragen. [Unterstütze](https://www.kuketz-blog.de/unterstuetzen/) auch du unsere Arbeit und werde Teil dieser großartigen Community! ❤️

items.body:
Timothy Williamson will be the inaugural speaker in a new lecture series accompanying a new journal: *[The Chinese Journal of Philosophy](https://academic.oup.com/cjp?)* (CJP).

Published by Oxford University Press, the CJP is an open-access (including no cost to authors) general philosophy journal.

It is edited by Roger T. Ames (Hawaii), Wei Cheng (Peking), Nicolas De Warren (Penn State), Sebastian Sunday Grève (Peking), and You Zhao (Peking).

The journal is open to submissions “from anyone working in philosophy and on all philosophical topics.” According to its [website](https://academic.oup.com/cjp?),

> the journal aims to represent the multitude of topics and approaches that may fall under the heading of ‘philosophy’ in the world today, with a special focus on philosophical research that has the potential to make different traditions of thought more fruitful for one another.

That is to say, it is not a journal primarily about Chinese philosophy, anymore than the *Canadian Journal of Philosophy* is a journal about Canadian philosophy, or the *Australasian Journal of Philosophy* is about Australasian philosophy. The [note](https://phil.pku.edu.cn/xzqk/cjp/intro.htm), “like these other journals, the *Chinese Journal of Philosophy* originates in a particular region whilst editing and publishing as an international collective, operating in English, and promoting work from around the world.”

CJP is currently open for submissions and plans to begin publishing articles in April.

The launch of the journal includes the start of a new lecture series from the [Department of Philosophy and Religious Studies at Peking University](https://phil.pku.edu.cn/index.htm). Williamson’s inaugural lecture is this Wednesday, and will be delivered in person and [online](https://us06web.zoom.us/j/86727223234).

Learn more about the journal [↗ academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/cjp?).

**Novation aktualisiert die Firmware der Controller-Keyboards Launchkey MK4 und FLkey 2 auf Version 2.0, die viele interessante Neuerungen mit sich bringt.**

Launchkey MK4 und FLkey 2 Firmware 2.0 (Bildquelle: Novation)

Inhalte

- Launchkey MK4 und FLkey 2 Firmware 2.0
- Arpeggiator
- OLED Display und NKS
- Pot Style
- Novation Play
- Preis und Verfügbarkeit: Novation Launchkey Serie MK4
- Preis und Verfügbarkeit: Novation FLkey Serie
- Novation Launchkey MK4 & FLkey 2 Firmware Update 2.0: Features
- Links

## Launchkey MK4 und FLkey 2 Firmware 2.0

Novation präsentiert das Firmware Update 2.0 für seine Controller Keyboards Launchkey MK4 und FLkey 2. Das Update bringt neue Abspielrichtungen für den Arpeggiator und das Verhalten der Regler lässt sich anpassen

Launchkey MK4 Serie und Launchkey Mini MK4 (Bildquelle: Novation)

## Wie update ich Launchkey MK4 und FLkey 2?

Launchkey MK4 und FLkey 2 lassen sich über Novation Components auf die Firmware v2.0 aktualisieren.

## Arpeggiator

Der Arpeggiator von Launchkey MK4 und FLkey 2 wurde mit sechs neuen Abspielrichtungen ausgestattet. Er verfügt jetzt insgesamt über 14 Möglichkeiten. Die drei Chord Modi können jetzt den Arpeggiator triggern, wodurch man sehr einfach Sequenzen erstellen kann. Die Arpeggiator Snapshots erlauben es, acht verschiedene Arp Einstellungen im Gerät zu speichern.

FLkey 2 Serie (Bildquelle: Novation)

## OLED Display und NKS

Die Novation Controller Keyboards unterstützen jetzt auch Native Instruments NKS. Dieses Steuerungsprotokoll unterstützt mittlerweile über 2.000 Plug-ins. Mit den Novation Keyboards können diese dank NKS jetzt einfach kontrolliert werden.

Das OLED Display zeigt an, welche Parameter gerade geregelt werden, wodurch sich der Controller noch mehr wie ein echtes Hardware Instrument anfühlt.

## Pot Style

Laut Novation hat sich die Community gewünscht, dass sich die Regler wie klassische Potis verhalten. Diesem Wunsch erfüllt Novation mit der Encoder Charakteristik Pot Style.

Launchkey MK4 White Serie (Bildquelle: Novation)

## Novation Play

Als Besitzer eines Launchkey MK4 oder FLkey 2 bekommt ihr jetzt auch noch kostenlos das Software Instrument Novation Play geschenkt, das speziell für die beiden Controller Keyboard Serien entwickelt wurde. Das OLED Display zeigt an, welche Parameter gerade geregelt werden.

Launchkey 88 MK4 (Bildquelle: Novation)

## Preis und Verfügbarkeit: Novation Launchkey Serie MK4

**Die Novation Launchkey Serie MK4 ist mit 88, 61, 49,[37](https://www.bonedo.de/artikel/novation-launchkey-37-mk4/)und [25](https://www.bonedo.de/artikel/novation-launchkey-25-37-mk4-test/) Tasten erhältlich. Darüber hinaus gibt es die Launchkey Mini Modelle mit [37](https://www.bonedo.de/artikel/novation-launchkey-mini-37-mk4-test/)und 25 Minitasten. Die regulären Modelle decken eine Preisspanne von 444,00 bis 99,00 Euro ab.**

**Während der Thomann Cyber Deals ist das Launchkey 37 auf 159,00 Euro reduziert. Das Launchkey 25 kostet 139,00 Euro. Das Launchkey Mini 37 ist für 119,00 Euro und das Launchkey Mini 25 für 99,00 Euro erhältlich.**

## Preis und Verfügbarkeit: Novation FLkey Serie

**Die Novation FLkey Serie ist mit 61, 49, [37](https://www.bonedo.de/artikel/novation-launchkey-37-mk4/) und 25 Tasten erhältlich. Die Preise liegen regulär zwischen 125,00 und 314,00 Euro. Während der Thomann Cyber Deals ist das Novation FLkey 61 auf 199,00 Euro und das FLkey 49 auf 179,00 Euro reduziert.**

## Novation Launchkey MK4 & FLkey 2 Firmware Update 2.0: Features

- Sechs neue Arp Typen. Insgesamt stehen jetzt 14 zur Auswahl
- Arpeggiator Routing: Route den Output der Chord Modi oder externes MIDI in den Arpeggiator
- Arpeggiator Snapshots: Speichere bis zu acht Arpeggiator Einstellungen in den Keyboards
- Mit der Encoder Charakteristik Pot Style verhalten sich die Regler wie klassische Potis
- Mit der Software Novation Play werden auf dem OLED Display angezeigt, welche Parameter angesteuert werden. Volle NKS 2.0 Unterstützung

items.body:
Hi there,

When an AI project disappoints, the first reaction is to blame the model. Try a bigger one, tweak the prompt, add more instructions.

But most of the time the weak link is upstream: where the AI finds the information it needs. Chatbot, agent or search, it’s only as good as what it can retrieve.

That’s the job of a **vector database**, which stores your data so AI can find what’s relevant by meaning, not just keywords. AWS Marketplace put together a guide on how to choose one.

[Download the evaluation guide ›](https://aws.amazon.com/marketplace/build-learn/vector-databases-for-ai)

**One building block behind three AI patterns:**

- Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines retrieve relevant context so your model responds from your data, not its training set.
- Agentic memory gives agents semantic recall across sessions instead of replaying conversation histories.
- Semantic search matches intent, not keywords.

All three depend on the same layer: **a vector database**.

[Explore what to evaluate for your use case](https://aws.amazon.com/marketplace/build-learn/vector-databases-for-ai):

- Architecture diagrams: Each pattern mapped with Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
- Evaluation framework: Hybrid search, scaling, hosting trade-offs, embedding pipeline fit, and metadata filtering
- Free trials: Test vector databases in AWS Marketplace and start building

Get the guide and find the right vector database for your stack.

[Download the evaluation guide ›](https://aws.amazon.com/marketplace/build-learn/vector-databases-for-ai)

- Tools are designed to plug in to your AWS workflows and integrate with your favorite AWS services
- Evaluate fast with free trials and developer-tier pricing to support fast prototyping
- Avoid upfront license fees and pay only for what you use, consolidating billing with your AWS account
- A broad selection of tools across AI, data, observability, security and more can enhance how you build with AWS

items.body:
Anfang November hat das Landesschulamt Sachsen-Anhalt die [Abmahnung des Lehrers Max Heckel aus dessen Personalakte gelöscht](https://www.spiegel.de/panorama/bildung/afd-in-sachsen-anhalt-ein-lehrer-eine-abmahnung-und-der-streit-ueber-die-neutralitaetspflicht-a-2a9dc291-a9d7-46fd-b6ce-00fcc109998c), die es ihm wegen AfD-kritischer Aussagen im Unterricht vor knapp eineinhalb Jahren erteilt hatte. Drei Wochen vor dem geplanten Gerichtstermin am Arbeitsgericht Magdeburg hat sich damit der Gegenstand der gerichtlichen Auseinandersetzung erledigt. Der Fall gibt dennoch Anlass, sich vor Augen zu führen, was der Begriff der Neutralität in der Schule aus rechtlicher Sicht bedeutet, wozu Lehrkräfte im Unterricht verpflichtet sind und wie sie sich verhalten müssen, wenn parteipolitische Positionen thematisiert werden.

Der Neutralitätsbegriff in der Schule hat einen unmissverständlichen verfassungsrechtlichen Rahmen. Er fordert von den Lehrkräften, sich aktiv und ständig zur freiheitlich demokratischen Grundordnung sowie den verfassungsrechtlichen Grundwerten zu bekennen. Eine normative Wertneutralität umfasst der Begriff gerade nicht. Zudem ist es Lehrkräften verboten, in religiös-weltanschaulicher sowie parteipolitischer Hinsicht Druck auf die Schüler*innen auszuüben und ihnen eigene Positionen aufzudrängen. Hieraus abzuleiten, dass menschenverachtende Positionen in der Schule als legitim dargestellt werden müssen, ist falsch und verfassungswidrig.

## Der Fall Max Heckel

Mit dem Klagegegenstand hat sich jetzt auch die Hoffnung auf eine verbindliche Klarstellung der rechtlichen Fragen erledigt, die angesichts der [verbreiteten](https://www.spiegel.de/panorama/bildung/lehrkraefte-umfrage-die-grosse-angst-vor-politischen-debatten-im-klassenzimmer-a-3454943f-9ceb-42c5-b046-2e1c419fa608) und [von der AfD bewusst herbeigeführten](https://verfassungsblog.de/lehrermeldeportale-darf-der-staat-nicht-akzeptieren/) Verunsicherung von Lehrkräften über den Fall hinaus bedeutsam gewesen wäre. [Seit 2018](https://www.gew.de/die-meldeportale-der-afd) betreibt die AfD online Meldeportale unter dem Titel „Neutrale Schule“, die dazu auffordern, angeblich neutralitätswidriges Verhalten von Lehrkräften bei den AfD-Fraktionen zu melden. Das Ziel dieses Vorgehens scheint die Einschüchterung von Lehrkräften zu sein, die Positionen der AfD im Unterricht kritisieren.

Der Lehrer Max Heckel wurde im Unterricht an einer Sekundarschule in Stendal von einem Schüler gefragt, ob er bei der letzten Bundestagswahl die AfD gewählt habe. In einem [Spiegel-Interview](https://www.spiegel.de/panorama/bildung/afd-der-lehrer-max-heckel-aus-stendal-will-einen-praezedenzfall-schaffen-a-20444482-fb06-4259-bea5-d7ad40ac0955) berichtet Heckel den Verlauf des hieraus entstandenen Gesprächs über die politischen Positionen der AfD: Selbst nicht die AfD gewählt zu haben, begründete er mit der Steuerpolitik der AfD sowie ihren Plänen zum Abbau schulischer Inklusion und zur Durchsetzung von „Remigration“. Dabei stellte er Vergleiche zu den Positionen anderer politischer Parteien an und erklärte, worauf sich seine persönliche Position gründet. Hierzu zeigte er den Schüler*innen eine Statistik des Leibniz-Instituts für Europäische Wirtschaftsforschung, gab ein Zitat von Björn Höcke wieder, bildete Beispiele zur praktischen Umsetzung von Inklusion in der Schule und erklärte, woher der „Remigrationsbegriff“ stammt und was er bedeutet. Zudem betonte er der Klasse gegenüber, dass für ihn alle Schüler*innen gleich viel wert sind und er inklusives Lernen für sinnvoll hält – und nahm damit implizit Bezug auf Werte wie die Menschenwürde aus Art. 1 Abs. 1 GG und das in der UN-Behindertenrechtskonvention verankerte Recht auf inklusive Bildung. Zum Ende des Gesprächs sagte er, wenn man die AfD wähle, müsse man „a) reich, b) frei von Moral oder c) nicht bei Verstand sein“, fügte aber auch hinzu, dass es natürlich trotzdem jedem freistehe, die AfD zu wählen, der zu einem anderen Schluss käme.

Fünf Wochen später erteilte das Schulamt Sachsen-Anhalt ihm eine Abmahnung und vertrat darin die Ansicht, dass Heckel mit seinen Äußerungen die Neutralitätspflicht verletzt habe und sie nicht der Aufklärung, sondern allein dem Ziel gedient hätten, die Schüler*innen davon zu überzeugen, nicht die AfD zu wählen. Zuvor hatte der AfD-Spitzenkandidat Ulrich Siegmund, dessen Ehefrau an derselben Schule arbeitet, im [Landtag von einem „Fall in Stendal“ berichtet](https://www.spiegel.de/panorama/bildung/afd-in-sachsen-anhalt-ein-lehrer-eine-abmahnung-und-der-streit-ueber-die-neutralitaetspflicht-a-2a9dc291-a9d7-46fd-b6ce-00fcc109998c) und mitgeteilt, die AfD habe eine Dienstaufsichtsbeschwerde erhoben und nach einiger Zeit noch einmal Druck auf das Landesschulamt ausgeübt. In der anschließenden Auseinandersetzung drohte das Schulamt dem Lehrer mit Kündigung. Schließlich entschied sich Max Heckel, rechtlich gegen die Abmahnung vorzugehen, um die relevanten Fragen verbindlich klären zu lassen: War die Abmahnung rechtmäßig? Durfte er das geschilderte Gespräch auf diese Weise mit den Schüler*innen führen? Durfte er sagen, AfD-Wähler*innen müssten wohl „reich, frei von Moral oder nicht bei Verstand“ sein, oder hat er damit die Grundsätze der schulischen Neutralität verletzt? Welche Anforderungen bestehen konkret an das Verhalten von Lehrkräften im Unterrichtsgespräch über parteipolitische Positionen?

## Der rechtliche Rahmen der Neutralität in der Schule

Es gibt in Deutschland keine explizit normierte Definition des Begriffs „Neutralität in der Schule“. Stattdessen ergibt sich der Inhalt des Neutralitätsgebots aus dem Grundgesetz, den Landesverfassungen, den Schulgesetzen der Bundesländer, dem Beamten- und Arbeitsrecht sowie den internationalen Menschenrechtsverträgen.

In Art. 7 Abs. 1 GG enthält die Verfassung den Bildungs- und Erziehungsauftrag des Staates. Er verpflichtet den Staat dazu, ein funktionsfähiges Schulsystem sicherzustellen, das Wissen, Fertigkeiten und soziale Kompetenzen vermittelt. Dieser Auftrag dient dem Ziel, eine chancengleiche Entwicklung der Kinder und Jugendlichen zu eigenverantwortlichen Persönlichkeiten zu ermöglichen, die sich an demokratischen Prozessen beteiligen. Die Schulgesetze der Bundesländer stellen klar, dass die Schule einen Auftrag zur demokratischen Bildung und Erziehung der Schüler*innen auf der normativen Grundlage der Verfassung hat. So bestimmt beispielsweise § 1 des Schulgesetzes Sachsen-Anhalt:

items.body:
Eczema causes itchy, inflamed rashes on the skin

Evgeniia Gordeeva/Getty Images

Over a third of people with moderate to severe eczema taking part in a clinical trial have seen their skin completely or almost completely clear up after taking an experimental pill for four months. The drug targets a part of the immune system that causes eczema when it gets stuck in overdrive, and it may be preferable to the current standard treatment, which has to be injected.

“It definitely looks promising,” says [Gayle Ross](https://www.thermh.org.au/our-people/gayle-ross) at the Royal Melbourne Hospital.

[Read more Chronic inflammation messes with your mind. Here’s how to calm it](https://www.newscientist.com/article/2491017-chronic-inflammation-messes-with-your-mind-heres-how-to-calm-it/)

Eczema, or atopic dermatitis, is a chronic skin condition characterised by itchy, inflamed rashes and broken skin that can become infected. It is driven by an overactive immune pathway involving two signalling proteins called interleukin-4 and interleukin-13.

In 2017, the companies Sanofi and Regeneron received approval in the US for their jointly developed eczema drug dupilumab, which blocks interleukin-4 and interleukin-13 signalling. But, although the medication is [effective](https://www.dupixenthcp.com/atopicdermatitis/efficacy-safety/adult-real-world-results), it has had [limited uptake](https://www.sciencedirect.com/org/science/article/pii/S256209592300065X) in the US because it must be injected under the skin and costs up to $59,000 per year for those without insurance coverage.

Now, another company, Kymera Therapeutics, has developed an alternative treatment that can be taken in pill form, called KT-621. It targets the same immune pathway as dupilumab but degrades a protein called STAT6 that is activated downstream from interleukin-4 and interleukin-13 in the development of eczema.

Free newsletter

#### Sign up to Health Check

[Sign up to newsletter](https://www.newscientist.com/sign-up/health/)

In the [clinical trial](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07217015), 244 adults with an average age of 39 and moderate to severe eczema were randomised to take KT-621 at three different doses or a placebo pill every day for 16 weeks.

Those taking the most effective dose experienced an average [72 per cent reduction](https://investors.kymeratx.com/news-releases/news-release-details/kymera-therapeutics-announces-positive-results-broaden2-phase-2b) in their eczema severity on a standard scale, compared to 27 per cent in the placebo group. What’s more, 38 per cent of participants taking KT-621 had completely healed skin or almost completely healed skin by the end of the trial.

“These results exceeded our expectations,” said [Terence Rooney](https://www.kymeratx.com/about-us/leadership/terence-rooney-md/), the chief medical officer of Kymera Therapeutics, when announcing the results in a [webcast](https://investors.kymeratx.com/news-releases/news-release-details/kymera-therapeutics-announces-positive-results-broaden2-phase-2b) on 23 November. He showed before-and-after photos of one man who had had severe eczema all over his torso at the beginning of the trial, which disappeared by the end.

“It’s obviously early days and the trial had relatively small patient numbers, but [KT-621] looks like it has similar efficacy to dupilumab, which is currently the standard of care for moderate to severe atopic dermatitis, and it would be nice to have an oral option as opposed to an injection,” says Ross.

[Read more You can upgrade your immune system, but not in the way you think](https://www.newscientist.com/article/2507511-you-can-upgrade-your-immune-system-but-not-in-the-way-you-think/)

The medication also appeared safe. A small proportion of participants developed conjunctivitis as a side-effect, but it tended to be mild and didn’t cause anyone to discontinue treatment, said Rooney. In fact, since the trial, almost every participant has chosen to continue taking the daily pill as part of an ongoing study, he said.

People taking dupilumab can develop conjunctivitis too, so “we’re pretty used to dealing with that”, says Ross.

Kymera Therapeutics is now planning a larger trial of KT-621 for treating eczema that is scheduled to begin in mid-2027. The company is also currently running a [trial of KT-621 in people with asthma](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07323654), since the condition is caused by the same overactive immune pathway operating in the lungs. It hasn’t yet said how much the drug will cost if it eventually receives regulatory approval.

items.body:
**Lachen als Persönlichkeitstest: Die Bewertung von Cartoons und Internet-Memes könnte Hinweise auf bestimmte problematische Charakterzüge liefern. In einer Studie konnten Computermodelle aus solchen Bewertungen vor allem auf erhöhte Fragebogenwerte für Psychopathie und Alltagssadismus schließen. Für die Beurteilung einzelner Menschen eignet sich dieses Verfahren jedoch nicht.**

**St. Petersburg (Russland).** Was für den einen ein harmloser Witz ist, empfindet der andere vielleicht als geschmacklos oder verletzend. Solche Unterschiede im Humor sind auch für die Persönlichkeitspsychologie interessant. Denn in ihnen könnten sich charakterliche Eigenheiten widerspiegeln, die Menschen bei einer direkten Befragung nicht unbedingt preisgeben.

Vier besonders problematische Persönlichkeitsmerkmale werden als dunkle Tetrade zusammengefasst. Sie umfasst neben der Psychopathie, die unter anderem mit Gefühlskälte und mangelndem Mitgefühl einhergeht, auch den Narzissmus, den manipulativen Machiavellismus und den Alltagssadismus. Letzterer beschreibt die Neigung, Gefallen am Leid anderer zu finden. Doch wie lassen sich solche Eigenschaften erfassen, wenn die Befragten ihre eigenen Schwächen verschleiern oder nicht erkennen?

### 71 Bilder als indirekter Persönlichkeitstest

Ein Team der National Research University Higher School of Economics (HSE) hat nun untersucht, ob sich die dunkle Tetrade auch anhand von Humorbewertungen erfassen lässt. Dazu bekamen 200 russischsprachige Erwachsene zwischen 18 und 72 Jahren jeweils 71 Cartoons, Memes und andere humoristische Bilder in zufälliger Reihenfolge zu sehen.

Die Testpersonen beurteilten jedes Motiv danach, wie witzig und wie freundlich oder grausam sie es fanden. Zusätzlich sollten sie einschätzen, ob sich der Witz gegen seinen Urheber oder gegen andere richtete. Ein Fragebogen erfasste anschließend, wie ausgeprägt die vier dunklen Persönlichkeitsmerkmale bei den Teilnehmern waren.

Anhand dieser Fragebogenwerte teilten die Wissenschaftler die Testpersonen für jedes Persönlichkeitsmerkmal separat in zwei Gruppen ein. Den 30 Prozent mit den jeweils höchsten Werten standen die übrigen 70 Prozent gegenüber. Sechs verschiedene Verfahren des maschinellen Lernens sollten anhand der Bildbewertungen zwischen diesen Gruppen unterscheiden. Die Modelle wurden mit Daten eines Teils der Teilnehmer trainiert und an den übrigen überprüft.

### Humorbewertungen hängen mit Charakterzügen zusammen

Die statistischen Analysen ergaben: Bei höheren Psychopathie- oder Sadismuswerten empfanden die Testpersonen die Bilder tendenziell als witziger, stuften den Humor aber zugleich als weniger freundlich ein. Auch stärker narzisstisch geprägte Teilnehmer bewerteten die Bilder im Mittel als lustiger. Ein statistisch signifikanter Zusammenhang mit der wahrgenommenen Freundlichkeit fehlte bei ihnen jedoch.

Am besten konnten die Computermodelle erhöhte Psychopathiewerte erkennen. Der beste Wert für die Trennschärfe (AUC) lag bei 0,819. Auf dieser Skala steht 0,5 für die Trennschärfe einer Zufallsentscheidung und 1 für eine perfekte Unterscheidung der Gruppen. Alltagssadismus ließ sich weniger gut, Narzissmus nur mäßig gut vorhersagen. Bei Machiavellismus war die Unterscheidung nicht besser als zufällig.

### Kein Instrument für die Individualdiagnostik

Allerdings bleiben Fragebögen auch bei diesem indirekten Ansatz ein zentraler Bestandteil der Methode. Sind die Selbstauskünfte verzerrt, kann sich das auf die Modellvorhersagen übertragen. Zudem erwiesen sich die Fragen zum Machiavellismus als vergleichsweise wenig konsistent, was die Interpretation des fehlenden Zusammenhangs erschwert.

Auch ist offen, ob die Befunde auf andere Kulturen und Humorformen übertragbar sind. Hinzu kommt, dass 172 der 200 Testpersonen einen Hochschulabschluss hatten. Aus der Freude an schwarzem Humor lässt sich daher keineswegs auf eine Psychopathie schließen. Die Untersuchung liefert lediglich einen ersten Hinweis auf die Eignung von Humorbewertungen für die Persönlichkeitsforschung, nicht auf die Verlässlichkeit eines diagnostischen Tests.

**Quellen:**

- Originalstudie im Fachmagazin [Journal of Individual Differences](https://econtent.hogrefe.com/doi/10.1027/1614-0001/a000465), doi: [10.1027/1614-0001/a000465](https://doi.org/10.1027/1614-0001/a000465)

items.title: Data centers are getting their own natural gas power plants
items.subtitle: Need for speed: Data center developers are bypassing years-long grid connection waits by building their own private natural gas power plants.
items.feedText: Over 100 such facilities have been announced in the US since early 2025, with combined capacity exceeding 115 gigawatts. A dirtier shortcut: If all planned US projects proceed, they could emit 152 million metric tons more CO₂ annually than if those data centers were grid connected, according to BloombergNEF tracking. Fossil fuel lock-in is a real risk: Though developers pitch private gas plants as temporary bridges until grid connections come through, experts warn that once built, operators are unlikely to simpl…
items.body:
One of the biggest roadblocks to starting up a data center is getting approval to connect to the electric grid—a wait that could last as long as a decade. Some developers aren’t willing to wait and are instead opting to build their own off-grid, or behind-the-meter, gas power plants to fuel the AI boom.

xAI’s Memphis campus has famously used dozens of natural gas turbines, some of them without permits, as far back as 2024. At the time, that facility was a rarity, and it faced scrutiny from regulators. It remains the subject of [ongoing legal battles](https://yaleclimateconnections.org/2026/10/why-the-naacp-is-suing-xai/). But the strategy of going off-grid for power has since become a lot more common.

As of October 2026, data center developers have announced plans for more than 100 behind-the-meter gas power plants at facilities in the US, according to data from Cleanview, a market intelligence company. The facilities have a combined planned capacity of over 115 gigawatts, more than double the peak power demand of California. The vast majority of these announcements have come since the beginning of 2025.

It’s possible that not all these facilities will be built; only a small fraction are under construction or operating today. But there’s a growing trend of large data centers looking to build their own power supply, and this could shape the grid—and its climate impacts—for decades to come.

Building your own power plant is generally more expensive than just hooking up to the grid, but the AI rush has made developers willing to pay a significant premium to get online faster. “The biggest motivator for on-site power right now from data centers is speed,” says Musfika Mishi, an associate at BloombergNEF, an energy consultancy.

When developers want to build a new industrial facility—like a data center—that requires a lot of electricity, they need to request a grid connection from a local utility or regional grid operator. That request kicks off a yearslong process in which grid planners study the existing grid to understand what would need to be built to safely deliver power to the facility without compromising reliability. Upgrades might be required, like building new transmission lines or larger transformers, and the developer might be on the hook to help pay for them.

Rather than waiting for that process to play out, developers can opt to instead build their own power plants. These facilities are referred to as “behind the meter” because they sit on the customer’s side of a utility meter—supplying the building directly, rather than relying on a utility via a grid hookup.

“This shift in the data center developers’ power strategies towards off-grid gas raises some important questions about how data centers will be powered going forward,” says Brendan Pierpont, director of electricity at the think tank Energy Innovation.

Behind-the-meter doesn’t always mean being totally disconnected from the grid, however. Some facilities may build such plants as a temporary measure, eventually connecting to the grid and tapping their own power plants only as backup. “It’s really just a very expensive way to bridge that maybe five-to-seven-year timeline gap until these data centers can get a grid connection,” Pierpont says.

Even if gas plants are pitched as a near-term solution, building new fossil fuel infrastructure could lead to longer-term effects, since an operator might choose to continue running plants once they’ve spent money building them. “Even though data centers say that it’s a grid-bridging solution, the probability that it is going to be in use much longer is a real risk, and that leads to fossil fuel lock-in,” Mishi says.

The on-site gas rush could have major implications for greenhouse-gas emissions. Today, the US grid is still reliant on fossil fuels, but nuclear and renewables together make up about 40% of electricity generation. That means making a grid connection is generally a lower-emissions option than relying entirely on an on-site gas plant. (That’s not the case everywhere—India, for example, is expecting to see a data center boom in the next decade, and its grid is largely served by emissions-intensive coal-fired power plants today.)

Utilities are already planning to build more natural gas power plants on the grid to meet rising electricity demand. Equipment manufacturers are struggling to keep up with the surge, and it’s pushing developers of behind-the-meter plants toward less-efficient alternatives.

Today, large natural gas plants generally use combined-cycle turbines. These capture heat to generate additional electricity, making them more efficient than single-cycle turbines, which are generally cheaper to build. Very few of the planned behind-the-meter facilities, however, will use combined-cycle turbines, Mishi says. That means these off-grid plants will likely produce more greenhouse-gas emissions than even other natural gas resources.

BloombergNEF is also [tracking](https://about.bnef.com/insights/data-centers/data-center-power-demand-is-set-to-surge-raising-new-climate-challenges-bloombergnef/) on-site natural gas plants at data centers, finding 181 gigawatts’ worth of announced projects globally, with 90% of that capacity designated for the US. If all planned behind-the-meter gas plants for data centers in the US go ahead, they could emit 345 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent each year by 2035, according to a BloombergNEF [report](https://about.bnef.com/insights/data-centers/data-center-power-demand-is-set-to-surge-raising-new-climate-challenges-bloombergnef/). That’s 152 million metric tons more than if those data centers pulled power from the US grid—a difference greater than the total annual emissions of the Netherlands.

And while it might seem logical that data centers bringing their own power could ease communities’ energy bills, those facilities going off-grid doesn’t protect prices for everyone else, says Matthias Fripp, director of global policy research at Energy Innovation. More demand for natural gas could push its price higher, he explains, which could in turn raise rates for the roughly 60% of American households that use natural gas for heating and cooking. That effect may also trickle into electricity prices.

There’s still a lot of uncertainty about how much of this gas rush will come to fruition, so this future isn’t set in stone. Today, just 4.9 gigawatts of behind-the-meter gas projects tied to data centers are operating, and 15.8 gigawatts are under construction, according to Cleanview’s data.

Creative solutions could also help limit the climate burden of the on-site gas buildout, BloombergNEF’s Mishi says. Building gas alongside on-site renewables or energy storage could help limit how often a gas plant needs to fire up, she says, though the economics of building multiple energy sources can be tricky.

items.title: AI-generated video falsely shared as Crimean Bridge damage
items.subtitle: The fake footage doesn’t match official photos of the bridge, and Google says the clip contains a SynthID watermark.
items.feedText: A video shows damage caused to the Crimean Bridge after Ukrainian strikes in November 2026. This video isn’t real and was made with AI. A viral video supposedly showing damage to the Crimean Bridge after it was attacked by Ukraine in November 2026 isn’t real and was made with AI. The structure in the fake clip doesn’t match the real bridge, and Google’s SynthID detector told us the video contained an invisible SynthID watermark which suggests that it was made or edited with Google AI. The video has been 'liked' thousands of times online. It was first shared by an Instagram account on 16 November with claims it showed the damage caused by an initial drone attack .
items.body:
# AI-generated video falsely shared as Crimean Bridge damage – Full Fact

## AI-generated video falsely shared as Crimean Bridge damage

## What was claimed

A video shows damage caused to the Crimean Bridge after Ukrainian strikes in November 2026.

## Our verdict

False. This video isn’t real and was made with AI.

A viral video supposedly showing damage to the Crimean Bridge after it was attacked by Ukraine in November 2026 isn’t real and was made with AI.

The structure in the fake clip doesn’t match the real bridge, and Google’s SynthID detector told us the video contained an invisible SynthID watermark which suggests that it was made or edited with Google AI.

The video has been 'liked' thousands of times online. It was first shared by an Instagram account on 16 November with claims it showed the damage caused by an initial drone attack .

The first attack on 16 November reportedly damaged the arch over the road section of the bridge, but the fake footage does not match what the real bridge looks like.

Join 75,000 newsletter subscribers who trust us to check the facts

Sign up to get weekly updates on politics, immigration, health and more.

Subscribe to weekly email newsletters from Full Fact for updates on politics, immigration, health and more. Our fact checks are free to read but not to produce, so you will also get occasional emails about fundraising and other ways you can help. You can unsubscribe at any time. For more information about how we use your data see our Privacy Policy .

The fake version shows two road bridges. In reality , one of the bridges is a rail bridge . The real rail bridge arch also has a distinct criss-cross pattern on the lowest rung near the track that isn’t present in the fake version.

Ukraine attacked the bridge, which links occupied Crimea to Russia, again on 17 November, severing the road bridge , and on 19 November , reportedly damaging the rail bridge too.

Again, official photos of the damage caused by these later strikes do not match the fake video circulating online.

It can be difficult to tell the difference between real and AI-generated videos, particularly when they circulate after real events. Our misinformation toolkit can help you become more confident to spot AI-generated content.

Tags

This article is part of our work fact checking potentially false pictures, videos and stories on Facebook. You can read more about this—and find out how to report Facebook content— here . For the purposes of that scheme, we’ve rated this claim as altered because this video isn’t real and was made with AI.

## Was this helpful?

Full Fact fights for good, reliable information in the media, online, and in politics.

items.title: CoEVFold suite: User friendly pipelines to visually represent protein coevolution
items.subtitle: Graham, Liam Cremona, Robin Little, Christopher D.
items.feedText: Multiple sequence alignment (MSA) data underlies current principles in protein folding and protein-protein interaction prediction, from which deep-learning models trained on protein sequence and structure datasets can predict protein structure. However, what is missing are user-friendly tools that enable researchers to identify and visualise coevolution, the principal signal that these MSAs encode. items.body: Multiple sequence alignment (MSA) data underlies current principles in protein folding and protein-protein interaction prediction, from which deep-learning models trained on protein sequence and structure datasets can predict protein structure. However, what is missing are user-friendly tools that enable researchers to identify and visualise coevolution, the principal signal that these MSAs encode. Here we present tools to identify and visualize coevolution, through a pipeline (CoEVFold) that uses basic direct coupling algorithms derived from GREMLIN and an input alignment of sequences from MMseqs2. We also provide notebooks to calculate coevolution with alternative methods such as CCMpred or plmc. The pipeline generates a visual representation of coevolution for a single protein but can also represent coevolution of homomeric or heteromeric protein complexes, as well as coevolution within protein networks. The input for this pipeline can be an amino acid sequence, or protein structures from AlphaFold/RoseTTAFold, the user’s own files or the PDB. Using proteins from well-studied prokaryotic and eukaryotic model systems (Bacillus subtilis, Escherichia coli and Saccharomyces cerevisiae), as well as phage proteins, we show that CoEVFold detects coevolution between proteins known to interact, between protomers of known oligomers, and within known protein complexes. Benchmarked against 18 heteromeric complexes of known structure, the top-ranked inter-protein couplings identified interface contacts with a precision of 0.8 or more in 7 complexes, and CoEVMapper rankings agreed with STRING associations for an Escherichia coli cell-wall synthesis network (ROC AUC 0.72–0.74). For homo-oligomers, the top-ranked coevolution pairs not explained by the monomer structure were protomer–protomer contacts in 25% (SpoIIIE) and 47% (MlaD) of cases, against 2% or less expected by chance. The coupling calculation for a ~ 950-residue complex took 114 s with GREMLIN, compared with 116 s for CCMpred and 2,060 s for plmc. Collectively, this suite of tools, named ‘CoEVFold suite’, has broad applicability and provide a useful toolkit to those interested in dissecting protein-protein interactions and networks.

items.body:
Thomas Mann ca. 1925–1945. Photograph by the Los Angeles Daily News. Courtesy of the UCLA Charles E. Young Research Library Department of Special Collections.

Colm Tóibín has been writing about Thomas Mann and his family—his wife, Katia; brother Heinrich;  daughters Erika, Monika, and Elisabeth; and sons Klaus, Golo, and Michael—for thirty years. The Irish novelist read Mann’s first novel, Buddenbrooks, as a teenager; in 1996, he was assigned to review three hefty biographies of Mann for the London Review of Books, to which he has subsequently contributed still more essays on the writer.

In 2021, Tóibín published his monumental novel The Magician, which recreates in vignette Mann’s childhood in Lübeck, youth in Munich and Italy, international fame as a Nobel laureate, wartime exile in France and the United States, and death in Switzerland at the age of eighty. Tóibín’s Mann is a luftmensch of a patriarch, impassively observing his own drift through time when he’s not absorbed by his craft. Der Zauberer, the children call him: the magician. Inscrutable and magnetic, he has the ability to make things appear as if from thin air.

Earlier this year, the Polish filmmaker Paweł Pawlikowski’s seventh feature, Fatherland, premiered at the Cannes Film Festival. The film follows Mann (Hanns Zischler) and his daughter Erika (Sandra Hüller) as they return to a divided Germany after the war to accept the Goethe Prize. Fatherland began as an adaptation of The Magician, though Pawlikowski’s script departs quite liberally from both the novel and historical fact: notably, it was Katia, mostly absent from the film, who traveled with Mann, rather than Erika, who refused to go. Tóibín, who is thanked in the credits, maintains that there is “not a line” of his dialogue in the film, yet certain phrasings ring familiar, as does the tone, a deadpan reckoning with loss, love, and fear. This fall, I called Tóibín at his home in Los Angeles, where he wrote much of The Magician, to discuss the Mann family, exile, and the author’s enmeshment in the politics of his day.

INTERVIEWER

Seven Palms, the Pacific Palisades home of the Manns from 1942 to 1952, is not open to the public, and yet you were allowed to pay it a visit on your first trip to Los Angeles, in 2005. How did that come about?

COLM TÓIBÍN

I had won the Los Angeles Times Book Prize, but the schlep from Dublin to L.A. for the award ceremony didn’t interest me. It’s a long journey. I said to the L.A. Times, “Look, if you can get me into Thomas Mann’s house, then I’ll come.” The people who bought the house from the Manns were still living there, though they were loath to let anyone in. But for some reason, they had relented just that week and admitted David Rieff, whose mother, Susan Sontag, was Mann’s guest there in the forties. They let me in too. It was the most fascinating thing to see. This is the house the Manns built. This was their refuge. This is where Doctor Faustus was written. This is the study. This is the kitchen. I was already toying with the idea of the book at that time, so it began a process of visiting the Manns’ houses and drawing a lot of energy from being in them, or even outside, looking in on them in Lübeck, in Munich, in rural Bavaria, and particularly in Princeton, where their house is now owned by the Catholic Church.

INTERVIEWER

Were there any details that struck you?

TÓIBÍN

There is a study away from the rest of the house that you can almost make into a little Germany just by closing the door, obscuring the California light. What’s very strange about Mann’s moving around is that he brought his desk from Munich—it came all the way to Princeton with him and then to California, when the things of refugees flew in the night. Certainly the Manns’ moving was done in a much more stylish way. It’s easy to mock the phrase, “Wherever I am is German culture,” but by separating his study from the house and by continuing his routines there, he was saying, “There is one person who maintains his decency and connection to tradition in the middle of all this, and that’s me.”

INTERVIEWER

Was he trying to balance a desire for comfort with a craving for solitude?

TÓIBÍN

He needed four hours in the morning. After that, he needed domestic life. Bohemian life and parties didn’t interest him much. He and Katia went for their walk, they might have to go somewhere in the evening, and then they got home as quickly as they could. Their life was centered around the children coming and going. They had gardeners, they had servants—in Munich, they had a chauffeur. Keeping all that going took a lot of time and energy.

The question of money is at the center of all this. His publisher, Alfred A. Knopf, managed to make Mann into a writer whose works every civilized household in America had to have—and the books sold in enormous quantities. Doctor Faustus was in the Book-of-the-Month club.

INTERVIEWER

Generational struggle is at the heart of The Magician. For Mann, the son of a senator, pursuing literature was itself a radical prospect. Meanwhile, his children Erika and Klaus, who came of age in the Weimar era, could express even their sexuality unabashedly, and openly committed themselves to antifascism early on. Could Mann have been jealous of his children’s sense of liberation?

TÓIBÍN

There’s a very strange letter from Mann writing them to say, “You have all the fun. I envy the fun you’re having.” His ways of dealing with his homosexuality were so closeted, so strange, so inward-looking, so framed by his weird gaze. There was a wildness in his imagination that was not matched by his suits.

INTERVIEWER

One of my favorite parts of The Magician is when W. H. Auden, whom Erika married for British citizenship, and Christopher Isherwood, the “family pimp” who set them up, come to Princeton for a Life photoshoot of the family in 1939. How did Auden and Isherwood feel about their attachment to the Manns?

TÓIBÍN

Klaus bored them, Erika bored them, and the family bored them. When Auden was asked who the most boring writer in the world was, he replied, “My father-in-law.”

I found that Life magazine issue in some secondhand place. Looking at the portrait of this family whose daughter married Auden sitting together, I could only think, This is a terrible lie.

INTERVIEWER

Like The Master, your 2004 novel about Henry James, The Magician is a deeply researched work of fiction. When undertaking these projects, were you tempted to veer from what actually happened?

TÓIBÍN

## Lisa Hanawalt's "I Can't Stop Thinking About Horses and Sex" (permalink)

[↗ Primärquelle: pluralistic.net](https://pluralistic.net/2026/11/20/intrusive-horse-thoughts/#lisa-hanawalt)

The title of animator Lisa Hanawalt's new graphic memoir *I Can't Stop Thinking About Horses and Sex* is a perfect encapsulation of the book's contents: a frank, self-aware, funny, horny, horsey exploration of Hanawalt's life, relationships, gender, and digestive issues:

[https://drawnandquarterly.com/books/i-cant-stop-thinking-about-horses-and-sex/](https://drawnandquarterly.com/books/i-cant-stop-thinking-about-horses-and-sex/)

Hanawalt is probably best known as the character designer for *Bojack Horseman*, but is also much loved in animation circles for her all-too-short-lived show *Tuca & Bertie*:

[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuca_%26_Bertie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuca_%26_Bertie)

She lived with the comedian/podcaster/showrunner Adam "Ruins Everything" Conover for 14 years, and the memoir revolves around the couple's breakup.

As the title promises, Hanawalt is also a lifelong horse-lover, who spent her childhood developing scars on her knees and calluses on the tops of her feet from endless all-fours sessions of pretending to be a horse. As an adult, she rides at the Los Angeles Equestrian Center, where she meets other horse people, who are beautifully depicted as the mix of posh sociopaths, obsessive animal-lovers, and lovable misfits (my daughter's middle school was around the corner from the LAEC and she grew up shoveling manure and tacking up at a teaching barn there; I can vouch for Hanawalt's faithful portrayal of the vibe).

Horses are Hanawalt's touchstone, the thing that brings her thoughts and emotions back into equilibrium, no matter what life throws at her. Eventually – inevitably – she acquires a horse, and just as inevitably, that horse proves to be her savior and her heartbreak. Horses are massive, majestic, impossibly powerful animals that are nevertheless forever on the verge of death, one weird disease or inexplicable fall from being maimed for life or keeling over.

The story of Hanawalt's pony Juni is intertwined with the story of her and Conover's breakup and her post-breakup relationships. Both threads of the tale are developed through beautiful, *extremely* funny, deeply personal vignettes that are brought to life by Hanawalt's art, which depicts bodies (animal, human, and animalistic human avatars) as hilarious, weird, and sexy all at once.

These two motifs criss-cross as we journey through Hanawalt's dating life, her childhood sexual trauma, her IBS, and her fears and hopes about her fertility (two of the major subplots involve Hanawalt's experiences with egg-freezing and bowel problems, and the way that the medical system treats women).

Hanawalt has a gift for compact, revealing character studies that leave the reader feeling both warm affection and exasperation with everyone in her life (including Hanawalt herself). It's a world without heroes and villains, where flaws and virtues are almost always flip-sides of the same coin. Everyone is crazy sometimes, including Hanawalt, and Hanawalt is self-aware enough to know when she's getting in her own way, and even why that happens, and also (just like all of us) can't always stop herself from tripping herself up.

Hanawalt's written and drawn a wise, funny, horny book that wrings comedy *and* insight out of trauma and melancholy. It's a gorgeous read that lingers.

Hanawalt isn't the only person who made smart, funny media out of her and Conover's breakup. Conover's comedy special about the breakup and its aftermath is called "Big Divorce Energy" and it was released the same week that *Can't Stop Thinking* hit the shelves:

[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CVB-SUX7zgk](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CVB-SUX7zgk)

I saw Conover perform this set live and it was terrific – and it got even better by the time he recorded it for the special. It makes for a perfect bookend for Hanawalt's memoir, a fact that both Conover and Hanawalt affirm in a lovely, warm conversation they recorded for Conover's *Factually* podcast. It's an interview that raises the bar for the kind of affection and even love a mature couple can salvage from a breakup:

[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BUXEDUiICM4](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BUXEDUiICM4)

The book itself is from Montreal's Drawn and Quarterly, who have a well-deserved reputation for publishing quality graphic novels, especially memoirs. D&Q always puts together a beautiful physical artifact, and *Can't Stop Thinking* is no exception: a handsome hardcover with luxurious, thick semi-matte pages and a bookmark ribbon sewn into the binding. It's the perfect gift for any friend going through a breakup (or thinking about buying a horse).

items.body:
On a summer day at UC Berkeley, four teenagers jostled at a whiteboard, vying to write down their solutions to an important public health concern. They were having fun even as they took on a heavy task: helping researchers design programs to reduce the skyrocketing suicide rate among Black youth.

In the United States, deaths by suicide have been surging among Black kids and teens for decades. For those between 10 and 17 years of age, the suicide rate [rose 144% from 2007 to 2020](https://publichealth.jhu.edu/sites/default/files/2023-08/2023-august-still-ringing-alarm.pdf). What’s more, Black boys die by suicide more than twice as frequently as Black girls, although the suicide rate for Black girls [increased by 182% between 2001 and 2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10900-019-00678-x).

As the teenagers brainstormed, [Jasmin Brooks Stephens](https://psychology.berkeley.edu/people/jasmin-brooks-stephens), a Berkeley assistant professor of psychology, watched nearby. The moment was a highlight in research she was conducting with the Homeless Children’s Network on improving mental health outcomes for Black youth. Brooks Stephens believed that teens themselves have meaningful ideas to share, and she had worked for eight weeks with these particular teenagers, who were part of the network’s [Jabali Youth Advocacy](https://www.hcnkids.org/jabali-youth-advocacy) organization, culminating in their trip to campus.

“One of the most exciting things was seeing them all jump up and say, ‘Wait, we can make a program for making us feel better? We have the power to do that?’” Brooks Stephens recalled. “Seeing them find and discover that sense of agency in themselves—that was invaluable to me.” It also was one of the few times any of the teens had visited a college campus, she said, an added bonus. In future work, Brooks Stephens plans to translate the results of her study for clinicians and policymakers who are trying to improve suicide prevention for Black youth.

The ongoing project is just one example of how Brooks Stephens is working to address rising suicide rates among Black youth by engaging them in participatory research—an unusual and hopeful approach in suicide prevention studies. “This summer I had the incredible opportunity to work alongside young people to design a program that would help other young people want to live,” she said. “Rather than waiting until a young person is already in crisis, I’m interested in understanding what helps youth thrive—what gives them hope and a sense of possibility and helps them recognize the brilliance they have inside them.”

## A pathway to hope in the face of racism

Despite the growing crisis among Black youth, [suicide rates are dropping for adolescents in the U.S. overall](https://www.samhsa.gov/data/sites/default/files/reports/rpt57150/2025-nsduh-annual-national-report.pdf). Brooks Stephens finds these statistics revealing: “To me, that suggests that the approaches we have relied on have not adequately addressed the conditions driving suicide risk in Black communities,” she said.

It’s easy to talk about [structural racism](https://news.berkeley.edu/2025/08/14/watch-berkeley-scholar-explain-structural-racism/) as an abstract concept, or personal encounters with racists as disturbing but bounded moments. But grappling with racism heavily impacts Black youth and increases their suicide risk, according to a 2023 report from the [Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health](https://publichealth.jhu.edu/sites/default/files/2023-08/2023-august-still-ringing-alarm.pdf). Indeed, Brooks Stephens has published work documenting how racial discrimination and the COVID-19 pandemic, which disproportionately harmed Black Americans, together [worsened suicide risk for Black young adults](https://psycnet.apa.org/record/2025-01327-001).

Brooks Stephens’s work is informed by both her research and her own experience of how race can shape young people’s sense of self. “I became aware very early on that Black children are often navigating expectations about who they are supposed to be before they have even had the opportunity to figure out who they are for themselves,” she said. “That has stayed with me—the importance of creating space for Black young people to define themselves, recognize their strengths, and imagine who they want to become.” At the same time, she saw how the stigma surrounding mental health could make it harder for Black youth and families to seek support, even as racism and other chronic stressors were impacting their well-being.

When she took an African American psychology class as an undergraduate at the University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill, with Enrique Neblett, a renowned scholar of race and health who became her mentor, Brooks Stephens saw the connection between those experiences—and found her passion. “I realized that there was an entire field devoted to understanding how racism affects mental health and how Black children come to understand themselves and their racial identity,” she said.

Later, during her doctoral research at the University of Houston, Brooks Stephens worked with Rheeda Walker, an expert on suicide science and African American adult mental health research. Brooks Stephens noticed that there was very limited discussion about building upstream resilience in suicide prevention research—an approach that focuses on child well-being and happiness before the development of a mental health crisis.

“We’re studying why people choose to end their life without understanding what makes people want to live,” she said. For Brooks Stephens, that realization opened up a different way of thinking about suicide prevention, one that made room for the strengths that were often absent from traditional models, such as racial identity, spirituality, family connection, belonging, or hope.

## Focusing on strengths to prevent suicide

Brooks Stephens knows she can’t single-handedly eliminate the racial traumas faced by young Black people. Nor can she end other factors that lead to higher suicide rates in her community, such as systemic injustice or poverty. Instead, she’s focusing on where she can make a difference through her research.

“While I may not be able to eradicate racism, I can help build programs that change how Black young people see themselves and their futures—programs that help them feel grounded in their identity and able to imagine a life that feels worth living,” she said.

*Brooks Stephens and her colleagues identified six positive factors that reduce suicidality among Black youth (courtesy of Jasmin Brooks Stephens).*

items.title: ‘The World It Was’
items.subtitle: For poet Chase Twichell, Zen practice and writing have long been deeply intertwined.
