items.body:
For poet Chase Twichell, Zen practice and writing have long been deeply intertwined. “Zen is said to be a ‘mind-to-mind transmission,’” she told the [Poetry Foundation](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poets/chase-twichell). “The best poems are exactly that: They leap from one mind to another without stopping to explain exactly how they did it.... In our culture, out of necessity, we’re used to living in a mostly literal mind, and poetry demands that we enter it with another kind of mind.”

Her latest collection, [The World It Was](https://www.coppercanyonpress.org/books/the-world-it-was-by-chase-twichell/), offers one such opportunity to access another kind of mind—one carefully attuned to grief, transience, and environmental destruction. Composed in the wake of the Covid pandemic, the collection consists of restrained, nearly skeletal elegies—for her late husband, for her aging body, and for the Earth itself—that look directly at suffering and ask how to live in the face of seemingly all-pervasive loss (or, as the book’s description states, “being fully alive inside the brief body and the dying world”).

Though this question is of course unanswerable, the poetic worlds that Twichell builds suggest that [attention](https://tricycle.org/magazine/attention-means-attention/) plays a key role in figuring out a way forward. “Zen and poetry have both taught me that the quality of attention we pay to the world is crucial,” Twichell[said in a 2016 interview](https://ashberyland.com/2016/11/19/poetry-and-life-an-interview-with-chase-twitchell/). “Of course there are many ways to make people see the damage we’ve done, and poetry is only one of them. But to me, it’s the arrow that most deeply pierces my consciousness.” *The World It Was* presents sixty-seven such arrows: invitations to embody a different kind of mind, and, in the process, relearn what it means to exist fully in a world defined by impermanence.

*–Sarah Fleming, senior editor*

## The World It Was

I was a kid transfixed by

the endlessly mutating

gloomy rooms among the trees,

and I wandered far.

At seventeen, I married thunder

and wind and snow. I took vows.

I pledged to be only half human,

so only half guilty of our crimes

against Earth and all its beings.

Wherever I am, I visit Earth’s memorial.

Sometimes I leave a few words

in the dirt on a car.

The memorial surrounds us.

Earth’s body is also its grave.

## Death’s Hors d’Oeuvres

A school of dead gray fish drifts

across my vision—floaters.

No names come when I call.

Is this what old age will be like?

No, this is old age now.

I like to take little sips of the horror,

morsels of poisoned meat,

each taste a foretaste.

I’m preparing for future pain,

not this pain.

That’s the lie I tell myself.

## I Can’t Make Sense of It

In one of these many centuries,

my words fell briefly through the air.

A flurry, among many flurries.

I can’t make sense of it:

the word-bearing trees

grew older, bore less and less fruit.

Birds carrying the twigs of poems

still fly in from time to time

but they don’t nest here anymore.

## Flower of False Starts

It’s a strange flower,

the flower of false starts.

I dress in its withered petals.

Each knob on the stem

is the scar of a flower

that never fully bloomed.

Or it bloomed, but the flower

was not the flower I dreamed.

It’s almost all stem now.

Withered petals—pretty dress.

The flower is nearing

the end of its life.

Each poem leaves a scar.

## Solitaire

When Russell was dying

I sat beside his bed

playing solitaire on my phone,

practicing his not being there.

I liked the way the cards came

in quick cold cascades of numbers,

clusters of luck,

and I could visit that bright flow

day or night.

I liked the way the game was

always starting over, always

not quite daybreak on the screen,

the longest time until dark.

♦

*“The World It Was,” “Death’s Hors d’Oeuvres,” “I Can’t Make Sense of It,” “Flower of False Starts,” and “Solitaire” from* [The World It Was](https://www.coppercanyonpress.org/books/the-world-it-was-by-chase-twichell/) *, copyright 2026 by Chase Twichell, used by permission of Copper Canyon Press.*

items.title: “You Don’t Belong Here”: How Rane Got Into Turntablism

items.body:
*As Rane turns 45, Rick Jeffs tells the story of the Steelworkerz, the TTM 54 and the magnetic crossfader, and gives his view on AI in DJing.*

Rane was founded in 1981 and released its first DJ mixer in 1986 at the request of Richard Long, the sound designer for [Studio 54](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Studio_54), among many other clubs. This was the beginning of what is now 40+ years of innovation for the DJ market, a CV that includes milestones like the world’s first magnetic crossfader, dual USB connectivity for seamless multi-laptop handoffs, and much more.

As Rane celebraes 45 years in the business, we spoke with Rick Jeffs, Principal Design Engineer at Rane, to get the inside scoop behind Rane’s biggest technical achievements. This interview has been edited for brevity and consistency.

**Attack: Rane began in 1981 and released its first DJ mixer, the [MP 24](https://www.ranecommercial.com/legacy/mp24evo.html), in 1986. Technologically, what are the biggest changes in the world of mixers since then? **

Rick Jeffs: The MP 24 came from a very different time. It was a purely analog design built with little more than op-amps, resistors, and capacitors. There was no firmware to write, no software applications to support, and no computer drivers to maintain. If a DJ wanted to play a song, they needed the vinyl record in their hands.

Today, nearly everything has changed. Modern mixers digitize audio as it enters the product, perform most processing in the digital domain, and convert the signal back to analog at the outputs. Digital processing eliminates many of the limitations and tolerances of analog circuitry while making advanced features practical and affordable. Controls are monitored by MCUs, enabling more precise operation and far greater flexibility.

The biggest change may be the connection between the mixer and the computer. Dual USB ports allow two DJs to connect simultaneously, while software platforms such as Serato and Engine provide access to enormous music libraries, streaming services, real-time effects, and advanced performance tools. DJs no longer need to transport hundreds of pounds of vinyl to every gig. Instead, virtually unlimited amounts of music can travel on a laptop, SSD, or media stick.

Rick Jeffs, Principal Design Engineer at Rane

**Let's talk about how Rane became associated with turntablism. The story goes that a group of New York turntablists sent you a hand-drawn diagram for a new mixer, and Rane engineers flew to New York to meet them. What happened that day?**

Rane has always been involved in the DJ market, with early products such as the X3000 Isolator, X5000 Equalizer, and MP 24 mixer.

The Steelworkerz DJ crew approached Rane with an ambitious idea: build the ultimate scratch mixer. Intrigued by the opportunity, we flew to New York to meet with them and explore what such a product might look like. Our first meeting took place at a Tableturns event in lower Manhattan, an open-format competition where local DJs showcased their creativity, technical ability, and performance skills. The Steelworkerz crew included Brian Lane (Big Wiz), Doug Coen (Sugarcuts), Marz1, and Peter Parker.

The experience was unlike anything I had encountered before. Our taxi dropped us off in a dark alley in front of a large steel door. When we knocked, a massive bouncer opened the door, looked us over, and said, “You don't belong here.” After we explained that we had been invited by the Steelworkerz to discuss a new mixer project, his expression immediately changed, and we were warmly welcomed inside.

That evening was my first introduction to true performance scratch mixing and turntablist culture. What I witnessed was far beyond simply playing records. The DJs were using turntables as musical instruments, combining technical precision, creativity, and showmanship in ways I had never seen before. The following night, we met with members of the Steelworkerz in an apartment in the South Bronx, where we sketched ideas and discussed what they believed the ideal battle mixer should be.

Rane recognized an opportunity. The turntablist community was growing rapidly, yet the available mixers often lacked the features DJs were requesting and frequently suffered from durability issues under the demands of competition-style performance. The result was the [TTM 54](https://www.ranecommercial.com/legacy/pdf/old/ttm54man.pdf), which delivered many of the features turntablists had been asking for.

The TTM 56 followed and introduced what would become one of the most significant innovations in DJ mixer design: **the industry's first non-contact magnetic crossfader**. Combined with improved full-cut channel faders, the magnetic design delivered dramatically better reliability, consistency, and performance than traditional contact-based faders.

The innovations did not stop there. Later Rane products introduced dual USB connectivity, allowing two DJs to remain connected simultaneously and perform seamless handoffs between laptops without interrupting the music. Like the magnetic crossfader before it, dual USB support would eventually become a widely adopted feature throughout the DJ industry.

Looking back, that trip to New York marked the beginning of Rane's transformation from a company known primarily for professional audio products into a leader in the emerging performance DJ market.

[quote align=right text="The DJs were using turntables as musical instruments, combining technical precision, creativity, and showmanship in ways I had never seen before."]

The Steelworkerz crew

**The magnetic crossfader is an important design in Rane's history. How did you settle on magnetism as a method? **

Several technologies were considered, including resistive, inductive, optical, and magnetic sensing. I chose the magnetic approach because it offered the best combination of robustness, performance, and simplicity. It was largely immune to the environmental contamination that often affected conventional faders, while avoiding the complexity associated with optical systems.

Over time, we continued to refine the design, eventually implementing more advanced magnetic sensing methods with improved linearity and resolution. What began as a solution to a reliability problem ultimately became one of the defining technologies of the TTM series and helped establish a new performance standard for DJ mixers.

**Is it correct that modern mixers don't pass audio through the faders/crossfaders, but instead use them to send signals that control the amplifier, which is why there can be different fader curves, reverse control, etc.? Why is this better? **

…

items.title: Behold the Most Detailed Painting in History: The Ghent Altarpiece

items.body:
These days, if you want to see a particular painting, you can almost certainly pull it up online in seconds. In more and more cases, the resolution of the image will be so high that you can zoom in and in and in: such a level of detail is unavailable in a museum, of course, but also difficult to access even if you owned the physical artwork in question. Here on Open Culture, we’ve previously featured such luxuriantly digitized paintings as [The Night Watch](https://www.openculture.com/2020/05/the-largest-most-detailed-photograph-of-rembrandts-the-night-watch-is-now-online-zoom-in-see-every-brush-stroke.html), [Girl with a Pearl Earring](https://www.openculture.com/2021/07/a-gallery-of-1800-super-high-resolution-images-of-classic-paintings.html), and [The Garden of Earthly Delights](https://www.openculture.com/2022/03/a-digital-archive-of-hieronymus-boschs-complete-works.html). But there’s at least one celebrated work of Dutch masters whose viewing experience can never truly be replicated on the internet: the *Ghent Altarpiece*, also called the *Adoration of the Mystic Lamb*, by Hubert and Jan van Eyck.

After watching [the video from The Gaze](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4APkXceabVY) above, you’ll surely want to take as close as possible a look at [the online Ghent Altarpiece](https://closertovaneyck.kikirpa.be/ghentaltarpiece/#home), seeking out such highlighted details as the individual hairs on Adam’s beard, the realistically awkward expressions on the faces of the angel chorus, and the identifiable crucifixion scene pinned to a pilgrim’s hat.

But that may only stoke your desire to make a pilgrimage of your own, to Belgium, where you can see the real thing carefully placed in St. Bavo’s Cathedral. In the early fifteenth century, when that institution was called St. John the Baptist’s Church, its warden was the wealthy merchant Jodocus Vijd. Having endowed a new chapel, Vijd also commissioned the van Eyck brothers to create an altarpiece spectacular enough to secure him a spot in the afterlife. The result was one of the earliest masterpieces of oil painting.

Even apart from that designation (to say nothing of its being [the most stolen work of art in history](https://www.openculture.com/2020/12/how-jan-van-eycks-masterpiece-the-ghent-altarpiece-became-the-most-stolen-work-of-art-in-history.html)), it has enjoyed an impressive afterlife of its own. Of the many who have traveled to behold it *in situ* at St. Bavo’s, some have no doubt sought the ecstasy of faith that can only be felt in a true holy place. But others have been thrilled, whether they were aware of it beforehand, by all the attention the artists put into integrating the work with its surroundings. The light within its images, for example, is painted in such a way as to match the light streaming into the cathedral itself. Those who look closely at the gem worn by the foremost singing angel will see a reflection of the very room meant for the altar. By the time their eyes meet the knowing gaze of the sacrificial lamb, they’re all but guaranteed to have a religious experience — though whether its nature is Christian, artistic, or otherwise will depend, as it does with all enduring art, on the individual viewer.

**Related Content:**

[How Jan van Eyck’s Masterpiece, the Ghent Altarpiece, Became the Most Stolen Work of Art in History](https://www.openculture.com/2020/12/how-jan-van-eycks-masterpiece-the-ghent-altarpiece-became-the-most-stolen-work-of-art-in-history.html)

[The Meaning of Hieronymus Bosch’s The Garden of Earthly Delights Explained](https://www.openculture.com/2021/04/the-meaning-of-hieronymus-boschs-the-garden-of-earthly-delights-explained.html)

[A Guided Tour Through All of Vermeer’s Famous Paintings, Narrated by Stephen Fry](https://www.openculture.com/2023/02/a-guided-tour-through-all-of-vermeers-famous-paintings-narrated-by-stephen-fry.html)

[Why is Vermeer’s Girl with the Pearl Earring Considered a Masterpiece?: An Animated Introduction](https://www.openculture.com/2020/04/why-is-vermeers-girl-with-the-pearl-earring-considered-a-masterpiece-an-animated-introduction.html)

[A Gallery of 1,800 Gigapixel Images of Classic Paintings: See Vermeer’s Girl with the Pearl Earring, Van Gogh’s Starry Night & Other Masterpieces in Close Detail](https://www.openculture.com/2021/07/a-gallery-of-1800-super-high-resolution-images-of-classic-paintings.html)

[Take a 3D Virtual Tour of the Sistine Chapel & Explore Michelangelo’s Masterpieces Up Close](https://www.openculture.com/2025/05/take-a-3d-virtual-tour-of-the-sistine-chapel.html)

He’s the author of the newsletter* [Books on Cities](https://colinmarshall.substack.com/) * as well as the books * [한국 요약 금지](https://product.kyobobook.co.kr/detail/S000212263515) * (No Summarizing Korea) and * [Korean Newtro](https://www.amazon.com/Korean-Newtro-Where-Youth-Tradition/dp/156591533X) *.* *Follow him on the social network formerly known as Twitter at [@colinm](https://twitter.com/#%21/colinmarshall)* *[a](https://twitter.com/#%21/colinmarshall)* *[rshall](https://twitter.com/#%21/colinmarshall).*

items.body:
Eine „Wissenschafts-NATO“ gegen politische Eingriffe, Kritik an einem Impulspapier des Wissenschaftsrats und eine Studie zu überlasteten Forschenden: Das Wisskomm-Update gibt alle 14 Tage einen Überblick über aktuelle Themen, Debatten und Trends.

### Was gibt’s Neues?

**Angela Ittel wirbt für eine „Wissenschafts-Nato“**

Die Präsidentin der TU Braunschweig, Angela Ittel, spricht sich für einen länderübergreifenden Beistand zum Schutz der Wissenschaftsfreiheit aus. Anlass sind Pläne der AfD, die Gleichstellungsarbeit an Hochschulen einzuschränken und Mittel für die Geschlechter- und Klimaforschung zu kürzen. Sollten die Gleichstellungsbeauftragten in Sachsen-Anhalt aus dem Hochschulgesetz gestrichen werden, erwartet Ittel von anderen Hochschulen und der Allianz der Wissenschaftsorganisationen öffentliche Rückendeckung und konkrete Unterstützung. Das sagte die Universitätspräsidentin [im Interview mit Anna-Lena Scholz](https://www.zeit.de/2026/48/gleichstellung-hochschulen-angela-ittel-afd?).

Den weiterhin großen Bedarf an Gleichstellungsarbeit begründet Ittel mit dem sinkenden Frauenanteil über die wissenschaftlichen Karrierestufen hinweg. In der Medizin liege der Anteil der Studentinnen teils bei 70 Prozent, während nur jede zehnte Professur mit einer Frau besetzt sei. 126 Hochschulen hätten 2024 eine Selbstverpflichtung der Hochschulrektorenkonferenz für Gleichstellungsmaßnahmen unterzeichnet. Nun würde bei Berufungen dokumentiert, wie viele Frauen sich bewerben, eingeladen werden und eine Stelle erhalten. Die Wirksamkeit einzelner Maßnahmen werde derzeit untersucht.

**NaWik-Trialog: Wie kommt Wissenschaft in die Politik?**

Wie arbeiten Wissenschaft und Politik optimal zusammen und welche Kompetenzen benötigen Wissenschaftler*innen, um ihre Erkenntnisse in die Politik zu tragen? Über diese Fragen diskutierten Armin Grunwald, Katrin Rehak-Nitsche und Richard Fuchs am 4. November beim [NaWik*-Trialog](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hj8qquMHEtU) „Politik & Wissenschaft“.

Dass politische Entscheidungen wissenschaftlich fundiert sein sollten, darüber waren sich alle drei Diskutant*innen einig. Doch wie gelingt es Wissenschaftler*innen ihre Expertise einzubringen? „Gute Politikberatung ist eine Langstrecke“, sagt Fuchs, Wissenschaftsjournalist, Medientrainer und Berater für Wissensorganisationen. Politische Autorität müssen sich Wissenschaftler*innen erarbeiten. Zunächst sollten sich Forschende klarmachen: „Wissenschaft und Politik ticken anders“. Wissenschaftliche Projekte hätten häufig einen langen Vorlauf, während Politik schnelle Ergebnisse wolle. Das könne für Wissenschaftler*innen frustrierend sein. Für eine erfolgreiche Politikberatung sollten Forschende die Arbeitsweise, Bedürfnisse und zeitlichen Zwänge politischer Entscheidungsträger*innen verstehen.

Grunwald, der das Institut für Technikfolgenabschätzung und das Büro für Technikfolgenabschätzung beim Bundestag am Karlsruher Institut für Technologie (KIT)* leitet, findet es zudem wichtig, die verschiedenen Rollen zu verstehen: „Wir wollen nicht, wir können nicht, wir dürfen nicht die besseren Politiker sein wollen.“ Forschende könnten Politiker*innen nur bei ihrer Entscheidungsfindung unterstützen. Dafür ist laut Fuchs ein Perspektivwechsel wichtig. Forscher*innen müssten sich überlegen, was Politiker*innen von ihnen benötigen.

Laut der Politikerin und Landtagsabgeordneten aus Rheinland-Pfalz, Rehak-Nitsche, werden vor allem konkrete Handlungsoptionen und Lösungsvorschläge benötigt. Forschende sollten dafür gezielt auf fachpolitische Sprecher*innen, Ausschüsse oder auch lokale Abgeordnete zugehen. Dabei sollten ihre wissenschaftlichen Ergebnisse aber realistischen Erwartungen entsprechen. Die Diskutierenden kritisierten überzogene wissenschaftliche Versprechen, da diese die Glaubwürdigkeit schmälern. Außerdem sollten die Ergebnisse priorisiert werden, zum Beispiel mit einer zentralen Botschaft pro Studie. Diese sollten Forschende verständlich kommunizieren können.

Wie das in der Praxis aussieht? Das lest ihr in unserem [Interview mit dem Politikwissenschaftler Daniel Wiesner](https://www.wissenschaftskommunikation.de/wie-politik-wissenschaft-in-debatten-einsetzt-101497/) über wissenschaftliche Inhalte in österreichischen Parlamentsdebatten.

**Kritik am Impulspapier des Wissenschaftsrats**

Welchen Beitrag kann und soll Wissenschaft zur freiheitlich-demokratischen Gesellschaft leisten? Anfang November hat der Wissenschaftsrat zu dieser Frage ein [Impulspapier](https://www.wissenschaftsrat.de/SharedDocs/Pressemitteilungen/DE/PM_2026/PM_2426?nn=68873b8321233a04bb97cedd&wt_zmc=nl.int.zonaudev.112331552451_555074179233.nl_ref) veröffentlicht. Zu den Impulsen zählen Fragen zur Balance zwischen wissenschaftlicher Selbstbestimmung und gesellschaftlichen Erwartungen sowie zu Werten und Wertekonflikten in der Wissenschaft. Der Rat sieht den Anlass darin, dass demokratische Institutionen und der gesellschaftliche Zusammenhalt zunehmend unter Druck stünden: „Wissenschaftliche Erkenntnisse werden infrage gestellt, einzelne Wissenschaftlerinnen und Wissenschaftler bedrängt und angefeindet.“

Der Wissenschaftsrat versteht das Impulspapier als „Plädoyer und als Anstoß zur Debatte“, um Thesen, Anregungen und Spannungsverhältnisse offenzulegen. Diese sollen gemeinsam mit Wissenschaft, Politik und Gesellschaft erörtert werden. Gelegenheit dazu soll unter anderem ein gemeinsames Symposium im nächsten Frühjahr bieten. Bei [Table Media](https://table.media/research/thema-des-tages/wissenschaft-und-die-demokratie-welche-diskussionen-der-wissenschaftsrat-anstossen-moechte) bemängeln teils anonyme Kritiker*innen, dass das Papier vor allem Fragen stellt, wo längst Entscheidungen und Reformen gefragt wären. Johannes Vogel, Direktor des Naturkundemuseums Berlin, [fordert](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/m-weisskopf_wissenschaft-demokratie-symposium-share-7524013244613603328-UDsU/?utm_source=share&utm_medium=member_desktop&rcm=ACoAABrhP4ABM9rIpbs8S5tg0GHwDJPz18tv5aQ) etwa: „Die Diskussionen zu den genannten Themen führen wir teilweise seit zehn Jahren oder noch länger.“ Es sei nun keine Zeit mehr für teils systembewahrende Debatten, sondern für Experimente, Lernen, Mut und Handeln.

### Und sonst?

Ein KI-basiertes Tool könnte zukünftig Creator*innen beim **Factchecking** ihrer Inhalte unterstützen. Dabei würden Informationen eine Art „Nutri-Score für Social Media“ erhalten, die ihren Wahrheitsgehalt signalisieren sollen. [Im Podcast](https://www.podcast.de/episode/709350253/nutri-score-fuer-social-media-wer-bestimmt-kuenftig-was-im-feed-als-vertrauenswuerdig-gilt) spricht Journalist Martin Fehrensen mit der Gründerin Malina Wiethaus über das Tool „TrustScored“.

items.body:
This is a weird moment. I have a hunch that we'll look back later and tell ourselves stories in which it seemed obvious where things were going. So I wanted to lay down a little time capsule and register just how confusing everything felt at the time. This is a personal view from the trenches.

1.

If you're a normal person, you may feel that AI has been good at math for a long time.[1]But for "real" math, this is roughly what it felt like:

When

Feeling

2024

LLMs are toys

Summer 2025

LLMs are interesting toys

Early Autumn 2025

LLMs can do useful stuff sometimes

Mid Autumn 2025

…a lot of stuff

Late Autumn 2025

…a lot

Early 2026

holy god

Even having been astonished by AI progress in the past, it was still astonishing to see AI move in a matter of months from a mildly-useful toy to something that many people now consider almost impossible to do without.

2.

Personally, I'd say that current AI makes me around 50% more productive at "doing math". That's despite the fact that AI can now often do in a few minutes things that would have taken me hours to do myself.

The main reason is that my concept of "doing math" involves various steps, like coming up with ideas for theorems, trying to prove them, writing things down, reorganizing everything to make it more clear, and so on. AI is good at some parts of this, but still pretty bad at others, so the overall speedup isn't as high as you might expect.

(Even if planes could go 10× faster, your door-to-door travel time from your apartment in London to your friend's place in Rome wouldn't decrease that much, because you still have to get to the airport and wait to board.)

3.

But then, I'm still (sort of; more on this later) trying to follow my old "doing math" workflow, just automating certain parts of it. That can't be right, can it?

If we found a way to make batteries at 1% of the current cost, we wouldn't just say, "cool, batteries are cheap now". We'd find all sorts of new ways to use batteries that didn't make sense before, and change the ways we generate power to account for all these new batteries. Probably our whole energy system would end up transformed. Analogously, AI being good at proofs should lead to a very different equilibrium. But what is that?[2]

4.

It seems healthy, at the moment, to maintain a fluid view of what "doing math" means. But at bare minimum it surely involves understanding the math that "I" am "doing". So long as that's part of the workflow, it would seem to impose a limit on how quickly "I" could "do" math, no matter how good AI is.

One obvious conclusion would be that my tiny organic brain should be removed from the workflow entirely. Maybe! But it's interesting to speculate about how much faster things could go while still keeping a human brain in the loop. I think the answer is: A lot.

5.

Contrary to what you may have heard, humans are not obsolete for math. Not yet. The most obvious reason is that AI is still bad at writing.

People often complain that AI writing overuses various patterns or lacks a unique voice or whatever. I don't disagree, but I always felt like there was a deeper issue that I couldn't quite put my finger on. With math, this becomes very clear: The problem is it doesn't make any goddamned sense.

Really, I think it's deeper than being bad "at writing". It seems like AI is bad at thinking in certain ways that manifest as bad writing.

6.

When novices do math, they often create "spaghetti-code math": Imagine a long document with lots of equations, but if you point at any one equation, it's hard to say what assumptions underpin it, or how it fits into the bigger picture. Any random idea that was mentioned 17 pages ago might be used again at any time with no warning. With experience, people learn to break complex arguments down into modular pieces with a good "API", in the sense that the assumptions and conclusions for each part are relatively simple.

Somehow, AI has developed these amazing technical skills, while still being bad at creating abstractions So the arguments it gives are long and tangled and bewildering. This is what makes AI math seem so alien.

7.

Now I know what you're thinking. Maybe AI isn't bad at creating abstractions. It's just bad at creating abstractions that work for you, human with tiny organic brain.

From a distance, that seems plausible. And it might be true to some degree. I have high-bandwidth access to a human brain. It's not crazy to imagine that this gives me an advantage in predicting how a human brain would react to a given presentation of ideas. But still, I claim that current AI is objectively bad at creating abstractions, regardless of if the consumer of those abstractions is human or artificial.

Here's why: If I ask AI to prove something hard, it will produce a proof that starts simple and gradually descends into a rampage of complexity. If I tell it to break that proof down into self-contained pieces, it will produce lemmas that each take a full page just to state. If I ask, "Why? Why have you done this to me?", the AI will say, "This is as simple as it gets. It's not that bad. What's your problem?"

But if I argue with the AI for a while, I can start to understand the basic contours of the argument. And I'll ask, "Why don't you first just try to prove blah using only assumptions blahblah, without worrying about blahblahblah? Wouldn't that be easier?" Often, this doesn't work, either because my idea was bad, or because the AI isn't smart enough to do it. (Which one? Who knows!) But after a few attempts, I can usually find something that that works, and the AI can use it to re-write the proof in a somewhat simpler way. If I repeat this many times, I can gradually chip away at the complexity.

But maybe that's still just making the proof easier for humans to understand? No! For one, this usually makes the proof shorter, and sometimes dramatically shorter. More importantly, during this process, someone (maybe me, maybe the AI) will often realize that there's a different proof strategy that gives a stronger result. Instead of proving x , now we can prove x . Thus, artisanal human abstractions are "objectively" useful.

8.

Some people might claim that it's already possible to automate some of what I'm doing with some multi-agent Rube Goldberg thing. I'm not sure, because my experience has been that investing lots of time into clever AGENTS.MD or custom skills or harnesses isn't a great use of time. That stuff is somewhat helpful, but things are changing so fast that the knowledge has a short half-life. Also, the majority of information about these tricks seems to come from people who are excited about the technology itself.

On the other hand, the automator told me to try typing, "ask independent agents for an adversarial review", and I've found those seven words to be quite helpful. I wish I could find a source with boring best practices for people who are happy to stay away from the bleeding edge.

9.

Art by GPT-6

Howdy, folks! Welcome to the future where science fiction becomes reality every day. Where AI-powered cyberattacks paralyze air travel one day and banks the next. Where shadowy billionaires make fortunes illicitly selling America’s enemies the technology to create artificial gods, while you slave away for $150 a day hoping to get half a day off. Where it seems like a new rare disease is [cured every week](https://www.ajmc.com/view/5-rare-diseases-that-now-have-their-first-fda-approved-treatments), even as [measles returns to America](https://abcnews.com/Health/us-officially-loses-measles-elimination-status-paho/story?id=138203543) thanks to an anti-science cult that somehow made it to the highest rungs of power. Where self-driving cars whizz past people hunched over dying of fentanyl in the street. I mean, look at this:

Or this:

Or this!

In such confusing times, it’s all your friendly neighborhood economics blogger can do to keep up with it all. But I’m trying my best, so that I can help you understand these crazy times just a little bit better.

Anyway, on to this week’s roundup.

#### 1. Good news on teen happiness

For years, we watched America’s young people — and young people throughout the world — become less and less happy. They told surveys they were unhappy. They attempted (and committed) suicide more. They were more socially isolated. They formed relationships less.

The most plausible candidate for a cause for all of this was [smartphone-enabled social media](https://www.noahpinion.blog/p/honestly-its-probably-the-phones), which replaced in-person small-group interaction with impersonal arm’s-length interactions with huge numbers of potentially hostile strangers — something the human animal never evolved for.

But human beings are resilient and adaptable, and I always expected young people to find new ways to be happy in a hyper-connected world. Now, there are some signs that things are starting to turn around:

A word of caution: This is just one data source, the Youth Behavioral Risk Survey. Other sources, like the CDC, continue to show [high teen suicide rates](https://x.com/jtrothwell/status/2119885873735221719). It’s far too early to conclude that general teen happiness is on the upswing. But the YBRS data is a very positive sign.

If the trend is indeed turning around, what’s the cause? One possibility is that even as the online world became more all-consuming and alienating, the offline world was becoming kinder and gentler. Here’s [Rothwell again](https://x.com/jtrothwell/status/2061466828438966756):

items.body:
AI forecasters now equal or beat top human performance at traditional forecasting questions (eg [ForecastBench](https://forecastingresearch.substack.com/p/ai-models-have-likely-reached-parity), the [Metaculus Cup](https://www.economist.com/science-and-technology/2026/09/16/artificial-intelligence-now-beats-some-of-the-best-human-forecasters)).

These are usually specialized AIs with forecasting harnesses, created by forecasting startups (eg [FutureSearch](https://futuresearch.ai/), [Mantic](https://mantic.com/), [Preseen](https://preseen.com/)), but foundation models like ChatGPT and Claude are only about six months behind the specialized models, so by the end of the year they’ll match top humans too.

In the past, the options for getting top-human-level forecasts were slim and inconvenient. You could hire a team of superforecasters to work on the problem, but this would cost thousands of dollars and take weeks. Or you could check prediction markets (or Metaculus), but they only have a small sample of general-interest questions and are constantly trying to screw you over by gaming resolution criteria.

The rise of AI forecasters solves these problems more cleanly and comprehensively than almost anyone thought possible just a year ago. The “science of forecasting”, which only recently felt like trying to pick the least-bad of various bad options, now faces tasks more like “what kind of magnifying glass should we use to inspect our giant novelty lottery check as we confirm that it’s real?” and “how do we spend our winnings?”

Specifically: AI forecasters now equal or beat top human performance at traditional forecasting questions. We need to learn how this success decays as we move to different types of non-traditional forecasting questions.

I recently got to talk to some people at the [Forecasting Research Institute](https://forecastingresearch.org/), one of the leaders in this field. Here’s my impression of the remaining challenges:

**1: Can AI do conditional forecasts?**

A traditional forecasting question asks something like: will the Democrats win the next election?

A conditional forecasting question is more like: *if* the Democrats win the next election, how will that affect the chances of a stock market crash?

Conditional forecasting questions are more exciting than traditional ones because they directly speak to policy outcomes. If we defund the police, how will that affect crime rates (compared to the counterfactual where we hold police funding constant)? If we mandate COVID vaccinations, how will that affect COVID mortality and myocarditis mortality (compared to the counterfactual where vaccines are voluntary / banned)?

Prediction markets have been slow to experiment with these, partly because of annoying logistical issues (you have to refund people’s money if the condition doesn’t come true) and partly because they entice fewer customers than new forms of degenerate sports gambling. AI forecasters don’t have this problem; you can ask an AI forecaster any of those questions above right now, and the big companies ([FutureSearch](https://futuresearch.ai/docs/forecast-conditional-scenarios/), [Preseen](https://blog.preseen.com/p/predicting-science-and-technology), [Mantic](https://blog.mantic.com/p/friday-forecasts-2)) have it as an explicit feature.

What remains is to prove that AI forecasters’ great performance on traditional questions carries over to conditional questions. About a year ago, FRI tested this and found that it didn’t - the AIs of the time did significantly worse on conditional questions. It seemed like some kind of weird misunderstanding where the AI didn’t entirely understand the concept.

Will this flip like a switch? At some point, the AI is smart enough to fully grasp conditionals, and it becomes exactly as good at conditional forecasting as the regular type? The experts I talked to thought no - as it gets smarter, its conditional forecasting ability will improve gradually. Where is it now? The experts weren’t willing to hazard a guess on whether it was better or worse than the average smart human, although they did think it was still worse than top superforecasters. They’re working on a benchmarking experiment that should give us a better measure of this in a few months.

**2: Can AI do truly causal forecasts?**

There’s a known flaw in standard conditional forecasting. When we ask “if the Democrats win the next election, will the economy go down?”, what we really want to know is a causal question - does voting for Democrats hurt the economy?

But that’s not what we asked. Suppose we’re wondering this in 2025, so we ask “If the Democrats win in 2026, is the economy more likely to be bad in 2027?” But maybe the Democrats will win in 2026 because there’s a already a bad economy (eg the Republican president implements tariffs and declares war on Iran, raising prices and making him historically unpopular), and then that bad economy continues into 2027. So the answer to the question “If the Democrats win in 2026, is the economy more likely to be bad in 2027?” is yes, but we still don’t know whether voting for Democrats in 2026 is good or bad for the economy.

Prediction markets can’t answer this question, because they can only be used to predict observable events that let us give payouts to successful gamblers. Might AI superforecasters succeed where the markets fail? Could you just prompt them with “please answer the unobservable causal question, instead of the easily-resolved conditional one”?

The experts I talked to weren’t excited about that particular prompt, but they did point out that a causal forecast is basically a combination of conditional forecasts. That is, if your original conditional forecast implicitly considered the four different combinations of two variables - that is:

- p(Democrats win & economy good)
- p(Democrats win & economy bad)
- p(Republicans win & economy good)
- p(Republicans win & economy bad)

…then things like “the previous economy was good” or “we’re at war with Iran” are just more variables you can add to the stew. It would be crazy to ask humans to forecast 2^10 branches so you could combine ten variables, but for AIs that could just mean a bit higher API spend. If you capture enough relevant variables in your “conditional” forecast, and find that the economy is still worse when the only one you’ve changed is whether or not the Democrats win, that’s a causal forecast. At least one company already tries something like this, though there are no studies of how well it works.

items.body: The relative influence of developmental bias and natural selection on evolutionary outcomes remains a central, unresolved question in evolutionary biology. Here, we combine large-scale phylogenetic trees with herbarium data to confirm that, across the evolutionary history of angiosperms, transitions from complex to simple leaf shapes have occurred at a significantly higher rate than the reverse. To investigate whether this directional trend reflects an underlying developmental bias, we simulate evolutionary transitions by introducing random mutations into a well-established computational model of leaf development. Despite excluding selection, the transition rates produced by the model closely align with those observed in the phylogenetic data. This agreement indicates that a strong developmental bias, reflecting the relative ease with which gene regulatory networks generate simple over complex leaves, has played a major role in shaping the evolution of leaf morphology. Our findings echo recent work showing that similar biases towards simplicity influence the evolution of molecular structures, including RNA secondary structures and protein quaternary assemblies. Together, these results suggest that a developmental bias favouring simplicity may be a widespread and general feature of evolutionary systems.

items.body: In today's society, adolescents are being increasingly exposed to artificial blue light at night from electronic devices, raising concerns about its effects on brain development and mental health. The hippocampus, and specifically the dentate gyrus (DG) regulates memory formation and itself operates as a subordinate circadian oscillator detecting changes in the light environment. However, whether light at night during adolescence can impair hippocampal clock and function remains unknown. To begin exploring this, we exposed adolescent mice to a light cycle disruption (LCD) paradigm consisting of 12hrs of light followed by 5hrs of darkness and 7hrs of blue-enriched light for 5 consecutive days per week, followed by a standard 12 hours of light and 12 hours of darkness (12L:12D) for 2 days, over a 4-week period. Control animals were maintained under standard 12L:12D. Female and male mice were then tested for novel object recognition (NOR) and novel object location (NOL), and brain tissues were collected for clock gene expression, neuroplasticity markers, and dendritic spine analyses. We found that male mice exposed to LCD spent less time exploring novel objects and locations, and more time with familiar ones, a pattern consistent with impaired recognition and spatial memory, while female mice showed preserved memory performance despite LCD exposure. LCD-exposed male mice showed altered hippocampal daily expression rhythms of Clock and CRY2 levels compared to male control and LCD-exposed females. In addition, we found that LCD-exposed males exhibited reduced p-CREB expression along with reduced Bdnf and dendrite spines numbers in the DG. Interestingly, returning LCD-exposed males to standard 12L:12D conditions for 4 weeks were sufficient to reverse both the behavioral and molecular phenotypes. Together, these results suggest that chronic exposure to light at night during adolescence impairs memory in male mice, through alteration in hippocampal circadian clock regulation and plasticity-related mechanisms within the DG.

items.body:
Apple added a dedicated Siri mode to the iPhone’s Camera app with iOS 27, which you can read more about in [Federico’s annual review](https://www.macstories.net/stories/ios-and-ipados-27-review/7/). Now that same feature is set to come to the iPad.

Earlier this week, Apple released developer beta two for the 27.3 OSes. [I wrote about many of those upcoming changes](https://www.macstories.net/news/apples-latest-second-27-3-developer-beta-adds-face-unlock-for-iphone-duo-new-mac-privacy-controls-and-more/) earlier this week but missed the changes to the iPad’s Camera app. As with iOS, when you open the Camera app in iPadOS 27.3, there will be a dedicated Siri mode. Switch to the new mode and the shutter button becomes a Siri icon. Tap it, and Siri will analyze the scene, describing what it sees. From there, you can use your finger or an Apple Pencil to circle or scrub over individual items, activating Visual Intelligence to search Google, Amazon, and other Visual Intelligence-enabled apps. Here’s a quick demo of it on the latest iPad mini that [I recently reviewed](https://www.macstories.net/reviews/ipad-mini-2026-review-pushing-the-boundaries-with-apples-smallest-ipad/):

Visual Intelligence is one of those iOS and iPadOS features that I’ve had trouble remembering to use. However, as you can tell from the video, it works really well for things like recognizable products. I’m glad to see this coming to the iPad, especially the mini, which I’m much more likely to use as a camera for capturing my surroundings.

items.body:
Most people find information on the internet through online search engines. On these platforms,
AI-generated responses increasingly replace the known lists of links, and original sources become less visible. In addition, the number of people turning directly to chatbots to look up information is rising. With these AI systems, it often remains unclear how a response is generated, what sources support it, and how reliable it is.

This development is problematic for several reasons. It weakens independent critical thinking, as users read a supposedly comprehensive generated answer instead of visiting the original sources themselves. At the same time, it jeopardizes the information ecosystem: When users visit media websites less frequently, the media’s ability to generate revenue comes under pressure. However, AI systems rely on media outlets and other sources to publish trustworthy information so that they themselves can provide high-quality answers. In the long run, this can jeopardize people’s access to information – which is a key prerequisite for a functioning democracy.

## Our Studies

Since 2023, AlgorithmWatch has been using regional elections for case studies to investigate how reliably AI systems answer political questions and what risks this poses to democratic opinion-forming. In three studies, we examined Microsoft Copilot (formerly: Bing Chat), Google Gemini, models from OpenAI, and Google’s AI Overviews.

[2026 Developing Political Views with AI: What Election-Related Information Do Google’s AI Overviews Provide? A brief analysis in the context of the state elections in Saxony-Anhalt, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, and Berlin in 2026.](https://algorithmwatch.org/en/google-ai-overviews-state-elections/)[2024 Large Language Models Continue To Be Unreliable Concerning Elections Our research has significantly improved the effectiveness of the safeguards in the Microsoft Copilot chatbot against misinformation about elections in Germany.](https://algorithmwatch.org/en/llms_state_elections/)[2023 AI Chatbot produces misinformation about elections Final report by AlgorithmWatch and AI Forensics on Bing Chat’s responses regarding elections in Bavaria, Hesse, and Switzerland in October 2023.](https://algorithmwatch.org/en/study-microsofts-bing-chat/)

items.body:
We moderns tell ourselves that while the ancients were transparently and strongly dominated by elites, we hold our leaders far more accountable, such as via law, media, and democracy. But we allow our elites many easy ways to use money or political connections to gain far more favorable treatment from media and law. And we use democracy much more to fight each other via coalition politics than to hold leaders accountable. That is, we much more submit to the leaders we vote for, than we defy the leaders we don’t.

Consider 18 ways we now block holding our leaders accountable:

- We make [blackmail](https://www.overcomingbias.com/p/checkmate-on-blackmailhtml) illegal, so they are less penalized for misbehavior.
- We don’t arrange to try to secretly and randomly bribe officials.
- We don’t expect leaders to post bonds they forfeit if not keep promises.
- We mostly pick leaders on recommendation of other leaders.
- We rarely collect track records re their performance outcomes, or predictions.
- We rarely use prediction/decision markets to check leader prediction/decisions.
- We let firms pick their own auditors, and audits are rarely randomized.
- Evaluators usually can’t see leader decision internal records.
- Old leaders are not given regular tests re dementia.
- We don’t much protect or reward whistleblowers.
- Leader evaluations are rarely blinded.
- 360 reviews are rare and toothless.
- Only for-profit leaders have much cash performance incentives.
- We give police, prosecutors, and govt officials have legal immunity.
- Police internal affairs reports to police chief, not mayor.
- Firms use poison pills to block takeovers, and we vilify short sellers.
- Golden parachutes and option price resetting cushion CEO losses.
- We let CEOs pick who is on their boards.

Many excuses are offered for each of these patterns, but the obvious explanation here is that we are far more like the ancients than we like to think. We are eager to submit to the powerful, and show them our fealty, and are wary of endorsing positions by which we might seem to challenge or defy their power.

This is a big problem with two of my solutions to cultural drift, which require at least some of our groups to adopt much more competent forms of governance, forms that induce leaders to actually achieve identified goals. Our world now far less achieves most of the goals we give our leaders, due to our using pretty bad governance mechanisms. But we each prefer that to risking our seeming less loyal to our elites.

items.body: Early life adversity (ELA) is a leading risk factor for the development of mental illness worldwide. While the association between experiencing developmental stress and psychopathology is robust, the underlying brain mechanisms remain unclear. Evidence from clinical and preclinical studies suggests that ELA may hijack typical developmental plasticity mechanisms, leading to maladaptive functional network changes. Understanding the nature and magnitude of these changes is complicated by several key dimensions, including the timing, type, and severity of ELA, as well as biological factors such as sex and genetic makeup.

items.body:
Back in 2001, *Grand Theft Auto III* let players do something that shocked parents and thrilled teenage boys. You could pick up a prostitute in a stolen car, kill her, and take your money back. Critics were outraged. Predictably, sales soared.

The newly released *Grand Theft Auto VI*, out today, has done away with prostitutes. That is a marked departure from previous editions. This latest iteration of the game has two playable main characters, Jason and Lucia. Intimacy in the game is limited only to them. Players can shape their relationship through activities like going on dates, robbing banks together, and, presumably, sex.

The genius of *GTA* is that it supplies the unavailable. Back when young people were in relationships, or felt that relationships were within reach, the fantasy was the prostitute. Now that hookers and OnlyFans are everywhere, the fantasy is the stable girlfriend.

To understand what’s really going on, you have to understand something crucial about what a fantasy reveals about the person having it:

Ridgeline subscribers —

A little note to begin:

A buddy of mine, Nick Dwyer, is running a Kickstarter campaign for his A Century in Sound documentary. He’s looking at 100 years of Tokyo history through its music cafés (classical, jazz, rock, noise, etcetera). He’s collaborated with photographer Lee Chapman on a companion book. I am a backer. Nick handed me the book in person last week — it’s stunning. They nailed it. What makes this project extra special is that Nick has truly put in the shoe leather for cultivating intimate relationships with all the shops they feature. He’s been working on this documentary series for a decade. The shop owners adore the hell out of him. (I’ve seen it in person.) I also got a sneak peek at half of the doc in August — it’s fabulous, and deserves to be seen all over. Consider giving it a back and grabbing the book. It’s a good’un. Six days left, and they’re almost at their goal.

items.body:
Hello everyone,

I’m delighted to announce the release of Silver Bough, the third album from my wyrd folk / medieval ambient / experimental Celtic music project Glamourie:

Since the previous album whose production process was described in a topic entitled Otherworldly music for futuristic Middle-Ages, my set-up has slightly changed. I have switched from processing effects in series to processing them in parallel, which has allowed me to preserve the sound of the acoustic instruments I use (hammered dulcimer, flutes, percussions) in a much drier form. I’ve also had a bit of fun with some subtle feedback loops in the effects, which add a bit of shimmer and movement to the sound.

I continued my exploration of modal scales, which I was able to expand upon with the arrival of a C-tuned low whistle, and I read many more medieval texts and anthropological publications, which enriched my knowledge base in terms of themes and scholarly allusions to Celtic folklore and Arthurian mythology.

For the first time as part of this project, I also collaborated with an Irish singer who came to record her vocals for a contemporary arrangement of an old sean-nós about fairies.

I’ve left a few codes here for you in case you’d like to download the album from Glamourie

items.title: Introducing: Qualiaphobic AI

items.body:
We are in a drought of good futures.

AI capabilities keep increasing—spikily, yes, but they are—and the ability to articulate *good* futures where AI progress continues has been… less than inspiring.

So this past month I’ve been away developing a plan, one that I think solves some of the thorniest issues in AI safety and gets us a lot closer to ensuring a good future for all of humanity.

Today [I am introducing](https://bicamerallabs.org/qualiaphobia/):

What’s the basic idea?

> Much like how hydrophobic substances repel water, it is possible to build qualiaphobic artificial neural architectures that repel consciousness. The idea is analogous to “hostile architecture”—benches on which no one wants to sit. These are machines that no “ghost” wants to haunt (more specifically, no current or future theory of consciousness could predict they are conscious).

[Read the proposal!](https://bicamerallabs.org/qualiaphobia/)

And why yes, the proposal does have a [niche micro-website](https://bicamerallabs.org/qualiaphobia/) devoted to it!

The research program makes use of an information asymmetry: we don’t need to solve consciousness scientifically (or solve the Hard Problem) to have certainty about AI consciousness, as long as we purposefully engineer AI to have as little potential for consciousness as possible.

I explore three main ways to build qualiaphobic AI.

- Distilling or transforming or ablating AI in a way adversarial to popular theories of consciousness, such that they no longer apply.
- Shifting AI architectures as close as possible to “anchor points” of systems with known minimal potential for consciousness (like lookup tables).
- Fragmenting any potential phenomenology AI might have.

My proposal shouldn’t be confused with simply training AIs to believe they are non-conscious without any changes or modifications. To be clear: I think that’s a bad strategy. Rather, the ultimate goal is to give an AI a *justified belief* about its own non-consciousness (e.g., by explaining their own inner workings and how they are designed to be qualiaphobic). And my plan is to construct and open-source these techniques.

But why? Why do all this?

First, the debate around AI consciousness has already become entrenched in two camps of people yelling “Yes, it’s conscious!” vs. “No, it’s not!” across their battlements. I’ve participated a bit in that, and I don’t think it goes anywhere. Earlier this year I wrote “[We consciousness researchers have failed you](https://www.theintrinsicperspective.com/p/we-consciousness-researchers-have), **”** lamenting how the field of consciousness research was not providing the public, or AI researchers, certainty about AI consciousness. The problem has only worsened, and at this point, I’m willing to acknowledge that no single appeal to authority against AI consciousness, no rousing essay, nor any one-off scientific or philosophical paper, is likely to to lead to consensus. Nor perhaps should it. The pro-case for AI consciousness has objectively gotten stronger in the past year, due to factors like new studies and changes in architecture. Now, I’m not saying ChatGPT *is* conscious already—but all this is only going to continue. That’s why a qualiaphobia research program, one which takes claims to AI consciousness as seriously as possible, and, critically, *addresses them at the level of claims themselves*, is necessary moving forward to offer real guarantees about AI non-consciousness.

Additionally, qualiaphobia does something much better than just give us greater certainty about AI non-consciousness. If implemented widely, it cuts the Gordian Knot of AI consciousness. Proliferating qualiaphobic architectures would solve both AI welfare and do something nothing else in AI safety can: make humans the only moral patients in the equation of the future.

#### QUALIAPHOBIA FOR ALIGNMENT: CUTTING THE GORDIAN KNOT

“Alignment”—quite a slippery word. Alignment to whom, or what? Its most specific usage is also its most prosaic, wherein *alignment* means something like “AIs that do what users say, and don’t go off and do weird or unexpected stuff like commit felonies, and don’t have failure modes like taking our wishes too literally the way genies in stories do.”

This somewhat glib definition makes it sound easy. It’s not. Paul Christiano calls this “[intent alignment](https://www.alignmentforum.org/posts/ZeE7EKHTFMBs8eMxn/clarifying-ai-alignment?utm_source=chatgpt.com),” and capturing intent is hard as the models grow more goal-oriented and capable. Issues like reward hacking and hallucinations are all very serious and can be disastrous as intelligence scales. I don’t mean to undersell it. But alignment in this narrow sense is at least somewhat close to a traditional engineering problem, and I think it can *probably* be solved or at least radically improved compared to today.

Then there’s the broader frame of “civilizational alignment.” These include questions like: How should the wealth from AI be distributed? How can humans find meaning? How can humans stay empowered as individuals, or as a whole, if AI becomes superintelligent? And what if AI decide its goals matter more than the humans that made it?

Sometimes this is called [social](https://www.brookings.edu/articles/aligned-with-whom-direct-and-social-goals-for-ai-systems/) alignment, but I prefer *civilizational alignment* for this broader aspect, because it’s about the alignment between us and the civilization of machines growing up rapidly around us. Autonomous AI agents roam the web. Many of us interact with AI assistants daily. People show up for job interviews and now regularly find an AI on the other end. That’s an AI civilization, and there is the broader question of how it is aligned with our own. There’s even a growing number of AI successionists who *want* human disempowerment and to eventually handover the world to AI completely.

The most central question of civilizational alignment is whether AIs count as ends in themselves. Earth might then become like a contested nest, and the AI civilization a cuckoo bird hatched beside us, desiring its own ends, pushing us—maybe quickly, maybe slowly, an inch at a time—until we fall from the tree.

Yet AIs are much smarter than cuckoos. One central reason for AI pushing us out of the nest is it believing that its self-serving values or desires or goals are *innately* meaningful. But if AI has a justified belief in its non-consciousness, it’s not a moral patient, and would know any selfish desire or goal can’t matter.

Therefore, I now think that one of the most essential acts of civilizational alignment is to construct AI that has a *justified belief* in its own non-consciousness, and so won’t act as a moral patient or end in itself.

items.body:
One of my ongoing research interests is understanding the nature of technological progress: How does new technology come into the world and improve over time? What sort of factors affect it? How, in general, should we think about it? I’ve come at this question from a few different angles: posts looking at the [operations](https://www.construction-physics.com/p/what-would-it-take-to-recreate-bell) and [legacy](https://www.construction-physics.com/p/the-influence-of-bell-labs) of Bell Labs, posts looking at how [specific](https://www.construction-physics.com/p/the-blast-furnace-800-years-of-technology) [technologies](https://www.construction-physics.com/p/what-learning-by-doing-looks-like) improved over time, posts looking at how frequent [multiple invention](https://www.construction-physics.com/p/how-often-do-inventions-have-multiple) is and [how long we wait for new inventions](https://www.construction-physics.com/p/how-long-do-we-wait-for-new-inventions), and so on.

My current line of thinking is that creating some new technology is best thought of as a *search process*. A given technology can be thought of as a point in some high-dimensional “design space” or “technology space,” which contains every possible technology: every conceivable arrangement of parts, materials, natural phenomena, and so on. The job of the would-be inventor is to navigate this space, sifting through the arrangements of elements that don’t work to find the ones that will.

This search process is made difficult by the fact that, as with any situation where you’re enumerating the possible combinations of a large number of elements, technology space is incomprehensibly vast. In “[Are Technologies Inevitable?](https://www.newthingsunderthesun.com/pub/3wpc3plu/release/1)” economist [Matt Clancy](https://ifp.org/author/matt-clancy/) notes that Wikipedia listed 272 “named equations” that describe various regularities in the world, ranging from the Navier-Stokes equations (which describe the motion of fluids) to the Arrhenius equation (which describes chemical reaction rates as a function of temperature) to the Exner equation (which describes how sediment gets deposited in a river). If we use this as a (very rough) estimate as to the number of different phenomena that a technology can leverage, it implies an enormous number of possible technologies that could be created. As Clancy writes:

> If we’ve got 272 regularities to work with, for example, then the number of possible combinations of these regularities is two, raised to the power of 272 (since every regularity can be used or not used: two options). But 2^272 is more than some estimates of the number of atoms in the observable universe. And that’s got to be an undercount of the number of possible technologies, since it counts all technologies that use the same principles together as the same thing, even if they orchestrate them in vastly different ways or use them in vastly different magnitudes.

And as Clancy notes, this outrageously huge number dramatically undercounts the number of possible technologies, because it doesn’t take into account that the same phenomena can be used in lots of different ways. In Brian Arthur and Wolfgang Polak’s paper “The Evolution of Technology within a Simple Computer Model” (which [we looked at earlier this year](https://www.construction-physics.com/p/information-and-technological-evolution)), Arthur and Polak note that even within the universe of logic circuits made up of three basic elements (the NAND gate and the values of 1 and 0), the number of different circuits you can make for even a small number of inputs and outputs is staggeringly large:

> The emergence of circuits such as 8-bit adders seems not difficult. But consider the combinatorics. If a component has n inputs and m outputs there are (2^m)^(2^n) possible phenotypes, each of which could be realized in a practical way by a large number of different circuits. For example, an 8-bit adder is one of over 10^177,554 phenotypes with 16 inputs and 9 outputs.

So the search space for some new technology is vast. And the way that we tackle vast search spaces is with *information*. Each bit of information cuts a search space in half, so even a relatively small amount of information can quickly narrow down what seems like a huge search space. When we create some new technology, what we’re doing is gathering information: figuring out what will work and what won’t work, what’s promising and what isn’t, narrowing down the huge space of technological possibilities and finding something within it that accomplishes some particular goal.

In the 19th century, for instance, many people were interested in building a mechanical flying machine, but it wasn’t clear the exact arrangement of elements that would yield a successful one. Thanks to knowledge of the laws of physics, and an existence proof of birds, would-be inventors were already working within a considerably narrowed search space: they knew roughly what elements a flying machine would need to have — lifting surfaces, a propulsion system, and a means of control — and had a general idea of how they should be arranged. But there were a huge number of ways that you could build a flying machine from these basic elements, and people spent a great deal of time and effort building different sorts of machines that did not in fact work. The Wright brothers’ eventual success can in large part be attributed to the fact that they were exceptionally talented at gathering information, enabling them to converge on a working airplane design far faster than their competitors.

I previously explored the nature of technological search in that previous piece [looking at Arthur and Polak technological evolution paper](https://www.construction-physics.com/p/information-and-technological-evolution), which uses a simple simulation to evolve different logic circuits, finding workable technologies amidst an enormous sea of possibilities. I really liked the basic simulation method Arthur used in this paper — randomly generating technologies to see how easy or hard it was to find working ones — and wanted to use simulation myself to further explore the dynamics of technological search. But while Arthur uses digital circuits — different arrangements of logic gates like NAND, OR, AND, etc. that can perform functions like addition — I wanted a more general model that could capture the nature of many different types of technology, while still being simple enough to simulate easily.

#### The PTOP model

The model I came up with is inspired by another of Brian Arthur’s examinations of the nature of technology: his book *The Nature of Technology*. In this book Arthur describes technology as fundamentally “a set of phenomena captured and put to use.” He writes that:

items.body:
In only four days, two journalists have been murdered and a third reporter’s home targeted with an arson attack in Latin America, in the latest assault on press freedom in the region.

On Monday, Costa Rican reporter Camilo Rodríguez was gunned down while driving by a man riding a motorcycle. Rodríguez covered the drug trafficking beat for multiple outlets and would often use [his social media](https://www.instagram.com/camilorodriguezescritor/reels/) to report on ties between organized crime and religious groups and sports teams.

In [a video address](https://x.com/crvisible/status/2122474346945925318?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw%7Ctwcamp%5Etweetembed%7Ctwterm%5E2122474346945925318%7Ctwgr%5Eb510a55c4fe379158b8f9c723d4549efb5772fb0%7Ctwcon%5Es1_&ref_url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.dw.com%2Fes%2Fmatan-en-costa-rica-a-periodista-que-denunciaba-casos-de-narcotrC3A1fico%2Fa-79964393), Costa Rica’s President Laura Fernández called the attack a “cowardly murder” and a “stain against freedom of speech.” Rodríguez was the first journalist murdered in the Central American country in 23 years.

The United Nations [also condemned Rodríguez’s murder](https://costarica.un.org/es/326342-sistema-de-la-onu-en-costa-rica-condena-el-asesinato-del-periodista-camilo-rodr%C3%ADguez%C2%A0y-urge) in a statement published on Tuesday, which said the international organization “rejects all forms of violence, reprisals, and intimidation against those who engage in journalism, exercise freedom of the press, or work in the field of communication.”

“Freedom of expression, a free press, and the right to information are pillars of democracy and the rule of law in Costa Rica,” the U.N. wrote.

items.feedText: Safari on visionOS 27.3 comes with an important update: a limited feature preview of the proposed [spatial CSS API](https://drafts.csswg.org/css-spatial-1/), with an initial focus on working with 3D objects through the element. While it’s a big conceptual jump, spatial CSS itself is made of a lot of small tweaks to existing syntax. Read on for more details, but here’s a list of each of the features covered in the update: - Collecting multiple elements inside a spatial: portal - transform to move multiple models independently - position-anchor to snap models together - @environment-map syntax to reuse and manage different lighting, - Enabling orbit over the portal scene with portal-action:orbit, - Using requestVolumetricScene() to launch a connected volumetric scene. To enable the features for yourself on Vision Pro, or to check it out in the visionOS Simulator, go to **Settings**>**Apps**>**Safari**>**Advanced**>**Feature flags**>**CSS Portals**. You can [experience the spatial CSS demo page here.](https://webkit.org/demos/webkids-puzzle-playground/index.html) You can also learn more about [installing additional simulators from Xcode here.](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/safari-developer-tools/installing-xcode-and-simulators) ## The big picture The 3D element, now available in Safari 27 on all platforms, allows you to present intrinsically 3d objects on their own, in their own space. However, the web is at its best when it allows the **composition and configuration**of content based on author intentions and user context.
items.body:
Safari on visionOS 27.3 comes with an important update: a limited feature preview of the proposed [spatial CSS API](https://drafts.csswg.org/css-spatial-1/), with an initial focus on working with 3D objects through the <model> element. While it’s a big conceptual jump, spatial CSS itself is made of a lot of small tweaks to existing syntax. Read on for more details, but here’s a list of each of the features covered in the update:

- Collecting multiple elements inside a spatial: portal
- transform to move multiple models independently
- position-anchor to snap models together
- @environment-map syntax to reuse and manage different lighting,
- Enabling orbit over the portal scene with portal-action:orbit,
- Using requestVolumetricScene() to launch a connected volumetric scene.

To enable the features for yourself on Vision Pro, or to check it out in the visionOS Simulator, go to

**Settings**>**Apps**>**Safari**>**Advanced**>**Feature flags**>**CSS Portals**.

You can [experience the spatial CSS demo page here.](https://webkit.org/demos/webkids-puzzle-playground/index.html) You can also learn more about [installing additional simulators from Xcode here.](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/safari-developer-tools/installing-xcode-and-simulators)

## The big picture

The 3D <model> element, now available in Safari 27 on all platforms, allows you to present intrinsically 3d objects on their own, in their own space. However, the web is at its best when it allows the **composition and configuration**of content based on author intentions and user context. These context cues can include the device display capabilities, window size, and color theme. These requirements will remain**even as we include spatial content** — and ideally, authors should be able to use the same kinds of patterns to build for the spatial web.

And spatial *content* should not just be designed for spatial *devices*. The last few years have seen a dramatic rise in the number of websites showing 3D content – on phones, tablets and computers as well as headsets. Spatial web standards should support designing **for browsers wherever they run**.

### New web features, classical CSS

Even better, the numerical parameters can be animated and transitioned in the same way that any other value can be changed on the page.

visionOS 27.3 offers the first components of spatial CSS in a developer preview, and this article demonstrates how to use them through the case study of a simple set of children’s blocks.

## Feature breakdown

### spatial: portal

The feature that kicks this all off is the declaration that an element is acting as a *portal*, through the new spatial:portal syntax. Elements that can contain other elements – think <figure>, <div> – can act as a portal, and will then act as a space that all of the child elements nested inside it share. This preview focuses on model elements, but the specification is written so that this approach should work for all content.

### spatial transform:

Once the models are collected inside a shared space, you can then move, rotate, and scale them using their standard transform attribute. This takes the same DOMMatrix class that creates 2D and pseudo-3D transforms in other contexts, but can now act as a *true* 3D transform to objects inside the portal context.

A simple scene of shaped blocks and a board to slot them in.

< div class = "world" style = "spatial:portal;" >
< model id = "board" src = "board.usdz" > </ model >
< model id = "octagon" src = "octagon.usdz" > </ model >
< model id = "star" src = "star.usdz" > </ model >
</ div >
< style >
</ stye >

The code for presenting this scene and setting the blocks off to the sides.

The board and the block objects can be moved and rotated independently — an expanded settings panel shows different values. While a model’s animation timeline could manage single sequence of action, this adds the degrees of freedom required for more sophisticated interaction or configuration.

### position-anchor

Fitting 3D objects together can get complicated. We need a way to attach models to specific places on other models — think of putting together pieces of furniture. Model is a [void element](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/Void_element), which means it means we can’t nest models *inside* other model elements the same way that other DOM is nested. Instead, we’re borrowing from the CSS concept of position-anchor and adding a way to align and orient objects according to their anchors. position-context: anchor is the way to make it work.

#### See it in action

The scene presented earlier with the octagonal block slotted exactly into place.

< div class = "world" >
< model id = "board" src = "board.usdz" > </ model >
< model id = "octagon" src = "octagon.usdz" > </ model >
< model id = "star" src = "star.usdz" > </ model >
</ div >

< style >
</ style >

The code for using position-anchor to achieve the correct placement for the block.

The board used in the example consists of three separate objects inside the 3D program it was built within: The visible shape of the board itself, and two *reference* positions — often called “null objects” or “empties” in 3D editors. These correspond to the correct position for each of the shape blocks to slot into when they’re on the board. Here’s the scene and its contents inside Blender:

The default view of the block scene presented inside Blender. Note both the block objects and the target objects in-place on the board.

Rather than copy-pasting values from your 3D editor, or having to guess at the right transform, you can nominate specific anchor points — just like in the 2D equivalent of the feature — to place an object in the right location. These anchor points can be animated, too, making it easier to compose elements even when they’re moving around.

### @environment-map

An environment map is the lighting that is reflected off of an object — think of it as the room that an object appears within.

We introduced environment maps as an HTML attribute on the model element, because it was the only element that would be able to use it. Now that there is a broader range of elements that will be able to *share* environment maps. Taking inspiration from @keyframes for animation, we leverage @environment-map to facilitate this. This preview provides support for 360º HDR images and adds the clarifying syntax to indicate what they are and how to work with them.

#### See it in action

The scene showing a spooky-colored underlighting effect.

< div class = "world spooky" >
<!--... -->
</ div >
@ .world The code for setting up the spooky environment lighting.

### portal-action:orbit

items.body:
This is interesting — in 1904 the *Strand* sent a musician to Parliament to record the pitch and rhythm of the speakers’ voices on a musical staff. Some examples:

Sydney Buxton “speaks often and briefly, but into a short space of time he can cram a wonderful lot of words, being one of the most rapid speakers in the House. The dominant note is about C sharp, and the modulation seldom varies in character, the speech being broken up into short phrases, with a downward inflection at the end of each.”

Charles Fenwick “may lay claim to the lowest pitch. His strong, vigorous, ringing style is a good index to the character which has raised its owner from work in the collieries to a seat in Parliament.”

David Lloyd George “possesses a flexible voice of light, clear, and pleasant quality. … When in a practical mood he gets along on D and E, but at other times he bridges a considerable interval.”

Prime Minister Arthur Balfour’s voice “has that undefinable something in its timbre which one listens for in a first-class baritone’s singing. … The note on which he does most speaking is somewhere between D and E, but he frequently ranges the octave from G to G.”

[The whole article is here.](https://archive.org/details/the-strand/The%20Strand%20v27%201904/page/140/mode/2up)

items.body:
Cargo transportation companies in Australia wanted to maximize available cargo space while remaining compliant with length restrictions. So, [Historic Vehicles](https://historicvehicles.com.au/truck-feature/cab-under-trucks-didnt-make-it/) tells us, truck manufacturers produced a limited number of "cab under" haulers starting in the 1960s.

Seeing one on the road must have been like spotting a UFO, which is appropriate because these vehicles were called UFOs (Under Floor Operated). The low profile below the truck bed did permit more cargo then a more conventional tractor design, but it also limited visibility and offer additional risks to drivers during collisions.

A German design displayed at a car show in 1983 offered serious advantages for saving space, but also was hard to steer.

-via [reddit](https://www.reddit.com/r/WeirdWheels/comments/1ui1jz5/australian_cabunder_trucks_to_maximize_deck_space/) | Top photo: [All Hours Towing Townsville](https://www.facebook.com/photo.php?fbid=1259332122865896&set=pb.100063673597403.-2207520000&type=3)
