Die CAD-Dateien zeigen beim iPhone Air 2 zwei Kameras nebeneinander und decken sich damit weitgehend mit den Dummy-Modellen, die der Leaker Sonny Dickson vor Kurzem veröffentlicht hat. Auf den Dummys sitzen beide Kameras im linken Teil der Kameraleiste, w…
items.body:
Auf CAD-Dateien, die [Engadget](https://www.engadget.com/2325828/new-leaks-reveal-the-iphone-18e-will-have-a-redesigned-camera-plateau/) einsehen konnte, ist die Kameraerhebung des iPhone Air 2 und des iPhone 18 jeweils 3,8 statt bisher 3,45 Millimeter dick. Während sich am Aussehen des iPhone 18 gegenüber dem iPhone 17 sonst nichts ändert, bekommt das iPhone Air 2 eine zweite Kamera. Sein Gehäuse bleibt mit 5,6 Millimetern trotzdem so dünn wie beim aktuellen Modell.

Fotocredit: Apple

## Ausstattung des iPhone Air 2

Die CAD-Dateien zeigen beim iPhone Air 2 zwei Kameras nebeneinander und decken sich damit weitgehend mit den Dummy-Modellen, die der Leaker Sonny Dickson vor Kurzem veröffentlicht hat. Auf den Dummys sitzen beide Kameras im linken Teil der Kameraleiste, während Blitz und Mikrofon wie bisher auf der rechten Seite liegen. Mehreren Berichten zufolge handelt es sich bei der zweiten Kamera um eine Ultraweitwinkelkamera. Der Analyst Jeff Pu geht davon aus, dass sie mit 48 Megapixeln auflöst.

Neben dem A20 Pro soll das iPhone Air 2 Apples C2-Modem, den Funkchip N2 und einen Akku mit längerer Laufzeit bekommen. Laut Pu bleibt es beim 6,5-Zoll-Display, bei 12 GB Arbeitsspeicher und bei der Frontkamera mit 18 Megapixeln und Center Stage.

Wie Engadget angibt, stammen die Dateien von einem Leaker aus der Lieferkette, der bereits die Farben des iPhone 17 und des iPhone 18 Pro korrekt vorhergesagt hat. Apple soll das iPhone Air 2 und das iPhone 18 Anfang 2027 gemeinsam mit dem iPhone 18e vorstellen.

items.body:
# Parlamentswahlen in Spanien: Wählen mit dem Taschenrechner

## Parlamentswahlen in Spanien : Wählen mit dem Taschenrechner

Spaniens sozialistischer Premier Pedro Sánchez setzt seine letzte Hoffnung in die kleineren linken Parteien. Auch taktisches Wählen kann ausschlaggebend sein.

24.11.2026

7:12 Uhr

teilen

Diesen Artikel teilen

Will die Hoffnung nicht aufgeben: Pedro Sánchez (links) nach einer TV-Debatte mit seinem konvervativen Herausforderer Alberto Núñez Feijoo Foto: Manu Fernandez/ap

Aus Madrid

Am 29. November wählt Spanien ein neues Parlament. Fast alle Umfragen gehen von einem klaren Sieg der Rechten aus. Die konservative Partido Popular (PP) von Alberto Núñez Feijóo wird demnach gemeinsam mit der rechtsextremen Vox von Santiago Abascal eine absolute Mehrheit erzielen. Eine Brandmauer gibt es in Spanien nicht.

Doch der seit acht Jahren regierende sozialistische Ministerpräsident Pedro Sánchez will die Hoffnung auf eine erneute Regierungsbildung nicht aufgeben. Dafür braucht er die Unterstützung der linken Parteien, links von Sánchez PSOE.

Doch gerade die schwächelt. Nicht zuletzt deshalb, weil die Sozialisten viele der Errungenschaften, wie etwa die Arbeitsmarktreform, die auf Druck der Linken zustande kamen, für sich vermarkten konnte. Nach der Wahl 2013 kam das Bündnis Sumar, der Juniorpartner in der bisherigen in Minderheit regierenden Koalition, auf 31 Abgeordnete. Die Umfragen sehen die Nachfolgeorganisation Frente Amplio (Breite Front), unter der einstigen Bürgermeisterin von Barcelona Ada Colau, nur noch bei 10.

Obwohl Frente Amplio 11 Parteien vereint, tritt die linke gespalten zu den Wahlen an. Die linksalternative Podemos, deren Angeordnete einst aus Sumar ausgetreten waren, nach dem sie keine Ministerposten erhielten, stellt sich alleine zur Wahl und wird aller Voraussicht nach, keine Vertreter ins neue Parlament entsenden. Es könnten somit wertvolle Stimmen verloren gehen. Dass Podemos und Frente Amplio nicht zusammenkamen, liegt weniger an inhaltlichen Punkten als an persönlichen Animositäten.

Von den drei linken Kräften vertritt Podemos, bei Wohnungs-, Verteidigungs- und Wirtschaftspolitik die radikalsten Positionen, während die PSOE am moderatesten auftritt. Beim Thema Migration sind sich die Parteien weitgehend einig.

## Auch mit Regionalparteien wird es eng

Darüber hinaus gibt es in mehreren Regionen, wie dem Baskenland, Galizien, Katalonien und Andalusien, eigene linke Kräfte. Diese vertreten neben sozialen Forderungen mehr oder weniger nationalistische oder regionalistische Bestrebungen. Sie werden wohl besser Abschneiden, als 2023. So sehen die Umfragen EH Bildu aus dem Baskenland etwa mit einem starken Zuwachs, ebenso die Republikanische Linke Kataloniens (ERC). Beide haben in den letzten acht Jahren Sánchez unterstützt.

Hinzu kommt das spanische Wahlsystem, in dem nach dem sogenannten D'Hondt-Verfahren ausgezählt wird, das großen Parteien Vorteile verschafft. Während die Methode bei großen Mengen zu vergebener Sitze relativ gerecht ist, kann es bei einer kleinen Zahl das Ergebnis stark verzerren. Und das ist in Spanien der Fall. Denn die Sitze werden auf Provinzebene vergeben. Manche Provinzen haben nur drei oder fünf Abgeordnete. Selbst Parteien mit über zehn Prozent der Stimmen können so einfach außen vor bleiben.

Angesicht der Befürchtung, die rechtsextreme Vox könnte schon bald in der Regierung sitzen, macht sich im linken Teil der Gesellschaft ein Gefühl breit, dass es so noch nie gab. Es geht vielen darum, das die Linke als Block gewinnt. Ob sie dafür letztendlich Frente Amplio, PSOE oder eine regionale Option wählen ist zweitrangig. Die Rede vom „taktischen Wählen“ macht die Runde.

In den sozialen Netzwerken und in einigen Zeitungen wird Provinz für Provinz analysiert, welche Parteien die besten Chancen haben, im Auszählungssystem der Rechten einen Sitz zu entreißen. Das bietet breiten Raum für Spekulation.

In vielen kleineren Provinzen etwa ist eine Stimme für Frente Amplio eine verlorene Stimme. So mancher vergisst darüber seine langjährige Ablehnung der Sozialdemokratie und wird wohl zum Stimmzettel der PSOE greifen. In Galizien ist es angebracht die linksnationalistische BNG zu wählen, im Baskenland die PSOE oder die linksnationalistische EH Bildu, in Andalusien je nach Provinz PSOE oder auch die linke Regionalpartei Adelante Andalucia.

Nur eine Option ist wackelig: Podemos. Diese Partei könnte knapp draußen bleiben und zu Folge haben, dass der letzte Sitz eben nicht an Frente Amplio oder PSOE, sondern an Vox geht.

Laut der O nlinezeitung eldiario.es sind 48 der 350 Parlamentssitze offen und hängen oft nur von einigen Hundert Stimmen ab. Taktisches Wählen kann so bei einem engen Wahlausgang ausschlaggebend sein.

items.body:
Die neue [Thüringen App](https://apps.apple.com/de/app/th%C3%BCringen-app/id6830136194) soll den Zugriff auf die digitalen Verwaltungsangebote des Bundeslands vereinfachen und zugleich regionale Informationen in einer für Smartphones optimierten Form bereitstellen. Die Anwendung steht kostenlos für iPhones und Android-Geräte zur Verfügung.

Nach Angaben der Landesregierung sollen damit insbesondere die bislang auf verschiedene Internetseiten und Portale verteilten Behördenangebote zusammengeführt werden. Nutzer können darüber beispielsweise einen Kita-Platz beantragen, ihren Wohnsitz ummelden oder Informationen zur Erneuerung ihres Personalausweises abrufen.

#### Screenshots aus dem App Store

## Behörden, Nahverkehr und Veranstaltungen

Eine Suchfunktion soll das Auffinden der passenden Verwaltungsleistungen erleichtern. Nutzer sollen ihr Anliegen mit eigenen Worten beschreiben können und daraufhin entsprechende Vorschläge angezeigt bekommen.

Über die Verwaltungsangebote hinaus soll die Thüringen App auch über die Abfahrtszeiten von Bussen und Bahnen informieren, Veranstaltungen in der Umgebung anzeigen und Nachrichten aus Thüringen bereitstellen. Auch Stellenangebote im Freistaat sollen sich über die App abrufen lassen.

#### Das offizielle Video zur App-Vorstellung

Nach Angaben des Thüringer Ministeriums für Digitales und Infrastruktur werden auch die Inhalte der bisherigen Familien-App des Landes in die neue Anwendung übernommen. Weitere digitale Verwaltungsleistungen sollen schrittweise hinzukommen.

## Kostenlos und ohne Benutzerkonto nutzbar

Für die Nutzung der allgemeinen Informationsangebote ist keine Registrierung erforderlich. Wer dagegen Verwaltungsleistungen direkt über die App in Anspruch nehmen möchte, kann sich dafür mit der BundID anmelden. Welche Behördengänge sich bereits vollständig digital erledigen lassen, hängt vom jeweiligen Angebot ab.

Die App wird nach Angaben des Freistaats von der Landesverwaltung selbst betrieben. Nutzerdaten würden dabei nicht an Dritte weitergegeben. Bei der Entwicklung sei zudem auf eine barrierefreie Gestaltung mit klarer Struktur und gut erkennbaren Bedienelementen geachtet worden.

# The U.S. and Iran Are Back to Trading Strikes

## The U.S. and Iran Are Back to Trading Strikes

## A roughly two-month lull in the fighting is seemingly over.

- United States
- Iran
- Middle East and North Africa
- Rishi Iyengar

### Iran War

Welcome back to Foreign Policy ’s Situation Report. We sincerely thank all of you for reading this week’s edition when you could be playing Grand Theft Auto VI. As a quick note, SitRep will be off next week for the U.S. Thanksgiving holiday.

Alright, here’s what’s on tap for the day: Iran and the United States engage in a new tit-for-tat , Pete Hegseth makes an unexpected visit to Venezuela , and Donald Trump meets with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in China .

Welcome back to Foreign Policy ’s Situation Report. We sincerely thank all of you for reading this week’s edition when you could be playing Grand Theft Auto VI. As a quick note, SitRep will be off next week for the U.S. Thanksgiving holiday.

Alright, here’s what’s on tap for the day: Iran and the United States engage in a new tit-for-tat , Pete Hegseth makes an unexpected visit to Venezuela , and Donald Trump meets with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in China .

### Past the Expiration Date

The Iran war appears to be heating up (again), as diplomatic talks have hit a wall (again). The United States and Iran resumed strikes over the past week, ending a roughly two-month lull in the conflict.

The renewed fighting has come as Iran continues to attack shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and amid an ongoing U.S. blockade on Iranian oil exports.

Tit-for-tat. Over the past six days, Iran launched a series of strikes on U.S. assets in Bahrain, which hosts the U.S. Navy’s 5th Fleet, and an air base in Kuwait that hosts U.S. forces.

Iran targeted a U.S. early warning radar facility in Bahrain on Friday and took aim at a radar system at a helicopter base in the tiny island nation on Sunday. No damage was reported. Tehran said the attacks were in retaliation for U.S. strikes on Iranian communications towers as well as ongoing drone surveillance operations.

On Tuesday, Iran targeted another radar facility in Bahrain with drones, which were reportedly intercepted; the United States retaliated with a strike on an Iranian missile launch site on Qeshm Island. Iran responded on Wednesday with an attack on Ali Al Salem air base in Kuwait. There were no reports of damage. Bahrain also said it intercepted Iranian aerial attacks on Wednesday.

Under pressure. U.S. President Donald Trump has been vague about his plans in the war, and some reports suggest he is mulling over ordering expansive strikes. But Trump on Thursday indicated that he’s not in a hurry to escalate. “I am not rushing into any decision. We will see what happens after the beginning of the year,” Trump told Axios.

Trump’s comments came as Israel is reportedly pressing the White House to escalate with a fresh bombing campaign. Roman Gofman, the director of the Israeli intelligence agency Mossad, visited Washington this week, where he is said to have expressed concerns to U.S. officials over alleged Iranian chemical weapons development.

The United States also has intelligence that Iran has drawn up plans to potentially use a dirty bomb or chemical weapon in Washington, according to a CNN report . Trump on Tuesday said the United States was looking into the dirty bomb report and takes it “very seriously.” But he later downplayed the prospect of Iran actually using such a weapon in Washington, and he warned that “if it does happen, we’ll wipe them out.” Trump this week also told Fox News there’s “indication that Iran is looking at gasses, looking at bio, because we’ve shut them out with the nuclear.”

“And they’re looking at gas and biological weapons. Not nice. And we’ll see,” he said.

Expired. If Trump does decide to ramp up the war, experts have warned that it would be a huge gamble and would undoubtedly lead to further retaliatory attacks on U.S. forces and assets in the region. The U.S. intelligence community reportedly assesses that Iran has a stockpile of up to 2,500 missiles in its arsenal, despite prior claims from the Trump administration of such capabilities being destroyed. Iran also remains defiant in the face of continued U.S. economic pressure, and Tehran appears emboldened by major Republican losses in the midterm elections.

The United States still has significant military assets in the region, including two aircraft carriers (after yet another reshuffling that saw the USS George Washington leave the Middle East this week, following the arrival of the USS Theodore Roosevelt ). But the United States is also facing significant constraints, and the war has depleted stockpiles of key munitions. Due to such shortages, acting U.S. Navy Secretary Hung Cao this week told senators that U.S. forces resorted to firing expired munitions in the war.

### Let’s Get Personnel

U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth made a surprise trip to Venezuela, where he signed a defense cooperation agreement with the country that the United States invaded in January. The Defense Department did not share details of the trip with the U.S. press, with the main images and details coming from Venezuelan state media.

Meanwhile, Politico reported that Hegseth’s personal lawyer, Tim Parlatore, also works for the son of a Libyan warlord who has been accused of war crimes.

The Pentagon nominated Gen. Christopher LaNeve to be permanent chief of staff of the U.S. Army, a role that he has been carrying out in an acting capacity since the ouster of Gen. Randy George in April.

Democrats on Wednesday officially nominated Hakeem Jeffries to be speaker of the House, making him the first black person to serve in that role should he be confirmed.

### On the Button

What should be high on your radar, if it isn’t already.

Rohingya genocide verdict. The International Court of Justice ruled on Thursday that Myanmar committed a genocide against its Rohingya ethnic minority population, the first time that the court has found a state responsible for genocide. The judgment is expected to set a number of international legal precedents, including those concerning standards of evidence and reparations, as journalist Andrew Nachemson wrote in FP.

Trump’s big trilateral. Trump capped off his Asia visit this week by meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China. In a joint “peace declaration” following their meeting, the three leaders committed to “reform” the United Nations, vowed to increase the supply of petroleum products “for the benefit of all nations,” and warned that the International Criminal Court and other similar entities “must not abuse their jurisdiction.” They also agreed to “conduct a dialogue” on nuclear risk and nonproliferation, saying that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.”

items.body:
The subtitle of [the paper](https://www.nber.org/papers/w36025#fromrss) is Natural Experiment in Alpha-Gal Syndrome, and the authors are [Vishal Patel](https://www.nber.org/people/vishal_patel_1), [Christopher M. Worsham](https://www.nber.org/people/chris_worsham), [Michael Liu-Hass](https://www.nber.org/people/michael_liu) & [Anupam Jena](https://www.nber.org/people/anupam_jena). The abstract:

> Observational associations between red meat consumption and cardiometabolic disease are confounded by diet and other health behaviors. Alpha-gal syndrome, a tick-borne allergy to mammalian meat, leads to an abrupt and involuntary cessation of red meat consumption. Using national electronic health records, we compared changes in weight and cardiometabolic health over two years before and after newly detected alpha-gal syndrome with those in patients with other tick-borne diseases, who were also bitten and sought care but whose diagnoses carry no dietary restriction. Relative to this comparison group, diagnosis of alpha-gal syndrome led to a sustained 0.8 kg (95% CI, 0.6 to 1.0) reduction in body weight that increased with the degree of sensitization, as well as small reductions in triglycerides, glycated hemoglobin, glucose, and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol. Not eating red meat appears to yield modest but measurable cardiometabolic benefits.

Those results will not make everyone happy.

items.body:
Slap fighting is the world’s newest combat sport. Built for short attention spans and super-viral moments, it’s aiming for global dominance. No flinching

In the days before Power Slap 22, in Belgrade, Serbia, in late July, the organisers of the world’s newest combat sport were taking no chances. At the Crowne Plaza hotel, where competitors were booked to stay, those facing off had been separated by floor, lest any unauthorised violence took place.

It turned out there was little need. The night before the main event, contestants mingled amiably in the lobby and bar. The atmosphere was more specialist sales conference than brewing barroom brawl. In the lobby, I joined Louis “Razor” Robinson, and Ryan “the Punisher” Kenny. “We’re all friends in slap,” Robinson said, earnestly, by way of a greeting. Robinson, a Brit from Stalybridge, Greater Manchester, is 30, stout, intense. Kenny, a Canadian, is 34, lofty, laid back.

items.body:
arXiv:2611.31345v1 Announce Type: new
Abstract: In recent years, multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved significant progress in chart-to-code generation. However, existing benchmarks mainly focus on static charts, overlooking interactive charts that enable richer and more expressive data exploration. Unlike static chart-to-code generation, which emphasizes visual consistency, interactive chart-to-code evaluation targets behavioral consistency, requiring chart states to evolve correctly under sequences of user interactions, thereby rendering traditional one-step evaluation paradigms ineffective. To address this gap, we introduce ChartInt, the first benchmark specifically designed for interactive chart-to-code generation. ChartInt consists of 2,779 carefully annotated examples covering common interaction patterns such as hover, highlight, and tooltips. Additionally, ChartInt incorporates editing tasks such as data updates, style adjustments, and cross-chart style transfer to expand real-world application scenarios. To enable reliable evaluation of interaction behavior, we propose a preset state snapshot protocol that predefines target interaction states and deterministically triggers interaction events, transforming dynamic behaviors into reproducible evaluation targets. Based on this protocol, we design a multi-dimensional evaluation framework measuring semantic and stylistic consistency. Experiments show that while current MLLMs perform well on static charts, their performance drops significantly on interactive tasks, highlighting the need for interaction-aware benchmarks.

sourceReferences.author: Yuhan Bian, Haoyu Liu, Siyu Li, Hanpei Guo, Jingrong Gao, Zhixu Li

items.title: The War Against Slop and an Emerging Weapon to Fight it: Formal Verification
items.subtitle: The word of the year in the AI industry over 2026 has been “slop” — meaning low-quality output from a large language model.
items.feedText: And with so much code being AI-generated now, avoiding slop has become a daily concern for software engineers. So how to do that? One way is to use formal verification systems, which use mathematical proofs and logic to verify the correctness of software or hardware. With AI’s growing prowess at solving math problems, there’s now a number of AI companies offering formal verification systems. items.body:
The word of the year in the AI industry over 2026 has been **“slop”**— meaning low-quality output from a large language model. And with so much code being AI-generated now, [avoiding slop](https://www.slopmanifesto.com/?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv) has become a daily concern for software engineers. So how to do that? One way is to use**formal verification systems**, which use**mathematical proofs and logic** to verify the correctness of software or hardware.

With [AI’s growing prowess at solving math problems](https://latent.space/p/ainews-quasi-riemann-hypothesis-openai/?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv), there’s now a number of AI companies offering formal verification systems. They include [Harmonic](https://www.harmonic.fun/?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv), [Theorem](https://theorem.dev/?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv), [Axiom Math](https://axiommath.ai/?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv), and a new entrant called [&Truth](https://andtruth.com/?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv) (pronounced ‘and truth’). In this article we’ll look at some of the approaches these companies are taking.

## How formal verification is used in software and AI today

In order to better understand the landscape of formal verification systems, we spoke to one of its leading proponents: [Clark Barrett](https://theory.stanford.edu/~barrett/?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv), &Truth’s co-founder and co-CEO. He’s also Corbel Professor (Research) of Computer Science at Stanford and was the **co-creator of** [cvc5](https://cvc5.github.io/?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv), a popular automated reasoning engine used in formal verification.

Without getting too in the weeds, cvc5 is what’s called **a “solver” for satisfiability modulo theories (SMT)**, which Barrett says is widely used in companies like Amazon. For instance, [cvc5 is used](https://www.amazon.science/news/how-academic-collaboration-delivers-real-world-security-to-amazon-customers?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv) for**specification analysis and test generation in Kiro**, Amazon’s agentic development environment.

“It's been fun to see my tools go from a good idea in the lab to cvc5 is now called billions of times a day in production pipelines at Amazon,” Barrett told us.

*Via* [a 2022 paper about cvc5](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/359546891_cvc5_A_Versatile_and_Industrial-Strength_SMT_Solver?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv) *co-authored by Clark Barrett.*

When AI coding agent companies talk about “verifying” their work, it typically means agents **running tests, critiquing their own output, or having another AI model judge it.** So I asked Barrett how far short of real verification does that fall?

“The main difference is really just, how do you know when you're done,” he replied. “So if you're testing, patching, scanning — using all these existing tools — they're quite good. I mean, they find a ton of problems. They raise those issues. **But you're never quite sure, did I find all of them [the issues]** or is there one more lurking there that my tool can't find?”

*&Atlas, the first tool of &Truth; it’s “a map of the world’s open-source code, starting with code written in the C programming language.”*

## Lean’s role in formal verification

&Truth builds on [Lean](https://lean-lang.org/?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv), **an open-source programming language and proof assistant**. The company combines AI with automated reasoning techniques to construct proofs that Lean can check.

Lean is a language used by frontier models to **solve all manner of supremely difficult math problems**. For instance, just this week GPT-6.2 Astra produced [what Vals believes](https://x.com/ValsAI/status/2123129591292432513?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv) is “the first Lean proof of Smoktunowicz’s Gap Theorem.” Vals added that Anthropic also used Lean to formalize Fermat’s Last Theorem, a project of 13 million lines.

The latest big math news is a report that Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claims [he used Claude to prove the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/anthropic-mathematician-claims-to-prove-riemann-hypothesis-most-famous-problem-in-all-of-math/?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv) — and **he posted the proof in Lean**.

*Example of Lean code; via Lean project website*

&Truth is building what it calls a **“verification machine”**on top of the Lean framework, with the ambition of reading code “in any language,**proving whether it satisfies precisely stated requirements**, and enabling humans to trust it without having to understand every line.”

“What Lean does is it just checks that you didn't make a mistake,” explained Barrett. “So you can think of it as a very sophisticated checker for mathematics.”

This has implications for model training too. **Axiom Math uses formal verification to provide correctness feedback for training** its mathematical reasoning systems, with proof attempts helping improve future models.

In [an interview with Latent Space in June](https://latent.space/p/axiom/?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv), Axiom CEO **Carina Hong** made the point that formal verification — and what Lean enables — isn’t just a defensive measure.

“Formal verification, or verified AI, to us it's not just about handling or kicking out the lousiness, the hallucinations, the mistakes. **It's about scaling brilliance.** It's about super-intelligence.”

Axiom develops [AxiomProver](https://wal.sh/research/axiomprover-2026/?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv), an AI system that generates Lean proofs, alongside [AXLE](https://api.axle.axiommath.ai/?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv), its toolkit for exploring, validating, and manipulating those proofs.

**Harmonic’s** [Aristotle](https://www.harmonic.fun/aristotle/?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv), an “[automated theorem prover](https://www.harmonic.fun/news/intro-harmonic/?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv)”, uses Lean heavily in its offering. “Inside Aristotle, AI writes the proofs and Lean checks every step of them, so a result never rests on the AI being right,” states the company on its website.

As of now, space agencies track more than 30,000 objects larger than a softball, with an expected one million more bullet-sized pieces of debris orbiting Earth that are too small to spot from the ground.. Government agencies and private commercial entities are planning to have up to 100,000 active spacecraft in orbit by the early 2030s, turning some orbital shells into crowded highways. And according to a new paper, available in preprint on arXiv by Federico Toson, a researcher at the University of Padova in Italy, the math that regulatory agencies use to determine whether a satellite is “safe” in these highly congested spaces is fundamentally flawed.

A jury has [found Huawei guilty](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/chinese-tech-giant-huawei-and-subsidiaries-convicted-sanctions-violations-fraud-conspiracy) of stealing US trade secrets, as reported earlier by [NBC News](https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/chinese-tech-company-huawei-convicted-federal-charges-rcna611189) and [Bloomberg](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-24/huawei-found-guilty-of-us-criminal-charges-in-landmark-case). The verdict, handed down in a federal court in New York, concludes a years-long legal battle that accused the Chinese telecom giant of stealing source code and proprietary technology from several companies, [including T-Mobile](https://www.theverge.com/tech/997132/a-jury-was-shown-this-video-of-a-huawei-employee-allegedly-stealing-t-mobile-robot-parts), Cisco, and Motorola.

The Department of Justice's 2018 criminal indictment against Huawei came to light following the [arrest of the company's CFO, Wanzhou Meng](https://www.theverge.com/2018/12/7/18131188/huawei-cfo-fraud-bail-defense-bail-us-canada), whom the agency accused of fraud. Though the [indictment against Meng](https://www.reuters.com/legal/us-judge-dismisses-indictment-against-huawei-cfo-that-strained-us-china-2022-12-02/) was eventually dismissed, she admitted to misleading banks over Huawei's operations …

[Read the full story at The Verge.](https://www.theverge.com/tech/1041820/huawei-guilty-trade-secrets-trial)

items.body:
Prime Video's new "[Blade Runner 2099](https://www.space.com/everything-we-know-about-blade-runner-2099)" series arrives Nov. 25, 2026, and it flips the cyberpunk universe on its head. The new show casts replicants as the dominant species on Earth, with humans relegated to second-class citizens after a global uprising.

This dreary dystopian cyberpunk realm originates from sci-fi legend Phillip K. Dick's 1968 novel, "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?," and was then so vividly brought to life in Ridley Scott’s seminal 1982 adaptation, "[Blade Runner](https://www.space.com/blade-runner-ridley-scott-40th-anniversary)." The 2017 sequel, "Blade Runner 2049," was directed by "Arrival’s" and "Dune’s" Denis Villeneuve.

Starring Michelle Yeoh, Hunter Schafer, Matthew Needham, Dimitri Abold, and Lewis Gribben, "[Blade Runner 2099](https://www.space.com/entertainment/space-movies-shows/new-blade-runner-2099-trailer-is-a-space-fans-dream-with-sinister-starships-and-strange-exoplanets-video)" hails from creator and showrunner Silka Louisa and Alcon Entertainment founders Andrew Kosove and Broderick Johnson, who executive produce with Ridley Scott's Scott Free Productions.

Here, Yeoh's dying replicant blade runner Olwen unites with Schafer’s Cora, a human masquerading as a synthetic, to hunt down a dangerous rogue replicant that holds the key to a dark secret.

We spoke to Kosove and Johnson about being respectful keepers of "Blade Runner's" creative flame, the pitch that sold them, and dipping back into Dick's original novel.

"When the original film came out in 1982, and even when "2049" came out about a decade ago, a lot of things that these movies envisioned seemed far, far away and hard to comprehend," Kosovo tells Space. "The creation of artificial sentient beings. Today, sitting here in November of 2026, the world is catching up quicker to the world of 'Blade Runner,' with artificial technology and concerns of how do humans use this technology for our benefit without it taking over."

"Silka came in several years ago and pitched her very simple idea, which was, the next chapter of 'Blade Runner' should be what happens when the replicants overtake their creators." explains Kosovo.

"We thought that idea was going to be particularly resonant. It was simple to understand so new fans could enter the world without being steeped in the first two movies. And we thought it had logical continuity to the story canon that came before it. It checked a number of key boxes for us. Even though we talked to a number of showrunners who were much more established in their careers than Silka was at that point, she won the day with the most elegant idea in our opinion."

(Image credit: Prime Video)

Johnson admits that Louisa's pitch approval was just the opening round of a multitude of responsible decisions to be ruminated over as the production process advanced.

"Once you agree that this is the story we’re telling, then it becomes a multi-year partnership in honoring all the artists and visionaries that came before as it relates to visual design and music," he notes. "Everything needs to be of the highest quality. Even though it's a TV show we feel it has theatrical level visual effects. It’s practical and tactile and analog. There’s a lot of things that come along with how you produce the show. At its core that becomes a partnership when you decide these are the characters I’m going to spend hours with and you go down that journey."

With nearly 60 years of "Blade Runner" material to play with, there’s bound to be easter eggs dropped into the tale over the course of "[Blade Runner 2099's](https://www.space.com/entertainment/our-1st-look-at-blade-runner-2099-shows-replicants-ruling-future-los-angeles-its-our-time-now)" 8-episode season.

Michelle Yeoh stars as a dying replicant in "Blade Runner 2099" (Image credit: Prime Video)

"You’ve got Tyrell as a critical aspect of our story, but Wallace creeps into the story as well," Kosove teases. "One of the keys things was, from an architectural standpoint, things that exist in "2049" had to exist in this. You see the Wallace spires when you see the Tyrell pyramid. You have the sea wall when they're going south with the spinner.

"There’s some story easter eggs too. Silka did something really cool which has not been done in either movie. She brought in concepts that go back to Philip K. Dick's novel, "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?" That was really interesting. We’re really excited for people to see it and see how they respond.”

"Blade Runner 2099" arrives on Nov. 25, 2026 exclusively on Prime Video.

items.body:
# 19 rumors about insider trading, prediction markets we've investigated

For years, accusations of insider trading have targeted politicians and celebrities. But with the second administration of U.S. President Donald Trump coinciding with the rise of online prediction markets such as Polymarket and Kalshi, rumors have multiplied that the president and his inside circle have gambled using privileged information before it's public, a practice that has yet to be fully outlawed .

In November, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who admitted to several affairs , including one with a suspected Chinese spy, was removed by the company's board, then quickly reinstated. Trump said he intervened in Huang's favor .

This resulted in reports that Trump, who owns Nvidia shares , financially benefited from Huang's return. Some critics suspected Trump even traded on this information . This would constitute insider trading, which is illegal, according to the Securities and Exchange Commission .

Here are 19 claims about online betting platforms and insider trading that we've investigated:

### Did Trump propose these rules limiting Congress members' privileges?

### Did House Democrats vote against banning congressional stock trading?

### Did Trump say his children benefit from 'inside information' when they invest in stocks, crypto?

### Did Mike Johnson say members of Congress should be able to 'engage in some stock trading'? Here's context

### Did Elizabeth Warren sell Spirit Airlines stock before budget carrier went out of business? Here's the truth

### Analyzing claim Trump insider bet $51M on oil prices dropping before US announced Iran ceasefire

### Did Polymarket user bet Trump would praise Allah on Easter?

### Eric Trump invested in drone maker shortly before Iran war

### Markwayne Mullin bought Chevron, Raytheon stock days before Maduro capture

### Did Barron Trump buy $30M in oil days before Iran war began? Claim lacks evidence

### Unpacking claims Polymarket bets on Iran strikes point to insider knowledge

### Why unverified claim Barron Trump made $400K from insider trading on Maduro capture spread online

### Yes, Marjorie Taylor Greene bought Palantir shares days before ICE granted tech giant $30M contract

### Martha Stewart quote comparing her crimes to allegations of Trump's insider trading is not real

### No proof Trump sold $2.3B in Truth Social stock before April 2 tariffs announcement

### UnitedHealthCare CEO Brian Thompson Was Not Set to Testify Against Pelosi in Insider Trading Case

### 'Something's Up' With US Economy Due to High-Profile Stock Sales?

### Did Moderna CEO Suddenly Dump $400M in Stock?

### Did Nancy Pelosi Invest Up to $1M in Tesla?

items.body:
*τρία* is the third instalment in **Aeson Zervas’** ongoing sequence for Heat Crimes, continuing the numbering of his untitled pieces from the self-titled debut (1–8), through *Hazlom* (9–17), and now from “Χωρίς τίτλο 18” to “Χωρίς τίτλο 29”. That continuity matters. Zervas’ reclusiveness, the absence of explanatory titles and the progressive numbering make the three albums feel like fragments of one unresolved archive. On *τρία*, Greek folk memory, rebetika, damaged soundtrack music and dubby electronics repeatedly surface and disappear. “Χωρίς τίτλο 20” slips into filmic suspense; “Χωρίς τίτλο 21” gives itself over to rebetika; the almost unbearably melancholic “Χωρίς τίτλο 22” is followed by the repeated scream of “Χωρίς τίτλο 23”; later, “Χωρίς τίτλο 25” places traditional material over an electronic dub framework. The album keeps circling between fairground unease, glitchy tapes, folk citation and invented memory. Is this, as Mark Fisher would have it, a harrowing investigation of memory disorder?

Mark Fisher’s hauntology is an obvious reference point: damaged repetition, obsolete media and sounds that appear to belong to futures that never arrived. [Matt Bluemink](https://shop.becoming.press/products/the-future-is-not-lost-music-technology-and-the-creation-of-worlds-2026-by-matt-bluemink) takes that diagnosis and pushes against its pessimism, arguing that anti-hauntology can use the past as material for new cultural forms rather than remaining trapped in mourning. But the work of Egyptian-born producer [Abadir](https://acloserlisten.com/2026/09/18/abadir-the-primitivist/), whom we interviewed recently, complicates the argument further. Abadir rejects the assumption that “newness” must be tied to an abstract future at all, especially when that future is defined through a Western critical vocabulary. For him, the more interesting question is how the past can be used creatively “without mourning it” while remaining grounded in the present; he is equally suspicious of escaping backwards through nostalgia and forwards through futurism. That position feels particularly useful for *τρία*. Zervas is clearly, but also self-consciously, nostalgic, yet nostalgia here is unstable and frequently unpleasant. Rebetika is not restored as heritage; it is scratched, looped, interrupted, displaced and contaminated by technologies and musical languages from elsewhere.

This also makes the Mediterranean dimension of the record more important than a simple Fisherian reading might allow. Zervas’ Greece is not an isolated national memory but a sedimented space in which Greek, Anatolian, Ottoman, North African and contemporary electronic histories overlap. The idea of Mediterranean music as a form of historical recomposition—taking materials already in circulation and assembling them into new cultural possibilities—fits *τρία* closely. Its imagined past may never have existed, but that does not make it escapist; it can also be a way of refusing a museumised, Eurocentric version of Greek antiquity as suggested by the label notes.

Marc Armand’s cover captures this beautifully. A broken archaeological piece lies on the floor of what appears to be a museum, caught in a shaft of light, while intact artefacts remain displayed on the walls. *τρία* behaves similarly: it removes cultural memory from the wall, breaks chronology and leaves the fragments where they can interfere with the present. The question, then, may not be whether Zervas is producing the music of the future. Abadir is right to make that category suspect. Perhaps the more urgent music now comes from artists for whom neither past nor future offers an easy refuge—artists forced to work inside an unstable present and to make something from whatever histories, technologies and damaged materials remain available.

The album raises many questions that deserve further elaboration. For what it is worth, I personally believe that those making the music of the future today—whatever that might mean—are often those for whom the future is not a given: artists in Ukraine and elsewhere confronting imperialism, war and genocide, and those faced with the very impossibility of the present. ( **Gianmarco Del Re** )

items.body:
Does a video show a real instance of "powerful waves" passing the shoreline of Gordon's Bay in South Africa? No, that's not true: An earlier version of the video on TikTok carries the platform's "Contains AI-generated media" label. Lead Stories found no reports from established news outlets of such waves at Gordon's Bay in November 2026.

The claim appeared in [a post](https://www.threads.com/@thebnsmedia/post/DgFVYmKld9r) (archived [↗ web.archive.org](https://web.archive.org/web/20261123193335/https://www.threads.com/@thebnsmedia/post/DgFVYmKld9r) ) made on Threads by the account @thebnsmedia on Nov. 23, 2026. The post included a video with a caption that read:

> Powerful ocean waves are surging over the beachfront at Gordon's Bay, South Africa, raising concerns over potential flooding and damage to coastal properties.
> #southafrica #gordonsbay #massivewaves #coastalweather #oceanwaves #bnsmedia #bnsnews #thebnsmedia

This is what a screenshot from the video looked like at the time of publication:

*(Image source: post by @thebnsmedia on Threads.)*

The post is embedded below:

> [View on Threads](https://www.threads.com/@thebnsmedia/post/DgFVYmKld9r)

A version of the video without the BNS Media watermark and text overlay was [posted on TikTok](https://www.tiktok.com/@._._._._940/video/7710336058319293718) by the account @._._._._940 on Nov. 20, 2026 (archived [↗ web.archive.org](https://web.archive.org/web/20261123204029/https://www.tiktok.com/@._._._._940/video/7710336058319293718) ). The video contained [a label](https://www.tiktok.com/tns-inapp/pages/ai-generated-content?enter_from=web_fyp&hide_nav_bar=1&lang=en) reading, "Contains AI-generated media" (archived [↗ web.archive.org](https://web.archive.org/web/20261123204706/https://www.tiktok.com/tns-inapp/pages/ai-generated-content?enter_from=web_fyp&hide_nav_bar=1&lang=en) ).

Although Google's [SynthID AI detection tool](https://synthid.com/) did not identify the video as containing a SynthID watermark (archived [↗ web.archive.org](https://web.archive.org/web/20261123205914/https://synthid.com/video-detection) ), the video shows signs of being AI-generated. For example, there are vehicles on top of what appear to be residential buildings. The beachfront is littered with cars, but no people are in sight. The water gathers unnaturally around the buildings without causing any visible structural damage.

Searches on [Google News](https://news.google.com/search?q=Powerful%20ocean%20waves%20AND%20Gordon%E2%80%99s%20Bay%20AND%20South%20Africa&hl=en-US&gl=US&ceid=US%3Aen) (archived [↗ web.archive.org](https://web.archive.org/web/20261123200437/https://news.google.com/search?q=Powerful%20ocean%20waves%20AND%20Gordon%E2%80%99s%20Bay%20AND%20South%20Africa&hl=en-US&gl=US&ceid=US%3Aen) ) and [Yahoo News](https://search.yahoo.com/news/search;_ylt=A2RRZvLNnARrxQIAq6RXNyoA;_ylu=Y29sbwN1cy1lYXN0LTEEcG9zAzIEdnRpZAMEc2VjA3BpdnM-?p=Powerful+ocean+waves+AND+Gordon%E2%80%99s+Bay+AND+South+Africa&fr2=piv-web&fr=uh3_news_web) (archived [↗ web.archive.org](https://web.archive.org/web/20261123200718/https://search.yahoo.com/news/search;_ylt=A2RRZvLNnARrxQIAq6RXNyoA;_ylu=Y29sbwN1cy1lYXN0LTEEcG9zAzIEdnRpZAMEc2VjA3BpdnM-?p=Powerful+ocean+waves+AND+Gordon%E2%80%99s+Bay+AND+South+Africa&fr2=piv-web&fr=uh3_news_web) ) for the claim did not return any matching results from established news outlets. A [Google image search](https://www.google.com/search?sa=X&sca_esv=404a6062959aa475&lns_surface=26&authuser=0&hl=en&sxsrf=AKL5yDiVyW1f6JchqfGuY7fglFBWiJTXHg:1795463722730&udm=44&vsint=CAIqDAoCCAcSAggKGAEgATojChYNAAAAPxUAAAA_HQAAgD8lAACAPzABEI4FGIAIJQAAgD8&lns_mode=un&source=lns.web.gsbubb&vsdim=654,1024&gsessionid=JGdoOkc-wv6OHHE8i1JRPzXHDmGqoxBs5jorZGLYn82nnv-9nnRe2w&lsessionid=F_m2DSCmMn13dPAwtC32Fj5UgbqYB2AYTn2gRKKVz5OwGbDlU8uuTg&vsrid=CL6RoeqQgemP4gEQAhgBIiQyYzU4MTY0Ni01NjM5LTRlY2MtOTU5ZS05OWI5YzRjNzg5ZjcyggEiAmJpKANCdAoubGZlLWR1bW15OjZkZmJmMzA5LTBiYzctNDg0OS1hNTA3LTM2NzMwMDRiMDg0ZBJCCkAvYm5zL2JpL2JvcmcvYmkvYm5zL2xlbnMtZnJvbnRlbmQtYXBpL3Byb2QubGVucy1mcm9udGVuZC1hcGkvMTE3WgQKAmJpOPmZ54PvnpgDUAA&q=&ved=2ahUKEwiXxJnL756YAxUbLFkFHe2dCbYQs6gLegQIFhAB&biw=1280&bih=631&dpr=2) (archived [↗ web.archive.org](https://web.archive.org/web/20261123195859/https://www.google.com/search?sa=X&sca_esv=404a6062959aa475&lns_surface=26&authuser=0&hl=en&sxsrf=AKL5yDiVyW1f6JchqfGuY7fglFBWiJTXHg:1795463722730&udm=44&vsint=CAIqDAoCCAcSAggKGAEgATojChYNAAAAPxUAAAA_HQAAgD8lAACAPzABEI4FGIAIJQAAgD8&lns_mode=un&source=lns.web.gsbubb&vsdim=654,1024&gsessionid=JGdoOkc-wv6OHHE8i1JRPzXHDmGqoxBs5jorZGLYn82nnv-9nnRe2w&lsessionid=F_m2DSCmMn13dPAwtC32Fj5UgbqYB2AYTn2gRKKVz5OwGbDlU8uuTg&vsrid=CL6RoeqQgemP4gEQAhgBIiQyYzU4MTY0Ni01NjM5LTRlY2MtOTU5ZS05OWI5YzRjNzg5ZjcyggEiAmJpKANCdAoubGZlLWR1bW15OjZkZmJmMzA5LTBiYzctNDg0OS1hNTA3LTM2NzMwMDRiMDg0ZBJCCkAvYm5zL2JpL2JvcmcvYmkvYm5zL2xlbnMtZnJvbnRlbmQtYXBpL3Byb2QubGVucy1mcm9udGVuZC1hcGkvMTE3WgQKAmJpOPmZ54PvnpgDUAA&q=&ved=2ahUKEwiXxJnL756YAxUbLFkFHe2dCbYQs6gLegQIFhAB&biw=1280&bih=631&dpr=2) ) of a screenshot from the video only showed matching results posted on social media. The accounts were not connected to established news outlets.

There was a powerful [spring high tide](https://www.citizen.co.za/news/spring-high-tide-bikini-beach-gordons-bay/) (archived [↗ web.archive.org](https://web.archive.org/web/20261123205419/https://www.citizen.co.za/news/spring-high-tide-bikini-beach-gordons-bay/) ) that threatened property and vehicles at Gordon's Bay in September 2023. However, footage from the high tide did not match the scene shown in the video in question.

items.title: Trump Makes False and Misleading Claims About Funding for HBCUs
items.subtitle: President Donald Trump falsely claimed that former Presidents Barack Obama and Joe Biden “did nothing” in terms of funding for historically Black c…
items.feedText: During his first presidential term, Trump signed a bipartisan bill in late 2019 that made mandatory federal funding for HBCUs permanent. But HBCUs also received that same mandatory funding each year under Obama and Biden, and Obama and Biden also authorized additional money for HBCUs during their presidencies. items.body:
President Donald Trump falsely claimed that former Presidents Barack Obama and Joe Biden “did nothing” in terms of funding for historically Black colleges and universities that Trump said he “saved” from bankruptcy.

During his first presidential term, Trump signed a bipartisan bill in late 2019 that made mandatory federal funding for HBCUs permanent. That was after the funding briefly lapsed earlier that year amid negotiations in Congress.

But HBCUs also received that same mandatory funding each year under Obama and Biden, and Obama and Biden also authorized additional money for HBCUs during their presidencies. The mandatory money is a fraction of all federal funding for HBCUs.

Trump made those and other claims about HBCUs in an [interview](https://rollcall.com/factbase/trump/transcript/donald-trump-interview-stephen-a-smith-online-show-november-12-2026/) with sports media personality Stephen A. Smith that aired Nov. 12. Smith is an [alumnus](https://www.wssu.edu/about/news/articles/2025/09/wssu-alumnus-stephen-a-smith-to-be-inducted-into-national-black-college-alumni-hall-of-fame.html) of Winston-Salem State University in North Carolina, one of about 100 HBCUs [recognized](https://nces.ed.gov/COLLEGENAVIGATOR/?s=all&sp=4&pg=6) by the Department of Education, and he is [an ambassador](https://sports.yahoo.com/articles/stephen-smith-makes-money-move-045839964.html) for the HBCU Week Foundation. About 289,000 students were attending HBCUs as of 2022, [according to](https://nces.ed.gov/fastfacts/display.asp?id=667) the National Center for Education Statistics.

Trump was talking about what he has done for “the Black community” when he said, “I saved the historically Black colleges and universities. They were out of business.” When Smith brought up the fact that HBCUs also received federal funding during the Obama and Biden administrations, Trump said, “They were going bankrupt during my administration. The money that they gave was stolen and it didn’t fund. They were going bankrupt.”

The president added later: “I got them financed, and I got them more than they wanted. Barack Obama did nothing for it, and Biden did nothing for it.”

Trump has been [claiming](https://www.insidehighered.com/news/2020/01/23/trumps-claim-about-saving-hbcus-was-false-his-administration-has-largely-backed) to have “saved” HBCUs since his 2020 presidential campaign. But his analysis is a combination of false, misleading and exaggerated claims, and the White House did not provide an explanation for them when we asked. We also don’t know what Trump meant when he said funding from Obama and Biden “was stolen.”

## What Trump Did

Trump later said that he got “10-year financing” for HBCUs, an apparent reference to the Fostering Undergraduate Talent by Unlocking Resources for Education Act, or [FUTURE Act](https://www.congress.gov/bill/116th-congress/house-bill/5363), which he signed in December 2019.

Among other things, the legislation, which [passed](https://www.congress.gov/bill/116th-congress/house-bill/5363/all-actions) with bipartisan support, amended Title III of the 1965 Higher Education Act to [provide](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R46400) permanent mandatory grant funding for HBCUs and other minority-serving institutions. The bill made $255 million available in total each year, and about $85 million of it was specifically for HBCUs, [according](https://www.nbcnews.com/news/nbcblk/congress-finalizes-bill-restoring-funding-black-colleges-n1099676) [to](https://apnews.com/article/c4834e48841d97c5a93312b1bf75302a) breakdowns of the funding. The law [says](https://www.congress.gov/bill/116th-congress/house-bill/5363/text) the funding is available for “fiscal year 2020 and each fiscal year thereafter” – not just for 10 years.

But the FUTURE Act reinstated annual funding that was first [approved](https://www.congress.gov/bill/110th-congress/house-bill/2669) in 2007 by Congress and then President George W. Bush. The authority to grant that funding was [extended](https://www.congress.gov/bill/111th-congress/house-bill/4872/text/statute?format=txt) through fiscal year 2019, when Obama signed a 2010 healthcare and education bill. The funding then [lapsed](https://www.insidehighered.com/quicktakes/2019/10/15/hbcus-plan-cuts-after-congress-misses-funding-deadline) in 2019, when Congress initially could not agree on an extension before the Sept. 30 deadline.

The compromise legislation that was enacted under Trump was negotiated for months by a bipartisan group of lawmakers. While one Republican involved in the negotiations gave Trump [some credit](https://www.insidehighered.com/news/2020/08/31/some-hbcus-bristle-being-held-sign-trumps-concern-race) for the legislation becoming law, some Democrats said he played a minor role, if any.

Students walk past a building on the campus of Howard University in Washington, D.C., in August 2024. Photo by Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP via Getty Images.

It’s true that some HBCUs were preparing to make staff and program cuts if the funding was not renewed, [according to](https://www.insidehighered.com/sites/default/files/media/Post-Deadline%20FUTURE%20Act%20-TMCF.pdf) a letter sent to Congress in October 2019 by [Harry L. Williams](https://tmcf.org/wp-content/uploads/Dr.-Harry-L.-Williams-1.pdf), president and CEO of the Thurgood Marshall College Fund, a nonprofit organization that represents dozens of HBCUs. But it’s an exaggeration to claim that the colleges and universities were “saved” from “going bankrupt,” as Trump said.

While the mandatory funding is a significant funding source for the schools, it is not their only source of funding. It’s not even the only source of funding from the federal government, as [Education Department records](https://web.archive.org/web/20240528221741/https://www.ed.gov/programs/iduestitle3b/funding.html#top#top) show that Congress has regularly appropriated three times as much in discretionary funding for HBCUs than the required mandatory funding.

Discretionary funding authorized during the Obama administration ranged from a low of about $216 million in fiscal year 2013 to a high of almost $266 million in fiscal year 2010. Those discretionary funding amounts then increased in Trump’s first term and again under Biden.

Furthermore, the discretionary and mandatory funding totals do not include other grants and contracts that HBCUs can be awarded by federal departments and agencies.

…

items.title: People who just won tough races should try to win again — and hold Trump accountable
items.subtitle: Josh Turek campaigns in Iowa on November 1, 2026.
items.feedText: The sheer scale of the 2026 blue wave — an anti-MAGA swing large enough to carry Democrats in places like Mississippi and South Carolina — poses a question of democratic theory that I think is a lot more interesting than the tired empirical debates about moderation. items.body:
The sheer scale of the 2026 blue wave — an anti-MAGA swing large enough to carry Democrats in places like Mississippi and South Carolina — poses a question of democratic theory that I think is a lot more interesting than the tired empirical debates about moderation. What should a person who won somewhere they “shouldn’t” have do with their term (or terms) in office, knowing that it’s objectively unlikely that the terrain will be as favorable in future cycles?

My perception is that most mainstream Democrats adhere to an ethic I would call Pragmatic Progmaxxing.

They understand that [Ayanna Pressley tweeting about reparations](https://x.com/RepPressley/status/2122109986306195477) is bad politics, that politicians like Josh Turek and James Talarico are going to have to stay away from 100-proof left-wing politics, and that even Abdul El-Sayed needs to do some picayune localism related to the auto industry. But their basic orientation is as [intense policy demanders](https://read.dukeupress.edu/jhppl/article/43/2/271/133583/How-Intense-Policy-Demanders-Shape-Postreform) who are trying to maximize the amount of progressive change by pushing elected officials to be as left-wing as they can possibly get away with.

Pragmatic Progmaxxing has especially interesting implications for the people who won the real reach seats. From a Progmaxxing point of view, you accept a certain amount of moderation from Sherrod Brown and Roy Cooper so they can win re-election. But Scott Colom needed a D+13 national political climate *and* an amateur hour opponent to barely win, so he should just give up and vote like Ed Markey. It’s basically a free Senate seat for six years.

I want to push back against this.

I think American democracy has been in a really dangerous place for the past 10 years. That’s proximately due to Donald Trump and the MAGA movement. But the intense policy demanders have been creating an underlying structural weakness by framing thumbing your nose at your constituents as noble and trying to be a loyal servant of the people as cowardly.

I would like to see Colom and Annie Andrews and the couple dozen House Democrats who won deep red seats make a good-faith effort to represent their constituents. That doesn’t mean they answer every policy question with a poll of public opinion in Mississippi. But it does mean they have to take seriously the question of whether a particular piece of legislation aligns with what their constituents are asking for. Because it’s not “brave” or “fearless” to ignore the public will in order to curry favor with your side’s interest groups. That pattern of behavior has made voters cynical about the democratic process, eroded faith in party politics, and given us the bad phenomenon of “safe seats” where the incumbents barely even care what’s happening.

To the extent that newly elected members run big political risks, I hope they look into their own hearts about what motivated them to run for office as Democrats at a time when large swaths of the business community were deciding to bandwagon with the MAGA movement. My guess is that in most cases, the Democrats who ran in 2026 were both aware that the “save our democracy” messaging of 2024 was not persuasive and also (rightly) believed in the merits of that messaging.

If I’m right about that, I think the best way to behave consistent with that ethic is to:

- Fight for democracy by being willing to take risks to hold Trump and his cronies accountable for violations of the law.
- Practice democracy by acting as if you care more about the policy views and interests of the voters in your constituency than the views and interests of ideological donors and the groups.

My fear is that in practice the opposite combination is more likely. The Democratic base is in some sense very fired up about the issues in bucket (1). But in terms of [concrete political power](https://www.slowboring.com/p/from-the-veal-pen-to-the-groups) — campaign dollars and the endorsements that can win you primaries — it’s all about the greens and the labor unions and the civil rights orgs and the child care advocates and the immigration lawyers.

If you feel that you need to break with party leadership on something, the thing you’re most likely to get latitude on is Trump accountability. This is more or less “how things work” in the modern era of American political parties — they demand a lot of party loyalty on votes about policy ideas — but it’s terrible for the country.

#### The nobility of winning

In his [classic 1974 book “Congress: The Electoral Connection,”](https://politicalscience.yale.edu/publications/congress-electoral-connection) David Mayhew says we should understand members of Congress as single-minded seekers of re-election.

In a world where that’s broadly true, it’s also true that when a member of Congress deviates from the rule, that’s usually driven by courage and prescience. All of your colleagues are looking at the Voting Rights Act through the narrow lens of re-election, but you decide that the most important thing is whether you can tell your granddaughter that you did the right thing, so you vote yes. Maybe you lose in 1966, maybe you don’t. But either way, it’s the right thing to do.

It’s important to understand, though, that a lot has changed since then. American political parties used to be basically patronage operations whose business model was winning elections so they could hand out jobs and contracts. Around the time that Mayhew wrote his book, these old patronage parties were dissolving in the face of amateur political activists who were rapidly forming professionalized issue-advocacy groups.

Those groups have now formed into quasi-stable coalitions that are aligned with and finance the political parties. The business model now is to deliver wins for intense policy demanders. And to accomplish that, you do need to win power sometimes — it’s Pragmatic Progmaxxing, not doctrinaire left-wing politics — but that’s quite different from Mayhew’s singular focus on winning.

Similarly, just being a member of Congress has become a significantly less elite job even as high-end income inequality has exploded. I wouldn’t say anyone is deliberately losing elections just for the pay raise, but it’s objectively true that going down in defeat and then becoming a media personality or a senior fellow at the Center for Pragmatic Progmaxxing is going to mean your living standards go up rather than down.

In this post-Mayhew universe, it’s of course still possible for a member to risk their re-election prospects for the sake of a transcendent moral cause.

But we don’t actually have any issues that are as titanically significant as civil rights. And I would say a much more typical case is a situation like the 2025 Congressional Review Act vote to disallow the state of California from imposing a de facto ban on internal combustion engine cars.

…

items.body:
My little auto-hiding palette features connections to file servers, SSH shortcuts, screen-sharing shortcuts, Keyboard Maestro macros, and more.

A thousand beta builds later, John Siracusa has finally launched his new app, a dock-and-palette utility called [Jetty Pro](http://hypercritical.co/2026/11/23/jetty-pro):

> I’d like to introduce Jetty Pro: an app that creates customizable Dock-like floating palettes around the edges of your Mac’s displays. These palettes can contain any combination of files, folders, volumes, apps, Shortcuts, spacers, dividers, and even the Trash. If you’ve ever been unsatisfied with some aspect of how the Dock works, or if you’ve just wanted to augment the Dock with some additional palettes, try Jetty Pro and make your Mac’s interface work the way you want it to.

I’ve been using this app for months and I love it. It has very specifically filled a space in my Mac’s interface that has been empty [since DragThing died in 2019](https://www.dragthing.com), namely a palette full of arbitrary stuff like SSH connections, folders, macros, and URLs that I want to get to with a single click.

For a guy who has a reputation for liking things *just so*, you might think Jetty Pro does things only one way. That’s not true. One of the things John wants *just so* is for his apps to have a lot of user-configurable options. You can make palettes of various looks, with various behaviors, and have their behavior remain consistent or vary depending on what display you’re using.

(And yes, it is a *thorough* Dock replacement, so I can finally have a second Dock appear on the right side of my secondary display whenever I have it open.)

In John’s [unsurprisingly detailed FAQ page](https://hypercritical.co/jetty-pro/) he explains why the app [is available only on a subscription basis](https://hypercritical.co/jetty-pro/#subscription)—mostly, it’s because it will require a lot of maintenance due to its use of private Apple APIs. Those private APIs are also why it’s not available in the Mac App Store, but only direct from John.

Jetty Pro has a 14-day free trial, and then costs $10 for the first year. Oh, and there’s no non-Pro version of Jetty in the Mac App Store. John worked on one for a while, but it didn’t make sense. All the goodness of Jetty Pro is happening with John’s circumvention of Apple’s rules. He’s a rebel! And his attempt to slowly rebuild every feature of DragThing continues.

[Go to the linked site](http://hypercritical.co/2026/11/23/jetty-pro).

[Read on Six Colors](https://sixcolors.com/link/2026/11/john-siracusa-launches-jetty-pro/).

items.title: Spotted on the D.C. Metro: Trump Staffer Accidentally Reveals Plan for Smithsonian Overhaul
items.subtitle: A commuter riding the Metro in Washington, D.C., snapped photos of a man working on a document titled “Smithsonian Institution Renewal Plan.” Obtai…
items.feedText: Now the plan may have been revealed — inadvertently — in a crowded car on Washington, D.C.’s Metro transit system. In the last week of October, as political Washington was focused on the coming midterm elections, a commuter on the Orange Line from the Northern Virginia suburbs was startled to see displayed, on the laptop of a man seated adjacent in a gray tartan suit, a document titled “Smithsonian Institution Renewal Plan.” The commuter snapped a few phone photos over the man’s shoulder and dispatched them to P…
items.body:
A commuter riding the Metro in Washington, D.C., snapped photos of a man working on a document titled “Smithsonian Institution Renewal Plan.” Obtained by ProPublica

Since the Trump administration erupted this summer with criticism of the Smithsonian National Museum of American History for promoting “radical activist ideology” and precipitated the planned departure of Smithsonian secretary Lonnie Bunch, the White House’s next step on this front of the culture wars has been unclear.

Now the plan may have been revealed — inadvertently — in a crowded car on Washington, D.C.’s Metro transit system.

In the last week of October, as political Washington was focused on the coming midterm elections, a commuter on the Orange Line from the Northern Virginia suburbs was startled to see displayed, on the laptop of a man seated adjacent in a gray tartan suit, a document titled “Smithsonian Institution Renewal Plan.” The commuter snapped a few phone photos over the man’s shoulder and dispatched them to ProPublica.

### Do You Have a Tip for ProPublica?

If you see something in public you think ProPublica should know about, there are a few ways you can reach us securely.

Send Us a Tip

The 25-item list laid bare a comprehensive effort to completely transform the history museum, which employs several hundred people, is home to several million artifacts and draws close to 2 million visitors per year. If implemented in anything like the proposed form, it would represent an unprecedented assertion of White House control over the Smithsonian, which is structured to be independent.

Among the actions listed on the plan: firing the museum’s director, Anthea Hartig, and a dozen other top administrators and curators; announcing a new permanent exhibit called “The Riches of Our Western Civilization Inheritance” and an exhibit on “Great Families of American History”; and announcing a new “Colossus Statue” of George Washington for the museum’s entrance.

Other items on the list harkened back to a scathing 162-page critique of the museum released by the White House on July 4. That report was followed by back-to-back congressional hearings and a Trump executive order requiring signs to be erected outside the museum warning about the “ideological capture” on display there. While the pressure helped prompt Bunch’s decision to retire as head of the Smithsonian at the end of the year, the warning signs have yet to go up, and it was unknown exactly what fixes the White House had in mind for the flaws that it so loudly decried.

Until now, perhaps. The plan displayed on the staffer’s laptop would issue new interpretative guidelines for exhibits, ending the museum’s reliance on a diversity style guide. It would review the Smithsonian’s strategy for traveling exhibitions, including halting one now underway, “The Bias Inside Us.” It would review the Smithsonian’s financial grants to “woke third parties” such as the American Alliance of Museums. And it would overhaul the museum’s online K-12 curriculum to “realign educational materials with patriotism, not ideology.” For instance, the website would drop the “Becoming US” module on immigration and launch a “Founders-focused curriculum titled something like Architects of Liberty: The Heroic Journey of America’s Founders OR Profiles in Liberty: Washington and America’s Heroic Men of Courage.”

The plan was apparently still a work in progress, given that the staffer had scribbled other proposals on a sheet of paper, also in plain view. They included “announce exciting cool exhibit on D-Day” and “no X rated exhibitions policy.” The latter item was a likely reference to something that drew a great deal of opprobrium in the July report and two congressional hearings that followed: a gay history exhibit that included a two-piece chrome and rubber crotch harness designed for sadomasochism.

At first, the identity of the staffer was undetermined, beyond a few clues including the fact that his initials were either B.S. or S.B., as displayed on his laptop. ProPublica reporters scoured White House staffing records to narrow down the list of candidates and took to the Orange Line to see if he would pop up again. Sure enough, there we saw the likeliest candidate, carrying the same style of brown leather satchel and same type of phone. He disembarked in Washington for the short walk to a White House employee checkpoint. It was Sam Bock, a 27-year-old associate policy adviser with the Domestic Policy Council, the White House office that produced the July report.

The White House did not respond to a query about the draft plan. Bock, who previously worked on the staff of Rep. Jim Jordan, the Ohio Republican elected last week as House Minority Leader, did not respond to messages. The Smithsonian, which bid farewell to Bunch at a board meeting last month, declined to comment.

The Smithsonian encompasses 20 museums beyond the American history one. It has a 17-member board that is led by the chief justice of the Supreme Court and comprises the U.S. vice president, three members of Congress from each party and nine private citizens nominated by other board members. But it relies on the federal government for the majority of its funding, receiving more than $1 billion per year, and its leadership is in a state of flux: Not only is it seeking to replace Bunch, but the board itself is riddled with vacancies as private citizen terms expire without replacements. Until President Donald Trump attempted to fire the director of the National Portrait Gallery last year, no president had tried to remove a Smithsonian executive. (The institution resisted, but the director, Kim Sajet, decided to leave anyway.)

Three Smithsonian museums, dedicated to African American history, American history, and natural history, seen from the Washington Monument Andrew Harnik/Getty Images

As [recounted by ProPublica in September](https://www.propublica.org/article/how-smithsonian-museum-american-history-became-target-trump-culture-war), the American history museum has faced scrutiny over the years. Since its founding in 1964, it has struggled with the mission of telling the story of a vast and variegated nation; in 2001, an earlier round of criticisms prompted a blue-ribbon commission to produce a report urging the museum to offer a more unified approach to the national story, with fewer nods to political correctness. The Smithsonian underwent another identity crisis following the murder of George Floyd in Minneapolis in 2020, as Bunch and others led an institution-wide self-reckoning.

…

items.body:
Last week, international health authorities formally announced that the US had lost its measles-elimination status, meaning that the virus is once again endemic. But the official determination is a bit like getting the technical readout of a cracked dam while the country is already feet under water.

The national tally of measles cases is nearing 6,000 for the year, the highest count since 1991. Transmission is widespread, with 47 states and jurisdictions reporting cases. There have been 43 outbreaks this year, which account for 96 percent of the cases. Four states have case counts above 500, including Pennsylvania, which leads with [1,638 cases as of November 23](https://www.pa.gov/agencies/health/diseases-conditions/infectious-disease/measles). Nearly 650 people have been hospitalized nationwide. As of today, 14 people have died.

## Deaths and transmission

On November 23, Pennsylvania's health department announced its ninth confirmed death, an unvaccinated resident of Centre County. On November 24, Wisconsin reported its [third measles death](https://www.dhs.wisconsin.gov/news/releases/112426.htm), an adult in Lafayette County. The report follows two other deaths in the state, [an infant](https://www.dhs.wisconsin.gov/news/releases/110526.htm) and [a child](https://www.dhs.wisconsin.gov/news/releases/111326.htm). New York has also reported a [death, which was of a 7-month-old baby](https://publications.aap.org/aapnews/news/36693/AAP-president-Child-s-death-in-New-York-another?autologincheck=redirected). On November 20, Virginia reported the death of [a child between the age of 0 and 4](https://www.vdh.virginia.gov/news/public-relations-contacts/2026-news-releases/vdh-1st-measles-death-2026/).

items.title: Outage Chaos: Who Turned Off All The Computer?

items.body:
It's been a tough couple of weeks for anyone trying to use email, fly, spend money, use an Apple device*, or do signals intelligence. Technical service outages are nothing new, but why do so many big ones seem to be happening all at once? Are hackers, AI, and international conflicts to blame? And what can we do about it?

Since most service interruptions don't make the news, it's hard to get a baseline on how often we see them happen normally. But after a major incident like the Microsoft cloud outage on November 12, any smaller disruption is more likely to become a story as part of a pattern instead of an isolated incident. We would have heard plenty about the Air Traffic Control problems anyway, but the November 18 disruption to the PlayStation Network might have gotten less attention. There might appear to be a spike or an upward trend in outages, but we can't easily verify that, and the increased coverage will tend to make it seem more significant and interconnected than it necessarily is regardless.

One boring reason we might see an uptick in problems right now is the date on the calendar. With Thanksgiving travel, Black Friday, Cyber Monday, Giving Tuesday, and Surveillance Sunday (we assume) all coming up, organizations often schedule major system updates for the first three weeks of November. This helps them prepare for holiday traffic, and lets them shift the outage risk to the time before those dates when they may consider it far more important to maintain reliable service.

While none of these particular outages have yet been directly attributed to AI (or to malicious hackers), bank CEOs and the NSA briefed congress and reportedly attributed at least some of them to rushed attempts to patch vulnerabilities found by AI. That’s understandable: all software updates carry risk, and companies and governments are having to deploy more updates, and faster, than they’ve ever needed to before. Some of those updates are to important infrastructure, where an outage would be very disruptive, but the impact of leaving vulnerabilities unpatched would be even worse.

Vulnerabilities are a type of software bug that affects security. Once a vulnerability is found in a given piece of software and disclosed, typically the software maker will release a patch fixing that vulnerability. That’s why so many update notes say things like “performance improvements and security fixes” — the security fixes are patches to vulnerabilities.

Companies and governments that run infrastructure face a challenging tradeoff: deploy patches quickly or slowly and cautiously? Patching quickly is important to keep systems secure. But every software update runs a risk: any change to a deployed system can have unintended consequences that snowball into a disastrous outage.

This exacerbates a much deeper problem long discussed in the engineering culture of many, if not most organizations. Keeping networks, servers, and applications not just secure but resilient in the face of patches, reboots, and capacity changes requires an investment in staff, time, hardware, and processes for frequent maintenance, redundant systems, realistic staging environments, automated rollbacks, monitoring, and pre-deployment testing. These investments are rarely as attractive to decision-makers as a new product or feature, or at times, sadly, as layoffs.

This should come as no surprise when we think of our apps, web sites, airlines, and bank cards as supported by electronic infrastructure. As in the more visible physical world, maintenance can only be deferred for so long before the costs become immediate and dramatic. We accept the cost of an occasional short term bridge closure to reduce the risk of a bridge collapse, and highway departments schedule road work nearly every night of the year to repair and prevent the worst potholes.

When this kind of work is endlessly deferred in the world of software, we speak of technical debt: issues we already know about that aren't causing a big enough problem right now to divert us from other work, but that, if left unaddressed, can easily multiply and interact to cause outages or other complications. This can show up as routine steps that have to be done by hand instead of automatically on a schedule, a programmer's shortcut that works well in one specific situation but is more fragile in general, an operating system six months (or years) overdue for a reboot, or a piece of networking hardware no longer supported for patches by its manufacturer. On the other hand, when maintenance work is well-resourced and routine, it should be rare for even major security updates to cause significant issues.

What’s needed in the short term is a big investment in the people and training needed to roll out patches promptly and safely. What’s needed in the long term is a big investment in software security, eliminating entire classes of vulnerabilities, like memory safety, before they are ever written.

For organizations that have gotten used to patching slowly and cautiously, suddenly switching gears to patching quickly is a big challenge. And the flood of vulnerability disclosures enabled by AI means that everyone is being asked to switch gears like that at once.

Fortunately, it’s not a zero-sum game: patches can be rolled out quickly and cautiously, with investments in reducing technical debt and expanding maintenance budgets as described above. These measures are expensive and time-consuming, but necessary. For governments asking how to respond to AI-enabled cybersecurity threats, investing in the people and training necessary to stay on top of patches will pay big dividends in reliability and security.

For individuals, consider the trade-offs when relying on a single provider for many services you rely on. Consumer cloud and device offerings tie together many of the things we need to function on a daily basis like email, messaging, file storage, and even payments, but that convenience and simplicity comes with the risk of losing access to it all if that service goes offline (or suspends your account). Trying out interoperable alternatives is a great way to reduce your reliance on a single company.

Finally, for any critical data, learn the 3-2-1 rule for backups: Keep three different copies on two different types of storage with one copy in a different physical location. For many users, a laptop or other personal device, cloud storage, and a local backup disk exemplify this rule, as long as the laptop stores data on its own drives, not only in the cloud.

Among other things, the accelerated rollout of AI has made it all the more critical  to reinvest in people and systems to keep our software, networks, governments, and interconnected world stable.

*Apple is an EFF donor. EFF donors do not influence our agenda or our positions.

items.title: Private Prison Told ICE Its Jail Was Worth $67 Million. ICE Bought It for Nearly Half a Billion.
