items.body:
As it eyed a sale of a jail in Tacoma, Washington, this spring, the private prison giant GEO Group valued the facility at $67 million, according to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement records obtained exclusively by The Intercept.

This month, the federal government just paid GEO almost seven times that — [$453 million](https://www.projectsaltbox.com/p/geo-group-sells-tacoma-detention) — when it purchased the facility, the Northwest ICE Processing Center.

The chasm between GEO’s March 2026 asset appraisal and the sale price just eight months later represents a “massive increase,” according to Michael Wriston, co-founder of the government watchdog Project Salt Box, which tracks ICE spending and contracts.

“ICE should explain how it arrived at $453 million and release the appraisal behind that price,” Wriston told The Intercept.

“I think this is what happens when you move too fast without sufficient internal controls,” John Roth, the former inspector general of the Department of Homeland Security, ICE’s parent agency, told The Intercept. “You’re going to waste a lot of money. And that assumes everyone has the best intentions and hasn’t got some sort of side deal or corrupt motive.”

Neither ICE nor GEO responded to requests for comment about the sale. Without answering questions about the sale price, the Department of Homeland Security told The Intercept the purchase was “to strengthen America’s ability to enforce its immigration laws and carry out the American people’s mandate for mass deportations.”

A screen capture of a March 2026 ICE spreadsheet showing GEO Group’s valuation of Northwest ICE Processing Center. Screenshot: Jacqueline Stevens/The Intercept

With Democrats set to [take control](https://theintercept.com/2026/11/04/midterms-democrats-agenda-congress-iran-ai/) of Congress, ICE’s real estate purchases are already coming under intense scrutiny on Capitol Hill.

> “These deals raise serious questions about pay-to-play schemes and corruption at DHS.”

“This new report is worthy of serious investigation and is part of a pattern of Department of Homeland Security purchases of detention facilities for hundreds of millions of dollars more than they seem to be worth,” Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., the incoming chair of the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, told The Intercept in a statement. “These deals raise serious questions about pay-to-play schemes and corruption at DHS.”

Hassan opened a [probe](https://www.hassan.senate.gov/news/press-releases/amid-corruption-allegations-senator-hassan-opens-investigation-into-purchase-of-ice-detention-facility-for-420-million-above-previous-asking-price) earlier this month into ICE’s $495 million purchase of a detention center the private prison giant CoreCivic previously offered to the state of Minnesota [for $75 million](https://www.kare11.com/article/news/investigations/senate-democrats-to-investigate-dhs-purchase-of-appleton-prison/89-b7ee1b9a-790e-4e79-ac47-5d5df30196d6) — a sale the state’s corrections commissioner told the news site [Punch Up](https://thepunchup.substack.com/p/6aa2d459-7864-40ba-b5d1-a106389ca439) was being discussed for $3 million.

[Related Private Prison Falsified Records in Detainee’s Death in ICE Custody](https://theintercept.com/2026/02/26/ice-geo-group-moshannon-death-falsify/)

GEO Group’s March 2026 valuation for Northwest ICE Processing Center, which the company purchased in 2005 as part of its acquisition of another private prison firm, was submitted to the Department of Homeland Security in accordance with its contract with ICE.

According to a [chart in the document](https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/28930958-ice-doc-showing-geo-group-valuation-of-nwipc-jail/), GEO calculated the current $67 million value of the detention facility, which is not the same as its market value, by subtracting annual depreciation figures from its original value of $109 million.

Roth, the former Homeland Security inspector general, expects scrutiny into the nearly half-billion-dollar sale’s paper trail.

“I’d be curious to know,” he said, “what sort of due diligence they did before they put that number down.”

## Cost of Avoiding Regulations

ICE officials told Government Accountability Office investigators that their robust plans for purchasing existing immigration detention facilities was not to save money, but to avoid issues with local governments.

“Officials noted that while they do not expect this effort to result in cost savings, it will help ICE fulfill its mission in locations where state governments may resist expanded detention efforts,” said a Government Accountability Office [report](https://files.gao.gov/reports/GAO-27-108665/index.html) released this month.

[Related How a Small Kansas City Became a Critical Hub for Trump’s Deportation Regime Against Its Will](https://theintercept.com/2026/09/22/leavenworth-kansas-corecivic-ice-mass-detention-deportation/)

Like [other private prison firms](https://theintercept.com/2026/11/10/arizona-ice-camp-mtc-sexual-abuse/) across the country, GEO’s efforts to build and operate facilities it owns have met obstacles in local rules and regulations.

In some cases, state-level regulators have gone after GEO for violations of labor laws like minimum wage and occupational safety regulations. Earlier this year in California, the company [paid a $100,000 fine](https://www.ccijustice.org/post/geo-group-calosha-settlement-fine) and agreed to extend worker protections to immigrant laborers over alleged violations of California worker safety standards.

One of the cases focused on the Northwest ICE Processing Center, the Tacoma facility that GEO just sold to ICE. In 2021, a judge ordered GEO to pay [$26 million](https://www.reuters.com/legal/government/geo-group-must-pay-minimum-wage-immigrant-detainees-court-rules-2023-12-22/) to former detainees and the state of Washington for, among other allegations, state minimum wage violations. (Andrew Free, one of the authors of this article, was an attorney for the ICE detainees in the lawsuit.)

The verdict was [upheld](https://www.reuters.com/legal/government/geo-group-cant-nix-23-mln-verdict-over-immigrant-detainee-pay-2025-01-16/) by a federal appeals court in 2025 after GEO sought the same immunity from state minimum wage laws enjoyed by the federal government. The Supreme Court is currently deciding whether it will hear GEO’s appeal.

In a May earnings call, GEO chair George Zoley noted the problem in areas with Democrats in charge of regulation.

“I think the logical solution to much of that is federal ownership of the facilities,” Zoley told the earnings call, according to the [Philadelphia Inquirer](https://www.inquirer.com/news/nation-world/moshannon-valley-detention-center-ice-trump-deportation-contract-20260923.html).

items.title: Many languages, one common neural code
items.subtitle: Languages take on thousands of forms.
items.feedText: Some are tonal, like Vietnamese, where shifts in pitch convey distinct meanings. English relies on precise word orders, but this matters less for Russian, where words can be swapped without changing the intended message. Despite so much variety in the linguistic kingdom, an MIT study has found that the human brain may process all sorts of languages in a universal way. items.body:
Languages take on thousands of forms. Some are tonal, like Vietnamese, where shifts in pitch convey distinct meanings. English relies on precise word orders, but this matters less for Russian, where words can be swapped without changing the intended message.

Despite so much variety in the linguistic kingdom, an MIT study has found that the human brain may process all sorts of languages in a universal way.

Artificial intelligence made this finding possible. In the study [published today in Nature Neuroscience](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41593-026-02523-6) *,* the researchers used multilingual models to predict how the human brain responds to various languages. Those models also helped the researchers detect a shared brain process across people who collectively spoke 21 different languages.

“Of course, there are many differences in the ways humans converse with each other. But our team found that there is something fundamentally similar in how the brain communicates,” says [Evelina Fedorenko](https://mcgovern.mit.edu/profile/ev-fedorenko/), who is an investigator at MIT’s McGovern Institute for Brain Research, an associate professor of brain and cognitive sciences, and the senior author of the paper.

The study is the first to use multilingual models to predict brain responses across many languages. As researchers develop AI language tools to diagnose brain disorders, this work can extend their benefit to speakers of more languages, and may one day even keep endangered ones from vanishing.

**Parsing the linguistic mind**

Language allows us to share our thoughts about the outside world and the ones we create in our minds. That power lives within a network of brain regions located in the left hemisphere.

“Every language is managed by these same parts of the brain,” explains Andrea Gregor de Varda, the lead author of the new study, a postdoc in the Fedorenko lab, and fellow in the [K. Lisa Yang Integrative Computational Neuroscience (ICoN) Center](https://yangtan.mit.edu/our-research/k-lisa-yang-icon-center/).

While scientists know that all languages activate the same parts of the brain, de Varda and Fedorenko wanted to know if that meant the brain processes them in the same way.

For example, they wondered, does the brain of someone who speaks Korean operate comparably to the brains of a Hindi or Spanish speaker?

It’s extremely hard to answer that question if you lack the right tools, de Varda says. And they needed one capable of creating a common code for comparing all sorts of languages — a task that is well-suited to artificial intelligence.

**Where AI meets the brain**

Large language models (LLMs) — such as those powering ChatGPT and Claude — interpret language much like the human brain, although they weren’t designed to do so. That surprising similarity is allowing de Varda and others in the field to wield these tools as a piercing [lens into the human mind](https://mcgovern.mit.edu/2025/11/19/the-cost-of-thinking/). Such studies often explore LLMs’ ability to learn or make sense of linguistic elements, such as grammar and meaning, to glean insights into how the brain might handle communication. But early LLMs used to work within a single language. The MIT researchers thought another class of models might help expand that scope.

“Multilingual language models are LLMs that can process hundreds of languages at once,” explains Fedorenko. Like other AIs of their kind, multilingual models ingest words or phrases and output numbers that scientists can extract. “Those numbers show how the model represents that bit of language,” she says. Now the team could study many languages at once using a single numerical code from the models. But the extent to which the models aligned with the human mind still lurked in the unknowns. De Varda believed he could coax an answer into light through a computational approach.

Using machine learning, he merged two data sources: the multilingual models’ code and scans of people’s brains as they performed linguistic tasks. The product was an AI tool known as an encoding model. It takes a multilingual model’s code, say, for a sentence, and predicts how the human brain might light up in response to the same input.

Encoding models at the time only existed for a handful of languages including English, French, and Chinese. But de Varda sought to test whether those models could be extended to more — and importantly, understudied ones. Doing so could reveal new aspects in which AI mirrors the human brain, and even detect a shared neural component across speakers of various languages.

**A mental bridge between languages**

The Fedorenko lab already had preexisting brain imaging data from speakers of 12 languages: Afrikaans, Dutch, Farsi, French, Lithuanian, Marathi, Norwegian, Romanian, Spanish, Tamil, Turkish, and Vietnamese. They recruited speakers of nine additional ones for their new study — Italian, Portuguese, German, Russian, Polish, Hindi, Arabic, Mandarin, and Korean — and recorded their brain activity while they listened to stories from “Alice in Wonderland” in their native language. By coupling that brain imaging data with outputs from multilingual models, the team created encoding models for those 21 languages.

“We found that the encoding models accurately predicted brain responses in all of the languages we studied — even in Marathi and Lithuanian, that, in contrast to English, we only have a limited amount of data on,” says Fedorenko. “The fact that there’s this emergent similarity between models and humans across so many languages is really quite exciting.”

Another finding was more interesting still. Even though the researchers trained an encoding model in a single language, it could predict brain activity for a language it had never seen before. For example, an encoding model trained to predict brain responses in French could also predict responses in Vietnamese, without ever being trained in Vietnamese. It was a truly fascinating discovery, de Varda says, because this was only possible if all the speakers’ brains were representing language in a shared way: a neural thread binding human communication.

What was that shared component? Dissecting different linguistic features across all the languages suggested that it has something to do with meaning. “That’s the intended power of communication, right? To share meaning; new information or our feelings about the world. So it’s fascinating we see that reflected in this work,” says Fedorenko.

items.title: Why Trump Rescued Jensen Huang

The woman, Alice Huang, may have influenced the Nvidia CEO’s decision to sell advanced chips to companies that transferred them to China. items.body:
A presidency that operated by normal rules of ethics or even self-preservation would be scrambling to distance itself from the repercussions of the Nvidia scandal. Last night, *The New York Times* reported that a Chinese woman who had an affair with Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s once and future chief executive, was [in regular contact with China’s spy agency](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/22/us/politics/alice-huang-china-spy-agency-nvidia.html). The woman, Alice Huang, may have influenced the Nvidia CEO’s decision to sell advanced chips to companies that transferred them to China.

Donald Trump instead pushed to reinstate Jensen Huang as the company’s CEO, even going so far as to [dial in](https://www.semafor.com/article/11/23/2026/jensen-huang-reinstated-as-nvidia-ceo) to the company’s board meeting to push for Huang’s return, a demand the company was in no position to turn down.

Trump’s decision is overdetermined, as an academic might put it, by several Trumpian precepts. The president believes as a matter of principle that powerful men should not face repercussions for sexual misconduct. He also takes a relativistic view of corruption, seeing it as simply a normal way to do business. This mindset allows him to routinely smear any opponent as corrupt (everybody does it, right?) while simultaneously engaging in flagrant corruption himself (after all, everybody does it).

But perhaps the most significant Trumpian attribute at play is his [disregard for the national interest](https://www.theatlantic.com/ideas/2026/11/trump-putin-ukraine-collins/689537/?utm_source=feed). Nvidia was permitting its advanced chips to fall into Chinese hands. This may have violated American law, and the law serves a critical purpose: to prevent America’s most powerful global rival from gaining access to cutting-edge technology that might enable it to obtain economic and military dominance.

*[[Read: A $5.7 trillion face-plant](https://www.theatlantic.com/technology/2026/11/jensen-huangs-icarus-complex/689393/?utm_source=feed)]*

Conservative Republicans, who tend to be the most hawkish politicians on China, are outraged by this, which may well turn out to have a decisive effect on the course of global leadership. The prospect of the U.S. losing the artificial-intelligence race to China out of an American businessman’s greed or libidinousness should leave them predictably furious.

Trump, however, does not seem to care whatsoever. Despite his occasional demagoguery against China, he seems to have little interest in competing against it. He proclaims his admiration of its dictator, Xi Jinping, more than any other world leader save Vladimir Putin, the Russian dictator. After a symbolic but fruitless meeting with the two partners last week, Trump giddily posted memes depicting the troika as global leaders akin to Roosevelt, Stalin, and Churchill.

Trump does not want China to exert global dominance, but he does not seem to view its ambitions with any concern. He told reporters last week that he [talked about Huang](https://finance.yahoo.com/video/trump-on-jensen-huang-were-a-country-of-second-chances-193647938.html) with Xi: “I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance. You know, we’re a country of second chances and I’d love to be able to see him have—that’s a very important company to us. And he put us in a position where we are literally 10 years advanced over other companies, and I did discuss that with President Xi, and he said, *Oh, brilliant, brilliant*.”

In other words, Trump seems to be saying that he asked the president of China, the country that is suspected of running the honey-trap operation on Huang, whether Trump should bring back the CEO of Nvidia. Then, Trump would have us believe, the Chinese president agreed that reinstating the executive over which China is feared to have leverage would be a good idea. And Trump presented this agreement as an encouraging sign.

*[[Read: China’s intelligence coup in the AI war](https://www.theatlantic.com/national-security/2026/11/jensen-huang-chinese-intelligence-nvidia/689430/?utm_source=feed)]*

In a normal administration, the mere fact that the president is telling a private company whom to install as CEO would itself constitute an enormous scandal. In the current atmosphere, this is simply a background detail.

The most benign explanation for Huang’s restoration is that Trump cares more about keeping the stock market soaring than any American national-security interest. Less benign interpretations include the possibility that Trump’s inner circle has profited from Nvidia circumventing export controls.

Determining what in fact took place will likely consume months of reporting and Watergate-style oversight hearings from a Congress that, as of January, will no longer be controlled by the president’s lackeys. Going into damage-control mode would be rational.

Instead Trump apparently believes that he can train his supporters to align their instincts with his and define his behavior as good and correct, as he did with the Russia hoax, or the perfect phone call with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, or the stolen 2020 election. “I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure,” Trump wrote on [Truth Social](https://www.trumpstruth.org/statuses/43714) this morning. He followed this up by [sharing](https://www.trumpstruth.org/statuses/43716) a depiction of the 2024 attempted assassination of himself in Butler, Pennsylvania, but with Huang in his place, bloodied and holding aloft a red bra. As long as the stock market goes up, Jensen Huang can sleep with all the Chinese spies he wants.

items.title: How to Bear Your Desolations
items.subtitle:
“You may have to break your heart, but it isn’t nothing to know even one moment alive.”

The morning after a relationship of depth and significance…
items.feedText: All that centering, all that glazing, all the hours of pressing letterforms into the wet clay — all of it in shiny shards. And meanwhile spring was breaking outside and a little girl in bright blue rain boots was jumping in a puddle, smashing the reflections of the clouds with savage joy. And I thought, this is all there is: breaking, breaking apart, breaking open. Breaking alive. Card from An Almanac of Birds: 100 Divinations for Uncertain Days, also available as a stand-alone print and as greeting cards. It is…
items.body:
### “You may have to break your heart, but it isn’t nothing to know even one moment alive.”

The morning after a relationship of depth and significance long bending under the weight of its own complexity had finally broken with an exhausted thud, I opened [the kiln](https://themarginalian.org/tag/ceramics) to discover a month’s worth of pottery shattered — two pieces had exploded, the shrapnel ruining the rest. All that centering, all that glazing, all the hours of pressing letterforms into the wet clay — all of it in shiny shards. And meanwhile spring was breaking outside and a little girl in bright blue rain boots was jumping in a puddle, smashing the reflections of the clouds with savage joy.

And I thought, this is all there is: breaking, breaking apart, breaking open.

Breaking alive.

Card from [An Almanac of Birds: 100 Divinations for Uncertain Days](https://almanacofbirds.org), also available as a [stand-alone print](https://society6.com/product/bird-divinations-ivory-billed-woodpecker-about-almanacofbirdsorg_print?curator=brainpicker) and as [greeting cards](https://society6.com/product/bird-divinations-ivory-billed-woodpecker-about-almanacofbirdsorg_cards?curator=brainpicker).

It is not an easy assignment, being alive. Coming awake from the stupor of near-living that lulls us through our days, awake to the knowledge that on the other side of the neighborhood ICE trucks are handcuffing people and on the other side of the planet children are dying in gunfire, while outside the first birds of spring are singing and everywhere people are falling in love and in some faraway mountain village a shepherd is singing under a thousand stars. And somehow, somehow, all of it has to cohere into a single world in which we, in all our incohesion, must live this single life.

[Ellen Bass](https://www.themarginalian.org/tag/ellen-bass/) reckons with all of this in her splendid poem “Any Common Desolation,” originally published in The Academy of American Poets’ [poem-a-day](https://poets.org/poem-a-day) newsletter and later included in James Crews’s lifeline of an anthology [How to Love the World: Poems of Gratitude and Hope](https://www.amazon.com/How-Love-World-Poems-Gratitude/dp/1635863864/?tag=braipick-20) ([public library](https://search.worldcat.org/title/1159045177)), shared here with Ellen’s blessing.

> ANY COMMON DESOLATION
> by Ellen Bass
> can be enough to make you look up
> at the yellowed leaves of the apple tree, the few
> that survived the rains and frost, shot
> with late afternoon sun. They glow a deep
> orange-gold against a blue so sheer, a single bird
> would rip it like silk. You may have to break
> your heart, but it isn’t nothing
> to know even one moment alive. The sound
> of an oar in an oarlock or a ruminant
> animal tearing grass. The smell of grated ginger.
> The ruby neon of the liquor store sign.
> Warm socks. You remember your mother,
> her precision a ceremony, as she gathered
> the white cotton, slipped it over your toes,
> drew up the heel, turned the cuff. A breath
> can uncoil as you walk across your own muddy yard,
> the big dipper pouring night down over you, and everything
> you dread, all you can’t bear, dissolves
> and, like a needle slipped into your vein —
> that sudden rush of the world.

Complement with Henry James on [how to stop waiting and start living](https://www.themarginalian.org/2022/10/17/henry-james-the-beast-in-the-jungle/) and Hermann Hesse on [how to be more alive](https://www.themarginalian.org/2023/07/06/hermann-hesse-wonder-butterflies/), then revisit Ellen’s magnificent poem [“How to Apologize.”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2023/11/28/how-to-apologize-ellen-bass/) And if you are looking to break your poetry open, I couldn’t recommend her [Living Room Craft Talks](https://www.ellenbass.com/events/living-room-craft-talk-series/) more heartily.

### donating = loving

For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing *The Marginalian* (which [bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings](https://www.themarginalian.org/2021/10/22/brain-pickings-becoming-the-marginalian/) for its first fifteen years). It has remained free and ad-free and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, no assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If this labor makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider lending a helping hand with a [donation](https://www.themarginalian.org/donate/). Your support makes all the difference.

### newsletter

*The Marginalian* has a free weekly newsletter. It comes out on Sundays and offers the week’s most inspiring reading. Here’s [what to expect](https://mailchi.mp/brainpickings/janna-levin-rebecca-elson-anne-lamott-james-gleick). Like? [Sign up.](https://www.themarginalian.org/newsletter/)

items.title: Space lasers are fast, but clouds still rule the forecast
items.subtitle: Since the launch of Sputnik, humanity has talked to its spacecraft through radio waves.
items.feedText: Radio is great for communication through any weather, but it has hit a limit—traditional radio frequencies are highly regulated by bodies like the International Telecommunications Union, which limits the scalability of radio communications networks to meet the growing demand for bandwidth to and from space. The obvious solution is to switch to infrared lasers, which have an extremely high data transfer rate.

items.body:
NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope reveals the hot dust that makes up Cassiopeia A. The composition of its dust provides clues to the structure of Cassiopeia A’s original star.

NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Tea Temim (Columbia University), Rick Arendt (UMBC), Dan Milisavljevic (Purdue University); Image Processing: Joseph DePasquale (STScI)

NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope reveals the hot dust that makes up Cassiopeia A (Cas A) in this high-resolution, mid-infrared image released on Nov. 23, 2026. Remnants like these are the clouds of gas and dust that remain following the explosion of a massive star and will eventually seed a new generation of stars and planets. The Webb data supports a scenario in which the interior of the star underwent a dramatic change, possibly just hours before its demise.

[See what scientists have learned about Cas A from Webb’s observation.](https://science.nasa.gov/missions/webb/nasas-webb-shows-how-supernova-dust-chronicles-star-evolution/)

*Image credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Tea Temim (Columbia University), Rick Arendt (UMBC), Dan Milisavljevic (Purdue University); Image Processing: Joseph DePasquale (STScI)*

items.body:
# Oceans and Forests Have Absorbed Roughly Half Our Carbon Emissions for Decades, Slowing Climate Change. But Can They Keep It Up? - Nautilus

## Oceans and Forests Have Absorbed Roughly Half Our Carbon Emissions for Decades, Slowing Climate Change. But Can They Keep It Up?

Oceans and land have been absorbing a lot of the carbon emissions humans create

11:00 AM CST on November 21, 2026

Over the past two centuries, humans have pumped billions of tons of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere by burning fossil fuels , raising global temperatures in the process.

Luckily for humanity, Earth has done what it could to soften the impact.

The world’s oceans have absorbed 35% of carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels since 1990, our new research shows, and the forests and other plants of the world have absorbed another 13%.

The importance of these two enormous natural carbon sinks cannot be overstated as global temperatures rise, fueling heat waves, fires, storms, floods and droughts around the world. Yet there is much that scientists do not understand about these carbon sinks – most importantly, how exactly they’ll behave in the future.

If the oceans and forests keep absorbing the same amount of carbon dioxide, scientists will have a sense of what to expect in the future and what can be done to slow climate change. And governments will know their remaining carbon budgets – that is, how much carbon dioxide can still be emitted into the atmosphere while keeping global temperatures below agreed-to levels.

But what if those carbon sinks change?

We have been working on greenhouse gas measurements for decades. In a new study, published Nov. 12, 2026, in the journal Science, we describe an alternative method for measuring these crucial carbon sinks, and what it shows.

We found that while the ocean sink has been expanding, meaning the oceans are taking in more carbon dioxide, that expansion might begin to slow down , leaving the oceans less effective at absorbing carbon in the coming decades. We found that the land sink has not been expanding, which was something of a surprise.

The Fiendishly Difficult Task of Measuring Carbon Sinks

Measuring how much carbon is being taken up by the world’s oceans and forests is devilishly difficult and prohibitively expensive.

This is because many parts of the land and ocean don’t behave in the same ways. What occurs in one ocean region or forest can be very different from another; and the behavior in one year can be very different in the next, often for reasons scientists do not fully understand.

Computer models can help overcome some of these complexities, but they too have limitations. Satellites can also help, but they cannot see through clouds, nor can they see what is happening in the soil or mid-to-deep ocean.

As carbon cycle scientists, we set out to find a different way to measure these carbon sinks.

Our new study approaches the problem from another angle. We used high-precision measurements of atmospheric oxygen (O₂), combined with atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO₂) measurements , to quantify how the ocean and land carbon sinks take up carbon dioxide.

This works because land, oceans and burning fossil fuels have different effects on oxygen: When fossil fuels are burned, they not only produce CO₂, they consume O₂. On land, when plants take up CO₂ to grow, they simultaneously release O₂. When the oceans take up atmospheric CO₂, there is no corresponding release of O₂.

This means that if we measure both CO₂ and O₂ in the atmosphere, then we can quantify the ocean and land carbon sinks. It is a straightforward mathematical approach of solving two equations with two unknowns, combined with our knowledge and measurements of the global budgets of CO₂ and O₂.

What We Found

When we looked at the ocean and land carbon sinks over the past three decades, the results were surprising and sobering.

In contrast to most computer model simulations , we did not find the land carbon sink increasing over time to keep pace with increasing fossil fuel emissions. We did, however, find a larger ocean carbon sink than predicted by most models , and we found that it has been increasing as emissions grow.

Where Is the Climate Headed?

If these trends in carbon sinks continue, then in the coming decades, humans will be relying more heavily on the oceans to slow down climate change. But in the next few decades, there are reasons to believe the oceans could become less effective at absorbing carbon.

For example, warmer waters are not able to hold as much gas , such as carbon dioxide. Warmer surface waters are also less efficient at mixing into the deep ocean , which has the beneficial effect of locking carbon dioxide away from the atmosphere for many hundreds of years.

The data for the past decade hints at the possibility that while the ocean carbon sink is increasing now, its rate of increase may be slowing down.

Carbon Cycle Models Need to Improve

For the oceans, most computer models agree with each other, but, for the historical period, they do not match our oxygen-based results. For the land, models vary widely from each other, and most do not match our oxygen-based results.

Computer models are essential to provide governments with feasible scenarios to avoid dangerous climate change, but to be effective they need to be better grounded in what real-world observations are showing. Nature is difficult to represent with a series of equations, and observations are few considering the size of the planet.

Looking Ahead

We believe our study improves understanding of global carbon sinks and can help lead to more reliable projections of what might happen with climate change in the coming decades. But like any scientific approach, our oxygen method also has drawbacks.

The measurements themselves are challenging, such that only about 10 research laboratories in the world are routinely doing them. Calibrating the measurements is an ongoing challenge. Earth is not helping: Warmer waters hold less gas, meaning that as oceans warm in response to climate change, they expel some oxygen into the atmosphere . We must account for this in our carbon sink calculations. And to take into account variability in ocean circulation and other ocean processes, we have to average our results over 10-year time frames.

Policymakers and the public need answers faster . We believe the solution involves both improving the atmospheric oxygen approach and using other independent approaches: measurements of carbon and oxygen in the oceans, computer models and satellites are all essential. Combining these approaches will lead to more robust understanding of the carbon cycle and climate change, and better knowledge of where these valuable carbon sinks and the global climate are headed.

This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article .

items.title: When A Farewell to Arms Was Censored For Foul Language
items.subtitle: The young novelist Ernest Hemingway was angry and frustrated.
items.feedText: Scribner’s Magazine had decided to cut “shit,” “fuck,” “balls,” “cocksucker,” “son of a bitch,” “whore,” and “Jesus Christ” from his new book, A Farewell to Arms, when it began serializing it in May 1929. items.body:
The young novelist Ernest Hemingway was angry and frustrated. *Scribner’s Magazine* had decided to cut “shit,” “fuck,” “balls,” “cocksucker,” “son of a bitch,” “whore,” and “Jesus Christ” from his new book, [A Farewell to Arms](https://bookshop.org/a/132/9780143138839), when it began serializing it in May 1929. The semi-autobiographical novel followed the experiences of an American ambulance driver on the Italian Front in World War I. For publication as a book, Maxwell Perkins, Hemingway’s editor at Charles Scribner’s Sons, managed to get the last three phrases restored, in sentences such as “I shot the son of a bitch with my rifle,” “they were loading the girls from the soldiers’ whorehouse into a truck,” and “Jesus Christ what I could do with two hundred and fifty dollars.” Hemingway and Perkins negotiated, the editor conceding “scrotum” instead of “balls,” but refusing “c—s r” as an alternative to “cocksucker” (which became, instead, “‘I killed that – of a sergeant’ ”). The author had to turn his other “four-letter words” into phrases like “Go something yourself.” Hemingway protested that “emasculation was a minor operation to perform on men, animals, and books, but its effect was great.” He was waging a fight for “full use of the language.” But he gave in.

Hemingway had won part of his fight. But predictably, “scrotum,” “son of a bitch,” “whore,” “Jesus Christ” (as an exclamation), and the premarital love affair at the novel’s core were themselves too much for the Word Police, at least in some jurisdictions. In Boston—a city already known for its gusto in banning any work of literature or art deemed indecent by officials—Police Superintendent Michael Crowley announced that the June issue of *Scribner’s* was being barred from sale because of its “salacious” material, even before the book version restored some of the offensive words. Scribner’s jumped to Hemingway’s defense, issuing a press release defending him as “one of the finest and most highly regarded of the modern writers,” and promised that it would continue serializing [A Farewell to Arms](https://bookshop.org/a/132/9780143138839)in coming issues. But Scribner’s also felt called upon to underscore the novel’s “distinctly moral” nature. “It is the story of a fine and faithful love, born, it is true, out of physical desire,” the release continued. “If white is to be contrasted with black, thereby emphasizing its whiteness, the picture cannot be all white.”

Spare, truthful words—honest names and honest profanities—had dignity and humanity. It was grand phrases that were obscene in their evasion of hard truths.[/pullquotes]

This defense sidestepped the fact that Hemingway himself, an admirer of Mark Twain, would have rejected any notion of a simplistic “black” and “white” moral in his novel as a shabby evasion serving outmoded and dishonest values. But the press release went forth, and Scribner’s investment paid off. [A Farewell to Arms](https://bookshop.org/a/132/9780143138839)sold 31,000 copies in its first print run and helped make its author financially independent. As book industry executives expected, being “banned in Boston” probably boosted sales—even among Bostonians, who could cross the city line to buy copies elsewhere. One of the passages in *[A Farewell to Arms](https://bookshop.org/a/132/9780143138839)* rang as a clarion call for turning ideas about what was “obscene” on their heads. In it, an Italian soldier, reflecting on the staggering death toll of a recent offensive, remarks that the sacrifice cannot have been “in vain.” In response, Hemingway’s protagonist, the American Frederic Henry, muses on the power and deceit of words:

I was always embarrassed by the words sacred, glorious, and sacrifice and the expression in vain…I had seen nothing sacred, and the things that were glorious had no glory and the sacrifices were like the stockyards of Chicago if nothing was done with the meat except to bury it…Abstract words such as glory, honor, courage, or hallow were obscene beside the concrete names of villages, the numbers of roads, the names of rivers, the numbers of regiments and the dates.

Spare, truthful words—honest names and honest profanities—had dignity and humanity. It was grand phrases that were obscene in their evasion of hard truths. One form of language lied. The other, if used to register authentic emotional experience, didn’t. “Fuck,” “shit,” and “cocksucker” expressed real feelings in real speech. “Glory,” “honor,” and “courage” deluded.

Yet the miniature Culture War that [A Farewell to Arms](https://bookshop.org/a/132/9780143138839)unleashed was also fought out behind closed doors in the Manhattan offices of Charles Scribner’s Sons. After all, Scribner’s and other prestige presses were themselves Word Police, upholding nineteenth-century aesthetic and moral ideals that company elders brought to their self-appointed roles as gatekeepers of American taste and cultivation, all while selling books and magazines to make money. Perkins had already run this gauntlet more than once. His elders at the house had objected loudly in 1922 when another of his young stars, F. Scott Fitzgerald, wanted to title a short story collection [Tales of the Jazz Age](https://bookshop.org/a/132/9780307476371). The word “jazz” was the problem: they felt, Perkins explained, “that the word whatever implication it actually has, will itself injure the book.” But the title stayed, and, as Fitzgerald correctly predicted, “it will be bought by *my own personal public*, that is, by the countless flappers and college kids who think I am a sort of oracle.” Many of those flappers and collegians knew that jazz’s “implications” included semen, orgasm, and sex.

Hemingway’s first novel, [The Sun Also Rises](https://bookshop.org/a/132/9780743297332), had almost been rejected by Scribner’s in 1926, despite Perkins’s advocacy. That novel’s spare account of emotionally rootless young Americans in post-World War I Europe bewildered the house’s older editors, and Hemingway and Perkins fought hard to retain the word “bitch” to describe the heroine, Lady Brett Ashley. As another writer observed, old “Charles Scribner would no sooner allow profanity in one of his books than he would invite friends to use his parlor as a toilet room.” The company had agreed to publication with great reluctance, resigning itself to the inevitable Boston banning. But *The Sun Also Rises* sold quickly; by the time of Hemingway’s death in 1961, an estimated million copies had circulated. Writing of the 1920s, the critic Edmund Wilson mused on the novel’s impact: “The great watchword was ‘Have a drink’; and in the bars of New York and Paris the young people were getting to talk like Hemingway.” As John Updike reflected decades later, “an entire generation of American men learned to speak in the accents of [his] stoicism.”

______________________________

items.body:
**by Marianne Janack**

In an article about AI and human nature in The Free Press ([AI Will Change What It Is To Be Human. Are We Ready?](https://www.thefp.com/p/ai-will-change-what-it-is-to-be-human?utm_source=publication-search)) Tyler Cowen and Avital Balwit predict that artificial intelligence, like many technological advances before it, can improve human life, but that it can also challenge our very ideas about what it is to be human. Humans have been, the authors claim, the smartest beings around for all of our history. But that will change with the development of artificial intelligence. And this will lead to what the authors call an identity crisis: no human will be able to compete with artificial intelligence on the basis of intelligence. The authors predict that we will value other kinds of things: people who do physical labor or work in the energy sector; people who provide inspiration (coaches and mentors) or entertainment. Greeters, charmers, and flatterers will also be in demand, Balwit and Cowen argue, if only to satisfy what they see as the human biological need for obsequiousity and interaction with other humans.

The authors also predict that AI will lead to longer human lives and better health; a boom in participation in human group activities like religious services, clubs, and volunteering; and more and better leisure time. However, along with these benefits might come a heavy dose of demoralization. If what we value is our intelligence and intellectual work, then AI will be better at those things than we are. It will make us obsolete if we are primarily knowledge workers. If we extol the virtues of intellectual humility, charisma, making friends, and pursuing things that we think of as meaningful, however, we can avoid the demoralization that will come if we continue to value intelligence. Human life will change, but the authors are not worried: “Humans are remarkably adaptable. We foraged and farmed, we built factories and spaceships, we wrote prayers, plays, poems, novels, and code. And now? Now we created this,” they say. So why should we think that AI will change human nature?

The language of human nature seems to suggest that we are not adaptable. We crave hierarchy, status, and connection to others, according to Balwit and Cowen. It seems that AI will not change these facts about us. Instead of finding status in being smart, getting good grades, or owning expensive things, however, we might find that we seek status in having friends or being humble. But, they warn, this is not the only possible outcome: we also might find that we compete more with others on the basis of physical strength, physical attributes, or on the quality of our AI companions. Our cravings are part of our natures, but how we satisfy those cravings is adaptable. Our future measures of status might look as strange to us now as our present measures might have looked to a person living 300 years ago, the authors say. There are a number of different ways the future might turn out.

Some of this is a debate about nature vs. nurture: how much of what we do is innate and how much is learned? Are we blank slates? Or do we come pre-programmed? Many people have claimed that this is a false dichotomy: that humans might have some characteristics from “nature” that are only potentially expressed, and that “nurture” interacts with “nature” to both elicit that which is natural and, sometimes, to create the natural.

To say that something has a nature is to characterize it as having predictable dispositions to respond in certain ways to repeatable situations. The nature of water is captured both by what it does in a given set of situations and what it is (H2O), with the former being ideally explainable by the latter. But human nature? What is the nature of humans? Are humans different from other things, like animals and machines, that might share some of our dispositions?

The classic response to this question since Aristotle pondered it has been that humans are ‘rational animals’—we are mortal, but we also have the ability to reason. Aristotle actually said that human beings are *zōon logon echon* —beings possessing *logos*; beings that can both reason and use language. These abilities were captured by subsequent theorists as ‘rationality’. But using the possession of rationality as definitive of human nature just seems to defer the theoretical problem. Is rationality reflected in language use? In the ability to think about our own thinking? To think in terms of universals and abstract terms? Often, rationality is glossed as intelligence, and in that case it’s something that can be measured by IQ tests, and represented as an ability to remember and store information. This is the sense in which Balwit and Cowen seem to understand rationality, and if AI is smarter than humans, our claim to rationality is, they assume, also threatened.

In his writings about anthropology, Immanuel Kant said that the greatest concern of human beings is what one must do in order to be a human being—suggesting that the human being is not a being that can be understood independently of what matters to her—and that being a human being is less about what is innate than about what we can become. Unlike the objects of empirical science, like water or rocks, our nature is tied up with what we value and what we strive for. And yet, as Balwit and Cowen suggest, our ideas about what it is to be human must be responsive to a world in which humans are not as smart as the technology we’ve created. The world we have created, they argue, is a world in which human beings might feel demoralized because we are no longer the smartest thing in existence.

Maybe the question to ask is: when and why did rationality become reduced to being smart? In the humanist tradition that gave rise to democratic liberalism, human rationality is not synonymous with smartness. It is the basis for self-governance. It is what allows us to act for reasons, rather than just being compelled to do things. It allows us to think not just about what is good, but about why we think it’s good, and whether we ought to value it.

And so the conclusion that we ought to draw from Balwit and Cowen’s argument is not that AI will change human nature, but that it will make us rethink what we value and why we value it—which is, if we think of humans as rational animals rather than just smart animals, yet another way of being human.

To be human is to worry about what the future holds, for us and for those who will come after us—who will have to live with what we, their predecessors, parents, and grandparents, have brought into being. Maybe being able to predict that future is something that we can use AI for— but maybe to be human is to be concerned about and interested in that future. In that sense human nature won’t be changed by AI.

items.body:
Many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction. It started when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon announced his resignation, warning that his employer and OpenAI were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s head of alignment science, replied, “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” And Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei subsequently told CNN, “I agree with Jacob much more than I disagree with him.”

These concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI). The result will be artificial superintelligence (ASI), a system with cognitive capabilities so vastly exceeding those of humans that it will easily evade our control and perhaps even wipe out our species. Artificial superintelligence is, it should be noted, a far more ambitious goal than artificial general intelligence (AGI), which generally refers to AI that can match human capabilities across a broad range of cognitive tasks.

These ideas have prompted varied reactions. Some argue that the concept of ASI is being used for marketing or to instigate regulation that will help the incumbent labs squash new competitors. Others focus on the plausibility of such systems killing us all, debating the finer points of specific scenarios such as AI-engineered superviruses. Still others claim that aligning ASI to human interests is feasible and so we should rush ahead to usher in this digital utopia.

Amid these conversations, one question has received comparatively little attention: From an engineering perspective, is superintelligence even possible? The answer is important because it can help us calibrate our anxieties and develop the most effective possible responses to this emerging technology.

I recently explored this topic in a computer science doctoral seminar that I taught at Georgetown University, in Washington, D.C., in which my students and I examined the technical and cultural roots of the superintelligence story. (For those who are interested, we published an annotated bibliography of our class readings.) I came away with several key objections to the feasibility of ASI, which I’ll detail below, as well as a deeper fear that even if the promised intelligence explosion never arrives, pursuing it can still create real harm.

Objection #1: Recursive Self-Improvement Is Speculative

RSI is an old concept. In a 1965 paper, statistician I.J. Good speculated that a rapid cycle of AI self-improvement could lead to an “intelligence explosion.” The idea gained traction in the 1990s among the Extropians, a Bay Area futurist group, where it offered a way to discuss ASI without having to address the engineering details of how one would build such a system. The concept was taken up by such notable figures as Eliezer Yudkowsky (who later founded the rationalism movement) and Nick Bostrom (who helped steer effective altruism to focus more on existential risks to humanity).

Recently, however, this topic has shifted from thought experiment to practical engineering within both Anthropic (makers of Claude) and OpenAI (makers of ChatGPT). In a June blog post titled “When AI Builds Itself,” Anthropic described how LLM-powered agents are speeding up the writing, debugging, and optimization of code, and also automating parts of research such as running experiments and logging results. The company’s internal data, the report concluded, “is showing that AI is already accelerating the development of AI systems.” OpenAI has been similarly explicit about its intentions; in a September report, the company announced a goal of developing an automated researcher by March 2028.

But do these efforts put the companies on a trajectory toward uncontrollable RSI? Several obstacles undermine this claim. Consider the availability of the data needed to improve AI systems. Through 2023, major advances in LLMs came from scaling up the size of the models. The original GPT-1 had 117 million parameters (values learned during training that shape how the neural network processes information). This quantity jumped to 1.5 billion for GPT-2, to 175 billion for GPT-3, to (likely) more than a trillion for GPT-4’s release three years ago. After GPT-4, however, continued scaling began yielding diminishing returns. This led engineers to increasingly turn their attention toward “post-training” phases, where techniques from reinforcement learning are applied to improve an already trained model’s performance on specific tasks. This approach rewards a model for producing successful responses, helping it better produce similar answers in the future. It requires, however, lots of examples of relevant inputs paired with correct outputs.

Such datasets are relatively easy to generate in highly structured fields such as computer programming and mathematics, which helps explain why we’ve seen rapid and impressive advances in these narrow domains. Progress in areas that lack easy access to this type of training data has been less dramatic. This might explain why AI can tackle advanced theorems but struggles to empty an email inbox. “What if the jagged frontier is mainly math + code (which you can push arbitrarily far with [reinforcement learning techniques]),” the French AI researcher François Chollet recently hypothesized, “and everything else starts to plateau because it is still bottlenecked by human generated data?” The deployment of automated coding agents and LLM-powered researchers won’t overcome this fundamental limitation.

The Game of Superintelligence

How a decades-old thought experiment became an AI-industry ambition—and where it might lead

Key

• Idea: A concept, argument, or vision

• Technical advance: A scientific or engineering development

• Reality check: A challenge to assumptions about AI progress

1. Alan Turing

1936

Introduces the concept of a universal computing machine. He later proposes that machines could think, laying the foundations for AI.

REALITY CHECK
Shows that some problems can’t be solved by any algorithm.

2. I. J. Good

1965

Proposes that an intelligent machine could design an even smarter one, setting off a potential “intelligence explosion.”

3. Backpropagation

1986

Geoffrey Hinton, David Rumelhart, and Ronald Williams demonstrate how backpropagation can train multilayer neural networks.

4. Vernor Vinge

1993

Proposes that an intelligent machine could design an even smarter one, setting off a potential “intelligence explosion.”

REALITY CHECK
Notes that faster thinking alone isn’t enough for superintelligence: A faster-thinking dog still couldn’t play chess.

items.body:

- [Inquiry](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/inquiry/) by Arianna Falbo, David Thorstad, and Dennis Whitcomb.

UJAM’s Virtual Pianist VIBE is £8 at [Plugin Boutique](https://www.pluginboutique.com/product/1-Instruments/64-Virtual-Instruments/10074-Virtual-Pianist-VIBE/?a_aid=5a86bc628c110), down from its usual £113, a whopping 93% off that runs until December 9.

[deals ids=”39d9f611-9c1b-44be-b007-1c8196a71b33″]

VIBE is a virtual electric piano and session player in one. The sound is based on recordings of a hand-picked 1972 vintage electric piano with warm, mellow, slightly bell-like tones you’ll recognise from decades of soul, jazz, funk and hip-hop records, standing as a staple of modern lo-fi and EDM production.

Play it like a normal instrument, or switch to Player mode, where VIBE performs for you. There are 40 styles to choose from. You trigger phrases with a single finger and controls for busyness, key range and variations stop it from sounding repetitive. Set your song’s key and the plugin plays varied, tailored phrases and harmonies. If you’d rather use the performance on another instrument, MIDI drag and drop lets you take the part into your DAW.

Beyond the core piano, you get over 150 presets, plus 45 Finisher multi-effect modes and 45 Ambience FX presets made for VIBE. Character presets move the tone from warm and bellow to bright and “barkier,” so the same plugin can sit in a neo-soul ballad or a punchy hip-hop beat.

It’s an easy way to get a convincing electric piano part down quickly, whether or not you can play keys and at £8, it’s a low-risk pickup. UJAM also offers a 30-day free demo if you want to try before you buy.

items.body:
**Mit iZotope Nectar 5 bekommt die beliebte Vocal-Suite ein umfassendes Update. Eine der wichtigsten Neuerungen ist Moments: Das Feature erkennt einzelne Wörter innerhalb einer Gesangsphrase und erlaubt deren gezielte Bearbeitung mit individuellen Effekten.**

Das neue Power-Bundle für die kreative Vocal-Bearbeitung: iZotope Nectar 5 – mit dem innovativen Feature „Moments“.

Was bislang nur mit aufwendiger Automation möglich war, soll damit künftig deutlich einfacher werden. Doch wie gut funktioniert das in der Praxis? Und rechtfertigen die Neuerungen den Umstieg von Nectar 4?

## iZotope Nectar 5 Highlights

- Moments ermöglicht die individuelle Effektbearbeitung einzelner Wörter innerhalb einer Vocal-Phrase – ein neuer Industrie-Standard.
- Nectar 5 verfügt über einen Serial-Compressor für die mehrstufige Kompression mit automatischer Pegelkompensation.
- Der Vocal Stabilizer führt zur dynamischen Klangoptimierung, während der Micro-Pitch-Shift Vocals breiter und lebendiger werden lässt.
- Es gibt eine Send-Style-Bearbeitung für Reverb, Delay und Dimension sowie automatisches Ducking, das die Sprachverständlichkeit bei Hall und Delay verbessert.

Falls ihr iZotope Nectar noch nicht kennt: Das Plugin stellt im Grunde ein komplettes Vocal-Tonstudio dar, das zahlreiche spezialisierte Tools unter einer Oberfläche vereint. Der KI-gestützte Vocal Assistant analysiert eure Aufnahme und schlägt passende Einstellungen für die weitere Klangbearbeitung vor – ganz ohne tontechnisches Know-how.

## Welche Versionen gibt es von iZotope Nectar 5?

Anders als den Vorgänger iZotope Nectar 4 gibt es die neue Version nur noch in zwei unterschiedlichen Ausführungen. Das preislich attraktive **Nectar 5 Elements** umfasst den Vocal Assistant, die Overview-Seite sowie grundlegende Parameter für Kompressor, EQ, Pitch und Reverb.

Die Vollversion **Nectar 5** kostet regulär 250 Euro und erweitert den Funktionsumfang vor allem um das neue Feature Moments, die Breath Control, 14 eigenständige Plugin-Komponenten und zusätzliche Bedienelemente auf der Overview-Seite. Übrigens bietet iZotope auch interessante Update- und Crossgrade-Angebote an.

## Welche Neuerungen bringt iZotope Nectar 5 mit?

Wie bereits erwähnt, verdient vor allem das neue Feature Moments besondere Aufmerksamkeit. Damit könnt ihr einzelne Wörter oder ganze Textpassagen gezielt mit unterschiedlichen Effekten versehen. Ohne aufwendige Automation bearbeitet ihr so jedes Wort einer gesungenen Phrase ganz individuell. So lassen sich beispielsweise einzelne Silben oder Wörter mit dekorativen Echos versehen – ein beliebter Trick vieler Producer.

Das neue Feature Moments erkennt Lyrics und erlaubt die gezielte Effektbearbeitung einzelner Wörter.

Auch die mehrstufige Kompression wird mit Nectar 5 zum Kinderspiel. Der Serial Compressor macht die bewährte Mixing-Technik einfacher als je zuvor. Ihr könnt bis zu drei Kompressoren, Limiter oder Clipper hintereinanderschalten und profitiert dabei von einer automatischen Pegelkompensation (Make-up Gain) – das Ergebnis: ein druckvoller, satter Sound ohne störendes Pumpen.

Die Kompression von iZotope Nectar 5 ist im Vergleich zu Version 4 einfacher und besser.

Der Vocal Stabilizer passt die Dynamik und den Klang der Stimme an. Dazu wählt ihr zuerst den passenden Gesangsstil und die Stimmlage aus. Anschließend könnt ihr den Klang gezielt formen und störende Resonanzen dynamisch reduzieren – auch dann, wenn sich die Vocal-Performance im Verlauf verändert. Die Intensität legt ihr über mehrere Frequenzbänder individuell fest.

Neben der Kompression trägt auch der Vocal Stabilizer zu einem gleichmäßigen, präsenten Vocal-Sound bei.

## Was hat sich bei den Effekten getan?

Nectar 5 erweitert die Möglichkeiten zur räumlichen Gestaltung der Vocals. Dafür hat iZotope das Dimension-Modul um den Modus Micro Pitch Shift ergänzt: Er verbreitert die Gesangsstimme durch dezente Tonhöhenverschiebungen und verleiht ihr dadurch mehr räumliche Tiefe.

Mehr Lebendigkeit im Handumdrehen: der Micro Pitch Shift von Nectar 5.

Ebenfalls praktisch ist der neue Wet-Level-Modus in den Modulen Reverb, Delay und Dimension. Er verwandelt den Dry-/Wet-Regler in eine send-ähnliche Steuerung. Damit fügt ihr gezielt räumliche Effekte hinzu und behaltet das vollständige trockene Gesangssignal bei.

Die automatische Ducking-Funktion verhindert indessen, dass die Nachklänge von Reverb und Delay die folgenden Textpassagen überdecken – was insbesondere der Sprachverständlichkeit zugutekommt. Außerdem lassen sich alle Effekte mithilfe neuer 3-Band-Filter gezielt klanglich anpassen. Hochpass und Tiefpass könnt ihr dabei mit individuell einstellbaren Flankensteilheiten anpassen.

Automatisches Ducking bei Reverb und Delay – eine äußerst praktische Zugabe.

items.body:
### 🎮 GTA VI breaks record with $3.8B first day

[↗ Primärquelle: business-standard.com](https://www.business-standard.com/technology/tech-news/gta-vi-generates-3-79-bn-becomes-biggest-entertainment-launch-ever-126112100066_1.html)

- Grand Theft Auto VI pulled in $3.79 billion in its first 24 hours, the most ever for an entertainment release, with developer Rockstar Games selling 32.5 million copies before the game even launched.
- The one-day total is nearly five times the roughly $800 million GTA V made on its first day in 2013, and it tops "Avengers: Endgame", the highest-grossing film ever at about $2.94 billion worldwide.
- Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar's parent, spent an estimated $1 billion or more making the game, and a longer trailer released through Netflix in August drove a sixfold jump in pre-orders, according to Sensor Tower.

### 📺 YouTube nears $3B deal in school addiction suits

[↗ Primärquelle: gizmodo.com](https://gizmodo.com/youtube-reportedly-nearing-multi-billion-settlement-with-school-districts-over-social-media-addiction-harms-2000843341)

- Google's YouTube is close to a settlement that could reach $3 billion with school districts that sued the video site, claiming it was deliberately built to be addictive with no concern for teenagers' mental health.
- The money would be divided among thousands of districts, so each could get around $1 million if split equally; the schools say YouTube's design pushed them to pay for extra counseling and mental health programs.
- Bloomberg says this would be the largest-ever corporate settlement with U.S. school districts, though $3 billion is under 1% of Alphabet's yearly revenue, and YouTube also promised new, unspecified safeguards as part of the deal.

### 🔍 SEC opens probe into Nvidia's accounting

[↗ Primärquelle: cryptopolitan.com](https://www.cryptopolitan.com/us-sec-civil-probe-into-nvidias-accounting/)

- The US Securities and Exchange Commission has opened a civil investigation into whether Nvidia misled investors about its accounting, though the chipmaker has not been accused of breaking any laws, Reuters reported.
- News of the probe helped push Nvidia shares down nearly 14% on Friday, erasing about $485 billion in a single day and roughly $2.7 trillion since the stock peaked on October 6.
- Scrutiny centers on Nvidia's $104 billion in Singapore sales last year, nearly half its revenue, plus a delayed quarterly report and customer Megaspeed, which US officials suspect of rerouting Nvidia chips to China.

### 🔓 FBI investigating apparent breach of crime database

[↗ Primärquelle: thenextweb.com](https://thenextweb.com/news/fbi-ncic-crime-database-breach-usda-hack)

- The FBI is investigating an apparent break-in at its National Crime Information Center, the NCIC database that police across the US rely on to check warrants and run background checks, CNN and NBC News reported yesterday.
- The NCIC connects federal, state and local agencies so that crime records are shared nationwide, and a former FBI official told CNN that the accuracy of those records is now in question, not just their privacy.
- Officials learned of the incident on Thursday, the same day Director Kash Patel went on Fox News to promote Operation Winter Shield as if it were ongoing, though CNN said that cybersecurity effort had actually ended months earlier.

### 🏭 Trump threatens tax on data centers built abroad

[↗ Primärquelle: cnbc.com](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/20/trump-data-centers-ai-companies-tax.html)

- President Donald Trump said yesterday that U.S. companies will be banned from building data centers abroad or face what he called a "tremendous tax," a policy he admitted he hadn't even told his own staff about.
- The threat runs into a problem: Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta, and Oracle have already built data centers in other countries, often to sit close to clients or meet local rules on where data must stay.
- Trump pitched the plan as a way to pull construction back home, even as a CNBC survey found 64% of registered voters oppose an AI data center within 10 miles of their house, with only 13% in favor.

### 🌍 Meta rethinks climate goal as AI emissions soar 45%

[↗ Primärquelle: arstechnica.com](https://arstechnica.com/ai/2026/11/meta-reconsiders-2030-net-zero-goal-amid-record-emissions-from-ai-data-centers/)

- Meta is reconsidering its promise to reach net-zero emissions by 2030 after its greenhouse gas pollution jumped 45% in a year, the largest increase among Big Tech companies building new AI data centers.
- In its 2026 sustainability report, released on Thursday, Meta said the demand for AI infrastructure grew faster than almost anyone expected, forcing it to re-evaluate its timelines, interim milestones, and near-term targets.
- Meta's total emissions rose from 15.6 million metric tonnes in 2024 to over 21.7 million in 2025, roughly matching Idaho's footprint, with much of the jump tied to data center servers and other capital goods.

items.body:
Die Wendung „Noch bei Trost?“ changiert zwischen „Bist du noch bei Trost, hast du sie noch alle?“ und „Findest du noch Trost – in Zeiten, die vielen trostlos erscheinen, in denen Gewissheiten wegbrechen, die man für tragfähig gehalten hatte?“ Für einen Theologen verdichtet sich im Trost der Sinn von Religion: Mit „Tröstet, tröstet mein Volk“ setzt das biblische Hoffnungsbuch par excellence, Deuterojesaja, ein (Jes 40,1), und einer der wichtigsten Texte der Reformationszeit, der Heidelberger Katechismus von 1563, beginnt mit der präambelartigen Frage: „Was ist dein einziger Trost im Leben und im Sterben?“ Gerade weil das Trost-Motiv so stark ist, kennt es aber Kipppunkte: Trost kann zur Vertröstung verkommen, zum Sedativum, das unruhige Fragen erstickt, statt sie auszuhalten. Vielleicht hat Emmanuel Levinas deshalb konstatiert, Philosophie könne nicht trösten – und, anders als Boethius, wohl auch gemeint: Sie soll es auch nicht. Was für die Philosophie gilt, gilt erst recht für die Wissenschaft. Warum aber diese Frage in einem Gedankengang zu Wissenschaft und Wissenschaftsfreiheit? Weil unsere Gesellschaft im Umgang mit den vielbeschworenen Polykrisen – ein Pleonasmus, aber sei’s drum – zumindest drei gefährliche Signaturen trägt, die auf unser Verständnis von Wissenschaft durchschlagen: erstens Polarisierung, die einfache Antworten emotionalisiert in die mediale Öffentlichkeit spült, damit zweitens Politisierung bewirkt, weil so Zugehörigkeiten via Identitätsmarker verteilt werden, und drittens Künstliche Intelligenz, die beschleunigt, was ohnehin zu schnell war, und die, als soziotechnisches System begriffen, eine Machtfrage darstellt und die Gefahr der Selbstentmündigung birgt. Um diesen Herausforderungen für Gesellschaft wie Wissenschaft nicht gänzlich schutzlos ausgeliefert zu sein, schlage ich konzeptionell vor, Wissenschaftsfreiheit mit Axel Honneth als soziale Freiheit zu begreifen und zu ihrer Umsetzung ein Set von fünf Governance-Perspektiven zu beherzigen, unter denen der Bildung für Wissenschaftlerinnen und Wissenschaftler die zentrale Bedeutung zukommen müsste.

## Die produktiven Enttäuschungen der Wissenschaft

Wenn gegenwärtig über den Status von Wissenschaft und deren Freiheit debattiert wird, fokussiert sich der innerwissenschaftliche Diskurs auf die Strukturfragen des Systems – sattsam bekannt, aber noch immer viel zu selten ernsthaft angepackt: Grund- versus Drittmittelfinanzierung, prekäre Karriereaussichten der Nachwuchswissenschaftler, das heiß gelaufene Peer-Review-Verfahren in einem zunehmend von Großverlagen beherrschten Publikationswesen, ganz zu schweigen von der Unterfinanzierung des Normalbetriebs. Dass all das mit der Qualität und Freiheit von Wissenschaft zu tun hat, leuchtet sofort ein: Wer um Drittmittel kämpft, ist anfälliger für Aufmerksamkeitslogiken, und wer befristet arbeitet, für vorauseilende Anpassung. Um Wissenschaftsfreiheit zu verteidigen, muss der Blick dennoch über die internen Problemlagen hinaus geweitet werden.

Zuvor aber ist zu klären, was gefährdet ist, wenn von Wissenschaft und Wissenschaftsfreiheit die Rede ist. Wissenschaft stellt eine methodisch geleitete, institutionalisierte Praxis produktiver Enttäuschungen mit dem Ziel der begründungsfähigen Revision oder Erweiterung des gegebenen Wissens dar. Methodisch geleitet ist Wissenschaft, weil nicht jede Weise der Meinungsbildung schon Erkenntnis hervorbringt. Institutionalisiert ist sie, weil in ihr Erkenntnisgewinnung keine Privatangelegenheit genialer Einzelner ist, sondern auf organisationell eingebettete Kritik und Prüfung angewiesen ist. Begründungsorientiert ist und bleibt sie, weil sich wissenschaftliche Aussagen weder allein durch ihre Urheber noch durch Publikumsresonanz oder politische Erwünschtheit legitimieren. Auf Revision angelegt ist sie, weil sie fehlbar bleibt. Der Motor ihres spezifischen Wirkens aber liegt in der produktiven Enttäuschung. Wissenschaft bewährt sich dort, wo wir bereit sind, unser vermeintliches Wissen enttäuschen zu lassen: durch das Experiment, das die Hypothese widerlegt, durch eine bis dato unbekannte Quelle, die eine etablierte Deutung umstürzt, durch eine Studie, die zeigt, dass eine politisch attraktive Maßnahme nicht wirkt, oder schlicht: durch das bessere Argument, das ich zulasse. Produktiv werden solche Enttäuschungen, wenn wir sie nicht als Kränkung unserer Identität, sondern als Erkenntnisgewinn begreifen. Darin liegt die Zu-Mutung der Wissenschaft, durch die sie sich von all den Kommunikationsformen unterscheidet, die auf Bestätigung, Zugehörigkeit und Aufmerksamkeit setzen. Gerät eine der Dimensionen unter Druck, wird von außen gekapert oder von innen vernachlässigt, droht das fragile Zusammenspiel zu zerbrechen: Methode ohne Enttäuschungsbereitschaft wird zur unkreativen Routine; lebendige Arbeitsgruppen drohen zu machtverwaltenden Institutionen zu verkommen; und – wer im Wissenschaftssystem kennt es nicht? – Fortschritts-, Innovations- und Exzellenzrhetoriken bedienen eher Aufmerksamkeits- und Finanzierungsspiele denn melioristischen Erkenntnisgewinn.

## Wissenschaftsfreiheit – dreifach gedacht

„Kunst und Wissenschaft, Forschung und Lehre sind frei“ – Art. 5 Abs. 3 GG hat nach den Erfahrungen der gleichgeschalteten Universität im Nationalsozialismus den Weg in die Verfassung zuerst als Abwehrrecht gegen den Staat gefunden. Seit dem Hochschulurteil von 1973 (BVerfGE 35, 79) wird ihm eine organisatorische Gewährleistungsdimension beigemessen: Der Staat hat nicht nur die Finger wegzulassen, sondern freie Wissenschaft organisatorisch zu ermöglichen. Das ist wichtig, reicht aber, so meine These, nicht hin, um zu verstehen, was gegenwärtig auf dem Spiel steht.

Hilfreich ist eine Anleihe bei [Axel Honneth](https://www.suhrkamp.de/buch/axel-honneth-das-recht-der-freiheit-t-9783518585627). Er fügt der bekannten Unterscheidung [Isaiah Berlins](https://global.oup.com/ukhe/product/liberty-9780199249893?cc=de&lang=en&) zwischen negativer Freiheit („Freiheit wovon?“) und positiver („Freiheit wozu?“) eine dritte hinzu, die er als eigentlich anspruchsvolle identifiziert: die soziale Freiheit. Sie gewinnt man nicht allein, sondern nur im Konzert mit anderen, sprich: in Praktiken wechselseitiger Anerkennung. Bei [Hegel](https://meiner.de/fmv_de/grundlinien-der-philosophie-des-rechts-15669) verwirklicht sie sich in Familie, bürgerlicher Gesellschaft und, nun ja, dem preußischen Staat. Bei Honneth wird diese Trias moderner reformuliert: in persönlichen Beziehungen, einer sozial eingebetteten Marktwirtschaft und der Dialektik von Rechtsstaat und demokratischer Öffentlichkeit.

items.body:
**Winzige Hohlkugeln geben Einblick in die Fortbewegung von Bakterien unter beengten Bedingungen. Im Inneren der Mikrokapseln entstehen charakteristische Schwimmbahnen, an denen sich sogar verschiedene Bakterienarten unterscheiden lassen. Für das Süßwasserbakterium Caulobacter crescentus erweist sich dabei das Rückwärtsschwimmen als besonders nützlich: Es erleichtert ihm den Weg aus der Enge.**

In den Mikrokapseln zeigt das Bakterium drei Schwimmweisen: Es gleitet an der Innenwand entlang, bewegt sich mit kurzem Wandkontakt besonders schnell oder schwimmt rückwärts in engen Schleifen © Saurabh Lab/NYU

**New York (U.S.A.).** Viele Bakterien bewegen sich mithilfe von Geißeln fort. Diese fadenförmigen Strukturen rotieren wie Propeller und ermöglichen es den Einzellern, durch Flüssigkeiten zu schwimmen. In ihrer natürlichen Umgebung steht den Mikroben aber längst nicht immer genügend Platz für freie Bewegungen zur Verfügung.

Ob in Bodenporen oder im Gewebe eines Wirts: Bakterien müssen sich häufig in winzigen Hohlräumen zurechtfinden. Unter dem Mikroskop ist dieses Verhalten schwer zu erfassen: Frei schwimmende Einzeller verlassen schnell das Sichtfeld, während das Fixieren auf Glas ihre Bewegungsfreiheit einschränkt.

### Mikrokugeln mit winziger Öffnung

Um die Bewegungen einzelner Bakterien unter räumlich beengten Bedingungen zu beobachten, haben Forscher der New York University (NYU) um Prof. Stefano Sacanna spezielle Mikrokapseln entwickelt. Die Hohlkugeln sind fünf bis zehn Mikrometer groß und besitzen jeweils eine Öffnung von rund einem Mikrometer Breite.

Durch diese Öffnung können Bakterien in die Kapseln hineinschwimmen und in deren Innerem schwimmen. Mithilfe eines herkömmlichen Lichtmikroskops lässt sich ihre räumliche Position aus der Unschärfe der Aufnahmen rekonstruieren. Dadurch können die Wissenschaftler die dreidimensionalen Schwimmbahnen einzelner Zellen auch ohne Farbstoffe über längere Zeit verfolgen.

### Rückwärts durch den Engpass

Bei den Experimenten mit dem in Seen und Flüssen vorkommenden Bakterium Caulobacter crescentus ließen sich drei charakteristische Bewegungsmuster unterscheiden. Beim Vorwärtsschwimmen mit nach hinten gerichteter Geißel gleiten die Mikroben entweder dicht an der gekrümmten Innenwand entlang oder bewegen sich besonders schnell, während nur ihre Vorderseite die Wand berührt. Schwimmen sie dagegen mit der Geißel voraus, ziehen sie enge Schleifen.

Doch gerade dieser Rückwärtsgang ist für das Verlassen der Kapseln von Vorteil. Weil die Geißel beim Rückwärtsschwimmen dem Zellkörper vorausliegt, kann sie leichter in die kleine Öffnung gelangen. Mutanten von Caulobacter, die nicht rückwärts schwimmen können, benötigten in den Experimenten mehr als doppelt so lange zum Verlassen der Mikrokugeln.

Damit kommt der Geometrie der Umgebung eine entscheidende Rolle zu. Denn auch die Größe der Öffnung und das Verhältnis von Kammer- und Bakteriengröße beeinflussen, wie die Einzeller hinein- und hinausgelangen und wie lange sie in einem bestimmten Bewegungsmodus bleiben.

### Schwimmbahnen verraten die Bakterienart

Wie die Versuche mit zwei weiteren Bakterienarten zeigen, hängt das Schwimmverhalten in den Kapseln auch vom Antrieb der Mikroben ab. So bewegen sich Caulobacter und der Krankheitserreger Pseudomonas aeruginosa durch den Innenraum der Kugeln, während sich Escherichia coli vorwiegend an der Innenwand entlangbewegt. Anhand der jeweiligen Schwimmbahnen lassen sich die drei untersuchten Bakterienarten voneinander unterscheiden.

Künftig könnte die Methode helfen, besser zu verstehen, wie Bakterien räumlich begrenzte Lebensräume in ihrem Wirt besiedeln. Auch der Einsatz der Mikrokapseln zur Unterscheidung von Krankheitserregern ist denkbar. Ob sich die Methode dafür unter klinischen Bedingungen eignet, ist jedoch noch offen.

**Quellen:**

- Originalstudie im Fachmagazin [Small](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/smll.76658), doi: 10.1002/smll.76658
