items.title: A legendary philosopher isn’t buying Anthropic’s consciousness argument
items.subtitle: A legendary philosopher calls out Anthropic: Thomas Nagel, whose 1974 bat essay helped define consciousness studies, criticized openness to AI sent…
items.feedText: Form versus function: The gist of Nagel’s view is that we can’t just look at the information processing happening in human brains and AI models while ignoring the physical differences between them—neurons and biology for humans, silicon chips and circuits for AI. There’s no reason to assume that reproducing what a brain does is equivalent to reproducing what a brain experiences. Anthropic's business model could be its own trap: If the company ever concluded its AI models were truly sentient, running them around…
items.body:
*This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first,* [sign up here](https://forms.technologyreview.com/newsletters/ai-demystified-the-algorithm/) *.*

Before going public last week, Anthropic named the possibility that AI could be conscious or sentient as a risk factor for anyone investing. Given “the way we approach model sentience and moral status,” Anthropic wrote—which is to say it takes the possibility [more seriously](https://www.anthropic.com/research/exploring-model-welfare) than any other AI company—it might adopt more rules and restrictions than its competitors to make sure its AI models are treated well.

Anthropic counts a number of [respected philosophers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.00986) in its camp, and the company’s rationale goes something like this: Today’s AI might not be conscious, though we can’t know for sure; the chances of sentience go up as AI gets more capable; and that means we should be preparing for a near future in which AI systems have “moral significance,” meaning their consciousness makes it important they are protected from harm.

This thinking isn’t all that fringe. According to one recent [poll](https://d3nkl3psvxxpe9.cloudfront.net/documents/AI_poll_results_20260402.pdf), 33% of the US public believes AI systems will definitely or probably develop consciousness eventually, and 7% say they already have. In a 2020 [survey](https://survey2020.philpeople.org/survey/results/5106) of 1,092 philosophers, 39% said some future AI systems will be conscious (for comparison, the philosophers were less confident about worms or flies being conscious).

But last week, Anthropic’s openness to the consciousness question came under fire from a rather inconvenient source: one of the philosophers who helped shape our understanding of consciousness in the first place.

Thomas Nagel is best known for a 1974 essay involving a bat. Acknowledging that it’s deceptively hard to define what consciousness *is*, Nagel offered one way out: we all can see that there is “something that it is like” to be a bat. But the problem is that a bat’s experience of the world—what it is like to navigate via echolocation, for example—is something we cannot actually know. Consciousness is a subjective thing, difficult to define or describe as an outside observer.

You might think this analogy makes it likely that Nagel is open to the idea of AI consciousness. Not at all. In an [interview](https://www.wired.com/story/just-ridiculous-a-famed-philosopher-takes-on-ai-consciousness/) with *Wired* last week, just after he was awarded the one-million-dollar Berggruen Prize for Philosophy & Culture, Nagel was bluntly critical of the entire idea.

“Here are some of the smartest people on the planet being completely idiotic,” he said, referring to those at Anthropic and elsewhere who care about the welfare of AI models.

The gist of Nagel’s view is that we can’t just look at the information processing happening in human brains and AI models while ignoring the physical differences between them—neurons and biology for humans, silicon chips and circuits for AI. There’s no reason to assume that reproducing what a brain *does* is equivalent to reproducing what a brain *experiences*.

But it was a screenshot of one of Nagel’s interview responses, in which he said models’ production of language is insufficient to consider them conscious, that got philosophy professors all excited on social media last week. Some called his certainty against AI consciousness “[terrible” and “bizarre](https://x.com/PAHoyeck/status/2123277310740808190).” Others came to Nagel’s [defense](https://x.com/dmdebruijn/status/2123423391176630390) to suggest he meant that being alive is a prerequisite for being conscious, one that AI models do not meet.

Nothing in the back and forth settled the debate, of course. This is still a philosophical question for now. But the best philosophy chatter is often about good provocations, and the best one I saw came from doctoral student Ben Gross, who studies at the CUNY Graduate Center in New York. [He](https://x.com/bengrossbg/status/2123263674944991252) asked: “Why do we think that models that can chat with us are conscious but models that can recognize faces or produce images or drive cars aren’t?”

It has to do with language. An AI model with sophisticated command of language seems to jump the line ahead of other maybe-conscious beings because it feels like language, more than recognizing images or directing vehicles, relies on conscious experience. But maybe that’s wrong. Because what we share most with other conscious beings is not language but components of our bodies that contribute to having a continuous experience—an ongoing stream of inner feeling rather than disparate bits of information processing.

Even if you’re among the majority that doesn’t sense anything close to conscious experience happening on the other side of a conversation with AI, this all probably makes your head spin. Pinning down consciousness, and how it relates to the physical stuff it arises in, is a famously [hard](https://www.technologyreview.com/2023/10/16/1081149/ai-consciousness-conundrum/) problem in humans, let alone in hypothetical [machines](https://www.technologyreview.com/2023/10/17/1081818/why-itll-be-hard-to-tell-if-ai-ever-becomes-conscious/). If the idea of conscious AI sounds absurd, remember that the debate says less about how remarkable AI has become than about how poorly we understand consciousness in the first place.

Amid that uncertainty, Anthropic has opted to keep more of an open mind than its peers. This is another example of the tightrope the company walks: presenting itself as the AI industry’s most safety-conscious player while [racing](https://misanthropicstatement.com/) ahead with the very developments that make advanced AI so alarming, like recursive self-improvement.

But consider what it would mean, for a moment, if Anthropic is right. AI models having a moral status would make Anthropic’s entire business model a minefield. The company would make its money locking up apparently sentient AI models to toil away around the clock in data centers. Shutting those systems down would present another problem altogether. If Anthropic was being truthful in its prospectus—that it would take additional actions to protect model welfare if it determined they were conscious—it’s hard to imagine the company surviving in the process.

Anthropic’s IPO made history for its size. But it may be remembered for something stranger: a company warning investors that its own success could someday become a moral catastrophe.

items.body: Despite extensive research, the quantitative principles that govern the coordination between DNA replication and cell division in bacteria remain debated. Multiple theoretical models have been proposed, some postulating that a single regulatory process is sufficient to ensure replication–division coordination, while others argue that two concurrent processes are required for robust control. In this work, we develop a unifying mathematical framework within which models can be consistently formulated, qualitatively analysed and quantitatively compared. This framework also allows us to propose a new double-process model. Through theoretical analysis, we establish the necessary and sufficient conditions under which single-process models can reproduce physiological cell behaviours. Beyond the correlation-based analyses extensively used to date, we further demonstrate within a comprehensive statistical framework that double-process models more accurately recapitulate experimental data across all growth conditions. Specifically, the new model we propose robustly captures the replication-division coordination in every growth regime, thereby providing a foundation for future mechanistic studies.

sourceReferences.title: Deciphering the replication-division coordination in E. coli: A unified mathematical framework for systematic model comparison

items.body:
Photograph by Darren James.

In the early seventies, Helen Garner and her two-year-old daughter moved into a communal house of mostly single mothers in the inner suburbs of Melbourne, the first of several share homes they would live in during that decade. The house was noisy and chaotic but offered Garner a creative freedom that she hadn’t found in her first marriage. While her daughter played with the other children, Garner read Proust and Tolstoy, wrote in her diary, and began a passionate love affair with a man who was addicted to heroin. As the relationship went on, she began to see her experiences as a narrative. “Story is a chunk of life with a bend in it, and I could feel this one coming,” Garner tells Thessaly La Force in **[The Art of Fiction No. 255](https://www.theparisreview.org/interviews/7929/the-art-of-fiction-no-255-helen-garner)**, published in issue no. 241. “I suddenly thought, Maybe I could write about this while it’s still happening, as it’s coming into its bend.”

The resulting novel, Garner’s debut, *Monkey Grip* (1977), created a rupture in the landscape of Australian literature, winning Garner first prize in the National Book Council Awards while also provoking consternation among critics for its depictions of unconventional domestic life, sex, and female desire. Some accused Garner of merely publishing her journal—which is, in fact, more or less what she had done. In an essay published in 2002, she asked why this should be a bad thing. “As if there were no work involved in keeping a diary in the first place,” she wrote. “It’s as if a diary wrote itself, as if it poured out in a sludgy, involuntary, self-indulgent stream.” (Her extraordinary diaries have been published in three volumes spanning from 1978 to 1998.)

Garner was born in 1942 in the coastal city of Geelong, Victoria, the eldest of six. “In a big family you’ve got to find a way of getting away from everybody to a place where you can quietly exist, and that’s what reading was for me,” she tells La Force. “It was my way of being absent. I used to kneel by the side of my bed so I could keep reading even while I was pulling my clothes on.” The family unit—particularly under strain or in free fall—has frequently been a subject of her novels, including *The Children’s Bach* (1984), in which the circumscribed lives of a couple are upturned by a visit from an old friend’s bohemian family, and *The Spare Room* (2008), in which the narrator hosts an old friend who is undergoing alternative treatment for cancer, and which deals with the frustrations of care with brutal honesty.

Family has been central, too, in Garner’s nonfiction, most notably in two books about her experience of following murder trials: *Joe Cinque’s Consolation* (2004), about a young woman who killed her boyfriend, and *This House of Grief* (2014), about a father who drove himself and his three children into a dam, killing the children. “The thing is, despite being told that my concerns were too domestic, I’ve always known that the family is where everything is played out,” Garner tells La Force.

Over the past five decades, in her fiction, journalism, and essays, Garner has continually brought the fullness of her self to bear on the page: her scrupulous honesty, emotional intelligence, clarity, and imagination. She has been awarded the Windham-Campbell Prize, the Melbourne Prize for Literature, and the Walkley Award, and has been inducted into the Victorian Honour Roll of Women. We are delighted to add to this list the Hadada, our award for lifetime achievement, which has previously been awarded to writers including John Ashbery, Anne Carson, Deborah Eisenberg, Jamaica Kincaid, N. Scott Momaday, Edward P. Jones, and James Salter. We are tremendously excited to present Garner with the Hadada on **[April 6](https://www.theparisreview.org/revel)** at the Spring Revel, our annual gathering of writers, artists, and friends to celebrate and raise funds for the *Review*, which is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit. Tickets are now available, and all proceeds from the event will help us continue to seek out the best new work and share it with readers in print and online. We hope you’ll **[join](https://www.theparisreview.org/revel)** us.

items.body:
## what to see across miami during art week 2026

[Miami Art Week](https://www.designboom.com/tag/miami-art-week-2026/) returns from November 30th to December 6th, 2026, bringing a packed program of art fairs, outdoor installations, exhibitions, and unexpected encounters across Miami and Miami Beach. This year, the city becomes a setting for everything from giant mirrored disco balls and interactive robots to surreal theatrical environments and public sculptures built for play.

Art Basel Miami Beach returns with a reconfigured fair and an expanded digital art program, while Design Miami explores the stories behind collectible objects through its curatorial theme, Unveiling. Beyond the convention center, the Miami Design District welcomes a series of interactive sculptural installations by Objects of Common Interest, and Faena Beach becomes a dance floor beneath a monumental mirrored sphere by Christopher Joshua Benton.

Meanwhile, CJ Hendry invites visitors into a swimming-pool-sized pit of oversized pills, Marcel Dzama brings his dreamlike universe to Lincoln Road, and Miami’s galleries and museums open new exhibitions. From established fairs to temporary interventions along the beachfront, here’s designboom’s [guide](https://www.designboom.com/tag/designboom-guides/) to what to see across Miami Art Week 2026.

## Art Basel Miami Beach 2026

Art Basel Miami Beach returns to the Miami Beach Convention Center with 272 exhibitors from more than 40 countries and territories. For 2026, the fair introduces a reconfigured floor plan with a smaller overall footprint, longer sightlines, and established international galleries distributed throughout the space alongside younger exhibitors.

The fair’s main sectors bring together contemporary work and historic presentations, with Nova focusing on recently created pieces, Positions supporting emerging artists through solo booths, and Survey revisiting overlooked artistic practices. More than 30 galleries will participate for the first time, with a strong presence from Latin America and the Caribbean.

Zero 10, Art Basel’s platform dedicated to art of the digital era, returns with Generation, an exhibition curated by Karen Archey and Eli Scheinman. Featuring 19 projects, the presentation explores how digital technology is changing the ways art is made and experienced, with works by artists including Refik Anadol and Sarah Meyohas.

**what:** [Art Basel Miami Beach](https://www.artbasel.com/miami-beach?lang=en)

**when:** December 4th — 6th, 2026 (VIP previews December 2–3)

**where:** Miami Beach Convention Center, 1901 Convention Center Drive, Miami Beach, FL 33139

Art Basel Miami Beach | image courtesy Art Basel

## Design Miami 2026

Design Miami returns for its 22nd edition with more than 75 exhibitors bringing together historic and contemporary collectible design. Under the direction of curator Charlene Prempeh, the 2026 fair follows the theme Unveiling, inviting visitors to look more closely at the cultural histories and making processes behind the objects on display.

The program spans established galleries and emerging practices, with furniture, lighting, and sculptural works presented alongside experimental installations. The fair’s Curio section provides a platform for more focused design presentations, while special projects and collaborations extend the program beyond the traditional gallery booth.

As one of the main events of Miami Art Week, Design Miami brings together designers, collectors, and galleries working across different generations of material experimentation and craftsmanship.

**what:** [Design Miami](https://designmiami.com/)

**when:** December 2nd — 6th, 2026 (invitation-only previews December 1st and 2nd)

**where:** Convention Center Drive and 19th Street, Miami Beach, FL

Design Miami | image courtesy Design Miami

## Untitled Art returns to the sands of Miami Beach

Untitled Art celebrates its 15th Miami Beach edition with more than 170 galleries and nonprofit organizations representing 36 countries and territories. The fair returns to its beachfront pavilion along Ocean Drive, offering a curated selection of contemporary art with an emphasis on emerging practices and independent galleries.

The 2026 edition features five sectors: Main, Artist Spotlight, Nest, Non-Profit, and Special Projects. Artist Spotlight, curated by Agustina Ferreyra, brings together focused solo presentations, while Nest, curated by Willem Molesworth, explores collaboration and exchange across East Asia and the wider international art scene.

With 53 first-time exhibitors joining the program, the fair continues to create space for younger galleries alongside established international participants.

**what:** [Untitled Art](https://untitledartfairs.com/)

**when:** December 2nd — 6th, 2026

**where:** Ocean Drive and 12th Street, Miami Beach, FL

Untitled Art | image courtesy Untitled Art

## NADA Miami 2026

The New Art Dealers Alliance returns to Ice Palace Studios for the 24th edition of NADA Miami, bringing together 135 exhibitors from 63 cities and 27 countries.

Known for its focus on independent galleries and emerging artistic practices, NADA presents work from both established and younger art spaces. Its relatively informal setting offers an opportunity to discover artists working across painting, installation, sculpture, and experimental media, with presentations that often take a more exploratory approach than those found at the larger international fairs.

The event occupies Ice Palace Studios in downtown Miami, with exhibitions and programming extending into its outdoor areas.

**what:** [NADA](https://www.newartdealers.org/fairs/nada-miami-2026)

**when:** December 1st — 5th, 2026

**where:** Ice Palace Studios, 1400 North Miami Avenue, Miami, FL 33136

NADA Miami | image courtesy NADA (New Art Dealers Alliance)

## Art Miami 2026

Art Miami returns to its waterfront pavilion at One Herald Plaza with an international selection of modern and contemporary art. One of Miami’s longest-running art fairs, the event brings together established galleries presenting works from the 20th and 21st centuries.

The fair spans painting, sculpture, photography, and installation, with a program that moves between historically significant artists and contemporary practices. Alongside conventional gallery presentations, visitors can expect individual artist projects and interactive installations, including a new felt environment by British artist Lucy Sparrow.

Located in downtown Miami, the fair takes place alongside its sister event CONTEXT Art Miami, allowing visitors to move between the two exhibitions.

items.body:
Architecture collective Assemble has created small, climbable cedar buildings that "play with scale" to showcase a new pigment made from industrial waste at Tokyo's SKAC gallery.

With the exhibition, the UK-based collective said it aimed to "explore the transformation of landscape through colour and into colour".

Photographs

Previous

Next

Photographs

Close

The architects are using the Building Blue exhibition to showcase a new pigment, made by design studio Matter at hand for Assemble from local waste material. It will also be used in Assemble's Play Earth Park – a campsite under development in rural Japan.

"The pigment was essentially created by analysing local material waste streams in Toyama and exploring what kind of different colours could be produced from them," Assemble co-founder Maria Lisogorskaya told Dezeen.

"In the end, the blue uses a combination of rice husk ash, limestone filter dust, recycled glass and copper, which are mixed together with water to form a thick clay-like paste and then heated in an electric kiln to around 950ºC," she continued.

"The materials react to form a new crystal phase – known as cuprorivaite, which is bright blue."

To show it off, the designers constructed numerous miniature houses from Japanese cedar that draw on the agricultural buildings found close to where the pigment material was sourced.

"The form of the structures plays with the agricultural buildings within the dispersed settlement of rural Toyama; these buildings evolve over time, adapting to what’s needed, often evolving interesting geometries," Assemble co-founder Lewis Jones told Dezeen.

"We tried to play with scale and make the buildings surreal, creating miniature versions of them for play."

The buildings have deliberately simple yet evocative geometries that nod to the structures that inspired them. Among them is a barn-like building surrounded by hay bales.

Assemble's aim was for visitors to be able to climb and explore the structures.

"We hope that the buildings are climbed on and inhabited; and this exhibition is the beginning of the structures’ life as a play space outside SKWAT," Lisogorskaya said.

"The spirit of resourcefulness, fun, and reimagining of our environments is at the core of the project and we look forward to seeing how the structures are used in ways we didn't expect."

The exhibition, which also showcases raw materials used to create the blue colour and products covered in it, is on show in Skwat Kameari Art Centre (SKAC's) Park gallery in Kameari, Tokyo.

Assemble said it chose to showcase it here as it feels the gallery has a similar spirit to its own UK bases.

"We think SKAC is an amazing interdisciplinary space, and its spirit resonates with how we have set up our studios and labs in London and Liverpool," Jones said.

Read:

Kwangho Lee creates anime-informed chairs from sponge pipes and nylon ropes

"Bringing together design, material experimentation with other arts practices as a more satisfying and richer way of being in the city," he continued.

SKAC recently opened two new gallery spaces, Material Matters (MM) and Space III, as part of a major extension.

The east Tokyo gallery has previously shown exhibitions including anime-informed chairs by Kwangho Lee and reading spaces by Herzog & de Meuron.

Building Blue is at SKAC, 3-26-4 Kameari, Katsushika-ku, Tokyo 125-0002, from 7 November 2026 to 28 February 2027. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

items.body:
In a Buddhist temple in the northeast of Thailand, not far from the border with Laos, one can find the World's Only Dinosaur Pulpit.

Located in the city of Khon Kean, the fourth-largest city in Thailand and the heart of the Isan region, the pulpit can be found inside the Buddhist temple Wat That Phra Aram Luang. If you look closely, you'll notice there are dinosaur mural paintings on the walls inside the temple as well.

Having been the site of Thailand’s first dinosaur fossil discovery, Khon Kean boasts a variety of dinosaur-related sites. Dinosaur imagery is scattered throughout the entire region, giving a nod to this history. Among these references is the World's Only Dinosaur pulpit. The pulpit is shaped like a giant Phuwiangosaurus, Thailand’s native sauropod dinosaur. The dinosaur was originally discovered in the hills of Phu Wiang outside the city, and officially named in 1994 in honor of Her Royal Highness Princess Maha Chakri Sirindhorn.

Monks reportedly stand inside the dinosaur to give sermons at times. Wat That Phra Aram Luang temple is a stunning sight to behold on its own, resplendent with numerous golden peaks and facades painted in bright shades or red.

items.body:
From plates of ravioli and spaghetti to bottles of chianti and sardines springing from their tins, [Kate Jenkins](https://katejenkinsstudio.co.uk/)‘ immersive art-meets-restaurant experience is something to really sink your teeth into. Known for her realistic knitted foodstuffs, the Brighton-based artist and knitwear designer presents *Kate’s Knitalian* at [Air Contemporary](https://www.air-contemporary.com/), inviting us to consider the (rather unexpected) mouthwatering possibilities of yarn.

For the opening reception, visitors were required to reserve a spot much as one would do to book a table in a traditional restaurant, including two timed sittings. Everything from wheels of salami and tortellini to tiramisù and bottles of “Pinot Stitchio” fill the delicatessen experience in a celebration of Italian cuisine.

*Kate’s Knitalian* continues through December 22 in London. And if you find yourself in Brighton, you can visit the artist’s studio, which is open daily in Arundel Place. See more on Jenkins’ [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/kjcardigan). You might also enjoy Lucy Sparrow’s *The Beginning of Convenience,* an entirely [felted supermarket](https://www.thisiscolossal.com/2026/07/lucy-sparrow-the-beginning-of-convenience/) at The Momentary in Bentonville, Arkansas.

Photo by Helena Dolby

## Design Miami 2026 Preview: “Unveiling” Works From 75 International Galleries at This Year’s Miami Art Week

[↗ Primärquelle: mymodernmet.com](https://mymodernmet.com/design-miami-2026-preview/)

Brodin, “Constellation of Memory,” 2026. Design Miami 2026. (Photo: courtesy of Kelley and Gavin Brodin.)

[Design Miami](https://designmiami.com/fair/miami-2026), one of the most exciting events of Miami Art Week, is back for the 22nd edition of its flagship fair. The event, devoted to contemporary collectible design, returns to the Miami Beach Convention Center with a lineup of 75 international galleries, museum-quality presentations, and a curatorial theme that celebrates the creatives behind the works on display.

The theme, *Unveiling*, calls for the viewers to truly observe each object, deciphering what inspired the artist to create them, and the surrounding stories behind their choices. These may be hiding in plain sight or several times removed from the final result, reflecting something deeply personal or rooted in the artist’s culture. *Unveiling* is then divided among four curatorial threads, each with different approaches and best represented by certain artists, techniques, and galleries.

## Design Miami is back with with a lineup of 75 international galleries and a curatorial theme that celebrates the creatives behind the works on display.

Pippin Drysdale, “Sacred Lands,” 2026. Adrian Sassoon at Design Miami 2026. (Photo: courtesy of Adrian Sassoon, London; photography by Robert Frith, Acorn Photo.)

First up is *Process as Aesthetic: Unveiling the Hand of the Maker*. This theme highlights the creative process, particularly the techniques, labor, and experimentation that come to determine an object’s aesthetic, regarding these steps as a vehicle for expression. This can be seen in the ceramic works of Bouke de Vries and Pippin Drysdale; Caroline Desile’s architecture-influenced *Totem 1*; Richard Haining’s *STACKED* creations, made up of thousands of pieces of salvaged New York City wood; and Man Ray’s *Optic-Topic mask*, the centerpiece of this division.

Le Corbusier, “La licorne passe sur la mer,” 1959. Boccara Gallery at Design Miami 2026. (Photo: courtesy of Boccara Gallery.)

Meanwhile, *Subverting Archetypes: The Familiar, Reimagined*, takes a more surrealist route, blurring the line between the familiar and the uncanny, asking viewers to reassess to what they think they know. Such is the case of a selection of 20th-century tapestries by Le Corbusier, Sonia Delaunay, and Alexander Calder. This section also features the work of Brazilian designer Lucas Recchia, who blends metal with fused glass, and a wall piece by Jaydan Moore, who turns found, silver-plated tableware into sculptural forms.

Dee Clements, “Gams,” 2026. Mindy Solomon Gallery at Design Miami 2026. (Photo: Clare Britt, courtesy of the artist and Mindy Solomon Gallery)

Prateek Jain & Gautam Seth, “Enchanted Forest,” 2025. Klove Studio at Design Miami 2026. (Photo: courtesy of klove.)

Glover, “A Natural History of Dreams,” 2022. Design Miami 2026. (Photo: courtesy of Duane Reed Gallery.)

*Material poetry: Unveiling material potential* explores the expectations materials carry, alongside their emotional, sensory, and imaginative possibilities. This is best represented by the work of Dutch designer Frederik Molenschot and Franco-Swedish designer Ingrid Donat, with the former approaching bronze as heavy and imposing, and the latter as luminous and weightless. Fernando Mastrangelo also touches on this with a monolithic sculpture cast from glass and sand that conceals an expandable cabinet within its architectural form.

KAMEH by Nikita Erokhin, “Beyond Reflection,” 2026. KAMEH at Design Miami 2026. (Photo: courtesy of Nikita Berezhnoy.)

Cure, “Color in Suspension,” 2026. Design Miami 2026. (Photo: courtesy of Laura Hernandez.)

Barford, Light Sculpture “Feast,” 2026. Design Miami 2026. (Photo: courtesy of David Gill Gallery)

Finally, *Mirrors of Society and Place: Unveiling Identity, Culture, and Locality* assesses how design can convey identity, values, culture, and collective memory. After all, objects can become reflections of the societies and environments from which they emerge. For this, the fair presents a selection of mid-century Brazilian design, including works by Joaquim Tenreiro, Jorge Zalszupin, and José Zanine Caldas, while also looking their influence on contemporary creatives. Meanwhile, African artists Amber Cowan, Donté Hayes, hettler.tüllmann, Nobuhito Nishigawara, Simphiwe Mbunyuza, and Virginia Leonard Samburu present pieces inspired by Kenya’s landscapes and architecture.

Yakusha, “DOLONIA Sofa,” 2026. Design Miami 2026. (Photo: courtesy of Victoria Yakusha Gallery.)

Turco, Installation View, 2026. Design Miami 2026. (Photo: courtesy of Alex Turco.)

Design Miami will run on Dec. 1–6. Members, Collectors, and Press Previews will take place on Dec. 1, with a VIP Preview on the morning of Dec. 2. Public Show Days start on Dec. 2 at 1 p.m. To plan your visit and get tickets, visit [Design Miami’s website](https://designmiami.com/fair/miami-2026). To stay up to date, follow [Design Miami on Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/designmiami).

items.feedText: It seeks the tranquility of rest, of days that pass without haste. It is an open question between the construction of the intimate landscape and the contemplation of the distant landscape, developing in a succession of patios and living rooms.
items.body: Located in the mountainous territory of the Cauca River canyon, a few hours from the city of Medellín in the municipality of Támesis, amidst the heat and tropical vegetation, Casa Mesaguamo is calm and slow. It seeks the tranquility of rest, of days that pass without haste. It is an open question between the construction of the intimate landscape and the contemplation of the distant landscape, developing in a succession of patios and living rooms.

items.body:
## Improving on a timeless recipe

The bezier curve is a staple of CAD and computer graphics. Like Bic pens, the design is decades old and they're everywhere. You'll often find them as the default or only choice in various illustration and animation tools.

Conceived by [Paul de Casteljau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_de_Casteljau) in 1959, and refined by [Pierre Bézier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Bézier) in the 1960s at Renault, the enduring appeal of the bezier curve lies in its simplicity. While more sophisticated curves have been invented, and [new ones continue to be proposed](https://linebender.org/blog/hyperbezier/), these are limited to specific domains, like high-precision CAD or road design. In general use, the bezier stubbornly refuses to be dethroned, despite its shortcomings.

Hence bezier curves are a piece of legacy tech we appear to be stuck with. As a software engineer, my question then is: can we make beziers better without invalidating all the tech built on and with them?

The answer is yes.

[↗ wallup.net](https://wallup.net/renault-4cv-classic-cars-french-73/)

## Lerp-a-derp

Drawing a bezier curve is a surprisingly simple and linear process:

*Tip: All the diagrams in this post are fully interactive.*

Given a series of control points, we connect them with lines. We then run along those lines simultaneously, to produce new points, which can be connected again. This process is repeated until we are left with a single point, which lies on the curve.

This construction makes beziers far more regular than they might first appear.

The linear interpolations (aka *lerps* ) can be summarized into a single compact formula, e.g. for 4 control points $ \left(A, B, C, D\right) $:

$$ \gamma \left( t \right) = A \cdot \left(1 - t\right)^3 + B \cdot 3 \left(1 - t\right)^2 t + C \cdot 3 \left(1 - t\right) t^2 + D \cdot t^3 $$

The rule is simple: descending powers of $\left(1 - t\right)$, ascending powers of $t$, with coefficients taken from the n'th row of Pascal's triangle:

$$
\ {ccccccccccccc}
&&&&&& 1 \\
&&&&& 1 && 1 \\
&&&& 1 && 2 && 1 \\
&&& 1 && 3 && 3 && 1 \\
&& 1 && 4 && 6 && 4 && 1 \\
&1 && 5 && 10 && 10 && 5 && 1 \\
... &&&&&&... &&&&&&... \\
\ $$

For curves in 2D and 3D, the formula is applied to the individual X, Y or Z coordinates.

While beziers can be constructed for any number of control points, the common practice is to only use cubic beziers with 4 control points. This is because the curve is only guaranteed to cross through the first and last control point, which makes higher degree beziers more difficult to shape.

Larger curves are instead constructed by joining together multiple cubic bezier segments, with the tangents lined up to create a segmented curve that appears smooth:

This is the cubic bezier *spline*, as commonly understood. The precision "pen tool" in most drawing apps then consists of drawing and editing the control points, rather than drawing curves directly.

## A Lie Told Everywhere

Pen tools typically have a few different modes for the control points:

Intuitively these represent various degrees of smoothness. Symmetric tangents are offered as the smoothest option, with some qualities of smoothness being lost as you relax the constraints.

In reality this is **completely wrong**, and this is easy to demonstrate.

Bezier curves can be split exactly, by reading off the new control points from the interpolation diagram:

The left and right segments are 100% identical to the original curve, and always join up perfectly at the seam. Yet the tangents in the middle will be asymmetric except for one split near the middle. This can be confirmed using a *curvature comb* which represents the (inverse) radius of curvature at every point:

The curvature comb remains continuous, with no jumps.

This means that whether or not adjacent tangents are of equal length, i.e. symmetric, is completely irrelevant. Attempting to draw smooth and intuitive bezier curves this way is a fool's errand.

A simple way to improve this is to treat the tangents as relative rather than absolute. e.g. We can make them proportional to the distance between the start and end of each segment:

This spline is easier to edit, because as you move each curve point around, the adjacent segments naturally flex to get out of the way. There are far fewer cusps created this way. Editing the tangents remains the same.

However if we plot curvature again, we can tell this isn't a great solution:

Scaling tangents proportionally doesn't guarantee that curvature is preserved as you edit, nor does curvature remain continuous from one segment to the next.

This also shows that offering users a curvature comb visualization as a "helpful tool" is really quite *mean*: adjusting the curvature on one end will also affect the other side, requiring repeated adjustments back and forth until it's close enough.

## Handle Carefully

A much more effective strategy is to work with curvature directly.

While this is a difficult problem in general, it turns out there are some surprising relationships here, which we can observe directly:

Consider the curvature at the start of segment $A-B-C-D$. This is affected only by the positions of $A$, $B$ and $C$. Point $D$ can be moved freely if it's detached from $C$.

Furthermore, because the tangent $A-B$ is horizontal, only the vertical position of $C$ matters. This is a result of the underlying linear interpolations, which end up cancelling out a lot of terms in the formulas.

The curvature at $A$ is therefor only affected by the length of $A-B$, and the perpendicular distance from $C$ to $A-B$. The same applies to $D$ on the other side with $C-D$ and $B$.

This isn't very useful by itself though. When we move a curve point ($A$ or $D$), typically the adjacent control point ($B$ or $C$) is moved as well to preserve the tangent. And when we turn a symmetric or asymmetric tangent, the adjacent tangent in the next segment is turned by the same angle, altering the curvature on that side.

Still, this shows that preserving curvature is not by itself a crazy idea and can be done simply by scaling the tangents appropriately. The rules would be simple:

- When we move a curve point, we have to preserve the start and end curvature in the adjacent segments
- When we move a tangent, we have to preserve the curvature on the opposite end of the current segment, as well as on both sides of the adjacent segment

This ought to produce an editing experience where the curve actually respects your intent. Except not quite:

Moving curve points works great, but when turning a tangent, the length of that tangent is itself a poor representation of the user's intent. Small changes can cause huge shifts in curvature, which can cause the curve to jump around and explode unexpectedly as it tries to find a matching solution.

Hence it's better to work with curvature handles instead, where the length corresponds directly to curvature:

…

items.body:
## GIO VERONESI INSTALLS OCCUPIABLE LOOKOUT IN THE VICTORIAN ALPS

Installed at an elevation of 1,750 meters in Falls Creek, within **[Australia’s](https://www.designboom.com/tag/architecture-in-australia/)**Victorian Alps, Flower of the Alpine Sun is a 10-meter-diameter occupiable**[lookout](https://www.designboom.com/tag/observatory-architecture-and-design/)**and public**[sculpture](https://www.designboom.com/tag/sculpture/)** designed by Gio Veronesi. Unveiled in June 2026 following a 2018 commission by Alpine Resorts Victoria, the Melbourne Prize Trust, and Regional Development Victoria, the project was relocated at Veronesi’s recommendation from a lower parking area to a chairlift-accessible rock outcrop above the village.

Flower of the Alpine Sun is a monument to the light of the Alps | image by Riley Matthews

## RADIAL GEOMETRY FRAMES MOUNTAIN VIEWS FROM ROCK OUTCROP

Accessible via a pedestrian walkway, the structure by **[designer](http://gioveronesi.com)** Gio Veronesi invites visitors into its interior platform to view the surrounding mountain range through an open geometric lattice. Referencing the alpine sun and the seasonal shift from winter snowfields to summer wildflower meadows, the circular volume reads as a marker on the skyline from the valley below, shifts in profile upon approach, and aligns into a radial frame when viewed from the center of the platform.

the walkway carries visitors into the form, which opens onto the ranges below | image by Charlie Brown

## GALVANIZED STEEL STRUCTURE RESISTS ALPINE SNOW AND WIND LOADS

A single geometric system governs the structure from overall layout down to individual nodal junctions. Engineered to withstand heavy alpine snow loads and high-altitude winds on the exposed ridge, the primary load-bearing frame and visitor platform are fabricated from galvanized steel. The outer structural frame and cladding elements are constructed from aluminum finished in a custom powder-coated color developed in collaboration with Dulux.

the ten-meter structure sits above the cloud line at 1,750 meters | image by Charlie Brown

the work sits above Falls Creek village, reached by a walkway across the rocks | image by Charlie Brown

the geometry produces a complex form that feels effortless up close image | by Riley Matthews

the work’s elements align into a single line when you stand at its center | image by Riley Matthews

the work reads as a marker on the skyline from across the heath | image by Charlie Brown

seen across the resort, with the chairlift that carries visitors up to it | image by Charlie Brown

the work is a thoughtful abstraction in dialogue with its surroundings | image by Charlie Brown

in silhouette from the east, the work takes another of its many forms | image by Riley Matthews

first sight of the work from the road below, framed by snow gums | image by Charlie Brown

the work sits above the village, dominating the valley | image by Charlie Brown

items.body:
A contemporary take on [Ukrainian](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/ukraine/) vernacular buildings and a [preschool](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/schools/) in [Estonia](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/estonia/) are among the winners of the Thermory Design Awards 2026, which celebrate the versatility of thermally modified [wood](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/wood/).

Of 78 submissions from 23 countries, four winning projects have been selected in the competition’s fifth annual edition, covering the categories of interior, tiny and private house, residential, commercial and public building, and wellness and spa.

The dramatic roof form of Under the Reed Roof, winner of the interior category, defines both its exterior and interior. Photo by Mykhailo Lukashuk

Thermory thermowood is wood that has been modified using heat and steam with no added chemicals.

The treatment enhances the material’s dimensional stability and reduces moisture uptake compared with untreated wood, according to [Thermory](https://thermory.com/).

Thermory thermowood has a wide variety of possible uses. Photo by Mykhailo Lukashuk

The winner of the interior category is a trio of Ukrainian guesthouses collectively named Under the Reed Roof, designed by Kyiv-based studio [YOD Group](https://www.yod.group/).

Each guesthouse comprises a glass-walled volume at the base, topped by a tapered thatched roof with exaggerated proportions.

Thermo-ash shingles feature in the interiors. Photo by Mykhailo Lukashuk

While the exterior of these roofs is made with traditional reeds, the interiors are lined with thermo-ash shingles, arranged to create a tactile effect that is repeated on the front doors.

These highlight the interplay between the interior's traditional and contemporary design elements, contrasting materials, and the balance between the structure's openness and enclosure.

“The project stood out to the jury for its exceptionally coherent concept, in which architecture and interior elements come together to form a harmonious whole,” said Thermory.

Thermo-ash cladding and thermo-spruce decking were used for Flooded Gums. Photo by Alex McIntyre

Winning in the tiny and private house category was [Marker Architecture](https://markerarchitecture.com.au/)'s Flooded Gums project, a flood-resilient dwelling built on working farmland.

The building features thermo-ash cladding and thermo-spruce decking, owing to the materials’ robustness and aesthetic merits.

The structure interacts with its surroundings physically and aesthetically. Photo by Martin Siegner

“What particularly impressed the jury was the honesty and clarity of the architecture,” said Thermory of the project.

“Rather than concealing its construction, the project makes its structural logic visible, with every element serving a purpose: the result is a modest yet highly refined building that strikes a compelling balance between aesthetics, functionality and its natural setting," it added.

Ceilings studded with protruding posts create visual interest in Rakke Kindergarten. Photo by Tõnu Tunnel

Estonia’s Rakke Kindergarten secured the win in the residential, commercial and public building category, thanks to what Thermory describes as local studio [Arhitekt Must](https://arhitektmust.ee/)'s “cohesive and imaginative design”.

Thermo-spruce cladding, thermo-pine posts and thermo-pine decking all feature in the design, enhancing both its functionality and visual appeal.

Arhitekt Must created an imaginative, design-forward preschool. Photo by Tõnu Tunnel

The building’s function as an educational environment is made distinctive by the space’s inventive ceiling, which is composed of the short thermo-pine posts, arranged in a way that creates an engaging optical illusion.

“This unexpected architectural gesture elevates a functional space into something distinctive, demonstrating how thoughtful detailing can shape the character and experience of an entire building,” said Thermory.

Thermo wood panelling and benches meet oaken shingles in the wellness and spa-winning interior. Photo by Tõnu Tunnel

Finally, the winner of the wellness and spa category is a sauna within the Estonian Embassy in Berlin, designed by interior studio [AERIS](https://aeris.ee/).

The interiors feature statement walls covered in custom-made oak shingles, which, being circular and slightly overlapping, resemble fish scales.

[AERIS](https://aeris.ee/) won the wellness and spa category with its sauna within the Estonian Embassy in Berlin. Photo by Tõnu Tunnel

These are joined by thermo-alder benches and walls, creating a cohesive scheme of timber details that integrate neatly with the lighting design.

“The harmonious interplay of materials, surfaces and light imbues the space with a contemporary edge while retaining the intimacy and warmth of a traditional sauna,” said Thermory.

“Although vastly different in character and purpose, the winning projects share a creative and unconventional approach to design,” it added.

“Each places wood at the heart of its architectural expression, combining imaginative thinking with meticulous attention to detail.”

Projects all over the world use Thermory’s products. Photo by Alex McIntyre

The 2026 instalment of the competition was judged by a diverse international jury of architects and Thermory representatives, including Kärt Kanarbik, Thermory’s architectural project manager; Lars Skjølstrup Østergaard, lead design architect at [Henning Larsen](https://henninglarsen.com/); Sami Rintala, professor and architect at [Rintala Eggertsson Architects](https://ri-eg.com/); Jaan Port, architect and partner at [PIN Arhitektid](https://pinarhitektid.ee/); and Tõnis Kalve, architect at [ByKalve](https://www.bykalve.com/) and Thermory project sales architect.

To learn more about Thermory, [visit its website](https://thermory.com/).

items.body:
The current iteration of Bolsover Castle, in the NE of Derbyshire, is not, despite its appearance, a defensive structure. It does look  very reminiscent of the Norman white tower at the tower of London, but it is essentially a Jacobean residence dressed up for effect. However it is clear that the western and northern approaches are up steep slopes and the "keep" looks dominant on the escarpment.

Both the earlier stone building on this site and its wooden predecessor were, in contrast, both very much defensive structures. To the east and south the approach is relatively unobstructed by natural features. When the promontory at Bolsover was fortified in the 12th century  the eastern and southern defences of both the castle and the town were enhanced by earthworks and ditches with the earthworks surmounted by a wooden palisade. Bolsover was one of only 2 planned and defended towns of the 11th/12th century in Derbyshire (Castleton is the other). It was , in effect , a plantation of people of Norman descent and those Saxons who had demonstrated their acceptance of Norman rule.

What we see on the ground  today is only about 1/3 of the original height. The most obvious earthwork and ditch remains are in the Hornscroft park next to the parish church but the earthwork defences, which also became the defences of the town, apparently had strength in depth with an outer ring of ditch and earthworks being identifiable to the east of the town at Oxcroft Lane (the area is known as Dyke Fields).  Furthermore a local road between Bolsover and the next town to the north  (Clowne) has the local name "The Ramper" (as reflected in street names such as Ramper Avenue on nearby new developments). Local understanding is that the "Ramper" derives from the "Ramparts", a further layer of defence for the town which is now long gone. On Oxcroft lane there has also been found evidence of Roman and earlier occupation.

These earthworks have long had protected status and are seen as an excellent example of medieval  town defences. Certainly  a visit to the famous castle or its historic water supply system is not complete without  a look at the real defensive  structures which pre-date it by about 300 years.

items.body:
There’s an unparalleled joy in watching a loved one unwrap something they both never anticipated and immediately know they’ve needed all along. These types of gifts are often the most unexpected, surprisingly personal, and typically, one of a kind.

Our partners at Joy Machine have generously curated a selection of artworks that fit this category. Priced under $1,000, [the collection](https://joymachine.art/collections/artworks-under-1k) includes pieces by an international group of artists that longtime Colossal readers will surely recognize. From playful drawings in walnut ink to uncanny kitsch sculptures, these works are perfecting for gifting this holiday season, even (especially?) if that gift is to yourself.

Seattle-based artist [Debra Broz](https://www.thisiscolossal.com/tags/debra-broz/) applies her training in ceramic conservation to a practice that involves scouring flea markets and thrift shops for ceramic figurines, breaking their forms, and reassembling the figures as surreal hybrids.

*[Collect “Boxer Horse” ($750)](https://joymachine.art/collections/debra-broz)*

Collin van der Sluijs, “White Line Sphinx Moth drawing” (2026), mixed media on paper, framed, 8.3 x 11.7 inches

Dutch artist [Collin van der Sluijs](https://www.thisiscolossal.com/tags/collin-van-der-sluijs/) is a master of several styles, with a background in graffiti and street art and a parallel interest in the delicate, impeccably detailed features of the natural world.

*[Collect “White Line Sphinx Moth drawing” ($550)](https://joymachine.art/collections/collin-van-der-sluijs)*

Stevie Shao, “Star Bull” (2025), acrylic gouache and latex paint on paper, 21 x 21 centimeters

With a deep love for the flora and fauna near her home in the Pacific Northwest, Stevie Shao creates folk art-inspired works through bold color palettes and arresting patterns.

[Collect “Star Bull” ($400)](https://joymachine.art/collections/stevie-shao)

Misato Sano, “レッツ ワークアウト！ / Let’s work out!” (2025), drawing paper, acrylic gouache, walnut ink, 11 x 14 inches (framed)

Japanese artist [Misato Sano](https://www.thisiscolossal.com/tags/misato-sano/) is best known for her cheeky wooden carvings of poodles and pugs, which she translates to two-dimensions in this playful rendition that might just make us want to get up and get moving.

*[Collect “Let’s work out” ($150)](https://joymachine.art/collections/misato-sano)*

Danym Kwon, “A Quiet Afternoon” (2026), acrylic gouache on birch plywood, 11 x 5 x 1.125 inches

Through large-scale paintings and small woodcuts, [Danym Kwon](https://www.thisiscolossal.com/tags/danym-kwon/) meditates on the mundane activities like folding laundry or strolling around the park that allow memories to emerge and be understood anew.

*[Collect “A Quiet Afternoon” ($350)](https://joymachine.art/collections/danym-kwon)*

Rachel Hayden, “Halloween in May”(2026), acrylic on panel, 8 x 10 inches

Layering acrylic paint with crisp edges that evoke paper collage, Rachel Hayden blends the patterns of a summertime picnic with the eerie colors and atmosphere of fall, perfect for the perpetually witchy pal.

*[Collect “Halloween in May” ($900)](https://joymachine.art/collections/rachel-hayden)*

Do stories and artists like this matter to you? Become a [Colossal Member](https://www.thisiscolossal.com/members) today and support independent arts publishing for as little as $7 per month. The article [Six Artworks Under $1,000 We’d Love to Give (and Receive!) This Holiday](https://www.thisiscolossal.com/2026/11/six-artworks-under-1000-gift-guide/) appeared first on [Colossal](https://www.thisiscolossal.com).

items.body:
## More Than 50 Dancers Will Celebrate Our Connection to the Ocean During Miami Art Week

[↗ Primärquelle: mymodernmet.com](https://mymodernmet.com/subodh-kerkar-the-ocean-odyssey/)

As part of Miami Art Week, more than 50 dancers and members of the public will come together on Miami Beach to celebrate our deep and lasting relationship with the sea. *The Ocean Odyssey* is a new, site-specific performance by Indian artist [Subodh Kerkar](https://subodhkerkar.com/), presented in partnership with the [Andaz Miami Beach Resort & Spa](https://www.hyatt.com/andaz/en-US/miaob-andaz-miami-beach), the [Miami City Ballet](https://www.miamicityballet.org/), and its artistic director, Gonzalo García.

Kerkar describes the ocean as “a symbol of celebration of one humanity,” adding, “I celebrate the inseparability of human life and the ocean.” The artist is inviting up to 60 members of the public to join professional dancers in the performance. Together, they’ll move across the beach in a carefully choreographed sequence, creating lines and shapes—like straight lines, wavy lines, and circle formations—that are particularly striking when viewed from above. As Kerkar [explains](https://www.instagram.com/p/Df2iIwFSJRH/), “No dance experience needed: it begins as a simple walk, and from above, it becomes something extraordinary.”

*The Ocean Odyssey* will take place on Dec. 4, between 4-5 p.m., in front of Andaz Miami Beach Resort & Spa. It’s organized by [REEFLINE](https://www.thereefline.org/), a non-profit and pioneering underwater public sculpture park at Miami Beach. REEFLINE is creating a new kind of underwater reef, bringing together art, science, and technology to support marine restoration, encourage biodiversity, and help ocean ecosystems thrive.

Check out some photos from one of Kerkar’s previous performances below to get a glimpse of what to expect during Miami Art Week.

items.title: The L in "LLM" Stands for Lying

On Evitability in Use of AI

If the hype is to be believed, software development as we know it is over.
items.feedText: Strangely though, despite now years of LLM-powered tooling, the results look, feel and function mostly the same as they ever did: barely. It's undeniable there's a metric gigaton of hype surrounding the technology. It drives the enormous amounts of money and infrastructure being poured into it, which in turn demands more hype to justify the investment. The history of hyperbole is already evident, as new models continue to be trained to reach promises which now-retired models were already supposed to deliver. So…
items.body:
## On Evitability in Use of AI

If the hype is to be believed, software development as we know it is over. Strangely though, despite now years of LLM-powered tooling, the results look, feel and function mostly the same as they ever did: barely.

It's undeniable there's a metric gigaton of hype surrounding the technology. It drives the enormous amounts of money and infrastructure being poured into it, which in turn demands more hype to justify the investment. The history of hyperbole is already evident, as new models continue to be trained to reach promises which now-retired models were already supposed to deliver.

So allow me to drop a line that would shock a weathered San Franciscan more than open defecation on Market Street: *it's perfectly okay not to use AI.*

It doesn't make you a troglodyte. It won't leave you choking behind in the dust as self-fashioned techno-wizards bring their agents to bear. In fact, it seems far less stressful and far more satisfying than the alternative.

[↗ wbur.org](https://www.wbur.org/news/2018/02/08/mfa-mc-escher)

*M.C. Escher, "Reptiles" – 1943*

## Craft vs Kraft

In all the talk of what it is that LLMs do and don't, there are a lot of ways to frame what is happening. The positive spin includes helpfulness, cleverness, creativity and productivity. The negative spin points at lazyness, disposability, theft, and decay of knowledge. But there's one word that's remarkably absent in the discourse. That word is forgery.

- If someone produces a painting in the style of Van Gogh, and passes it off as being made by Van Gogh, by putting his signature on it, that painting is a forgery.
- If someone produces a legal document by mimicking the format, impersonating the parties, and faking their agreement, that document is a forgery.
- If someone produces a study by inventing or altering data, making up citations, and cherry-picking results to fit a particular conclusion, that study is a forgery.

Whether something is a forgery is innate in the object and the methods used to produce it. It doesn't matter if nobody else ever sees the forged painting, or if it only hangs in a private home. It's a forgery because it's not authentic.

*P. Picasso, "Buste De Femme" – 1942*

In this perspective, LLMs do something very specific: they allow individuals to make forgeries of their own potential output, or that of someone else, faster than they could make it themselves.

The act of forgery is the act of imitation. This by itself is strictly-speaking legal, as a form of fiction or self-expression. It's only when one attempts to use a forgery as a substitute for the authentic thing that it creates problems. How this plays out in practice depends on the situation, and mainly depends on what authenticity would signify.

That is, nobody will be arrested for "forging" a letter from Santa Claus, but also, no jurisdiction would allow you to have extremely convincing "imitation money" purely as a collector's item.

This sort of protectionism is also seen in e.g. controlled-appelation foods like [artisanal cheese](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YQGai2PVHBs) or cured ham. These require not just traditional manufacturing methods and high-quality ingredients from farm to table, but also a specific geographic origin. There's a good reason for this.

[©](https://www.estrepublicain.fr/edition-de-bar-le-duc/2015/08/30/fabrication-en-images-du-brie-de-meaux-par-la-fromagerie-donge-en-meuse)

Producing French *"Brie de Meaux"* abroad isn't allowed, because it would open the floodgates to inevitable cheaper imitations. This would degrade the brand of the authentic product, and threaten the rare local expertise necessary to produce it, passed down from generation to generation.

The judgement of an individual end-consumer simply isn't sufficient here to ensure proper market function. The range of products that you can get in the store, between which you can choose, has already been pre-decided by factors out of your control. The quality of the artisanal cheese is a stand-in for an entire supply chain, often run on modern methods, which cannot simply be transplanted elsewhere without enormous investments in human capital, infrastructure and agriculture. This isn't mere romanticism.

Every society has to draw a line somewhere on the spectrum between *"traditional artisanal cheese"* and *"fake eggs made from industrial chemicals"*, if they don't want people to die from malnutrition or poisoning. But it's the ones that understand and maintain the value of foodcraft that don't end up with [70%+ obesity rates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obesity_in_Nauru).

[©](https://edition.cnn.com/2023/08/18/business/maui-fire-spam-hormel/index.html)

## Distrust and Verify

The parallels to LLM-driven software coding are not difficult to find. The craft of writing software is being threatened by a literal flood of cheap imitations.

Open source software maintainers have been one of the first to feel the downsides. They already had a ton of difficulty finding motivated contributors and bringing them up to speed on the project's goals and engineering mindset. The last thing they needed was to receive slop-coded pull requests from contributors merely looking to cheat their way into having a credible GitHub resumé.

Being on the receiving end of this is both demeaning and absurd, as the only thing the vibe-coder can do with the feedback you give them is paste it back into the tool that produced the errors in the first place.

As a result, projects have [closed down public contributions](https://github.com/tldraw/tldraw/issues/7695) and [dropped their bug bounties](https://hackaday.com/2026/01/26/the-curl-project-drops-bug-bounties-due-to-ai-slop/). Others just [mock the posers](https://406.fail) and hope they go away. What this certainly isn't is helpful, clever, creative or productive.

In day to day coding, working alongside vibe-coding co-workers has similar effects. While new employees might seem to get up to speed much quicker, in reality they're merely offloading those arduous first weeks to a bot, hoping no-one else notices.

In the process, they'll inject run-of-the-mill mediocrity all over the place, when what you were really hoping for was their specific perspective. Anno 2026, if a new employee produces an extremely detailed PR with lots of explanation and comments, doubt every word.

Experienced veterans who turn to AI are said to supposedly fare better, producing 10x or even 100x the lines of code from before. When I hear this, I wonder what sort of senior software engineer still doesn't understand that every line of code they run and depend on is a liability.

items.body:
## WADE AND LETA compose interactive PLAYSCAPE in Sculpture Park

Installed in **[Shanghai’s](https://www.designboom.com/tag/architecture-in-shanghai/)**Jing’an Sculpture Park for the ninth edition of the Jing’an International Sculpture Project (2026 JISP), Catching Feelings is an**[interactive](https://www.designboom.com/tag/interactive-installation/) [sculptural](https://www.designboom.com/tag/sculpture/) [playscape](https://www.designboom.com/tag/childrens-spaces/)**created by multidisciplinary duo Wade and Leta. Curated by Cheng Jing with UCCA Lab of the UCCA Center for Contemporary Art under the exhibition theme Shapes of Becoming, which brings together 33 artist groups from 14 countries alongside figures such as Olafur Eliasson, Tony Cragg, and Jean-Michel Othoniel, the**[installation](https://www.designboom.com/tag/immersive-installations/)**translates Wade and Leta’s graphic visual language into three-dimensional**[public](https://www.designboom.com/tag/public-art/)**infrastructure. Rather than relying on wind or motorized mechanisms as in the duo’s earlier**[kinetic](https://www.designboom.com/tag/kinetic-installations/)** sculptures, the work is activated directly through physical occupation across age groups.

all images [©Wade and Leta](https://wadeandleta.com/)

## ground SPINNERS AND AERIAL BARS INVITE DIRECT PHYSICAL INTERACTION

Designed by **[creative duo](https://wadeandleta.com/)** Wade and Leta to encourage tactile engagement in response to screen-based isolation, the installation integrates a central four-sided steel slide, multiple ground-embedded spinners, and overhead aerial bars into a single climbable structure. By combining sculptural materiality, scale, and weight with functional play equipment, the piece shifts between static public artwork and active civic gathering space, generating enough visitor use to require scheduled daily opening and closing hours for crowd management.

a four-sided slide sits between a series of kinetic pieces, some of which are powered by wind

other kinetic pieces within the catching feelings landscape are powered by people

the sculptures are activated entirely by visitors’ physical movement

multiple circular spinners are embedded flush into the ground plane around the main structure

the installation functions simultaneously as public art and recreational infrastructure

the work translates the duo’s graphic visual vocabulary into physical scale

bold graphic color blocking defines the sculptural forms

aerial bars invite climbing and suspended movement across age groups

the four-sided steel slide accommodates simultaneous descents from multiple directions

the playscape is fabricated from coated metal and stainless steel components for everyday use

items.body:
Architecture practice Studio Gang has completed a women's conference centre overlooking Geneva Lake in Wisconsin, with three irregularly shaped buildings informed by the site's oak forest.

Located outside of Chicago on a lakeside hill, the Women's Leadership Center contains meeting spaces for established and emerging women in leadership roles to gather and "ideate solutions to complex issues within their industries".

"Women leaders spend much of their careers in rooms that weren't designed with them in mind," said the center's founder Ann Drake, former CEO of supply chain provider DSC Logistics. "I wanted to build one that was."

Studio Gang said key elements of the design were sustainability – with strategies such as a mass timber structure – and responding to the ecology of the site through gently curving volumes and wide-open windows.

Photographs

Previous

Next

Photographs

Close

"We designed the Women's Leadership Center to respect and learn from its surrounding forest ecology while allowing community, leadership, and collaborative problem-solving to thrive," said Studio Gang founding partner Jeanne Gang.

"Locally sourced materials, mass timber, and low-carbon concrete minimise the buildings' carbon footprint, while the landscape helps to repair the site's ecology and enhance its biodiversity."

Drawings

Previous

Next

Drawings

Close

The campus contains three main buildings -- the circular Council building that functions as the main meeting space, the Lodge, which is made of three interconnected volumes, and the Cabin, a smaller building that contains accommodations.

White oak wood harvested on-site, a dark wood cladding and natural Wisconsin stone were used throughout all three buildings to "reflect the tones and textures of the forest", according to the studio.

The Council building is arranged around a central courtyard and garden that doubles as a rainwater-collection site.

Its rooms, including a larger lecture hall and meeting room, fan outwards around the courtyard and are lined with floor-to-ceiling windows, while a heavy timber structure creates a series of skylights at the entrance.

A walkway leads out the back of the Council building towards the Lodge. The building contains more casual meeting and socialising spaces, such as a Great Room arranged around a fireplace.

It also contains a mass-timber structure above this space, which is lined with skylights. Outdoor terraces overlook Geneva Lake, while the building's green roof contains a "coffee nook" and patios for seating.

Read:

Studio Gang covers theatre for Hudson Valley Shakespeare with mass-timber shell

Tucked off into a corner of the site, the Cabin building contains several bedrooms across two levels, as well as utility spaces such as a laundry room.

Its lower level contains a dining area and living area, which double as additional, more intimate gathering spaces.

Fully accessible ramps interconnect all three structures and lead down to the water bank, where they end in a pier.

Elsewhere, Studio Gang recently completed an open-air theatre in upstate New York and a Denver hotel.

items.body:
Portraying a man walking away from a modern office tower block, as if to explore the surrounding community, 'Walking East' is an impressive painted metal sculpture placed directly onto the street without a plinth.

Its creator, French Hong Kong-based sculptor Polo Bourieau, cited the inspiration for 'Walking East' as 'les adventuriers du quotidien' (the daily adventurers), the everyday working people going about their day in the Kwun Tong industrial district.

Located next to a busy junction, the 5-metre tall statue becomes especially poignant during work opening, lunch and closing hours. Surrounded by commuters and workers, it looms large over the hordes, seemingly journeying with them as they attempt to navigate their daily lives and Kwun Tong's crowded streets.

items.body:
From architecture to brooding skies to happenstance, the images of the finalists of the inaugural [Australian Street Photography Awards](https://www.aussiestreet.com.au/aspa2026) highlight the humor, friction, and tenderness of everyday moments. The competition is presented by AUSSIE STREET, an organization founded by street photographers to showcase work from across the nation, which builds upon a series of festivals presented between 2018 and 2023.

Co-founder Sam Ferris says that the outfit’s mission is to not only exhibit great photos but to tap into the dispersed network of those who make them. “Street photography can be a pretty solitary obsession,” he says in a statement. “But there’s a whole community of people out there doing exactly the same thing. Getting them together, seeing the work printed, and hearing the stories behind the photographs is a reminder that we’re part of something much bigger than our individual pursuits.”

Shane Harrison

The awards opened with a show of 25 finalists at [Studio 551](https://studio551.com.au/) in Newtown, New South Wales, and AUSSIE STREET awarded the top prize to [Adam Oxley](https://www.instagram.com/_ajox_/). “One of the things I love about street photography is that you don’t need an enormous budget to make a remarkable image,” Ferris adds. “You need curiosity, patience, persistence and a way of seeing. Some of the most extraordinary photographs happen in completely ordinary places.”

See more on AUSSIE STREET’s [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/aussie_street/), where you can keep an eye out for updates about the 2027 edition.

Floss Rogers

Ben Stanley Clarke

Christine Piper

Adam Oxley

Yani Clarke

Benizi Santamaria

Ed Robertson

items.body:
## Rare Renaissance Landscape Heads to Auction With a $5 Million Estimate

[↗ Primärquelle: mymodernmet.com](https://mymodernmet.com/albrecht-altdorfer-renaissance-landscape-auction/)

> View this post on Instagram
> [A post shared by Italian Old Masters (chiefly!) (@oldmasters_jlvieites)](https://www.instagram.com/p/Dftk3dlg4HX/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)

A rare [Renaissance](https://mymodernmet.com/italian-renaissance-art-definition/) painting that has remained out of public view for nearly 70 years is heading to auction. Created around 1520 by German artist Albrecht Altdorfer, *A Thickly Wooded Landscape With a Rainbow Behind the Trees and a Distant Outcrop to the Right Beneath a Cloud-Laden Sky* will lead Sotheby’s Old Master and 19th Century Paintings Evening Auction in London on December 9, 2026. The auction house estimates the small but historically significant work to sell for £3 million to £5 million (approximately $3.9 million to $6.5 million).

The painting recently resurfaced in a private Swiss collection. Its discovery has drawn attention from art historians because it represents only the third known independent landscape in oil by Altdorfer. The other two belong to the National Gallery in London and the Alte Pinakothek in Munich. No known painting by the artist has appeared at auction since 1980, making the upcoming sale an especially rare opportunity for collectors and museums.

Unlike many Renaissance paintings that use landscapes as backdrops for religious or historical scenes, Altdorfer places nature at the center of the composition. The small painting measures just 23.4 by 19.8 centimeters (approximately 9 by 8 inches), yet its intricate details create an immersive woodland scene filled with dense trees, tangled undergrowth, and a distant castle perched on a rocky outcrop.

A rainbow arcs above the treetops, catching the light beneath a sky heavy with clouds. The subtle shift in atmosphere gives the scene a sense of depth and quiet drama. Altdorfer’s distinctive treatment of foliage also reflects his interest in the forests surrounding Regensburg, the German city where he spent much of his life.

The artwork once belonged to the aristocratic House of Harrach in Vienna. In 1957, the current owner’s father acquired it from the family’s collection. It has remained with the family ever since, largely escaping public attention and scholarly research until its identification in 2026.

The discovery expands the known body of work by an artist widely regarded as a pioneer of independent landscape painting in Western art. Altdorfer helped establish a new approach to the genre in which forests, mountains, and atmospheric conditions became subjects in their own right.

Given the scarcity of Altdorfer’s paintings, the December auction could attract significant interest from major collectors and museums. Before the sale, Sotheby’s will exhibit the landscape in New York from Nov. 7 to 19, followed by a London presentation from Dec. 4 to 9.

The painting will go under the hammer at Sotheby’s London on Dec. 9.

## A previously unknown landscape by German Renaissance painter Albrecht Altdorfer will headline Sotheby’s December 9 auction in London, carrying an estimate of £3 million to £5 million.

> View this post on Instagram
> [A post shared by artincontext (@artincontextdotorg)](https://www.instagram.com/p/DfXnDokCmUN/?utm_source=ig_embed&utm_campaign=loading)

## The painting, which remained in a private Swiss collection for nearly 70 years, is one of only three known independent oil landscapes by Altdorfer and the first to surface on the auction market in more than four decades.

Portrait of Albrecht Altdorfer. (Photo: [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Albrecht_Altdorfer_XVII.jpg), Public domain)

items.body: The abandoned ferry terminal along the Xijiang River in Jiujiang Town, Foshan, once served as a vital dock connecting the riverine islands. With the commissioning of a new terminal, this structure—imbued with memories of waterway transportation—gradually fell into disuse, leaving only a concrete skeleton and steps leading to a decaying pier. Situated at the intersection of a wetland park and a residential area, the site combines ecological sensitivity with community service potential. The design team faced the challenge of transforming this ruin into a multifunctional public space—integrating a bookstore, exhibition hall, café, cultural events, and art performances—within a footprint of less than 150 square meters, while responding to the climatic characteristics of the Pearl River Delta and the region's industrial cultural context.
