items.body:
Full Page Ad in Conde Nast’s Traveler magazine, March 1988 ([via](https://michaelcrichton.com/works/travels/))

I was talking to my friend Jamie about therapy a few months ago and he recommended the “Psychiatry” chapter in Michael Crichton’s 1988 memoir, [Travels](https://michaelcrichton.com/works/travels/).

Around 1971, Crichton was separated from his wife. She suggested he see a psychiatrist. “I refused,” Crichton wrote. “I didn’t think psychiatry did any good for people. It was just a lot of hand-holding.”

Then his wife gave him the name of a prominent psychiatrist at UCLA but suggested that the doctor was probably too busy to see him. Crichton took offense at the idea he wasn’t important enough to be seen, and made an appointment. (It’s a very funny chapter.)

“I now found myself in a peculiar situation,” he wrote. “I didn’t really believe in psychiatry, I didn’t want to see a psychiatrist, and I didn’t think there was anything wrong with me, but I was challenged to present myself to Dr. Norton in a fascinating way.”

After a fine performance, Dr. Norton took Crichton on as a patient.

> But I still wasn’t sure psychiatry did any good. And it was expensive, sixty dollars an hour. Anything that cost so much must surely be an indulgence. Rich lazy people went to psychiatrists.
> I decided to keep track of how much it was costing me to see Dr. Norton, and I assessed each session when it was over to determine if it had been worth the sixty dollars.
> I found Dr. Norton puzzling because he was so normal. I’d tell him my story and he’s say things like ‘Time will tell’ or ‘You can’t make an omelet without breaking eggs.’
> I thought, Sixty dollars an hour to hear you can’t make an omelette without breaking eggs? What good is this?

But Crichton enjoyed “complaining about my life” and kept going back.

On the fifth session, “three hundred dollars down the drain,” as he put it, they had a breakthrough: it turns out that Crichton was an insecure person.

> I felt amazed. Just as amazed as if he had shown me that I had a third arm coming out of my chest, an arm I had never noticed before. How could I not have noticed this before? But I never thought I was insecure. If anything, I saw myself as astoundingly confident.
> Could I really have held such an incorrect view of myself?
> Dr. Norton tried to soften the blow, and explained that many things about ourselves were difficult to see without outside help. That was the whole point of a therapist. He was an objective outsider.
> This was a new idea to me, that there might be some things about myself that I couldn’t see without outside help. But it obviously was true.
> I never kept track of how much I was spending again.

Crichton then goes on to tell a funny story about getting involved with several women and how Dr. Norton warns him that things are going to go very badly. Crichton doesn’t think so. He thinks he can handle it.

“Time will tell,” Dr. Norton says.

And it does: things go very badly for Crichton.

> “What a mess” I said.
> “Hell hath no fury like a woman scorned,” Dr. Norton said.
> By now I saw the point of these homilies. Dr. Norton was trying to get me to understand that certain rules of life had been around for a long time and that life probably wasn’t going to make an exception for me.

Crichton gets divorced, goes to a psychic, becomes totally depressed after achieving all his goals in life (it happens!), reads Ram Dass’s [Be Here Now](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Be_Here_Now_(book)), and starts traveling again.

But he never really talks about psychiatry again in that chapter.

So I searched around, seeing if anything came up about Crichton and psychiatry.

The first thing that surfaced was [this 1970 clip of his appearance on The Dick Cavett Show](https://www.youtube.com/watch?si=lI1aj1DSOB2ekSfJ&t=326&v=eB8NapR3_rM&feature=youtu.be) to promote his first non-fiction book, [Five Patients](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_Patients):

Around [5:26,](https://www.youtube.com/watch?si=lI1aj1DSOB2ekSfJ&t=326&v=eB8NapR3_rM&feature=youtu.be) Cavett asks Crichton about psychiatry.

> Cavett: What’s happening in psychiatry these days? There’s always something peculiar going on there. The latest thing I heard about is they’re using computers as psychoanalysts.
> Crichton: There is a computer program which I put in the book because it was mostly amusing. It was done as a joke by a fellow named Weizenbaum at MIT several years ago. What he set out to do is to see if you could program a computer to interact in something approaching a conversation with a person. And he did it by a series of kind of tricks. So for example, the computer will pick up something in your sentence and play it back to you. If you mention parents it’ll pop something back, “Can you tell me more?” or “Why do you say that about [blank]?” and put in the parents. But it turns out in practice to be kind of successful, kind of frighteningly successful.
> Cavett: It sounds ludicrous to begin with. I mean, it would seem like the idea of therapy would be that the genius of the therapist would be that he treats every person as individual and finds out what this individual’s problems are and he’s unlike any other individual. But how can a machine do that?
> Crichton: That particular point is why this thing is kind of frightening the psychiatrist.
> Cavett: Because it’s succeeding?
> Crichton: Yeah!

There are at several things that are interesting to me about this clip.

- This was filmed 56 years ago.
- Crichton, seen here, is about one year away from going to therapy himself.
- Cavett sort of completely gets wrong what therapy is about, which Crichton later discovers for himself: seen through the eye of an attentive but impartial observer, your problems aren’t actually that unique at all.

But by far the most interesting is the story of MIT professor and computer scientist [Joseph Weizenbaum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Weizenbaum) himself, and how his experience ELIZA caused him [to turn against AI](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2023/jul/25/joseph-weizenbaum-inventor-eliza-chatbot-turned-against-artificial-intelligence-ai).

From [his MIT obituary](https://news.mit.edu/2008/obit-weizenbaum-0310):

items.title: HTML is Dead, Long Live HTML
items.subtitle:

Browsers are in a very weird place.

items.body:
## Rethinking DOM from first principles Browsers are in a very weird place. While WebAssembly has succeeded, even on the server, the client still feels largely the same as it did [10 years ago](https://acko.net/blog/shadow-dom/). Enthusiasts will tell you that accessing native web APIs via WASM is a solved problem, with some [minimal JS glue](https://queue.acm.org/detail.cfm?id=3746174). But the question not asked is why you would want to access the DOM. It's just the only option. So I'd like to explain why it really is time to send the DOM and its assorted APIs off to a farm somewhere, with some ideas on how. I won't pretend to know everything about browsers. Nobody knows everything anymore, and that's the problem. ## The 'Document' Model Few know how bad the DOM really is. In Chrome, document.body now has 350+ keys, grouped roughly like this: This doesn't include the CSS properties in document.body.style of which there are... **660**. The boundary between properties and methods is very vague. Many are just facades with an invisible setter behind them. Some getters may trigger a just-in-time re-layout. There's ancient legacy stuff, like all the onevent properties nobody uses anymore. The DOM is not lean and continues to get fatter. Whether you notice this largely depends on whether you are making web pages or web applications. Most devs now avoid working with the DOM directly, though occasionally some purist will praise pure DOM as being superior to the various JS component/templating frameworks. What little declarative facilities the DOM has, like innerHTML, do not resemble modern UI patterns at all. The DOM has too many ways to do the same thing, none of them nice. connectedCallback() { const shadow = this.attachShadow({ mode: 'closed' }), template = document.getElementById('hello-world') .content.cloneNode(true), hwMsg = `Hello ${ this.name }`; Array.from(template.querySelectorAll('.hw-text')) .forEach(n => n.textContent = hwMsg); shadow.append(template); } Web Components deserve a mention, being the web-native equivalent of JS component libraries. But they came too late and are unpopular. The API seems clunky, with its Shadow DOM introducing new nesting and scoping layers. Proponents kinda [read like apologetics](https://kinsta.com/blog/web-components/). The achilles heel is the DOM's SGML/XML heritage, making everything stringly typed. React-likes do not have this problem, their syntax only *looks* like XML. Devs have learned not to keep state in the document, because it's inadequate for it. For HTML itself, there isn't much to critique because nothing has changed in 10-15 years. Only [ARIA](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA) (accessibility) is notable, and only because this was what Semantic HTML was supposed to do and didn't. Semantic HTML never quite reached its goal. Despite dating from around 2011, there is e.g. no or tag, when those were well-established idioms. Instead, an article inside an article [is probably](https://www.w3.org/TR/2011/WD-html5-author-20110809/the-article-element.html) a comment. The guidelines are... weird. There's this feeling that HTML always had paper-envy, and couldn't quite embrace or fully define its hypertext nature, and did not trust its users to follow clear rules. Stewardship of HTML has since firmly passed to WHATWG, really the browser vendors, who have not been able to define anything more concrete as a vision, and have instead just added epicycles at the margins. Along the way even CSS has grown expressions, because every templating language wants to become a programming language. Editability of HTML remains a sad footnote. While technically supported via contentEditable, actually wrangling this feature into something usable for applications is a dark art. I'm sure the Google Docs and Notion people have horror stories. Nobody really believes in the old gods of progressive enhancement and separating markup from style anymore, not if they make apps. Most of the applications you see nowadays will kitbash HTML/CSS/SVG into a pretty enough shape. But this comes with immense overhead, and is looking more and more like the opposite of a decent UI toolkit. *The Slack input box* *Off-screen clipboard hacks* Lists and tables must be virtualized by hand, taking over for layout, resizing, dragging, and so on. Making a chat window's scrollbar stick to the bottom is somebody's TODO, every single time. And the more you virtualize, the more you have to reinvent find-in-page, right-click menus, etc. The web blurred the distinction between UI and fluid content, which was novel at the time. But it makes less and less sense, because the UI part is a decade obsolete, and the content has largely homogenized. ## CSS is inside-out CSS doesn't have a stellar reputation either, but few can put their finger on exactly why. Where most people go wrong is to start with the wrong mental model, approaching it like a constraint solver. This is easy to show with e.g.:
...
...
...
...
The first might seem reasonable: divide the parent into two halves vertically. But what about the second? Viewed as a set of constraints, it's contradictory, because the parent div is twice as tall as... itself. What will happen instead in *both cases* is the height is ignored. The parent height is unknown and CSS doesn't backtrack or iterate here. It just shrink-wraps the contents. If you set e.g. height: 300px on the parent, then it works, but the latter case will still just spill out. *Outside-in and inside-out layout modes* Instead, your mental model of CSS should be applying two passes of constraints, first going outside-in, and then inside-out. When you make an application frame, this is *outside-in*: the available space is divided, and the content inside does not affect sizing of panels. When paragraphs stack on a page, this is *inside-out*: the text stretches out its containing parent. This is what HTML wants to do naturally. CSS is always inside-out by default, reflecting its document-oriented nature. The outside-in is not obvious, because it's up to you to pass all the constraints down, starting with . This is why they always say vertical alignment in CSS is hard. *Use flex grow and shrink for spill-free auto-layouts with completely reasonable gaps* The scenario above is better handled with a CSS3 flex box ( display: flex ), which provides explicit control over how space is divided. Unfortunately flexing muddles the simple CSS model. To auto-flex, the [layout algorithm](https://www.w3.org/TR/css-flexbox-1/#algo-main-item) must measure the "natural size" of every child. This means laying it out twice: first speculatively, as if floating in aether, and then again after growing or shrinking to fit: …

items.body:
## a new museum envisioned for Kistefos

Architecture studio [SO–IL](https://www.designboom.com/tag/so-il/) presents its design for the Kistefos Museum in Jevnaker, [Norway](https://www.designboom.com/tag/architecture-in-norway/), where an enveloping [skin](https://www.designboom.com/tag/facades/) of translucent glass scales would take on the changing colors of the surrounding forest. The architects imagine a building with a swollen, almost organic silhouette that appears to float just above the forest floor. In the renderings, its pale green exterior takes on a silvery glow under the low Norwegian sun.

The proposal was developed as part of an international competition for a new museum at Kistefos, an art destination about an hour north of Oslo. The site occupies the grounds of a historic wood pulp mill and is already home to an extensive outdoor sculpture collection and BIG’s twisting, bridge-like gallery, completed in 2019.

The new [museum](https://www.designboom.com/tag/museums-galleries/) was conceived as a permanent home for the collection of Norwegian art collector Christen Sveaas. SO–IL was among eight finalists in the competition, which ultimately saw Swiss architecture studio Christ & Gantenbein selected to develop the building in December 2025.

visualizations © SO–IL

## an inhabitable facade of timber and glass

Much of the character of SO–IL’s architecture comes from its unusually deep facade. The [architects](https://solidobjectives.com/) call this space the ‘thicket,’ a timber-framed environment that occupies the perimeter of the museum. Custom glass elements are arranged in a repeating, scale-like pattern across its curved outer surface, with larger openings cut into the skin to expose the structure beneath.

From within the thicket, visitors would find themselves among a network of exposed wooden beams and elevated walkways. Metal staircases wind between floors, while platforms extend out toward the trees. There is enough room here for large sculptural works, some of which appear suspended within the timber framework.

The use of locally sourced wood recalls the industrial origins of Kistefos, where the production of wood pulp began in the late nineteenth century. Through the translucent glass, the forest would remain partially visible even as visitors move deeper into the museum.

large openings in the glass skin reveal the timber structure beneath

## a journey through SO–IL’s kistefos museum

The team at SO–IL organizes the interior around a central oculus, which visitors encounter after passing through a compressed entrance from the public plaza. From this point, several routes lead through the collection. Openings between floors introduce views into neighboring galleries, so visitors might catch sight of an artwork well before they reach the room in which it is displayed.

The exhibition spaces occupy two levels, with smaller galleries downstairs dedicated to craft and historic artworks. On the upper floor, rooms for modern and contemporary art vary in height and exposure to daylight. SO–IL’s renderings explore these differences in atmosphere, from a deep blue-green lobby beneath a curved skylight to expansive, pale exhibition rooms.

Throughout the proposal, opportunities to step away from the enclosed galleries are built into the museum’s architecture. A visitor could emerge from an exhibition onto a platform among the trees, where the glass overhead filters the sunlight and the sculptures of Kistefos’s outdoor collection are visible below.

outdoor platforms extend from the galleries toward the forest

elevated walkways wind through the timber-framed ‘thicket’

a translucent suspended canopy filters daylight into the exhibition space

a curved skylight introduces daylight into the museum lobby

the upper-level galleries accommodate large-scale contemporary artworks

the proposed museum sits among the artworks of Kistefos’s sculpture park

items.title: Dezeen reports from New York's new November design week
items.subtitle: A collection of showcases, old and new, took place in New York this November, effectively adding a second design week to a city already loaded with…

items.body:
A collection of showcases, old and new, took place in [New York](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/new-york-city/) this November, effectively adding a second design week to a city already loaded with events. Dezeen's US editor Ben Dreith explores the offerings.

The as-yet-unofficial design week in the first weeks of November came into focus earlier this year, when trade fair ICFF, anchor fair of [NYCxDesign](https://nycxdesign.org/), [announced that in 2027 it will take place simultaneously](https://www.dezeen.com/2026/05/12/icff-new-york-november-2027/) with sister fair BDNY, which has been held in November for years.

The move has prompted questions in the city about the future of the NYCxDesign festival in May and what a November design week would look like.

Dudd Haus at Collectible design fair was a standout booth from the week. Photo by Matthew Gordon

While BDNY and high-end showcase [Salon Art + Design](https://www.thesalonny.com/) have always been held in November, other design fairs have sprouted to take advantage of the opportunity to show during this busy period.

The week is positioning itself, without any explicit organisation, as a massive event in the New York design calendar.

Even NYCxDesign, still scheduled for May as usual in 2027, held a November event bringing in designers [Ross Lovegrove](https://www.rosslovegrove.com/), [Karim Rashid](https://www.karimrashid.com/) and [Rem D Koolhaas](https://www.instagram.com/rem_un/?hl=en) for a talk moderated by New York-based design writer [Camille Okhio](https://camilleokhio.com/).

The panellists spoke about the potential for AI and derided the inclusion of craft in conversations about design. However, as writer Debika Ray noted in an opinion piece for Dezeen, [crafted, one-off pieces have lately come to dominate design shows](https://www.dezeen.com/2026/09/16/how-craft-conquered-design/).

NYCxDesign staking out a talk with well-known industrial designers suggests that its May event could be devoted to industrial design, while November complements it with a focus on collectible furniture.

This was definitely true this year, when collectible designs dominated the November showcases.

A screen by Wiktoria & Filip Bielicki at Objekt Gallery's Collectible booth showcased a trend towards reliefs during the design week. Photo by Simon Leung

Among these was the Brussels-founded design fair [Collectible](https://collectible.design/). For its third New York iteration, it moved from office tower-turned creative hub WSA to a defunct movie theatre on the Upper East Side that is being developed by entities [related to WSA](https://therealdeal.com/new-york/2026/09/22/stellbergers-happier-grocery-heads-to-upper-east-side/).

While the unfinished theatre fit the experimental nature of the work, the execution was, by some accounts, chaotic, with one worker being sent to the hospital after an unstable light fell onto her head.

Collectible called it an "isolated occurrence involving an exhibitor's equipment".

"The safety of our exhibitors, staff and visitors is a priority, and we take any reported incident seriously," a representative for Collectible told Dezeen.

"Collectible maintains safety procedures for the fair and expects all exhibitors to ensure that their own equipment is installed and secured appropriately."

[Read: Eighteen weird, wonderful and well-made objects from NYCxDesign 2026](https://www.dezeen.com/2026/05/27/eighteen-objects-nycxdesign-2026/)

Despite some chaos, including recently laid cement, there were strong showings. Philadelphia-based [Dudd Haus](https://www.duddhaus.com/?srsltid=AYCX9vIyaH2V17-zeh1tz7VhlvjqLSL2DcCwQCyXkGEAr9oH6VCMhiHC) showed a pared-down booth with its usual mix of conceptual one-offs. Particularly of note was a milled-aluminium floor lamp by [Jordan Maurice](https://www.instagram.com/jordan__maurice/?hl=en) and a paravent made with telephone cords by [Overt Cove](https://www.overtcove.com/).

Also eye-catching was a booth of droopy glass lamps and shades with erotic overtones by [Upstate New York gallery Freaks](https://freaksny.com/), and another sensual booth with drapes and lacquered furniture by [Iitem studio](https://iitem.nyc/).

The fair's scenography carried the sleek, modern, USM-laden feel from the prior additions. Curators [Alex Tieghi-Walker](https://alextiwa.com/) and [Lynette Nylander](https://www.instagram.com/lynettesaid/?hl=en) designed special sections.

Bas-reliefs were popular on otherwise modern furniture, including a battened screen by Polish studio [Wiktoria & Filip Bielicki](https://www.instagram.com/wiktoria.and.filip/) for [Objekt Gallery](https://objekt.gallery/) and a coffee table with raised ceramic on its base by [Small Things Studio](https://www.smallthingsstudios.com/) for [Salon 21](https://www.salontwenty-one.com/).

Montreal collective Ensemble took over Yabu Pushelberg's New York office, creating a plywood gallery within the office. Photo by Simon S Belleau

At Collectible, [Montreal design collective Ensemble](https://www.instagram.com/ensssemble/) showcased its members' work on nooks in a wall made with USM panels.

This was just a taste of what Ensemble had in store for the week. The collective brought their signature experimentation to [Yabu Pushelberg](https://www.yabupushelberg.com/)’s Tribeca studio, creating a plywood room-within-a-room to showcase work, including new lamps by [Zebulon Perron](https://zebulonperron.com/), sculptural glass lamps by [Alex Joncas](https://alexjoncas.com/), metal works by [Jérémy Paguet](https://studiopaguet.com/), leather lamps by [Jeta Studio](https://www.jeta.studio/en) and brass-lined mirrors by [Jeremy Le Chatelier](https://www.jeremylechatelier.com/).

It was an extremely focused showing that proved sometimes you can do more with less.

Zarolat showed a light by Natural Urbano and Polybion at Salon Art + Design. Photo by Peter Baker

At Salon Art + Design, a few younger galleries stuck out from the historical work and ultra-high-end designs that usually characterise the fair.

Brooklyn-based [Zarolat’](https://www.zarolat.com/)s showing included ash-wood lamps with cellulose shades by Natural Urbano and [Polybion](https://www.polybion.bio/stories/lapso-lamp-celium-natural-urbano/), while New York-based hub for Brazilian furniture, [Bossa Furniture,](https://www.bossafurniture.com/) showcased a greatest hits of mid-century São Paulo makers, including Joaquim Tenreiro.

Marquel Williams showcased his eye for curation at Basic Space. Photo by Alexa Bendek

items.body:
At Macdonald Book Shop, a cozy and beloved store in the Colorado mountain town of Estes Park, selling books began as a side hustle.

J. Edward Macdonald bought a small log cabin in Estes Park in 1908 and opened a hardware and general store next door — with one corner full of books for sale. When he retired, his wife Jessica turned the parlor of their home into a proper bookstore, also selling magazines, stationery, and school supplies. That was 1928. Books have been the focus ever since.

Over the decades, the shop expanded to claim more of the original house. Four generations of Macdonald women kept it going. After J. Edward died in 1932, Jessica ran the store on her own until her death in 1957. Ownership passed to their daughter Louise, and when Louise died in 1971, her daughter Paula Steige took over. Steige retired from teaching in 1976 and reopened the shop year-round — it had been a summer-only operation.

Then, in July 1982, the Lawn Lake Dam failed. Four feet of water tore through the bookstore, destroying two-thirds of the inventory. But the community showed up to help: More than 100 volunteers helped rebuild the foundation, rip out and replace the floor joists, paint, clean, and shelve new stock. The store reopened 18 days later. Steige later called it “a blessing in disguise” — the old house needed renovation anyway.

The Macdonald name is still on the door, though ownership changed again in 2020, when Anastacia Galloway Reed and Kevin Reed, who also own the neighboring Inkwell & Brew, bought the shop.

The bookstore still operates in the same cabin on Elkhorn Avenue, still stocks around 15,000 titles, and still does what it’s done since Jessica first set up in the parlor: It gives people a place to find a book and a welcoming vibe to those who want to sit down and read.

items.body:
From vintage tomes and encyclopedic volumes, British artist [Su Blackwell](https://sublackwell.co.uk/) carves, slices, and reconfigures text-laden pages into enchanting sculptures. Her latest body of work, opening this week in a solo show titled *Pathway of Crumbs*, draws on fairytales and folklore, a fitting topic for such dreamlike scenes.

Nodding to the enduring children’s story of *Hansel and Gretel*, the exhibition roots in nature and the stories we draw from the world around us. “In Flight,” for example, stretches nearly 3.5 feet as a swarm of butterflies emerges from the flared pages of a book. “Break off my Branches” is similarly dynamic, with a flock of multi-colored birds perched on the spindly stems that burst from a splayed edition.

“Break off my Branches” (2025), paper cut sculpture and wooden frame without glass, 115 x 16 x 85 centimeters

Blackwell selected this particular set of books because they’ve been in her collection for several years, allowing the artist to digest their contents and ruminate on how they might emerge over time. Some she’s left in the same condition since purchasing them from a secondhand shop, and others she’s minimally cut and spliced for earlier projects. All, though, have remained a compelling artifact of human knowledge and a collective desire to create, one she transforms anew into striking compositions at the intersection of nature and culture.

*Pathway of Crumbs* is on view from November 25 to January 25 at [Long & Ryle](https://longandryle.com/) in London. Find more from Blackwell on [her website](https://sublackwell.co.uk/).

items.body:
## Art Basel Spotlights Multimedia Collaboration Between Refik Anadol and Indigenous Artists

[↗ Primärquelle: mymodernmet.com](https://mymodernmet.com/art-basel-winds-of-yawanawa/)

Yawanawa & Refik Anadol, “Winds of Yawanawa (NFT Data Sculpture),” 2023, NFT Data Sculpture (dictated by real-time weather data) Format: 4k Resolution Video File: 8 minute loop. Original music. Signed Certificate of Authenticity.

Artist [Refik Anadol](https://refikanadol.com/) is known around the world for his pioneering work highlighting the use of generative AI in art. Despite the tech-forward components of his practice, his creations continue to engage with the natural world and more traditional techniques. This balance is at the heart of *The Forest Remembers: Winds of Yawanawa*, a collaboration between Anadol and the Yawanawa people of the Brazilian Amazon, to be showcased at [Art Basel Miami Beach](https://www.artbasel.com/).

The project, presented as part of Zero 10, Art Basel’s initiative for art of the digital era, builds on the 2023 collaboration between the Yawanawa and Anadol. The presentation features the original artworks by Yawanawa artists Nawashahu and Mukashahu alongside three new canvases and the 1,000 digital works Anadol created around these creatives’ compositions.

Anadol’s works will be featured in an installation comprising 12 towering screens. Meanwhile, Nawashahu and Mukashahu’s physical artworks will be presented beside the digital displays, engaging in a creative dialogue about tradition, creativity, and the future of art.

The event also includes the limited release of new collector’s prints. There are 25 numbered sets, each featuring high-resolution reproductions of the original drawings and paintings by Nawashahu and Mukashahu. “In the paintings,” the Yawanawa sisters share, “every stroke carries the strength of our ancestry, the beauty of nature, and the magic of our spiritual world.”

In addition to shining a light on Yawanawa heritage, proceeds from the project will continue to support Indigenous-led initiatives through Instituto Nixiwaka across the Yawanawa territory. This includes cultural preservation and community infrastructure projects in several villages, helping their communities and uplifting future generations.

“For us, the forest is not a resource, it is a living being that we are a part of,” says Chief Biraci Brasil Nixiwaka Yawanawa, president of Instituto Nixiwaka. “Through this work with Refik, our art and our spirituality have found new ways to travel, carrying the voice of our ancestors into new worlds.”

As for Anadol, he is aware of the conversations around AI in art, but hopes to inspire a more nuanced vision around it. “People think AI can take over the world and create problems,” he says. “But AI can also be used to connect cultures and create visibility.”

*The Forest Remembers: Winds of Yawanawa*, presented by Scorpios in collaboration with HOFA Gallery and Instituto Nixiwaka, will be on view at Art Basel Miami Beach 2026. VIP Previews are on Dec. 2–3, with the public displays running Dec. 4–6. To learn more, plan your visit, and book your tickets, visit[Art Basel’s website](https://www.artbasel.com/).

items.body:
“About Texas,” newspaper + marker, 2024

My [Friday newsletter](https://austinkleon.substack.com/p/this-is-how-we-do-it) began:

> [Molly Ivins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molly_Ivins) called Texas “the laboratory for bad government,” and that’s been the case my entire adult life. I was a 17-year-old in Ohio during the 2000 election, and since I couldn’t vote, I went around waving a copy of [Shrub: The Short But Happy Political Life of George W. Bush](https://geni.us/jzBru4C) at my family members, warning them that the whole country could become Texas. (Whenever other Americans joke that they wish Texas would go ahead and secede, I reply, “But then you’d lose your [early warning system](https://austinkleon.com/2020/12/04/art-is-an-early-warning-system/)!”) 19 summers ago, Meg and I moved to Austin so she could go to grad school. We stayed. She gave birth to a couple of native Texans during the Obama administration (I was able to become a full-time writer thanks to the Affordable Care Act), and since then we’ve been raising them in a sunny city full of friendly people and great food, all the while knowing that just five miles down the road, some of the most corrupt men in the world do their best to wreck the place. So you can imagine how it felt on Tuesday night, when a good number of those creeps were [sent packing by our fellow Texans](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/05/us/texas-democrats-statewide-sweep.html?unlocked_article_code=1.OFE.jOl1.9KtaJ39zOo9a&smid=url-share). The vibe around here is: [jubilant](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/jubilant).

Filed under: Texas

items.body:
## Modern SSAO in a modern run-time

[Use.GPU](https://usegpu.live) 0.14 is out, so here's an update on my declarative/reactive rendering efforts.

The highlights in this release are:

- dramatic inspector viewing upgrades
- a modern ambient-occlusion (SSAO/GTAO) implementation
- newly revised render pass infrastructure
- expanded shader generation for bind groups
- more use of generated WGSL struct types

*SSAO with Image-Based Lighting*

The main effect is that out-of-the-box, without any textures, Use.GPU no longer looks like early 2000s OpenGL. This is a problem every home-grown 3D effort runs into: how to make things look good without premium, high-quality models and pre-baking all the lights.

Use.GPU's reactive run-time continues to purr along well. Its main role is to enable doing at run-time what normally only happens at build time: dealing with shader permutations, assigning bindings, and so on. I'm quite proud of the [line up of demos](https://usegpu.live/demo/rtt/cube-target) Use.GPU has now, for the sheer diversity of rendering techniques on display, including an example path tracer. The new inspector is the cherry on top.

A lot of the effort continues to revolve around mitigating flaws in GPU API design, and offering something simpler. As such, the challenge here wasn't just implementing SSAO: the basic effect is pretty easy. Rather, it brings with it a few new requirements, such as temporal accumulation and reprojection, that put new demands on the rendering pipeline, which I still want to expose in a modular and flexible way. This refines the efforts [I detailed previously](https://acko.net/blog/use-gpu-goes-trad/) for 0.8.

Good SSAO also requires deep integration in the lighting pipeline. Here there is tension between modularizing and ease-of-use. If there is only one way to assemble a particular set of components, then it should probably be provided as a prefab. As such, occlusion has to remain a first class concept, tho it can be provided in several ways. It's a good case study of pragmatism over purity.

In case you're wondering: WebGPU is still not readily available on every device, so Use.GPU remains niche, tho it already excels at in-house use for adventurous clients. At this point you can imagine me and the browser GPU teams eyeing each other awkwardly from across the room: I certainly do.

## Inspector Gadget

The first thing to mention is the upgraded the Use.GPU inspector. It already had a lot of quality-of-life features like highlighting, but the main issue was finding your way around the giant trees that Use.GPU now expands into.

*Old*

*New*

*Highlights show data dependencies*

The fix was filtering by type. This is very simple as a component already advertises its inspectability in a few pragmatic ways. Additionally, it uses the data dependency graph between components to identify relevant parents. This shows a surprisingly tidy overview with no additional manual tagging. For each demo, it really does show you the major parts first now.

If you've checked it out before, give it another try. The layered structure is now clearly visible, and often fits in one screen. The main split is how Live is used to reconcile different levels of representation: from data, to geometry, to renders, to dispatches. These points appear as different reconciler nodes, and can be toggled as a filter.

It's still the best way to see Live and Use.GPU in action. It can be tricky to grok that each line in the tree is really a plain function, calling other functions, as it's an execution trace you can inspect. It will now point you more in the right way, and auto-select the most useful tabs by default.

The inspector is unfortunately far heavier than the GPU rendering itself, as it all relies on HTML and React to do its thing. At some point it's probably worth to remake it into a Live-native version, maybe as a 2D canvas with some virtualization. But in the mean time it's a dev tool, so the important thing is that it still works when nothing else does.

Most of the images of buffers in this post can be viewed live in the inspector, if you have a WebGPU capable browser.

## SSAO

Screen-space AO is common now: using the rendered depth buffer, you estimate occlusion in a hemisphere around every point. I opted for Ground Truth AO (GTAO) as it estimates the correct visibility integral, as opposed to a more empirical 'crease darkening' technique. It also allows me to estimate bent normals along the way, i.e. the average unoccluded direction, for better environment lighting.

*Hemisphere sampling*

This image shows the debug viz in the demo. Each frame will sample one green ring around a hemisphere, spinning rapidly, and you can hold ALT to capture the sampling process for the pixel you're pointing at. It was invaluable to find sampling issues, and also makes it trivial to verify alignment in 3D. The shader calls printPoint(…) and printLine(…) in WGSL, which are provided by a print helper, and linked in the same way it links any other shader functions.

*Bent normal and occlusion samples*

SSAO is expensive, and typically done at half-res, with heavy blurring to hide the sampling noise. Mine is no different, though I did take care to handle odd-sized framebuffers correctly, with no unexpected sample misalignments.

It also has accumulation over time, as the shadows change slowly from frame to frame. This is done with temporal reprojection and motion vectors, at the cost of a little bit of ghosting. Moving the camera doesn't reset the ambient occlusion, as long as it's moving smoothly.

*Motion vectors example*

*Accumulated samples*

As Use.GPU doesn't render continuously, you can now use <Loop converge={N}> to decide how many extra frames you want to render after every visual change.

Reprojection requires access to the last frame's depth, normal and samples, and this is trivial to provide. Use.GPU has built-in transparent history for render targets and buffers. This allows for a classic front/back buffer flipping arrangement with zero effort (also, n > 2).

*Depth history*

You bind this as virtual sources, each accessing a fixed slot history[i], which will transparently cycle whenever you render to its target. Any reimagined GPU API should seriously consider buffer history as a first-class concept. All the modern techniques require it.

*IGN*

Rather than use e.g. blue noise and hope the statistics work out, I chose a very precise sampling and blurring scheme. This uses interleaved gradient noise (IGN), and pre-filters samples in alternating 2x2 quads to help diffuse the speckles as quickly as possible. IGN is designed for 3x3 filters, so a more specifically tuned noise generator may work even better, but it's a decent V1.

items.body:
## MACHINED ALUMINUM STREET FURNITURE REGULATES URBAN CIRCULATION

Founded in 2026 as a family-run practice working across industrial design, urban planning, and architecture, Terminal Design has introduced a collection of **[street furniture](https://www.designboom.com/tag/street-furniture/)**engineered to regulate circulation and occupation in public spaces. Developed in collaboration with civic partners and refined through full-scale prototype testing, the line encompasses slatted**[benches](https://www.designboom.com/tag/chair-design/)**, staggered lean bars, barriers, and cantilevered shelters produced in limited runs for municipal plazas, corporate courtyards, commercial streets, and transit hubs. Each component is proportioned around calculated inclines, intervals, and facets that support brief stops while discouraging prolonged lounging, maintaining pedestrian flow in congested zones.

calm bench in orange | all images [©Terminal Design Solutions](https://www.terminaldesignsolutions.com)

## BRUSHED GRAIN AND RED, PINK, AND VIOLET tones form CIVIC COLLECTION

Fabricated from machined aluminum with a directional brushed grain and finished in anodized tones of red, pink, and deep violet, the pieces pair orthogonal geometry with weather-resistant durability. Beyond visual contrast, **[the studio](https://www.terminaldesignsolutions.com)** utilizes the thermal conductivity of uninsulated aluminum as a passive behavioral mechanism: by absorbing and radiating seasonal heat in summer and cold in winter, the metal surfaces naturally limit seating duration without active enforcement.

items.title: "Intensely physical patterns" cloak Gerhard Richter's self-designed gallery in Doha

items.body:
Kaleidoscopic [patterns](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/patterns/) adorn the exterior of this [pavilion](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/pavilions-tag/) in Doha, Qatar, designed by artist Gerhard Richter with US studio [Selldorf Architects](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/selldorf-architects/) as an [art gallery.](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/galleries/)

Simply called Doha Pavilion, the psychedelic structure was conceived a work of both art and architecture for MIA Park – a public space outside the [Museum of Islamic Art by IM Pei](https://www.dezeen.com/2025/01/14/museum-of-islamic-art-im-pei-21st-century-architecture/).

### Photographs

Previous

Next

### Photographs

Close

It serves as a permanent pavilion for the site and as a gallery for Richter's own work.

Richter designed the Doha Pavilion with[Selldorf Architects](https://www.selldorf.com/) as a reference to his Strip paintings – a series that involved digitally dividing his Abstract Painting artwork into vertical stripes, building on his earlier explorations of colour, pattern and repetition.

"My trip to Doha in 2013 came two years into developing my Strip paintings, and the city’s architecture and history sparked an idea for a pavilion that could unite the thematic threads of that body of work," said Richter.

"The pavilion’s exterior features decorative tiles based on the patterns that first led me to the Strips," he continued. "Doha is the right place and the only place for my pavilion.”

Doha Pavilion has a six-sided form, wrapped in psychedelic tiles displaying repeating, kaleidoscopic patterns that recall geometries seen in Islamic art, nodding to the project's context.

Selldorf Architects founder Annabelle Selldorf said the design reflects a "profound culmination of many years of [Richter's] research into abstraction".

"I am grateful for the welcome that Gerhard Richter extended to me, and for the wonderful dialogue that ensued, as my studio made manifest the work that had existed in his mind," she said.

"This pavilion is the profound culmination of many years of his research into abstraction, with intensely physical patterns that invite you to immerse yourself in their endlessness," she continued.

"The more I look at them, the more fascinating they become to me as an architectural space to experience."

Inside, Richter's paintings and sculptures are displayed throughout the hexagonal gallery space. This includes both archival and new works made especially for the pavilion.

Among the new works is the Strip Tower – a freestanding tripartite sculpture.

[Read: David Chipperfield Architects builds concrete gallery around singular artwork in Germany](https://www.dezeen.com/2026/10/20/anselm-kiefer-pavilion-david-chipperfield-architects-germany/)

The opening of Doha Pavilion coincides with the inaugural edition of Rubaiya Qatar 2026, which is an international visual arts quadrennial.

Elsewhere, [Selldorf Architects recently completed the controversial remodel of the National Gallery’s Sainsbury Wing](https://www.dezeen.com/2025/05/06/sainsbury-wing-renovation-national-gallery-selldorf-architects-london/). In an interview with Dezeen after the opening, founder Selldorf said that ["what matters is I know why we did things"](https://www.dezeen.com/2025/05/06/annabelle-selldorf-gallery-renovation-sainsbury-wing-frick-collection-interview/).

items.title: Historic Park Theatre in Estes Park, Colorado
items.subtitle: The Historic Park Theatre’s most famous feature was born from heartbreak.

items.body:
The Historic Park Theatre’s most famous feature was born from heartbreak. Its tower, added by owner Ralph Gwynn in 1929, is known locally as the Tower of Love — not for the romance it celebrates but for the one that fell apart. Legend has it that Gwynn was left at the altar, and he built the tower as a tribute to the woman who broke his heart. Decades later, when a new Estes Park sign ordnance threatened the glittering neon that outlines it, residents took the matter to a ballot and won the theater a variance. So the Tower of Love kept its glow.

Construction on the theater itself began in 1913. The architect Joseph R. Anderson designed the building in the Classical Revival style, with parts of it fabricated in the city of Longmont and hauled up to Estes Park for assembly.

Gwynn, a projectionist from Denver, bought the theater in 1922 at the height of the silent-film era and ran it until his death in 1963. He added the lobby in his first year, the tower in 1929, and the neon lights in 1938.

Mickey and Ola Stanger began running the theater in 1967, initially on a lease from businessman Vic Walker before eventually buying the building. What started as a two-person operation eventually became a family affair, stretching across multiple generations, with a Stanger granddaughter, Jenna MacGregor, running it today. The theater was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1984.

Today the Park Theatre operates year-round, screening classics, documentaries, independent films, and first-run blockbusters alongside live music and other events. The concessions offerings have recently been updated, and adult visitors are encouraged to enjoy their movies with a cold beer. The projection technology has also come a long way from Gwynn’s era: A digital projector, Dolby 3-D, and Dolby 5.1 surround sound arrived in 2013, a new screen in 2015, and new auditorium seating in 2024. A historic designation, it turns out, doesn’t require you to sit in the original seats.

items.body:
[Catherine Lepage](https://catherinelepage.com/) will have you leaping out of your desk chair with her self-directed “Dancing on Osees.” The irresistible animation features a quirky troupe of characters who can’t help but get down to “Together Tomorrow.” As the energetic track bolts forward, so do the hand-drawn dancers, who Lepage captures through stop-motion collages on paper.

The Montréal-based artist graciously shares glimpses behind the scenes on [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/catlepage/).

items.body:
## Melinda French Gates Let 12 People Decide How To Give Away $240 Million

[↗ Primärquelle: mymodernmet.com](https://mymodernmet.com/melinda-french-gates-20-million-donations/)

In 2024, Melinda French Gates launched the $240 million Global Leaders program, in which she gave $20 million apiece to 12 influential figures to distribute to causes of their choice by the end of 2026. She did this through her [philanthropic](https://mymodernmet.com/marlene-engelhorn-donates-inheritance/) organization, Pivotal, which works to enact social progress for women and young people both in the U.S. and around the world. Now, we’re getting to see the results of her generosity in real time.

French Gates started the program because she recognized the limits of her own perspective when it came to making donations. She wanted the money to reach places where it could make the most impact.

“There are so many great ideas out there that might never cross my path but might cross someone else’s,” she told the Associated Press. “That’s one reason I started the Global Leaders program: to partner with experts whose firsthand knowledge could broaden Pivotal’s perspective and deepen our impact.”

One of the recipients of the money, Dr. Alfiee Breland-Noble, was surprised to be included in the program and has since used the money to fund a wide variety of projects. Breland-Noble, who founded the AAKOMA Project—which stands for African American Knowledge Optimized for Mindfully Healthy Adolescents—to address the mental health needs of young people of color, used the $20 million to establish the MATTIE Fund, short for Mindful Advocacy for Totally Transformative Inclusion and Equity. The fund was also named for and inspired by her mother, Mattie McLeod Breland.

When it came to deciding where the money should go, Breland-Noble even turned to her Instagram followers for suggestions. Among the organizations she supported were BackSpinz Music Academy in North Carolina and Daddy Stroller Social Club, an organization that brings fathers together and raises awareness of paternal postpartum depression.

Another recipient of French Gates’ money was former New Zealand Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern, who took a slightly different approach with her Matariki Fund for Women. Rather than exclusively donating to existing programs, Ardern wanted to help bring new ones to life. She partnered with the International Rescue Committee to support the creation of Safer Births in Crises, an initiative that works to prevent maternal deaths in areas affected by humanitarian crises. The program is now focusing its efforts on South Sudan, Burkina Faso, and Papua New Guinea.

For Gary Barker, founder and CEO of Equimundo, the money opened the door to even more funding opportunities. Barker established the Caring Masculinity Fund, which supports organizations that promote gender equality by actively involving men and boys. His work also caught the attention of Australia’s Minderoo Foundation, which expressed interest in supporting similar efforts in its own country.

What’s particularly interesting about French Gates’ approach is where the money ended up. According to Pivotal, 91% of the donations went to organizations that had never received funding from Pivotal before, with the average grant amounting to approximately $240,000. By putting the decision of where to donate into the hands of others, French Gates was able to reach communities and organizations that might otherwise have never crossed her path.

#### Source: How three leaders donated the $20 million Melinda French Gates gave them with no strings attached

items.title: People not excited about AI
items.subtitle: Our World in Data collected results from several polls about sentiment around AI.
items.feedText: The results are about what you’d expect, with more people concerned than excited. I imagine sentiment is only more negative through the past month. Although I wonder what sentiment was like for the internet in the early days of wider adoption. Tags: Our World in Data, sentiment
items.body:
Our World in Data collected results [from several polls about sentiment around AI](https://ourworldindata.org/no-matter-how-you-ask-more-americans-are-negative-than-positive-about-ai). The results are about what you’d expect, with more people concerned than excited.

I imagine sentiment is only more negative through the past month. Although I wonder what sentiment was like for the internet in the early days of wider adoption.

**Tags:** [Our World in Data](https://flowingdata.com/tag/our-world-in-data/), [sentiment](https://flowingdata.com/tag/sentiment/)
